Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.

Aṅguttaranikāye

The Numerical Discourses

Ekakanipāta-ṭīkā

Subcommentary on the Book of the Ones

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Anantañāṇaṃ [V 1.0001][M 1.0001] karuṇāniketaṃ,

Namāmi nāthaṃ jitapañcamāraṃ;

Dhammaṃ visuddhaṃ bhavanāsahetuṃ,

Saṅghañca seṭṭhaṃ hatasabbapāpaṃ.

I pay homage to the Lord, of infinite wisdom, the abode of compassion, the conqueror of the five Māras; to the pure Dhamma, the cause for the destruction of existence; and to the excellent Saṅgha, who have destroyed all evil.

Kassapaṃ taṃ mahātheraṃ, saṅghassa pariṇāyakaṃ;

Dīpasmiṃ tambapaṇṇimhi, sāsanodayakārakaṃ.

To that great elder Kassapa, the leader of the Saṅgha, the establisher of the Dispensation on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.

Paṭipattiparādhīnaṃ, sadāraññanivāsinaṃ;

Pākaṭaṃ gagane canda-maṇḍalaṃ viya sāsane.

To him who is devoted to the practice, constantly dwelling in the forest, manifest in the Dispensation like the orb of the moon in the sky.

Saṅghassa [V 1.0002] pitaraṃ vande, vinaye suvisāradaṃ;

Yaṃ nissāya vasantohaṃ, vuḍḍhippattosmi sāsane.

I venerate the father of the Saṅgha, highly skilled in the Vinaya, relying on whom I dwell and have attained growth in the Dispensation.

Anutheraṃ mahāpaññaṃ, sumedhaṃ sutivissutaṃ;

Avikhaṇḍitasīlādi-parisuddhaguṇodayaṃ.

To the anuthera of great wisdom, intelligent and renowned in learning, in whom have arisen the utterly pure qualities headed by unbroken morality.

Bahussutaṃ satimantaṃ, dantaṃ santaṃ samāhitaṃ;

Namāmi sirasā dhīraṃ, garuṃ me gaṇavācakaṃ.

Learned, mindful, tamed, peaceful, and concentrated, I bow my head to that steadfast one, my teacher, the reciter for the community.

Āgatāgamatakkesu[M 1.0002], saddasatthanayaññusu;

Yassantevāsibhikkhūsu, sāsanaṃ suppatiṭṭhitaṃ.

The Dispensation is well-established among his disciple monks, who are skilled in scripture, tradition, and logic, and who know the meaning and method of the true teaching.

Yo sīhaḷindo dhitimā yasassī,

Uḷārapañño nipuṇo kalāsu;

Jāto visuddhe ravisomavaṃse,

Mahabbalo abbhutavuttitejo.

That Sinhala lord, resolute and glorious, of vast wisdom and skilled in the arts, born in the pure lineage of the sun and moon, of great strength, wondrous conduct, and splendor.

Jitvārivaggaṃ atiduppasayhaṃ,

Anaññasādhāraṇavikkamena;

Pattābhiseko jinadhammasevī,

Abhippasanno ratanattayamhi.

Having conquered the hostile forces so very hard to overcome with his unparalleled prowess, he attained consecration, a devotee of the Victor's Dhamma, deeply confident in the Triple Gem.

Ciraṃ vibhinne jinasāsanasmiṃ,

Paccatthike suṭṭhu viniggahetvā;

Sudhaṃva sāmaggirasaṃ pasatthaṃ,

Pāyesi bhikkhū parisuddhasīle.

Having thoroughly subdued the adversaries, he caused the monks of pure virtue in the Victor's Dispensation, which had long been divided, to drink the praised taste of harmony, which is like nectar.

Katvā vihāre vipule ca ramme,

Tatrappitenekasahassasaṅkhe;

Bhikkhū [V 1.0003] asese catupaccayehi,

Santappayanto suciraṃ akhaṇḍaṃ.

Having built vast and delightful monasteries, for a very long time and without interruption he satisfied the many thousands of monks there in their entirety with the four requisites.

Saddhammavuddhiṃ abhikaṅkhamāno,

Sayampi bhikkhū anusāsayitvā;

Niyojayaṃ ganthavipassanāsu,

Akāsi vuddhiṃ jinasāsanassa.

Desiring growth in the good Dhamma, having himself instructed the monks and engaged them in the study of the texts and in insight meditation, he brought about the growth of the Victor's Dispensation.

Tenāhamaccantamanuggahīto,

Anaññasādhāraṇasaṅgahena;

Yasmā parakkantabhujavhayena,

Ajjhesito bhikkhugaṇassa majjhe.

By him, the one named Parakkantabhuja, I was exceedingly favored with a unique kindness and was requested in the midst of the assembly of monks.

Tasmā [M 1.0003] anuttānapadānamatthaṃ,

Seṭṭhāya aṅguttaravaṇṇanāya;

Sandassayissaṃ sakalaṃ suboddhuṃ,

Nissāya pubbācariyappabhāvaṃ.

Therefore, relying on the authority of the ancient teachers, I will explain the meaning of the abstruse passages of the excellent commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya in its entirety, so that it may be easily understood.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā

The Explanation of the Introduction

1. Saṃvaṇṇanārambhe ratanattayaṃ namassitukāmo tassa visiṭṭhaguṇayogasandassanatthaṃ “karuṇāsītalahadaya”ntiādimāha. Visiṭṭhaguṇayogena hi vandanārahabhāvo, vandanārahe ca katā vandanā yathādhippetamatthaṃ sādheti. Ettha ca saṃvaṇṇanārambhe ratanattayappaṇāmakaraṇappayojanaṃ tattha tattha bahudhā papañcenti ācariyā, mayaṃ pana idhādhippetameva payojanaṃ dassayissāma, tasmā saṃvaṇṇanārambhe ratanattayappaṇāmakaraṇaṃ yathāpaṭiññātasaṃvaṇṇanāya anantarāyena parisamāpanatthanti veditabbaṃ. Idameva hi payojanaṃ ācariyena idhādhippetaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati –

1. Wishing to pay homage to the Triple Gem at the beginning of the subcommentary, in order to show its connection with distinguished qualities, he said the words beginning 'with a heart cooled by compassion.' For it is because of its connection with distinguished qualities that it is worthy of veneration, and veneration paid to what is worthy of veneration accomplishes the intended purpose. Here, though the teachers have explained in many ways the purpose of making an obeisance to the Triple Gem at the beginning of a subcommentary, we will show only the purpose intended here. Therefore, it should be understood that making an obeisance to the Triple Gem at the beginning of the subcommentary is for the sake of completing the promised subcommentary without obstruction. This, indeed, is the purpose intended here by the author. For he will say:

“Iti me pasannamatino, ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ puññaṃ;

Yaṃ suvihatantarāyo, hutvā tassānubhāvenā”ti.

'By the power of this merit consisting in the veneration of the Triple Gem, which I have performed with a confident mind, having become one for whom obstacles are well removed...'

Ratanattayappaṇāmakaraṇena [V 1.0004] cettha yathāpaṭiññātasaṃvaṇṇanāya anantarāyena parisamāpanaṃ ratanattayapūjāya paññāpāṭavato, tāya paññāpāṭavañca rāgādimalavidhamanato. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Here, the unobstructed completion of the promised subcommentary by making an obeisance to the Triple Gem comes about because veneration of the Triple Gem leads to keenness of wisdom; and this keenness of wisdom, in turn, comes from the destruction of the mental stains of lust and so on. For it has been said:

“Yasmiṃ, mahānāma, samaye ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hotī”tiādi (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11).

'Mahānāma, on an occasion when a noble disciple recollects the Tathāgata, his mind is not obsessed by lust, not obsessed by hatred, and not obsessed by delusion. On that occasion his mind is simply upright....'

Tasmā ratanattayapūjanena vikkhālitamalāya paññāya pāṭavasiddhi.

Therefore, through veneration of the Triple Gem, keenness is accomplished for a wisdom whose stains have been washed away.

Atha vā ratanattayapūjanassa paññāpadaṭṭhānasamādhihetuttā paññāpāṭavaṃ. Vuttañhi tassa samādhihetuttaṃ –

Alternatively, there is keenness of wisdom because veneration of the Triple Gem is a cause for concentration, which is the proximate cause of wisdom. For its being a cause for concentration has been stated:

“Ujugatacitto [M 1.0004] kho pana, mahānāma, ariyasāvako labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ, pamuditassa pīti jāyati, pītimanassa kāyo passambhati, passaddhakāyo sukhaṃ vediyati, sukhino cittaṃ samādhiyatī”ti (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11).

'With an upright mind, Mahānāma, a noble disciple gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains gladness connected with the Dhamma. When he is gladdened, rapture is born in him. In one who is rapturous in mind, the body becomes tranquil. One whose body is tranquil experiences happiness. The mind of a happy person becomes concentrated.'

Samādhissa ca paññāya padaṭṭhānabhāvo vuttoyeva – “samāhito yathābhūtaṃ pajānātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.5; 4.99; 5.1071). Tato evaṃ paṭubhūtāya paññāya paṭiññāmahattakataṃ khedamabhibhuyya anantarāyena saṃvaṇṇanaṃ samāpayissati.

And that concentration is the proximate cause of wisdom has been stated thus: 'One who is concentrated understands things as they really are.' Therefore, with wisdom that has thus become keen, having overcome the weariness from the great task he has undertaken, he will complete the subcommentary without obstruction.

Atha vā ratanattayapūjāya āyuvaṇṇasukhabalavaḍḍhanato anantarāyena parisamāpanaṃ veditabbaṃ. Ratanattayappaṇāmena hi āyuvaṇṇasukhabalāni vaḍḍhanti. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Alternatively, the unobstructed completion should be understood as resulting from the increase of lifespan, beauty, happiness, and strength through veneration of the Triple Gem. For by paying homage to the Triple Gem, lifespan, beauty, happiness, and strength increase. As it has been said:

“Abhivādanasīlissa, niccaṃ vuḍḍhāpacāyino;

Cattāro dhammā vaḍḍhanti, āyu vaṇṇo sukhaṃ bala”nti. (dha. pa. 109) –

'For one who is habitually respectful and constantly honors the elders, four things increase: lifespan, beauty, happiness, and strength.'

Tato āyuvaṇṇasukhabalavuddhiyā hoteva kāriyaniṭṭhānaṃ.

Therefore, because of the increase in lifespan, beauty, happiness, and strength, the task is indeed completed.

Atha [V 1.0005] vā ratanattayagāravassa paṭibhānāparihānāvahattā. Aparihānāvahañhi tīsupi ratanesu gāravaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Alternatively, it is because reverence for the Triple Gem is conducive to the non-decline of ready wit. For reverence toward the three gems is indeed conducive to non-decline. As it has been said:

“Sattime, bhikkhave, aparihānīyā dhammā. Katame satta? Satthugāravatā, dhammagāravatā, saṅghagāravatā, sikkhāgāravatā, samādhigāravatā, sovacassatā, kalyāṇamittatā”ti (a. ni. 7.34).

'Bhikkhus, there are these seven principles of non-decline. What seven? Reverence for the Teacher, reverence for the Dhamma, reverence for the Saṅgha, reverence for the training, reverence for concentration, amenability to correction, and good friendship.'

Hoteva ca tato paṭibhānāparihānena yathāpaṭiññātaparisamāpanaṃ.

And so, through the non-decline of ready wit, there is indeed the completion of the work as promised.

Atha vā pasādavatthūsu pūjāya puññātisayabhāvato. Vuttañhi tassā puññātisayattaṃ –

Alternatively, it is because veneration of the objects of confidence results in a superabundance of merit. For its resulting in a superabundance of merit has been stated:

“Pūjārahe pūjayato, buddhe yadi va sāvake;

Papañcasamatikkante, tiṇṇasokapariddave.

‘For one who venerates those worthy of veneration, whether Buddhas or their disciples, who have overcome proliferation and crossed beyond sorrow and lamentation...’

Te [M 1.0005] tādise pūjayato, nibbute akutobhaye;

Na sakkā puññaṃ saṅkhātuṃ, imettamapi kenacī”ti. (dha. pa. 195-196; apa. thera 1.10.1-2);

‘...for one who venerates such as these, the quenched and fearless, it is not possible for anyone to measure his merit by saying, “It is this much.”’

Puññātisayo ca yathādhippetaparisamāpanūpāyo. Yathāha –

And a superabundance of merit is a means for accomplishing one's intended purpose. As it is said:

“Esa devamanussānaṃ, sabbakāmadado nidhi;

Yaṃ yadevābhipatthenti, sabbametena labbhatī”ti. (khu. pā. 8.10);

‘This is a treasure for gods and humans that bestows all that they desire. Whatever they long for, all that is obtained by this.’

Upāyesu ca paṭipannassa hoteva kāriyaniṭṭhānaṃ. Ratanattayapūjā hi niratisayapuññakkhettasambuddhiyā aparimeyyappabhāvo puññātisayoti bahuvidhantarāyepi lokasannivāse antarāyanibandhanasakalasaṃkilesaviddhaṃsanāya pahoti, bhayādiupaddavañca nivāreti. Tasmā vuttaṃ – “saṃvaṇṇanārambhe ratanattayappaṇāmakaraṇaṃ yathāpaṭiññātasaṃvaṇṇanāya anantarāyena parisamāpanattha”nti.

For one who has undertaken the means, the completion of the task is indeed assured. For veneration of the Triple Gem is a superabundance of merit of immeasurable power, since the Triple Gem is understood to be an unsurpassed field of merit. Thus, in this world with its many kinds of obstacles, it is able to destroy all defilements that are a basis for obstacles, and it averts dangers, calamities, and so on. Therefore it was said: ‘Making an obeisance to the Triple Gem at the beginning of the subcommentary is for the sake of completing the promised subcommentary without obstruction.’

Evañca sappayojanaṃ ratanattayavandanaṃ kattukāmo paṭhamaṃ tāva bhagavato vandanaṃ kātuṃ tammūlakattā [V 1.0006] sesaratanānaṃ “karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ…pe… gativimutta”nti āha. Tattha yassā desanāya saṃvaṇṇanaṃ kattukāmo, sā na vinayadesanā viya karuṇāpadhānā, nāpi abhidhammadesanā viya paññāpadhānā, atha kho karuṇāpaññāpadhānāti tadubhayappadhānameva tāva sammāsambuddhassa thomanaṃ kātuṃ “karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ, paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha kiratīti karuṇā, paradukkhaṃ vikkhipati apanetīti attho. Atha vā kiṇātīti karuṇā, paradukkhe sati kāruṇikaṃ hiṃsati vibādhatīti attho. Paradukkhe sati sādhūnaṃ kampanaṃ hadayakhedaṃ karotīti vā karuṇā. Atha vā kamiti sukhaṃ, taṃ rundhatīti karuṇā. Esā hi paradukkhāpanayanakāmatālakkhaṇā attasukhanirapekkhatāya kāruṇikānaṃ sukhaṃ rundhati vibandhatīti attho. Karuṇāya sītalaṃ karuṇāsītalaṃ, karuṇāsītalaṃ hadayaṃ assāti karuṇāsītalahadayo, taṃ karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ.

Wishing to offer this purposeful veneration to the Triple Gem, and because the other two gems are rooted in the Blessed One, the author first pays homage to him, saying: ‘...a heart cooled by compassion... liberated from all destinies.’ Here, the teaching on which he wishes to write a subcommentary is not predominantly about compassion like the teaching of the Vinaya, nor predominantly about wisdom like the teaching of the Abhidhamma, but is predominant in both compassion and wisdom. Therefore, to praise the Perfectly Enlightened One as being preeminent in both, it is said: ‘with a heart cooled by compassion, and with the darkness of delusion dispelled by the radiance of wisdom.’ Herein, compassion (karuṇā) is so called because it scatters (kirati); the meaning is that it disperses, it removes the suffering of others. Or, compassion (karuṇā) is so called because it injures (kiṇāti); the meaning is that when there is suffering in others, it hurts and afflicts the compassionate person. Or, compassion (karuṇā) is so called because when there is suffering in others, it causes the good to tremble and makes their hearts sorrowful. Or, kaṃ means happiness; that which obstructs (rundhati) it is karuṇā. The meaning is that this compassion, which has the characteristic of desiring to remove the suffering of others, obstructs and hinders the happiness of compassionate persons on account of their indifference to their own happiness. Cooled by compassion is ‘cooled-by-compassion’ (karuṇāsītalaṃ). One who has a heart cooled by compassion is ‘one-with-a-heart-cooled-by-compassion’ (karuṇāsītalahadayo). Hence the phrase ‘to him with a heart cooled by compassion’ (karuṇāsītalahadayaṃ).

Tattha kiñcāpi paresaṃ hitopasaṃhārasukhādiaparihānicchanasabhāvatāya, byāpādāratīnaṃ ujuvipaccanīkatāya ca sattasantānagatasantāpavicchedanākārappavattiyā mettāmuditānampi cittasītalabhāvakāraṇatā upalabbhati, tathāpi dukkhāpanayanākārappavattiyā parūpatāpāsahanarasā avihiṃsabhūtā [M 1.0006] karuṇā visesena bhagavato cittassa cittappassaddhi viya sītibhāvanimittanti vuttaṃ – “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti. Karuṇāmukhena vā mettāmuditānampi hadayasītalabhāvakāraṇatā vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā asādhāraṇañāṇavisesanibandhanabhūtā sātisayaṃ niravasesañca sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ viya savisayabyāpitāya mahākaruṇābhāvaṃ upagatā karuṇāva bhagavato atisayena hadayasītalabhāvahetūti āha – “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti. Atha vā satipi mettāmuditānaṃ sātisaye hadayasītibhāvanibandhanatte sakalabuddhaguṇavisesakāraṇatāya tāsampi kāraṇanti karuṇāva bhagavato “hadayasītalabhāvakāraṇa”nti vuttā. Karuṇānidānā hi sabbepi buddhaguṇā. Karuṇānubhāvanibbāpiyamānasaṃsāradukkhasantāpassa hi bhagavato paradukkhāpanayanakāmatāya anekānipi asaṅkhyeyyāni kappānaṃ akilantarūpasseva niravasesabuddhakaradhammasambharaṇaniratassa samadhigatadhammādhipateyyassa ca sannihitesupi sattasaṅkhārasamupanītahadayūpatāpanimittesu na īsakampi cittasītibhāvassa aññathattamahosīti. Etasmiñca atthavikappe tīsupi avatthāsu bhagavato karuṇā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Herein, although it is found that loving-kindness and sympathetic joy are also a cause for the cooling of the mind—due to their nature of wishing for the welfare and happiness of others, their being the direct opposite of ill will and discontent, and their operating by way of cutting off the torment present in the mental continuum of beings—still, it is compassion, which is a state of non-harming, that is especially the cause of the cooling of the Blessed One’s mind, like tranquility of mind, because it operates by way of removing suffering and its essence is the inability to endure the torment of others. Thus it is said: ‘one whose heart is cooled by compassion.’ Or it should be seen that the fact that loving-kindness and sympathetic joy are a cause for the cooling of the heart is stated by way of compassion. Or else, just as the knowledge of omniscience, which is based on extraordinary knowledge, is unsurpassed and complete, so too compassion, having reached the state of great compassion by pervading its entire domain, is the cause for the supreme cooling of the Blessed One’s heart. Thus he said: ‘one whose heart is cooled by compassion.’ Or again, although loving-kindness and sympathetic joy are a basis for the supreme cooling of the heart, because compassion is the cause of all the special qualities of a Buddha, it is also their cause, and thus compassion alone is said to be ‘the cause for the cooling of the heart’ of the Blessed One. For all the qualities of a Buddha are rooted in compassion. For the Blessed One—whose torment from the suffering of saṃsāra was being extinguished by the power of compassion, who was dedicated to gathering all the things that make a Buddha without tiring for countless aeons out of a desire to remove the suffering of others, and who had attained sovereignty over the Dhamma—the coolness of his mind did not undergo even the slightest alteration even when signs that torment the heart, brought on by the formations of beings, were present. In this alternative explanation, it should be seen that the Blessed One’s compassion is included in all three periods.

Pajānātīti paññā, yathāsabhāvaṃ pakārehi paṭivijjhatīti attho. Paññāva ñeyyāvaraṇappahānato pakārehi dhammasabhāvāvajotanaṭṭhena pajjototi paññāpajjoto. Savāsanappahānato visesena hataṃ samugghātitaṃ vihataṃ. Paññāpajjotena vihataṃ paññāpajjotavihataṃ[V 1.0007], muyhanti tena, sayaṃ vā muyhati, mohanamattameva vā tanti moho, avijjā. Sveva visayasabhāvappaṭicchādanato andhakārasarikkhatāya tamo viyāti mohatamo, paññāpajjotavihato mohatamo etassāti paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo, taṃ paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ. Sabbesampi hi khīṇāsavānaṃ satipi paññāpajjotena avijjandhakārassa vihatabhāve saddhādhimuttehi viya diṭṭhippattānaṃ sāvakehi paccekasambuddhehi ca savāsanappahānena sammāsambuddhānaṃ kilesappahānassa viseso vijjatīti sātisayena avijjāpahānena bhagavantaṃ thomento āha – “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti.

‘One understands’ (pajānāti), thus it is wisdom (paññā); the meaning is that one penetrates things in their own-being in various ways. Wisdom itself is a light (pajjota) because it illuminates the nature of phenomena in various ways by abandoning the obstruction to the knowable; thus it is the ‘light of wisdom’ (paññāpajjota). It is especially struck down, eradicated, and dispelled by the abandonment of the latent dispositions. ‘Dispelled by the light of wisdom’ is paññāpajjotavihata. ‘One is deluded by it, or one is deluded oneself, or it is mere delusion’; this is delusion (moha), that is, ignorance (avijjā). Because it conceals the own-being of its object, it is like darkness (tamo); thus it is the ‘darkness of delusion’ (mohatamo). ‘For him the darkness of delusion is dispelled by the light of wisdom,’ thus he is paññāpajjotavihatamohatamo; him, paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ. For although the darkness of ignorance has been dispelled by the light of wisdom for all whose taints are destroyed, there is a distinction in the abandonment of defilements for the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas compared to the disciples liberated by faith, the disciples who have attained to view, and the Paccekabuddhas, namely, the abandonment of the latent dispositions. Thus, praising the Blessed One for his supreme abandonment of ignorance, he says: ‘one whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the light of wisdom.’

Atha [M 1.0007] vā antarena paropadesaṃ attano santāne accantaṃ avijjandhakāravigamassa nibbattitattā, tattha ca sabbaññutāya balesu ca vasībhāvassa samadhigatattā, parasantatiyañca dhammadesanātisayānubhāvena sammadeva tassa pavattitattā bhagavāva visesato mohatamavigamena thometabboti āha – “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti. Imasmiñca atthavikappe “paññāpajjoto”ti padena bhagavato paṭivedhapaññā viya desanāpaññāpi sāmaññaniddesena, ekasesanayena vā saṅgahitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Alternatively, because he brought about the complete removal of the darkness of ignorance in his own mental continuum without the instruction of others, and because he attained omniscience and mastery over the powers, and because through the surpassing power of his Dhamma teaching it was rightly set in motion in the mental continuums of others, the Blessed One is especially to be praised for the removal of the darkness of delusion. Thus he says: ‘one whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the light of wisdom.’ In this alternative explanation of the meaning, it should be understood that by the term ‘light of wisdom,’ the Blessed One’s wisdom of teaching is included as well as his wisdom of penetration, either by way of a general designation or by the principle of ellipsis.

Atha vā bhagavato ñāṇassa ñeyyapariyantikattā sakalañeyyadhammasabhāvāvabodhanasamatthena anāvaraṇañāṇasaṅkhātena paññāpajjotena sabbañeyyadhammasabhāvacchādakassa mohandhakārassa vidhamitattā anaññasādhāraṇo bhagavato mohatamavināsoti katvā vuttaṃ – “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti. Ettha ca mohatamavidhamanante adhigatattā anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ kāraṇopacārena sasantānamohatamavidhamanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Abhinīhārasampattiyā savāsanappahānameva hi kilesānaṃ ñeyyāvaraṇappahānanti, parasantāne pana mohatamavidhamanassa kāraṇabhāvato anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ “mohatamavidhamana”nti vuccatīti.

Alternatively, because the Blessed One’s knowledge encompasses all that is knowable, the darkness of delusion, which conceals the nature of all knowable phenomena, has been dispelled by the light of wisdom, that is, by the unobstructed knowledge which is capable of awakening to the nature of all knowable phenomena. Therefore, on the grounds that the Blessed One’s destruction of the darkness of delusion is not shared by others, it is said: ‘one whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the light of wisdom.’ Here, the unobstructed knowledge, being attained upon the dispelling of the darkness of delusion, should be understood as the dispelling of the darkness of delusion in one’s own continuum by a metaphorical application of the cause. For it is precisely the abandonment of the defilements together with their latent dispositions, through the fulfillment of the aspiration, that is the abandonment of the obstruction to the knowable. In the mental continuums of others, however, since it is the cause for dispelling the darkness of delusion, the unobstructed knowledge is called ‘the dispelling of the darkness of delusion.’

Kiṃ pana kāraṇaṃ avijjāsamugghātoyeveko pahānasampattivasena bhagavato thomanānimittaṃ gayhati, na pana sātisayaniravasesakilesappahānanti? Tappahānavacaneneva tadekaṭṭhatāya sakalasaṃkilesagaṇasamugghātassa vuttattā. Na hi so tādiso kileso atthi, yo niravasesaavijjāpahānena na pahīyatīti.

But what is the reason that the eradication of ignorance alone is taken as the mark of praise for the Blessed One with respect to the accomplishment of abandonment, and not the unsurpassed, complete abandonment of all defilements? Because by the very statement of its abandonment, the eradication of the entire host of defilements is stated, since they have the same meaning. For there is no such defilement that is not abandoned with the complete abandonment of ignorance.

Atha vā vijjā viya sakalakusaladhammasamuppattiyā, niravasesākusaladhammanibbattiyā saṃsārappavattiyā [V 1.0008] ca avijjā padhānakāraṇanti tabbighātavacanena sakalasaṃkilesagaṇasamugghāto vutto eva hotīti vuttaṃ – “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti.

Or, since ignorance is the principal cause for the arising of all unwholesome states and for the continuation of saṃsāra—just as knowledge is for the arising of all wholesome states—by the statement of its destruction, the eradication of the entire host of defilements is thereby stated. Thus it is said: ‘one whose darkness of delusion is dispelled by the light of wisdom.’

Narā ca amarā ca narāmarā, saha narāmarehīti sanarāmaro, sanarāmaro ca so loko cāti sanarāmaraloko, tassa garūti sanarāmaralokagaru, taṃ sanarāmaralokagaruṃ. Etena devamanussānaṃ viya tadavasiṭṭhasattānampi yathārahaṃ guṇavisesāvahatāya bhagavato upakārataṃ [M 1.0008] dasseti. Na cettha padhānappadhānabhāvo codetabbo. Añño hi saddakkamo, añño atthakkamo. Īdisesu hi samāsapadesu padhānampi appadhānaṃ viya niddisīyati yathā “sarājikāya parisāyā”ti (cūḷava. 336). Kāmañcettha sattasaṅkhārabhājanavasena tividho loko, garubhāvassa pana adhippetattā garukaraṇasamatthasseva yujjanato sattalokassa vasena attho gahetabbo. So hi lokīyanti ettha puññapāpāni tabbipāko cāti “loko”ti vuccati. Amaraggahaṇena cettha upapattidevā adhippetā.

‘Humans (narā) and immortals (amarā)’ are narāmarā. ‘With humans and immortals’ is sanarāmaro. ‘That world with humans and immortals’ is sanarāmaraloko. ‘A venerable one (garu) of that world’ is sanarāmaralokagaru; him, sanarāmaralokagaruṃ. By this he shows the Blessed One’s helpfulness in bringing special qualities to other beings as appropriate, just as to devas and humans. Here the issue of primary and secondary should not be raised. For the order of words is one thing, the order of meaning another. In such compound terms, even the primary element is indicated as if it were secondary, as in ‘the assembly with its king.’ Although the world is threefold—as the world of beings, the world of formations, and the world as receptacle—since venerability is intended here, the meaning should be taken in terms of the world of beings, as it is only they who are capable of showing reverence. For it is called ‘world’ (loka) because merit and demerit and their results are experienced therein. And here, by the term ‘immortals,’ devas by rebirth are intended.

Atha vā samūhattho lokasaddo samudāyavasena lokīyati paññāpīyatīti. Saha narehīti sanarā, sanarā ca te amarā cāti sanarāmarā, tesaṃ lokoti sanarāmaralokoti purimanayeneva yojetabbaṃ. Amarasaddena cettha visuddhidevāpi saṅgayhanti. Tepi hi maraṇābhāvato paramatthato amarā. Narāmarānaṃyeva ca gahaṇaṃ ukkaṭṭhaniddesavasena yathā “satthā devamanussāna”nti (dī. ni. 1.157). Tathā hi sabbānatthapariharaṇapubbaṅgamāya niravasesahitasukhavidhānatapparāya niratisayāya payogasampattiyā sadevamanussāya pajāya accantūpakāritāya aparimitanirupamappabhāvaguṇavisesasamaṅgitāya ca sabbasattuttamo bhagavā aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu aparimāṇānaṃ sattānaṃ uttamagāravaṭṭhānaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “sanarāmaralokagaru”nti.

Alternatively, the word ‘loka’ (world) has the meaning of a collection, since it is seen or designated as a collection. ‘With humans’ is sanarā; ‘those who are with humans and are immortals’ are sanarāmarā; ‘their world’ is sanarāmaraloko. This should be construed in the same way as before. Here, by the word ‘immortals,’ the devas of purity are also included, for they too are immortals in the ultimate sense because of the absence of death. The mention of only humans and immortals is a way of indicating the most excellent, as in ‘the Teacher of devas and humans.’ For the Blessed One, the foremost of all beings, is the supreme object of reverence for immeasurable beings in immeasurable world-systems because of his unsurpassed accomplishment in practice, which is preceded by the avoidance of all harm and is intent on providing for the complete welfare and happiness of all; because of his extreme helpfulness to the populace with its devas and humans; and because he is endowed with special qualities of immeasurable, incomparable power and majesty. Therefore it is said: ‘the venerable one of the world with its humans and immortals.’

Sobhanaṃ gataṃ gamanaṃ etassāti sugato. Bhagavato hi veneyyajanūpasaṅkamanaṃ ekantena tesaṃ hitasukhanipphādanato sobhanaṃ, tathā lakkhaṇānubyañjanappaṭimaṇḍitarūpakāyatāya dutavilambitakhalitānukaḍḍhananippīḷanukkuṭikakuṭilākuṭilatādi- dosarahitamavahasitarājahaṃsavasabhavāraṇamigarājagamanaṃ kāyagamanaṃ ñāṇagamanañca vipulanimmalakaruṇāsativīriyādiguṇavisesasahitamabhinīhārato yāva mahābodhi anavajjatāya sobhanamevāti. Atha vā sayambhuñāṇena sakalampi lokaṃ pariññābhisamayavasena parijānanto ñāṇena sammā gato avagatoti sugato, tathā lokasamudayaṃ pahānābhisamayavasena pajahanto anuppattidhammataṃ āpādento sammā gato atītoti sugato, lokanirodhaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikiriyābhisamayavasena sammā [V 1.0009] gato adhigatoti [M 1.0009] sugato, lokanirodhagāminipaṭipadaṃ bhāvanābhisamayavasena sammā gato paṭipannoti sugato. “Sotāpattimaggena ye kilesā pahīnā, te kilese na puneti na pacceti na paccāgacchatīti sugato”tiādinā (cūḷani. mettagūmāṇavapucchāniddeso 27) nayena ayamattho vibhāvetabbo. Atha vā sundaraṃ ṭhānaṃ sammāsambodhiṃ, nibbānameva vā gato adhigatoti sugato, yasmā vā bhūtaṃ tacchaṃ atthasaṃhitaṃ veneyyānaṃ yathārahaṃ kālayuttameva ca dhammaṃ bhāsati, tasmā sammā gadatīti sugato, da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā. Iti sobhanagamanatādīhi sugato, taṃ sugataṃ.

“His going is beautiful,” thus he is the Well-Gone One. For the Blessed One’s approach to those to be trained is entirely beautiful because it brings about their welfare and happiness. Likewise, his bodily gait—his form adorned with the major and minor marks, free from faults such as haste, delay, stumbling, dragging, pressing, squatting, or crookedness—resembles the graceful gait of a royal swan, a lordly elephant, or a king of beasts. His going, both bodily and mental, is accompanied by vast, stainless qualities such as compassion, mindfulness, and energy; from his initial resolve up to the great enlightenment, it is flawless and thus beautiful. Or else, by his self-originated knowledge, having fully understood the entire world through the direct knowledge of full understanding, he has gone rightly, has comprehended—thus he is the Well-Gone One. Similarly, having abandoned the origin of the world through the direct knowledge of abandonment, he has gone rightly, having brought it to a state of non-arising—thus he is the Well-Gone One. Having realized the cessation of the world, Nibbāna, through the direct knowledge of realization, he has gone rightly, has attained—thus he is the Well-Gone One. Having developed the path leading to the cessation of the world through the direct knowledge of development, he has gone rightly, has practiced—thus he is the Well-Gone One. This meaning should be elaborated in this way, as stated in the Cūḷaniddesa: “By the path of stream-entry, he does not return to, does not come back to, does not revert to the defilements that have been abandoned—thus he is the Well-Gone One.” Or else, he has gone to the beautiful state, perfect enlightenment, or to Nibbāna itself—thus he is the Well-Gone One. Or because he speaks what is factual, true, beneficial, timely, and appropriate for those to be trained, he speaks rightly—thus he is the Well-Spoken One (by changing the ‘da’ to a ‘ta’). Thus, because of his beautiful going and so on, he is the Well-Gone One—that Sugata.

Puññapāpakammehi upapajjanavasena gantabbato gatiyo, upapattibhavavisesā. Tā pana nirayādivasena pañcavidhā. Tāhi sakalassapi bhavagāmikammassa ariyamaggādhigamena avipākārahabhāvakaraṇena nivattitattā bhagavā pañcahipi gatīhi suṭṭhu mutto visaṃyuttoti āha – “gativimutta”nti. Etena bhagavato katthacipi gatiyā apariyāpannataṃ dasseti, yato bhagavā “devātidevo”ti vuccati. Tenevāha –

Destinations are places to be gone to through rebirth based on meritorious and demeritorious kamma; they are specific modes of existence. These are fivefold, beginning with the hells. Since, by the attainment of the noble path, all kamma leading to existence has been made to cease by being rendered incapable of producing a result, the Blessed One is well freed and disjoined from all five destinations. Thus it is said, “freed from destinations.” This shows that the Blessed One is not included in any destination whatsoever, which is why he is called “the god beyond gods.” Therefore it is said:

“Yena devūpapatyassa, gandhabbo vā vihaṅgamo;

Yakkhattaṃ yena gaccheyyaṃ, manussattañca abbaje;

Te mayhaṃ āsavā khīṇā, viddhastā vinaḷīkatā”ti. (a. ni. 4.36);

“By which I might be reborn as a god, or as a gandhabba or a bird; by which I might reach the state of a yakkha, or attain the human state—those taints of mine are destroyed, shattered, and annihilated.”

Taṃtaṃgatisaṃvattanikānañhi kammakilesānaṃ aggamaggena bodhimūleyeva suppahīnattā natthi bhagavato gatipariyāpannatāti accantameva bhagavā sabbabhavayonigativiññāṇaṭṭhitisattāvāsasattanikāyehi suparimutto, taṃ gativimuttaṃ. Vandeti namāmi, thomemīti vā attho.

Because the kamma and defilements that lead to various destinations have been thoroughly abandoned by the supreme path at the very root of enlightenment, the Blessed One is not included in any destination. Thus, the Blessed One is completely liberated from all realms of existence, sources of rebirth, destinations, stations of consciousness, abodes of beings, and classes of beings. To him, the one freed from destinations. Vande means: ‘I pay homage,’ or ‘I praise.’

Atha vā gativimuttanti anupādisesanibbānadhātuppattiyā bhagavantaṃ thometi. Ettha hi dvīhi ākārehi bhagavato thomanā veditabbā attahitasampattito parahitappaṭipattito ca. Tesu attahitasampatti anāvaraṇañāṇādhigamato savāsanānaṃ sabbesaṃ kilesānaṃ accantappahānato anupādisesanibbānappattito ca veditabbā, parahitappaṭipatti lābhasakkārādinirapekkhacittassa sabbadukkhaniyyānikadhammadesanato viruddhesupi niccaṃ hitajjhāsayato ñāṇaparipākakālāgamanato ca. Sā panettha āsayato payogato ca duvidhā, parahitappaṭipatti tividhā ca, attahitasampatti [M 1.0010] pakāsitā hoti. Kathaṃ? “Karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti etena āsayato parahitappaṭipatti[V 1.0010], sammāgadanatthena sugatasaddena payogato parahitappaṭipatti, “paññāpajjotavihatamohatamaṃ gativimutta”nti etehi catusaccasampaṭivedhanatthena ca sugatasaddena tividhāpi attahitasampatti, avasiṭṭhena “paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti etena cāpi attahitasampatti parahitappaṭipatti pakāsitā hotīti.

Or, the phrase “freed from destinations” praises the Blessed One for his attainment of the Nibbāna-element without residue remaining. Here, the praise of the Blessed One should be understood in two aspects: through the accomplishment of his own welfare and through his practice for the welfare of others. Among these, the accomplishment of his own welfare is to be understood as the attainment of unobstructed knowledge, the utter abandonment of all defilements together with their latent tendencies, and the attainment of Nibbāna without residue. The practice for the welfare of others is to be understood as teaching the Dhamma that leads out from all suffering with a mind indifferent to gain and honor, with a constant intention for the welfare even of the hostile, and by awaiting the time for the maturation of their knowledge. Herein, the practice for the welfare of others is twofold: by way of intention and by way of application. And the threefold accomplishment of his own welfare is also shown. How? By “with a heart cooled by compassion,” the practice for the welfare of others by way of intention is shown. By the word sugata in the sense of speaking well, the practice for the welfare of others by way of application is shown. By the phrases “dispelling the darkness of delusion with the lamp of wisdom” and “freed from destinations,” and by the word sugata in its sense of penetrating the four truths, the threefold accomplishment of his own welfare is shown. And by the phrase “dispelling the darkness of delusion with the lamp of wisdom,” both the accomplishment of his own welfare and the practice for the welfare of others are also shown.

Atha vā tīhi ākārehi bhagavato thomanā veditabbā hetuto, phalato, upakārato ca. Tattha hetu mahākaruṇā, sā paṭhamapadena dassitā. Phalaṃ catubbidhaṃ ñāṇasampadā, pahānasampadā, ānubhāvasampadā, rūpakāyasampadā cāti. Tāsu ñāṇappahānasampadā dutiyapadena saccappaṭivedhanatthena ca sugatasaddena pakāsitā honti, ānubhāvasampadā tatiyapadena, rūpakāyasampadā yathāvuttakāyagamanasobhanatthena sugatasaddena lakkhaṇānubyañjanapāripūriyā vinā tadabhāvato. Upakāro anantaraṃ abāhiraṃ karitvā tividhayānamukhena vimuttidhammadesanā. So sammāgadanatthena sugatasaddena pakāsito hotīti veditabbaṃ.

Alternatively, the praise of the Blessed One is to be understood in three aspects: cause, fruit, and benefit. Herein, the cause is great compassion, which is shown by the first phrase. The fruit is fourfold: the accomplishment of knowledge, the accomplishment of abandonment, the accomplishment of power, and the accomplishment of the form-body. Among these, the accomplishments of knowledge and abandonment are shown by the second phrase and by the word sugata in its sense of penetrating the truths; the accomplishment of power by the third phrase; and the accomplishment of the form-body by the word sugata in the sense of the beauty of the bodily gait as described above, since that beauty is impossible without the fulfillment of the major and minor marks. The benefit is the teaching of the Dhamma of liberation through the entrance of the threefold vehicle, without making a distinction between the internal and the external. This, it should be understood, is shown by the word sugata in the sense of speaking rightly.

Tattha “karuṇāsītalahadaya”nti etena sammāsambodhiyā mūlaṃ dasseti. Mahākaruṇāsañcoditamānaso hi bhagavā saṃsārapaṅkato sattānaṃ samuddharaṇatthaṃ katābhinīhāro anupubbena pāramiyo pūretvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ adhigatoti karuṇā sammāsambodhiyā mūlaṃ. “Paññāpajjotavihatamohatama”nti etena sammāsambodhiṃ dasseti. Anāvaraṇañāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi maggañāṇaṃ, maggañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca anāvaraṇañāṇaṃ “sammāsambodhī”ti vuccatīti. Sammāgamanatthena sugatasaddena sammāsambodhiyā paṭipattiṃ dasseti līnuddhaccapatiṭṭhānāyūhanakāmasukhallikattakilamathānuyogasassatucchedābhinivesādiantadvayarahitāya karuṇāpaññāpariggahitāya majjhimāya paṭipattiyā pakāsanato sugatasaddassa. Itarehi sammāsambodhiyā padhānappadhānabhedaṃ payojanaṃ dasseti. Saṃsāramahoghato sattasantāraṇañhettha padhānaṃ payojanaṃ, tadaññamappadhānaṃ. Tesu padhānena parahitappaṭipattiṃ dasseti, itarena attahitasampattiṃ. Tadubhayena attahitāya [M 1.0011] paṭipannādīsu catūsu puggalesu bhagavato catutthapuggalabhāvaṃ dasseti. Tena ca anuttaradakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ uttamavandaneyyabhāvaṃ attano ca vandanakiriyāya khettaṅgatabhāvaṃ dasseti.

Here, “with a heart cooled by compassion” indicates the root of perfect enlightenment. For the Blessed One, his mind spurred by great compassion, having made the resolve to rescue beings from the swamp of saṃsāra, fulfilled the perfections in sequence and attained unsurpassed perfect enlightenment; thus, compassion is the root of perfect enlightenment. “With the lamp of wisdom dispelling the darkness of delusion” indicates perfect enlightenment itself. For path knowledge has unobstructed knowledge as its proximate cause, and unobstructed knowledge has path knowledge as its proximate cause; this is called “perfect enlightenment.” By the word sugata in the sense of “one who has gone rightly,” the practice for perfect enlightenment is indicated, because the word sugata reveals the middle path, which is free from the two extremes—such as sloth and agitation, indulgence in sensual pleasures and self-mortification, and adherence to eternalism and annihilationism—and is embraced by compassion and wisdom. By the other phrases, the purpose of perfect enlightenment is shown with its distinction between principal and subordinate. Here, the principal purpose is the ferrying of beings across the great flood of saṃsāra; the other is subordinate. Through the principal purpose, the practice for the welfare of others is shown; through the other, the accomplishment of one's own welfare. By both, the Blessed One's status as the fourth of the four kinds of persons—that is, the one who practices for the welfare of both himself and others—is shown. And by this, his status as an unsurpassed recipient of offerings, as one supremely worthy of veneration, and as a field for one's own act of veneration is shown.

Ettha ca karuṇāgahaṇena lokiyesu mahaggatabhāvappattāsādhāraṇaguṇadīpanato bhagavato sabbalokiyaguṇasampatti dassitā hoti, paññāgahaṇena sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānamaggañāṇadīpanato sabbalokuttaraguṇasampatti. Tadubhayaggahaṇasiddho hi attho “sanarāmaralokagaru”ntiādinā papañcīyatīti[V 1.0011]. Karuṇāgahaṇena ca upagamanaṃ nirupakkilesaṃ dasseti, paññāgahaṇena apagamanaṃ. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena lokasamaññānurūpaṃ bhagavato pavattiṃ dasseti lokavohāravisayattā karuṇāya, paññāgahaṇena samaññāya anatidhāvanaṃ. Sabhāvānavabodhena hi dhammānaṃ samaññaṃ atidhāvitvā sattādiparāmasanaṃ hotīti. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena mahākaruṇāsamāpattivihāraṃ dasseti, paññāgahaṇena tīsu kālesu appaṭihatañāṇaṃ catusaccañāṇaṃ, catupaṭisambhidāñāṇaṃ, catuvesārajjañāṇaṃ. Karuṇāgahaṇena mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇassa gahitattā sesāsādhāraṇañāṇāni, cha abhiññā, aṭṭhasu parisāsu akampanañāṇāni, dasa balāni, cuddasa buddhañāṇāni, soḷasa ñāṇacariyā, aṭṭhārasa buddhadhammā, catucattālīsa ñāṇavatthūni, sattasattati ñāṇavatthūnīti evamādīnaṃ anekesaṃ paññāpabhedānaṃ vasena ñāṇacāraṃ dasseti. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena caraṇasampattiṃ, paññāgahaṇena vijjāsampattiṃ. Karuṇāgahaṇena attādhipatitā, paññāgahaṇena dhammādhipatitā. Karuṇāgahaṇena lokanāthabhāvo, paññāgahaṇena attanāthabhāvo. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena pubbakāribhāvo, paññāgahaṇena kataññutā. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena aparantapatā, paññāgahaṇena anattantapatā. Karuṇāgahaṇena vā buddhakaradhammasiddhi, paññāgahaṇena buddhabhāvasiddhi. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena paresaṃ tāraṇaṃ, paññāgahaṇena sayaṃtaraṇaṃ. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena sabbasattesu anuggahacittatā, paññāgahaṇena sabbadhammesu virattacittatā dassitā hoti.

Here, by the taking up of compassion, the Blessed One's accomplishment in all worldly qualities is shown by the illumination of the uncommon qualities attained in the exalted states belonging to the mundane; by the taking up of wisdom, his accomplishment in all supramundane qualities is shown by the illumination of the path-knowledge, which is the basis for the knowledge of omniscience. For the meaning established by taking up both is elaborated by such phrases as 'the teacher of the world with its devas and humans.' By the taking up of compassion, his approach is shown to be without defilement; by the taking up of wisdom, his withdrawal. Likewise, by the taking up of compassion, the Blessed One’s conduct in conformity with worldly convention is shown, since compassion has worldly parlance as its sphere; by the taking up of wisdom, his not overstepping convention is shown. For it is by not understanding the intrinsic nature of things that one oversteps convention and misapprehends a 'being,' and so on. Further, by the taking up of compassion, his abiding in the attainment of great compassion is shown; by the taking up of wisdom are shown the unimpeded knowledge of the three times, the knowledge of the four truths, the knowledge of the four analytical knowledges, and the knowledge of the four grounds of self-confidence. Since the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion is included by the taking up of compassion, by the taking up of wisdom his range of knowledge is shown by way of the many divisions of wisdom, such as the remaining uncommon knowledges: the six direct knowledges, the unshaken knowledges in the eight assemblies, the ten powers, the fourteen Buddha-knowledges, the sixteen modes of knowledge-conduct, the eighteen distinct qualities of a Buddha, the forty-four bases of knowledge, and the seventy-seven bases of knowledge. Similarly, by the taking up of compassion, the accomplishment in conduct is shown; by the taking up of wisdom, the accomplishment in knowledge. By the taking up of compassion, sovereignty over oneself; by the taking up of wisdom, sovereignty of the Dhamma. By the taking up of compassion, his state as a protector for the world; by the taking up of wisdom, his state as his own protector. Likewise, by the taking up of compassion, his being one who acts first; by the taking up of wisdom, his gratitude. By the taking up of compassion, his devotion to others; by the taking up of wisdom, his lack of devotion to self. By the taking up of compassion, the accomplishment of the qualities that make a Buddha; by the taking up of wisdom, the accomplishment of the state of a Buddha. Similarly, by the taking up of compassion, the ferrying across of others; by the taking up of wisdom, his own ferrying across. Thus, by the taking up of compassion, a mind of helpfulness towards all beings is shown; by the taking up of wisdom, a mind of dispassion towards all phenomena is shown.

Sabbesañca buddhaguṇānaṃ karuṇā ādi tannidānabhāvato, paññā pariyosānaṃ tato uttarikaraṇīyābhāvato. Iti ādipariyosānadassanena [M 1.0012] sabbe buddhaguṇā dassitā honti. Tathā karuṇāgahaṇena sīlakkhandhapubbaṅgamo samādhikkhandho dassito hoti. Karuṇānidānañhi sīlaṃ tato pāṇātipātādiviratippavattito, sā ca jhānattayasampayoginīti. Paññāvacanena paññākkhandho. Sīlañca sabbesaṃ buddhaguṇānaṃ ādi, samādhi majjhe, paññā pariyosānanti evampi ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇā sabbe buddhaguṇā dassitā honti nayato dassitattā. Eso eva hi niravasesato buddhaguṇānaṃ dassanupāyo, yadidaṃ nayaggahaṇaṃ, aññathā ko nāma samattho bhagavato guṇe anupadaṃ niravasesato dassetuṃ? Tenevāha –

Among all the qualities of a Buddha, compassion is the beginning because it is their cause, and wisdom is the culmination because there is nothing further to be done beyond it. Thus, by showing the beginning and the culmination, all the qualities of a Buddha are shown. Similarly, by the taking up of compassion, the aggregate of concentration, which is preceded by the aggregate of virtue, is shown. For virtue has compassion as its cause, since it proceeds from it as abstinence from the destruction of life, etc.; and that compassion is associated with the three jhānas. By the word 'wisdom,' the aggregate of wisdom is shown. And since virtue is the beginning of all a Buddha's qualities, concentration the middle, and wisdom the culmination, in this way too all the qualities of a Buddha, good in the beginning, the middle, and the end, are shown, because they are shown by way of a method. This indeed is the means for showing the Buddha's qualities without remainder, that is, the grasping of a method. Otherwise, who indeed would be able to show the Blessed One's qualities without remainder, one by one? Therefore he said:

“Buddhopi buddhassa bhaṇeyya vaṇṇaṃ,

Kappampi ce aññamabhāsamāno;

Khīyetha [V 1.0012] kappo ciradīghamantare,

Vaṇṇo na khīyetha tathāgatassā”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.304; 3.141; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 2.425; udā. aṭṭha. 53; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 4.4; apa. aṭṭha. 2.7.parappasādakattheraapadānavaṇṇanā);

A Buddha himself might speak the praise of a Buddha, for an entire eon, speaking of nothing else; that eon would be spent in that long stretch of time, but the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.

Teneva ca āyasmatā sāriputtattherenapi buddhaguṇaparicchedanaṃ pati anuyuttena “no hetaṃ, bhante”ti paṭikkhipitvā “apica me, bhante, dhammanvayo vidito”ti vuttaṃ.

And for this very reason, the Venerable Sāriputta, when questioned about defining the extent of the Buddha's qualities, rejected this, saying, 'No, venerable sir,' and stated, 'However, venerable sir, the course of the Dhamma is known to me.'

2. Evaṃ saṅkhepena sakalasabbaññuguṇehi bhagavantaṃ abhitthavitvā idāni saddhammaṃ thometuṃ “buddhopī”tiādimāha. Tattha buddhoti kattuniddeso. Buddhabhāvanti kammaniddeso. Bhāvetvā sacchikatvāti ca pubbakālakiriyāniddeso. Yanti aniyamato kammaniddeso. Upagatoti aparakālakiriyāniddeso. Vandeti kiriyāniddeso. Tanti niyamanaṃ. Dhammanti vandanakiriyāya kammaniddeso. Gatamalaṃ anuttaranti ca tabbisesanaṃ.

2. Having thus briefly extolled the Blessed One with all the qualities of an omniscient one, he now, in order to praise the good Dhamma, says what begins with “A Buddha too…” Herein, 'Buddha' is a designation of the agent. 'The state of a Buddha' is a designation of the object. 'Having developed and having realized' is a designation of a prior action. 'Which' is a designation of the object indefinitely. 'Has attained' is a designation of a subsequent action. 'I revere' is a designation of the action. 'That' is a specification. 'Dhamma' is a designation of the object of the action of revering. 'Stainless' and 'unsurpassed' are its qualifiers.

Tattha buddhasaddassa tāva “bujjhitā saccānīti buddho, bodhetā pajāyāti buddho”tiādinā (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddeso 97; paṭi. ma. 1.162) niddesanayena attho veditabbo. Atha vā savāsanāya aññāṇaniddāya accantavigamato, buddhiyā vā vikasitabhāvato buddhavāti buddho jāgaraṇavikasanatthavasena. Atha vā kassacipi ñeyyadhammassa anavabuddhassa abhāvena ñeyyavisesassa kammabhāvena aggahaṇato kammavacanicchāya abhāvena avagamanatthavaseneva [M 1.0013] kattuniddeso labbhatīti buddhavāti buddho yathā “dikkhito na dadātī”ti. Atthato pana pāramitāparibhāvito sayambhuñāṇena saha vāsanāya vihataviddhaṃsitaniravasesakileso mahākaruṇāsabbaññutaññāṇādiaparimeyyaguṇagaṇādhāro khandhasantāno buddho. Yathāha –

Here, first, the meaning of the word 'Buddha' should be understood according to the method of the Niddesa, in such passages as: 'He is a Buddha because he has understood the truths; he is a Buddha because he awakens the populace.' Or else, he is a Buddha because of the final departure of the sleep of ignorance together with its latent dispositions, or because of the blossoming of his wisdom; thus 'Buddha' is used in the sense of awakening and blossoming. Or else, because there is no knowable thing whatsoever that he has not understood, and because he does not grasp any particular knowable thing as an object, and because there is no desire for a passive construction, the designation of the agent is obtained simply in the sense of understanding. Thus he is a 'Buddha' (one who has understood), just as in the phrase 'a consecrated person does not give.' But in terms of meaning, a 'Buddha' is a continuity of aggregates that has been brought to maturity by the perfections, who possesses self-originating knowledge, who has, along with their latent dispositions, struck down, demolished, and eradicated without remainder all defilements, and who is a receptacle for a collection of immeasurable qualities such as great compassion, the knowledge of omniscience, and so on. As it is said:

“Buddhoti yo so bhagavā sayambhū anācariyako pubbe ananussutesu dhammesu sāmaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhi, tattha ca sabbaññutaṃ patto balesu ca vasībhāva”nti (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddeso 97; paṭi. ma. 1.161).

That Blessed One is a 'Buddha' who, being self-become, without a teacher, has by himself fully awakened to the truths concerning things unheard before, and has therein attained omniscience and mastery in regard to the powers.

Api-saddo sambhāvane. Tena “evaṃ guṇavisesayutto sopi nāma bhagavā”ti vakkhamānaguṇadhamme [V 1.0013] sambhāvanaṃ dīpeti. Buddhabhāvanti sammāsambodhiṃ. Bhāvetvāti uppādetvā vaḍḍhetvā ca. Sacchikatvāti paccakkhaṃ katvā. Upagatoti patto, adhigatoti attho. Etassa buddhabhāvanti etena sambandho. Gatamalanti vigatamalaṃ, niddosanti attho. Vandeti paṇamāmi, thomemi vā. Anuttaranti uttararahitaṃ, lokuttaranti attho. Dhammanti yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjamāne apāyato ca saṃsārato ca apatamāne katvā dhāretīti dhammo. Ayañhettha saṅkhepattho – evaṃ vividhaguṇagaṇasamannāgato buddhopi bhagavā yaṃ ariyamaggasaṅkhātaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā, phalanibbānaṃ pana sacchikatvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ adhigato, tamevaṃ buddhānampi buddhabhāvahetubhūtaṃ sabbadosamalarahitaṃ attano uttaritarābhāvena anuttaraṃ paṭivedhasaddhammaṃ namāmīti. Pariyattisaddhammassapi tappakāsanattā idha saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo.

The word 'api' is in the sense of affirmation. Thereby it indicates the affirmation of the qualities of the Dhamma to be spoken of, as if to say: 'That Blessed One, endowed with such special qualities, too…' 'The state of a Buddha' means perfect self-enlightenment. 'Having developed' means having produced and augmented it. 'Having realized' means having made it directly present. 'Has attained' means has reached, has acquired. This is connected with 'the state of a Buddha.' 'Stainless' means with stains departed; the meaning is 'faultless.' 'I revere' means I pay homage, or I praise. 'Unsurpassed' means without a superior; the meaning is 'supramundane.' It is 'Dhamma' because it holds those who practice it as instructed, preventing them from falling into the planes of misery and into saṃsāra. Herein, this is the concise meaning: That Blessed One, a Buddha endowed with such a variety of qualities, having developed the Dhamma designated as the noble path and having realized the fruit, Nibbāna, attained unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment; I pay homage to that very good Dhamma of penetration, which is the cause of the state of a Buddha even for Buddhas, which is free from all faults and stains, and which is unsurpassed because there is nothing superior to it. The good Dhamma of the scriptures should be seen as included here too, because it makes that known.

Atha vā “abhidhammanayasamuddaṃ adhigañchi, tīṇi piṭakāni sammasī”ti ca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttattā pariyattidhammassapi sacchikiriyāsammasanapariyāyo labbhatīti sopi idha vutto evāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā “yaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā sacchikatvā”ti ca vuttattā buddhakaradhammabhūtāhi pāramitāhi saha pubbabhāge adhisīlasikkhādayopi idha dhammasaddena saṅgahitāti veditabbā. Tāpi hi vigatappaṭipakkhatāya gatamalā, anaññasādhāraṇatāya anuttarā cāti. Tathā hi sattānaṃ sakalavaṭṭadukkhanissaraṇāya katamahābhinīhāro mahākaruṇādhivāsanapesalajjhāsayo [M 1.0014] paññāvisesapariyodātanimmalānaṃ dānadamasaññamādīnaṃ uttamadhammānaṃ satasahassādhikāni kappānaṃ cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni sakkaccaṃ nirantaraṃ niravasesānaṃ bhāvanāpaccakkhakaraṇehi kammādīsu adhigatavasībhāvo acchariyācinteyyamahānubhāvo adhisīlaadhicittānaṃ paramukkaṃsapāramippatto bhagavā paccayākāre catuvīsatikoṭisatasahassamukhena mahāvajirañāṇaṃ pesetvā anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ abhisambuddhoti.

Or, since it is said in the commentary, 'He fathomed the ocean of the Abhidhamma method and comprehended the three Piṭakas,' it should be seen that the aspect of realization and comprehension of the Dhamma of the scriptures is also stated here. Likewise, since it is said, 'having developed and realized which Dhamma,' it should be understood that the trainings in higher virtue and so on in the preliminary stage, together with the perfections that are the qualities that make a Buddha, are also included here by the word 'Dhamma.' For they are stainless because they are unopposed, and they are unsurpassed because they are not common to others. Thus, he who had made the great aspiration for the liberation of all beings from all the suffering of the round, whose disposition was amiable through being imbued with great compassion; who for four incalculable eons and a hundred thousand more, by developing and directly experiencing them respectfully, continuously, and without remainder, attained mastery over actions and so on in regard to the supreme qualities such as giving, taming, and restraint, which are spotless, being purified by special wisdom; the Blessed One, of wonderful, inconceivable great power, who had reached the ultimate, supreme perfection of higher virtue and the higher mind, having sent forth the great diamond knowledge through twenty-four hundred thousand crore openings in the structure of conditionality, fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect self-enlightenment.

Ettha ca “bhāvetvā”ti etena vijjāsampadāya dhammaṃ thometi, “sacchikatvā”ti etena vimuttisampadāya. Tathā paṭhamena jhānasampadāya, dutiyena vimokkhasampadāya. Paṭhamena vā samādhisampadāya, dutiyena samāpattisampadāya. Atha vā paṭhamena khayañāṇabhāvena, dutiyena anuppādañāṇabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā vijjūpamatāya, dutiyena vajirūpamatāya. Purimena vā virāgasampattiyā, dutiyena nirodhasampattiyā. Tathā paṭhamena niyyānabhāvena, dutiyena nissaraṇabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā hetubhāvena, dutiyena asaṅkhatabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā dassanabhāvena, dutiyena vivekabhāvena. Paṭhamena vā adhipatibhāvena, dutiyena amatabhāvena dhammaṃ thometi. Atha vā “yaṃ dhammaṃ bhāvetvā buddhabhāvaṃ upagato”ti etena svākkhātatāya dhammaṃ thometi, “sacchikatvā”ti [V 1.0014] etena sandiṭṭhikatāya. Tathā purimena akālikatāya, pacchimena ehipassikatāya. Purimena vā opaneyyikatāya, pacchimena paccattaṃ veditabbatāya dhammaṃ thometi. “Gatamala”nti iminā saṃkilesābhāvadīpanena dhammassa parisuddhataṃ dasseti, “anuttara”nti etena aññassa visiṭṭhassa abhāvadīpanena vipulaparipuṇṇataṃ. Paṭhamena vā pahānasampadaṃ dhammassa dasseti, dutiyena pabhavasampadaṃ. Bhāvetabbatāya vā dhammassa gatamalabhāvo yojetabbo. Bhāvanāguṇena hi so dosānaṃ samugghātako hotīti. Sacchikātabbabhāvena anuttarabhāvo yojetabbo. Sacchikiriyānibbattito hi taduttarikaraṇīyābhāvato anaññasādhāraṇatāya anuttaroti. Tathā “bhāvetvā”ti etena saha pubbabhāgasīlādīhi sekkhā sīlasamādhipaññākkhandhā dassitā honti. “Sacchikatvā”ti etena saha asaṅkhatāya dhātuyā asekkhā sīlasamādhipaññākkhandhā dassitā hontīti.

Here, by 'having developed' he praises the Dhamma for its accomplishment in knowledge, and by 'having realized,' for its accomplishment in liberation. Similarly, by the first, for its accomplishment in jhāna; by the second, for its accomplishment in release. Or by the first, for its accomplishment in concentration; by the second, for its accomplishment in attainment. Alternatively, by the first, for its nature as the knowledge of destruction; by the second, for its nature as the knowledge of non-arising. Or by the first, for its likeness to lightning; by the second, for its likeness to a diamond. By the former, for the attainment of dispassion; by the latter, for the attainment of cessation. Similarly, by the first, for its nature as deliverance; by the second, for its nature as escape. Or by the first, for its nature as a cause; by the second, for its nature as the unconditioned. Or by the first, for its nature as vision; by the second, for its nature as seclusion. Or by the first, for its nature as sovereignty; by the second, for its nature as the deathless, he praises the Dhamma. Alternatively, by 'having developed the Dhamma and attained Buddhahood,' he praises the Dhamma for being well-proclaimed; by 'having realized,' for being directly visible. Similarly, by the former, for being timeless; by the latter, for being 'come and see.' Or by the former, for being leading onward; by the latter, for being 'to be known personally,' he praises the Dhamma. With 'stainless,' he shows the purity of the Dhamma by indicating the absence of defilements; and with 'unsurpassed,' its vastness and completeness by indicating the absence of anything superior. By the first, he shows the Dhamma's accomplishment in abandoning; by the second, its accomplishment in eminence. The state of being stainless should be connected with the Dhamma's quality of being developed, for through the virtue of development, it becomes the uprooter of faults. The state of being unsurpassed should be connected with its quality of being realized, for having been brought to fulfillment by realization, it is unsurpassed because there is nothing further to be done and because it is not shared by others. Similarly, by 'having developed,' together with the preliminary virtue and so on, the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the trainee are shown. By 'having realized,' together with the unconditioned element, the aggregates of virtue, concentration, and wisdom of the adept are shown.

3. Evaṃ [M 1.0015] saṅkhepeneva sabbadhammaguṇehi saddhammaṃ abhitthavitvā idāni ariyasaṅghaṃ thometuṃ “sugatassā”tiādimāha. Tattha sugatassāti sambandhaniddeso. “Tassa puttāna”nti etena sambandho. Orasānanti puttavisesanaṃ. Mārasenamathanānanti orasaputtabhāve kāraṇaniddeso tena kilesappahānameva bhagavato orasaputtabhāve kāraṇaṃ anujānātīti dasseti. Aṭṭhannanti gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso. Tena ca satipi tesaṃ sattavisesabhāvena anekasatasahassabhāve imaṃ gaṇanaparicchedaṃ nātivattantīti dasseti maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhabhāvānativattanato. Samūhanti samudāyaniddeso. Ariyasaṅghanti guṇavisiṭṭhasaṃhatabhāvaniddeso. Tena asatipi ariyapuggalānaṃ kāyasāmaggiyaṃ ariyasaṅghabhāvaṃ dasseti diṭṭhisīlasāmaññena saṃhatabhāvato.

3. Having thus briefly praised the good Dhamma with all its qualities, now, in order to praise the Noble Sangha, he says, 'of the Sugata,' and so on. Herein, 'of the Sugata' is an indication of relationship. The relationship is with 'his sons.' 'True-born' is a qualifier of 'sons.' 'Crushers of Māra’s army' is an indication of the reason for being true-born sons; thus it shows that the abandoning of defilements is the very reason for being the Blessed One’s true-born sons, which he sanctions. 'Eight' is an indication of numerical limitation. And by this, it shows that even though they, by their individual distinctions, are many hundreds of thousands, they do not exceed this numerical limitation, because they do not go beyond the states of those on the path and those who have attained the fruit. 'Group' is an indication of a collection. 'Noble Sangha' is an indication of a community distinguished by qualities. By this, it shows that even when there is no physical gathering of the noble individuals, the state of a Noble Sangha exists because of their being united by common view and virtue.

Tattha urasi bhavā jātā saṃbaddhā ca orasā. Yathā hi sattānaṃ orasaputtā attajatāya pitu santakassa dāyajjassa visesena bhāgino honti, evametepi ariyapuggalā sammāsambuddhassa savanante ariyāya jātiyā jātatāya bhagavato santakassa vimuttisukhassa ariyadhammaratanassa ekantena bhāginoti orasā viya orasā. Atha vā bhagavato dhammadesanānubhāvena ariyabhūmiṃ okkamamānā okkantā ca ariyasāvakā bhagavato ure vāyāmajanitābhijātitāya nippariyāyena orasaputtāti vattabbataṃ arahanti. Sāvakehi pavattiyamānāpi hi dhammadesanā “bhagavato dhammadesanā”icceva vuccati taṃmūlakattā lakkhaṇādivisesābhāvato ca.

Herein, those who arise in the breast, are born, and are connected are 'true-born.' Just as beings’ own true-born sons, being born of oneself, are special heirs to their father’s property, his inheritance; so too, these noble individuals, having been born of the noble birth upon hearing the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, are the sole heirs to the Blessed One’s property: the bliss of liberation and the jewel of the noble Dhamma. Thus, like true-born sons, they are true-born. Or alternatively, noble disciples who are entering and have entered the noble plane through the power of the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma, being born from the Blessed One’s breast through the noble birth generated by striving, deserve to be called 'true-born sons' without qualification. For even a teaching of the Dhamma set in motion by disciples is called 'the Blessed One’s teaching of the Dhamma' because he is its source and because it is without any difference in characteristics.

Yadipi ariyasāvakānaṃ ariyamaggādhigamasamaye bhagavato viya tadantarāyakaraṇatthaṃ devaputtamāro[V 1.0015], māravāhinī vā na ekantena apasādeti, tehi pana apasādetabbatāya kāraṇe vimathite tepi vimathitā eva nāma hontīti āha – “mārasenamathanāna”nti. Imasmiṃ panatthe “māramārasenamathanāna”nti vattabbe “mārasenamathanāna”nti ekadesasarūpekaseso katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Atha vā khandhābhisaṅkhāramārānaṃ viya devaputtamārassapi guṇamāraṇe sahāyabhāvūpagamanato kilesabalakāyo “senā”ti vuccati. Yathāha – “kāmā te paṭhamā senā”tiādi [M 1.0016] (su. ni. 438; mahāni. 28, 68, 149). Sā ca tehi diyaḍḍhasahassabhedā, anantabhedā vā kilesavāhinī satidhammavicayavīriyasamathādiguṇappaharaṇehi odhiso vimathitā vihatā viddhastā cāti mārasenamathanā, ariyasāvakā. Etena tesaṃ bhagavato anujātaputtataṃ dasseti.

Although at the time when noble disciples attain the noble path, the devaputta Māra or Māra’s army does not entirely assail them to create an obstacle as they did for the Blessed One, yet when the causes that can be assailed by them are crushed, they too are indeed crushed. Hence he says: 'of the crushers of Māra’s army.' In this sense, it should be understood that although 'of the crushers of Māra and Māra’s army' should have been said, a partial ellipsis of a similar form has been made, resulting in 'of the crushers of Māra’s army.' Alternatively, just as there are the Māras of the aggregates and formations, so the host of defilements is called an 'army' because the devaputta Māra also becomes an ally in killing good qualities. As it is said: 'Sensual pleasures are your first army,' etc. (Snp 436). And that army of defilements, with its one and a half thousand or infinite divisions, is completely crushed, struck down, and scattered by them with the weapons of such good qualities as mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, energy, and serenity. Thus the noble disciples are crushers of Māra’s army. By this he shows their status as the Blessed One’s true-born sons.

Ārakattā kilesehi, anaye na iriyanato, aye ca iriyanato ariyā niruttinayena. Atha vā sadevakena lokena saraṇanti araṇīyato upagantabbato, upagatānañca tadatthasiddhito ariyā, ariyānaṃ saṅghoti ariyasaṅgho, ariyo ca so saṅgho cāti vā ariyasaṅgho, taṃ ariyasaṅghaṃ. Bhagavato aparabhāge buddhadhammaratanānampi samadhigamo saṅgharatanādhīnoti assa ariyasaṅghassa bahūpakārataṃ dassetuṃ idheva “sirasā vande”ti vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

According to the etymological method, they are 'noble' because they are far from defilements, because they do not fare in what is not the right way, and because they fare in the right way. Or, they are 'noble' because they are to be gone to for refuge by the world with its gods, that is, they are to be approached, and because those who have approached them achieve their aim. The Sangha of the noble ones is the Noble Sangha. Or, that which is noble and is a Sangha is the Noble Sangha. To that Noble Sangha. It should be understood that 'I revere with my head' is said right here in order to show the great helpfulness of this Noble Sangha, since in the period after the Blessed One, the attainment even of the Buddha and Dhamma jewels is dependent on the Sangha jewel.

Ettha ca “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti etena ariyasaṅghassa pabhavasampadaṃ dasseti, “mārasenamathanāna”nti etena pahānasampadaṃ sakalasaṃkilesappahānadīpanato. “Aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti etena ñāṇasampadaṃ maggaṭṭhaphalaṭṭhabhāvadīpanato. “Ariyasaṅgha”nti etena pabhavasampadaṃ dasseti sabbasaṅghānaṃ aggabhāvadīpanato. Atha vā “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti ariyasaṅghassa visuddhanissayabhāvadīpanaṃ, “mārasenamathanāna”nti sammāujuñāyasāmīcippaṭipannabhāvadīpanaṃ, “aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti āhuneyyādibhāvadīpanaṃ, “ariyasaṅgha”nti anuttarapuññakkhettabhāvadīpanaṃ. Tathā “sugatassa orasānaṃ puttāna”nti etena ariyasaṅghassa lokuttarasaraṇagamanasabbhāvaṃ dīpeti. Lokuttarasaraṇagamanena hi te bhagavato orasaputtā jātā. “Mārasenamathanāna”nti etena abhinīhārasampadāsiddhaṃ pubbabhāge sammāpaṭipattiṃ dasseti. Katābhinīhārā hi sammāpaṭipannā māraṃ māraparisaṃ vā abhivijinanti. “Aṭṭhannampi samūha”nti etena viddhastavipakkhe sekkhāsekkhadhamme dasseti puggalādhiṭṭhānena maggaphaladhammānaṃ pakāsitattā. “Ariyasaṅgha”nti aggadakkhiṇeyyabhāvaṃ dasseti. Saraṇagamanañca sāvakānaṃ sabbaguṇānaṃ ādi, sapubbabhāgappaṭipadā sekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo majjhe, asekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo [V 1.0016] pariyosānanti ādimajjhapariyosānakalyāṇā saṅkhepato sabbe ariyasaṅghaguṇā pakāsitā honti.

Here, by 'the true-born sons of the Sugata' he shows the Noble Sangha’s accomplishment in eminence; by 'the crushers of Māra’s army,' its accomplishment in abandoning, by indicating the abandoning of all defilements; by 'the group of eight,' its accomplishment in knowledge, by indicating the state of being on the path and at the fruit; by 'Noble Sangha,' its accomplishment in eminence, by indicating its state as the foremost of all Sanghas. Alternatively, 'the true-born sons of the Sugata' indicates the Noble Sangha’s state of pure dependence; 'the crushers of Māra’s army' indicates their state of having practiced rightly, uprightly, properly, and correctly; 'the group of eight' indicates their state of being worthy of gifts, etc.; 'Noble Sangha' indicates their state as an unsurpassed field of merit. Similarly, 'the true-born sons of the Sugata' illuminates the Noble Sangha’s true state of having gone for supramundane refuge. For it is by going for supramundane refuge that they are born as the Blessed One’s true-born sons. 'The crushers of Māra’s army' shows the right practice in the preliminary stage, accomplished by the fulfillment of their aspiration. For those who have made the aspiration and practice rightly conquer Māra and his retinue. 'The group of eight' shows the qualities of the trainee and the adept, whose opponents have been vanquished, since the qualities of the path and fruit are declared with the individual as the basis. 'Noble Sangha' shows their state as the foremost of those worthy of offerings. The going for refuge is the beginning of all the disciple’s virtues; the practice along with its preliminary part—the aggregates of virtue, etc., of the trainee—is the middle; the aggregates of virtue, etc., of the adept are the end. Thus, in brief, all the qualities of the Noble Sangha are declared to be good in the beginning, the middle, and the end.

4. Evaṃ [M 1.0017] gāthāttayena saṅkhepato sakalaguṇasaṃkittanamukhena ratanattayassa paṇāmaṃ katvā idāni taṃnipaccakāraṃ yathādhippete payojane pariṇāmento “iti me”tiādimāha. Tattha ratijananaṭṭhena ratanaṃ, buddhadhammasaṅghā. Tesañhi “itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā yathābhūtaguṇe āvajjentassa amatādhigamahetubhūtaṃ anappakaṃ pītipāmojjaṃ uppajjati. Yathāha –

4. Thus, having paid homage to the Triple Gem in three stanzas by way of briefly extolling all their qualities, now, dedicating that reverence to its intended purpose, he says, 'Thus for me,' etc. Here, 'gem' means that which generates delight; these are the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. For when one adverts to their real qualities with the words, 'Thus is the Blessed One,' etc., abundant joy and gladness arise, which become a cause for the attainment of the deathless. As it is said:

“Yasmiṃ, mahānāma, samaye ariyasāvako tathāgataṃ anussarati, nevassa tasmiṃ samaye rāgapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, na dosa…pe… na mohapariyuṭṭhitaṃ cittaṃ hoti, ujugatamevassa tasmiṃ samaye cittaṃ hoti tathāgataṃ ārabbha. Ujugatacitto kho pana, mahānāma, ariyasāvako labhati atthavedaṃ, labhati dhammavedaṃ, labhati dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ pāmojjaṃ, pamuditassa pīti jāyatī”tiādi (a. ni. 6.10; 11.11).

“Mahānāma, at a time when a noble disciple is recollecting the Tathāgata, his mind is not obsessed by lust, nor by hatred, nor by delusion. At that time his mind is straight, with the Tathāgata as its object. With a straight mind, Mahānāma, a noble disciple gains inspiration in the meaning, gains inspiration in the Dhamma, and gains joy connected with the Dhamma. For one who is joyful, rapture arises,” and so on (AN 6.10; 11.11).

Cittīkatādibhāvo vā ratanaṭṭho. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Or, the quality of being esteemed, and so on, is the meaning of ‘jewel.’ For this has been said:

“Cittīkataṃ mahagghañca, atulaṃ dullabhadassanaṃ;

Anomasattaparibhogaṃ, ratanaṃ tena vuccatī”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.33; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 3.5.223; khu. pā. aṭṭha. 6.3; su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.226);

“Prized and of great value, incomparable and rare to see, fit for the use of superior beings—for that reason it is called a jewel” (DN-a 2.33; SN-a 3.223; Khp-a 6.3; Snp-a 1.226).

Cittīkatabhāvādayo ca anaññasādhāraṇā buddhādīsu eva labbhantīti.

And these qualities, such as being esteemed, are not common to others but are found only in the Buddha and the other jewels.

Vandanāva vandanāmayaṃ yathā “dānamayaṃ, sīlamaya”nti (dī. ni. 3.305; itivu. 60). Vandanā cettha kāyavācācittehi tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇaninnatā, thomanā vā. Pujjabhāvaphalanibbattanato puññaṃ, attano santānaṃ punātīti vā. Suvihatantarāyoti suṭṭhu vihatantarāyo. Etena attano pasādasampattiyā, ratanattayassa ca khettabhāvasampattiyā taṃ puññaṃ atthappakāsanassa upaghātakaupaddavānaṃ vihanane samatthanti dasseti. Hutvāti pubbakālakiriyā. Tassa “atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti etena sambandho. Tassāti yaṃ ratanattayavandanāmayaṃ puññaṃ, tassa. Ānubhāvenāti balena.

The term `vandanāmayaṃ` means consisting of veneration, just as in `dānamayaṃ`, ‘consisting of giving,’ and `sīlamayaṃ`, ‘consisting of virtue’ (DN 3.305; It 60). Herein, veneration is the inclination of body, speech, and mind towards the qualities of the Three Jewels, or it is praise. It is merit (`puñña`) because it generates the fruit of being worthy of veneration, or because it purifies (`punāti`) one’s own mental continuum. `Suvihatantarāyo` means one whose obstacles are thoroughly removed. By this it is shown that this merit, through the attainment of one’s own confidence and through the attainment of the Three Jewels’ status as a field of merit, is capable of removing the detrimental disturbances to the explanation of the meaning. `Hutvā` is a gerund expressing a prior action. It is connected with the clause, “I will explain the meaning.” `Tassa` (of that) refers to that merit consisting of veneration for the Three Jewels. `Ānubhāvena` (by the power) means by the strength.

5. Evaṃ [V 1.0017][M 1.0018] ratanattayassa nipaccakārakaraṇe payojanaṃ dassetvā idāni yassā dhammadesanāya atthaṃ saṃvaṇṇetukāmo, tassā tāva guṇābhitthavanavasena upaññāpanatthaṃ “ekakadukādipaṭimaṇḍitassā”tiādimāha, ekakādīni aṅgāni uparūpari vaḍḍhetvā desitehi suttantehi paṭimaṇḍitassa visiṭṭhassāti attho. Etena “aṅguttaro”ti ayaṃ imassa āgamassa atthānugatā samaññāti dasseti. Nanu ca ekakādivasena desitāni suttāniyeva āgamo. Kassa pana ekakadukādīhi paṭimaṇḍitabhāvoti? Saccametaṃ paramatthato, suttāni pana upādāya paññatto āgamo. Yatheva hi atthabyañjanasamudāye suttanti vohāro, evaṃ suttasamudāye āgamoti vohāro. Ekakādīhi aṅgehi uparūpari uttaro adhikoti aṅguttaro, āgamissanti ettha, etena, etasmā vā attatthaparatthādayoti āgamo, ādikalyāṇādiguṇasampattiyā uttamaṭṭhena taṃtaṃabhipatthitasamiddhihetutāya paṇḍitehi varitabbato varo, āgamo ca so varo ca seṭṭhaṭṭhenāti āgamavaro, āgamasammatehi vā varoti āgamavaro. Aṅguttaro ca so āgamavaro cāti aṅguttarāgamavaro, tassa.

5. Having thus shown the purpose of paying homage to the Three Jewels, now, wishing to comment on the meaning of that Dhamma teaching, in order to introduce it by way of praising its qualities, he says: “of that which is adorned with the ones, twos, etc.” The meaning is: of that which is distinguished by being adorned with suttas taught with factors that increase one by one. By this he shows that “Aṅguttara” is a designation for this collection that accords with its meaning. But is it not the case that the suttas themselves, taught by way of ones, twos, etc., are the collection? To whom, then, does the quality of being adorned with ones, twos, etc. belong? This is true in an ultimate sense, but the collection is a designation made in dependence on the suttas. For just as the term ‘sutta’ is used for a collection of meaning and phrasing, so the term ‘āgama’ is used for a collection of suttas. It is ‘further by a factor’ (aṅga-uttara) because it is successively higher (uttara) or more (adhika) by factors of one and so on. It is an ‘āgama’ (collection) because one’s own welfare, the welfare of others, etc., come (āgamissanti) to it, by it, or from it. It is ‘excellent’ (vara) because it is to be chosen (varitabbato) by the wise, being supreme in the sense that it is a cause for the fulfillment of various aspirations on account of its possession of qualities such as being good in the beginning. It is an excellent collection (āgamavara) because it is a collection (āgama) and it is excellent (vara) in the sense of being the best; or it is excellent (vara) among the esteemed collections (āgama). It is the excellent collection of discourses in further-factored arrangement (Aṅguttarāgamavara) because it is the Aṅguttara and it is the Āgamavara; the passage refers to that.

Puṅgavā vuccanti usabhā, asantasanaparissayasahanassa paripālanādiguṇehi taṃsadisatāya dhammakathikā eva puṅgavāti dhammakathikapuṅgavā, tesaṃ. Hetūpamādippaṭimaṇḍitanānāvidhadesanānayavicittatāya vicittapaṭibhānajananassa. Sumaṅgalavilāsinīādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.ganthārambhakathā; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.ganthārambhakathā; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.ganthārambhakathā) pana “buddhānubuddhasaṃvaṇṇitassā”ti vuttaṃ. Buddhānañhi saccappaṭivedhaṃ anugamma paṭividdhasaccā aggasāvakādayo ariyā buddhānubuddhā. Ayampi āgamo tehi atthasaṃvaṇṇanāvasena guṇasaṃvaṇṇanāvasena ca saṃvaṇṇito eva. Atha vā buddhā ca anubuddhā ca buddhānubuddhāti yojetabbaṃ. Sammāsambuddheneva hi tiṇṇaṃ piṭakānaṃ atthavaṇṇanākkamo bhāsito, yā “pakiṇṇakadesanā”ti vuccati. Tato saṅgāyanādivaseneva sāvakehīti ācariyā vadanti. Idha pana “dhammakathikapuṅgavānaṃ vicittapaṭibhānajananassa”icceva thomanā katā. Saṃvaṇṇanāsu cāyaṃ ācariyassa pakati, yā taṃtaṃsaṃvaṇṇanāsu ādito tassa tassa saṃvaṇṇetabbassa dhammassa visesaguṇakittanena thomanā. Tathā hi sumaṅgalavilāsinīpapañcasūdanīsāratthappakāsanīsu aṭṭhasālinīādīsu [M 1.0019] ca yathākkamaṃ “saddhāvahaguṇassa, paravādamathanassa, ñāṇappabhedajananassa, tassa gambhīrañāṇehi ogāḷhassa abhiṇhaso nānānayavicittassā”tiādinā thomanā katā.

`Puṅgavā` means bulls. Because of their similarity to them through such qualities as enduring dangers without trembling and giving protection, Dhamma speakers are called ‘bulls’; hence the term `dhammakathikapuṅgavā` (bulls among Dhamma speakers). The phrase refers to them. The next phrase is: ‘of that which generates brilliant readiness of speech.’ This is because of the variety of its manifold methods of teaching adorned with reasons, similes, and so on. In the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī and other commentaries, however, it is said: “praised by the Buddhas and the anubuddhas.” For the noble ones, such as the chief disciples, who have penetrated the truth in conformity with the Buddhas’ penetration of the truth, are `anubuddhas` (those who have understood after). This collection, too, has been praised by them by way of explaining its meaning and praising its qualities. Alternatively, `buddhānubuddhā` should be construed as ‘the Buddhas and the anubuddhas.’ For the method of commenting on the meaning of the three Piṭakas was spoken by the Perfectly Enlightened One himself; this is what is called the ‘scattered teaching.’ The teachers say that afterwards this was done by the disciples by way of the councils and so on.
