Here, however, the praise is given simply as: “of that which generates brilliant readiness of speech in the bulls among Dhamma speakers.” This is the author’s custom in the commentaries, that is, the praise at the beginning of each commentary by proclaiming the special qualities of the particular Dhamma to be commented upon. Thus, in the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī, Papañcasūdanī, Sāratthappakāsinī, Aṭṭhasālinī, and others, praise is given respectively with such phrases as: “of that which has the quality of inspiring faith,” “of that which crushes opposing views,” “of that which generates the analysis of knowledge,” “of that which has been fathomed by deep knowledge,” and “of that which is variegated by manifold methods.”

6. Attho kathīyati etāyāti atthakathā, sā eva aṭṭhakathā, ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā yathā “dukkhassa pīḷanaṭṭho”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.17; 2.8). Āditotiādimhi paṭhamasaṅgītiyaṃ[V 1.0018]. Chaḷabhiññatāya paramena cittavasībhāvena samannāgatattā jhānādīsu pañcavidhavasitāsabbhāvato ca vasino, therā mahākassapādayo, tesaṃ satehi pañcahi. Yāti yā aṭṭhakathā. Saṅgītāti atthaṃ pakāsetuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne “ayaṃ etassa attho, ayaṃ etassa attho”ti saṅgahetvā vuttā. Anusaṅgītā ca yasattherādīhi pacchāpi dutiyatatiyasaṅgītīsu. Iminā attano saṃvaṇṇanāya āgamanavisuddhiṃ dasseti.

6. ‘The meaning (attha) is told (kathīyati) by means of it’; hence `atthakathā` (commentary). This itself becomes `aṭṭhakathā` by changing `ttha` to `ṭṭha`, as in `pīḷanaṭṭho` for `pīḷana-attho` in the phrase ‘the meaning of suffering is oppression’ (Paṭis-M 1.17, 2.8). `Ādito` means in the beginning, at the First Council. The elders, Mahākassapa and the others, were masters (`vasino`) because they possessed the six superknowledges with supreme mastery over the mind and because they possessed the five kinds of mastery over the jhānas and so on. The phrase refers to the five hundred of them. `Yā` refers to the commentary. `Saṅgītā` (chanted) means it was recited, having been collected together at the appropriate places to explain the meaning, saying, ‘This is the meaning of this, this is the meaning of that.’ And `anusaṅgītā` (subsequently chanted) later by the Elder Yasa and others at the Second and Third Councils. By this he shows the purity of the transmission of his own commentary.

7. Sīhassa lānato gahaṇato sīhaḷo, sīhakumāro. Taṃvaṃsajātatāya tambapaṇṇidīpe khattiyānaṃ, tesaṃ nivāsatāya tambapaṇṇidīpassa ca sīhaḷabhāvo veditabbo. Ābhatāti jambudīpato ānītā. Athāti pacchā. Aparabhāge hi asaṅkaratthaṃ sīhaḷabhāsāya aṭṭhakathā ṭhapitāti. Tena sā mūlaṭṭhakathā sabbasādhāraṇā na hotīti idaṃ atthappakāsanaṃ ekantena karaṇīyanti dasseti. Tenevāha – “dīpavāsīnamatthāyā”ti. Tattha dīpavāsīnanti jambudīpavāsīnaṃ, dīpavāsīnanti vā sīhaḷadīpavāsīnaṃ atthāya sīhaḷabhāsāya ṭhapitāti yojanā.

7. ‘Sīhaḷa’ comes from ‘seizing’ (`lānato gahaṇato`) the lion; this refers to the lion-prince. It should be understood that the island of Tambapaṇṇi is called Sīhaḷa because the khattiyas on the island were born in his lineage, and because it was their dwelling place. `Ābhatā` means brought from Jambudīpa. `Atha` means afterwards. For in a later period, the commentary was established in the Sinhala language in order to prevent corruption. He shows that because that original commentary is thus not common to all, this explanation of the meaning must definitely be undertaken. Therefore he said: “for the benefit of the island-dwellers.” Here, the construction is either: for the benefit of the ‘island-dwellers,’ that is, the inhabitants of Jambudīpa; or, it was established in the Sinhala language for the benefit of the ‘island-dwellers,’ that is, the inhabitants of the island of Sri Lanka.

8. Apanetvānāti kañcukasadisaṃ sīhaḷabhāsaṃapanetvāna. Tatoti aṭṭhakathāto. Ahanti attānaṃ niddisati. Manoramaṃ bhāsanti māgadhabhāsaṃ. Sā hi sabhāvaniruttibhūtā paṇḍitānaṃ manaṃ ramayatīti. Tenevāha – “tantinayānucchavika”nti, pāḷigatiyā anulomikaṃ pāḷicchāyānuvidhāyininti attho. Vigatadosanti asabhāvaniruttibhāsantararahitaṃ.

8. `Apanetvāna` means having removed the Sinhala language, which is like a cloak. `Tato` means from that commentary. `Ahaṃ` (I) indicates himself. `Manoramaṃ bhāsaṃ` (the delightful language) means the Māgadhī language. For it, being the natural mode of expression, delights the minds of the wise. Therefore he said: `tantinayānucchavikaṃ`, meaning suitable to the textual method. The meaning is: conforming to the course of the Pāḷi, following the style of the Pāḷi. `Vigatadosaṃ` (faultless) means free from other languages that are not the natural mode of expression.

9. Samayaṃ avilomentoti siddhantaṃ avirodhento. Etena atthadosābhāvamāha. Aviruddhattā eva hi theravādāpi idha pakāsīyissanti. Theravaṃsadīpānanti thirehi sīlakkhandhādīhi samannāgatattā therā[M 1.0020], mahākassapādayo, tehi āgatā ācariyaparamparā theravaṃso. Tappariyāpannā hutvā āgamādhigamasampannattā paññāpajjotena tassa samujjalanato theravaṃsadīpā, mahāvihāravāsino therā, tesaṃ. Vividhehi ākārehi nicchīyatīti vinicchayo, gaṇṭhiṭṭhānesu khīlamaddanākārena pavattā vimaticchedakathā. Suṭṭhu nipuṇo saṇho vinicchayo etesanti sunipuṇavinicchayā. Atha vā vinicchinotīti vinicchayo, yathāvuttatthavisayaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Suṭṭhu nipuṇo cheko vinicchayo etesanti sunipuṇavinicchayā. Etena mahākassapādittheraparamparābhato, tatoyeva ca aviparīto saṇhasukhumo mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ vinicchayoti tassa pamāṇabhūtataṃ dasseti.

9. `Samayaṃ avilomento` means not contradicting the established doctrine. By this he states the absence of faults in meaning. Indeed, because it is uncontradicted, the Theravāda doctrine will also be explained herein. `Theravaṃsadīpānaṃ`: The elders (`therā`), Mahākassapa and others, are so called because they are endowed with the firm (`thira`) aggregates of virtue and so on. The lineage of teachers that has come down from them is the Theravaṃsa (Lineage of the Elders). Because they are included in that lineage, are accomplished in the scriptures and in realization, and illuminate that lineage with the lamp of wisdom, they are the ‘lamps of the Theravaṃsa’ (`theravaṃsadīpā`); this refers to the elders dwelling in the Mahāvihāra. The phrase refers to them. A `vinicchaya` (decision) is so called because a matter is decided upon in various ways; it is a discourse that cuts off doubt, proceeding in the manner of driving a stake into knotty points. `Sunipuṇavinicchayā` means those whose decision is very skillful and subtle. Alternatively, a `vinicchaya` is that which decides, that is, the knowledge concerning the aforesaid subject matter. `Sunipuṇavinicchayā` means those whose decision is very skillful and expert. By this he shows that the decision of the Mahāvihāra dwellers is authoritative because it has been transmitted in the lineage of elders beginning with Mahākassapa and for that very reason is unerring, subtle, and fine.

10. Sujanassa [V 1.0019] cāti ca-saddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena “na kevalaṃ jambudīpavāsīnaṃyeva atthāya, atha kho sādhujanānaṃ tosanatthañcā”ti dasseti. Tena ca “tambapaṇṇidīpavāsīnampi atthāyā”ti ayamattho siddho hoti uggahaṇādisukaratāya tesampi bahūpakārattā. Ciraṭṭhitatthanti ciraṭṭhitiatthaṃ, cirakālāvaṭṭhānāyāti attho. Idañhi atthappakāsanaṃ aviparītabyañjanasunikkhepassa atthasunītassa ca upāyabhāvato saddhammassa ciraṭṭhitiyā saṃvattati. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

10. The particle 'ca' in 'sujanassa cāti' has a collective sense. It thereby indicates: 'Not only for the benefit of the inhabitants of Jambudīpa, but also for the satisfaction of good people.' Through this, the meaning 'it is also for the benefit of the inhabitants of the island of Tambapaṇṇi' is established, because it is of great help to them too, being easy to learn, etc. 'Ciraṭṭhitatthanti' means for the sake of long stability, that is, for the purpose of its lasting for a long time. For this exposition of the meaning, since it is a means for well-placed phrasing that is not distorted and for a meaning that is well-guided, it conduces to the long stability of the good Dhamma. For this has been said by the Blessed One:

“Dveme, bhikkhave, dhammā saddhammassa ṭhitiyā asammosāya anantaradhānāya saṃvattanti. Katame dve? Sunikkhittañca padabyañjanaṃ, attho ca sunīto”ti (a. ni. 2.21).

"Bhikkhus, these two things conduce to the stability, non-confusion, and non-disappearance of the good Dhamma. What two? Well-placed words and phrases, and a meaning that is well-guided." (AN 2.21)

11-12. Yaṃ atthavaṇṇanaṃ katthukāmo, tassā mahantattaṃ pariharituṃ “sāvatthipabhūtīna”ntiādimāha. Tenāha – “na idha vitthārakathaṃ karissāmi, na taṃ idha vicārayissāmī”ti ca. Tattha dīghassāti dīghanikāyassa. Majjhimassāti majjhimanikāyassa. “Saṅgītīnaṃ dvinnaṃ yā me atthaṃ vadantenā”tipi pāṭho. Tatthapi saṅgītīnaṃ dvinnanti dīghamajjhimanikāyānanti attho gahetabbo. Meti karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ, mayāti attho. Sudanti nipātamattaṃ. Heṭṭhā dīghassa majjhimassa ca atthaṃ vadantena sāvatthipabhutīnaṃ nagarānaṃ yā vaṇṇanā katā, tassā vitthārakathaṃ na idha bhiyyo karissāmīti [M 1.0021] yojetabbaṃ. Yāni ca tattha vatthūni vitthāravasena vuttāni, tesampi vitthārakathaṃ na idha bhiyyo karissāmīti sambandho.

11–12. Wishing to compose a commentary on the meaning, and to avoid its great length, he says 'sāvatthipabhūtīnaṃ,' etc. Therefore he says: 'I will not give a detailed account here, nor will I investigate it here.' Therein, 'dīghassāti' means 'of the Dīgha Nikāya,' and 'majjhimassāti' means 'of the Majjhima Nikāya.' There is also the reading: 'Saṅgītīnaṃ dvinnaṃ yā me atthaṃ vadantenā.' There too, 'of the two recitations' should be understood to mean 'of the Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāyas.' 'Me' is a genitive used in the instrumental sense; it means 'by me' (mayā). 'Sudaṃ' is merely a particle. The passage should be construed thus: 'The description of the cities beginning with Sāvatthī that was made previously when explaining the meaning of the Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāyas—I will not give a further detailed account of it here.' The connection is: 'And of those stories that were told there in detail, I will not give a further detailed account of them here either.'

13. Idāni “na idha vitthārakathaṃ karissāmī”ti sāmaññato vuttassa atthassa pavaraṃ dassetuṃ – “suttānaṃ panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Suttānaṃ ye atthā vatthūhi vinā na pakāsantīti yojetabbaṃ.

13. Now, to show the special significance of the general statement, 'I will not give a detailed account here,' the passage beginning 'suttānaṃ panā' was stated. This should be construed as referring to those meanings of the suttas that do not become clear without the background stories.

14. Yaṃ aṭṭhakathaṃ kattukāmo, tadekadesabhāvena visuddhimaggo ca gahetabboti kathikānaṃ upadesaṃ karonto tattha vicāritadhamme uddesavasena dasseti – “sīlakathā”tiādinā. Tattha sīlakathāti cārittavārittādivasena sīlassa vitthārakathā. Dhutadhammāti piṇḍapātikaṅgādayo terasa kilesadhunanakadhammā. Kammaṭṭhānāni sabbānīti pāḷiyaṃ āgatāni aṭṭhatiṃsa, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ dveti niravasesāni yogakammassa bhāvanāya pavattiṭṭhānāni. Cariyāvidhānasahitoti rāgacaritādīnaṃ sabhāvādividhānena sahito. Jhānāni cattāri rūpāvacarajjhānāni, samāpattiyo catasso āruppasamāpattiyo[V 1.0020]. Aṭṭhapi vā paṭiladdhamattāni jhānāni samāpajjanavasībhāvappattiyā samāpattiyo. Jhānāni vā rūpārūpāvacarajjhānāni, samāpattiyo phalasamāpattinirodhasamāpattiyo.

14. Wishing to compose the commentary, while instructing the reciters that the Visuddhimagga should be adopted as a part of it, he indicates by way of summary the topics discussed therein, beginning with 'the talk on virtue.' Therein, 'the talk on virtue' is the detailed discourse on virtue by way of conduct and restraint, etc. 'The ascetic practices' are the thirteen practices that shake off the defilements, such as the alms-food-eater's practice. 'All meditation subjects' means the thirty-eight found in the Pāli Canon and the two in the commentaries—all without exception, being the grounds for the development of the yogi's practice. 'Together with the classification of temperaments' means together with the classification by way of the nature, etc., of those of lustful temperament, etc. 'The jhānas' are the four form-sphere jhānas, and 'the attainments' are the four formless attainments. Alternatively, the eight jhānas are jhānas merely upon being attained, while the attainments are those that have reached the state of mastery in entering them. Or, 'the jhānas' are the form and formless-sphere jhānas, and 'the attainments' are the attainment of fruition and the attainment of cessation.

15. Lokiyalokuttarabhedā cha abhiññāyo sabbā abhiññāyo. Ñāṇavibhaṅgādīsu āgatanayena ekavidhādinā paññāya saṃkaletvā sampiṇḍetvā nicchayo paññāsaṅkalananicchayo.

15. 'All the direct knowledges' means the six direct knowledges with their division into mundane and supramundane. 'The synthesis and determination of wisdom' is the determination arrived at by synthesizing and condensing with wisdom in the onefold way, etc., according to the method found in the Ñāṇavibhaṅga and other texts.

16. Paccayadhammānaṃ hetuādīnaṃ paccayuppannadhammānaṃ hetupaccayādibhāvo paccayākāro, tassa desanā paccayākāradesanā, paṭiccasamuppādakathāti attho. Sā pana ghanavinibbhogassa sudukkaratāya saṇhasukhumā, nikāyantaraladdhisaṅkararahitā, ekattanayādisahitā ca tattha vicāritāti āha – “suparisuddhanipuṇanayā”ti. Paṭisambhidādīsu āgatanayaṃ avissajjetvāva vicāritattā avimuttatantimaggā.

16. 'The mode of conditions' (paccayākāro) is the state of being a condition, such as a root condition, for conditionally arisen phenomena on the part of conditioning phenomena. 'The exposition of the mode of conditions' is the teaching of that, which means the discourse on dependent origination. And because the analysis of the compact is extremely difficult, that discourse is subtle and refined; and because it was investigated there free from admixture with the tenets of other schools and endowed with the method of unity, etc., he says: 'by the supremely purified and subtle method.' It is 'a path not deviating from the textual lineage' because it was investigated without abandoning the method found in the Paṭisambhidāmagga and other texts.

17. Iti pana sabbanti iti-saddo parisamāpane, pana-saddo vacanālaṅkāre, etaṃ sabbanti attho. Idhāti imissā aṭṭhakathāya na vicārayissāmi punaruttibhāvatoti adhippāyo.

17. In 'iti pana sabbaṃ,' the particle 'iti' denotes conclusion, and the particle 'pana' is a verbal ornament; the meaning is 'all this.' 'Here' means 'in this commentary'; the intention is: 'I will not investigate it, because it would be a repetition.'

18. Idāni [M 1.0022] tasseva avicāraṇassa ekantakāraṇaṃ niddhārento “majjhe visuddhimaggo”tiādimāha. Tattha “majjhe ṭhatvā”ti etena majjhabhāvadīpanena visesato catunnaṃ āgamānaṃ sādhāraṇaṭṭhakathā visuddhimaggo, na sumaṅgalavilāsinīādayo viya asādhāraṇaṭṭhakathāti dasseti. “Visesato”ti ca idaṃ vinayābhidhammānampi visuddhimaggo yathārahaṃ atthavaṇṇanā hoti evāti katvā vuttaṃ.

18. Now, determining the decisive reason for that non-investigation, he says, 'the Visuddhimagga in the middle,' etc. Therein, by this indication of its central position with the words 'standing in the middle,' he shows that the Visuddhimagga is a general commentary especially for the four Nikāyas, not a specific commentary like the Sumaṅgalavilāsinī and others. And the word 'especially' is said because the Visuddhimagga also serves, as is fitting, as a commentary explaining the meaning of the Vinaya and Abhidhamma.

19. Iccevāti iti eva. Tampīti visuddhimaggampi. Etāyāti manorathapūraṇiyā. Ettha ca “sīhaḷadīpaṃ ābhatā”tiādinā atthappakāsanassa nimittaṃ dasseti, “dīpavāsīnamatthāya sujanassa ca tuṭṭhatthaṃ ciraṭṭhitatthañca dhammassā”ti etena payojanaṃ, apanetvāna tatohaṃ, sīhaḷabhāsa”ntiādinā. “Sāvatthipabhutīna”ntiādinā ca karaṇappakāraṃ. Heṭṭhimanikāyesu visuddhimagge ca vicāritānaṃ atthānaṃ avicāraṇampi hi idha karaṇappakāro evāti.

19. 'Iccevāti' is 'iti eva.' 'Tampīti' is 'visuddhimaggam pi.' 'Etāyāti' is 'by this, the Manorathapūraṇī.' And here, with 'sīhaḷadīpaṃ ābhatā,' etc., he shows the occasion for the exposition of the meaning; with 'dīpavāsīnamatthāya sujanassa ca tuṭṭhatthaṃ ciraṭṭhitatthañca dhammassā' he shows the purpose; and with 'apanetvāna tatohaṃ, sīhaḷabhāsaṃ,' etc., and 'sāvatthipabhutīnaṃ,' etc., he shows the mode of execution. For the non-investigation here of meanings investigated in the earlier Nikāyas and in the Visuddhimagga is itself the mode of execution.

Ganthārambhakathāvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the introductory discourse is finished.

1. Rūpādivaggavaṇṇanā

1. Commentary on the Chapter on Form and So Forth

Nidānavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Introduction

Vibhāgavantānaṃ [V 1.0021] sabhāvavibhāvanaṃ vibhāgadassanavaseneva hotīti paṭhamaṃ tāva nipātasuttavasena vibhāgaṃ dassetuṃ “tattha aṅguttarāgamo nāmā”tiādimāha. Tattha tatthāti “aṅguttarāgamassa atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti yadidaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmiṃ vacane, “yassa atthaṃ pakāsayissāmī”ti paṭiññātaṃ, so aṅguttarāgamo nāma nipātasuttavasena evaṃ vibhāgoti attho. Atha vā tatthāti “aṅguttaranissitaṃ attha”nti etasmiṃ vacane yo aṅguttarāgamo vutto, so nipātasuttādivasena edisoti attho.

The manifestation of the intrinsic nature of things that are divided comes about by way of seeing their divisions. Therefore, in order to first show the division by way of the suttas in numerical collections, he states, beginning with: 'Therein, the Aṅguttara collection is so named….' Here, 'therein' refers to that statement where it was said, 'I will explain the meaning of the Aṅguttara collection.' In that statement, what was pledged as 'the meaning of which I will explain' is the Aṅguttara collection, which is divided in this way by way of the suttas in numerical collections; this is the meaning. Alternatively, 'therein' refers to this statement: 'the meaning based on the Aṅguttara.' The Aṅguttara collection mentioned there is of such a kind by way of the suttas in numerical collections and so on; this is the meaning.

Idāni taṃ ādito paṭṭhāya saṃvaṇṇitukāmo attano saṃvaṇṇanāya paṭhamamahāsaṅgītiyaṃ nikkhittānukkamena pavattabhāvadassanatthaṃ “tassa nipātesu…pe… vuttaṃ nidānamādī”tiādimāha. Tattha yathāpaccayaṃ tattha tattha desitattā paññattattā ca vippakiṇṇānaṃ dhammavinayānaṃ saṅgahetvā gāyanaṃ kathanaṃ saṅgīti. Etena taṃtaṃsikkhāpadānaṃ suttānañca ādipariyosānesu [M 1.0023] antarantarā ca sambandhavasena ṭhapitaṃ saṅgītikāravacanaṃ saṅgahitaṃ hoti. Saṅgīyamānassa atthassa mahantatāya pūjanīyatāya ca mahatī saṅgīti mahāsaṅgīti, paṭhamā mahāsaṅgīti paṭhamamahāsaṅgīti, tassā pavattikālo paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikālo, tasmiṃ paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle. Nidadāti desanaṃ desakālādivasena aviditaṃ viditaṃ katvā nidassetīti nidānaṃ. Yo lokiyehi upogghātoti vuccati, svāyamettha “evaṃ me suta”ntiādiko gantho veditabbo. Na “sanidānāhaṃ, bhikkhave, dhammaṃ desemī”tiādīsu (a. ni. 3.126) viya ajjhāsayādidesanuppattihetu. Tenevāha – “evaṃ me sutantiādikaṃ āyasmatā ānandena paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikāle vuttaṃ nidānamādī”ti.

Now, wishing to comment upon it from the beginning, in order to show that his own commentary proceeds in accordance with the sequence laid down at the First Great Council, he states, beginning with: 'Of that, in the Nipātas… the introduction beginning with… was spoken.' Here, saṅgīti means the collecting and chanting of the Dhamma and Vinaya, which had been taught and laid down in various places according to the occasion and were thus scattered. By this is included the word of the compilers of the council, which was placed at the beginning and end of the various training rules and suttas, and in between them, as a connecting thread. Because of the greatness and venerability of the meaning being chanted, a great chanting is a Great Council. The first Great Council is the First Great Council; the time of its occurrence is the time of the First Great Council; during that time of the First Great Council. A nidāna is so called because it lays down—that is, it reveals by making known what was unknown concerning the teacher, the time of the teaching, and so on. This should be understood here as the text beginning with 'Thus have I heard,' which is called an upogghāta (prologue) by worldly people. It is not the cause for the arising of the teaching, such as the intention, as in such passages as: 'Bhikkhus, I teach the Dhamma with its cause…' (AN 3.126). Therefore he said: 'The introduction beginning with “Thus have I heard” was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council.'

1. “Sā panesā”tiādinā bāhiranidāne vattabbaṃ atidisitvā idāni abbhantaranidānaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya saṃvaṇṇituṃ “yaṃ paneta”nti vuttaṃ. Tattha yasmā saṃvaṇṇanaṃ karontena saṃvaṇṇetabbe dhamme padāni padavibhāgaṃ tadatthañca dassetvā tato paraṃ piṇḍatthādinidassanavasena ca saṃvaṇṇanā kātabbā, tasmā padāni tāva dassento “evanti nipātapada”ntiādimāha[V 1.0022]. Tattha padavibhāgoti padānaṃ viseso, na padaviggaho. Atha vā padāni ca padavibhāgo ca padavibhāgo, padaviggaho ca padavibhāgo ca padavibhāgoti vā ekasesavasena padapadaviggahā padavibhāgasaddena vuttāti veditabbaṃ. Tattha padaviggaho “jetassa vanaṃ jetavana”ntiādinā samāsapadesu daṭṭhabbo.

1. Having applied by extension what is to be said on the external introduction with the words 'But this…,' now, in order to comment on the internal introduction from the beginning, it is said, 'But as to this….' Here, since one making a commentary should comment by first showing the words, the division of words, and their meaning in the teaching to be commented upon, and thereafter by way of showing the summary meaning and so on, he therefore first shows the words, stating, beginning with: 'The word evaṃ is a particle.' Here, 'division of words' means the distinction of words, not the analysis of words. Alternatively, it should be understood that by the principle of ellipsis, 'words and division of words' are called 'division of words,' or 'analysis of words and division of words' are called 'division of words'; thus both 'word' and 'analysis of a word' are expressed by the term 'division of words.' Here, the analysis of a word should be seen in compound words, such as 'Jeta's grove is Jetavana.'

Atthatoti padatthato. Taṃ pana padatthaṃ atthuddhārakkamena paṭhamaṃ evaṃ-saddassa dassento “evaṃ-saddo tāvā”tiādimāha. Avadhāraṇādīti ettha ādi-saddena idamatthapucchāparimāṇādiatthānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tathā hi “evaṃgatāni puthusippāyatanāni, evamādīnī”tiādīsu idaṃ-saddassa atthe evaṃ-saddo. Gata-saddo hi pakārapariyāyo, tathā vidhākāra-saddā ca. Tathā hi vidhayuttagatasadde lokiyā pakāratthe vadanti. “Evaṃ su te sunhātā suvilittā kappitakesamassū āmukkamaṇikuṇḍalābharaṇā odātavatthavasanā pañcahi kāmaguṇehi samappitā samaṅgībhūtā paricārenti seyyathāpi tvaṃ etarahi [M 1.0024] sācariyakoti. No hidaṃ, bho gotamā”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.286) pucchāyaṃ. “Evaṃ lahuparivattaṃ (a. ni. 1.48), evamāyupariyanto”ti (dī. ni. 1.244; pārā. 12) ca ādīsu parimāṇe.

'As to the meaning' means 'as to the meaning of the word.' Showing that meaning of the word first for the word evaṃ by the method of extracting the meaning, he states, beginning with: 'Now, the word evaṃ….' In 'emphasis, etc.,' by the word 'etc.' the inclusion of such meanings as 'this,' 'question,' 'measure,' and so on, should be seen. For in such phrases as 'such various crafts and skills' and 'such things as these,' the word evaṃ has the sense of the word 'this.' The word gata is a synonym for 'manner,' as are the words vidha and ākāra. For worldly people use the word gata together with vidha in the sense of 'manner.' For instance, in questions, as in: 'Are your disciples, well-bathed, well-anointed, with hair and beard trimmed, wearing jewel-earrings and ornaments, dressed in white clothes, endowed and provided with the five cords of sensual pleasure, enjoying themselves just as you are now with your teacher? Not so, Master Gotama' (DN 1.286). And in the sense of measure, as in: 'so quickly changing' (AN 1.48) and 'so limited in lifespan' (DN 1.244; Pārā 12).

Nanu ca “evaṃ su te sunhātā suvilittā evamāyupariyanto”ti ettha evaṃ-saddena pucchanākāraparimāṇākārānaṃ vuttattā ākārattho eva evaṃ-saddoti? Na, visesasabbhāvato. Ākāramattavācako hi evaṃ-saddo ākāratthoti adhippeto yathā “evaṃ byākho”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.234; pāci. 417; cūḷava. 65), na pana ākāravisesavācako. Evañca katvā “evaṃ jātena maccenā”tiādīni (dha. pa. 53) upamādiudāharaṇāni upapannāni honti. Tathā hi “yathā hi…pe… bahu”nti (dha. pa. 53) ettha puppharāsiṭṭhāniyato manussūpapattisappurisūpanissayasaddhammassavanayonisomanasikārabhogasampatti- ādidānādipuññakiriyāhetusamudāyato sobhāsugandhatādiguṇayogato mālāguṇasadisiyo pahūtā puññakiriyā maritabbasabhāvatāya maccena sattena kattabbāti jotitattā puppharāsimālāguṇāva upamā. Tesaṃ upamākāro yathā-saddena aniyamato vuttoti “evaṃ-saddo upamākāranigamanattho”ti vattuṃ yuttaṃ, so pana upamākāro niyamiyamāno atthato upamāva hotīti āha – “upamāyaṃ āgato”ti. Tathā “evaṃ iminā ākārena abhikkamitabba”ntiādinā upadisiyamānāya samaṇasāruppāya ākappasampattiyā yo tattha upadisanākāro, so atthato upadeso evāti vuttaṃ – “evaṃ te…pe… upadese”ti. Tathā evametaṃ [V 1.0023] bhagavā, evametaṃ sugatāti ettha bhagavatā yathāvuttamatthaṃ aviparītato jānantehi kataṃ tattha saṃvijjamānaguṇānaṃ pakārehi haṃsanaṃ udaggatākaraṇaṃ sampahaṃsanaṃ, yo tattha sampahaṃsanākāroti yojetabbaṃ.

But is it not so that here, in 'thus are your disciples…' and 'so limited in lifespan,' since the manner of questioning and the manner of measure are stated by the word evaṃ, the word evaṃ simply has the meaning of 'manner'? No, because of the existence of a distinction. For the word evaṃ is intended to mean 'manner' when it expresses just the manner, as in 'in such a way, a tiger…' (MN 1.234, etc.), but not when it expresses a specific manner. This being so, examples involving simile, etc., such as 'Thus by a mortal who is born…' (Dhp 53), become fitting. For there, in 'Just as… many…' (Dhp 53), from the standpoint of a heap of flowers, many meritorious actions—similar to the qualities of a garland on account of possessing qualities like beauty and fragrance, arising from the collective causes of meritorious deeds such as giving, which include human rebirth, association with good people, hearing the good Dhamma, wise attention, and attainment of wealth—should be done by a being who is mortal by nature. Thus the heap of flowers and the qualities of the garland are the simile. Since the manner of the simile is stated indefinitely by the word yathā, it is proper to say that the word evaṃ has the meaning of concluding the manner of the simile. But that manner of the simile, when being specified, is in substance a simile itself, so he says: 'it has come in a simile.' Similarly, with 'Thus, in this manner, one should go forth…,' the manner of instruction given there for the attainment of the deportment proper to a recluse is, in substance, instruction itself; thus it is said: 'Thus for you… in instruction.' Likewise, in 'So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Fortunate One,' the rejoicing (sampahaṃsana) is the gladdening and elation expressed in various ways about the qualities present there, made by those who know without distortion the meaning stated by the Blessed One. It should be connected as 'the manner of rejoicing there.'

Evamevaṃ panāyanti ettha garahaṇākāroti yojetabbaṃ, so ca garahaṇākāro “vasalī”tiādikhuṃsanasaddasannidhānato idha evaṃ-saddena pakāsitoti viññāyati. Yathā cettha, evaṃ upamākārādayopi upamādivasena vuttānaṃ puppharāsiādisaddānaṃ sannidhānatoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ, bhanteti khotiādīsu pana dhammassa sādhukaṃ savanamanasikārena niyojitehi bhikkhūhi attano tattha ṭhitabhāvassa paṭijānanavasena vuttattā [M 1.0025] ettha evaṃ-saddo vacanasampaṭicchanattho vutto, tena “evaṃ, bhante, sādhu bhante, suṭṭhu bhante”ti vuttaṃ hoti. Evañca vadehīti “yathāhaṃ vadāmi, evaṃ samaṇaṃ ānandaṃ vadehī”ti vadanākāro idāni vattabbo evaṃ-saddena nidassīyatīti nidassanattho vutto. Evaṃ noti etthāpi tesaṃ yathāvuttadhammānaṃ ahitadukkhāvahabhāve sanniṭṭhānajananatthaṃ anumatiggahaṇavasena “no vā, kathaṃ vo ettha hotī”ti pucchāya katāya “evaṃ no ettha hotī”ti vuttattā tadākārasanniṭṭhānaṃ evaṃ-saddena vibhāvitanti viññāyati. So pana tesaṃ dhammānaṃ ahitāya dukkhāya saṃvattanākāro niyamiyamāno avadhāraṇattho hotīti āha – “evaṃ no ettha hotītiādīsu avadhāraṇe”ti.

In 'Thus, thus they come…,' it should be connected as 'the manner of reproach.' And that manner of reproach is understood to be expressed here by the word evaṃ because of the proximity of abusive words such as 'outcaste.' Just as here, so too the manner of simile and so on should be seen from the proximity of words such as 'heap of flowers' that are stated by way of simile, etc. But in 'Yes, venerable sir,' etc., since it is spoken by the bhikkhus—who are engaged in carefully listening to and attending to the Dhamma—by way of acknowledging their state of being established therein, here the word evaṃ is said to have the meaning of assent to what is said. By this is meant: 'Yes, venerable sir,' 'Good, venerable sir,' 'Well, venerable sir.' In 'And speak thus,' the manner of speaking—'Speak to the recluse Ānanda just as I speak'—is now indicated by the word evaṃ, so it is said to have the meaning of demonstration. In 'Thus for us' too, since the question 'Or not? What do you think about this?' was asked in order to generate a conclusion about the unbeneficial and painful nature of those things as stated, by way of seeking their consent, and it was said, 'Thus it is for us,' it is understood that the conclusion about that manner is clarified by the word evaṃ. But since that manner of those things conducing to what is unbeneficial and painful is being determined, it has the meaning of emphasis. Thus he says: 'In “Thus it is for us,” etc., it is in the sense of emphasis.'

Nānānayanipuṇanti ekattanānattaabyāpāraevaṃdhammatāsaṅkhātā, nandiyāvaṭṭatipukkhalasīhavikkīḷitaaṅkusadisālocanasaṅkhātā vā ādhārādibhedavasena nānāvidhā nayā nānānayā. Nayā vā pāḷigatiyo, tā ca paññattiādivasena saṃkilesabhāgiyādilokiyāditadubhayavomissakatādivasena kusalādivasena khandhādivasena saṅgahādivasena samayavimuttādivasena padhānādivasena kusalamūlādivasena tikapaṭṭhānādivasena ca nānappakārāti nānānayā, tehi nipuṇaṃ saṇhaṃ sukhumanti nānānayanipuṇaṃ. Āsayova ajjhāsayo, te ca sassatādibhedena tattha ca apparajakkhatādibhedena ca aneke, attajjhāsayādayo eva vā samuṭṭhānaṃ uppattihetu etassāti anekajjhāsayasamuṭṭhānaṃ. Atthabyañjanasampannanti atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇaṃ upanetabbābhāvato. Saṅkāsanapakāsanavivaraṇavibhajanauttānīkaraṇapaññattivasena chahi atthapadehi akkharapadabyañjanākāraniruttiniddesavasena chahi byañjanapadehi ca samannāgatanti vā attho daṭṭhabbo.

"Skilled in various methods" means adept in the various methods, which are reckoned as the suchness of things in terms of non-operation in unity and multiplicity; or as the methods called the Nandiyāvaṭṭa, the Tipukkhala, the Lion's Play, the Goad, and the Examination of Directions, which are diverse based on distinctions of support and so on. Or, the methods are the courses of the Pāli, and these are of various kinds: based on concepts, etc.; based on what partakes of defilement, etc., what is worldly, etc., and what is a mixture of both, etc.; based on what is wholesome, etc.; based on the aggregates, etc.; based on inclusion, etc.; based on temporary liberation, etc.; based on striving, etc.; based on wholesome roots, etc.; and based on the Tika and Paṭṭhāna, etc. Thus they are "various methods." Being skilled in them means being subtle and fine; hence, "skilled in various methods." An inclination is a disposition, and these are many, distinguished by eternalism, etc., and therein by having little dust, etc. Or, dispositions such as the disposition towards self are the origin, the cause of arising, for this; hence, "arising from many inclinations." "Endowed with meaning and expression" means complete in meaning and expression, as there is nothing that needs to be added. Or, the meaning should be understood as being endowed with six aspects of meaning—elucidation, manifestation, opening up, analysis, making plain, and designation—and with six aspects of expression—letters, words, phrases, form, language, and exposition.

Vividhapāṭihāriyanti ettha pāṭihāriyapadassa vacanatthaṃ “paṭipakkhaharaṇato rāgādikilesāpanayanato ca pāṭihāriya”nti vadanti. Bhagavato pana paṭipakkhā rāgādayo na santi[V 1.0024], ye haritabbā. Puthujjanānampi vigatūpakkilese aṭṭhaguṇasamannāgate citte hatapaṭipakkhe iddhividhaṃ pavattati, tasmā tattha pavattavohārena ca na sakkā idha “pāṭihāriya”nti vatthuṃ. Sace pana mahākāruṇikassa bhagavato veneyyagatā ca kilesā [M 1.0026] paṭipakkhā, tesaṃ haraṇato “pāṭihāriya”nti vuttaṃ, evaṃ sati yuttametaṃ. Atha vā bhagavato ca sāsanassa ca paṭipakkhā titthiyā, tesaṃ haraṇato pāṭihāriyaṃ. Te hi diṭṭhiharaṇavasena ca diṭṭhippakāsane asamatthabhāvena ca iddhiādesanānusāsanīhi haritā apanītā hontīti. “Paṭī”ti vā ayaṃ saddo “pacchā”ti etassa atthaṃ bodheti “tasmiṃ paṭipaviṭṭhamhi, añño āgañchi brāhmaṇo”tiādīsu (su. ni. 985; cūḷani. pārāyanavaggo, vatthugāthā 4) viya, tasmā samāhite citte vigatūpakkilese katakiccena pacchā haritabbaṃ pavattetabbanti paṭihāriyaṃ, attano vā upakkilesesu catutthajjhānamaggehi haritesu pacchā haraṇaṃ paṭihāriyaṃ, iddhiādesanānusāsaniyo ca vigatūpakkilesena katakiccena ca sattahitatthaṃ puna pavattetabbā, haritesu ca attano upakkilesesu parasattānaṃ upakkilesaharaṇāni hontīti paṭihāriyāni bhavanti. Paṭihāriyameva pāṭihāriyaṃ, paṭihāriye vā iddhiādesanānusāsanisamudāye bhavaṃ ekamekaṃ pāṭihāriyanti vuccati. Paṭihāriyaṃ vā catutthajjhānaṃ maggo ca paṭipakkhaharaṇato, tattha jātaṃ, tasmiṃ vā nimittabhūte, tato vā āgatanti pāṭihāriyaṃ. Tassa pana iddhiādibhedena visayabhedena ca bahuvidhassa bhagavato desanāyaṃ labbhamānattā āha – “vividhapāṭihāriya”nti.

"Various miracles": Here, some say the etymological meaning of the word "pāṭihāriya" is "it is a 'pāṭihāriya' because it removes opposition and dispels defilements such as lust." But the Blessed One has no opposing defilements like lust that need to be removed. Even for ordinary people, when the mind is free from imperfections and endowed with eight qualities, with opposition destroyed, the kinds of psychic power operate. Therefore, based on the usage in that context, one cannot say "pāṭihāriya" here. If, however, for the greatly compassionate Blessed One, the defilements present in those to be trained are the opposition, and it is called "pāṭihāriya" because it removes them, then this is fitting. Or, the adherents of other sects are the opposition to the Blessed One and his Dispensation, and their removal is a "pāṭihāriya." For they are removed and dispelled by the miracles of psychic power, telepathy, and instruction, by way of refuting their views and by their inability to proclaim their own views. Or, the word "paṭi" conveys the meaning "after," as in such passages as: "When he had gone back in, another brahmin came." Therefore, what is to be brought forth and set in motion afterwards by one who has accomplished his task in a concentrated mind free from imperfections is a "pāṭihāriya." Or, after one's own imperfections have been removed by the fourth jhāna and the path, the subsequent removal is a "pāṭihāriya." The miracles of psychic power, telepathy, and instruction are to be set in motion again for the welfare of beings by one who is free from imperfections and has accomplished his task. When one's own imperfections are removed, the acts of removing the imperfections of other beings become "pāṭihāriyas." A "pāṭihāriya" is simply a "pāṭihāriya"; or, in the collection of the miracles of psychic power, telepathy, and instruction, each one that occurs is called a "pāṭihāriya." Or, the fourth jhāna and the path are a "pāṭihāriya" because they remove opposition; what is born from that, or has that as its basis, or comes from that is a "pāṭihāriya." Since this is found in the Blessed One's teaching in many forms, distinguished by psychic power, etc., and by its domain, it is said: "various miracles."

Na aññathāti bhagavato sammukhā sutākārato na aññathāti attho, na pana bhagavato desitākārato. Acinteyyānubhāvā hi bhagavato desanā. Evañca katvā “sabbappakārena ko samattho viññātu”nti idaṃ vacanaṃ samatthitaṃ bhavati, dhāraṇabaladassanañca na virujjhati sutākārāvirujjhanassa adhippetattā. Na hettha atthantaratāparihāro dvinnaṃ atthānaṃ ekavisayattā, itarathā thero bhagavato desanāya sabbathā paṭiggahaṇe samattho asamattho cāti āpajjeyyāti.

"Not otherwise": This means not otherwise than the way it was heard in the presence of the Blessed One, not, however, otherwise than the way it was taught by the Blessed One. For the Blessed One's teaching is of inconceivable power. This being so, the statement, "Who is capable of understanding in every way?" is supported, and the demonstration of the power of retention is not contradicted, since what is intended is non-contradiction with the way it was heard. Here there is no exclusion of a different meaning, because the two meanings have a single domain. Otherwise, it would follow that the elder was both capable and incapable of grasping the Blessed One's teaching in every way.

“Yo paro na hoti, so attā”ti evaṃ vuttāya niyakajjhattasaṅkhātāya sasantatiyaṃ vattanato tividhopi me-saddo kiñcāpi ekasmiṃyeva atthe dissati, karaṇasampadānasāminiddesavasena pana vijjamānabhedaṃ sandhāyāha – “me-saddo tīsu atthesu dissatī”ti.

According to the statement, 'That which is not other is self,' the word 'me' occurs in reference to one's own continuity, which is reckoned as one's own and internal. Although this threefold word 'me' is seen in a single sense, with reference to the existing distinctions in its designation as instrument, dative, and owner, it is said: 'The word "me" is seen in three meanings.'

Kiñcāpi [M 1.0027] upasaggo kiriyaṃ viseseti, jotakabhāvato pana satipi tasmiṃ suta-saddo eva taṃ tamatthaṃ vadatīti anupasaggassa suta-saddassa atthuddhāre saupasaggassa gahaṇaṃ na virujjhatīti [V 1.0025] dassento “saupasaggo ca anupasaggo cā”ti āha. Assāti sutasaddassa. Kammabhāvasādhanāni idha sutasadde sambhavantīti vuttaṃ – “upadhāritanti vā upadhāraṇanti vā attho”ti. Mayāti atthe satīti yadā me-saddassa kattuvasena karaṇaniddeso, tadāti attho. Mamāti atthe satīti yadā sambandhavasena sāminiddeso, tadā.

Although a prefix qualifies the action, nevertheless, even when it is present, it is the word 'suta' itself that expresses that particular meaning, because it is an indicator. To show that in extracting the meaning of the unprefixed word 'suta,' taking up the prefixed form is not contradictory, he said, 'both with a prefix and without a prefix.' 'Of this' (assa) means of the word 'suta.' It is said that here, for the word 'suta,' derivations in the sense of object and state are possible: 'the meaning is "ascertained" or "ascertainment."' 'When the meaning is "by me"': this is when there is the designation of instrument for the word 'me' as agent. 'When the meaning is "of me"': this is when there is the designation of owner by way of relation.

Sutasaddasanniṭṭhāne payuttena evaṃ-saddena savanakiriyājotakena bhavitabbanti vuttaṃ – “evanti sotaviññāṇādiviññāṇakiccanidassana”nti. Ādi-saddena sampaṭicchanādīnaṃ sotadvārikaviññāṇānaṃ tadabhinīhaṭānañca manodvārikaviññāṇānaṃ gahaṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sabbesampi vākyānaṃ evakāratthasahitattā “suta”nti etassa sutamevāti ayamattho labbhatīti āha – “assavanabhāvappaṭikkhepato”ti. Etena avadhāraṇena niyāmataṃ dasseti. Yathā ca sutaṃ sutamevāti niyāmetabbaṃ, taṃ sammā sutaṃ hotīti āha – “anūnādhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Atha vā saddantaratthāpohanavasena saddo atthaṃ vadatīti sutanti assutaṃ na hotīti ayametassa atthoti vuttaṃ – “assavanabhāvappaṭikkhepato”ti. Iminā diṭṭhādivinivattanaṃ karoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – na idaṃ mayā diṭṭhaṃ, na sayambhuñāṇena sacchikataṃ, atha kho sutaṃ, tañca sammadevāti. Tenevāha – “anūnādhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Avadhāraṇatthe vā evaṃ-sadde ayamatthayojanā – “karīyatī”ti tadapekkhassa suta-saddassa ayamattho vutto “assavanabhāvappaṭikkhepato”ti. Tenevāha – “anūnādhikāviparītaggahaṇanidassana”nti. Savana-saddo cettha kammattho veditabbo “suyyatī”ti.

It is said that the word 'evaṃ', being used in connection with the word 'suta', must be an indicator of the action of hearing; thus it is said: ''Evaṃ' is an indication of the function of ear-consciousness and other consciousnesses.' By the word 'ādi' (etc.), one should understand the inclusion of the ear-door consciousnesses such as receiving consciousness, and the mind-door consciousnesses brought forth from that. Because all sentences contain the meaning of the particle 'eva' (only), from 'suta' the meaning 'heard only' is obtained. Thus he says: 'by way of rejecting the state of not-hearing.' By this emphasis, he shows definiteness. And just as what is heard should be defined as 'heard only,' so that it is 'well heard,' he says: 'an indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or distortion.' Or, because a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meaning of other words, 'suta' means 'it is not unheard.' This is its meaning. Thus it is said: 'by way of rejecting the state of not-hearing.' By this, he effects the exclusion of what is seen, etc. This is what is said: 'This was not seen by me, nor realized by self-originating knowledge, but it was heard, and that correctly.' Therefore he says: 'an indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or distortion.' Or, when the word 'evaṃ' has the sense of emphasis, this is the application of the meaning: with reference to 'is done,' this meaning of the word 'suta' is stated: 'by way of rejecting the state of not-hearing.' Therefore he says: 'an indication of grasping without deficiency, excess, or distortion.' Here the word 'savana' (hearing) should be understood in the objective sense, as 'what is heard.'

Evaṃ savanahetusavanavisesavasena padattayassa ekena pakārena atthayojanaṃ dassetvā idāni pakārantarehi taṃ dassetuṃ – “tathā eva”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha tassāti yā sā bhagavato sammukhā dhammassavanākārena pavattā manodvāraviññāṇavīthi, tassā. Sā hi nānappakārena ārammaṇe pavattituṃ samatthā. Tathā ca vuttaṃ – “sotadvārānusārenā”ti. Nānappakārenāti vakkhamānānaṃ anekavihitānaṃ [M 1.0028] byañjanatthaggahaṇānaṃ nānākārena. Etena imissā yojanāya ākārattho evaṃ-saddo gahitoti dīpeti. Pavattibhāvappakāsananti pavattiyā atthibhāvappakāsanaṃ. Sutanti dhammappakāsananti yasmiṃ ārammaṇe vuttappakārā viññāṇavīthi nānappakārena pavattā, tassa dhammattā vuttaṃ, na sutasaddassa dhammatthattā. Vuttassevatthassa pākaṭīkaraṇaṃ “ayañhetthā”tiādi. Tattha viññāṇavīthiyāti karaṇatthe karaṇavacanaṃ, mayāti kattuatthe.

Thus, having shown in one way the application of meaning to the three words by way of the cause of hearing and the particular hearing, now to show it in other ways, 'just so,' etc., is said. Therein, 'of that' (tassā) refers to that cognitive series of mind-door consciousness which occurred in the presence of the Blessed One in the manner of hearing the Dhamma. For it is capable of occurring in various ways in relation to its object. And so it is said: 'in accordance with the ear-door.' 'In various ways' means in the various manners of grasping the many kinds of phrasing and meaning that will be spoken of. By this he indicates that in this application, the word 'evaṃ' is taken in the sense of 'manner.' 'Manifestation of the state of occurrence' means the manifestation of the existence of the occurrence. 'Suta' means the manifestation of the Dhamma: since that object in which the aforesaid cognitive series occurred in various ways is Dhamma, this is said; not because the word 'suta' means Dhamma. The making clear of this same meaning begins with 'Herein....' There, 'by the cognitive series' is the instrumental case in the sense of instrument; 'by me' is in the instrumental case in the sense of agent.

Evanti niddisitabbappakāsananti nidassanatthaṃ evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā vuttaṃ nidassetabbassa nidassitabbattābhāvābhāvato[V 1.0026]. Tena evaṃ-saddena sakalampi suttaṃ paccāmaṭṭhanti dasseti. Sutasaddassa kiriyāsaddattā savanakiriyāya ca sādhāraṇaviññāṇappabandhappaṭibaddhattā tattha ca puggalavohāroti vuttaṃ – “sutanti puggalakiccappakāsana”nti. Na hi puggalavohārarahite dhammappabandhe savanakiriyā labbhatīti.

'Evaṃ' is the manifestation of what is to be pointed out: This is said taking the word 'evaṃ' in the sense of indication, because what is to be indicated must indeed be indicated. He shows that by that word 'evaṃ', the entire sutta is referred to. Because the word 'suta' is a word of action, and because the action of hearing is connected with a general continuum of consciousness where there is conventional usage of 'person,' it is said: ''Suta' is the manifestation of a person's function.' For the action of hearing is not found in a continuum of phenomena devoid of the conventional usage of 'person.'

Yassa cittasantānassātiādipi ākāratthameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā purimayojanāya aññathā atthayojanaṃ dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha ākārapaññattīti upādāpaññatti eva dhammānaṃ pavattiākārupādānavasena tathā vuttā. Sutanti visayaniddesoti sotabbabhūto dhammo savanakiriyākattupuggalassa savanakiriyāvasena pavattiṭṭhānanti katvā vuttaṃ. Cittasantānavinimuttassa paramatthato kassaci kattuabhāvepi saddavohārena buddhiparikappitabhedavacanicchāya cittasantānato aññaṃ viya taṃsamaṅgiṃ katvā vuttaṃ – “cittasantānena taṃsamaṅgīno”ti. Savanakiriyāvisayopi sotabbadhammo savanakiriyāvasena pavattacittasantānassa idha paramatthato kattubhāvato, savanavasena cittapavattiyā eva vā savanakiriyābhāvato taṃkiriyākattu ca visayo hotīti katvā vuttaṃ – “taṃsamaṅgīno kattuvisaye”ti. Sutākārassa ca therassa sammānicchitabhāvato āha – “gahaṇasanniṭṭhāna”nti. Etena vā avadhāraṇatthaṃ evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā ayamatthayojanā katāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The phrase beginning 'Of which mental continuum' is also stated to show a different construction of the meaning from the previous one, by taking the word 'evaṃ' as signifying the mode. Therein, 'designation of mode' is a derivative designation, so called because it is derived from the mode of occurrence of phenomena. 'Sutaṃ is a designation of the object' is said because the Dhamma to be heard is the ground for the occurrence of the act of hearing for the person who is the agent of that act. Although in the ultimate sense there is no agent apart from the mental continuum, through verbal convention and the desire to express a conceptually fabricated distinction, it is spoken of by making the one endowed with it seem different from the mental continuum, thus: 'by the mental continuum of one endowed with it.' The Dhamma to be heard, the object of the act of hearing, is also the object for the agent of that act. This is said because here, in the ultimate sense, the mental continuum that occurs by way of the act of hearing is the agent, or because the act of hearing is simply the occurrence of the mind by way of hearing. Thus it is said: 'in the agent's domain of one endowed with it.' And because the Elder has correctly determined the mode of what was heard, he says: 'the determination of the apprehension.' Or it should be seen that this construction of the meaning has been made by taking the word 'evaṃ' in the sense of emphasis.

Pubbe sutānaṃ nānāvihitānaṃ suttasaṅkhātānaṃ atthabyañjanānaṃ upadhāritarūpassa ākārassa nidassanassa, avadhāraṇassa vā pakāsanasabhāvo [M 1.0029] evaṃ-saddoti tadākārādiupadhāraṇassa puggalapaññattiyā upādānabhūtadhammappabandhabyāpāratāya vuttaṃ – “evanti puggalakiccaniddeso”ti. Savanakiriyā pana puggalavādinopi viññāṇanirapekkhā natthīti visesato viññāṇabyāpāroti āha – “sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso”ti. Meti saddappavattiyā ekanteneva sattavisayattā viññāṇakiccassa ca tattheva samodahitabbato “meti ubhayakiccayuttapuggalaniddeso”ti vuttaṃ. Avijjamānapaññattivijjamānapaññattisabhāvā yathākkamaṃ evaṃsaddasutasaddānaṃ atthāti te tathārūpapaññattiupādānabyāpārabhāvena dassento āha – “evanti puggalakiccaniddeso, sutanti viññāṇakiccaniddeso”ti. Ettha ca karaṇakiriyākattukammavisesappakāsanavasena puggalabyāpāravisayapuggalabyāpāranidassanavasena gahaṇākāraggāhakatabbisayavisesaniddesavasena kattukaraṇabyāpārakattuniddesavasena ca dutiyādayo catasso atthayojanā dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The word 'evaṃ' has the nature of revealing the mode, the demonstration, or the determination of the form that has been ascertained of the meaning and phrasing of the various kinds of previously heard suttas. Because the ascertainment of that mode, etc., is an activity of the continuity of phenomena that is the basis for the designation of a person, it is said: 'Evaṃ is a designation of a person's function.' But since even for a personalist the act of hearing is not independent of consciousness, it is especially an activity of consciousness. Thus he says: 'Sutaṃ is a designation of consciousness's function.' Because the word 'me' by its occurrence refers exclusively to a being, and because the function of consciousness must be included right there, it is said: 'Me is a designation of the person connected with both functions.' The meanings of the words 'evaṃ' and 'sutaṃ' are, respectively, the nature of a non-existent designation and an existent designation. Showing them as being the activity of deriving such a designation, he says: 'Evaṃ is a designation of a person's function; sutaṃ is a designation of consciousness's function.' And here it should be seen that the four constructions of meaning, the second and so on, are shown: by way of explaining the distinction of instrument, action, agent, and object; by way of indicating the person's activity and its object; by way of designating the distinction of the mode of apprehension, the one who apprehends, and the object thereof; and by way of designating the agent in terms of the activity of the agent and instrument.

Sabbassapi saddādhigamanīyassa atthassa paññattimukheneva paṭipajjitabbattā sabbapaññattīnañca [V 1.0027] vijjamānādivasena chasu paññattibhedesu antogadhattā tesu “eva”ntiādīnaṃ paññattīnaṃ sarūpaṃ niddhārento āha – “evanti ca meti cā”tiādi. Tattha evanti ca meti ca vuccamānassatthassa ākārādino dhammānaṃ asallakkhaṇabhāvato avijjamānapaññattibhāvoti āha – “saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasena avijjamānapaññattī”ti. Tattha saccikaṭṭhaparamatthavasenāti bhūtatthauttamatthavasena. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yo māyāmarīciādayo viya abhūtattho, anussavādīhi gahetabbo viya anuttamattho ca na hoti, so rūpasaddādisabhāvo, ruppanānubhavanādisabhāvo vā attho saccikaṭṭho paramattho cāti vuccati, na tathā “evaṃ me”tipadānaṃ atthoti. Etamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “kiñhettha ta”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Sutanti pana saddāyatanaṃ sandhāyāha – “vijjamānapaññattī”ti. Teneva hi “yañhi taṃ ettha sotena upaladdha”nti vuttaṃ. “Sotadvārānusārena upaladdha”nti pana vutte atthabyañjanādi sabbaṃ labbhati. Taṃ taṃ upādāya vattabbatoti sotapathamāgate dhamme upādāya tesaṃ upadhāritākārādino paccāmasanavasena evanti, sasantatipariyāpanne khandhe upādāya meti vattabbattāti attho. Diṭṭhādisabhāvarahite saddāyatane pavattamānopi [M 1.0030] sutavohāro “dutiyaṃ tatiya”ntiādiko viya paṭhamādīni diṭṭhamutaviññāte apekkhitvā pavattoti āha – “diṭṭhādīni upanidhāya vattabbato”ti. Assutaṃ na hotīti hi sutanti pakāsito ayamatthoti.

Because all meaning attainable by words must be accessed only through the gateway of designation, and because all designations are included in the six kinds of designation, such as existent designation, the author, determining the nature of such designations as 'evaṃ' and 'me,' says: 'Evaṃ ca me ca,' etc. Therein, because the meaning of 'evaṃ' and 'me' when spoken—the mode, etc.—is not a characteristic of phenomena, it is a non-existent designation. Thus he says: 'a non-existent designation in the sense of real and ultimate meaning.' Here, 'in the sense of real and ultimate meaning' means in the sense of true and supreme meaning. This is what is meant: that meaning which is not unreal like a magical illusion or a mirage, and not non-supreme like what is to be grasped by oral tradition—that is, the nature of form, sound, etc., or the nature of being afflicted, of experiencing, etc.—is called 'real and ultimate meaning.' The meaning of the words 'evaṃ me' is not so. To make this very meaning clearer, the passage beginning 'What here is that?' is stated. But with reference to the sound base, he says of 'sutaṃ': 'It is an existent designation.' For that reason it is said: 'For what is apprehended here by the ear.' But when it is said, 'apprehended in accordance with the ear-door,' then everything—meaning, phrasing, etc.—is obtained. The meaning is that it should be spoken of by depending on this or that: 'evaṃ' is spoken by way of reviewing the ascertained mode of the phenomena that have come into the range of the ear; 'me' should be spoken of by depending on the aggregates included in one's own continuity. Although the convention 'heard' occurs in relation to the sound base, which is devoid of the nature of the seen, etc., it proceeds in dependence on the first, etc., which are seen, sensed, and cognized, just like 'second,' 'third,' etc. Thus he says: 'Because it is to be spoken of in reference to the seen, etc.' For this meaning is clarified thus: 'sutaṃ' is so called because it is not 'unheard.'

Attanā paṭividdhā suttassa pakāravisesā evanti therena paccāmaṭṭhāti āha – “asammohaṃ dīpetī”ti. Nānappakārappaṭivedhasamattho hotīti etena vakkhamānassa suttassa nānappakārataṃ duppaṭivijjhatañca dasseti. Sutassa asammosaṃ dīpetīti sutākārassa yāthāvato dassiyamānattā vuttaṃ. Asammohenāti sammohābhāvena, paññāya eva vā savanakālasambhūtāya taduttarikālapaññāsiddhi. Evaṃ asammosenāti etthāpi vattabbaṃ. Byañjanānaṃ paṭivijjhitabbo ākāro nātigambhīro, yathāsutadhāraṇameva tattha karaṇīyanti satiyā byāpāro adhiko, paññā tattha guṇībhūtāti vuttaṃ – “paññāpubbaṅgamāyā”tiādi “paññāya pubbaṅgamā”ti katvā. Pubbaṅgamatā cettha padhānabhāvo “manopubbaṅgamā”tiādīsu (dha. pa. 1, 2) viya, pubbaṅgamatāya vā cakkhuviññāṇādīsu āvajjanādīnaṃ viya appadhānatte paññā pubbaṅgamā etissāti ayampi attho yujjati, evaṃ satipubbaṅgamāyāti etthāpi vuttanayānusārena yathāsambhavamattho veditabbo. Atthabyañjanasampannassāti atthabyañjanaparipuṇṇassa, saṅkāsanappakāsanavivaraṇavibhajanauttānīkaraṇapaññattivasena chahi atthapadehi akkharapadabyañjanākāraniruttiniddesavasena chahi byañjanapadehi ca samannāgatassāti vā attho daṭṭhabbo.

'The special kinds of the sutta penetrated by himself are thus reviewed by the Elder.' Thus he says: 'It indicates non-delusion.' By this, he shows that he is capable of penetrating the various kinds, and thus shows the diversity and difficulty of penetration of the sutta about to be spoken. 'It indicates the non-forgetting of what was heard' is said because the mode of what was heard is shown as it really is. 'By non-delusion' means by the absence of delusion; or, by the wisdom that arose at the time of hearing, the attainment of subsequent wisdom is accomplished. The same should be said here for 'by non-forgetting.' The mode of the phrasing to be penetrated is not too profound; what should be done there is simply to retain it as heard. Thus the activity of mindfulness is predominant, and wisdom is secondary. So it is said: 'preceded by wisdom,' etc., taking it as 'wisdom is its forerunner.' Here, 'being the forerunner' can mean being primary, as in 'mind is the forerunner' (Dhp 1, 2). Or, 'being the forerunner' can mean being secondary, as attention, etc., are for eye-consciousness, etc. In that case, the meaning 'wisdom is its forerunner' is also fitting. Similarly, in the case of 'preceded by mindfulness,' the meaning should be understood as is appropriate according to the stated method. 'Endowed with meaning and phrasing' means complete in meaning and phrasing. Or, the meaning should be seen as: endowed with the six aspects of meaning—namely, indication, elucidation, exposition, analysis, making plain, and designation—and with the six aspects of phrasing—namely, letters, words, phrases, style, etymology, and definition.

Yonisomanasikāraṃ [V 1.0028] dīpeti evaṃ-saddena vuccamānānaṃ ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇatthānaṃ aviparītasaddhammavisayattāti adhippāyo. Avikkhepaṃ dīpetīti “cittapariyādānaṃ kattha bhāsita”ntiādipucchāvase pakaraṇappattassa vakkhamānassa suttassa savanaṃ samādhānamantarena na sambhavatīti katvā vuttaṃ. Vikkhittacittassātiādi tassevatthassa samatthanavasena vuttaṃ. Sabbasampattiyāti atthabyañjanadesakappayojanādisampattiyā. Aviparītasaddhammavisayehi viya ākāranidassanāvadhāraṇatthehi yonisomanasikārassa, saddhammassavanena viya ca avikkhepassa yathā yonisomanasikārena phalabhūtena attasammāpaṇidhipubbekatapuññatānaṃ siddhi vuttā [M 1.0031] tadavinābhāvato. Evaṃ avikkhepena phalabhūtena kāraṇabhūtānaṃ saddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayānaṃ siddhi dassetabbā siyā assutavato sappurisūpanissayarahitassa ca tadabhāvato. Na hi vikkhittacittotiādinā samatthanavacanena pana avikkhepena kāraṇabhūtena sappurisūpanissayena ca phalabhūtassa saddhammassavanassa siddhi dassitā. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo yutto siyā, saddhammassavanasappurisūpanissayā na ekantena avikkhepassa kāraṇaṃ bāhiraṅgattā, avikkhepo pana sappurisūpanissayo viya saddhammassavanassa ekantakāraṇanti. Evampi avikkhepena sappurisūpanissayasiddhijotanā na samatthitāva. No na samatthitā vikkhittacittānaṃ sappurisapayirupāsanābhāvassa atthasiddhattā. Ettha ca purimaṃ phalena kāraṇassa siddhidassanaṃ nadīpūrena viya upari vuṭṭhisabbhāvassa, dutiyaṃ kāraṇena phalassa siddhidassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ ekantavassinā viya meghavuṭṭhānena vuṭṭhippavattiyā.

It indicates wise attention. The intention is that the meanings of mode, demonstration, and determination, which are expressed by the word 'evaṃ,' have the undistorted good Dhamma as their object. It indicates non-distraction. This is said because, on the occasion of a question such as, 'Where is the mastery of the mind spoken of?', the hearing of the sutta about to be explained, which is relevant to the treatise, is not possible without concentration. The phrase beginning 'For one with a distracted mind' is stated to support this very meaning. 'By all accomplishment' means by the accomplishment of meaning, phrasing, the speaker, the purpose, etc. Just as the accomplishment of right self-direction and of having made merit in the past is stated through wise attention as the fruit—due to their inseparability—like the accomplishment of wise attention through the meanings of mode, demonstration, and determination, which have the undistorted good Dhamma as their object, and like that of non-distraction through hearing the good Dhamma. So too, by non-distraction as the fruit, the accomplishment of the causes—hearing the good Dhamma and association with superior persons—should be shown, because for one who has not heard and who lacks association with superior persons, it is absent. But by the supporting statement beginning 'For not for one with a distracted mind...', the accomplishment of hearing the good Dhamma, which is the fruit, is shown through non-distraction and association with superior persons as the cause. Here this intention would be fitting: hearing the good Dhamma and association with superior persons are not the exclusive cause of non-distraction, as they are external conditions. But non-distraction, like association with superior persons, is an exclusive cause of hearing the good Dhamma. Even so, the demonstration of the accomplishment of association with superior persons by means of non-distraction is not supported. No, it is not unsupported, because it is implicitly established that those with distracted minds do not associate with superior persons. And here, the first—the demonstration of the accomplishment of the cause by the fruit—should be seen like inferring the existence of rain upstream from the flooding of a river. The second—the demonstration of the accomplishment of the fruit by the cause—should be seen like the occurrence of rain from the rising of a cloud that will certainly bring rain.

Bhagavato vacanassa atthabyañjanappabhedaparicchedavasena sakalasāsanasampattiogāhanākāro niravasesaparahitapāripūritākāraṇanti vuttaṃ – “evaṃ bhaddako ākāro”ti. Yasmā na hotīti sambandho. Pacchimacakkadvayasampattinti attasammāpaṇidhipubbekatapuññatāsaṅkhātaguṇadvayaṃ. Aparāparaṃ vuttiyā cettha cakkabhāvo, caranti etehi sattā sampattibhavesūti vā. Ye sandhāya vuttaṃ – “cattārimāni, bhikkhave, cakkāni, yehi samannāgatānaṃ devamanussānaṃ catucakkaṃ vattatī”tiādi (a. ni. 4.31). Purimapacchimabhāvo cettha desanākkamavasena daṭṭhabbo. Pacchimacakkadvayasiddhiyāti pacchimacakkadvayassa atthitāya. Sammāpaṇihitatto pubbe ca katapuñño suddhāsayo hoti tadasiddhihetūnaṃ kilesānaṃ dūrībhāvatoti āha – “āsayasuddhi siddhā hotī”ti. Tathā hi vuttaṃ – “sammāpaṇihitaṃ cittaṃ, seyyaso naṃ tato kare”ti (dha. pa. 43), “katapuññosi tvaṃ, ānanda, padhānamanuyuñja, khippaṃ hohisi anāsavo”ti (dī. ni. 2.207) ca. Tenevāha – “āsayasuddhiyā adhigamabyattisiddhī”ti. Payogasuddhiyāti yonisomanasikārapubbaṅgamassa dhammassavanappayogassa visadabhāvena. Tathā cāha – “āgamabyattisiddhī”ti[V 1.0029], sabbassa vā kāyavacīpayogassa niddosabhāvena. Parisuddhakāyavacīpayogo hi vippaṭisārābhāvato avikkhittacitto pariyattiyaṃ visārado hotīti.

The manner of encompassing all the excellence of the Teaching through the classification of meaning and wording in the Blessed One’s speech is said to be complete in every way for the welfare of others—thus, it is said, “this is an excellent manner.” Because it is not thus—this is the connection. The attainment of the latter two wheels—this refers to the pair of qualities known as right self-resolution and previously performed merit. Here, the nature of a wheel lies in the continuous activity, or because beings fare on through fortunate existences by means of these. This is said with reference to: “Bhikkhus, there are these four wheels. When gods and humans possess them, the four wheels turn for them,” and so on (AN 4.31). Here, the earlier and later aspects should be understood according to the order of the teaching. By the accomplishment of the latter two wheels—that is, by their existence—one whose self is rightly directed and who has previously made merit has a pure disposition, since the defilements that are the causes of its non-accomplishment are far removed. Thus, it is said: “Purity of disposition is accomplished.” For it is said: “A rightly directed mind makes one better than that” (Dhp 43), and “You, Ānanda, have made merit. Apply yourself to striving, and you will quickly become free from taints” (DN 16). Therefore, it is said: “Through purity of disposition, the accomplishment of attainment and competence is achieved.” Through purity of practice—by the clarity of the practice of listening to the Dhamma, preceded by wise attention. Thus, it is also said: “The accomplishment of learning and competence is achieved,” or by the faultlessness of all bodily and verbal action. For one whose bodily and verbal action is entirely pure, being free from remorse and with an undistracted mind, becomes skilled in the scriptural learning.

Nānappakārapaṭivedhadīpakenātiādinā [M 1.0032] atthabyañjanesu therassa evaṃ-saddasuta-saddānaṃ asammohadīpanato catuppaṭisambhidāvasena atthayojanaṃ dasseti. Tattha sotappabhedapaṭivedhadīpakenāti etena ayaṃ suta-saddo evaṃ-saddasannidhānato, vakkhamānāpekkhāya vā sāmaññeneva sotabbadhammavisesaṃ āmasatīti dasseti. Manodiṭṭhikaraṇānaṃ pariyattidhammānaṃ anupekkhanasuppaṭivedhā visesato manasikārappaṭibaddhāti te vuttanayena yonisomanasikāradīpakena evaṃ-saddena yojetvā, savanadhāraṇavacīparicayā pariyattidhammā visesena sotāvadhānappaṭibaddhāti te avikkhepadīpakena suta-saddena yojetvā dassento sāsanasampattiyā dhammassavane ussāhaṃ janeti. Tattha dhammāti pariyattidhammā. Manasā anupekkhitāti “idha sīlaṃ kathitaṃ, idha samādhi, idha paññā, ettakā ettha anusandhayo”tiādinā nayena manasā anu anu pekkhitā. Diṭṭhiyā suppaṭividdhāti nijjhānakkhanti bhūtāya, ñātapariññāsaṅkhātāya vā diṭṭhiyā tattha tattha vuttarūpārūpadhamme “iti rūpaṃ, ettakaṃ rūpa”ntiādinā suṭṭhu vavatthapetvā paṭividdhā.

“By illuminating the various kinds of penetration,” etc.: in the meanings and expressions, the Elder demonstrates the connection of meaning through the fourfold analytical knowledge, as this dispels confusion regarding the words ‘thus’ and ‘heard.’ Herein, “by illuminating the penetration of the varieties of what is heard”: by this it is shown that the word ‘heard,’ either by its proximity to the word ‘thus’ or by consideration of what is to be said, generally touches upon the special qualities of the Dhamma to be heard. The teachings of the scriptural learning are objects for the mind and for view, are well penetrated by contemplation, and are especially connected to mental application. By connecting these with the word ‘thus,’ which illuminates wise attention in the way described, and by connecting the word ‘heard,’ which illuminates non-distraction, with the teachings of the scriptural learning—which through listening, retention, and verbal practice are especially connected to attentive hearing—he inspires enthusiasm for listening to the Dhamma as an accomplishment of the Teaching. Herein, ‘Dhamma’ refers to the teachings of the scriptural learning. ‘Contemplated by the mind’ means contemplated again and again by the mind in this way: “Here virtue is taught, here concentration, here wisdom; these are the connections here,” and so on. ‘Well penetrated by view’ means that the material and immaterial phenomena spoken of in the various contexts—such as “this is form, this much is form”—are thoroughly established and penetrated by the view that has become reflective acceptance, or by the view designated as full understanding by knowledge.

Sakalena vacanenāti pubbe tīhi padehi visuṃ visuṃ yojitattā vuttaṃ. Asappurisabhūminti akataññutaṃ, “idhekacco pāpabhikkhu tathāgatappaveditaṃ dhammavinayaṃ pariyāpuṇitvā attano dahatī”ti (pārā. 195) evaṃ vuttaṃ anariyavohārāvatthaṃ. Sā eva anariyavohārāvatthā asaddhammo. Nanu ca ānandattherassa “mamedaṃ vacana”nti adhimānassa, mahākassapattherādīnañca tadāsaṅkāya abhāvato asappurisabhūmisamatikkamādivacanaṃ niratthakanti? Nayidamevaṃ, “evaṃ me suta”nti vadantena ayampi attho vibhāvitoti dassanato. Keci pana “devatānaṃ parivitakkāpekkhaṃ tathāvacananti edisī codanā anavakāsā”ti vadanti. Tasmiṃ kira khaṇe ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi “bhagavā parinibbuto, ayañca āyasmā desanākusalo idāni dhammaṃ deseti, sakyakulappasuto tathāgatassa bhātā cūḷapituputto, kiṃ nu kho sayaṃ sacchikataṃ dhammaṃ deseti, udāhu bhagavato eva vacanaṃ yathāsuta”nti, evaṃ tadāsaṅkitappakārato asappurisabhūmisamokkamādito atikkamādi vibhāvitanti. Attano adahantoti “mameda”nti attani aṭṭhapento. Appetīti [M 1.0033] nidasseti. Diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthesu yathārahaṃ satte netīti netti, dhammoyeva netti dhammanetti.

“With the whole utterance”: this is said because it was previously connected separately with the three words. “The plane of an unworthy person” refers to ingratitude, the state of ignoble conduct spoken of thus: “Here, some bad bhikkhu, having learned the Dhamma and Vinaya proclaimed by the Tathāgata, claims it for himself” (Vin Pār 1:1). That very state of ignoble conduct is the ignoble teaching. But is not the statement about transcending the plane of an unworthy person and so on meaningless, since the Venerable Ānanda had no conceit of thinking, “This is my utterance,” and the great elders such as the Venerable Mahākassapa had no such suspicion of him? This is not so, for by saying, “Thus have I heard,” this meaning too is clarified by way of illustration. Some, however, say: “Such a statement is made in anticipation of the reflections of deities, and thus there is no room for such an objection.” At that moment, it is said, a thought arose in the minds of certain deities: “The Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, and this venerable one, skilled in teaching, now teaches the Dhamma. He was born into the Sakyan clan, a cousin of the Tathāgata, the son of his paternal uncle. Now, does he teach a Dhamma he has realized himself, or is it the Blessed One’s utterance just as he heard it?” Thus, by precluding this kind of suspicion, the transcending of the descent into the plane of an unworthy person is clarified. “Claiming it for oneself” means establishing it in oneself with the thought, “This is mine.” “He applies it” means he points it out as his. Because it leads beings appropriately in matters concerning the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal, it is a guide (netti); the Dhamma itself is the guide, the Dhamma-guide (dhammanetti).

Daḷhataraniviṭṭhā [V 1.0030] vicikicchā kaṅkhā. Nātisaṃsappanaṃ matibhedamattaṃ vimati. Assaddhiyaṃ vināseti bhagavatā bhāsitattā sammukhā cassa paṭiggahitattā khalitaduruttādiggahaṇadosābhāvato ca. Ettha ca pañcamādayo tisso atthayojanā ākārādiatthesu aggahitavisesameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā dassitā, tato parā catasso ākāratthameva evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā vibhāvitā, pacchimā pana tisso yathākkamaṃ ākāratthaṃ nidassanatthaṃ avadhāraṇatthañca evaṃ-saddaṃ gahetvā yojitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

Wavering (kaṅkhā) is doubt (vicikicchā) that is more firmly established. Perplexity (vimati) is not an excessive vacillation, but a mere difference of opinion. It destroys lack of faith because it was spoken by the Blessed One, because it was received in his presence, and because there is an absence of the fault of grasping slips, poor expressions, and so on. Here, the three applications of meaning beginning with the fifth are shown by taking the word ‘thus’ in the sense of characteristic, etc., without a specific instance being taken. Then, the next four are explained by taking the word ‘thus’ only in the sense of a characteristic. The final three, however, should be understood as being connected by taking the word ‘thus’ sequentially in the sense of a characteristic, in the sense of an illustration, and in the sense of emphasis.

Eka-saddo aññaseṭṭhaasahāyasaṅkhādīsu dissati. Tathā hesa “sassato attā ca loko ca, idameva saccaṃ moghamaññanti ittheke abhivadantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.27) aññatthe dissati, “cetaso ekodibhāva”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.228; pārā. 11) seṭṭhe, “eko vūpakaṭṭho”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.405; 2.215; ma. ni. 1.80; saṃ. ni. 3.63; cūḷava. 445) asahāye “ekova kho, bhikkhave, khaṇo ca samayo ca brahmacariyavāsāyā”tiādīsu (a. ni. 8.29) saṅkhāyaṃ. Idhāpi saṅkhāyanti dassento āha – “ekanti gaṇanaparicchedaniddeso”ti. Kālañca samayañcāti yuttakālañca paccayasāmaggiñca. Khaṇoti okāso. Tathāgatuppādādiko hi maggabrahmacariyassa okāso tappaccayappaṭilābhahetuttā. Khaṇo eva ca samayo. Yo khaṇoti ca samayoti ca vuccati, so eko evāti hi attho. Mahāsamayoti mahāsamūho. Samayopi khoti sikkhāpadapūraṇassa hetupi. Samayappavādaketi diṭṭhippavādake. Tattha hi nisinnā titthiyā attano attano samayaṃ pavadantīti. Atthābhisamayāti hitappaṭilābhā. Abhisametabboti abhisamayo, abhisamayo attho abhisamayaṭṭhoti pīḷanādīni abhisametabbabhāvena ekībhāvaṃ upanetvā vuttāni. Abhisamayassa vā paṭivedhassa visayabhūto attho abhisamayaṭṭhoti tāneva tathā ekattena vuttāni. Tattha [M 1.0034] pīḷanaṃ dukkhasaccassa taṃsamaṅgino hiṃsanaṃ avipphārikatākaraṇaṃ. Santāpo dukkhadukkhatādivasena santapanaṃ paridahanaṃ.

The word ‘one’ (eka) is seen in the senses of ‘other,’ ‘chief,’ ‘solitary,’ ‘number,’ etc. For it is seen in the sense of ‘other’ in such passages as: “‘The self and the world are eternal; this alone is true, anything else is wrong,’ thus some proclaim” (MN 102). It is seen in the sense of ‘chief’ in such passages as: “unification of mind” (DN 9). It is seen in the sense of ‘solitary’ in such passages as: “alone and secluded” (DN 16; MN 12; SN 35.63; Vin Cv 10). It is seen in the sense of ‘number’ in such passages as: “Bhikkhus, there is only one opportunity and occasion for living the holy life” (AN 8.29). Here too it indicates number, thus he says: “‘One’ is an indication defining a count.” “Time and occasion” means a suitable time and a conjunction of conditions. “Opportunity” (khaṇa) means a favorable chance. For the arising of a Tathāgata and so on is an opportunity for the holy life on the path, since it is a cause for obtaining the conditions for it. An opportunity is also an occasion (samaya). The meaning is that what is called an opportunity and an occasion is one and the same. “A great occasion” (mahāsamayo) means a great assembly. An occasion (samayo) is also a cause for fulfilling the training rules. “Proclaimers of doctrines” (samayappavādakā) means proclaimers of views. For there the sectarians sit and proclaim their respective doctrines. “Breakthrough to the goal” (atthābhisamayo) means the attainment of what is beneficial. That which is to be realized (abhisametabba) is a breakthrough (abhisamayo). The goal that is a breakthrough is the ‘goal of breakthrough’ (abhisamayaṭṭho); thus, things like ‘oppression’ are spoken of, having been brought to a state of unity by their nature of being things to be realized. Or, the goal that is the object of breakthrough or penetration is the ‘goal of breakthrough’ (abhisamayaṭṭho); therefore those same terms are spoken of as being unified in that way. Herein, ‘oppression’ (pīḷana), in relation to the truth of suffering, is the harming of one who possesses it and the causing of non-prosperity. ‘Torment’ (santāpo) is the burning and scorching by way of the suffering due to pain and so on.

Tattha sahakārikāraṇe sanijjhaṃ sameti samavetīti samayo, samavāyo. Sameti samāgacchati ettha maggabrahmacariyaṃ tadādhārapuggalehīti samayo, khaṇo. Sameti ettha, etena vā saṃgacchati satto, sabhāvadhammo vā sahajātādīhi, uppādādīhi vāti samayo, kālo. Dhammappavattimattatāya atthato abhūtopi hi kālo dhammappavattiyā adhikaraṇaṃ karaṇaṃ viya ca kappanāmattasiddhena rūpena voharīyatīti. Samaṃ, saha vā avayavānaṃ ayanaṃ pavatti avaṭṭhānanti samayo, samūho yathā “samudāyo”ti. Avayavasahāvaṭṭhānameva hi samūhoti. Avasesapaccayānaṃ [V 1.0031] samāgame eti phalaṃ etasmā uppajjati pavattati cāti samayo, hetu yathā “samudayo”ti. Sameti saṃyojanabhāvato sambaddho eti attano visaye pavattati, daḷhaggahaṇabhāvato vā saṃyuttā ayanti pavattanti sattā yathābhinivesaṃ etenāti samayo, diṭṭhi. Diṭṭhisaṃyojanena hi sattā ativiya bajjhantīti. Samiti saṅgati samodhānanti samayo, paṭilābho. Samassa yānaṃ, sammā vā yānaṃ apagamoti samayo, pahānaṃ. Abhimukhaṃ ñāṇena sammā etabbo abhisametabboti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ aviparīto sabhāvo. Abhimukhabhāvena sammā eti gacchati bujjhatīti abhisamayo, dhammānaṃ aviparītasabhāvāvabodho. Evaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ atthe samayasaddassa pavatti veditabbā. Samayasaddassa atthuddhāre abhisamayasaddassa udāharaṇaṃ vuttanayena veditabbaṃ. Assāti samayasaddassa. Kālo attho samavāyādīnaṃ atthānaṃ idha asambhavato, desadesakaparisānaṃ viya suttassa nidānabhāvena kālassa apadisitabbato ca.

Herein, in the sense of a contributory cause, because something comes together (sameti) or concurs (samaveti), it is a ‘samaya,’ a ‘conjunction’ (samavāya). Because the holy life of the path comes together (sameti) or converges (samāgacchati) here upon the persons who are its basis, it is a ‘samaya,’ an ‘occasion’ (khaṇo). Because a being or a natural phenomenon comes together (saṃgacchati) here, or by means of this, with its conascent conditions, etc., or with its arising, etc., it is a ‘samaya,’ ‘time’ (kālo). For although time is in reality non-existent, being merely the occurrence of phenomena, it is spoken of in a form established by mere convention as if it were a basis and an instrument for the occurrence of phenomena. Because the going (ayanaṃ), occurrence (pavatti), or state (avaṭṭhānaṃ) of parts is even (samaṃ) or simultaneous (saha), it is a ‘samaya,’ a ‘collection’ (samūho), as in ‘aggregate’ (samudāyo). For a collection is just the co-existence of parts. When the remaining conditions come together, the fruit ‘comes’ (eti) from this, it arises and proceeds, thus it is a ‘samaya,’ a ‘cause’ (hetu), as in ‘origin’ (samudayo). Because, being connected by way of being a fetter, it ‘comes together’ (sameti), ‘comes’ (eti), and proceeds in its own domain; or, because of being firmly grasped, beings, being yoked, ‘go’ (ayanti) and proceed according to their adherence by means of this, it is a ‘samaya,’ a ‘view’ (diṭṭhi). For beings are very tightly bound by the fetter of views. A meeting (samiti), a coming together (saṅgati), a convergence (samodhānaṃ) is a ‘samaya,’ an ‘attainment’ (paṭilābho). The ‘going’ (yānaṃ) to peace (samassa), or the right ‘going’ (sammā yānaṃ) which is departure, is a ‘samaya,’ ‘abandonment’ (pahānaṃ). Because it is to be rightly ‘gone to’ (sammā etabbo) or fully understood (abhisametabbo) directly with knowledge, it is ‘penetration’ (abhisamayo), which is the unperverted nature of phenomena. Because, by way of facing it directly, one rightly ‘comes’ (eti), goes (gacchati), and awakens (bujjhati), it is ‘penetration’ (abhisamayo), which is the understanding of the unperverted nature of phenomena. Thus the usage of the word ‘samaya’ is to be understood in each respective meaning. In the extraction of the meaning of the word ‘samaya,’ the example of the word ‘abhisamaya’ should be understood in the way stated. Of this word ‘samaya,’ the meaning is ‘time’ (kālo), because the meanings of conjunction, etc., are not possible here, and because time is to be indicated as the basis of the sutta, just as for the country, the teacher, and the assembly.

Kasmā panettha aniyamitavaseneva kālo niddiṭṭho, na utusaṃvaccharādivasena niyametvāti āha – “tattha kiñcāpī”tiādi. Utusaṃvaccharādivasena niyamaṃ akatvā samayasaddassa vacane ayampi guṇo laddho hotīti dassento “ye vā ime”tiādimāha. Sāmaññajotanā hi visese avatiṭṭhatīti. Tattha diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo devasikaṃ jhānasamāpattīhi vītināmanakālo, visesato sattasattāhāni. Suppakāsāti dasasahassilokadhātuyā pakampanaobhāsapātubhāvādīhi [M 1.0035] pākaṭā. Yathāvuttabhedesu eva samayesu ekadesaṃ pakārantarehi saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ “yo cāya”ntiādimāha. Tathā hi ñāṇakiccasamayo attahitappaṭipattisamayo ca abhisambodhisamayo, ariyatuṇhībhāvasamayo diṭṭhadhammasukhavihārasamayo, karuṇākiccaparahitappaṭipattidhammikathāsamayo desanāsamayoyeva.

Why is time indicated here in an unspecified way, not defined by way of seasons, years, and so on? He says: 'Therein, although,' etc. Showing that by not making a definition by way of seasons, years, etc., this advantage is also gained in the use of the word 'samaya,' he says: 'Or these,' etc. For a general indication stands on the particular. Therein, the 'occasion of dwelling happily in this very life' is the time of passing the days with the attainments of jhāna, especially the seven weeks. 'Well-proclaimed' means made manifest by the quaking, the appearance of a radiance, etc., in the ten-thousand-world-system. To show one part of the occasions with the distinctions as stated, by collecting them under other modes, he says: 'And this,' etc. For the 'occasion for the function of knowledge' and the 'occasion for the practice for one's own welfare' is the 'occasion of full enlightenment'; the 'occasion of noble silence' is the 'occasion of dwelling happily in this very life'; the 'occasion for the function of compassion, the practice for the welfare of others, and talk on the Dhamma' is the 'occasion of teaching' itself.

Karaṇavacanena niddeso katoti sambandho. Tatthāti abhidhammavinayesu. Tathāti bhummakaraṇehi. Adhikaraṇattho ādhārattho. Bhāvo nāma kiriyā, kiriyāya kiriyantaralakkhaṇaṃ bhāvenabhāvalakkhaṇaṃ.
