Tattha yathā kālo sabhāvadhammaparicchinno sayaṃ paramatthato avijjamānopi ādhārabhāvena paññāto taṅkhaṇappavattānaṃ tato pubbe parato ca abhāvato “pubbaṇhe jāto, sāyanhe gacchatī”ti ca ādīsu, samūho ca avayavavinimutto avijjamānopi kappanāmattasiddho avayavānaṃ ādhārabhāvena paññāpīyati “rukkhe sākhā, yavarāsiyaṃ sambhūto”tiādīsu, evaṃ idhāpīti dassento āha – “adhikaraṇaṃ…pe… dhammāna”nti. Yasmiṃ kāle, dhammapuñje vā kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ eva kāle, dhammapuñje [V 1.0032] ca phassādayopi hontīti ayañhi tattha attho. Yathā “gāvīsu duyhamānāsu gato, duddhāsu āgato”ti dohanakiriyāya gamanakiriyā lakkhīyati, evaṃ idhāpi “yasmiṃ samaye, tasmiṃ samaye”ti ca vutte “satī”ti ayamattho viññāyamāno eva hoti padatthassa sattāvirahābhāvatoti samayassa sattākiriyāya cittassa uppādakiriyā, phassādīnaṃ bhavanakiriyā ca lakkhīyatīti. Yasmiṃ samayeti yasmiṃ navame khaṇe, yasmiṃ yonisomanasikārādihetumhi, paccayasamavāye vā sati kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tasmiṃyeva khaṇe hetumhi paccayasamavāye ca phassādayopi hontīti ubhayattha samayasadde bhummaniddeso kato lakkhaṇabhūtabhāvayuttoti dassento āha – “khaṇa…pe… lakkhīyatī”ti.

The connection is: 'The indication is made with the instrumental expression.' 'Therein' means in the Abhidhamma and Vinaya. 'Thus' means by the locative and instrumental cases. The meaning of 'locative' is the meaning of 'basis.' 'Being' (bhāva) is an action; the marking of one action by another action is the 'locative absolute.' Therein, just as time, which is delimited by natural phenomena and is itself non-existent in the ultimate sense, is designated as a basis because of the non-existence before and after of things occurring at that moment, as in 'he was born in the morning, he goes in the evening,' etc.; and just as a collection, which is non-existent apart from its components and established by mere convention, is designated as a basis for its components, as in 'a branch on a tree,' 'produced in a heap of barley,' etc.; so too here, he shows this by saying: 'the basis… of phenomena.' When a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen at a certain time or in a certain collection of phenomena, at that very time and in that very collection of phenomena contact and so on also exist—this is the meaning here. Just as in 'he went while the cows were being milked, he returned when they had been milked,' the action of going is marked by the action of milking, so too here, when 'at which time... at that time' is said, the meaning 'being present' is understood, because the meaning of the word does not lack existence. Thus, by the action of the existence of the occasion, the action of the arising of consciousness and the action of the being of contact, etc., are marked. 'At which time' means: when a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen at the ninth moment, or when a cause such as wise attention is present, or when a conjunction of conditions is present, at that very moment, cause, or conjunction of conditions, contact and so on also exist. Thus, showing that in both places the word 'samaya' is indicated in the locative case, connected with the state of being a mark, he says: 'the moment… is marked.'

Hetuattho karaṇattho ca sambhavati “annena vasati, ajjhenena vasati, pharasunā chindati, kudālena khaṇatī”tiādīsu viya. Vītikkamañhi sutvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā otiṇṇe vatthusmiṃ taṃ puggalaṃ paṭipucchitvā [M 1.0036] vigarahitvā ca taṃ taṃ vatthuṃ otiṇṇakālaṃ anatikkamitvā teneva kālena sikkhāpadāni paññāpento bhagavā viharati sikkhāpadapaññattihetuñca apekkhamāno tatiyapārājikādīsu viya.

The meaning of 'cause' and 'instrument' are possible, as in such examples as 'he lives on food,' 'he dwells by study,' 'he cuts with an axe,' 'he digs with a spade.' For having heard of a transgression, the Blessed One has the Sangha of bhikkhus assembled, and when the case has come up, having interrogated and reproached that person, without letting the time when that case occurred pass by, he lays down the training rules at that very time, while also having regard for the reason for laying down the training rule, as in the case of the third pārājika and so on.

Accantameva ārambhato paṭṭhāya yāva desanāniṭṭhānaṃ parahitappaṭipattisaṅkhātena karuṇāvihārena. Tadatthajotanatthanti accantasaṃyogatthajotanatthaṃ. Upayogavacananiddeso kato yathā “māsaṃ ajjhetī”ti. Porāṇāti aṭṭhakathācariyā. Abhilāpamattabhedoti vacanamattena viseso. Tena suttavinayesu vibhattibyattayo katoti dasseti.

Continuously from the beginning right up to the conclusion of the discourse, with the abiding in compassion reckoned as the practice for the welfare of others. 'To illuminate its meaning' means to illuminate the meaning of continuous connection. The indication is made with an expression of duration, as in 'he studies for a month.' 'The ancients' means the commentary masters. 'A difference in mere phrasing' means a distinction by mere speech. By this he shows that in the Suttas and the Vinaya an interchange of case endings is made.

Idāni “bhagavā”ti imassa atthaṃ dassento āha – “bhagavāti garū”tiādi. Bhagavāti vacanaṃ seṭṭhanti seṭṭhavācakaṃ vacanaṃ, seṭṭhaguṇasahacaraṇaṃ seṭṭhanti vuttaṃ. Atha vā vuccatīti vacanaṃ, attho. Yasmā yo “bhagavā”ti vacanena vacanīyo attho, so seṭṭhoti attho. Bhagavāti vacanamuttamanti etthāpi eseva nayo. Gāravayuttoti garubhāvayutto garuguṇayogato. Garukaraṇaṃ vā sātisayaṃ arahatīti gāravayutto, gāravārahoti attho. Sippādisikkhāpakā garū honti, na ca gāravayuttā, ayaṃ pana tādiso na hoti, tasmā garūti vatvā gāravayuttoti vuttanti keci. Vuttoyeva, na idha vattabbo visuddhimaggassa imissā aṭṭhakathāya ekadesabhāvatoti adhippāyo.

Now, showing the meaning of 'Bhagavā,' he says: 'Bhagavā means venerable,' etc. 'The word Bhagavā is the best' means it is a word denoting the best, said to be the best because it is accompanied by the best qualities. Or, 'word' (vacana) is what is spoken, the meaning. Since the meaning to be expressed by the word 'Bhagavā' is the best, this is the meaning. The same method applies also here to 'The word Bhagavā is the highest.' 'Worthy of reverence' means endowed with the state of being venerable because of connection with venerable qualities. Or, he is 'worthy of reverence' because he deserves exceptional veneration; the meaning is 'deserving of reverence.' Teachers of crafts and so on are 'venerable,' but they are not 'worthy of reverence'; this one, however, is not like that. Therefore, some say, having said 'venerable,' it is said 'worthy of reverence.' It has already been said; it should not be repeated here. The intention is that the Visuddhimagga is a part of this commentary.

Dhammasarīraṃ paccakkhaṃ karotīti “yo vo, ānanda, mayā dhammo ca vinayo ca desito paññatto[V 1.0033], so vo mamaccayena satthā”ti (dī. ni. 2.216) vacanato dhammassa satthubhāvapariyāyo vijjatīti katvā vuttaṃ. Vajirasaṅghātasamānakāyo parehi abhejjasarīrattā. Na hi bhagavato rūpakāye kenaci sakkā antarāyo kātunti. Desanāsampattiṃ niddisati vakkhamānassa sakalasuttassa evanti niddisanato. Sāvakasampattiṃ niddisati paṭisambhidāpattena pañcasu ṭhānesu bhagavatā etadagge ṭhapitena mayā mahāsāvakena sutaṃ, tañca kho mayā sutaṃ, na anussutikaṃ, na paramparābhatanti imassa atthassa dīpanato. Kālasampattiṃ niddisati “bhagavā”ti padassa sannidhāne payuttassa samayasaddassa kālassa buddhuppādappaṭimaṇḍitabhāvadīpanato[M 1.0037]. Buddhuppādaparamā hi kālasampadā. Tenetaṃ vuccati –

'He makes the Dhamma-body directly perceptible.' This is said because, according to the statement, 'Ānanda, the Dhamma and Vinaya that I have taught and laid down for you, that shall be your Teacher after I am gone' (DN 16), there exists a way in which the Dhamma is the Teacher. His body is like a diamond conglomerate because his body is unbreakable by others. For no one is able to cause injury to the Blessed One's physical body. He indicates the perfection of the teaching by the indication of the entire sutta to be spoken with the word 'Thus.' He indicates the perfection of the disciple by explaining the meaning of: 'It was heard by me, a great disciple who has attained the analytical knowledges and was placed by the Blessed One as the foremost in five respects; and what was heard by me was truly heard, not from oral tradition, not handed down in a lineage.' He indicates the perfection of the time by explaining that the time of the word 'samaya,' used in proximity to the word 'Bhagavā,' is adorned with the arising of a Buddha. For the perfection of time is supreme with the arising of a Buddha. Therefore this is said:

“Kappakasāye kaliyuge, buddhuppādo aho mahacchariyaṃ;

Hutāvahamajjhe jātaṃ, samuditamakarandamaravinda”nti. (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.1; saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.1 devatāsaṃyutta);

In the Kali Yuga, the dregs of the aeon, the arising of a Buddha is a great wonder! It is like a lotus with its nectar arisen, born in the midst of a sacrificial fire.

Bhagavāti desakasampattiṃ niddisati guṇavisiṭṭhasattuttamagarugāravādhivacanabhāvato.

'Bhagavā' indicates the perfection of the speaker because it is a designation for the best of beings, who is distinguished by qualities, venerable, and worthy of reverence.

Evaṃnāmake nagareti kathaṃ panetaṃ nagaraṃ evaṃnāmakaṃ jātanti? Vuccate, yathā kākandassa isino nivāsaṭṭhāne māpitā nagarī kākandī, mākandassa nivāsaṭṭhāne māpitā mākandī, kusambassa nivāsaṭṭhāne māpitā kosambīti vuccati, evaṃ savatthassa isino nivāsaṭṭhāne māpitā nagarī sāvatthīti vuccati. Evaṃ tāva akkharacintakā vadanti. Aṭṭhakathācariyā pana bhaṇanti – “yaṃ kiñci manussānaṃ upabhogaparibhogaṃ, sabbamettha atthī”ti sāvatthi. Satthasamāyoge ca ‘kiṃ bhaṇḍamatthī’ti pucchite ‘sabbamatthī’ti vacanamupādāya sāvatthi.

Regarding the city so named, how did this city come to be so named? It is said: Just as the city built at the dwelling place of the sage Kākanda is called Kākandī, the one built at the dwelling place of Mākanda is called Mākandī, and the one built at the dwelling place of Kusamba is called Kosambī, so the city built at the dwelling place of the sage Savattha is called Sāvatthī. Thus say the etymologists. The commentators, however, say: 'Because whatever is for human consumption and use, all of it is here (sabbam ettha atthi),' it is called Sāvatthī. And because, at a gathering of a caravan, when asked, 'What goods are there?' the reply was, 'Everything is there (sabbam atthi),' it is called Sāvatthī.

“Sabbadā sabbūpakaraṇaṃ, sāvatthiyaṃ samohitaṃ;

Tasmā sabbamupādāya, sāvatthīti pavuccati. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.14; khu. pā. aṭṭha. 5.maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanā; udā. aṭṭha. 5; paṭi. ma. 2.1.184);

Always, all kinds of provisions are gathered in Sāvatthī; therefore, on account of 'everything,' it is called Sāvatthī.

“Kosalānaṃ puraṃ rammaṃ, dassaneyyaṃ manoramaṃ;

Dasahi saddehi avivittaṃ, annapānasamāyutaṃ.

The delightful city of the Kosalans, fair to see and charming, never devoid of the ten sounds, endowed with food and drink.

“Vuddhiṃ [V 1.0034] vepullataṃ pattaṃ, iddhaṃ phītaṃ manoramaṃ;

Āḷakamandāva devānaṃ, sāvatthipuramuttama”nti. (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.14; khu. pā. aṭṭha. 5.maṅgalasuttavaṇṇanā);

Having reached growth and full development, successful, prosperous, and delightful, the supreme city of Sāvatthī is like Āḷakamandā of the gods.

Avisesenāti na visesena, vihārabhāvasāmaññenāti attho. Iriyāpathavihāro…pe… vihāresūti iriyāpathavihāro dibbavihāro brahmavihāro ariyavihāroti etesu catūsu vihāresu. Samaṅgiparidīpananti samaṅgibhāvaparidīpanaṃ. Etanti viharatīti etaṃ padaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ “idhekacco gihisaṃsaṭṭho viharati sahanandī sahasokī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 4.241) iriyāpathavihāre āgataṃ, “yasmiṃ samaye, bhikkhave, bhikkhu vivicceva kāmehi [M 1.0038]… paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharatī”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 499; vibha. 624) dibbavihāre, “so mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.556; 3.308; ma. ni. 1.77, 459, 509; 2.309, 315, 451, 471; 3.230, vibha. 642, 643) brahmavihāre, “so khohaṃ, aggivessana, tassāyeva kathāya pariyosāne tasmiṃyeva purimasmiṃ samādhinimitte ajjhattameva cittaṃ saṇṭhapemi sannisādemi ekodiṃ karomi, samādahāmi, yena sudaṃ niccakappaṃ viharāmī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.387) ariyavihāre.

'Not specifically' means not in a special sense, but in the general sense of the state of dwelling; that is the meaning. 'Dwelling by way of posture... among the dwellings': this refers to these four dwellings: the dwelling by way of posture, the divine dwelling, the sublime dwelling, and the noble dwelling. 'An exposition of being endowed' means an exposition of the state of being endowed. 'This' refers to the word 'dwells.' For it is found in reference to the dwelling by way of posture in such passages as: 'Here, someone dwells associating with householders, rejoicing with them and sorrowing with them.' It is found in reference to the divine dwelling in such passages as: 'When, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu, quite secluded from sensual pleasures... having entered, dwells in the first jhāna.' It is found in reference to the sublime dwelling in such passages as: 'He dwells pervading one direction with a mind accompanied by loving-kindness.' It is found in reference to the noble dwelling in such passages as: 'Then I, Aggivessana, at the very conclusion of that talk, on that same, former sign of concentration, inwardly establish my mind, settle it down, unify it, and concentrate it, whereby I dwell for a very long time.'

Tattha iriyanaṃ pavattanaṃ iriyā, kāyappayogo. Tassā pavattanūpāyabhāvato ṭhānādi iriyāpatho. Ṭhānasamaṅgī vā hi kāyena kiñci kareyya gamanādīsu aññatarasamaṅgī vā. Atha vā iriyati pavattati etena attabhāvo, kāyakiccaṃ vāti iriyā, tassā pavattiyā upāyabhāvato pathoti iriyāpatho, ṭhānādi eva. So ca atthato gatinivattiādiākārena pavatto catusantatirūpappabandho eva. Viharaṇaṃ, viharati etenāti vā vihāro. Divi bhavo dibbo, tattha bahulappavattiyā brahmapārisajjādidevaloke bhavoti attho. Tattha yo dibbānubhāvo, tadatthāya saṃvattatīti vā dibbo, abhiññābhinīhāravasena mahāgatikattā vā dibbo, dibbo ca so vihāro cāti dibbavihāro, catasso rūpāvacarasamāpattiyo. Arūpasamāpattiyopi ettheva saṅgahaṃ gacchanti. Brahmānaṃ, brahmāno vā vihārā brahmavihārā, catasso appamaññāyo. Ariyo, ariyānaṃ vā vihāro ariyavihāro, cattāri sāmaññaphalāni. So hi ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanantiādi yadipi bhagavā ekenapi iriyāpathena cirataraṃ kālaṃ attabhāvaṃ pavattetuṃ sakkoti, tathāpi upādinnakasarīrassa ayaṃ sabhāvoti dassetuṃ vuttaṃ. Yasmā vā bhagavā yattha katthaci vasanto veneyyānaṃ dhammaṃ desento nānāsamāpattīhi [V 1.0035] ca kālaṃ vītināmento vasatīti sattānaṃ attano ca vividhahitasukhaṃ harati upaneti uppādeti, tasmā vividhaṃ haratīti viharatīti evamettha attho veditabbo.

Herein, moving, setting in motion, is iriyā; it is bodily application. Because it is a means for setting it in motion, standing and so on are called the iriyāpatha (path of movement). For one might do something with the body while endowed with the posture of standing, or while endowed with walking, and so on. Or, the individual existence (attabhāvo) is moved, is set in motion by this, or it is a bodily function, thus it is iriyā. Because it is a means for its movement, it is a path (patha), hence iriyāpatha, that is, standing and so on. In essence, this is just the continuum of the fourfold continuity of material form, proceeding by way of moving forward, stopping, etc. Dwelling (viharaṇaṃ), or that by which one dwells (viharati), is a dwelling (vihāro). 'Being in heaven' (divi bhavo) is divine (dibbo); the meaning is being in a deva world such as that of the Brahmā hosts, where it frequently occurs. Or it is 'divine' because it conduces to that divine state; or because it has a great range by the power of direct knowledge and aspiration. That which is divine and is a dwelling is a 'divine dwelling' (dibbavihāro); these are the four form-sphere attainments. The formless attainments are also included here. The dwellings of the Brahmas, or of Brahmas, are the 'sublime dwellings' (brahmavihārā); these are the four immeasurables. The noble dwelling, or the dwelling of the noble ones, is the 'noble dwelling' (ariyavihāro); these are the four fruits of recluseship. As to 'the affliction of one posture,' etc., although the Blessed One is able to sustain his individual existence for a very long time with a single posture, this is said to show that this is the nature of the body that has been clung to. Or, because the Blessed One, dwelling anywhere, teaching the Dhamma to those who can be trained and passing the time with various attainments, brings (harati), conveys, and generates diverse (vividha) welfare and happiness for beings and for himself, therefore 'he dwells' (viharati) means 'he brings diversely' (vividhaṃ harati). This is the meaning to be understood here.

Jetassa [M 1.0039] rājakumārassāti ettha attano paccatthikajanaṃ jinātīti jeto. Sotasaddo viya hi kattusādhano jetasaddo. Atha vā raññā pasenadikosalena attano paccatthikajane jite jātoti jeto. Rañño hi jayaṃ āropetvā kumāro jitavāti jetoti vutto. Maṅgalakāmatāya vā tassa evaṃnāmameva katanti jeto. Maṅgalakāmatāya hi jeyyoti etasmiṃ atthe jetoti vuttaṃ. Vitthāro panātiādinā “anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme”ti ettha sudatto nāma so, gahapati, mātāpitūhi katanāmavasena, sabbakāmasamiddhatāya pana vigatamaccheratāya karuṇādiguṇasamaṅgitāya ca niccakālaṃ anāthānaṃ piṇḍamadāsi. Tena anāthapiṇḍikoti saṅkhaṃ gato. Āramanti ettha pāṇino, visesena vā pabbajitāti ārāmo, tassa pupphaphalādisobhāya nātidūranaccāsannatādipañcavidhasenāsanaṅgasampattiyā ca tato tato āgamma ramanti abhiramanti, anukkaṇṭhitā hutvā nivasantīti attho. Vuttappakārāya vā sampattiyā tattha tattha gatepi attano abbhantaraṃyeva ānetvā rametīti ārāmo. So hi anāthapiṇḍikena gahapatinā jetassa rājakumārassa hatthato aṭṭhārasahiraññakoṭīhi santhārena kiṇitvā aṭṭhārasahiraññakoṭīhi senāsanāni kārāpetvā aṭṭhārasahiraññakoṭīhi vihāramahaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā evaṃ catupaññāsahiraññakoṭipariccāgena buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa niyyātito, tasmā “anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāmo”ti vuccatīti imamatthaṃ nidasseti.

Herein, regarding 'of Prince Jeta': he is called Jeta because he conquers (jināti) his enemies. The word jeta is an agent noun, like the word sota. Or, he is called Jeta because he was born after King Pasenadi of Kosala had conquered his enemies. For the victory was ascribed to the king, and the prince was called Jeta as if he had conquered. Or, out of a desire for an auspicious name, he was just named thus. For out of a desire for auspiciousness, he was called Jeta in the sense of 'one who should be victorious' (jeyya). By 'The detailed explanation...' etc., he indicates the meaning of 'in Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.' Herein, that householder's name given by his parents was Sudatta. But because he was successful in all his wishes, was free from avarice, and was endowed with such qualities as compassion, he always gave alms (piṇḍa) to the destitute (anātha). Thus he came to be known as Anāthapiṇḍika. 'Beings delight (āramanti) here, or especially the renunciants, thus it is a park (ārāmo).' The meaning is that because of the beauty of its flowers and fruits, and its possession of the five factors of a lodging—such as being not too far and not too near—they come from here and there and delight, take pleasure, and dwell there without anxiety. Or, because of its aforesaid assets, even when they have gone elsewhere, it brings them back into its fold, as it were, and makes them delight, thus it is a park. This park was purchased by the householder Anāthapiṇḍika from Prince Jeta by covering the ground with eighteen crores of gold coins; he had lodgings built for another eighteen crores; and he completed the monastery's dedication festival for another eighteen crores. Having thus made a donation of fifty-four crores of gold coins, he dedicated it to the Sangha of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head. Therefore it is called 'Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.' This is the meaning he indicates.

Tatthāti “ekaṃ samayaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ vākyaṃ, tattha. Siyāti kassaci evaṃ parivitakko siyā, vakkhamānākārena kadāci codeyya vāti attho. Atha tattha viharatīti yadi jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme viharati. Na vattabbanti nānāṭhānabhūtattā sāvatthijetavanānaṃ, “ekaṃ samaya”nti ca vuttattāti adhippāyo. Idāni codako tameva attano adhippāyaṃ “na hi sakkā”tiādinā vivarati. Itaro sabbametaṃ aviparītaṃ atthaṃ ajānantena tayā vuttanti dassento “na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabba”ntiādimāha. Tattha etanti “sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme”ti etaṃ vacanaṃ. Evanti “yadi tāva bhagavā”tiādinā [M 1.0040] yaṃ taṃ bhavatā coditaṃ, taṃ atthato evaṃ na kho pana daṭṭhabbaṃ, na ubhayattha apubbaṃ acarimaṃ vihāradassanatthanti attho. Idāni attanā yathādhippetaṃ aviparītamatthaṃ, tassa ca paṭikacceva vuttabhāvaṃ, tena ca appaṭividdhataṃ pakāsento “nanu avocumha…pe… jetavane”ti āha. Evampi [V 1.0036] “jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme viharati”cceva vattabbaṃ, na “sāvatthiya”nti codanaṃ manasi katvā vuttaṃ – “gocaragāmanidassanattha”ntiādi.

'Therein' refers to the statement: 'At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.' 'It might be': some person might have this thought; the meaning is that one might sometimes raise an objection in the way that will be stated. 'Then if he was dwelling there': if he was dwelling in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park, then 'at Sāvatthī' should not be said. The intention is that this is because Sāvatthī and Jeta's Grove are different places, and because 'at one time' has been said. Now the objector explains his own intention with 'For it is not possible....' The other, showing that 'all this was said by you without knowing the correct meaning,' says, 'But this should not be seen thus....' Herein, 'this' is the statement 'was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park.' 'Thus' means: what was objected to by you with the words 'If indeed the Blessed One...' should not be seen thus in its meaning. The meaning is that it is not for the purpose of showing a dwelling in both places simultaneously. Now, explaining the correct meaning as he himself intends it, and that it was stated from the start, and that this has not been penetrated by the objector, he says: 'Did we not say... in Jeta's Grove?' Even so, having kept in mind the objection that one should say only 'was dwelling in Jeta's Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika's Park,' and not 'at Sāvatthī,' it was said: 'For the purpose of indicating the alms-round village,' etc.

Avassañcettha gocaragāmakittanaṃ kattabbaṃ. Tathā hi taṃ yathā jetavanādikittanaṃ pabbajitānuggahakaraṇādianekappayojanaṃ, evaṃ gocaragāmakittanampi gahaṭṭhānuggahakaraṇādivividhapayojananti dassento “sāvatthivacanenā”tiādimāha. Tattha paccayaggahaṇena upasaṅkamapayirupāsanānaṃ okāsadānena dhammadesanāya saraṇesu sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpanena yathūpanissayaṃ uparivisesādhigamāvahanena ca gahaṭṭhānuggahakaraṇaṃ, uggahaparipucchānaṃ kammaṭṭhānānuyogassa ca anurūpavasanaṭṭhānapariggahenettha pabbajitānuggahakaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ. Karuṇāya upagamanaṃ, na lābhādinimittaṃ. Paññāya apagamanaṃ, na virodhādinimittanti upagamanāpagamanānaṃ nirupakkilesataṃ vibhāveti. Dhammikasukhaṃ nāma anavajjasukhaṃ. Devatānaṃ upakārabahulatā janavivittatāya. Pacurajanavivittañhi ṭhānaṃ devā upasaṅkamitabbaṃ maññanti. Tadatthaparinipphādananti lokatthanipphādanaṃ, buddhakiccasampādananti attho. Evamādināti ādi-saddena sāvatthikittanena rūpakāyassa anuggaṇhanaṃ dasseti, jetavanādikittanena dhammakāyassa. Tathā purimena parādhīnakiriyākaraṇaṃ, dutiyena attādhīnakiriyākaraṇaṃ. Purimena vā karuṇākiccaṃ, itarena paññākiccaṃ. Purimena cassa paramāya anukampāya samannāgamaṃ, pacchimena paramāya upekkhāya samannāgamaṃ dīpeti. Bhagavā hi sabbasatte paramāya anukampāya anukampati, na ca tattha sinehadosānupatito paramupekkhakabhāvato. Upekkhako ca na parahitasukhakaraṇe appossukko mahākāruṇikabhāvato. Tassa mahākāruṇikatāya lokanāthatā, upekkhakatāya attanāthatā.

And here the praise of the alms-resort village should be made. For just as the praise of Jetavana and so on serves many purposes, such as supporting the renunciants, so the praise of the alms-resort village serves various purposes, such as supporting the householders. To show this, he says, “by the word Sāvatthī,” and so on. Here, support for householders is to be understood as the granting of opportunity for them to approach and attend upon him by accepting their requisites, as teaching them the Dhamma, establishing them in the refuges and precepts, and leading them to the attainment of higher distinctions in accordance with their supporting conditions. Support for the renunciants is to be understood as the selection of a suitable dwelling place for study, inquiry, and the practice of the meditation subject. He clarifies the unblemished nature of his approaching and departing, thus: his approaching is out of compassion, not for the sake of gain and so on; his departing is through wisdom, not on account of conflict and so on. Righteous happiness means blameless happiness. The great helpfulness of the deities is due to its seclusion from people; for deities consider a place secluded from many people as fit to be approached. “The accomplishment of that purpose” means the accomplishment of the world’s welfare; the meaning is the accomplishment of the Buddha’s mission. By “and so on”: with this word he shows that the praise of Sāvatthī indicates the maintenance of the physical body, and the praise of Jetavana and so on, the maintenance of the Dhamma body. So too, the former indicates the performance of an action dependent on others, the second the performance of an action dependent on oneself. Or the former is the task of compassion, the latter the task of wisdom. The former shows his possession of supreme compassion, the latter his possession of supreme equanimity. For the Blessed One has compassion for all beings with supreme compassion, yet he is not drawn into the fault of affection because he possesses supreme equanimity. And though equanimous, he is not unconcerned with promoting the welfare and happiness of others because he is greatly compassionate. Through his great compassion he is the protector of the world; through his equanimity he is his own protector.

Tathā hesa bodhisattabhūto mahākaruṇāya sañcoditamānaso sakalalokahitāya ussukkamāpanno mahābhinīhārato paṭṭhāya [M 1.0041] tadatthanipphādanatthaṃ puññañāṇasambhāre sampādento aparimitaṃ kālaṃ anappakaṃ dukkhamanubhosi, upekkhakatāya sammā patitehi dukkhehi na vikampitatā. Mahākāruṇikatāya saṃsārābhimukhatā, upekkhakatāya tato nibbindanā. Tathā upekkhakatāya nibbānābhimukhatā, mahākāruṇikatāya tadadhigamo. Tathā mahākāruṇikatāya paresaṃ ahiṃsāpanaṃ, upekkhakatāya sayaṃ parehi abhāyanaṃ. Mahākāruṇikatāya paraṃ rakkhato attano rakkhaṇaṃ, upekkhakatāya attānaṃ rakkhato paresaṃ rakkhaṇaṃ. Tenassa attahitāya paṭipannādīsu catutthapuggalabhāvo siddho hoti. Tathā mahākāruṇikatāya saccādhiṭṭhānassa ca cāgādhiṭṭhānassa ca pāripūrī, upekkhakatāya upasamādhiṭṭhānassa ca paññādhiṭṭhānassa ca pāripūrī[V 1.0037]. Evaṃ purisuddhāsayappayogassa mahākāruṇikatāya lokahitatthameva rajjasampadādibhavasampattiyā upagamanaṃ, upekkhakatāya tiṇāyapi amaññamānassa tato apagamanaṃ. Iti suvisuddhaupagamāpagamassa mahākāruṇikatāya lokahitatthameva dānavasena sampattīnaṃ pariccajanā, upekkhakatāya cassa phalassa attano apaccāsīsanā. Evaṃ samudāgamanato paṭṭhāya acchariyabbhutaguṇasamannāgatassa mahākāruṇikatāya paresaṃ hitasukhatthaṃ atidukkarakāritā, upekkhakatāya kāyampi analaṅkāritā.

Thus, when he was a Bodhisatta, with a mind impelled by great compassion, he exerted himself for the welfare of the entire world. Beginning from his great aspiration, in order to accomplish that purpose, he fulfilled the accumulations of merit and knowledge and endured no little suffering for an immeasurable time; yet through his equanimity he was not shaken by the sufferings that rightly befell him. Through his great compassion he faced towards saṃsāra; through his equanimity he was disenchanted with it. So too, through his equanimity he faced towards Nibbāna; through his great compassion he attained it. So too, through his great compassion he caused others no harm; through his equanimity he himself was not harmed by others. Through his great compassion, in protecting others he protected himself; through his equanimity, in protecting himself he protected others. Thereby his status as the fourth person—one who is practicing for the welfare of both himself and others—was established. So too, through his great compassion there was the fulfillment of the resolution on truth and the resolution on relinquishment; through his equanimity there was the fulfillment of the resolution on calm and the resolution on wisdom. Thus for him, whose intention and effort were pure, through his great compassion he took up royal fortune and other forms of worldly success only for the welfare of the world; through his equanimity he departed from them, regarding them as no more than a blade of grass. Thus for him, whose approaching and departing were utterly pure, through his great compassion he relinquished his acquisitions by way of giving only for the welfare of the world; through his equanimity he did not hope for any fruit for himself. Thus, from the time of his first arising, being endowed with wonderful and marvelous qualities, through his great compassion he performed extremely difficult deeds for the welfare and happiness of others; through his equanimity he did not even adorn his body.

Tathā mahākāruṇikatāya carimattabhāve jiṇṇāturamatadassanena sañjātasaṃvego, upekkhakatāya uḷāresu devabhogasadisesu bhogesu nirapekkho mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhami. Tathā mahākāruṇikatāya “kicchaṃ vatāyaṃ loko āpanno”tiādinā (dī. ni. 2.57; saṃ. ni. 2.4, 10) karuṇāmukheneva vipassanārambho, upekkhakatāya buddhabhūtassa satta sattāhāni vivekasukheneva vītināmanaṃ. Mahākāruṇikatāya dhammagambhīrataṃ paccavekkhitvā dhammadesanāya appossukkanaṃ āpajjitvāpi mahābrahmuno ajjhesanāpadesena okāsakaraṇaṃ, upekkhakatāya pañcavaggiyādiveneyyānaṃ ananurūpasamudācārepi anaññathābhāvo. Mahākāruṇikatāya katthaci paṭighātābhāvenassa sabbattha amittasaññābhāvo, upekkhakatāya katthacipi anurodhābhāvena sabbattha sinehasanthavābhāvo. Mahākāruṇikatāya paresaṃ pasādanā, upekkhakatāya [M 1.0042] pasannākārehi na vikampanā. Mahākāruṇikatāya dhammānurāgābhāvena tattha ācariyamuṭṭhiabhāvo, upekkhakatāya sāvakānurāgābhāvena parivāraparikammatābhāvo. Mahākāruṇikatāya dhammaṃ desetuṃ parehi saṃsaggamupagacchatopi upekkhakatāya na tattha abhirati. Mahākāruṇikatāya gāmādīnaṃ āsannaṭṭhāne vasatopi upekkhakatāya araññaṭṭhāne eva viharaṇaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “purimenassa paramāya anukampāya samannāgamaṃ dīpetī”ti.

So too, through great compassion, in his last existence, he felt a sense of urgency on seeing an old man, a sick man, and a dead man; and through equanimity, being unconcerned with magnificent enjoyments similar to divine enjoyments, he went forth in the great renunciation. So too, through great compassion, his commencement of insight was by way of compassion, with the thought: “Alas, this world has fallen into trouble”; through equanimity, after he became a Buddha, he passed seven weeks solely in the bliss of seclusion. Through great compassion, though he had become disinclined to teach the Dhamma after reflecting on its profundity, he granted the opportunity on the pretext of Mahābrahmā’s request; through equanimity, he was unperturbed even by the improper conduct of the group of five and other disciples. Through great compassion, since he had no aversion toward anyone, he had no perception of an enemy anywhere; through equanimity, since he had no partiality toward anyone, he had no affection or intimacy anywhere. Through great compassion, he inspired confidence in others; through equanimity, he was not shaken by their expressions of confidence. Through great compassion, since he had no attachment to the Dhamma, he did not have a “teacher’s fist” in regard to it; through equanimity, since he had no attachment to his disciples, he did not groom a retinue. Through great compassion, though he associated with others to teach the Dhamma, through equanimity he took no delight in that. Through great compassion, though he lived in a place near a village, etc., through equanimity he dwelt as if in a forest. Therefore it was said: “The former shows his possession of supreme compassion.”

Tanti tatrāti padaṃ. “Desakālaparidīpana”nti ye desakālā idha viharaṇakiriyāvisesanabhāvena vuttā, tesaṃ paridīpananti dassento “yaṃ samayaṃ…pe… dīpetī”ti āha. Taṃ-saddo hi vuttassa atthassa paṭiniddeso, tasmā idha kālassa desassa vā paṭiniddeso bhavitumarahati, na aññassa. Ayaṃ tāva tatra-saddassa paṭiniddesabhāve atthavibhāvanā. Yasmā pana īdisesu ṭhānesu tatra-saddo dhammadesanāvisiṭṭhaṃ desakālañca vibhāveti, tasmā vuttaṃ – “bhāsitabbayutte vā desakāle dīpetī”ti. Tena tatrāti yatra bhagavā dhammadesanatthaṃ bhikkhū ālapati bhāsati, tādise dese, kāle vāti attho. Na hītiādinā tamevatthaṃ samattheti. Nanu ca yattha ṭhito bhagavā “akālo kho tāvā”tiādinā [V 1.0038] bāhiyassa dhammadesanaṃ paṭikkhipi, tattheva antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhito tassa dhammaṃ desesīti? Saccametaṃ, adesetabbakāle adesanāya idaṃ udāharaṇaṃ. Tenevāha – “akālo kho tāvā”ti.

The word is tatra. “Clarification of place and time”: To show that this means the clarification of the places and times that have been stated here as qualifiers of the act of dwelling, he says: “It indicates the time when… etc.” That word is a reference to what has been stated; therefore here it must be a reference to the time or place, not to anything else. This, in the first place, is the explanation of the meaning of the word tatra in its function as a reference. But since in such contexts the word tatra clarifies the place and time specified for the teaching of the Dhamma, it is therefore said: “Or it indicates the place and time suitable for speaking.” Thus the meaning of tatra is: in such a place or at such a time when the Blessed One addresses the bhikkhus in order to teach the Dhamma. By “For not…” etc., he supports this same meaning. But did not the Blessed One, standing in the very place where he had rejected Bāhiya’s request to teach the Dhamma, saying, “It is not the time, Bāhiya,” then teach him the Dhamma right there in the middle of the street? This is true. This is an example of not teaching at an unsuitable time. For that reason he said: “It is not the time, Bāhiya.”

Yaṃ pana tattha vuttaṃ – “antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhamhā”ti, tampi tassa akālabhāvasseva pariyāyena dassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Tassa hi tadā addhānaparissamena rūpakāye akammaññatā ahosi, balavapītivegena nāmakāye. Tadubhayassa vūpasamaṃ āgamento papañcaparihāratthaṃ bhagavā “akālo kho”ti pariyāyena paṭikkhipi. Adesetabbadese adesanāya pana udāharaṇaṃ “atha kho bhagavā maggā okkamma aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi (saṃ. ni. 2.154), vihārapacchāyāyaṃ paññatte āsane nisīdī”ti (dī. ni. 1.363) ca evamādikaṃ idha ādisaddena saṅgahitaṃ. “Atha kho so, bhikkhave, bālo idha pubbe nesādo idha pāpāni kammāni karitvā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.251) padapūraṇamatte kho-saddo, “dukkhaṃ kho agāravo viharati [M 1.0043] appatisso”tiādīsu (a. ni. 4.21) avadhāraṇe, “kittāvatā nu kho, āvuso, satthu pavivittassa viharato sāvakā vivekaṃ nānusikkhantī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.31) ādikālatthe, vākyārambheti attho. Tattha padapūraṇena vacanālaṅkāramattaṃ kataṃ hoti, ādikālatthena vākyassa upaññāsamattaṃ. Avadhāraṇatthena pana niyamadassanaṃ, tasmā āmantesi evāti āmantane niyamo dassito hoti.

As for what was said there, “We have entered among the houses,” that too was said to show indirectly that it was an unsuitable time for him. For at that time, his physical body was unwieldy due to the fatigue of the journey, and his mental body due to the powerful impact of joy. Waiting for both of these to subside, the Blessed One rejected him indirectly with the words, “It is not the time,” in order to avoid proliferation. An example of not teaching in an unsuitable place is included here by the word “and so on,” referring to such passages as: “Then the Blessed One stepped off the road and sat down at the foot of a certain tree” and “He sat down on the prepared seat in the shade of the monastery.” In such passages as, “Then, bhikkhus, that fool, having formerly been a fowler here, having done evil deeds here…,” the word kho is a mere expletive. In such passages as, “It is painful, indeed, to live without reverence, without deference,” it has the sense of emphasis. In such passages as, “To what extent, friends, do the disciples not train in seclusion when the Teacher is dwelling in seclusion?” it has the sense of initial time, meaning the start of a sentence. There, as an expletive it serves merely as a verbal ornament; as indicating initial time it merely introduces the statement. But in the sense of emphasis it shows a delimitation. Thus it shows the delimitation in the addressing, as “he addressed them indeed.”

Bhagavāti lokagarudīpananti kasmā vuttaṃ, nanu pubbepi bhagavāsaddassa attho vuttoti? Yadipi vutto, taṃ panassa yathāvutte ṭhāne viharaṇakiriyāya kattu visesadassanatthaṃ kataṃ, na āmantanakiriyāya, idha pana āmantanakiriyāya, tasmā tadatthaṃ puna “bhagavā”ti pāḷiyaṃ vuttanti tassatthaṃ dassetuṃ “bhagavāti lokagarudīpana”nti āha. Tena lokagarubhāvato tadanurūpaṃ paṭipattiṃ patthento attano santikaṃ upagatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ dhammaṃ desetuṃ te āmantesīti dasseti. Kathāsavanayuttapuggalavacananti vakkhamānāya cittapariyādānadesanāya savanayoggapuggalavacanaṃ. Catūsupi parisāsu bhikkhū eva edisānaṃ desanānaṃ visesena bhājanabhūtāti sātisayaṃ sāsanasampaṭiggāhakabhāvadassanatthaṃ idha bhikkhuggahaṇanti dassetvā idāni saddatthaṃ dassetuṃ “apicā”tiādimāha. Tattha bhikkhakoti bhikkhūti bhikkhanadhammatāya bhikkhūti attho. Bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti buddhādīhi ajjhupagataṃ bhikkhācariyaṃ, uñchācariyaṃ, ajjhupagatattā anuṭṭhitattā bhikkhu. Yo hi appaṃ vā mahantaṃ vā bhogakkhandhaṃ pahāya agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito, so kasigorakkhādijīvikākappanaṃ hitvā liṅgasampaṭicchaneneva [V 1.0039] bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatattā bhikkhu, parappaṭibaddhajīvikattā vā vihāramajjhe kājabhattaṃ bhuñjamānopi bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhu, piṇḍiyālopabhojanaṃ nissāya pabbajjāya ussāhajātattā vā bhikkhācariyaṃ ajjhupagatoti bhikkhūti evamettha attho daṭṭhabbo. Ādinā nayenāti “chinnabhinnapaṭadharoti bhikkhu, bhindati pāpake akusale dhammeti bhikkhu, bhinnattā pāpakānaṃ akusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ bhikkhū”tiādinā (vibha. 510) vibhaṅge āgatanayena. Ñāpaneti avabodhane, paṭivedaneti attho.

Why was it said, 'The Blessed One is the elucidation of the one revered by the world'? Was not the meaning of the word 'Blessed One' already explained before? Even if it was explained, that was done to show the distinction of the agent in the act of dwelling in the aforementioned place, not in the act of addressing. Here, however, it is for the act of addressing. Therefore, to show that meaning, it is said again in the Pāli, 'The Blessed One,' and to clarify its meaning, it is stated, 'The Blessed One is the elucidation of the one revered by the world.' By this, it shows that, because he is revered by the world, he addressed the bhikkhus who had come to him, desiring to teach them the Dhamma in accordance with their dispositions, as is befitting. 'A statement to persons fit to hear the discourse' refers to the discourse on the cleansing of the mind that is about to be spoken, a statement to persons suitable for hearing. Among the four assemblies, bhikkhus are especially the vessels for such teachings; hence the mention of 'bhikkhus' here is to highlight their exceptional capacity to receive the Dispensation. Now, to explain the meaning of the word, it begins with 'Moreover….' Here, 'bhikkhu' means one who begs; the meaning is 'bhikkhu' because of the nature of begging. 'One who has undertaken the alms-round': because one has undertaken the alms-round and the practice of gleaning undertaken by the Buddhas and others, and has not abandoned it, one is a bhikkhu. For whoever, having abandoned a small or great mass of wealth, goes forth from the household life into homelessness, and having given up livelihoods such as agriculture and cattle-herding, has undertaken the alms-round simply by accepting the emblem, is a bhikkhu. Or, because one's livelihood is dependent on others, even while eating food in the monastery, one has undertaken the alms-round and is thus a bhikkhu. Or, because zeal for the going-forth has arisen by relying on the meal of alms-morsels, one has undertaken the alms-round and is thus a bhikkhu. In this way the meaning should be understood here. 'By such a method' refers to the method found in the Vibhaṅga: 'A bhikkhu is one who wears patched and torn robes; a bhikkhu is one because he breaks up evil, unwholesome states; a bhikkhu is one because of the breaking up of evil, unwholesome states,' and so on. 'Making known' (ñāpana) is in the sense of awakening (avabodhana); the meaning is penetration (paṭivedana).

Bhikkhanasīlatāti [M 1.0044] bhikkhanena jīvanasīlatā, na kasivāṇijjādinā jīvanasīlatā. Bhikkhanadhammatāti “uddissa ariyā tiṭṭhantī”ti (jā. 1.7.59) evaṃ vuttā bhikkhanasabhāvatā, na yācanakohaññasabhāvatā. Bhikkhane sādhukāritāti “uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyyā”ti (dha. pa. 168) vacanaṃ anussaritvā tattha appamajjanā. Atha vā sīlaṃ nāma pakatisabhāvo, idha pana tadadhiṭṭhānaṃ. Dhammoti vataṃ. Sādhukāritāti sakkaccakāritā ādarakiriyā. Hīnādhikajanasevitanti ye bhikkhubhāve ṭhitāpi jātimadādivasena uddhatā unnaḷā, ye ca gihibhāve paresaṃ adhikabhāvampi anupagatattā bhikkhācariyaṃ paramakāruññataṃ maññanti, tesaṃ ubhayesampi yathākkamaṃ “bhikkhavo”ti vacanena hīnajanehi daliddehi paramakāruññataṃ pattehi parakulesu bhikkhācariyāya jīvikaṃ kappentehi sevitaṃ vuttiṃ pakāsento uddhatabhāvaniggahaṃ karoti. Adhikajanehi uḷārabhogakhattiyakulādito pabbajitehi buddhādīhi ājīvavisodhanatthaṃ sevitaṃ vuttiṃ pakāsento dīnabhāvaniggahaṃ karotīti yojetabbaṃ. Yasmā “bhikkhavo”ti vacanaṃ āmantanabhāvato abhimukhīkaraṇaṃ, pakaraṇato sāmatthiyato ca sussusājananaṃ sakkaccasavanamanasikāraniyojanañca hoti, tasmā tamatthaṃ dassento “bhikkhavoti iminā”tiādimāha. Tattha sādhukaṃ savanamanasikāreti sādhukasavane sādhukamanasikāre ca. Kathaṃ pana pavattitā savanādayo sādhukaṃ pavattitā hontīti? “Addhā imāya sammāpaṭipattiyā sakalasāsanasampatti hatthagatā bhavissatī”ti ādaragāravayogena kathādīsu aparibhavādinā ca. Vuttañhi “pañcahi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato suṇanto saddhammaṃ bhabbo niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammattaṃ. Katamehi pañcahi? Kathaṃ na paribhoti, kathitaṃ na paribhoti, na attānaṃ paribhoti, avikkhittacitto dhammaṃ suṇāti ekaggacitto, yoniso ca manasikaroti. Imehi kho, bhikkhave, pañcahi dhammehi samannāgato suṇanto saddhammaṃ bhabbo niyāmaṃ okkamituṃ kusalesu dhammesu sammatta”nti (a. ni. 5.151). Tenevāha – “sādhukaṃ savanamanasikārāyattā hi sāsanasampattī”ti.

The virtue of begging (bhikkhanasīlatā) means the virtue of living by begging, not by farming, trading, and the like. The nature of begging (bhikkhanadhammatā) is the disposition to beg as stated: 'The noble ones stand indicating their need,' not the disposition of importunate begging or hypocrisy. Diligence in begging (bhikkhane sādhukāritā) is not being heedless in this, recalling the verse: 'One should rise up and not be heedless.' Alternatively, sīla (virtue) is natural disposition, but here it is the determination for it. Dhamma is observance. Sādhukāritā (diligence) is acting carefully, an action done with respect. 'Frequented by lowly and eminent persons': This is said because the word 'bhikkhus' restrains the arrogance of those who, though established in the state of a bhikkhu, are arrogant and haughty on account of pride of birth, by pointing out that this way of life is followed by lowly, poor people who have attained supreme compassion and make their living by the alms-round in others' families. And it restrains the lowliness of those who were of humble station in lay life by pointing out that this way of life is followed by eminent persons—the Buddhas and others who have gone forth from wealthy khattiya families, etc.—for the sake of purifying their livelihood. This is how it should be construed. Because the word 'bhikkhus,' being an address, is a way of facing them, and by the power of the context, it generates a desire to listen and enjoins careful listening and attention, therefore, to show that meaning, it is said, 'By this word "bhikkhus"...' and so on. Here, 'listening and attending carefully' refers to careful listening and careful attention. But how do listening and so on, when undertaken, become undertaken carefully? By applying oneself with respect and reverence, thinking: 'Surely, through this right practice, the entire success of the Dispensation will come into my hands,' and by not disparaging the discourse, etc. For it is said: 'Bhikkhus, endowed with five qualities, a listener of the good Dhamma is capable of entering the fixed course, the rightness in wholesome states. What five? He does not disparage the discourse, he does not disparage the speaker, he does not disparage himself, he listens to the Dhamma with an unscattered and one-pointed mind, and he attends wisely. Bhikkhus, endowed with these five qualities, a listener of the good Dhamma is capable of entering the fixed course, the rightness in wholesome states.' Hence it is said: 'For the success of the Dispensation depends on careful listening and attention.'

Pubbe [V 1.0040] sabbaparisāsādhāraṇattepi bhagavato dhammadesanāya “jeṭṭhaseṭṭhā”tiādinā bhikkhūnaṃ eva āmantane kāraṇaṃ dassetvā idāni bhikkhū [M 1.0045] āmantetvāva dhammadesanāya payojanaṃ dassetuṃ “kimatthaṃ pana bhagavā”ti codanaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tattha aññaṃ cintentāti aññavihitā. Vikkhittacittāti asamāhitacittā. Dhammaṃ paccavekkhantāti hiyyo tato paraṃ divasesu vā sutadhammaṃ pati pati manasā avekkhantā. Bhikkhū āmantetvā dhamme desiyamāne ādito paṭṭhāya desanaṃ sallakkhetuṃ sakkontīti imamatthaṃ byatirekamukhena dassetuṃ “te anāmantetvā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Although previously the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma was common to all assemblies, having shown the reason for addressing only the bhikkhus with such terms as 'the eldest and the best,' now, to demonstrate the purpose of teaching the Dhamma only after addressing the bhikkhus, the commentary raises the objection: 'But for what reason...?' Here, 'thinking of something else' means their minds are directed elsewhere. 'With distracted minds' means with unconcentrated minds. 'Reflecting on the Dhamma' means mentally reviewing, again and again, the Dhamma heard on previous days. When the Dhamma is taught after addressing the bhikkhus, they are able to mark the teaching from the very beginning. To show this meaning by way of a negative example, it is said, 'without addressing them,' etc.

Bhikkhavoti cettha sandhivasena i-kāralopo daṭṭhabbo. Bhikkhavo itīti ayaṃ iti-saddo hetuparisamāpanādiatthapadatthavipariyāyapakārāvadhāraṇanidassanādianekatthappabhedo. Tathā hesa “ruppatīti kho, bhikkhave, tasmā rūpanti vuccatī”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.79) hetvatthe dissati. “Tasmātiha me, bhikkhave, dhammadāyādā bhavatha, mā āmisadāyādā. Atthi me tumhesu anukampā. Kinti me sāvakā dhammadāyādā bhaveyyuṃ, no āmisadāyādā”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 1.19) parisamāpane. “Iti vā iti evarūpā naccagītavāditavisūkadassanā paṭivirato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.13) ādiatthe. “Māgaṇḍiyoti tassa brāhmaṇassa saṅkhā samaññā paññatti vohāro nāmaṃ nāmakammaṃ nāmadheyyaṃ nirutti byañjanamabhilāpo”tiādīsu (mahāni. 73, 75) padatthavipariyāye. “Iti kho, bhikkhave, sappaṭibhayo bālo, appaṭibhayo paṇḍito, saupaddavo bālo, anupaddavo paṇḍito, saupasaggo bālo, anupasaggo paṇḍito”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.124) pakāre. “Atthi idappaccayā jarāmaraṇanti puṭṭhena satā, ‘ānanda, atthī’tissa vacanīyaṃ. ‘Kiṃ paccayā jarāmaraṇa’nti iti ce vadeyya. Jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ iccassa vacanīya”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.96) avadhāraṇe. “Atthīti kho, kaccāna, ayameko anto, natthīti kho, kaccāna, ayaṃ dutiyo anto”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 2.15; saṃ. ni. 3.90) nidassane. Idhāpi nidassane eva daṭṭhabbo. Bhikkhavoti hi āmantanākāro. Tamesa iti-saddo nidasseti “bhikkhavoti āmantesī”ti. Iminā nayena “bhaddante”tiādīsupi yathārahaṃ iti-saddassa attho veditabbo. Pubbe “bhagavā āmantesī”ti vuttattā “bhagavato paccassosu”nti [M 1.0046] idha “bhagavato”ti sāmivacanaṃ āmantanameva sambandhiantaraṃ apekkhatīti iminā adhippāyena “bhagavato āmantanaṃ paṭiassosu”nti vuttaṃ. “Bhagavato”ti pana idaṃ paṭissavasambandhena sampadānavacanaṃ yathā “devadattāya paṭissuṇotī”ti. Yaṃ nidānaṃ bhāsitanti sambandho. Imassa suttassa sukhāvagāhaṇatthanti kamalakuvalayujjalavimalasādurasasalilāya pokkharaṇiyā [V 1.0041] sukhāvataraṇatthaṃ nimmalasilātalaracanāvilāsasobhitaratanasopānaṃ vippakiṇṇamuttātalasadisavālukācuṇṇapaṇḍarabhūmibhāgaṃ titthaṃ viya suvibhattabhittivicitravedikāparikkhittassa nakkhattapathaṃ phusitukāmatāya viya paṭivijambhitasamussayassa pāsādavarassa sukhārohanatthaṃ dantamayasaṇhamuduphalakañcanalatāvinaddhamaṇigaṇappabhāsamudayujjalasobhaṃ sopānaṃ viya suvaṇṇavalayanūpurādisaṅghaṭṭanasaddasammissitassa kathitahasitamadhurassaragehajanavijambhitavicaritassa uḷāraissariyavibhavasobhitassa mahāgharassa sukhappavesanatthaṃ suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttāpavāḷādijutivissaravijjotitasuppatiṭṭhitavisāladvārabāhaṃ mahādvāraṃ viya ca atthabyañjanasampannassa buddhānaṃ desanāñāṇagambhīrabhāvasaṃsūcakassa imassa suttassa sukhāvagāhatthaṃ.

Herein, in bhikkhavoti, the elision of the vowel 'i' should be understood as due to sandhi. The word iti has various meanings, such as cause, conclusion, 'and so on,' reversal of a word's meaning, manner, delimitation, and illustration. For instance, it appears in the sense of cause in passages like: ‘It is afflicted, bhikkhus, therefore it is called form.’ It concludes discussions in statements such as: ‘Therefore, bhikkhus, be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things. I have compassion for you. How can my disciples be my heirs in the Dhamma, not my heirs in material things?’ It is used in the sense of 'and so on' in phrases like: ‘He abstains from such things as dancing, singing, music, and seeing shows.’ It reverses a word's meaning in expressions such as: ‘“Māgaṇḍiya”—this is the designation, term, concept, expression, name, act of naming, appellation, utterance, and label of that brahmin.’ It specifies the manner in statements like: ‘Thus, bhikkhus, the fool is with peril, the wise one is without peril; the fool is with affliction, the wise one is without affliction; the fool is with distress, the wise one is without distress.’ It serves for delimitation in passages such as: ‘When asked, “Does aging-and-death have this as its condition?” one should answer, “Yes, Ānanda, it does.” If asked, “With what as condition is there aging-and-death?” one should reply, “With birth as condition, there is aging-and-death.”’ It illustrates in phrases like: ‘“It exists,” Kaccāna, is one extreme; “it does not exist” is the second extreme.’ Here too, it should be understood as an illustration. For bhikkhavo is a form of address, and the word iti here points this out, as in ‘he addressed them, “Bhikkhus.”’ In the same way, the meaning of iti should be understood as appropriate in phrases like bhaddante, and so on. Since it was said previously, ‘The Blessed One addressed them,’ here the genitive bhagavato (of the Blessed One) implies a connection to the address. With this intention, it is said, ‘they replied to the Blessed One’s address.’ Alternatively, the word bhagavato is in the dative case in connection with the reply, just as in ‘he promises to Devadatta.’ The connection is that this introduction was spoken for the purpose of making this sutta easy to grasp. Just as for a lotus pond with clear, sweet, pure water, radiant with lotuses and water lilies, one might construct a bathing place with a jeweled staircase, beautiful with its construction from spotless stone slabs, and with a ground of white sand powder like a surface strewn with pearls, for the purpose of easy descent; or just as for a splendid palace, surrounded by well-proportioned walls and decorated railings, and so lofty it seems to want to touch the path of the stars, one might construct a staircase of fine, smooth ivory planks, entwined with golden creepers and radiant with the luster of a host of gems, for the purpose of easy ascent; or just as for a great mansion, resounding with the mingled sounds of speech, laughter, and sweet voices, with the bustling of its inhabitants, and splendid with the glory of great wealth and power, one might construct a great door with large, well-fixed doorposts illumined by the radiance of gold, silver, gems, pearls, and coral, for the purpose of easy entry; so too, this introduction is spoken for the purpose of making this sutta—which is endowed with meaning and phrasing and indicative of the profundity of the Buddhas’ knowledge of the teaching—easy to grasp.

Etthāha – “kimatthaṃ pana dhammavinayasaṅgahe kayiramāne nidānavacanaṃ, nanu bhagavatā bhāsitavacanasseva saṅgaho kātabbo”ti? Vuccate, desanāya ṭhitiasammosasaddheyyabhāvasampādanatthaṃ. Kāladesadesakanimittaparisāpadesehi upanibandhitvā ṭhapitā hi desanā ciraṭṭhitikā hoti asammosadhammā saddheyyā ca. Desakālakattuhetunimittehi upanibaddho viya vohāravinicchayo. Teneva ca āyasmatā mahākassapena “cittapariyādānasuttaṃ, āvuso ānanda, kattha bhāsita”ntiādinā desādipucchāsu katāsu tāsaṃ vissajjanaṃ karontena dhammabhaṇḍāgārikena “evaṃ me suta”ntiādinā imassa suttassa nidānaṃ bhāsitaṃ. Apica satthusampattippakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ. Tathāgatassa hi bhagavato pubbacaraṇānumānāgamatakkābhāvato sammāsambuddhabhāvasiddhi. Na hi sammāsambussa pubbacaraṇādīhi attho atthi sabbattha appaṭihatañāṇacāratāya ekappamāṇattā ca ñeyyadhammesu. Tathā ācariyamuṭṭhidhammamacchariyasāsanasāvakānānurāgābhāvato khīṇāsavabhāvasiddhi. Na hi sabbaso khīṇāsavassa te sambhavantīti suvisuddhassa parānuggahappavatti. Evaṃ [M 1.0047] desakasaṃkilesabhūtānaṃ diṭṭhisīlasampadādūsakānaṃ avijjātaṇhānaṃ accantābhāvasaṃsūcakehi ñāṇappahānasampadābhibyañjanakehi ca sambuddhavisuddhabhāvehi purimavesārajjadvayasiddhi, tato ca antarāyikaniyyānikadhammesu sammohābhāvasiddhito pacchimavesārajjadvayasiddhīti bhagavato catuvesārajjasamannāgamo attahitaparahitappaṭipatti ca nidānavacanena pakāsitā hoti. Tattha tattha sampattaparisāya ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ ṭhānuppattikappaṭibhānena dhammadesanādīpanato, idha pana rūpagarukānaṃ puggalānaṃ ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ ṭhānuppattikappaṭibhānena dhammadesanādīpanatoti yojetabbaṃ. Tena vuttaṃ – “satthusampattippakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacana”nti.

Here it is asked: 'But what is the purpose of stating the introduction when compiling the Dhamma and Vinaya? Surely, only the words spoken by the Blessed One should be compiled.' It is replied: It is for the purpose of establishing the teaching’s stability, incorruptibility, and credibility. For a teaching that is established by being linked with the time, place, speaker, occasion, and assembly remains long-lasting, is of an incorruptible nature, and is credible, like a legal decision that is bound up with the speaker, time, agent, cause, and occasion. And for this very reason, when the Venerable Mahākassapa asked such questions about the place and so on, saying, 'Friend Ānanda, where was the Cittapariyādāna Sutta spoken?' the treasurer of the Dhamma, in answering those questions, stated the introduction to this sutta beginning, 'Thus have I heard.' Furthermore, the statement of the introduction is for the purpose of revealing the Teacher’s accomplishment. For the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, the attainment of perfect self-enlightenment is established by the absence of prior practice, inference, tradition, and reasoning. For one who is perfectly self-enlightened has no need for prior practice and the like, because his knowledge ranges everywhere unobstructed and is of a single measure in regard to all knowable things. Likewise, the attainment of the state of one whose taints are destroyed is established by the absence of a teacher's closed fist, of stinginess with the Dhamma, and of lack of affection for the disciples of the teaching. For these do not exist at all for one whose taints are completely destroyed; thus, the activity of one who is perfectly pure proceeds for the welfare of others. In this way, through the perfectly pure states of the Buddha—which indicate the complete absence of ignorance and craving (the defilements of the speaker and corruptors of the accomplishment in view and virtue) and which manifest the accomplishment in knowledge and abandonment—the first pair of grounds of self-confidence is achieved. And from that, because of the achievement of non-delusion regarding obstructive and emancipating dhammas, the latter pair of grounds of self-confidence is achieved. Thus, the Blessed One’s possession of the four grounds of self-confidence and his practice for his own and others’ welfare are revealed by the statement of the introduction. It should be connected thus: 'because he illuminates the Dhamma teaching with ready wit concerning the right occasion, in accordance with the disposition of the assembly present on each occasion; but here, he illuminates the Dhamma teaching with ready wit concerning the right occasion, in accordance with the disposition of persons who hold form in high esteem.' Therefore it is said: 'The statement of the introduction is for the purpose of revealing the Teacher’s accomplishment.'

Tathā sāsanasampattippakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ. Ñāṇakaruṇāpariggahitasabbakiriyassa hi bhagavato [V 1.0042] natthi niratthakā paṭipatti, attahitatthā vā. Tasmā paresaṃ eva atthāya pavattasabbakiriyassa sammāsambuddhassa sakalampi kāyavacīmanokammaṃ yathāpavattaṃ vuccamānaṃ diṭṭhadhammikasamparāyikaparamatthehi yathārahaṃ sattānaṃ anusāsanaṭṭhena sāsanaṃ, na kapparacanā. Tayidaṃ satthucaritaṃ kāladesadesakaparisāpadesehi saddhiṃ tattha tattha nidānavacanehi yathārahaṃ pakāsīyati. “Idha pana rūpagarukānaṃ puggalāna”ntiādi sabbaṃ purimasadisameva. Tena vuttaṃ – “sāsanasampattippakāsanatthaṃ nidānavacana”nti. Apica satthuno pamāṇabhāvappakāsanena vacanena sāsanassa pamāṇabhāvadassanatthaṃ nidānavacanaṃ, tañca desakappamāṇabhāvadassanaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayānusārena “bhagavā”ti ca iminā padena vibhāvitanti veditabbaṃ. Bhagavāti hi tathāgatassa rāgadosamohādisabbakilesamaladuccaritadosappahānadīpanena vacanena anaññasādhāraṇasuparisuddhañāṇakaruṇādiguṇavisesayogaparidīpanena tato eva sabbasattuttamabhāvadīpanena ayamattho sabbathā pakāsito hotīti. Idamettha nidānavacanappayojanassa mukhamattanidassanaṃ.

Likewise, the introductory statement is for the purpose of revealing the accomplishment of the Teaching. For the Blessed One, all of whose actions are encompassed by knowledge and compassion, there is no practice that is useless or only for his own benefit. Therefore, all the bodily, verbal, and mental actions of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One—all of whose actions proceed only for the welfare of others—when they are recounted as they occurred, constitute the Teaching in the sense that they instruct beings appropriately in what pertains to the present life, the future life, and the ultimate good; they are not mere literary compositions. This conduct of the Teacher, together with the time, place, speaker, assembly, and occasion, is appropriately revealed by the introductory statements in each case. The phrase 'But here, for persons who hold form in high esteem,' and so on, is entirely similar to what was stated before. Hence it is said: 'The introductory statement is for the purpose of revealing the accomplishment of the Teaching.' Furthermore, the introductory statement serves to show that the Teaching is the authority by means of the statement that proclaims that the Teacher is the authority. This demonstration that the speaker is the authority should be understood as being clarified by the term 'Blessed One' in accordance with the method explained above. For the word 'Blessed One,' by revealing the Tathāgata’s abandonment of all defilements such as greed, hatred, and delusion, and the stains of misconduct, and by disclosing his possession of unparalleled, supremely pure qualities like knowledge and compassion, thereby fully reveals his status as the supreme among all beings. This here is just a brief indication of the purpose of the introductory statement.

Nikkhittassāti desitassa. Desanā hi desetabbassa sīlādiatthassa veneyyasantānesu nikkhipanato “nikkhepo”ti vuccati. Suttanikkhepaṃ vicāretvāva vuccamānā pākaṭā hotīti sāmaññato bhagavato desanāya samuṭṭhānassa vibhāgaṃ dassetvā “etthāyaṃ desanā evaṃsamuṭṭhānā”ti desanāya samuṭṭhāne dassite suttassa sammadeva nidānaparijānanena vaṇṇanāya suviññeyyattā vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā [M 1.0048] anekasataanekasahassabhedānipi suttantāni saṃkilesabhāgiyādipaṭṭhānanayavasena soḷasavidhataṃ nātivattanti, evaṃ attajjhāsayādisuttanikkhepavasena catubbidhabhāvanti āha – “cattāro hi suttanikkhepā”ti. Ettha ca yathā attajjhāsayassa aṭṭhuppattiyā ca parajjhāsayapucchāhi saddhiṃ saṃsaggabhedo sambhavati “attajjhāsayo ca parajjhāsayo ca, attajjhāsayo ca pucchāvasiko ca, aṭṭhuppattiko ca parajjhāsayo ca, aṭṭhuppattiko ca pucchāvasiko cā”ti ajjhāsayapucchānusandhisabbhāvato, evaṃ yadipi aṭṭhuppattiyā attajjhāsayenapi saṃsaggabhedo sambhavati, attajjhāsayādīhi pana purato ṭhitehi aṭṭhuppattiyā saṃsaggo natthīti na idha niravaseso vitthāranayo sambhavatīti “cattāro suttanikkhepā”ti vuttaṃ. Tadantogadhattā vā sesanikkhepānaṃ mūlanikkhepavasena cattārova dassitā. Yathādassanañhettha ayaṃ saṃsaggabhedo gahetabboti.

“Of the laid down” means of the taught. For the teaching is called a “laying down” (nikkhepa) because it lays down the meaning of virtue, etc., to be taught, in the mental continuities of those to be trained. It is said that after considering the laying down of the sutta, what is being spoken becomes clear. Thus, having generally shown the division of the origin of the Blessed One’s teaching, when the origin of the teaching is shown by the words, “Here, this teaching has such-and-such an origin,” the explanation becomes easily understandable through the correct knowledge of the sutta's source. Therein, just as the suttas, though of many hundreds and thousands of kinds, do not go beyond sixteen types by way of the method of the bases such as the portion of defilement, so too, by way of the laying down of suttas based on one’s own inclination, etc., they become fourfold. Thus he said: “For there are four layings down of suttas.” And here, just as a distinction by combination is possible for one's own inclination and for an occasion of utterance, together with another's inclination and questions—as in “one’s own inclination and another’s inclination; one’s own inclination and a question-based occasion; an occasion of utterance and another’s inclination; an occasion of utterance and a question-based occasion”—due to the existence of a connection between inclination and question, so too, although a distinction by combination is possible for an occasion of utterance with one's own inclination, since there is no combination of an occasion of utterance with one's own inclination, etc., when these stand first, an exhaustive detailed method is not possible here. Thus it is said, “There are four layings down of suttas.” Or, because the remaining layings down are included within these, only four are shown as the root layings down. And here this distinction by combination should be understood as it has been shown.

Tatrāyaṃ vacanattho – nikkhipīyatīti nikkhepo, suttaṃ eva nikkhepo suttanikkhepo. Atha vā nikkhipanaṃ nikkhepo, suttassa nikkhepo suttanikkhepo, suttadesanāti attho. Attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo, so assa atthi kāraṇabhūtoti attajjhāsayo. Attano ajjhāsayo etassāti [V 1.0043] vā attajjhāsayo. Parajjhāsayepi eseva nayo. Pucchāya vaso pucchāvaso, so etassa atthīti pucchāvasiko. Suttadesanāvatthubhūtassa atthassa uppatti atthuppatti, atthuppattiyeva aṭṭhuppatti ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā. Sā etassa atthīti aṭṭhuppattiko. Atha vā nikkhipīyati suttaṃ etenāti suttanikkhepo, attajjhāsayādi eva. Etasmiṃ atthavikappe attano ajjhāsayo attajjhāsayo. Paresaṃ ajjhāsayo parajjhāsayo. Pucchīyatīti pucchā, pucchitabbo attho. Pucchāvasena pavattaṃ dhammappaṭiggāhakānaṃ vacanaṃ pucchāvasikaṃ, tadeva nikkhepasaddāpekkhāya pulliṅgavasena vuttaṃ – “pucchāvasiko”ti. Tathā aṭṭhuppatti eva aṭṭhuppattikoti evamettha attho veditabbo.

Herein, this is the word-meaning: “It is laid down,” thus it is a “laying down” (nikkhepa); the sutta itself is a laying down, thus suttanikkhepa. Or, the act of laying down is a laying down; the laying down of the sutta is suttanikkhepo, meaning the teaching of the sutta. One's own inclination is attajjhāsayo. It exists for one as a cause, thus it is attajjhāsayo. Or, one's own inclination is of this one, thus attajjhāsayo. This same method applies to parajjhāsayo (another's inclination). Dependence on a question is pucchāvaso; this exists for one, thus one is pucchāvasiko (question-based). The arising (uppatti) of a reason (attha) that is the basis for the teaching of a sutta is atthuppatti (arising of a reason). Attha-uppatti itself becomes aṭṭhuppatti by changing the ttha to ṭṭha. This exists for one, thus one is aṭṭhuppattiko (based on an occasion of utterance). Or, the sutta is laid down by means of this, thus it is a suttanikkhepo; this refers to one's own inclination, etc. In this alternative meaning, one's own inclination is attajjhāsayo; the inclination of others is parajjhāsayo. “It is asked,” thus it is a question (pucchā), the meaning to be asked. The speech of the Dhamma-recipients that proceeds by way of a question is pucchāvasikaṃ. This same word, with reference to the word nikkhepa, is stated in the masculine gender as pucchāvasiko. Similarly, aṭṭhuppatti itself is aṭṭhuppattiko. Thus the meaning here should be understood.

Apicettha paresaṃ indriyaparipākādikāraṇanirapekkhattā attajjhāsayassa visuṃ suttanikkhepabhāvo yutto kevalaṃ attano ajjhāsayeneva dhammatantiṭṭhapanatthaṃ pavattitadesanattā. Parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ pana paresaṃ ajjhāsayapucchānaṃ desanāpavattihetubhūtānaṃ uppattiyaṃ pavattitānaṃ [M 1.0049] kathamaṭṭhuppattiyā anavarodho, pucchāvasikaaṭṭhuppattikānaṃ vā parajjhāsayānurodhena pavattitānaṃ kathaṃ parajjhāsaye anavarodhoti? Na codetabbametaṃ. Paresañhi abhinīhāraparipucchādivinimuttasseva suttadesanākāraṇuppādassa aṭṭhuppattibhāvena gahitattā parajjhāsayapucchāvasikānaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tathā hi brahmajāladhammadāyādasuttādīnaṃ vaṇṇāvaṇṇaāmisuppādādidesanānimittaṃ “aṭṭhuppattī”ti vuccati. Paresaṃ pucchaṃ vinā ajjhāsayaṃ eva nimittaṃ katvā desito parajjhāsayo, pucchāvasena desito pucchāvasikoti pākaṭoyamatthoti. Attano ajjhāsayeneva kathesīti dhammatantiṭṭhapanatthaṃ kathesi. Vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā saddhindriyādayo. Ajjhāsayanti adhimuttiṃ. Khantinti diṭṭhinijjhānakkhantiṃ. Mananti paññatticittaṃ. Abhinīhāranti paṇidhānaṃ. Bujjhanabhāvanti bujjhanasabhāvaṃ, paṭivijjhanākāraṃ vā. Rūpagarukānanti pañcasu ārammaṇesu rūpārammaṇagarukā rūpagarukā. Cittena rūpaninnā rūpapoṇā rūpapabbhārā rūpadassanappasutā rūpena ākaḍḍhitahadayā, tesaṃ rūpagarukānaṃ.

Moreover, here, because it is independent of such causes as the ripening of others' faculties, it is proper for “one's own inclination” to be a separate laying down of a sutta, since the teaching is set in motion solely by one's own inclination for the purpose of establishing the tradition of the Dhamma. But in the case of the “another's inclination” and “question-based” types, which are set in motion when the inclinations and questions of others arise as the cause for the teaching, how are they not included in the “occasion of utterance” type? Or, in the case of the “question-based” and “occasion of utterance” types, which are set in motion in conformity with another's inclination, how are they not included in the “another's inclination” type? This should not be questioned. For “occasion of utterance” is taken to be the arising of a cause for teaching a sutta that is free from others' aspiration, inquiry, etc. Therefore “another's inclination” and “question-based” are taken separately. For example, the ground for teaching the Brahmajāla Sutta, the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, etc.—the arising of praise and blame, material gain, and so on—is called an “occasion of utterance.” A teaching delivered by taking another's inclination as the ground, without their asking a question, is “another's inclination.” A teaching delivered by way of a question is “question-based.” This meaning is clear. “He spoke from his own inclination” means he spoke for the purpose of establishing the tradition of the Dhamma. Qualities that ripen for liberation are the faith faculty and so on. “Inclination” means resolve. “Acceptance” means the acceptance that comes from scrutinizing a view. “Mind” means the mind that makes concepts. “Aspiration” means resolution. “State of understanding” means the nature of understanding, or the mode of penetration. “Those who esteem form”: among the five sense objects, those who esteem the form object are “those who esteem form.” Their minds are inclined to form, sloping towards form, bent on form, devoted to seeing form, their hearts drawn by form—of these who esteem form.

Paṭisedhatthoti paṭikkhepattho. Kassa pana paṭikkhepatthoti? Kiriyāpadhānañhi vākyaṃ, tasmā “na samanupassāmī”ti samanupassanākiriyāpaṭisedhattho. Tenāha – “imassa pana padassā”tiādi. Yo paro na hoti, so attāti lokasamaññāmattasiddhaṃ sattasantānaṃ sandhāya – “aha”nti satthā vadati, na bāhirakaparikappitaṃ ahaṃkāravisayaṃ ahaṃkārassa bodhimūleyeva samucchinnattā. Lokasamaññānatikkamantā eva hi buddhānaṃ lokiye visaye desanāpavatti. Bhikkhaveti ālapane kāraṇaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva. Aññanti apekkhāsiddhattā aññatthassa [V 1.0044] “idāni vattabbaitthirūpato añña”nti āha. Ekampi rūpanti ekaṃ vaṇṇāyatanaṃ. Samaṃ visamaṃ sammā yāthāvato anu anu passatīti samanupassanā, ñāṇaṃ. Saṃkilissanavasena anu anu passatīti samanupassanā, diṭṭhi. No niccatoti ettha iti-saddo ādiattho, evamādikoti attho. Tena “dukkhato samanupassatī”ti evamādīni saṅgaṇhāti. Olokentopīti devamanussavimānakapparukkhamaṇikanakādigatāni rūpāni anavasesaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇena olokentopi. Sāmaññavacanopi yaṃ-saddo “ekarūpampī”ti rūpassa [M 1.0050] adhigatattā rūpavisayo icchitoti “yaṃ rūpa”nti vuttaṃ. Tathā purisasaddo pariyādiyitabbacittapuggalavisayoti rūpagarukassāti visesitaṃ. Gahaṇaṃ “khepana”nti ca adhippetaṃ, pariyādānañca uppattinivāraṇanti āha – “catubhūmakakusalacitta”nti. Tañhi rūpaṃ tādisassa parittakusalassapi uppattiṃ nivāreti, kimaṅgaṃ pana mahaggatānuttaracittassāti lokuttarakusalacittassapi uppattiyā nivāraṇaṃ hotuṃ samatthaṃ, lokiyakusaluppattiyā nivārakatte vattabbameva natthīti “catubhūmakakusalacittaṃ pariyādiyitvā”ti vuttaṃ. Na hi kāmaguṇassādappasutassa purisassa dānādivasena savipphārikā kusaluppatti sambhavati. Gaṇhitvā khepetvāti attānaṃ assādetvā pavattamānassa akusalacittassa paccayo hontaṃ pavattinivāraṇena muṭṭhigataṃ viya gahetvā anuppādanirodhena khepetvā viya tiṭṭhati. Tāva mahati lokasannivāse tassa pariyādiyaṭṭhānaṃ avicchedato labbhatīti āha – “tiṭṭhatī”ti yathā “pabbatā tiṭṭhanti, najjo sandantī”ti. Tenāha – “idha ubhayampi vaṭṭatī”tiādi.

“For the purpose of negation” means for the purpose of rejection. But for the rejection of what? A sentence is dominated by its verb; therefore, “I do not see” is for the purpose of negating the action of seeing. Hence he says: “but of this word,” etc. That which is not “other” is “self.” With reference to the continuity of a being, which is established merely by worldly convention, the Teacher says “I,” not with reference to the externally conceived object of “I-making,” since “I-making” was utterly eradicated at the very root of the Bodhi tree. For the teachings of the Buddhas proceed in the worldly sphere only without transgressing worldly convention. “Monks”: the reason for this vocative has been stated below. “Another”: because the meaning of “other” is established by relation, he says “other than the form of a woman to be spoken of now.” “Even one form” means one visible form base. “One sees again and again what is uniform and what is diverse, correctly, as it really is”—this is seeing (samanupassanā), that is, knowledge. “One sees again and again by way of defilement”—this is seeing, that is, view. “Not as permanent”: here the word iti has the meaning of “and so on.” Thereby it includes such phrases as “sees as suffering.” “Even when surveying”: even when surveying with the knowledge of omniscience all forms without exception, such as those found in the celestial and human mansions, celestial trees, gems, and gold. Although it is a general term, the word yaṃ (“whatever”) is intended to refer to form, because “even one form” has been mentioned. Thus it is said, “whatever form.” Similarly, the word “person” refers to a person whose mind is to be overcome; it is specified as “one who esteems form.” “Seizing” and “casting out” are intended, and “overcoming” is the prevention of arising. Thus he says: “the wholesome mind of the four planes.” For that form prevents the arising of even a limited wholesome state in such a person, to say nothing of an exalted or supramundane mind. Since it is capable of preventing the arising of even a supramundane wholesome mind, there is no need to speak of its being a preventer of the arising of a mundane wholesome mind. Therefore it is said, “overcoming the wholesome mind of the four planes.” Indeed, for a person devoted to enjoying the taste of sensual pleasures, the arising of wholesome states with far-reaching results, such as giving, is not possible. “Having seized and cast it out”: it stands, as it were, seizing and casting out by preventing the occurrence of the unwholesome mind that proceeds by savoring it and being a condition for it, like seizing something in one's fist and casting it out by non-arising and cessation. In this great world-abode, its state of overcoming is found uninterruptedly for so long. Thus he says, “it stands,” just as in “mountains stand, rivers flow.” Therefore he says: “Here both are applicable,” and so on.

Yathayidanti sandhivasena ākārassa rassattaṃ yakārāgamo cāti āha – “yathā ida”nti. Itthiyā rūpanti itthisarīragataṃ tappaṭibaddhañca rūpāyatanaṃ. Paramatthassa niruḷho, paṭhamaṃ sādhāraṇato saddasatthalakkhaṇāni vibhāvetabbāni, pacchā asādhāraṇatoti tāni pāḷivasena vibhāvetuṃ – “ruppatīti kho…pe… veditabba”nti āha. Tattha ruppatīti sītādivirodhipaccayehi vikāraṃ āpādīyati, āpajjatīti vā attho. Vikāruppatti ca virodhipaccayasannipāte visadisuppatti vibhūtatarā, kuto panāyaṃ visesoti ce? “Sītenā”tiādivacanato. Evañca katvā vedanādīsu anavasesarūpasamaññā sāmaññalakkhaṇanti sabbarūpadhammasādhāraṇaṃ rūppanaṃ. Idāni atthuddhāranayena rūpasaddaṃ saṃvaṇṇento “ayaṃ panā”tiādimāha. Rūpakkhandhe vattatīti “oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā”tiādivacanato (ma. ni. 1.361; 2.113; 3.86, 89; vibha. 2). Rūpūpapattiyāti ettha rūpabhavo rūpaṃ uttarapadalopena. Rūpabhavūpapattiyāti ayañhettha attho. Kasiṇanimitteti pathavīkasiṇādisaññite paṭibhāganimitte. Rūppati attano phalassa sabhāvaṃ karotīti rūpaṃ, sabhāvahetūti [V 1.0045][M 1.0051] āha – “sarūpā…pe… ettha paccaye”ti. Karacaraṇādiavayavasaṅghātabhāvena rūpīyati nirūpīyatīti rūpaṃ, rūpakāyoti āha – “ākāso…pe… ettha sarīre”ti.

Regarding 'yathayidaṃ,' he says this is 'yathā idaṃ,' indicating the shortening of the vowel 'ā' and the insertion of the consonant 'y' due to euphonic combination. 'The form of a woman' means the visible form base included in a woman's body and connected with it. The established meaning is in the ultimate sense. First, the characteristics of the word and its meaning should be explained in general, and afterwards in particular. To explain them according to the Pāli text, he says: 'It is afflicted… it should be understood.' Herein, 'is afflicted' (ruppati) means it is brought to a state of alteration by opposing conditions such as cold, or it undergoes it. And the arising of alteration—the dissimilar arising when opposing conditions converge—is more manifest. If it is asked, 'Whence this distinction?' From the statement beginning 'by cold.' Thus, affliction (ruppana) is the general characteristic common to all phenomena of form, the designation for form without remainder in contrast to feeling, etc. Now, commenting on the word 'form' by way of extracting its meanings, he says: 'But this…' It is used for the aggregate of form, because of the statement 'whether gross or subtle…' In the expression 'rūpūpapatti,' 'form' (rūpa) stands for form-existence (rūpabhava) by elision of the final member of the compound; the meaning here is 'rebirth in the form-existence.' In the expression 'kasiṇanimitta,' it refers to the counterpart sign cognized as the earth-kasiṇa, etc. It is 'form' (rūpa) because it forms (rūppati), that is, it produces the intrinsic nature of its own fruit; it is the cause of its intrinsic nature. Thus he says: 'of its own nature… here in the condition.' It is 'form' (rūpa) because it is formed (rūpīyati) or defined (nirūpīyati) as a composite of limbs such as hands and feet; it is the form-body. Thus he says: 'space… here in the body.'

Rūpayati vaṇṇavikāraṃ āpajjamānaṃ hadayaṅgatabhāvaṃ pakāsetīti rūpaṃ, vaṇṇāyatanaṃ. Ārohapariṇāhādibhedarūpagataṃ saṇṭhānasampattiṃ nissāya pasādaṃ āpajjamāno rūpappamāṇoti vuttoti āha – “ettha saṇṭhāne”ti. Piyarūpantiādīsu sabhāvattho rūpasaddo. Ādisaddena rūpajjhānādīnaṃ saṅgaho. “Rūpī rūpāni passatī”ti ettha ajjhattaṃ kesādīsu parikammasaññāvasena paṭiladdharūpajjhānaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ assa atthīti rūpīti vutto. Itthiyā catusamuṭṭhāne vaṇṇeti itthisarīrapariyāpannameva rūpaṃ gahitaṃ, tappaṭibaddhavatthālaṅkārādirūpampi pana purisacittassa pariyādāyakaṃ hotīti dassetuṃ – “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Gandhavaṇṇaggahaṇena vilepanaṃ vuttaṃ. Kāmaṃ “asukāya itthiyā pasādhana”nti sallakkhitassa akāyappaṭibaddhassapi vaṇṇo paṭibaddhacittassa purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭheyya, taṃ pana na ekantikanti ekantikaṃ dassento “kāyappaṭibaddho”tiāha. Upakappatīti cittassa pariyādānāya upakappati. Purimassevāti pubbe vuttaatthasseva daḷhīkaraṇatthaṃ vuttaṃ yathā “dvikkhattuṃ bandhaṃ subandha”nti. Nigamanavasena vā etaṃ vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Opammavasena vuttanti “yaṃ evaṃ purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī”ti sakalamevidaṃ purimavacanaṃ upamāvasena vuttaṃ, tattha pana upamābhūtaṃ atthaṃ dassetuṃ – “yathayidaṃ…pe… itthirūpa”nti vuttaṃ. Pariyādāne ānubhāvo sambhavo pariyādānānubhāvo, tassa dassanavasena vuttaṃ.

It is 'form' (rūpa) because it reveals (rūpayati), that is, it manifests the state of having reached the heart while undergoing a change of color; this is the visible form base. Depending on the perfection of shape, which is comprised in the form distinguished by height, girth, etc., one who attains confidence is said to be 'one who takes form as his measure.' Thus he says: 'here, in shape.' In expressions such as 'pleasing form,' the word 'form' has the meaning of intrinsic nature. The word 'etc.' includes the form jhānas and so on. In the phrase 'one with form sees forms,' 'form' here is the form jhāna attained internally by means of the perception of the preparatory sign in the hair of the head, etc. Because he has this, he is called 'one with form.' In the case of a woman, 'color' with its fourfold origin is taken as just the form included in the woman's body. But to show that even form connected with that, such as clothes and ornaments, can overwhelm a man's mind, the passage beginning 'Moreover…' was stated. By the mention of 'scent and color,' unguent is meant. Granted, even the color of something not connected to the body, when noted as 'the adornment of such and such a woman,' might overwhelm the mind of a man with an attached mind.
