But since this is not invariably so, to show what is invariably so, he says: 'connected to the body.' 'It is conducive' means it is conducive to the overwhelming of the mind. This was stated for the sake of reinforcing the meaning already stated before, as in 'a bond bound twice is a strong bond.' Or it should be seen that this was stated by way of a conclusion. It was stated by way of a simile. The entire preceding statement, 'which so overwhelms a man's mind,' was stated as a simile. But to show the meaning that is the simile there, it was said: 'just as… a woman's form.' The power to overwhelm is the potential for overwhelming; this was stated to show that.

Idaṃ pana “itthirūpa”ntiādivacanaṃ pariyādānānubhāve sādhetabbe dīpetabbe vatthu kāraṇaṃ. Nāgo nāma so rājā, dīghadāṭhikattā pana “mahādāṭhikanāgarājā”ti vutto. Asaṃvaraniyāmenāti cakkhudvārikena asaṃvaranīhārena. Nimittaṃ gahetvāti rāguppattihetubhūtaṃ rūpaṃ subhanimittaṃ gahetvā. Visikādassanaṃ gantvāti sivathikadassanaṃ gantvā. Tattha hi ādīnavānupassanā ijjhati. Vatthulobhena kuto tādisāya maraṇanti asaddahanto “mukhaṃ tumhākaṃ dhūmavaṇṇa”nti te daharasāmaṇere uppaṇḍento vadati.

But this statement beginning 'a woman's form' is the basis and reason to be explained and demonstrated when the power of overwhelming is to be established. That king was named Nāga, but because he had long tusks he was called 'the great-tusked Nāga king.' 'By the method of non-restraint' means by the procedure of non-restraint at the eye-door. 'Having grasped a sign' means having grasped the sign of beauty, the form that is a cause for the arising of lust. 'Having gone to see the street' means having gone to see the charnel ground. For there the contemplation of disadvantages is successful. Not believing that such a death could occur out of greed for the object, he taunts those young novices, saying: 'Your faces are the color of smoke.'

Ratanattaye suppasannattā kākavaṇṇatissādīhi visesanatthañca so tissamahārājā saddhāsaddena visesetvā vuccati. Daharassa cittaṃ pariyādāya [M 1.0052] tiṭṭhatīti adhikāravasena vuttaṃ. Niṭṭhituddesakiccoti gāme asappāyarūpadassanaṃ imassa anatthāya siyāti ācariyena nivāritagāmappaveso pacchā niṭṭhituddesakicco hutvā ṭhito. Tena vuttaṃ – “atthakāmānaṃ vacanaṃ aggahetvā”ti[V 1.0046]. Nivatthavatthaṃ sañjānitvāti attanā diṭṭhadivase nivatthavatthaṃ tassā matadivase sivathikadassanatthaṃ gatena laddhaṃ sañjānitvā. Evampīti evaṃ maraṇasampāpanavasenapi. Ayaṃ tāvettha aṭṭhakathāya anuttānatthadīpanā.

Because he had great confidence in the Three Jewels, and to distinguish him from others such as Kākavaṇṇatissa, the great king Tissa is designated by the word 'Saddhā' (Faithful). 'It overwhelms the mind of the young man': this is said in connection with the main character. 'Having completed the task of his recitation': Having been prevented by his teacher from entering the village, who thought, 'Seeing unsuitable forms in the village might be for his harm,' he later stood with the task of his recitation completed. Therefore it is said: 'Not having taken the words of those who wished for his welfare.' 'Recognizing the cloth she had worn': having recognized the cloth she had worn on the day he saw her, which he found when he went to the charnel ground on the day she died. 'Even thus': even by way of bringing about death thus. This, for its part, is the explanation of the meaning that was not plain in the commentary.

Nettinayavaṇṇanā

Exposition on the Method of the Guide

Idāni pakaraṇanayena pāḷiyā atthavaṇṇanaṃ karissāma. Sā pana atthasaṃvaṇṇanā yasmā desanāya samuṭṭhānappayojanabhājanesu piṇḍatthesu ca niddhāritesu sukarā hoti suviññeyyā ca, tasmā suttadesanāya samuṭṭhānādīni paṭhamaṃ niddhārayissāma. Tattha samuṭṭhānaṃ nāma desanānidānaṃ, taṃ sādhāraṇamasādhāraṇanti duvidhaṃ. Tattha sādhāraṇampi ajjhattikabāhirabhedato duvidhaṃ. Tattha sādhāraṇaṃ ajjhattikasamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma lokanāthassa mahākaruṇā. Tāya hi samussāhitassa bhagavato veneyyānaṃ dhammadesanāya cittaṃ udapādi, yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “sattesu ca kāruññataṃ paṭicca buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ volokesī”tiādi (ma. ni. 1.283; mahāva. 9; saṃ. ni. 1.173). Ettha ca hetāvatthāyapi mahākaruṇāya saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo yāvadeva saṃsāramahoghato saddhammadesanāhatthadānehi sattasantāraṇatthaṃ taduppattito. Yathā ca mahākaruṇā, evaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ dasabalañāṇādayo ca desanāya abbhantarasamuṭṭhānabhāvena vattabbā. Sabbañhi ñeyyadhammaṃ tesaṃ desetabbākāraṃ sattānañca āsayānusayādiṃ yāthāvato jānanto bhagavā ṭhānāṭṭhānādīsu kosallena veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ vicittanayadesanaṃ pavattesīti. Bāhiraṃ pana sādhāraṇaṃ samuṭṭhānaṃ dasasahassamahābrahmaparivārassa sahampatibrahmuno ajjhesanaṃ. Tadajjhesanuttarakālañhi dhammagambhīratāpaccavekkhaṇājanitaṃ appossukkataṃ paṭippassambhetvā dhammassāmī dhammadesanāya ussāhajāto ahosi. Asādhāraṇampi abbhantarabāhirabhedato duvidhameva. Tattha abbhantaraṃ yāya mahākaruṇāya yena ca desanāñāṇena [M 1.0053] idaṃ suttaṃ pavattitaṃ, tadubhayaṃ veditabbaṃ. Bāhiraṃ pana rūpagarukānaṃ puggalānaṃ ajjhāsayo. Svāyamattho aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto eva.

Now, we will explain the meaning of the Pāli text according to the method of the treatise. Because this explanation of meaning is easy to understand and comprehend when the origins, purposes, and recipients of the teaching are clarified along with the summary meaning, we will therefore first clarify the origins and so forth of the sutta teaching. Here, 'origin' refers to the cause of the teaching, which is of two kinds: common and uncommon. Among these, the common origin is also twofold: internal and external. The common internal origin is the great compassion of the Lord of the World. For it was due to this that the Blessed One, stirred by compassion, resolved to teach the Dhamma to those capable of being guided. This is referred to in such statements as: 'Out of compassion for beings, he surveyed the world with the Buddha-eye,' etc. (Majjhima Nikāya 1.283; Mahāvagga 9; Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.173). Here, the inclusion of great compassion should be understood even in the sense of the cause, from its very arising for the sake of rescuing beings from the great flood of saṃsāra by extending the hand of the True Dhamma teaching. Just as with great compassion, so too the knowledge of omniscience, the ten powers, and other knowledges should be regarded as internal origins of the teaching. For the Blessed One, knowing as they really are all knowable phenomena, the manner in which they should be taught, and the inclinations and latent tendencies of beings, skillfully sets in motion a teaching of various methods suited to the dispositions of those capable of being guided, with his expertise in what is possible and impossible, etc. The external common origin is the request of Brahmā Sahampati along with his retinue of ten thousand great brahmās. For after that request, having dispelled the lack of enthusiasm generated by reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma, the Lord of Dhamma became energized to teach the Dhamma. The uncommon origin is also twofold: internal and external. Among these, the internal should be understood as the great compassion and the knowledge of teaching by which this sutta was delivered—both of them. The external is the inclination of individuals who esteem form. This meaning has already been stated in the commentary.

Payojanampi sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇato duvidhaṃ. Tattha sādhāraṇaṃ yāva anupādāparinibbānaṃ vimuttirasattā bhagavato desanāya. Tenevāha – “etadatthā kathā, etadatthā mantanā”tiādi. Asādhāraṇaṃ pana tesaṃ rūpagarukānaṃ puggalānaṃ rūpe chandarāgassa jahāpanaṃ, ubhayampetaṃ bāhirameva. Sace pana veneyyasantānagatampi desanābalasiddhisaṅkhātaṃ payojanaṃ adhippāyasamijjhanabhāvato yathādhippetatthasiddhiyā mahākāruṇikassa bhagavatopi payojanamevāti gaṇheyya, iminā pariyāyenassa abbhantaratāpi siyā.

The purpose is also twofold: common and uncommon. Here, the common purpose of the Blessed One’s teaching is the taste of liberation, extending even to final Nibbāna without residue. Hence it is said: “For this purpose is the talk, for this purpose is the discussion,” and so on. The uncommon purpose, however, is causing those individuals who are attached to form to abandon desire and lust for form. Both these purposes are external. But if one were to consider that even the purpose termed 'the success of the power of teaching,' which arises in the mind-continuum of a trainee, is indeed a purpose for the greatly compassionate Blessed One—because it fulfills his intended aim through the fulfillment of their intention—then by this method, its internality could also be accepted.

Apica [V 1.0047] tesaṃ rūpagarukānaṃ puggalānaṃ rūpasmiṃ vijjamānassa ādīnavassa yāthāvato anavabodho imissā desanāya samuṭṭhānaṃ, tadavabodho payojanaṃ. So hi imāya desanāya bhagavantaṃ payojeti tannipphādanaparāyaṃ desanāti katvā. Yañhi desanāya sādhetabbaṃ phalaṃ, taṃ ākaṅkhitabbattā desakaṃ desanāya payojetīti payojananti vuccati. Tathā tesaṃ puggalānaṃ tadaññesañca veneyyānaṃ rūpamukhena pañcasu upādānakkhandhesu ādīnavadassanañcettha payojanaṃ. Tathā saṃsāracakkanivattisaddhammacakkappavattisassatādimicchāvādanirākaraṇaṃ sammāvādapurekkhāro akusalamūlasamūhananaṃ kusalamūlasamāropanaṃ apāyadvārapidahanaṃ saggamaggadvāravivaraṇaṃ pariyuṭṭhānavūpasamanaṃ anusayasamugghātanaṃ “mutto mocessāmī”ti purimapaṭiññāvisaṃvādanaṃ tappaṭipakkhamāramanorathavisaṃvādanaṃ titthiyadhammanimmathanaṃ buddhadhammapatiṭṭhāpananti evamādīnipi payojanāni idha veditabbāni.

Furthermore, for those individuals who are attached to form, the failure to understand as it really is the danger present in form is the origin of this teaching, while understanding it is the purpose. For that understanding employs the Blessed One for this teaching, since the teaching is dedicated to its accomplishment. For whatever fruit is to be achieved by the teaching, because it is to be desired, it employs the teacher for the teaching; therefore it is called 'purpose.' Moreover, for those individuals and other receptive beings, the purpose here is the perception of danger in the five aggregates of clinging by means of form. Furthermore, the purposes to be understood here include: halting the wheel of saṃsāra, turning the wheel of the True Dhamma, refuting eternalist and other wrong views, upholding right view, eradicating unwholesome roots, cultivating wholesome roots, closing the doors to the lower realms, opening the doors to heaven and the path, calming obsessive thoughts, uprooting latent tendencies, fulfilling the earlier declaration, 'Freed, I will free others,' without falsehood, frustrating the opposing desires of Māra, crushing the doctrines of sectarians, and establishing the Buddha's Dhamma. Such are the purposes to be recognized here.

Yathā te puggalā rūpagarukā, evaṃ tadaññe ca sakkāyagarukā sakkāyasmiṃ allīnā saṅkhatadhammānaṃ sammāsambuddhassa ca paṭipattiṃ ajānantā asaddhammassavanasādhāraṇaparicariyamanasikāraparā saddhammassavanadhāraṇaparicayappaṭivedhavimukhā ca bhavavippamokkhesino veneyyā imissā desanāya bhājanaṃ.

Just as those individuals are devoted to form, so too are others devoted to self-identity, clinging to self-identity, unaware of the practice of the Perfectly Enlightened One with regard to conditioned phenomena. They are devoted to listening to false teachings, common practices, and improper attention, and are turned away from listening to the True Dhamma, retaining it, becoming familiar with it, and penetrating it. These teachable beings, seeking liberation from existence, are suitable vessels for this teaching.

Piṇḍattā [M 1.0054] cettha rūpaggahaṇena rūpadhāturūpāyatanarūpakkhandhapariggaṇhanaṃ rūpamukhena catudhammānaṃ vaṭṭattayavicchedanūpāyo āsavoghādivivecanaṃ abhinandananivāraṇasaṅgatikkamo vivādamūlapariccāgo sikkhattayānuyogo pahānattayadīpanā samathavipassanānuṭṭhānaṃ bhāvanāsacchikiriyāsiddhīti evamādayo veditabbā.

In brief, here, through the grasping of form, the comprehension of the form element, the form base, and the form aggregate should be understood. By means of form, the following are to be understood: the method for cutting off the three rounds concerning the four truths, the discrimination of the cankers, floods, and so on, the restraint of delight, the overcoming of clinging, the abandonment of the root of disputes, the application of the threefold training, the exposition of the threefold abandonment, the practice of serenity and insight, and the accomplishment of development and realization—these and other such things.

Ito paraṃ pana soḷasa hārā dassetabbā. Tattha “rūpa”nti sahajātā tassa nissayabhūtā tappaṭibaddhā ca sabbe rūpārūpadhammā taṇhāvajjā dukkhasaccaṃ. Taṃsamuṭṭhāpikā tadārammaṇā ca taṇhā samudayasaccaṃ. Tadubhayesaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ. Nirodhappajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccaṃ. Tattha samudayena assādo, dukkhena ādīnavo, magganirodhehi nissaraṇaṃ, rūpārammaṇassa akusalacittassa kusalacittassa ca pariyādānaṃ phalaṃ. Yañhi desanāya sādhetabbaṃ payojanaṃ, taṃ phalanti vuttovāyamattho. Tadatthaṃ hidaṃ suttaṃ bhagavatā desitanti. Yathā taṃ kusalacittaṃ na pariyādiyati, evaṃ paṭisaṅkhānabhāvanābalapariggahitā indriyesu guttadvāratā upāyo. Purisassa kusalacittapariyādānenassa rūpassa aññarūpāsādhāraṇatādassanāpadesena atthakāmehi [V 1.0048] tato cittaṃ sādhukaṃ rakkhitabbaṃ. Ayamettha bhagavato āṇattīti ayaṃ desanāhāro. Assādādisandassanavibhāvanalakkhaṇo hi desanāhāro. Vuttañhetaṃ nettippakaraṇe –

Henceforth, the sixteen methods are to be shown. Herein, 'form' means all material and immaterial phenomena that are co-nascent with it, that are its support, and that are connected with it, excluding craving; this is the truth of suffering. The craving that originates from it and takes it as an object is the truth of the origin. The non-occurrence of both is the truth of cessation. The practice which is the understanding of cessation is the truth of the path. Herein, gratification is through the origin, danger is through suffering, and escape is through the path and cessation. The mastery over unwholesome consciousness and wholesome consciousness that have form as their object is the fruit. For the purpose to be accomplished by the teaching is called the fruit; this is the intended meaning. For that purpose, this discourse was taught by the Blessed One. So that that wholesome consciousness is not overcome, the means is the guarding of the sense doors, undertaken with the power of reflective development. By those who desire a person's welfare, his mind should be well guarded from that, by means of mastering wholesome consciousness, by way of showing the distinctive nature of this form from other forms. This here is the Blessed One's instruction—this is the method of teaching. For the method of teaching is characterized by demonstrating gratification, danger, escape, and so on. As it is said in the Nettippakaraṇa:

“Assādādīnavatā, nissaraṇampi ca phalaṃ upāyo ca;

Āṇattī ca bhagavato, yogīnaṃ desanāhāro”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

"Gratification and danger, and also escape, the fruit and the means, and the instruction of the Blessed One: this is the method of teaching for yogis." (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Desīyati saṃvaṇṇīyati etāya suttatthoti desanā, desanāya sahacaraṇato vā desanā. Nanu ca aññepi hārā desanāsaṅkhātassa suttassa atthasaṃvaṇṇanāto desanāya sahacārino vāti? Saccametaṃ, ayaṃ pana hāro yebhuyyena yathārutavaseneva viññāyamāno desanāya saha caratīti vattabbataṃ arahati, na tathāpare. Na hi assādādīnavanissaraṇādisandassanarahitā suttadesanā atthi. Kiṃ pana tesaṃ assādādīnaṃ anavasesānaṃ vacanaṃ desanāhāro, udāhu [M 1.0055] ekaccānanti? Niravasesānaṃyeva. Yasmiñhi sutte assādādīnavanissaraṇāni sarūpato āgatāni, tattha vattabbameva natthi. Yattha pana ekadesena āgatāni, na ca sarūpena, tattha anāgataṃ atthavasena niddhāretvā hāro yojetabbo.

It is called a teaching because the meaning of the sutta is taught and explained by it, or because it accompanies the teaching. But are not other methods also companions of the teaching, since they explain the meaning of the discourse designated as a teaching? That is true. However, this method, being for the most part understood just as it was heard, deserves to be called a companion of the teaching, but not so the others. For there is no discourse-teaching that is without the demonstration of gratification, danger, escape, and so on. But is the statement of those gratifications, dangers, etc., in this method complete or partial? It is complete. For in whichever discourse gratification, danger, and escape are presented in their own form, there is nothing further to be said. But where they are presented in part and not in their own form, the method should be applied by ascertaining through the meaning what is not stated.

Sayaṃ samantacakkhubhāvato taṃdassanena sabhāvato ca “aha”nti vuttaṃ. Bhikkhanasīlatādiguṇayogato abhimukhīkaraṇatthañca, “bhikkhave”ti vuttaṃ. Attābhāvato aparatādassanatthañca “añña”nti vuttaṃ. Ekassa anupalabbhadassanatthaṃ anekabhāvappaṭisedhanatthañca “ekarūpampī”ti vuttaṃ. Tādisassa rūpassa abhāvato adassanato ca “na samanupassāmī”ti vuttaṃ. Tassa paccāmasanato aniyamato ca “ya”nti vuttaṃ. Idāni vuccamānākāraparāmasanato tadaññākāranisedhanato ca “eva”nti vuttaṃ. Visabhāgindriyavatthuto sabhāgavatthusmiṃ tadabhāvato ca “purisassā”ti vuttaṃ. Nimittaggāhassa vatthubhāvato tathā parikappitattā ca “cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Evanti vuttākāraparāmasanatthañceva nidassanatthañca “yathā”ti vuttaṃ. Attano paccakkhabhāvato bhikkhūnaṃ paccakkhakaraṇatthañca “ida”nti vuttaṃ. Itthisantānapariyāpannato tappaṭibaddhabhāvato ca “itthirūpa”nti vuttanti evaṃ anupadavicayato vicayo hāro. Vicīyanti etena, ettha vā padapañhādayoti vicayo, viciti eva vā tesanti vicayo. Padapucchāvissajjanapubbāparānuggahanaṃ assādādīnañca visesaniddhāraṇavasena pavicayalakkhaṇo hi vicayo hāro. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Because he himself is all-seeing and by nature sees that, it is said as 'I.' Because of being endowed with qualities such as the habit of begging, and for the purpose of addressing them, it is said as 'monks.' Due to the absence of a self and for the purpose of showing otherness, it is said as 'another.' To show the non-existence of a single instance and to deny multiplicity, it is said as 'even a single form.' Because of the absence and non-perception of such a form, it is said as 'I do not perceive.' Due to its being touched upon and its indefiniteness, it is said as 'whatever.' Now, because of referring to the mode being spoken of and denying any other mode, it is said as 'thus.' Because it is an object for a dissimilar faculty and because of its absence as such for a similar faculty, it is said as 'of a man.' Because it is the basis for grasping signs and is thus conceived, it is said as 'it stands obsessing the mind.' For the purpose of referring to the mode thus spoken and as an illustration, it is said as 'just as.' Because of being directly evident to oneself and for making it evident to the monks, it is said as 'this.' Because it pertains to the continuum of a woman and is bound to that, it is said as 'a woman’s form.' Thus, the method of investigation is by way of word-by-word analysis. 'Investigation' (vicayo) is so called because questions concerning words and so on are investigated by it or in it; or it is simply their investigation. Indeed, the method of investigation is characterized by thorough analysis, by way of determining the specific characteristics of gratification and so on, involving the questioning and answering of words and the grasping of what precedes and follows. And this has been said:

“Yaṃ [V 1.0049] pucchitañca vissajjitañca, suttassa yā ca anugīti;

Suttassa yo pavicayo, hāro vicayoti niddiṭṭho”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“What is asked and what is answered, and the elucidation that follows the discourse; and the thorough analysis of the discourse—this method is designated as investigation.” (Netti. 4, Niddesavāra);

Anādimati saṃsāre itthipurisānaṃ aññamaññarūpābhirāmatāya “itthirūpaṃ purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatī”ti yujjatīti ayaṃ yuttihāro. Byañjanatthānaṃ yuttāyuttavibhāgavibhāvanalakkhaṇo hi yuttihāro. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

In the beginningless cycle of existence, due to the mutual delight of women and men in each other's form, the statement 'a woman’s form stands obsessing a man’s mind' is appropriate—this is the method of appropriateness. Indeed, the method of appropriateness is characterized by the clarification of the division between what is appropriate and inappropriate in terms of expressions and meanings. And this has been said:

“Sabbesaṃ hārānaṃ, yā bhūmī yo ca gocaro tesaṃ;

Yuttāyuttiparikkhā, hāro yuttīti niddiṭṭho”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“For all the methods, whatever is their ground and their range; the examination of what is appropriate and inappropriate—that method is designated as appropriateness.” (Netti. 4, Niddesavāra);

Yuttīti [M 1.0056] ca upapatti sādhanayutti, idha pana yuttivicāraṇā yutti uttarapadalopena “rūpabhavo rūpa”nti yathā. Yuttisahacaraṇato vā yutti.

And 'yutti' means appropriateness, the reasoning that establishes. But here, 'yutti' means the investigation of appropriateness, by way of eliding the latter term, just as 'rūpabhavo' becomes 'rūpa' (form-existence becomes form). Or 'yutti' arises from being associated with appropriateness.

Itthirūpaṃ ayoniso olokiyamānaṃ indriyesu aguttadvāratāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, sā kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ abhāvanāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, sā sabbassapi saṃkilesapakkhassa parivuddhiyā padaṭṭhānaṃ. Byatirekato pana itthirūpaṃ yoniso olokiyamānaṃ satipaṭṭhānabhāvanāya padaṭṭhānaṃ, sā bojjhaṅgānaṃ bhāvanāpāripūriyā padaṭṭhānaṃ, sā vijjāvimuttīnaṃ pāripūriyā padaṭṭhānaṃ, kusalassa cittassa pariyādānaṃ sammohābhinivesassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, so saṅkhārānaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ, saṅkhārā viññāṇassāti sabbaṃ āvattati bhavacakkaṃ. Byatirekato pana kusalassa cittassa apariyādānaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya pāripūriyā padaṭṭhānanti ayaṃ tāva avisesato nayo. Visesato pana sīlassa apariyādānaṃ avippaṭisārassa padaṭṭhānaṃ, avippaṭisāro pāmojjassātiādinā yāva anupādāparinibbānaṃ netabbaṃ. Ayaṃ padaṭṭhāno hāro. Sutte āgatadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānabhūte dhamme tesañca padaṭṭhānabhūteti sambhavato padaṭṭhānabhūtadhammaniddhāraṇalakkhaṇo hi padaṭṭhāno hāro. Vuttañcetaṃ –

A woman's form, being looked at unwisely, is the proximate cause of unguarded sense doors; that unguardedness is the proximate cause for the non-development of wholesome qualities; that is the proximate cause for the growth of the entire side of defilement. Conversely, a woman's form, being looked at wisely, is the proximate cause for the development of the foundations of mindfulness; that is the proximate cause for the complete fulfillment of the factors of enlightenment; that is the proximate cause for the fulfillment of true knowledge and liberation. The exhaustion of the wholesome mind is the proximate cause for delusion and adherence; that is the proximate cause for formations, and formations for consciousness—thus the entire wheel of existence revolves. Conversely, the non-exhaustion of the wholesome mind is the proximate cause for the arising and fulfillment of those various wholesome qualities. This, for a start, is the general principle. Specifically, the integrity of virtue is the proximate cause for absence of remorse, and absence of remorse for joy—and so on, it should be led up to final Nibbāna without clinging. This is the method of proximate causes. Indeed, the method of proximate causes is characterized by determining the phenomena that are proximate causes, based on the possibility that phenomena mentioned in the suttas are proximate causes for some things, and that those in turn are proximate causes for others. And this has been said:

“Dhammaṃ deseti jino, tassa ca dhammassa yaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ;

Iti yāva sabbadhammā, eso hāro padaṭṭhāno”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“The Conqueror teaches the Dhamma, and whatever is the proximate cause of that Dhamma; thus, up to all phenomena, this is the method of proximate causes.” (Netti. 4, Niddesavāra);

Padaṭṭhānanti [V 1.0050] āsannakāraṇaṃ. Idha pana padaṭṭhānavicāraṇā padaṭṭhānotiādi yuttihāre vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ.

‘Padaṭṭhāna’ means proximate cause. But here, that 'padaṭṭhāna' stands for 'the investigation of proximate causes', and so on, should be understood in the same manner as explained in the method of appropriateness.

Ekarūpanti ca rūpāyatanaggahaṇena channampi bāhirānaṃ āyatanānaṃ gahaṇaṃ bāhirāyatanabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā. Cittanti manāyatanaggahaṇena channampi ajjhattikānaṃ āyatanānaṃ gahaṇaṃ ajjhattikāyatanabhāvena ekalakkhaṇattā. Evaṃ khandhadhātādivasenapi ekalakkhaṇatā vattabbā. Ayaṃ lakkhaṇo hāro. Lakkhīyanti etena, ettha vā ekalakkhaṇadhammā avuttāpi ekaccavacanenāti lakkhaṇo. Sutte anāgatepi dhamme vuttappakāre āgate viya niddhāretvā yā saṃvaṇṇanā, so lakkhaṇo hāro. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

And 'one form' means that by grasping the form base, the six external bases are also grasped, because they have the single characteristic of being external bases. 'Mind' means that by grasping the mind base, the six internal bases are also grasped, because they have the single characteristic of being internal bases. Similarly, the single characteristic should be stated by way of aggregates, elements, and so on. This is the characteristic method. By this, or herein, phenomena with a single characteristic, even if unstated, are indicated by a single expression; this is the characteristic. In the Sutta, the explanation that determines even unmentioned phenomena as if they were mentioned in the stated manner, is the characteristic method. And this has been said:

“Vuttamhi [M 1.0057] ekadhamme, ye dhammā ekalakkhaṇā keci;

Vuttā bhavanti sabbe, so hāro lakkhaṇo nāmā”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“When one phenomenon is stated, whatever phenomena have a single characteristic, all those are thereby stated. That method is called the characteristic method.” (Netti. 4, Niddesavāra)

Nidāne imissā desanāya rūpagarukānaṃ puggalānaṃ rūpasmiṃ anādīnavadassitā vuttā, “kathaṃ nu kho ime imaṃ desanaṃ sutvā rūpe ādīnavadassanamukhena sabbasmimpi khandhapañcake sabbaso chandarāgaṃ pahāya sakalavaṭṭadukkhato mucceyyuṃ, pare ca tattha patiṭṭhāpeyyu”nti ayamettha bhagavato adhippāyo. Padanibbacanaṃ niruttaṃ, taṃ “eva”ntiādinidānapadānaṃ “nāha”ntiādipāḷipadānañca aṭṭhakathāyaṃ tassā līnatthavaṇṇanāya ca vuttanayānusārena sukarattā na vitthārayimha.

In the introduction to this discourse, for individuals who are attached to form, their non-seeing of danger in form is addressed, with the thought: ‘How then, having heard this teaching, might these individuals, by seeing the danger in form, abandon all desire and lust for the entire five aggregates, be freed from all the suffering of the cycle of existence, and establish others in that as well?’—this was the Blessed One’s intention here. The explanation of words, the etymology—for the introductory terms 'eva' and so on, and for the Pāli terms 'nāha' and so on—we have not elaborated, since it is easy to understand according to the method stated in the commentary and in its explanation of the subtle meaning.

Padapadatthadesanādesanānikkhepasuttasandhivasena pañcavidhā sandhi. Tattha padassa padantarena sambandho padasandhi. Padatthassa padatthantarena sambandho padatthasandhi, yo “kiriyākārakasambandho”ti vuccati. Nānānusandhikassa suttassa taṃtaṃanusandhīhi sambandho, ekānusandhikassa ca pubbāparasambandho desanāsandhi, yā aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “pucchānusandhi, ajjhāsayānusandhi, yathānusandhī”ti tidhā vibhattā. Ajjhāsayo cettha attajjhāsayo parajjhāsayoti dvidhā veditabbo. Desanānikkhepasandhi catunnaṃ suttanikkhepānaṃ vasena veditabbā. Suttasandhi idha paṭhamanikkhepavaseneva veditabbā. “Kasmā panettha idameva cittapariyādānasuttaṃ paṭhamaṃ nikkhitta”nti nāyamanuyogo katthaci na pavattati. Apica ime sattā anādimati saṃsāre paribbhamantā itthipurisā aññamaññesaṃ pañcakāmaguṇasaṅkhātarūpābhirāmā, tattha itthī purisassa rūpe sattā giddhā gadhitā laggā laggitā āsattā, sā cassā tattha āsatti dubbivecanīyā[V 1.0051]. Tathā puriso itthiyā rūpe, tattha ca dassanasaṃsaggo garutaro itaresañca mūlabhūto. Teneva hi bhagavā “kathaṃ nu kho mātugāme paṭipajjitabba”nti (dī. ni. 2.203) puṭṭho “adassanamevā”ti avoca. Tasmā bhagavā pañcasu kāmaguṇesu rūpe chandarāgahāpanatthaṃ idameva suttaṃ paṭhamaṃ desesi. Nibbānādhigamāya paṭipattiyā ādi resā paṭipattīti. Yaṃ pana ekissā desanāya desanantarena saṃsandanaṃ, ayampi desanāsandhi. Sā idha evaṃ veditabbā. “Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… tiṭṭhatī”ti ayaṃ desanā. “Ye kho, bhikkhave, cakkhuviññeyyā rūpā iṭṭhā kantā manāpā piyarūpā kāmūpasaṃhitā rajanīyā[M 1.0058], tañce bhikkhu abhinandati abhivadati ajjhosāya tiṭṭhati, tassa taṃ abhinandato abhivadato ajjhosāya tiṭṭhato uppajjanti aneke pāpakā akusalā dhammā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.118) imāya desanāya saṃsandati. Tathā “rūpe maññati, rūpesu maññati, rūpato maññati, rūpaṃ ‘me’ti maññati. Rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, anabhijānaṃ aparijānaṃ avirājayaṃ appajahaṃ abhabbo dukkhakkhayāyā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.112) evamādīhi desanāhi saṃsandatīti ayaṃ catubyūho hāro. Viyūhīyanti vibhāgena piṇḍīyanti etena, ettha vāti byūho, nibbacanādīnaṃ catunnaṃ byūhoti catubyūho, catunnaṃ vā byūho etthāti catubyūho. Nibbacanādhippāyādīnaṃ catunnaṃ vibhāgalakkhaṇo hi catubyūho hāro. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Cohesion is fivefold: by way of word, meaning, exposition, exposition-collection, and sutta. Among these, the connection of a word with another word is word-cohesion. The connection of a meaning with another meaning is meaning-cohesion, which is called 'the connection of action and agent.' For a sutta with various connections, the connection is by way of its respective connections; and for a sutta with a single connection, the connection of what precedes and follows is exposition-cohesion, which is divided in the commentary into three: 'question-connection, intention-connection, and appropriate-connection.' Here, intention should be understood as twofold: one's own intention and another's intention. Exposition-collection cohesion should be understood by way of the four modes of sutta exposition. Sutta-cohesion here should be understood by way of the first mode of exposition. The question, 'Why is this very Cittapariyādāna Sutta placed first here?' is not applicable anywhere. Moreover, these beings, wandering in beginningless saṃsāra, are men and women delighting in each other's forms, which are reckoned as the five strands of sensual pleasure. Among them, a woman is attached, greedy, fixated, bound, and clinging to a man's form, and her attachment there is hard to disentangle. Similarly, a man is to a woman's form, and there the contact through sight is more weighty and is the root of the others. For that very reason, when the Blessed One was asked, 'How should one behave toward womankind?' (Dī. Ni. 2.203), he replied, 'By not seeing them.' Therefore, to bring about the abandoning of desire and lust for forms among the five strands of sensual pleasure, the Blessed One first taught this very sutta. This practice is the beginning of the path for the attainment of Nibbāna. Furthermore, the connecting of one exposition with another exposition is also exposition-cohesion. Here, it should be understood thus: The exposition, 'Monks, I do not…pe… remains,' connects with the exposition, 'Monks, whatever forms cognizable by the eye—desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual pleasure, and arousing passion—if a monk delights in them, welcomes them, and remains obsessed with them, then many evil, unwholesome states arise in him' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.118). Similarly, it connects with expositions such as: 'One conceives form, conceives in forms, conceives from form, conceives form as “mine.” Monks, without fully knowing form, without fully understanding form, without being disenchanted with form, without abandoning form, one is incapable of the destruction of suffering' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.112). This is the fourfold array method. By this, or herein, things are analyzed and grouped by division; this is 'array' (byūho). It is the fourfold array because it is the array of the four—definition, intention, and so on; or it is the fourfold array because the array of the four is herein. Indeed, the fourfold array method is characterized by the division of the four: definition, intention, and so on. For it has been said:

“Neruttamadhippāyo, byañjanamatha desanānidānañca;

Pubbāparānusandhī, eso hāro catubyūho”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“Etymology, intention, expression, and the basis of the exposition; the connection of what precedes and follows: this is the fourfold array method.” (Netti. 4, Niddesavāra)

“Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ…pe… itthirūpa”nti etena ayonisomanasikāro dīpito. Yaṃ tattha cittaṃ pariyādiyati, tena yonisomanasikāro. Tattha ayonisomanasikaroto taṇhāvijjā parivaḍḍhanti, tāsu taṇhāgahaṇena nava taṇhāmūlakā dhammā āvaṭṭanti, avijjāgahaṇena avijjāmūlakaṃ sabbaṃ bhavacakkaṃ āvaṭṭati, yonisomanasikāraggahaṇena ca yonisomanasikāramūlakā dhammā āvaṭṭanti, catubbidhañca sampatticakkanti. Ayaṃ āvaṭṭo hāro. Āvaṭṭayanti etena, ettha vā sabhāgavisabhāgā ca dhammā, tesaṃ vā āvaṭṭananti āvaṭṭo. Desanāya gahitadhammānaṃ sabhāgāsabhāgadhammavasena āvaṭṭanalakkhaṇo hi āvaṭṭo hāro. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

“Monks, I do not see another…pe… a woman’s form”—by this, unwise attention is indicated. In that case where the mind is overwhelmed, wise attention is indicated. For one who attends unwisely, craving and ignorance increase. Through grasping craving, nine craving-rooted states revolve. Through grasping ignorance, the entire wheel of existence rooted in ignorance revolves. And through grasping wise attention, states rooted in wise attention revolve, as does the fourfold wheel of accomplishment. This is the revolving method. By this, or herein, similar and dissimilar states are made to revolve, or their revolving is 'revolving.' Indeed, the revolving method is characterized by the revolving of states as similar and dissimilar to the states taken up in the exposition. And this has been said:

“Ekamhi padaṭṭhāne, pariyesati sesakaṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ;

Āvaṭṭati paṭipakkhe, āvaṭṭo nāma so hāro”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“When one foundation is present, one seeks the remaining foundation; it revolves towards the counterpart. That method is called the revolving method.” (Netti. 4, Niddesavāra)

Rūpaṃ [V 1.0052] catubbidhaṃ kammasamuṭṭhānaṃ, cittasamuṭṭhānaṃ, utusamuṭṭhānaṃ, āhārasamuṭṭhānaṃ, tathā iṭṭhaṃ iṭṭhamajjhattaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ aniṭṭhamajjhattanti. Idha pana iṭṭhaṃ adhippetaṃ. Cittaṃ kusalacittamettha veditabbaṃ. Taṃ kāmāvacaraṃ, rūpāvacaraṃ, arūpāvacaraṃ, lokuttaranti catubbidhaṃ. Vedanādisampayuttadhammabhedato anekavidhanti [M 1.0059] ayaṃ vibhattihāro. Vibhajīyanti etena, ettha vā sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇānaṃ saṃkilesavodānadhammānaṃ bhūmiyoti vibhatti. Vibhajanaṃ vā etesaṃ bhūmiyoti vibhatti. Saṃkilesadhamme vodānadhamme ca sādhāraṇāsādhāraṇato padaṭṭhānato bhūmito vibhajanalakkhaṇo hi vibhattihāro. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Form is fourfold: kamma-originated, mind-originated, temperature-originated, and nutriment-originated. Likewise, it is desirable, desirable-neutral, undesirable, and undesirable-neutral. Here, however, the desirable is intended. Mind should be understood here as wholesome mind. It is fourfold: sense-sphere, form-sphere, formless-sphere, and supramundane. It is of many kinds due to the diversity of associated states such as feeling. This is the analytical method. By this, or herein, things are analyzed; or 'analysis' (vibhatti) is the ground for common and uncommon states of defilement and purification. Or 'analysis' is the analysis of these by their grounds. Indeed, the analytical method is characterized by analyzing states of defilement and states of purification as common or uncommon, by way of their foundation and ground. And this has been said:

“Dhammañca padaṭṭhānaṃ, bhūmiñca vibhajjate ayaṃ hāro;

Sādhāraṇe asādhāraṇe ca neyyo vibhattī”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“This method analyzes the state, the foundation, and the ground; it should be understood as analysis in terms of the common and the uncommon.” (Netti. 4, Niddesavāra)

Itthirūpaṃ purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhati ayoniso manasikaroto, yoniso manasikaroto na pariyādiyati susaṃvutindriyattā sīlesu samāhitassāti ayaṃ parivatto hāro. Paṭipakkhavasena parivattīyanti iminā, ettha vā sutte vuttadhammā, parivattanaṃ vā tesanti parivatto. Niddiṭṭhānaṃ dhammānaṃ paṭipakkhato parivattanalakkhaṇo hi parivatto hāro. Vuttañhetaṃ –

A woman's form stands overwhelming a man's mind when he attends unwisely, but it does not overwhelm when he attends wisely, due to well-restrained faculties and being composed in virtue—this is the transforming mode. By this, things are transformed by way of opposition; or here, the states stated in the sutta, or their transformation—this is the transforming mode. Indeed, the transforming mode is characterized by the transformation of the designated states by way of opposition. For this is said:

“Kusalākusale dhamme, niddiṭṭhe bhāvite pahīne ca;

Parivattati paṭipakkhe, hāro parivattano nāmā”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“Wholesome and unwholesome states, when specified, developed, and abandoned; it transforms in opposition, this is called the transforming mode.” (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Bhikkhave, samaṇā pabbajitāti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Aññaṃ paraṃ kiñcīti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Rūpaṃ vaṇṇaṃ cakkhuviññeyyanti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Samanupassāmi olokessāmi jānāmīti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Evaṃ itthaṃ imaṃ pakāranti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Purisassa puggalassāti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Cittaṃ viññāṇaṃ manoti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Pariyādāya gahetvā khepetvāti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Tiṭṭhati dharati ṭhātīti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Yathā yena pakārena yenākārenāti pariyāyavacanaṃ. Itthī nārī mātugāmoti pariyāyavacananti ayaṃ vevacano hāro. Vividhaṃ vacanaṃ ekassevatthassa vācakametthāti vivacanaṃ, vivacanameva vevacanaṃ. Vividhaṃ vuccati etena atthoti vā vivacanaṃ, vivacanameva vevacanaṃ. Ekasmiṃ atthe anekapariyāyasaddappayojanalakkhaṇo hi vevacano hāro. Vuttañhetaṃ –

“Monks, ‘ascetics who have gone forth’ is a synonym. ‘Another, beyond this’ is a synonym. ‘Form, color, cognizable by the eye’ is a synonym. ‘I attend, I look, I know’ is a synonym. ‘Thus, in this way, in this manner’ is a synonym. ‘A man, a person’ is a synonym. ‘Mind, consciousness, intellect’ is a synonym. ‘Having overwhelmed, having taken, having destroyed’ is a synonym. ‘Stands, lasts, remains’ is a synonym. ‘As, by which manner, by which way’ is a synonym. ‘A woman, a female, a member of the female sex’ is a synonym—this is the synonym mode. Here, 'vivacana' means diverse expressions that are indicative of one and the same meaning; 'vivacana' itself is 'vevacana'. Or 'vivacana' means that by which a meaning is expressed in diverse ways; 'vivacana' itself is 'vevacana'. Indeed, the synonym mode is characterized by the application of many synonymous words for a single meaning. This has been said:”

“Vevacanāni [V 1.0053] bahūni tu, sutte vuttāni ekadhammassa;

Yo jānāti suttavidū, vevacano nāma so hāro”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“Many synonyms for a single state are stated in the suttas; that mode which is understood by a knower of the suttas is called the synonym mode.” (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Rūpaṃ [M 1.0060] kāḷasāmādivasena anekadhā paññattaṃ. Puriso khattiyādivasena anekadhā paññatto. Cittaṃ parittamahaggatādivasena anekadhā paññattaṃ. “Pariyādāyā”ti ettha pariyādānaṃ pariyādāyakānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ vasena vītikkamapariyuṭṭhānādinā ca anekadhā paññattaṃ. Ayaṃ paññattihāro. Pakārehi, pabhedato vā ñāpīyanti iminā, ettha vā atthāti paññatti. Ekekassa dhammassa anekāhi paññattīhi paññāpetabbākāravibhāvanalakkhaṇo hi paññattihāro. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Form is designated in many ways, by way of black, dark, and so on. A person is designated in many ways, by way of Khattiya, and so on. The mind is designated in many ways, by way of limited, exalted, and so on. Here, in ‘pariyādāya’ (having overwhelmed), the act of overwhelming (pariyādāna) is designated in many ways by way of the unwholesome states that overwhelm, and by way of transgression, obsession, and so on. This is the designation mode. By this, things are made known by way of modes or distinctions; or here, ‘paññatti’ means that meaning exists. Indeed, the designation mode is characterized by clarifying the manner in which each state is to be designated by many designations. For this was said:

“Ekaṃ bhagavā dhammaṃ, paññattīhi vividhāhi deseti;

So ākāro ñeyyo, paññattī nāma so hāro”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“The Blessed One teaches one state with various designations; that mode is to be understood, that is called the designation mode.” (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Virodhipaccayasamavāye visadisuppattiruppanavaṇṇavikārāpattiyā taṃsamaṅgino hadayaṅgatabhāvappakāsanaṃ rūpaṭṭhoti aniccatāmukhena otaraṇaṃ, aniccassa pana dukkhattā dukkhatāmukhena, dukkhassa ca anattakattā suññatāmukhena otaraṇaṃ. Cittaṃ manoviññāṇadhātu, tassā pariyādāyikā taṇhā tadekaṭṭhā ca pāpadhammā dhammadhātūti dhātumukhena otaraṇaṃ. Evaṃ khandhāyatanādimukhehipi otaraṇaṃ vattabbanti ayaṃ otaraṇo hāro. Otārīyanti anuppavesīyanti etena, ettha vā suttāgatā dhammā paṭiccasamuppādādīsūti otaraṇo. Paṭiccasamuppādādimukhena suttatthassa otaraṇalakkhaṇo hi otaraṇo hāro. Vuttañhetaṃ –

The characteristic of form (rūpaṭṭho) is the manifestation of its being grasped by one endowed with it, through the arising of dissimilarity, affliction, and change of appearance in the combination of opposing conditions; this is penetration through the aspect of impermanence. Since what is impermanent is suffering, penetration occurs through the aspect of suffering. And since suffering is non-self, penetration occurs through the aspect of emptiness. The mind is the element of mental consciousness; the craving that consumes it, and the unwholesome states having the same basis as it, are the element of phenomena—thus, penetration occurs through the aspect of elements. In this way, penetration should be spoken of through the aspects of aggregates, sense bases, and so on. This is the method of penetration. By this, things are entered into, they are penetrated. Or, here, the teachings found in the suttas, such as dependent origination, are the means of penetration. For the method of penetration is characterized by entering into the meaning of the suttas through the gateway of dependent origination and so on. As it has been said—

“Yo ca paṭiccuppādo, indriyakhandhā ca dhātuāyatanā;

Etehi otarati yo, otaraṇo nāma so hāro”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“Whatever is dependent origination, and the faculties, aggregates, elements, and sense bases; whoever penetrates these, that is called the method of penetration.” (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Nāhaṃ, bhikkhave…pe… samanupassāmīti ārambho. Evaṃ purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatīti padasuddhi, na pana ārambhasuddhi. Yathayidantiādi padasuddhi ceva ārambhasuddhi cāti ayaṃ sodhano hāro. Sodhīyanti samādhīyanti etena, ettha vā sutte padapadatthapañhārambhāti sodhano. Sutte padapadatthapañhārambhānaṃ sodhanalakkhaṇo hi sodhano hāro. Vuttañhetaṃ –

“Monks, I do not…pe…perceive”—this is the beginning. “Thus, a person’s mind remains completely consumed”—this is purity of wording, but not purity of the beginning. “As it is,” etc., this is purity of wording and purity of the beginning—this is the method of purification. By this, they are purified, they are composed. Or, here, the words, the meanings of the words, the questions, and the beginnings in the sutta are purified; hence, it is the method of purification. For the method of purification is characterized by the purification of the words, the meanings of the words, the questions, and the beginnings in the sutta. As it has been said—

“Vissajjitamhi [V 1.0054] pañhe, gāthāyaṃ pucchitāyamārabbha;

Suddhāsuddhaparikkhā, hāro so sodhano nāmā”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“When the question has been answered, having begun with the verse that was asked; the examination of purity and impurity—that method is called purification.” (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Aññanti [M 1.0061] sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ kassaci visesassa anāmaṭṭhattā. Ekarūpampīti taṃ avikappetvā visesavacanaṃ. Yathayidanti sāmaññato adhiṭṭhānaṃ aniyamavacanabhāvato. Itthirūpanti taṃ avikappetvā visesavacananti ayaṃ adhiṭṭhāno hāro. Adhiṭṭhīyanti anuppavattīyanti etena, ettha vā sāmaññavisesabhūtā dhammā vinā vikappenāti adhiṭṭhāno. Suttāgatānaṃ dhammānaṃ avikappanavaseneva sāmaññavisesaniddhāraṇalakkhaṇo hi adhiṭṭhāno hāro. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

“Añña” (other) is the establishment in a general way because no particular is touched upon. “Even of one form” means, without conceptualizing it, a term of particularity. “As it is” means the establishment in a general way due to its nature of being unrestricted speech. “Female form” means, without conceptualizing it, a term of particularity—this is the method of establishment. By this, they are established, they are not produced. Or, here, the phenomena that are general and particular are established without conceptualization; hence, it is the method of establishment. For the method of establishment is characterized by the ascertainment of generality and particularity simply by way of non-conceptualization of the phenomena stated in the suttas. And this was also said—

“Ekattatāya dhammā, yepi ca vemattatāya niddiṭṭhā;

Tena vikappayitabbā, eso hāro adhiṭṭhāno”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“Those phenomena designated as one, and also those designated as diverse; by this they should be conceptualized—this method is establishment.” (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Rūpassa kammāvijjādayo kammacittādayo ca hetu. Samanupassanāya āvajjanādayo. Kusalassa cittassa yoniso manasikārādayo. Pariyādāyāti ettha pariyādānassa ayonisomanasikārādayoti ayaṃ parikkhāro hāro. Parikaroti abhisaṅkharoti phalanti parikkhāro, hetu paccayo ca. Parikkhāraṃ ācikkhatīti parikkhāro, hāro. Parikkhāravisayattā, parikkhārasahacaraṇato vā parikkhāro. Sutte āgatadhammānaṃ parikkhārasaṅkhātahetupaccaye niddhāretvā saṃvaṇṇanālakkhaṇo hi parikkhāro hāro. Vuttañhetaṃ –

The cause of form is kamma, ignorance, etc., and kamma-consciousness, etc. For sustained observation, attention, etc. For wholesome consciousness, wise attention, etc. Here, the accessories for consuming (pariyādāna) are unwise attention, etc.—this is the method of accessories. An accessory (parikkhāra) is that which prepares, conditions, and bears fruit; it is a cause and a condition. It explains the accessories, therefore it is the method of accessories. Or, it is called “parikkhāra” due to being the object of accessories or associating with the accessories. For the method of accessories is characterized by determining and explaining the phenomena stated in the suttas as causes and conditions, which are called accessories. As it has been said—

“Ye dhammā yaṃ dhammaṃ, janayantippaccayā paramparato;

Hetumavakaḍḍhayitvā, eso hāro parikkhāro”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“Those phenomena which give rise to other phenomena, successively through conditions; having drawn out the cause—this method is accessories.” (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhatīti ettha pariyādāyikā visesato taṇhāvijjā veditabbā tāsaṃ vasena pariyādānasambhavato. Tāsu taṇhāya rūpamadhiṭṭhānaṃ, avijjāya arūpaṃ. Visesato taṇhāya samatho paṭipakkho, avijjāya vipassanā. Samathassa cetovimutti, phalavipassanāya paññāvimutti. Tathā hi tā rāgavirāgā avijjāvirāgāti visesetvā vuccantīti ayaṃ samāropano hāro. Samāropīyanti etena, ettha vā padaṭṭhānādimukhena dhammāti samāropano. Sutte āgatadhammānaṃ padaṭṭhānavevacanabhāvanāpahānasamāropanavicāraṇalakkhaṇo hi samāropano hāro. Vuttañhetaṃ –

“The mind of a person remains consumed”—here, craving and ignorance are to be understood as particularly consuming, because through them, complete consumption arises. Among these, craving has form as its basis, while ignorance has the formless. Specifically, serenity is the antidote to craving, while insight is the antidote to ignorance. The liberation of mind comes from serenity, and the liberation by wisdom comes from the fruition of insight. Thus, they are distinguished as the fading away of lust and the fading away of ignorance—this is the method of inclusion. By this, they are included. Or, here, phenomena are included through the aspects of basis and so on; hence, it is the method of inclusion. For the method of inclusion is characterized by the investigation of phenomena stated in the suttas, through their basis, synonyms, development, abandonment, and inclusion. As it has been said—

“Ye [V 1.0055][M 1.0062] dhammā yaṃ mūlā, ye cekatthā pakāsitā muninā;

Te samāropayitabbā, esa samāropano hāro”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“Those phenomena that have a root, and those that have a single meaning explained by the Sage, these should be included; this is the method of inclusion.” (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Ettāvatā ca –

Thus far—

“Desanā vicayo yutti, padaṭṭhāno ca lakkhaṇo;

Catubyūho ca āvaṭṭo, vibhatti parivattano.

“The exposition, the investigation, the reasoning, the basis, and the characteristic; the fourfold analysis, the turning, the classification, and the reversal.

Vevacano ca paññatti, otaraṇo ca sodhano;

Adhiṭṭhāno parikkhāro, samāropano soḷaso”ti. (netti. 1 uddesavāra) –

The synonym and the designation, the penetration and the purification; the establishment, the accessories, the inclusion—these are the sixteen.” (Netti. 1 Uddesavāra)—

Evaṃ vuttā soḷasa hārā dassitāti veditabbā. Harīyanti etehi, ettha vā suttageyyādivisayā aññāṇasaṃsayavipallāsāti hārā. Haranti vā sayaṃ tāni, haraṇamattameva vāti hārā phalūpacārena. Atha vā harīyanti voharīyanti dhammasaṃvaṇṇakadhammappaṭiggāhakehi dhammassa dānaggahaṇavasenāti hārā. Atha vā hārā viyāti hārā. Yathā hi anekaratanāvalisamūho hārasaṅkhāto attano avayavabhūtaratanasamphassehi samupajaniyamānahilādasukho hutvā tadupabhogijanasarīrasantāpaṃ nidāghapariḷāhūpajanitaṃ vūpasameti, evameva tepi nānāvidhaparamattharatanappabandhā saṃvaṇṇanāvisesā attano avayavabhūtaparamattharatanādhigamena samuppādiyamānanibbutisukhā dhammappaṭiggāhakajanahadayaparitāpaṃ kāmarāgādikilesahetukaṃ vūpasamentīti. Atha vā hārayanti aññāṇādinīhāraṃ apagamaṃ karonti ācikkhantīti vā hārā. Atha vā sotujanacittassa haraṇato ramaṇato ca hārā niruttinayena yathā “bhavesu vantagamano bhagavā”ti (visuddhi. 1.144; pārā. aṭṭha. 1.verañjakaṇḍavaṇṇanā).

It should thus be understood that the sixteen methods have been shown. They are called “methods” (hāras) because by them [defilements] are carried away (harīyanti). Or, here, ignorance, doubt, and perversions concerning the domain of suttas, verses, etc., are the hāras (because they are carried away). Or, they themselves carry away (haranti) those, or they are merely the act of carrying away (haraṇamattameva)—hence, they are called “methods” metaphorically. Alternatively, they are called “methods” because they are carried away (harīyanti) and declared (voharīyanti) by those who praise the Dhamma and those who receive it, through the giving and accepting of the Dhamma. Or, they are called “methods” (hāras) because they are like necklaces. Just as a collection of many jeweled strands, called a necklace, brings joy through the contact of its component jewels, generating bliss and soothing the bodily heat born of summer’s scorching heat in those who enjoy it, so too do these various strands of supreme truth-jewels, distinguished by ways of praise, bring forth the bliss of Nibbāna through the realization of their component supreme truths and thereby pacify the heart’s torment—born of defilements like sensual lust—in those who receive the Dhamma. Or, they are called “methods” (hāras) because they cause the removal (hārayanti) of ignorance and other defilements, or because they declare (ācikkhanti) their removal. Or, they are called “methods” etymologically because they captivate (haraṇa) and delight (ramaṇa) the minds of listeners—just as it is said, “The Blessed One, who has abandoned journeying through states of existence…” (Visuddhimagga 1.144; Pārājika Aṭṭhakathā 1, Verañjakaṇḍa commentary).

Ito paraṃ pana nandiyāvaṭṭādipañcavidhanayā veditabbā – tattha taṇhāvijjā samudayasaccaṃ, tāsaṃ adhiṭṭhānādibhūtā rūpadhammā dukkhasaccaṃ, tesaṃ appavatti nirodhasaccaṃ, nirodhappajānanā paṭipadā maggasaccaṃ. Taṇhāgahaṇena cettha māyāsāṭheyyamānātimānamadappamādapāpicchatāpāpamittatāahirikaanottappādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo. Avijjāgahaṇena viparītamanasikārakodhūpanāhamakkhapaḷāsaissāmacchariya- sārambhadovacassatābhavadiṭṭhivibhavadiṭṭhiādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo. Vuttavipariyāyato [M 1.0063] kusalapakkho netabbo. Kathaṃ? Amāyāasāṭheyyādivasena aviparītamanasikārādivasena ca. Tathā samathapakkhiyānaṃ saddhindriyādīnaṃ[V 1.0056], vipassanāpakkhiyānaṃ aniccasaññādīnañca vasena vodānapakkho netabboti ayaṃ nandiyāvaṭṭassa nayassa bhūmi. Yo hi taṇhāavijjāhi saṃkilesapakkhassa suttatthassa samathavipassanāhi vodānapakkhassa ca catusaccayojanamukhena nayanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso, ayaṃ nandiyāvaṭṭanayo nāma. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Furthermore, this should be understood according to the fivefold method of Nandiyāvaṭṭa, etc. Herein, craving and ignorance are the truth of arising. The material phenomena that are their basis, etc., are the truth of suffering. The non-occurrence of these is the truth of cessation. The path, which is the understanding of cessation, is the truth of the path. Here, by taking craving as representative, the unwholesome side should be led through deceit, fraud, conceit, arrogance, intoxication, heedlessness, evil desires, bad companionship, shamelessness, lack of fear of wrongdoing, etc. By taking ignorance as representative, the unwholesome side should be led through wrong attention, anger, enmity, contempt, spite, envy, selfishness, rivalry, obstinacy, views of eternalism, and views of annihilation, etc. The wholesome side should be led in the opposite way, as stated. How? Through non-deceit, non-fraud, etc., and through right attention, etc. Likewise, the purified side should be led through the faculties of faith, etc., belonging to the side of serenity, and through the perceptions of impermanence, etc., belonging to the side of insight. This is the ground of Nandiyāvaṭṭa’s method. For that special exposition which is characterized by leading the meaning of the suttas, both the defiled side by craving and ignorance, and the purified side by serenity and insight, by way of connecting with the four truths—this is called the method of Nandiyāvaṭṭa. As it is said—

“Taṇhañca avijjampi ca, samathena vipassanāya yo neti;

Saccehi yojayitvā, ayaṃ nayo nandiyāvaṭṭo”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“Whoever leads craving and ignorance away by serenity and insight, having yoked them with the truths—this method is Nandiyāvaṭṭa.” (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Nandiyāvaṭṭassa viya āvaṭṭo etassāti nandiyāvaṭṭo. Yathā hi nandiyāvaṭṭo anto ṭhitena padhānāvayavena bahiddhā āvaṭṭati, evamayampi nayoti attho. Atha vā nandiyā taṇhāya pamodassa vā āvaṭṭo etthāti nandiyāvaṭṭo.

Its turning is like that of Nandiyāvaṭṭa, therefore it is Nandiyāvaṭṭa. For just as the Nandiyāvaṭṭa whirlpool swirls outward because of its main component remaining fixed within, so too does this method—such is the meaning. Alternatively, it is called Nandiyāvaṭṭa because the turning of delight (nandi), craving (taṇhā), or joy (pamoda) is here.

Heṭṭhā vuttanayena gahitesu taṇhāvijjātappakkhiyadhammesu taṇhā lobho, avijjā moho, avijjāya sampayutto lohite sati pubbo viya taṇhāya sati sijjhamāno āghāto doso iti tīhi akusalamūlehi gahitehi, tappaṭipakkhato kusalacittaggahaṇena ca tīṇi kusalamūlāni gahitāni eva honti. Idhāpi lobho sabbāni vā sāsavakusalamūlāni samudayasaccaṃ, tannibbattā tesaṃ adhiṭṭhānagocarabhūtā upādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccantiādinā saccayojanā veditabbā. Phalaṃ panettha vimokkhattayavasena niddhāretabbaṃ, tīhi akusalamūlehi tividhaduccaritasaṃkilesamalavisamaakusalasaññāvitakkādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo, tathā tīhi kusalamūlehi tividhasucaritasamakusalasaññāvitakkasaddhammasamādhivimokkhamukhādivasena vodānapakkho netabboti ayaṃ tipukkhalassa nayassa bhūmi. Yo hi akusalamūlehi saṃkilesapakkhassa kusalamūlehi vodānapakkhassa suttatthassa ca catusaccayojanāmukhena nayanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso, ayaṃ tipukkhalanayo nāma. Tīhi avayavehi [M 1.0064] lobhādīhi saṃkilesapakkhe, alobhādīhi ca vodānapakkhe pukkhalo sobhanoti tipukkhalo. Vuttañhetaṃ –

In the manner stated above, among the states included under craving, ignorance, and those pertaining to them: craving is greed; ignorance is delusion. When ignorance is associated with it, and just as pus arises from blood, so too, when craving is present, hatred (āghāta), which is ill-will (dosa), arises. Thus, the three unwholesome roots are understood. By counteracting them through the grasping of wholesome consciousness, the three wholesome roots are also understood. Here, greed, or all unwholesome roots accompanied by taints, is the truth of origin. The aggregates of clinging, which arise from them and serve as their basis and domain, are the truth of suffering—this connection to the truths should be understood. The result here should be determined in terms of the three liberations. The unwholesome side should be led on by the three unwholesome roots, manifesting as the threefold misconduct, defilements, impurities, wrong unwholesome perceptions, and thoughts. Similarly, the purified side should be led on by the three wholesome roots, manifesting as the threefold good conduct, right wholesome perceptions, thoughts, true Dhamma, concentration, the gateways to liberation, and so forth—this is the ground of the threefold analysis. For that special exposition which is characterized by leading the meaning of the suttas—the side of defilement through the unwholesome roots, and the side of purification through the wholesome roots—by way of connecting with the four truths, this is called the threefold analysis. With three components, the defilement side (greed and so forth) and the purification side (non-greed and so forth), the analysis is splendid, hence it is called the threefold analysis. As it is said—

“Yo akusale samūlehi,

Neti kusale ca kusalamūlehi;

Bhūtaṃ tathaṃ avitathaṃ,

Tipukkhalaṃ taṃ nayaṃ āhū”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

“He who leads the unwholesome with their roots, and the wholesome with their wholesome roots, (knows) the real, the true, the unfailing; that method they call the threefold analysis.” (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Vuttanayena [V 1.0057] gahitesu taṇhāvijjātappakkhiyadhammesu visesato taṇhādiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena asubhe “subha”nti, dukkhe “sukha”nti ca vipallāsā, avijjādiṭṭhīnaṃ vasena anicce “nicca”nti, anattani “attā”ti vipallāsā veditabbā. Tesaṃ paṭipakkhato kusalacittaggahaṇena siddhehi sativīriyasamādhipaññindriyehi cattāri satipaṭṭhānāni siddhāniyeva honti.

According to the method explained, among the states included under craving, ignorance, and those pertaining to them, distortions are to be understood especially in terms of craving and views: regarding the unattractive as “attractive,” and the painful as “pleasant.” In terms of ignorance and views: regarding the impermanent as “permanent,” and the non-self as “self.” By opposing them, with the taking up of wholesome consciousness, the four foundations of mindfulness are indeed established by the established faculties of mindfulness, energy, concentration, and wisdom.

Tattha catūhi indriyehi cattāro puggalā niddisitabbā. Kathaṃ? Duvidho hi taṇhācarito mudindriyo tikkhindriyoti, tathā diṭṭhicarito. Tesu paṭhamo asubhe “subha”nti vipariyesaggāhī satibalena yathābhūtaṃ kāyasabhāvaṃ sallakkhento bhāvanābalena taṃ vipallāsaṃ samugghātetvā sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamati. Dutiyo asukhe “sukha”nti vipariyesaggāhī “uppannaṃ kāmavitakkaṃ nādhivāsetī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.26; a. ni. 4.14; 6.58) vuttena vīriyasaṃvarabhūtena vīriyabalena paṭipakkhaṃ vinodento bhāvanābalena taṃ vipallāsaṃ vidhametvā sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamati. Tatiyo anicce “nicca”nti vipallāsaggāhī samathabalena samāhitacitto saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇikabhāvaṃ sallakkhento bhāvanābalena taṃ vipallāsaṃ samugghātetvā sammattaniyāmaṃ okkamati. Catuttho santatisamūhakiccārammaṇaghanavañcitatāya phassādidhammapuñjamatte anattani “attā”ti micchābhinivesī catukoṭikasuññatāmanasikārena taṃ micchābhinivesaṃ viddhaṃsento sāmaññaphalaṃ sacchikaroti. Subhasaññādīhi catūhipi vā vipallāsehi samudayasaccaṃ, tesamadhiṭṭhānārammaṇabhūtā pañcupādānakkhandhā dukkhasaccantiādinā saccayojanā veditabbā. Phalaṃ panettha cattāri sāmaññaphalāni, catūhi cettha vipallāsehi caturāsavoghayogaganthaagatitaṇhupādānasallaviññāṇaṭṭhitiapariññādivasena akusalapakkho netabbo, tathā catūhi satipaṭṭhānehi [M 1.0065] catubbidhajjhānavihārādhiṭṭhānasukhabhāgiyadhammaappamaññāsammappadhānaiddhipādādivasena vodānapakkho netabboti ayaṃ sīhavikkīḷitassa nayassa bhūmi. Yo hi subhasaññādīhi vipallāsehi sakalassa saṃkilesapakkhassa saddhindriyādīhi ca vodānapakkhassa catusaccayojanāvasena nayanalakkhaṇo saṃvaṇṇanāviseso, ayaṃ sīhavikkīḷito nāma. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Here, four types of individuals should be described by means of the four faculties. How? The craving-prone individual is twofold: one with dull faculties and one with sharp faculties; likewise for the view-prone individual. Among them, the first, who grasps the perversion 'beautiful' in what is foul, discerns the true nature of the body with the power of mindfulness and, through the power of development, uproots that perversion and enters the certainty of rightness. The second, who grasps the perversion 'pleasant' in what is suffering, dispels the opposing tendency with the power of energy—which is the restraint of energy spoken of in such passages as 'one does not tolerate an arisen sensual thought' (MN 2; AN 4.14; 6.58)—and, through the power of development, shatters that perversion and enters the certainty of rightness. The third, who grasps the perversion 'permanent' in what is impermanent, with a mind concentrated by the power of tranquility, discerns the momentary nature of formations and, through the power of development, uproots that perversion and enters the certainty of rightness. The fourth, deceived by the compactness of continuity, mass, function, and object, has the wrong adherence of 'self' in what is not-self, a mere heap of phenomena such as contact. Through attention to emptiness with its four aspects, he destroys that wrong adherence and realizes the fruit of recluseship. The connection to the truths should be understood thus: the truth of the origin is the four perversions, such as the perception of beauty; the truth of suffering is the five aggregates of clinging, which are their basis and object; and so on. Here, the result is the four fruits of recluseship. Furthermore, the unwholesome side should be led by the four perversions, by way of the non-full-understanding of the four cankers, floods, bonds, fetters, wrong courses, craving, clinging, darts, stations of consciousness, and so on. Likewise, the side of purification should be led by the four foundations of mindfulness, the four kinds of meditative dwellings, the determinations, the states partaking of happiness, the boundless states, the right efforts, the bases of psychic power, and so on. This is the ground for the method of 'the lion's play.' For that special exposition, characterized by leading the entire side of defilement by means of the perversions such as the perception of beauty, and the side of purification by means of the faculties such as faith, through the application of the four truths—this is called 'the lion's play.' As it is said:

“Yo neti vipallāsehi,

Kilese indriyehi saddhamme;

Etaṃ nayaṃ nayavidū,

Sīhavikkīḷitaṃ āhū”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

"He who leads the defilements by means of perversions, and the true Dhamma by means of the faculties; this method, those skilled in methods call 'the lion's play.'" (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Asantāsanajavaparakkamādivisesayogena [V 1.0058] sīho bhagavā, tassa vikkīḷitaṃ desanā vacīkammabhūto vihāroti katvā vipallāsatappaṭipakkhaparidīpanato sīhassa vikkīḷitaṃ etthāti sīhavikkīḷito, nayo. Balavisesayogadīpanato vā sīhavikkīḷitasadisattā nayo sīhavikkīḷito. Balaviseso cettha saddhādibalaṃ, dasabalāni eva vā.

The Blessed One is a lion due to his connection with special qualities such as fearlessness, swiftness, and exertion. Considering his teaching, which is his verbal action, as his sport, and because it illuminates the perversions and their opposites, the method is called 'the lion's play' (sīhavikkīḷita), for the lion's play is in this. Alternatively, the method is called 'the lion's play' because it resembles a lion's play in illuminating the application of special powers. Here, the special power refers to the powers of faith and so forth, or indeed the ten powers.

Imesaṃ pana tiṇṇaṃ atthanayānaṃ siddhiyā vohāranayadvayaṃ siddhameva hoti. Tathā hi atthanayattayadisābhāvena kusalādidhammānaṃ ālocanaṃ disālocanaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Now, for the accomplishment of these three methods of meaning, the two methods of expression are indeed established. For the examination of wholesome and other states, by way of the three methods of meaning serving as directions, is 'scrutiny of direction.' As it is said:

“Veyyākaraṇesu hi ye,

Kusalākusalā tahiṃ tahiṃ vuttā;

Manasā olokayate,

Taṃ khu disālocanaṃ āhū”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

"For in expositions, those wholesome and unwholesome states spoken of here and there, one contemplates with the mind. That, truly, they call 'scrutiny of direction.'" (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Tathā ālocitānaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ atthanayattayayojane samānayanato aṅkuso viya aṅkuso. Vuttañhetaṃ –

Likewise, because it brings together those states that have been scrutinized for application to the three methods of meaning, it is like a goad; it is the Goad. As it is said:

“Oloketvā disalocanena, ukkhipiya yaṃ samāneti;

Sabbe kusalākusale, ayaṃ nayo aṅkuso nāmā”ti. (netti. 4 niddesavāra);

"Having scrutinized with 'scrutiny of direction,' and having lifted up what it brings together—all wholesome and unwholesome states—this method is called 'the goad.'" (Netti. 4 Niddesavāra);

Tasmā manasāva atthanayānaṃ disābhūtadhammānaṃ locanaṃ disālocanaṃ, tesaṃ samānayanaṃ aṅkusoti pañcapi nayāni yuttāni honti.

Therefore, the scrutiny by the mind itself of states that are directions for the methods of meaning is 'scrutiny of direction'; and the bringing together of these is 'the goad.' Thus, all five methods are fitting.

Ettāvatā [M 1.0066] ca –

And thus far—

“Paṭhamo nandiyāvaṭṭo, dutiyo ca tipukkhalo;

Sīhavikkīḷito nāma, tatiyo nayalañjako.

"The first is Nandiyāvaṭṭa, and the second is Tipukkhalo; the third, named Sīhavikkīḷita, is the Method-Illuminator.

Disālocanamāhaṃsu, catutthaṃ nayamuttamaṃ;

Pañcamo aṅkuso nāma, sabbe pañca nayā gatā”ti. (netti. 1 uddesavāra) –

They declared Disālocana as the fourth, the supreme method; the fifth is called Aṅkusa—all five methods are thus understood." (Netti. 1 Uddesavāra) –

Evaṃ [V 1.0059] vuttapañcanayāpi ettha dassitāti veditabbā. Nayati saṃkilesaṃ vodānañca vibhāgato ñāpetīti nayo, lañjeti pakāseti suttatthanti lañjako, nayo ca so lañjako cāti nayalañjako. Idañca suttaṃ soḷasavidhe suttantapaṭṭhāne saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ byatirekamukhena nibbedhāsekkhabhāgiyanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aṭṭhavīsatividhe pana suttantapaṭṭhāne lokiyalokuttaraṃ sattadhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ ñāṇaññeyyaṃ dassanabhāvanaṃ sakavacanaṃ vissajjanīyaṃ kusalākusalaṃ anuññātaṃ paṭikkhittañcāti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, it should be understood that the five methods thus spoken of are also shown here. A method (nayo) is so called because it leads, making known defilement and purification distinctly. An illuminator (lañjako) is so called because it marks and illuminates the meaning of the sutta; it is a method and it is an illuminator, hence 'method-illuminator' (nayalañjako). This sutta, in the sixteenfold classification of sutta foundations, should be regarded as pertaining to defilement by way of contrast, and pertaining to penetration and the state of one beyond training. But in the twenty-eightfold classification of sutta foundations, it should be understood as worldly and supramundane, the sevenfold basis of phenomena, knowledge and the knowable, seeing and development, one's own statement, the rejoinder, the wholesome and unwholesome, and the permitted and the forbidden.

Tattha soḷasavidhasuttantaṃ paṭṭhānaṃ nāma “saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, vāsanābhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, asekkhabhāgiyaṃ suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, vāsanābhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, nibbedhabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, saṃkilesabhāgiyañca vāsanābhāgiyañca nibbedhabhāgiyañca asekkhabhāgiyañca suttaṃ, neva saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ na vāsanābhāgiyaṃ na nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ na asekkhabhāgiyaṃ sutta”nti (netti. 89) evaṃ vuttasoḷasasāsanapaṭṭhānāni.

Here, the sixteenfold foundation of discourses is as follows: "a discourse pertaining to defilement, a discourse pertaining to habitual tendencies, a discourse pertaining to penetration, a discourse pertaining to the state of one beyond training, a discourse pertaining to both defilement and habitual tendencies, a discourse pertaining to both defilement and penetration, a discourse pertaining to both defilement and the state of one beyond training, a discourse pertaining to both habitual tendencies and penetration, a discourse pertaining to both habitual tendencies and the state of one beyond training, a discourse pertaining to both penetration and the state of one beyond training, a discourse pertaining to defilement, habitual tendencies, and penetration, a discourse pertaining to defilement, habitual tendencies, and the state of one beyond training, a discourse pertaining to defilement, penetration, and the state of one beyond training, a discourse pertaining to habitual tendencies, penetration, and the state of one beyond training, a discourse pertaining to defilement, habitual tendencies, penetration, and the state of one beyond training, and a discourse pertaining to neither defilement, nor habitual tendencies, nor penetration, nor the state of one beyond training." (Netti. 89) Thus are these sixteen foundations of the Teaching stated.

Tattha saṃkilissanti etenāti saṃkileso, saṃkilesabhāge saṃkilesakoṭṭhāse pavattaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ. Vāsanā puññabhāvanā, vāsanābhāge pavattaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ, vāsanaṃ bhajāpetīti vā vāsanābhāgiyaṃ. Nibbijjhanaṃ lobhakkhandhādīnaṃ padālanaṃ nibbedho, nibbedhabhāge [M 1.0067] pavattaṃ, nibbedhaṃ bhajāpetīti vā nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ. Pariniṭṭhitasikkhā dhammā asekkhā, asekkhabhāge pavattaṃ, asekkhe bhajāpetīti vā asekkhabhāgiyaṃ. Tesu yattha taṇhādisaṃkileso vibhatto, idaṃ saṃkilesabhāgiyaṃ. Yattha dānādipuññakiriyavatthu vibhattaṃ, idaṃ vāsanābhāgiyaṃ. Yattha sekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo vibhattā, idaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyaṃ. Yattha pana asekkhā sīlakkhandhādayo vibhattā, idaṃ asekkhabhāgiyaṃ. Itarāni tesaṃ vomissakanayavasena vuttāni. Sabbāsavasaṃvarapariyāyādīnaṃ vasena sabbabhāgiyaṃ veditabbaṃ. Tattha hi saṃkilesadhammā lokiyasucaritadhammā sekkhā dhammā asekkhā dhammā ca vibhattā. Sabbabhāgiyaṃ pana “passaṃ na passatī”tiādikaṃ udakādianuvādavacanaṃ veditabbaṃ.

Therein, 'that by which one is defiled' is defilement; occurring in the portion of defilement, in the category of defilement, is 'pertaining to defilement.' Vāsanā is the cultivation of merit; occurring in the portion of vāsanā is 'pertaining to vāsanā,' or 'that which causes one to partake of vāsanā' is 'pertaining to vāsanā.' The piercing, the breaking apart of the aggregates of greed and so forth, is penetration; occurring in the portion of penetration, or 'that which causes one to partake of penetration,' is 'pertaining to penetration.' States of perfected training are the states of a non-trainee; occurring in the portion of the non-trainee, or 'that which causes one to partake of the states of a non-trainee,' is 'pertaining to the non-trainee.' Among these, where defilements such as craving are distinguished, this is 'pertaining to defilement.' Where the bases for meritorious action such as giving are distinguished, this is 'pertaining to vāsanā.' Where the aggregates of virtue and so forth of a trainee are distinguished, this is 'pertaining to penetration.' Where, however, the aggregates of virtue and so forth of a non-trainee are distinguished, this is 'pertaining to the non-trainee.' The others are spoken of by way of the method of combination. 'Pertaining to all portions' should be understood by way of the Discourse on the Restraint of All Taints and so forth. For therein, states of defilement, worldly states of good conduct, states of a trainee, and states of a non-trainee are distinguished. However, 'pertaining to all portions' should be understood as repetitive phrases such as 'seeing, he does not see,' which are words of reiteration concerning water and so forth.

Aṭṭhavīsatividhaṃ [V 1.0060] suttantapaṭṭhānaṃ pana “lokiyaṃ, lokuttaraṃ, lokiyañca lokuttarañca, sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ, dhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ, sattādhiṭṭhānañca dhammādhiṭṭhānañca, ñāṇaṃ, ñeyyaṃ, ñāṇañca ñeyyañca, dassanaṃ, bhāvanā, dassanañca bhāvanā ca, sakavacanaṃ, paravacanaṃ, sakavacanañca paravacanañca, vissajjanīyaṃ, avissajjanīyaṃ, vissajjanīyañca avissajjanīyañca, kammaṃ, vipāko, kammañca vipāko ca kusalaṃ, akusalaṃ, kusalañca akusalañca anuññātaṃ, paṭikkhittaṃ, anuññātañca paṭikkhittañca, thavo”ti (netti. 112) evamāgatāni aṭṭhavīsati sāsanapaṭṭhānāni. Tattha lokiyanti loke niyutto, loke vā vidito lokiyo. Idha pana lokiyo attho yasmiṃ sutte vutto, taṃ suttaṃ lokiyaṃ. Tathā lokuttaraṃ. Yasmiṃ pana sutte padesena lokiyaṃ, padesena lokuttaraṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ lokiyañca lokuttarañca. Sattaadhippāyasattapaññattimukhena desitaṃ sattādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Dhammavasena desitaṃ dhammādhiṭṭhānaṃ. Ubhayavasena desitaṃ sattādhiṭṭhānañca dhammādhiṭṭhānañca. Iminā nayena sabbapadesu attho veditabbo. Buddhādīnaṃ pana guṇābhitthavanavasena pavattaṃ suttaṃ thavo nāma –

The twenty-eightfold foundation of the suttas is as follows: 'mundane, supramundane, and both mundane and supramundane; founded on beings, founded on phenomena, and founded on both beings and phenomena; knowledge, the knowable, and both knowledge and the knowable; seeing, cultivation, and both seeing and cultivation; one's own word, another's word, and both one's own and another's word; to be explained, not to be explained, and both to be explained and not to be explained; action, result, and both action and result; wholesome, unwholesome, and both wholesome and unwholesome; permitted, prohibited, and both permitted and prohibited; and praise.' (Netti. 112) Thus are given the twenty-eight foundations of the teaching. Therein, 'mundane' means engaged in the world, or known in the world. Here, however, a sutta in which a mundane meaning is spoken is a 'mundane' sutta. Likewise for 'supramundane.' But a sutta in which the mundane is spoken of in part and the supramundane is spoken of in part is 'both mundane and supramundane.' Taught by way of the intention toward beings and the designation of beings, it is 'founded on beings.' Taught by way of phenomena, it is 'founded on phenomena.' Taught by way of both, it is 'founded on both beings and phenomena.' By this method, the meaning should be understood in all the terms. Furthermore, a sutta that proceeds by way of extolling the qualities of the Buddha and others is named 'praise'—

“Maggānaṭṭhaṅgiko seṭṭho, saccānaṃ caturo padā;

Virāgo seṭṭho dhammānaṃ, dvipadānañca cakkhumā”ti. (dha. pa. 273; netti. 170; peṭako. 30) ādikaṃ viya –

‘Of paths, the Eightfold is the best; of truths, the four statements are best; of states, dispassion is the best; and of bipeds, the one with vision is the best.’ (Dhp. 273; Netti. 170; Peṭ. 30), like this and so on—

Nettinayavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Netti Guide is concluded.

2. Saddagarukādīnanti [M 1.0068] ādisaddena gandharasaphoṭṭhabbagaruke saṅgaṇhāti. Āsayavasenāti ajjhāsayavasena. Utusamuṭṭhānopi itthisantānagato saddo labbhati, so idha nādhippetoti “cittasamuṭṭhāno”ti vuttaṃ. Kathitasaddo ālāpādisaddo. Gītasaddo sarena gāyanasaddo. Itthiyā hasanasaddopettha saṅgahetabbo tassapi purisena assādetabbato. Tenāha – “apica kho mātugāmassa saddaṃ suṇāti tirokuṭṭā vā tiropākārā vā hasantiyā vā bhaṇantiyā vā gāyantiyā vā, so tadassādetī”tiādi. Nivatthanivāsanassāti khalitthaddhassa nivāsanassa. Alaṅkārassāti nūpurādikassa alaṅkārassa. Itthisaddotveva veditabboti itthipaṭibaddhabhāvato vuttaṃ. Tenāha – “sabbopī”tiādi. Avidūraṭṭhāneti tassa hatthikulassa vasanaṭṭhānato avidūraṭṭhāne. Kāyūpapannoti sampannakāyo thirakathinamahākāyo. Mahāhatthīti mahānubhāvo hatthī. Jeṭṭhakaṃ katvāti yūthapatiṃ katvā.

2. ‘Of those who hold sound, etc., in high regard’: by the word ‘etc.,’ it includes those who hold smell, taste, and tangible objects in high regard. ‘By way of inclination’ means by way of underlying disposition. A sound originating from the season and occurring in a woman's continuity is also found, but that is not intended here; thus it is said, ‘mind-originated.’ ‘Spoken sound’ is sound such as conversation. ‘The sound of song’ is the sound of singing with the voice. Here, the sound of a woman laughing should also be included, because it too can be savored by a man. Therefore, it is said: ‘Moreover, he hears the sound of a woman from behind a wall or from behind a fence, laughing or speaking or singing, and he savors it,’ and so on. ‘Of the lower garment worn’ means of the lower garment of a harlot. ‘Of ornaments’ means of adornments such as anklets. ‘It should be understood as just a woman's sound’ is said because of its connection to a woman. Therefore, it is said: ‘All of this,’ and so on. ‘In a place not far’ means in a place not far from the dwelling place of that elephant herd. ‘Endowed with a body’ means having a complete body—firm, hard, and large. ‘A great elephant’ means an elephant of great power. ‘Having made him the chief’ means having made him the leader of the herd.

Kathinatikkhabhāvena [V 1.0061] siṅgasadisattā aḷasaṅkhātāni siṅgāni etassa atthīti siṅgī, suvaṇṇavaṇṇatāya mahābalatāya ca sīhahatthiādimigasadisattā migo viyāti migo. Tattha tattha kiccaṃ netubhāvena cakkhuyeva nettaṃ, taṃ uggataṭṭhena āyataṃ etassāti āyatacakkhunetto. Aṭṭhi eva taco etassāti aṭṭhittaco. Tenābhibhūtoti tena migena abhibhūto ajjhotthaṭo niccalaggahito hutvā. Karuṇaṃ rudāmīti kāruññapatto hutvā rodāmi viravāmi. Paccatthikabhayato mutti nāma yathā tathā sahāyavato hoti, na ekākinoti āha – “mā heva maṃ pāṇasamaṃ jaheyyā”ti. Tattha mā heva manti maṃ evarūpaṃ byasanaṃ pattaṃ attano pāṇasamaṃ piyasāmikaṃ tvaṃ māheva jahi.

Because they are hard and sharp and resemble a horn, it has horns known as ‘aḷa’; thus it is ‘siṅgī’ (horned). Because of its golden color and great strength, and because it resembles beasts such as lions and elephants, it is like a beast; thus it is ‘migo’ (beast). Here and there, because it is the nature of the eye to lead to action, it is a guide (nettaṃ); because this is prominent and long, it is ‘āyatacakkhunetto’ (having long, prominent eyes). ‘Bone is its skin’; thus it is ‘aṭṭhittaco’ (bone-skinned). ‘Overcome by that beast’ means: having been overcome, overwhelmed, and held motionless by that beast. ‘I cry pitifully’ means: having become pitiable, I weep and wail.
