Freedom from fear of an enemy comes to one who has a companion, not to one who is alone; thus, he says: ‘Do not abandon me, who is like your own life.’ Therein, ‘do not abandon me’ means: ‘You must not abandon me, your beloved husband who is like your own life and has met with such a disaster.’

Kuñce girikūṭe ramati abhiramati, tattha vā vicarati, koñjanādaṃ nadanto vā vicarati, ku vā pathavī, tadabhighātena jīratīti kuñjaro. Saṭṭhihāyananti jātiyā saṭṭhivassakālasmiṃ kuñjarā thāmena parihāyanti, taṃ sandhāya evamāha. Pathabyā cāturantāyāti catūsu disāsu samuddaṃ patvā ṭhitāya cāturantāya pathaviyā. Suppiyoti suṭṭhu piyo. Tesaṃ tvaṃ vārijo seṭṭhoti ye samudde vā gaṅgāya vā yamunāya vā nammadānadiyā vā kuḷīrā, tesaṃ sabbesaṃ vaṇṇasampattiyā mahantattena ca vārimhi [M 1.0069] jātattā vārijo tvameva seṭṭho pasatthataro. Muñca rodantiyā patinti sabbesaṃ seṭṭhattā tameva yācāmi, rodamānāya mayhaṃ sāmikaṃ muñca. Athāti gahaṇassa sithilakaraṇasamanantarameva. Etassāti paṭisattumaddanassa.

He delights and takes pleasure on the mountain peak (kuñca), or he wanders there, or he wanders while crying like a heron, or the earth (ku) wears away (jīrati) from his striking it; thus he is a kuñjara (elephant). ‘Sixty years old’: at the age of sixty years from birth, elephants decline in strength; with reference to this, he spoke thus. ‘Of the four-bordered earth’ means of the earth that is four-bordered, standing having reached the ocean in the four directions. ‘Very dear’ means exceedingly dear. ‘Among them, you, the water-born, are the best’: whatever crabs there are in the ocean, or in the Ganges, the Yamuna, or the Nammadā river, among all of them, because of your perfection of color and your greatness, and because you are born in the water, you, the water-born, are indeed the best, the most praiseworthy. ‘Release the husband of her who is weeping’: because you are the best of all, I beseech you: release the husband of me who is weeping. ‘Then’ means immediately after the loosening of the grip. ‘Of this one’ means of the one who crushes his adversaries.

Pabbatagahanaṃ nissāyāti tisso pabbatarājiyo atikkamitvā catutthāya pabbatarājiyaṃ pabbatagahanaṃ upanissāya. Evaṃ vadatīti “udetayaṃ cakkhumā”tiādinā (jā. 1.2.17) imaṃ buddhamantaṃ mantento vadati.

‘Relying on the mountain thicket’: having crossed three mountain ranges, he dwells relying on the mountain thicket of the fourth mountain range. ‘He speaks thus’: he speaks while chanting this Buddha-incantation, ‘This one with vision arises,’ and so on (Jā. 1.2.17).

Tattha udetīti pācīnalokadhātuto uggacchati. Cakkhumāti sakalacakkavāḷavāsīnaṃ andhakāraṃ vidhamitvā cakkhuppaṭilābhakaraṇena yantena tesaṃ dinnaṃ cakkhu, tena cakkhunā cakkhumā. Ekarājāti sakalacakkavāḷe ālokakarānaṃ antare seṭṭhaṭṭhena rañjanaṭṭhena ca ekarājā. Harissavaṇṇoti harisamānavaṇṇo, suvaṇṇavaṇṇoti attho. Pathaviṃ pabhāsetīti pathavippabhāso. Taṃ taṃ namassāmīti tasmā taṃ evarūpaṃ bhavantaṃ namassāmi vandāmi. Tayājja guttā viharemha divasanti tayā ajja rakkhitā hutvā imaṃ divasaṃ catuiriyāpathavihārena sukhaṃ vihareyyāma.

Therein, 'he arises' means he emerges from the eastern world-system. 'The Eye' means: having dispelled the darkness for all beings dwelling in the world-sphere, he is the eye given to them by the means that causes the regaining of sight; because of that eye, he is 'one with the eye'. 'The Sole Ruler' means: among those who make light in the entire world-sphere, he is the Sole Ruler on account of being the best and on account of delighting. 'Golden-colored' means of a color similar to gold; the meaning is golden-hued. 'He illuminates the earth' means the illuminator of the earth. 'Him, him I revere' means: therefore, I revere and bow to such a one as you. 'Protected by you today, may we live this day' means: being protected by you today, may we live happily this day by abiding in the four postures.

Evaṃ [V 1.0062] bodhisatto imāya gāthāya sūriyaṃ namassitvā dutiyagāthāya atīte parinibbute buddhe ceva buddhaguṇe ca namassati “ye brāhmaṇā”tiādinā. Tattha ye brāhmaṇāti ye bāhitapāpā parisuddhā brāhmaṇā. Vedagūti vedānaṃ pāraṃ gatā, vedehi pāraṃ gatāti vā vedagū. Idha pana sabbe saṅkhatadhamme vidite pākaṭe katvā katāti vedagū. Tenevāha – “sabbadhamme”ti. Sabbe khandhāyatanadhātudhamme salakkhaṇasāmaññalakkhaṇavasena attano ñāṇassa vidite pākaṭe katvā tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ matthakaṃ madditvā sammāsambodhiṃ pattā, saṃsāraṃ vā atikkantāti attho. Te me namoti te mama imaṃ namakkāraṃ paṭicchantu. Te ca maṃ pālayantūti evaṃ mayā namassitā ca te bhagavanto maṃ pālayantu rakkhantu. Namattu buddhānaṃ…pe… vimuttiyāti ayaṃ mama namakkāro atītānaṃ parinibbutānaṃ buddhānaṃ atthu, tesaṃyeva catūsu phalesu ñāṇasaṅkhātāya bodhiyā atthu, tathā tesaññeva arahattaphalavimuttiyā [M 1.0070] vimuttānaṃ atthu, yā ca nesaṃ tadaṅgavikkhambhanasamucchedappaṭippassaddhinissaraṇasaṅkhātā pañcavidhā vimutti, tāya vimuttiyāpi ayaṃ mayhaṃ namakkāro atthūti attho. Imaṃ so parittaṃ katvā, moro carati esanāti idaṃ pana padadvayaṃ satthā abhisambuddho hutvā āha. Tassattho – bhikkhave, so moro imaṃ parittaṃ imaṃ rakkhaṃ katvā attano gocarabhūmiyaṃ pupphaphalādīnaṃ atthāya nānappakārāya esanāya caratīti.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, having paid homage to the sun with this verse, then paid homage with the second verse, beginning with 'ye brāhmaṇā,' to the past, fully extinguished Buddhas and the virtues of the Buddhas. Therein, 'ye brāhmaṇā' means those brahmins who have cast out evil, who are purified. 'Vedagū' means those who have gone to the far shore of the Vedas, or who have gone beyond by means of the Vedas. Here, however, it means one is a 'vedagū' because of having made all conditioned phenomena known and manifest. Therefore, it is said: 'sabbadhamme'—all phenomena. The meaning is: having made all phenomena—the aggregates, sense bases, and elements—known and manifest to one's own knowledge by way of their specific and general characteristics, having crushed the heads of the three Māras, they have attained perfect enlightenment, or they have crossed over saṃsāra. 'Te me namo' means: may they accept this homage of mine. 'And may they protect me' means: thus revered by me, may those Blessed Ones protect and guard me. 'Namattu buddhānaṃ…pe… vimuttiyā' means: may this homage of mine be for the past, fully extinguished Buddhas; may it also be for their enlightenment, which is known as knowledge in the four fruits; and likewise for those liberated by the liberation of the fruit of arahantship. Moreover, the meaning is: may this homage of mine also be for their fivefold liberation, which consists of liberation by substitution of opposites, by suppression, by cutting off, by tranquilization, and by escape. 'Having made this protective recitation, the peacock roams in search'—these two lines the Teacher spoke after becoming fully enlightened. Its meaning is: 'Monks, that peacock, having made this protective recitation, this safeguard, roams in its feeding ground in various ways in search of flowers, fruits, and so on.'

Evaṃ divasaṃ caritvā sāyaṃ pabbatamatthake nisīditvā atthaṃ gacchantaṃ sūriyaṃ olokento buddhaguṇe āvajjetvā nivāsaṭṭhāne rakkhāvaraṇatthāya puna brahmamantaṃ vadanto “apetaya”ntiādimāha. Tenevāha – “divasaṃ gocaraṃ gahetvā”tiādi. Tattha apetīti apayāti atthaṃ gacchati. Imaṃ so parittaṃ katvā moro vāsamakappayīti idampi abhisambuddho hutvā āha. Tassattho – bhikkhave, so moro imaṃ parittaṃ imaṃ rakkhaṃ katvā attano nivāsaṭṭhāne vāsaṃ saṃkappayitthāti. Parittakammato puretaramevāti parittakammakaraṇato puretarameva. Morakukkuṭikāyāti kukkuṭikāsadisāya moracchāpikāya.

Having thus roamed during the day, in the evening he sits atop a mountain, watches the setting sun, reflects on the virtues of the Buddha, and then, for the sake of protection and shelter in his dwelling place, again reciting the Brahma mantra, says 'apetaya,' and so on. Therefore it is said: 'having spent the day in his feeding ground,' etc. Therein, 'apeti' means 'apayāti'—it goes away, it sets. 'Having made this protective recitation, the peacock prepared his dwelling'—this too the Teacher spoke after becoming fully enlightened. Its meaning is: 'Monks, that peacock, having made this protective recitation, this safeguard, arranged his dwelling in his own dwelling place.' 'Even before the protective act' means even before the performance of the protective act. 'Morakukkuṭikāya' means by a young peahen similar to a hen.

3. Tatiye rūpāyatanassa viya gandhāyatanassapi samuṭṭhāpakapaccayavasena viseso natthīti āha – “catusamuṭṭhānika”nti. Itthiyā sarīragandhassa kāyāruḷhaanulepanādigandhassa ca tappaṭibaddhabhāvato avisesena gahaṇappasaṅge idhādhippetagandhaṃ niddhārento “svāya”ntiādimāha. Tattha itthiyāti pākatikāya itthiyā. Duggandhoti pākatikāya itthiyā sarīragandhabhāvato duggandho hoti. Idhādhippetoti iṭṭhabhāvato assādetabbattā vuttaṃ. Kathaṃ pana itthiyā sarīragandhassa duggandhabhāvoti āha – “ekaccā hī”tiādi. Tattha assassa viya gandho [V 1.0063] assā atthīti assagandhinī. Meṇḍakassa viya gandho assā atthīti meṇḍakagandhinī. Sedassa viya gandho assā atthīti sedagandhinī. Soṇitassa viya gandho assā atthīti soṇitagandhinī. Rajjatevāti anādimati saṃsāre avijjādikilesavāsanāya parikaḍḍhitahadayattā phoṭṭhabbassādagadhitacittatāya ca andhabālo evarūpāyapi duggandhasarīrāya itthiyā rajjatiyeva. Pākatikāya itthiyā sarīragandhassa duggandhabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni visiṭṭhāya ekaccāya itthiyā tadabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ – “cakkavattino [M 1.0071] panā”tiādimāha. Yadi evaṃ īdisāya itthiyā sarīragandhopi idha kasmā nādhippetoti āha – “ayaṃ na sabbāsaṃ hotī”tiādi. Tiracchānagatāya itthiyā ekaccāya ca manussitthiyā sarīragandhassa ativiya assādetabbabhāvadassanato puna tampi avisesena anujānanto “itthikāye gandho vā hotū”tiādimāha. Itthigandhotveva veditabboti tappaṭibaddhabhāvato vuttaṃ.

3. In the third case, just as there is no distinction regarding the form-base, so too there is none regarding the smell-base in terms of its originating condition. Thus, it is said: 'It is four-origined.' Regarding a woman's body odor and the scent of perfumes or unguents applied to her body, since there is the possibility of taking them without distinction due to their being connected to her, the intended smell here is clarified by saying, 'her own,' and so on. Therein, 'a woman' refers to an ordinary woman. 'Foul-smelling' means that the body odor of an ordinary woman is foul. 'What is intended here' is said because it is desirable and to be enjoyed. But how is a woman's body odor foul? It is explained: 'For some women…' and so on. Therein, 'one with the smell of a horse' means she has a smell like a horse. 'One with the smell of a ram' means she has a smell like a ram. 'One with the smell of sweat' means she has a smell like sweat. 'One with the smell of blood' means she has a smell like blood. 'He lusts indeed' means that, because his heart is drawn by the latent tendencies of ignorance and other defilements in beginningless saṃsāra, and because his mind is obsessed with the pleasure of tangible objects, the blind fool still lusts after even such a woman with a foul-smelling body. After showing the foulness of an ordinary woman's body odor, now to show its absence in certain exceptional women, it is said: 'But for a universal monarch's [consort]…' and so on. If so, why is the body odor of such a woman not intended here? It is explained: 'This does not apply to all…' and so on. Because of showing that the body odor of certain female animals and certain human women is extremely enjoyable, it is again generally allowed by saying, 'whether there is a woman's body odor…' and so on. 'It should be understood simply as a woman's smell' is said because it is connected to her.

4. Catutthādīsu kiṃ tenāti jivhāviññeyyarase idhādhippete kiṃ tena avayavarasādinā vuttena payojanaṃ. Oṭṭhamaṃsaṃ sammakkhetīti oṭṭhamaṃsasammakkhano, kheḷādīni. Ādisaddena oṭṭhamaṃsamakkhano tambulamukhavāsādiraso gayhati. Sabbo so itthirasoti itthiyāvassa gahetabbattā.

4. In the fourth and following cases, 'what is the use of that?' means: if the taste cognizable by the tongue is what is intended here, what is the purpose of what was said about the taste of the limbs, and so on? 'He smears the lip-flesh' means the smearing of the lip-flesh, which includes saliva, etc. By the word 'etc.', the smearing of the lip-flesh, the taste of betel, mouth-fresheners, and so on, is included. 'All that is a woman's taste' means it is to be taken as belonging to a woman indeed.

5. Itthiphoṭṭhabboti etthāpi eseva nayo. Yadi panettha itthigatāni rūpārammaṇādīni avisesato purisassa cittaṃ pariyādāya tiṭṭhanti, atha kasmā bhagavatā tāni visuṃ visuṃ gahetvā desitānīti āha – “iti satthā”tiādi. Yathā hītiādinā tamevatthaṃ samattheti. Gametīti vikkhepaṃ gameti, ayameva vā pāṭho. Gametīti ca saṅgameti. Na tathā sesā saddādayo, na tathā rūpādīni ārammaṇānīti etena sattesu rūpādigarukatā asaṃkiṇṇā viya dassitā, na kho panetaṃ evaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ anekavidhattā sattānaṃ ajjhāsayassāti dassetuṃ – “ekaccassa cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Pañcagarukavasenāti pañcārammaṇagarukavasena. Ekaccassa hi purisassa yathāvuttesu pañcasupi ārammaṇesu garukatā hoti, ekaccassa tattha katipayesu, ekasmiṃ eva vā, te sabbepi pañcagarukātveva veditabbā yathā “sattisayo aṭṭhavimokkhā”ti. Na pañcagarukajātakavasena ekekārammaṇe garukasseva nādhippetattā. Ekekārammaṇagarukānañhi pañcannaṃ puggalānaṃ tattha āgatattā taṃ jātakaṃ “pañcagarukajātaka”nti vuttaṃ. Yadi evaṃ tena idha payojanaṃ natthīti āha – “sakkhibhāvatthāyā”ti. Āharitvā kathetabbanti rūpādigarukatāya ete anayabyasanaṃ pattāti dassetuṃ kathetabbaṃ.

5. Regarding 'a woman's tangible object,' here too the method is the same. But if in this case, the forms, sounds, etc., pertaining to women indiscriminately occupy a man’s mind, then why did the Blessed One teach them separately? To this, it is said: "Thus, the Teacher," etc. As in the phrase "yathā hi," etc., it confirms the same meaning. "Gameti" means it leads to distraction, or this may be the reading. "Gameti" also means it gathers. But the other sounds, etc., are not like that; nor are the objects like forms, etc. By this, it is shown that among beings, the high regard for forms, etc., is, as it were, unmixed. However, this should not be viewed in such a way, for the inclinations of beings are diverse. To illustrate this, it is said: "For some," etc. "Pañcagarukavasena" means by way of high regard for the five objects. For some men, high regard is placed on all five objects as described; for some, only on a few; and for others, on just one. Yet all should be understood as having fivefold high regard, just as in the case of "the seven sharp instruments and the eight liberations." This is not intended in the sense of the Pañcagaruka Jātaka, where only one with high regard for a single object is meant. For that Jātaka is called the 'Pañcagaruka Jātaka' because five persons, each with high regard for a single object, are mentioned therein. If it is so, then what is the purpose here? It is said: "For the sake of being a witness." "Āharitvā kathetabbaṃ" means it should be told to show that because of their high regard for forms, etc., these beings have met with misfortune and disaster.

6-8. Tesanti [V 1.0064][M 1.0072] suttānaṃ. Uppaṇḍetvā gaṇhituṃ na icchīti tassa thokaṃ virūpadhātukattā na icchi. Anatikkamantoti saṃsandento. Dve hatthaṃ pattānīti dve uppalāni hatthaṃ gatāni. Pahaṭṭhākāraṃ dassetvāti aparāhi itthīhi ekekaṃ laddhaṃ, mayā dve laddhānīti santuṭṭhākāraṃ dassetvā. Parodīti tassā pubbasāmikassa mukhagandhaṃ saritvā. Tassa hi mukhato uppalagandho vāyati. Hāretvāti tasmā ṭhānā apanetvā, “harāpetvā”ti vā pāṭho, ayamevattho.

6-8. Of those suttas: “She did not wish to take them after examining them” means she did not wish to because of her slight physical defect. “Not passing over” means comparing. “Two reached her hand” means two lotuses came into her hands. “Showing a delighted expression” means showing a satisfied look, thinking, “Other women received one each, I received two.” “She wept” means she wept, remembering the scent of her former husband's mouth. For the fragrance of lotuses wafted from his mouth. “Having taken away” means having removed from that place; or the reading is “having caused to be taken away,” the meaning is just this.

Sādhu sādhūti bhāsatoti dhammakathāya anumodanavasena “sādhu sādhū”ti bhāsato. Uppalaṃva yathodaketi yathā uppalaṃ uppalagandho mukhato nibbattoti. Vaṭṭameva kathitanti yathārutavasena vuttaṃ. Yadipi evaṃ vuttaṃ, tathāpi yathārutamatthe avatvā vivaṭṭaṃ nīharitvā kathetabbaṃ vimuttirasattā bhagavato desanāya.

“Speaking, ‘Well said, well said’” means speaking “Well said, well said” by way of approving of the Dhamma talk. “Like a lotus in water” means: just as a lotus is produced, so the lotus fragrance is produced from his mouth. “Only the round of existence is spoken of” means it is spoken according to the literal sense. Even though it is spoken thus, still, without stating the literal meaning, one should speak by bringing forth the meaning that leads beyond the round, for the Blessed One's teaching has the taste of liberation.

Rūpādivaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on Form, etc., is completed.

Iti manorathapūraṇiyā aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus in the Manorathapūraṇī, the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya,

Paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanāya anuttānatthadīpanā niṭṭhitā.

The Elucidation of the Abstruse Meaning in the Commentary on the First Chapter is completed.

2. Nīvaraṇappahānavaggavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Chapter on Abandoning the Hindrances

11. Dutiyassāti [V 1.0065] dutiyavaggassa. Ekadhammampīti ettha “ekasabhāvampī”ti iminā sabhāvatthoyaṃ dhammasaddo “kusalā dhammā”tiādīsu viyāti dassitaṃ hoti. Yadaggena ca sabhāvattho, tadaggena nissattattho siddho evāti “nissattaṭṭhena dhammo veditabbo”ti vuttaṃ. Subhanimittanti dhammapariyāyena vuttaṃ. Tañhi atthato kāmacchando vā siyā. So hi attano gahaṇākārena subhanti, tenākārena pavattanakassa aññassa kāmacchandassa nimittattā “subhanimitta”nti ca vuccati. Tassa ārammaṇaṃ vā subhanimittaṃ. Iṭṭhañhi iṭṭhākārena vā gayhamānaṃ rūpādiārammaṇaṃ “subhanimitta”nti vuccati. Ārammaṇameva cettha nimittaṃ. Tathā hi vakkhati – “subhanimittanti rāgaṭṭhāniyaṃ ārammaṇa”nti. Samuccayattho vā-saddo anekatthattā nipātānaṃ. Bhiyyobhāvāyāti punappunaṃ bhāvāya. Vepullāyāti vipulabhāvāya, vaḍḍhiyāti attho. Ajāto nijjāto. Sesapadāni tasseva [M 1.0073] vevacanāni. Kāmesūti pañcasu kāmaguṇesu. Kāmacchandoti kāmasaṅkhāto chando, na kattukamyatāchando na dhammacchando. Kāmanavasena rajjanavasena ca kāmo eva rāgo kāmarāgo. Kāmanavasena nandanavasena ca kāmo eva nandīti kāmanandī. Kāmanavasena taṇhāyanavasena ca kāmataṇhā. Ādisaddena “kāmasneho kāmapariḷāho kāmamucchā kāmajjhosāna”nti etesaṃ padānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tattha vuttanayeneva kāmatthaṃ viditvā sinehanaṭṭhena kāmasneho, pariḷāhanaṭṭhena kāmapariḷāho, mucchanaṭṭhena kāmamucchā, gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpanaṭṭhena kāmajjhosānaṃ veditabbaṃ. Kāmacchando eva kusalappavattito cittassa nīvaraṇaṭṭhena kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ, soti kāmacchando. Asamudācāravasenāti asamudācārabhāvena. Ananubhūtārammaṇavasenāti “idaṃ nāmeta”nti vatthuvasena utvā tasmiṃ attabhāve ananubhūtassa ārammaṇassa vasena. Rūpasaddādibhedaṃ pana ārammaṇaṃ ekasmimpi attabhāve ananubhūtaṃ nāma nattheva, kimaṅgaṃ pana anādimati saṃsāre.

11. 'Dutiyassāti' means 'of the second,' that is, of the second chapter. Here, by 'ekadhammampi' (even a single dhamma), it is shown that the word 'dhamma' has the meaning of 'intrinsic nature' (ekasabhāvampi), as in 'wholesome dhammas' (kusalā dhammā), etc. And inasmuch as it has the meaning of intrinsic nature, to that extent the meaning of 'non-sentient' (nissatta) is also established. Hence it is said: 'Dhamma should be understood in the sense of non-sentient.' 'Subhanimitta' (beautiful sign) is stated as a synonym. For in essence it could be sensual desire. For it is beautiful in its mode of being grasped, and because it is the sign for the arising of another sensual desire in that mode, it is called 'beautiful sign.' Alternatively, its object is the beautiful sign. For a pleasing object like form, when grasped as agreeable, is called a 'beautiful sign.' Here, the object itself is the sign. Thus it will be said: 'A beautiful sign is an object that is a basis for lust.' The word 'vā' (or) has the meaning of aggregation, as particles have many meanings. 'Bhiyyobhāvāya' means for repeated occurrence. 'Vepullāya' means for abundant growth, that is, for increase. 'Ajāto nijjāto' means unborn and unarisen. The remaining terms are synonyms for the same. 'Kāmesu' refers to the five strands of sensual pleasure. 'Kāmacchando' is desire reckoned as sensuality, not the desire to act nor the desire for Dhamma. Through the mode of desiring and the mode of being attached, sensuality itself is lust, hence 'sensual lust' (kāmarāgo). Through the mode of desiring and the mode of delighting, sensuality itself is delight, hence 'sensual delight' (kāmanandī). Through the mode of desiring and the mode of craving, it is 'sensual craving' (kāmataṇhā). By the word 'ādi' (etc.) the inclusion of terms like 'sensual affection' (kāmasneho), 'sensual fever' (kāmapariḷāho), 'sensual infatuation' (kāmamucchā), and 'sensual obsession' (kāmajjhosāna) should be understood. Here, having understood the meaning of sensuality in the manner stated, 'sensual affection' is to be understood in the sense of clinging; 'sensual fever' in the sense of burning; 'sensual infatuation' in the sense of delusion; and 'sensual obsession' in the sense of swallowing and fixation. Sensual desire itself, by being a hindrance to the mind's wholesome activity, is the 'sensual desire hindrance' (kāmacchandanīvaraṇa); that is, it is sensual desire. 'Asamudācāravasena' means by way of non-manifestation. 'Ananubhūtārammaṇavasena' means by way of an object not previously experienced in that very existence, having been identified as 'this particular thing' in terms of its substance. However, an object classified as form, sound, etc., is certainly not something that has not been experienced even once in a single existence, how much less in beginningless saṃsāra.

Yaṃ vuttaṃ – “asamudācāravasena cā”tiādi, taṃ atisaṃkhittanti vitthārato dassetuṃ – “tatthā”tiādimāha. Tattha bhavaggahaṇena mahaggatabhavo gahito. So hi oḷārikakilesasamudācārarahito. Tajjanīyakammakatādikāle pārivāsikakāle ca caritabbāni dveasīti khuddakavattāni nāma. Na hi tāni sabbāsu avatthāsu caritabbāni, tasmā tāni na mahāvattesu antogadhānīti “cuddasa mahāvattānī”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā āgantukavattaāvāsikagamika-anumodanabhattagga- piṇḍacārikaāraññakasenāsanajantāgharavaccakuṭiupajjhāya- saddhivihārikaācariya-antevāsikavattānīti [V 1.0066] etāni cuddasa mahāvattāni nāmāti vuttaṃ. Itarāni pana “pārivāsikānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ vattaṃ paññāpessāmī”ti (cūḷava. 75) ārabhitvā “na upasampādetabbaṃ, na chamāyaṃ caṅkamante caṅkame caṅkamitabba”nti (cūḷava. 81) vuttāni pakatatte caritabbavattāni chasaṭṭhi, tato paraṃ “na, bhikkhave, pārivāsikena bhikkhunā pārivāsikavuḍḍhatarena bhikkhunā saddhiṃ, mūlāyapaṭikassanārahena, mānattārahena, mānattacārikena, abbhānārahena bhikkhunā saddiṃ ekacchanne āvāse vatthabba”ntiādīni pakatatte caritabbehi anaññattā visuṃ visuṃ agaṇetvā pārivāsikavuḍḍhatarādīsu puggalantaresu caritabbattā [M 1.0074] tesaṃ vasena sampiṇḍetvā ekekaṃ katvā gaṇitāni pañcāti ekasattativattāni. Ukkhepanīyakammakatavattesu vattapaññāpanavasena vuttaṃ – “na pakatattassa bhikkhuno abhivādanaṃ paccuṭṭhānaṃ…pe… piṭṭhiparikammaṃ sāditabba”nti idaṃ abhivādanādīnaṃ assādiyanaṃ ekaṃ, “na pakatatto bhikkhu sīlavipattiyā anuddhaṃsetabbo”tiādīni (cūḷava. 51) ca dasāti evaṃ dvāsīti honti. Etesveva pana kānici tajjanīyakammakatādivattāni kānici pārivāsikādivattānīti aggahitaggahaṇena dvāvīsativattanti veditabbaṃ. “Cuddasa mahāvattānī”ti vatvāpi “āgantukagamikavattāni cā”ti imesaṃ visuṃ gahaṇaṃ imāni abhiṇhaṃ sambhavantīti katvā. Kileso okāsaṃ na labhati sabbadā vattappaṭipattiyaṃyeva byāvaṭacittatāya. Ayonisomanasikāranti aniccādīsu “nicca”ntiādinā pavattaṃ anupāyamanasikāraṃ. Sativossagganti satiyā vissajjanaṃ, sativirahanti attho. Evampīti vakkhamānāpekkhāya avuttasampiṇḍanattho pi-saddo.

What was said—'by way of proper conduct' and so on—is too brief; to explain it in detail, the text begins with 'herein.' Herein, by the term 'peak of existence,' the sublime state of existence is meant, for it is devoid of the transgression of gross defilements. The eighty-two minor duties are those to be observed during the time of an act of rebuke and the period of probation. Indeed, these are not to be observed in all circumstances; therefore, they are not included among the major duties. Hence it is said: 'the fourteen major duties.' Likewise, the duties for newcomers, residents, travelers, giving thanks, in the refectory, on alms-round, for forest-dwellers, concerning lodgings, steam-bath houses, restrooms, for preceptors, co-residents, teachers, and resident pupils—these are called the fourteen major duties. The remaining sixty-six duties to be observed by those in good standing are those stated beginning with 'I will prescribe the duties for monks under probation' (Cūḷavagga 75) up to 'One should not give ordination... nor walk on the walking path when another is walking on the ground' (Cūḷavagga 81). Furthermore, the five duties, which are not distinct from those to be observed by those in good standing but are counted separately as individual categories because they are to be observed toward different individuals such as senior probationers, etc., are those beginning with 'Monks, a monk under probation should not dwell under the same roof with a senior probationer, one deserving to be sent back to the beginning, one deserving mānatta, one undergoing mānatta, or one deserving rehabilitation.' Thus, there are seventy-one duties. Regarding the duties for those subject to the act of suspension, it is said by way of prescribing duties: 'One should not accept a greeting, being stood up for... or having one's back massaged from a monk in good standing.' This non-acceptance of greetings, etc., counts as one. And 'A monk in good standing should not be reproached for a breach of virtue' (Cūḷavagga 51) and so on—these are ten. Thus, there are eighty-two. Among these, some are duties for those subject to the act of rebuke, etc., and some are duties for those under probation, etc. By taking what was not taken before, twenty-two duties should be understood. Even after saying 'the fourteen major duties,' the separate mention of 'the duties for newcomers and travelers' is because these frequently occur. Defilement finds no opportunity because the mind is constantly engaged in the practice of these duties. 'Unwise attention' is attention that proceeds in an improper way, such as perceiving the impermanent as permanent, etc. 'Abandonment of mindfulness' is the relinquishing of mindfulness; the meaning is the absence of mindfulness. 'Even so'—this 'pi' particle has the meaning of summarizing what has not been stated, with reference to what will be said.

Anusandhivasenāti pucchānusandhiādianusandhivasena. Pubbāparavasenāti pubbāparaganthasallakkhaṇavasena. Gaṇhantassāti ācariyamukhato gaṇhantassa. Sajjhāyantassāti ācariyamukhato uggahitaganthaṃ sajjhāyantassa. Vācentassāti pāḷiṃ tadatthañca uggaṇhāpanavasena paresaṃ vācentassa. Desentassāti desanāvasena paresaṃ dhammaṃ desentassa. Pakāsentassāti attano attano saṃsayaṭṭhāne pucchantānaṃ yāthāvato atthaṃ pakāsentassa. Kileso okāsaṃ na labhati rattindivaṃ ganthakammesuyeva byāvaṭacittatāya. Evampīti vuttasampiṇḍanattho pi-saddo. Evaṃ sesesupi.

'By way of connection' means by way of the connection of inquiry and so on. 'By way of earlier and later' means by way of discerning the connection between the earlier and later parts of the text. 'For one who is learning' means for one who is learning from the mouth of a teacher. 'For one who is reciting' means for one who is reciting the text learned from the mouth of a teacher. 'For one who is teaching' means for one who is teaching others the Pāli and its meaning by way of causing them to learn it. 'For one who is expounding' means for one who is expounding the Dhamma to others by way of exposition. 'For one who is clarifying' means for one who is clarifying the meaning accurately to those asking about their own points of doubt. Defilement finds no opportunity because the mind is constantly occupied with textual work day and night. 'Even so'—this 'pi' particle has the meaning of summarizing what has been said. Similarly in the remaining cases as well.

Dhutaṅgadharo hotīti vuttamevatthaṃ pakāseti “terasa dhutaṅgaguṇe samādāya vattatī”ti. Bāhullāyāti cīvarādipaccayabāhullāya. Yathā cīvarādayo paccayā bahulaṃ uppajjanti, tathā āvattassa [V 1.0067] pavattassāti attho. Parihīnajjhānassāti jhānantarāyakarena visabhāgarūpadassanādinā kenaci nimittena parihīnajjhānassa. Vissaṭṭhajjhānassāti asamāpajjanavasena pariccattajjhānassa. Bhassādīsūti ādi-saddena gaṇasaṅgaṇikaniddānavakammādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Sattasu vā anupassanāsūti ettha satta anupassanā nāma aniccānupassanā dukkhānupassanā anattānupassanā nibbidānupassanā virāgānupassanā [M 1.0075] nirodhānupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā khayānupassanā vayānupassanā vipariṇāmānupassanā animittānupassanā appaṇihitānupassanā suññatānupassanā adhipaññādhammavipassanā yathābhūtañāṇadassanaṃ ādīnavānupassanā paṭisaṅkhānupassanā vivaṭṭānupassanāti imāsu aṭṭhārasasu mahāvipassanāsu ādito vuttā aniccānupassanādi-paṭinissaggānupassanāpariyantā satta. Ettha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ visuddhimaggasaṃvaṇṇanāto (visuddhi. mahāṭī. 2.741) gahetabbaṃ.

'He is one who observes the ascetic practices' explains the very meaning stated: 'He undertakes and practices the thirteen ascetic qualities.' 'For abundance' means for the abundance of requisites such as robes, etc. The meaning is that just as requisites like robes arise in abundance, so too does he turn towards and engage in them. 'One who has lost jhāna' refers to one whose jhāna is lost due to some sign, such as seeing incompatible forms, which acts as an obstacle to jhāna. 'One who has abandoned jhāna' refers to one who has given up jhāna by not attaining it. 'In talk, etc.'—here, the word 'etc.' includes group activities, socializing, sleep, new work, and so on. 'Or in the seven contemplations'—here, the seven contemplations are the contemplation of impermanence, the contemplation of suffering, the contemplation of non-self, the contemplation of disenchantment, the contemplation of dispassion, the contemplation of cessation, and the contemplation of relinquishment. These seven are those stated at the beginning, up to the contemplation of relinquishment, among these eighteen great insights: the contemplation of impermanence, the contemplation of suffering, the contemplation of non-self, the contemplation of disenchantment, the contemplation of dispassion, the contemplation of cessation, the contemplation of relinquishment, the contemplation of destruction, the contemplation of vanishing, the contemplation of change, the contemplation of the signless, the contemplation of the desireless, the contemplation of emptiness, the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena, the knowledge and vision of things as they are, the contemplation of danger, the reflective contemplation, and the contemplation of turning away. Whatever needs to be said here should be taken from the commentary on the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhimagga Mahāṭīkā 2.741).

Anāsevanatāyāti purimattabhāve jhānena vikkhambhitakilesassa kāmacchandādiāsevanāya abhāvato. Ananubhūtapubbanti tasmiṃ attabhāve ananubhūtapubbaṃ. Jātoti etasseva vevacanaṃ sañjātotiādi. Nanu ca khaṇikattā sabbadhammānaṃ uppannassa kāmacchandassa taṅkhaṇaṃyeva avassaṃ nirodhasambhavato niruddhe ca tasmiṃ puna aññasseva uppajjanato ca kathaṃ tassa punappunabhāvo rāsibhāvo cāti āha – “tattha sakiṃ uppanno kāmacchando”tiādi. Aṭṭhānametanti akāraṇametaṃ. Yena kāraṇena uppanno kāmacchando na nirujjhati, niruddho ca sveva puna uppajjissati, tādisaṃ kāraṇaṃ natthīti attho.

'By non-indulgence' means due to the absence of indulgence in sensual desire and other defilements, which were suppressed by jhāna in a prior existence. 'Never before experienced' means never before experienced in that existence. 'Born' is a synonym for 'arisen,' etc. Now, one might ask: Since all phenomena are momentary, and sensual desire, once arisen, must necessarily cease in that very moment, and once it has ceased, another arises—how then can there be repetition or accumulation of that same desire? To this he says: 'Here, sensual desire arises once...' 'This is impossible' means this is not a cause. The meaning is: there is no such cause by which an arisen sensual desire would not cease, or that, once ceased, the very same one would arise again.

Rāgaṭṭhāniyanti rāgajanakaṃ. Aniccādīsu niccādivasena viparītamanasikāro, idha ayonisomanasikāroti āha – “anicce nicca”ntiādi. Ayonisomanasikāroti anupāyamanasikāro, kusaladhammappavattiyā akāraṇabhūto manasikāroti attho. Uppathamanasikāroti kusaladhammappavattiyā amaggabhūto manasikāro. Saccavippaṭikūlenāti saccābhisamayassa anunulomavasena. Āvajjanātiādinā āvajjanāya paccayabhūtā tato purimuppannā manodvārikā akusalajavanappavatti phalavohārena tathā vuttā. Tassa hi vasena sā akusalappavattiyā upanissayo hoti. Āvajjanāti bhavaṅgacittaṃ āvajjayatīti āvajjanā. Anu anu āvajjetīti anvāvajjanā. Bhavaṅgārammaṇato aññaṃ ābhujatīti ābhogo. Samannāharatīti samannāhāro. Tadevārammaṇaṃ attānaṃ anubandhitvā uppajjamāno manasi karoti ṭhapetīti manasikāro. Ayaṃ vuccati ayonisomanasikāroti ayaṃ anupāyauppathamanasikāralakkhaṇo ayonisomanasikāro nāma vuccati.

'That which is a basis for lust' means that which generates lust. The inverted attention regarding the impermanent, etc., as permanent, etc., is here called 'unwise attention,' as stated: 'permanent in the impermanent,' and so on. 'Unwise attention' means inappropriate attention; the meaning is, attention that is a non-cause for the arising of wholesome states. 'Wrong-path attention' is attention that is a non-path for the arising of wholesome states. 'Opposed to the truth' means in a way not in accordance with the realization of the truth. By 'adverting' and so on, the unwholesome impulsion process arising through the mind-door, which precedes it and for which adverting is a condition, is described as such in terms of result. For through that, it becomes a supporting condition for the unwholesome process. 'Adverting' is what turns the life-continuum consciousness. 'Repeatedly adverting' is anvāvajjanā. 'Bending' towards an object other than that of the life-continuum is ābhogo. 'Bringing together' is samannāhāro. 'Attending' (manasikāra) is that which, arising in pursuit of that very object, places it and fixes it in the mind. This is called 'unwise attention'—this, characterized by inappropriate and wrong-path attention, is called 'unwise attention'.

12. Dutiye [V 1.0068][M 1.0076] bhattabyāpatti viyāti bhattassa pūtibhāvena vippakārappatti viya, cittassa byāpajjananti cittassa vikārabhāvāpādanaṃ. Tenevāha – “pakativijahanabhāvo”ti. Byāpajjati tena cittaṃ pūtikummāsādayo viya purimapakatiṃ jahatīti byāpādo. Paṭighoyeva uparūpari uppajjamānassa paṭighassa nimittabhāvato paṭighanimittaṃ, paṭighassa ca kāraṇabhūtaṃ ārammaṇaṃ paṭighanimittanti āha – “paṭighassapi paṭighārammaṇassapi etaṃ adhivacana”nti. Aṭṭhakathāyanti mahāaṭṭhakathāyaṃ.

12. In the second, 'the corruption of food' is like the state of being spoiled due to its putridity; similarly, 'the corruption of mind' means causing the mind to be in an altered state. Therefore, it is said, 'the state of abandoning its original nature.' The mind is corrupted by it, like spoiled rice gruel and so forth, abandoning its former nature; thus, it is called 'ill will' (byāpādo). Aversion itself is the 'sign of aversion' (paṭighanimitta), as it is the condition for aversion that arises repeatedly; and the object that is the cause of aversion is also the 'sign of aversion.' Thus, it is said: 'This is a designation for both aversion and for the object of aversion.' 'In the commentary' means in the Great Commentary.

13. Tatiye thinatā thinaṃ, sappipiṇḍo viya avipphārikatāya cittassa ghanabhāvo baddhatāti attho. Medhatīti middhaṃ, akammaññabhāvena hiṃsatīti attho. “Yā tasmiṃ samaye cittassa akalyatā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1162) thinassa, “yā tasmiṃ samaye kāyassa akalyatā”tiādinā (dha. sa. 1163) ca middhassa abhidhamme niddiṭṭhattā vuttaṃ – “cittassa akammaññatā thinaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ khandhānaṃ akammaññatā middha”nti. Satipi aññamaññāvippayoge cittakāyalahutādīnaṃ viya cittacetasikānaṃ yathākkamaṃ taṃtaṃviseso siyā, yā tesaṃ akalyatādīnaṃ visesapaccayatā, ayametesaṃ sabhāvoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kapimiddhassāti vuttamevatthaṃ vibhāveti “pacalāyikabhāvassā”ti. Akkhidalānaṃ pacalabhāvaṃ karotīti pacalāyiko, pacalāyikassa bhāvo pacalāyikabhāvo, pacalāyikattanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ubhinnanti thinamiddhānaṃ. “Vitthāro veditabbo”ti iminā sambandho veditabbo. Cittassa akalyatāti cittassa gilānabhāvo. Gilāno hi akalyakoti vuccati. Vinayepi vuttaṃ – “nāhaṃ, bhante, akalyako”ti (pārā. 151). Kālaṃ khamatīti hi kalyaṃ, arogatā, tassaṃ niyutto kalyako, na kalyako akalyako. Akammaññatāti cittagelaññasaṅkhātova akammaññatākāro. Olīyanāti olīyanākāro. Iriyāpathūpatthambhitañhi cittaṃ iriyāpathaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkontaṃ rukkhe vagguli viya khīle laggitaphāṇitavārako viya ca olīyati lambati, tassa taṃ ākāraṃ sandhāya – “olīyanā”ti vuttaṃ. Dutiyapadaṃ upasaggena vaḍḍhitaṃ. Kāyassāti vedanādikkhandhattayasaṅkhātassa nāmakāyassa. Akalyatā akammaññatāti heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Megho viya ākāsaṃ onayhatīti onāho. Onayhatīti ca chādeti avattharati vāti attho[M 1.0077]. Sabbatobhāgena onāhoti pariyonāho. Aratiādīnaṃ attho vibhaṅge (vibha. 856) vuttanayeneva veditabboti tattha vuttapāḷiyā dassetuṃ – “vuttaṃ heta”ntiādimāha.

13. In the third, sluggishness (thina) is the state of being thick, like a lump of ghee, meaning the mind is dense and bound due to lack of diffusion. Drowsiness (middha) means torpor, because it harms by making one unfit for action. As stated in the Abhidhamma: 'The unsuitability of the mind at that time is sluggishness,' and 'The unsuitability of the body at that time is drowsiness.' Thus, it is said: 'The mind's unworkability is sluggishness, the unworkability of the three aggregates is drowsiness.' Despite their inseparability, just as there are distinctions for lightness of mind and body, and so on, so too there may be a respective distinction for mind and mental factors in sequence; it should be understood that this is their intrinsic nature, which is the specific condition for their unsuitability, and so on. The phrase 'of a monkey's drowsiness' clarifies this very meaning: 'of the state of nodding.' It causes nodding of the eyelids—hence, it is called 'nodding' (pacalāyiko); the state of one who is nodding is 'the state of nodding' (pacalāyikabhāvo); it is said to be 'the quality of nodding' (pacalāyikattaṃ). 'Of both' refers to sluggishness and drowsiness. The connection should be understood with 'the detailed explanation should be understood.' 'The mind's unsuitability' means the mind's sickness. For a sick person is called 'unsuitable' (akalyaka). As stated in the Vinaya: 'I am not unsuitable, venerable sir.' For 'kalyaṃ' means 'suitable for the time,' i.e., health; one endowed with that is 'kalyaka'; not kalyaka is 'akalyaka.' 'Unworkability' is the mode of unworkability known as sickness of mind. 'Sinking' is the mode of sinking. For when the mind, supported by the postures, is unable to maintain the posture, it sinks and hangs down, like a bat on a tree, or a pot of molasses clinging to a stake—thus, it is called 'sinking.' The second word is augmented by a prefix. 'Of the body' refers to the mental body consisting of the three aggregates beginning with feeling. 'Unsuitability' and 'unworkability' are in the same way as stated above. Like a cloud covering the sky, it is 'covering' (onāho). 'Covering' means it conceals or overwhelms. A complete covering is 'overwhelming' (pariyonāho). The meanings of discontent (arati), etc., should be understood as explained in the Vibhaṅga. To illustrate this with the Pāli stated there, the text says: 'For this has been said,' etc.

Tattha pantesūti dūresu, vivittesu vā. Adhikusalesūti samathavipassanādhammesu. Aratīti ratippaṭikkhepo. Aratitāti aramanākāro. Anabhiratīti anabhiratabhāvo. Anabhiramanāti anabhiramanākāro[V 1.0069]. Ukkaṇṭhitāti ukkaṇṭhanākāro. Paritassitāti ukkaṇṭhanavaseneva paritassanā, ukkaṇṭhitasseva tattha tattha taṇhāyanāti vuttaṃ hoti. Paritassitāti vā kampanā. Tandīti jātiālasiyaṃ, pakatiālasiyanti attho. Tathā hi kusalakaraṇe kāyassa avipphārikatā līnatā jātiālasiyaṃ tandī nāma, na rogautujādīhi kāyagelaññaṃ. Tandiyanāti tandiyanākāro. Tandimanatāti tandiyā abhibhūtacittatā. Alasassa bhāvo ālasyaṃ, ālasyāyanākāro ālasyāyanā. Ālasyāyitassa bhāvo ālasyāyitattaṃ. Iti sabbehipi imehi padehi kilesavasena kāyālasiyaṃ kathitaṃ. Thinamiddhakāraṇānañhi rāgādikilesānaṃ vasena nāmakāyassa ālasiyaṃ, tadeva rūpakāyassāpīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Jambhanāti phandanā. Punappunaṃ jambhanā vijambhanā. Ānamanāti purato namanā. Vinamanāti pacchato namanā. Sannamanāti samantato namanā. Paṇamanāti yathā tantato uṭṭhitapesakāro kismiñcideva gahetvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ ussāpeti, evaṃ kāyassa uddhaṃ ṭhapanā. Byādhiyakanti uppannabyādhitā. Iti sabbehipi imehi padehi thinamiddhakāraṇānaṃ rāgādikilesānaṃ vasena kāyabaddhanameva kathitaṃ. Bhuttāvissāti bhuttavato. Bhattamucchāti bhattagelaññaṃ. Balavabhattena hi mucchāpatto viya hoti. Bhattakilamathoti bhattena kilantabhāvo. Bhattapariḷāhoti bhattadaratho. Tasmiñhi samaye pariḷāhuppattiyā upahatindriyo hoti, kāyo jīratīti. Kāyaduṭṭhullanti bhattaṃ nissāya kāyassa akammaññataṃ. Akalyatātiādi heṭṭhā vuttanayameva. Līnanti avipphārikatāya paṭikuṭitaṃ. Itare dve ākārabhāvaniddesā. Thinanti sappipiṇḍo viya avipphārikatāya ghanabhāvena ṭhitaṃ. Thiyanāti ākāraniddeso. Thiyibhāvo thiyitattaṃ[M 1.0078], avipphāravaseneva baddhatāti attho. Imehi pana sabbehipi padehi thinamiddhakāraṇānaṃ rāgādikilesānaṃ vasena cittassa gilānākāro kathitoti veditabbo. Purimā cattāro dhammāti arati, tandī, vijambhitā, bhattasammadoti ete cattāro dhammā. Yadā thinamiddhaṃ uppannaṃ hoti, tadā aratiādīnampi sambhavato “upanissayakoṭiyā pana hotī”ti vuttaṃ, upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo hotīti attho.

There, 'pantesu' means distant or secluded places. 'Adhikusalesu' refers to the qualities of tranquility and insight. 'Arati' means the opposite of delight. 'Aratitā' is the state of not finding pleasure. 'Anabhirati' is the state of dissatisfaction. 'Anabhiramanā' is the act of not delighting. 'Ukkaṇṭhitā' is the state of agitation. 'Paritassitā' is the trembling due to agitation; it is said that craving arises here and there in one who is agitated. Alternatively, 'paritassitā' means shaking. 'Tandī' refers to inborn laziness, meaning natural laziness. For when performing wholesome actions, the body's lack of vigor and sluggishness is called 'tandī,' inborn laziness, not the bodily weakness caused by illness or seasonal factors. 'Tandiyanā' is the act of being lazy. 'Tandimanatā' is the state of being overwhelmed by laziness. The nature of a lazy person is 'ālasya,' and the tendency toward laziness is 'ālasyāyanā.' The state of one who is lazy is 'ālasyāyitattaṃ.' Thus, all these terms describe bodily laziness caused by defilements. For the laziness of the mental body arises by way of defilements like lust, which are the causes of sloth and torpor; and the same should be understood for the physical body. 'Jambhanā' means yawning. 'Vijambhanā' is stretching. 'Ānamanā' is bending forward. 'Vinamanā' is bending backward. 'Sannamanā' is bending in all directions. 'Paṇamanā' is the straightening of the body upwards, just as a weaver, having risen from the loom, takes hold of something and raises his body straight. 'Byādhiyakaṃ' refers to the state of having an arisen illness. Thus, all these terms describe the binding of the body caused by defilements like lust, which are the causes of sloth and torpor. 'Bhuttāvissa' means of one who has eaten. 'Bhattamucchā' is sickness from food. For one who has eaten heavily becomes as if stupefied. 'Bhattakilamatho' is the fatigue from eating. 'Bhattapariḷāho' is the feverish distress caused by food. At that time, due to the arising of burning distress, the faculties are impaired, and the body wastes away. 'Kāyaduṭṭhullaṃ' is the body's unworkability on account of food. 'Akalyatā' and similar terms follow the same explanation as before. 'Līnaṃ' means contracted due to lack of vigor. The other two terms are designations of the state. 'Thīnaṃ' is like a lump of ghee, remaining dense due to lack of vigor. 'Thiyanā' describes the state. 'Thiyibhāvo' and 'thiyitattaṃ' mean being bound due to lack of expansion. All these terms, however, should be understood as describing the sickly state of the mind caused by defilements like lust, which are the causes of sloth and torpor. The first four factors—discontent (arati), laziness (tandī), stretching (vijambhitā), and food-stupefaction (bhattasammado)—are these four states. When sloth and torpor arise, these factors also arise, hence it is said, 'they occur in the category of decisive support,' meaning they serve as a condition in the category of decisive support.

14. Catutthe uddatassa bhāvo uddhaccaṃ. Yassa dhammassa vasena uddhataṃ hoti cittaṃ, taṃsampayuttā vā dhammā, so dhammo uddaccaṃ. Kucchitaṃ kataṃ kukataṃ, duccaritaṃ sucaritañca. Akatampi hi kukatameva. Evañhi vattāro honti “yaṃ mayā na kataṃ, taṃ kukata”nti. Evaṃ katākataṃ duccaritaṃ sucaritañca kukataṃ, taṃ ārabbha vippaṭisāravasena pavattaṃ pana cittaṃ idha kukatanti veditabbaṃ. Tassa bhāvo kukkuccaṃ. Cittassa uddhatākāroti cittassa avūpasamākārova vutto. Avūpasamalakkhaṇañhi uddhaccaṃ. Yathāpavattassa katākatākāravisiṭṭhassa duccaritasucaritassa [V 1.0070] anusocanavasena virūpaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ vippaṭisāro. Kukkuccassapi katākatānusocanavasena cittavikkhepabhāvato avūpasamākāro sambhavatīti āha – “cetaso avūpasamoti uddhaccakukkuccassevataṃ nāma”nti. Sveva ca cetaso avūpasamoti uddhaccakukkuccameva niddiṭṭhaṃ. Tañca attanova attanā sahajātaṃ na hotīti āha – “ayaṃ pana upanissayakoṭiyā paccayo hotī”ti. Upanissayapaccayatā ca purimuppannavasena veditabbā.

14. In the fourth, the state of being agitated is restlessness (uddhacca). That mental state by which the mind becomes agitated, or the mental states associated with it, that mental state is restlessness. What is badly done is 'badly done' (kukata), which includes both misconduct and good conduct. For even what is not done is indeed 'badly done.' Thus, people say, 'What I have not done is badly done.' In this way, both done and undone misconduct and good conduct are 'badly done.' However, the mind that arises by way of regret concerning that is here to be understood as 'badly done' (kukata). The state of that is remorse (kukkucca). The agitated characteristic of the mind means the uncomposed characteristic of the mind is stated. For restlessness has the characteristic of non-composure. Regarding misconduct and good conduct that has occurred, distinguished by the characteristic of being done or undone, the distorted reflection by way of sorrowing is regret (vippaṭisāra). Since remorse, too, has an uncomposed characteristic due to the mind's distraction through sorrowing over what was done and not done, it is said: 'The non-composure of the mind is the name for restlessness and remorse.' And this very non-composure of the mind is what is pointed out as restlessness and remorse. And that does not arise co-nascently with itself. Therefore, it is said: 'This, however, is a condition by way of a supporting condition.' And its nature as a supporting condition should be understood by way of what has arisen previously.

15. Pañcame vigatā cikicchā assāti vicikicchā. Sabhāvaṃ vicinanto tāya kicchatīti vā vicikicchā.

15. In the fifth, 'devoid of remedy' is doubt (vicikicchā). Or, while investigating its own nature, one is troubled by it; hence, it is doubt (vicikicchā).

16. Chaṭṭhe hetuṃ vā paccayaṃ vā na labhatīti ettha hetuggahaṇena janakaṃ kāraṇamāha, paccayaggahaṇena anupālanakaṃ kāraṇaṃ. Hetunti vā upādānakāraṇaṃ. Paccayanti sahakāraṇaṃ vuttaṃ. Tanti kilesaṃ. Vivaṭṭetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhātīti vivaṭṭābhimukhaṃ cittaṃ pesetvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento arahattaphalaṃ gaṇhāti. Bhikkhāya caranti etthāti bhikkhācāro, gocaragāmassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmiṃ bhikkhācāre. Vayaṃ āgammāti dārabharaṇānurūpaṃ vayaṃ āgamma. Āyūhantoti upacinanto. Aṅgārapakkanti vītaccikaṅgāresu pakkaṃ. Kiṃ nāmetanti bhikkhū garahanto āha. Jīvamānapetakasattoti [M 1.0079] jīvamāno hutvā “teneva attabhāvena petabhāvaṃ pattasatto bhavissatī”ti parikappavasena vuttaṃ. Kuṭanti pānīyaghaṭaṃ. Yāva dāruṇanti ativiya dāruṇaṃ. Vipāko kīdiso bhavissatīti tayā katakammassa āyatiṃ anubhavitabbavipāko kīdiso bhavissati.

16. In the sixth, regarding 'not obtaining a cause or condition,' here by the taking up of 'cause' (hetu) is meant the generative cause, and by the taking up of 'condition' (paccaya) is meant the sustaining cause. Or, 'cause' (hetu) is the material cause; 'condition' (paccaya) is said to be the co-operative cause. 'That' (taṃ) means a defilement. 'Having turned away, one attains arahantship' means: having directed the mind towards turning away and developing insight, one attains the fruit of arahantship. 'That wherein they wander for alms' is the alms-round (bhikkhācāra); this is a designation for the village for alms-resort; in that alms-round. 'Having come to age' (vayaṃ āgamma) means having come to an age suitable for supporting a wife. 'Accumulating' (āyūhanto) means increasing. 'Cooked on embers' (aṅgārapakkaṃ) means cooked on embers devoid of flame. 'What is this called?' (kiṃ nāmetaṃ)—he said this, reproaching the monks. 'A living ghost-being' (jīvamānapetakasatto) is said by way of supposition, meaning: 'while still living, he will become a being who has attained the state of a ghost by that very same existence.' 'A pot' (kuṭaṃ) means a water pot. 'So harsh' (yāva dāruṇaṃ) means exceedingly harsh. 'What kind of result will there be?' (vipāko kīdiso bhavissati) means: what kind of result of the deed done by you will have to be experienced in the future?

Visaṅkharitvāti chedanabhedanādīhi vināsetvā. Dīpakamigapakkhinoti attano nisinnabhāvassa dīpanato evaṃladdhanāmā migapakkhino, yena araññaṃ netvā nesādo tesaṃ saddena āgatāgate migapakkhino vadhitvā gaṇhāti. Theranti cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissattheraṃ. Iddhiyā abhisaṅkharitvāti adhiṭṭhānādivasena iddhiṃ abhisaṅkharitvā. Upayogatthe cetaṃ karaṇavacanaṃ. Aggipapaṭikanti accikaraṇaṃ, vipphuliṅganti attho. Passantassevāti anādare sāmivacanaṃ. Tassa therassāti tassa milakkhatissattherassa. Tassāti tassā aggipapaṭikāya. Paṭibalassāti uggahaṇasajjhāyādīsu paṭibalassa. Dukkhaṃ upanisā kāraṇametissāti dukkhūpanisā, dukkhanibandhanā dukkhahetukā saddhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Vattamukhena kammaṭṭhānassa kathitattā “vattasīse ṭhatvā”ti vuttaṃ. Palālavaraṇakanti palālapuñjaṃ.

'Having dismantled' (visaṅkharitvā) means having destroyed by cutting, breaking, and so on. 'Indicator animals and birds' (dīpakamigapakkhino) are animals and birds so named from indicating the fact of their own presence, by means of which a hunter, having led them into the forest, kills and captures the animals and birds that come near, attracted by their sound. 'The Elder' (theraṃ) refers to the Elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika Tissa. 'Having fashioned by psychic power' (iddhiyā abhisaṅkharitvā) means having fashioned psychic power by way of resolution, and so on. And this is an instrumental expression in the sense of application. 'A spark of fire' (aggipapaṭikaṃ) means that which makes a flame; the meaning is 'a spark' (vipphuliṅga). 'Even while he was looking on' (passantasseva) is a genitive expression in the sense of disregard. 'Of that elder' (tassa therassa) refers to that Elder Milakkha Tissa. 'Of that' (tassā) refers to that spark of fire. 'Of one who is capable' (paṭibalassa) means of one who is capable in learning, recitation, and so on. 'Suffering is the supporting condition and cause for it' is 'having suffering as its supporting condition' (dukkhūpanisā); this means that faith is said to be bound to suffering, to have suffering as its cause. Because the meditation subject was explained by way of the practice, it is said, 'standing at the head of the practice' (vattasīse ṭhatvā). 'A heap of straw' (palālavaraṇakaṃ) means a pile of straw.

Ārambhathāti samathavipassanādīsu vīriyaṃ karotha. Nikkamathāti kosajjato nikkhamatha, kāmānaṃ [V 1.0071] vā panūdanāya nikkhamatha, ubhayenapi vīriyameva vuttaṃ. Vīriyañhi ārambhanakavasena ārambho, kosajjato nikkhamanavasena “nikkamo”ti vuccati. Yuñjatha buddhasāsaneti buddhassa bhagavato pariyattipaṭipattipaṭivedhasaṅkhāte tividhasāsane yuñjatha yogaṃ karotha. Evamanuyuñjantā maccuno senaṃ dhunātha viddhaṃsetha. Tattha maccuno senanti –

'Strive' (ārambhatha) means exert effort in tranquility (samatha), insight (vipassanā), and so on. 'Depart' (nikkamatha) means depart from laziness, or depart for the expulsion of sensual pleasures; in both cases, effort is meant. For effort (vīriya) is called 'striving' (ārambha) in the sense of initiating, and 'departure' (nikkama) in the sense of departing from laziness. 'Apply yourselves to the Buddha’s dispensation' (yuñjatha buddhasāsane) means apply yourselves to the threefold dispensation of the Blessed One, the Buddha, namely, learning (pariyatti), practice (paṭipatti), and realization (paṭivedha). Thus applying yourselves, shake off and destroy the army of Death. Herein, the army of Death means:

“Kāmā te paṭhamā senā, dutiyā arati vuccati;

Tatiyā khuppipāsā te, catutthī taṇhā pavuccati.

"Sensual pleasures are your first army, the second is called discontent; your third is hunger and thirst, the fourth is declared to be craving."

“Pañcamaṃ thinamiddhaṃ te, chaṭṭhā bhīrū pavuccati;

Sattamī vicikicchā te, makkho thambho te aṭṭhamo.

"Your fifth is sloth and torpor, the sixth is called fear; your seventh is doubt, your eighth is hypocrisy and obstinacy."

“Lābho [M 1.0080] siloko sakkāro,

Micchāladdho ca yo yaso;

Yo cattānaṃ samukkaṃse,

Pare ca avajānāti.

"Gain, renown, and honor, and whatever fame is wrongly gained; whoever exalts themself and disparages others—"

“Esā namuci te senā, kaṇhassābhippahārinī;

Na naṃ asūro jināti, jetvā ca labhate sukha”nti. (su. ni. 438-441) –

"This, Namuci, is your army, the assaulting force of the Dark One; no coward conquers it, but having conquered it, one obtains happiness."

Evamāgataṃ kāmādibhedaṃ maccuno senaṃ. Ettha ca yasmā āditova agāriyabhūte satte vatthukāmesu kilesakāmā mosayanti, te abhibhuyya anagāriyabhāvaṃ upagatānaṃ pantesu senāsanesu aññataraññataresu vā adhikusalesu dhammesu arati uppajjati. Vuttañhetaṃ – “pabbajitena kho, āvuso, abhirati dukkarā”ti (saṃ. ni. 4.331). Tato te parappaṭibaddhajīvikattā khuppipāsā bādhati, tāya bādhitānaṃ pariyesanataṇhā cittaṃ kilamayati. Atha nesaṃ kilantacittānaṃ thinamiddhaṃ okkamati, tato visesamanadhigacchantānaṃ durabhisambhavesu araññavanapatthesu pantesu senāsanesu viharataṃ utrāsasaññitā bhīru jāyati. Tesaṃ ussaṅkitaparisaṅkitānaṃ dīgharattaṃ vivekarasamanassādayamānānaṃ viharataṃ “na siyā nu kho esa maggo”ti paṭipattiyaṃ vicikicchā uppajjati. Taṃ vinodetvā viharataṃ appamattakena visesādhigamena mānamakkhathambhā jāyanti. Tepi vinodetvā viharataṃ tato adhikataraṃ visesādhigamanaṃ [V 1.0072] nissāya lābhasakkārasilokā uppajjanti. Lābhādīhi mucchitvā dhammappatirūpakāni pakāsento micchāyasaṃ adhigantvā tattha ṭhitā jātiādīhi attānaṃ ukkaṃsenti, paraṃ vambhenti, tasmā kāmādīnaṃ paṭhamasenādibhāvo veditabbo. Naḷāgāranti naḷehi vinaddhatiṇacchannagehaṃ.

Thus has come the army of Death, with its divisions of sensual pleasures and so on. Herein, since from the very beginning defilements of desire delude beings who are householders in regard to sensual objects, for those who, having overcome these, have gone forth into the homeless life, discontent (arati) arises in regard to one or another of the higher wholesome states in remote dwellings and lodgings. For it has been said: 'For one gone forth, friends, delight is hard to achieve.' Then, because their livelihood is dependent on others, hunger and thirst afflict them. For those afflicted by these, the craving for seeking wearies their minds. Then, for those with wearied minds, sloth and torpor overcome them. Then, for those not attaining any distinction while dwelling in remote dwellings and lodgings in forest tracts that are difficult to endure, fear (bhīru), known as terror, arises. For those dwelling for a long time, suspicious and apprehensive, not savoring the taste of seclusion, doubt (vicikicchā) arises in their practice: 'Might this not be the path?' For those dwelling having dispelled that, conceit (māna), hypocrisy (makkha), and obstinacy (thambha) arise with even a slight attainment of distinction. For those dwelling having dispelled these too, gains, honors, and renown arise dependent on the attainment of a higher distinction. Infatuated by these gains and so on, proclaiming things that are counterfeit dhamma and achieving false fame, established therein they exalt themselves through birth and so on, and disparage others. Therefore, the state of being the first army and so on should be understood as belonging to sensual pleasures and the others. 'A reed hut' (naḷāgāraṃ) means a house thatched with grass and bound with reeds.

Vihassatīti uggahaṇasajjhāyanamanasikārādīhi viharissati. Jātisaṃsāranti punappunaṃ jātisaṅkhātasaṃsāravaṭṭaṃ. Dukkhassantaṃ karissatīti dukkhassa antasaṅkhātaṃ nibbānaṃ sacchikarissati. Palālapuñjāhanti palālapuñjaṃ ahanti padacchedo. Tatiyaṃ ṭhānanti anāgāmiphalaṃ sandhāya vadati.

'He will dwell' (vihassati) means he will dwell by way of learning, recitation, mental application, and so on. 'The cycle of birth' (jātisaṃsāra) means the round of saṃsāra, designated as repeated birth. 'He will make an end of suffering' (dukkhassantaṃ karissati) means he will realize Nibbāna, which is designated as the end of suffering. 'Palālapuñjāhaṃ' has the word division 'palālapuñjaṃ ahaṃ' (I am a heap of straw). 'The third state' (tatiyaṃ ṭhānaṃ) is said in reference to the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmiphala).

Tivassabhikkhukāleti upasampadato tīṇi vassāni assāti tivasso, tivasso ca so bhikkhu cāti tivassabhikkhu, tassa, tena vā [M 1.0081] upalakkhito kālo tivassabhikkhukālo, tasmiṃ. Yadā so tivasso bhikkhu nāma hoti, tadāti vuttaṃ hoti. Kammaṃ karotīti bhāvanākammaṃ karoti. Ganthakammanti ganthavisayaṃ uggahaṇādikammaṃ. Piṇḍāpacitiṃ katvāti antovasse temāsaṃ dinnapiṇḍassa kilesakkhayakaraṇena apacitiṃ pūjaṃ katvā. Piṇḍāpacitiṃ karonto hi bhikkhu yehi attano yo piṇḍapāto dinno, tesaṃ tassa mahapphalabhāvaṃ icchanto attano santānameva kilesakkhayakaraṇena visodhetvā arahattaṃ gaṇhāti.

'At the time of the three-year monk' means 'he has three years since his higher ordination,' thus 'three-year'; and he is a monk, thus 'three-year monk'; the time marked by him or by that is the 'time of the three-year monk.' It is said, 'when he is called a three-year monk.' 'He performs action' means he performs the practice of meditation. 'Textual work' means activities such as learning texts. 'Having honored the alms-food' means having shown reverence for the alms-food given during the three months of the rains-retreat by destroying the defilements. For a monk honoring the alms-food, wishing that the alms-food given to him by whomever may bring great fruit to them, purifies his own mental continuum by destroying the defilements and attains arahantship.

Mahābhūtīti ettha pūjāvacano mahantasaddo, bhūtīti ca nāmekadesena tissabhūtittheraṃ ālapati. Bhavati hi nāmekadesenapi vohāro yathā “devadatto datto”ti. Mahābhūtīti vā piyasamudāhāro, so mahati bhūti vibhūti puññañāṇādisampadā assāti mahābhūti. Channaṃ sepaṇṇigacchamūlanti sākhāpalāsādīhi channaṃ ghanacchāyaṃ sepaṇṇigacchamūlaṃ. Asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ pādakaṃ katvāti kesādiasubhakoṭṭhāsabhāvanāya paṭiladdhaṃ upacārasamādhiṃ appanāsamādhiṃ vā pādakaṃ katvā. Asubhavisayaṃ upacārajjhānādikammamevettha upari pavattetabbabhāvanākammassa kāraṇabhāvato ṭhānanti kammaṭṭhānaṃ.

Here, in 'Mahābhūti,' the word 'mahanta' is a term of respect, and by 'bhūti' he addresses the elder Tissa Bhūti by a part of his name. For it is customary to address someone partially by name, as in 'Devadatta is Datta.' Alternatively, 'Mahābhūti' may be an affectionate form of address, meaning 'he who possesses great prosperity, splendor, and accomplishment in merit, wisdom, and so forth, is Mahābhūti.' 'The foot of the covered sepaṇṇi tree' refers to the base of the sepaṇṇi tree, which is covered and densely shaded by its branches, leaves, and so forth. 'Having made the meditation on the repulsive its foundation' means having made either access concentration or absorption concentration, attained through the contemplation of repulsive parts such as hair, its foundation. Here, the very meditative work on the repulsive object, such as access jhāna, is called a 'meditation subject' because it is the foundation, being the cause, for the meditative practice to be developed further.

Sahassadvisahassasaṅkhāmattattā “mahāgaṇe”ti vuttaṃ. Attano vasanaṭṭhānato therassa santikaṃ gantvāti attano vasanaṭṭhānato ākāsena gantvā vihārasamīpe otaritvā divāṭṭhāne nisinnattherassa santikaṃ gantvā. Kiṃ āgatosīti kiṃkāraṇā āgatosi. Sabbesu rattidivasabhāgesu okāsaṃ alabhantoti so kira thero “tuyhaṃ okāso na bhavissati, āvuso”ti [V 1.0073] vuttepi “vitakkamāḷake ṭhitakāle pucchissāmi, bhante”ti vatvā “tasmiṃ ṭhāne aññe pucchissantī”ti vutte “bhikkhācāramagge, bhante”ti vatvā “tatrāpi aññe pucchantī”ti vutte dupaṭṭanivāsanaṭṭhāne, saṅghāṭipārupanaṭṭhāne, pattanīharaṇaṭṭhāne, gāme caritvā āsanasālāya yāgupītakāle, bhanteti. Tatthāpi therā attano kaṅkhaṃ vinodenti, āvusoti. Antogāmato nikkhamanakāle pucchissāmi, bhanteti. Tatrāpi aññe pucchanti, āvusoti. Antarāmagge, bhanteti. Bhojanasālāya bhattakiccapariyosāne, bhante. Divāṭṭhāne pādadhovanakāle, bhanteti. Tato paṭṭhāya [M 1.0082] yāva aruṇā apare pucchanti, āvusoti. Dantakaṭṭhaṃ gahetvā mukhadhovanatthaṃ gamanakāle, bhanteti. Tadāpi aññe pucchantīti. Mukhaṃ dhovitvā āgamanakāle, bhanteti. Tatrāpi aññe pucchissantīti. Senāsanaṃ pavisitvā nisinnakāle, bhanteti. Tatrāpi aññe pucchanti, āvusoti. Evaṃ sabbesu rattidivasabhāgesu yācamāno okāsaṃ na labhi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “evaṃ okāse asati maraṇassa kathaṃ okāsaṃ labhissathā”ti. Bhante, nanu mukhaṃ dhovitvā senāsanaṃ pavisitvā tayo cattāro pallaṅke uṇhāpetvā yonisomanasikārakammaṃ karontānaṃ okāsalābhena bhavitabbaṃ siyāti adhippāyena vadati. Maṇivaṇṇeti indanīlamaṇivaṇṇe.

Because the number was approximately one or two thousand, it was called a 'great assembly.' 'Having gone from his own dwelling place to the elder’s presence' means having gone from his own dwelling place through the sky, descended near the monastery, and approached the elder who was seated in his daytime dwelling. 'Why have you come?' means for what reason have you come? 'Not obtaining an opportunity at any time of day or night': it is said that when the elder told him, 'There will be no opportunity for you, friend,' he replied, 'I will ask when you are standing on the meditation walk, venerable sir.' When told, 'Others will ask in that place,' he said, 'On the alms-round path, venerable sir.' When told, 'Others ask there too,' he said, 'At the place for putting on the under-robe, at the place for draping the outer robe, at the place for taking out the bowl, after walking in the village, during the time of drinking rice-gruel in the assembly hall, venerable sir.' 'There too, friend, elders dispel their doubts.' 'I will ask when you are leaving the village, venerable sir.' 'Others ask there too, friend.' 'On the road between villages, venerable sir.' 'At the end of the meal duties in the dining hall, venerable sir.' 'At the daytime dwelling during the time for washing feet, venerable sir.' 'From then until dawn, others will ask, friend.' 'When taking a tooth-stick to go and wash your mouth, venerable sir.' 'Even then, others ask.' 'When returning after washing your mouth, venerable sir.' 'There too, others will ask.' 'After entering your lodging and sitting down, venerable sir.' 'There too, others ask, friend.' Thus, though requesting at all times of day and night, he did not obtain an opportunity. This is what is referred to by this: 'When there is no such opportunity, how will you find an opportunity at the time of death?' He speaks with this intention: 'Venerable sir, surely there must be an opportunity for those who, after washing their face, entering their lodging, warming up three or four cross-legged postures, are engaged in the work of proper attention?' 'Like a gem’s color' means like the color of an indranila sapphire.

Ghaṭentassevāti vāyāmantasseva. Visuddhipavāraṇanti “parisuddho aha”nti evaṃ pavattaṃ visuddhipavāraṇaṃ. Arahantānameva hesā pavāraṇā. Kāḷakaṃ vāti mahantaṃ kāḷakaṃ sandhāya vadati, tilako vāti khuddakaṃ sandhāya. Ubhayenapi sīlassa parisuddhabhāvameva vibhāveti.

'Of one who is striving' means of one who is making an effort. 'Invitation of purity' refers to the declaration 'I am pure'; this is called the invitation of purity. This invitation is indeed for the Arahants alone. 'Or a black mark' refers to a large black mark, while 'or a sesame seed mark' refers to a small one. By both, he illustrates the complete purity of virtue.

Padhānakammikāti padhānakamme niyuttā. Laddhamagganti laddhūpāyaṃ, paṭhamameva laddhūpadesanti vuttaṃ hoti. Apattānīti chaḍḍitāni. Alābūneva sāradeti saradakāle vātātapahatāni tattha tattha vippakiṇṇaalābūni viya. Kāpotakānīti kapotakavaṇṇāni. Tāni disvāna kā ratīti tāni evarūpāni aṭṭhīni disvā tumhākaṃ kā nāma rati, nanu appamattakāpi rati kātuṃ na vaṭṭatiyevāti attho. Dutiyakathaṃ akathitapubboti attano vuḍḍhatarena saddhiṃ vuttavacanassa paccanīkaṃ dutiyakathaṃ akathitapubbo.

'Those engaged in the primary practice' means those engaged in the main meditative striving. 'Having obtained the path' means having obtained the means; it is said to mean having received the initial instruction. 'Cast off' means discarded. 'Like gourds in autumn' means like gourds in the autumn season, struck by wind and sun, scattered here and there. 'Pigeon-colored' means having the color of a pigeon. 'Seeing them, what delight is there?' means: seeing such bones, what delight is there for you? The meaning is that it is not fitting to have even the slightest delight. 'One who has never before spoken a second word' means one who has never before spoken a second word that contradicts what was said by his elder.

Tadaṅgena, tadaṅgassa pahānaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ. Yañhi rattibhāge samujjalitena dīpena andhakārassa viya tena tena vipassanāya avayavabhūtena ñāṇaṅgena paṭipakkhavaseneva tassa tassa pahātabbadhammassa pahānamidaṃ tadaṅgappahānaṃ nāma. Yathā kāmacchandādayo na cittaṃ pariyuṭṭhāya tiṭṭhanti, evaṃ pariyuṭṭhānassa nisedhanaṃ appavattikaraṇaṃ vikkhambhanaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ. Yañhi [V 1.0074] sasevāle udake pakkhittena ghaṭena sevālassa viya tena tena lokiyasamādhinā nīvaraṇādīnaṃ paccanīkadhammānaṃ vikkhambhanamidaṃ vikkhambhanappahānaṃ nāma. Sammā upacchijjanti etena kilesāti samucchedo, pahīyanti etena kilesāti pahānaṃ, samucchedasaṅkhātaṃ [M 1.0083] pahānaṃ niravasesappahānanti samucchedappahānaṃ. Yañhi asanivicakkābhihatassa rukkhassa viya ariyamaggañāṇena saṃyojanādīnaṃ dhammānaṃ yathā na puna vattanti, evaṃ pahānamidaṃ samucchedappahānaṃ nāma. Paṭippassambhati vūpasammati kilesadaratho etāyāti paṭippassaddhi, phalaṃ, sāyeva pahānanti paṭippassaddhippahānaṃ. Sabbe kilesā sabbasaṅkhatā vā nissaranti apagacchanti etenāti nissaraṇaṃ, nibbānaṃ, tadeva pahānanti nissaraṇappahānaṃ. Paṭippassambhayamānanti paṭippassambhaṃ kilesavūpasamaṃ kurumānaṃ. Lokiyalokuttarehīti tadaṅgavikkhambhanappahānānaṃ lokiyattā, itaresaṃ lokuttarattā vuttaṃ.

The abandoning of a state by its specific opposite is 'abandoning by substitution.' Just as darkness is dispelled by a lamp burning in the night, so too, by each insight-knowledge acting as a counteragent, the abandoning of each defilement to be abandoned is called 'abandoning by substitution.' Just as sensual desire and other defilements do not persist by overwhelming the mind, the suppression, non-arising, and subduing of their obsession is called 'abandoning by suppression.' Just as algae in water are suppressed by a pot thrown into it, so too, by mundane concentration acting as an opposing force, the suppression of hindrances and other opposing states is called 'abandoning by suppression.' 'They are rightly cut off by this'—thus, it is 'eradication.' 'They are abandoned by this'—thus, it is 'abandoning.' The abandoning designated as eradication without remainder is called 'abandoning by eradication.' Just as a tree struck by lightning does not grow again, so too, the abandoning of fetters and other defilements by noble path-knowledge, ensuring they do not recur, is called 'abandoning by eradication.' 'The turmoil of defilements subsides and calms down by this'—thus, it is 'tranquillization.' The fruit itself is the abandoning—thus, it is 'abandoning by tranquillization.' 'All defilements and all conditioned phenomena escape and depart by this'—thus, it is 'escape.' Nibbāna itself is the abandoning—thus, it is 'abandoning by escape.' 'Tranquillizing' means bringing about tranquillization, the calming of the defilements. 'By the mundane and supramundane' is said because abandoning by substitution and by suppression are mundane, while the others are supramundane.

Nimīyati phalaṃ etena uppajjanaṭṭhāne pakkhipamānaṃ viya hotīti nimittaṃ, kāraṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Asubhassa nimittaṃ, asubhameva vā nimittanti asubhanimittaṃ. Asubhanissitampi hi jhānaṃ nissite nissayavohārena asubhanti voharīyati yathā “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti. Tenevāha – “dasasu asubhesu uppannaṃ sārammaṇaṃ paṭhamajjhāna”nti. Anicce aniccantiādinā nayena vuttassāti iminā catubbidhaṃ yonisomanasikāraṃ dasseti. Heṭṭhā cettha idha ca catubbidhassa ayonisomanasikārassa yonisomanasikārassa ca gahaṇaṃ niravasesadassanatthaṃ katanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tesu pana asubhe “asubha”nti manasikāro idhādhippeto, tadanukūlattā vā itaresampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

A sign (nimitta) is so called because by it a fruit is measured, as if it were being placed in the place of arising. This is a designation for 'cause'. The sign of the unattractive, or the unattractive itself as a sign, is the 'unattractive-sign'. For even a jhāna dependent on the unattractive is spoken of as 'unattractive' by way of conventional usage based on its support, just as it is said, 'The beds are crying out.' Therefore, he said: 'The first jhāna that has arisen with the ten unattractive things as its object.' By the phrase 'stated by the method of "in the impermanent as impermanent," etc.', he indicates the fourfold wise attention. It should be understood that the inclusion of the fourfold unwise attention and wise attention, both below and here, is done for the sake of showing it completely, without remainder. Among these, however, the attention to the unattractive as 'unattractive' is intended here; or, the inclusion of the others should be understood as being conducive to it.

Ekādasasu asubhesu paṭikūlākārassa uggaṇhanaṃ, yathā vā tattha uggahanimittaṃ uppajjati, tathā paṭipatti asubhanimittassa uggaho. Upacārappanāvahāya asubhabhāvanāya anuyuñjanaṃ asubhabhāvanānuyogo. Bhojane mattaññuno thinamiddhābhibhavābhāvā otāraṃ alabhamāno kāmacchando pahīyatīti vadanti. Bhojananissitaṃ pana āhāre paṭikūlasaññaṃ, tabbipariṇāmassa tadādhārassa tassa ca udariyabhūtassa asubhatādassanaṃ, kāyassa ca āhāraṭṭhitikatādassanaṃ yo uppādeti, so visesato bhojane pamāṇaññū nāma, tassa ca kāmacchando pahīyateva. Dasavidhañhi asubhanimittanti pākaṭavasena vuttaṃ. Kāyagatāsatiṃ pana gahetvā ekādasavidhampi asubhanimittaṃ veditabbaṃ.

In the eleven kinds of unattractiveness, the grasping of the repulsive aspect, or the practice whereby the learning sign arises there, is the grasping of the sign of unattractiveness. Devotion to the development of unattractiveness, which leads to access and absorption, is the practice of developing unattractiveness. They say that for one who knows moderation in food, since he is not overcome by sloth and torpor, sensual desire, not finding an opportunity, is abandoned. However, one who gives rise to the perception of repulsiveness in food, which is dependent on the meal; who sees the unattractiveness of its transformation, of its container, and of its becoming stomach-contents; and who sees the body's subsistence on food, is especially called one who knows the measure in eating, and for him, sensual desire is indeed abandoned. The tenfold sign of unattractiveness is spoken of in a manifest way. But by including mindfulness directed to the body, the elevenfold sign of unattractiveness should be understood.

Abhutvā udakaṃ piveti pānīyassa okāsadānatthaṃ cattāro pañca ālope abhutvā pānīyaṃ [V 1.0075] piveyyāti attho. Tena vuttaṃ – “catunnaṃ [M 1.0084] pañcannaṃ ālopānaṃ okāse satī”ti. Abhidhammaṭīkākārena panettha “cattāro pañca ālope, bhutvāna udakaṃ pive”ti pāṭhaṃ parikappetvā aññathā attho vaṇṇito, so aṭṭhakathāya na sameti. Asubhakammikatissatthero dantaṭṭhidassāvī.

'Having not eaten, one drinks water' means that for the purpose of allowing space for a drink, one should drink water without having eaten four or five mouthfuls. Therefore, it is said: 'When there is space for four or five morsels.' The author of the Abhidhamma sub-commentary, however, conjecturing the reading here as 'having eaten four or five morsels, one should drink water,' explains the meaning differently, which does not agree with the commentary. The Elder Tissa, a practitioner of the unattractive meditation, was one who saw a tooth-bone.

17. Sattame mijjati hitapharaṇavasena siniyhatīti mitto, hitesī puggalo, tasmiṃ mitte bhavā, mittassa vā esāti mettā, hitesitā. Tattha “mettā”ti vutte appanāpi upacāropi vaṭṭati sādhāraṇavacanabhāvatoti āha – “mettāti ettāvatā pubbabhāgopi vaṭṭatī”ti. Api-saddo appanaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Appanaṃ appattāya mettāya suṭṭhu muccanassa abhāvato cetovimuttīti “appanāva adhippetā”ti vuttaṃ.

17. In the seventh: a friend (mitta) is one who is affectionate and loved because he brings welfare; he is a person who desires one's welfare. That which exists in a friend, or that which belongs to a friend, is mettā (loving-kindness); the state of desiring welfare. Here, when 'mettā' is said, both absorption (appanā) and access concentration (upacāra) are suitable, because it is a general term. Thus, he said: 'By "mettā," even the preliminary part is suitable.' The word 'api' includes absorption. Since for loving-kindness that has not attained absorption there is no proper liberation of mind (cetovimutti), it is said that 'absorption is indeed intended'.

Sattesu mettāyanassa hitūpasaṃhārassa uppādanaṃ pavattanaṃ mettānimittassa uggaho. Paṭhamuppanno mettāmanasikāro parato uppajjanakassa kāraṇabhāvato mettāmanasikārova mettānimittaṃ. Kammaṃyeva sakaṃ etesanti kammassakā, sattā, tabbhāvo kammassakatā, kammadāyādatā. Dosamettāsu yāthāvato ādīnavānisaṃsānaṃ paṭisaṅkhānavīmaṃsā idha paṭisaṅkhānaṃ. Mettāvihārīkalyāṇamittavantatā idha kalyāṇamittatā. Odissakaanodissakadisāpharaṇānanti attaatipiyamajjhattaverivasena odissakatā, sīmāsambhede kate anodissakatā, ekādidisāpharaṇavasena disāpharaṇatā mettāya uggahaṇe veditabbā. Vihāraracchagāmādivasena vā odissakadisāpharaṇaṃ. Vihārādiuddesarahitaṃ puratthimādidisāvasena anodissakadisāpharaṇaṃ. Evaṃ vā dvidhā uggahaṇaṃ sandhāya – “odissakaanodissakadisāpharaṇa”nti vuttaṃ. Uggaho ca yāva upacārā daṭṭhabbo. Uggahitāya āsevanā bhāvanā. Tattha sabbe sattā, pāṇā, bhūtā, puggalā, attabhāvapariyāpannāti etesaṃ vasena pañcavidhā. Ekekasmiṃ averā hontu, abyāpajjhā, anīghā, sukhī attānaṃ pariharantūti catudhā pavattito vīsatividhā anodhisopharaṇā mettā. Sabbā itthiyo, purisā, ariyā, anariyā, devā, manussā, vinipātikāti sattādhikaraṇavasena pavattā sattavidhā aṭṭhavīsatividhā vā, dasahi disāhi disādhikaraṇavasena pavattā dasavidhā ca, ekekāya [M 1.0085] vā disāya sattādiitthādiaverādibhedena asītādhikacatusatappabhedā ca odhisopharaṇā veditabbā. Mettaṃ bhāventassāti mettājhānaṃ bhāventassa. Tvaṃ etassa kuddhotiādi paccavekkhaṇāvidhidassanaṃ. Appaṭicchitapaheṇakaṃ viyāti asampaṭicchitapaṇṇākāraṃ viya. Paṭisaṅkhāneti vīmaṃsāyaṃ. Vattaniaṭaviyaṃ attaguttattherasadise.

The arising and maintaining of bringing welfare to beings, which is the act of loving-kindness, is the grasping of the sign of loving-kindness. The initially arisen mental attention to loving-kindness is itself the sign of loving-kindness, because it is the cause for what arises subsequently. Deeds are their own, thus beings are 'owners of their deeds' (kammassakā). That state is ownership of kamma (kammassakatā), heirship to kamma. Here, 'reflection' (paṭisaṅkhāna) is the reflective investigation of the dangers and benefits of hatred and loving-kindness as they really are. Here, 'good friendship' (kalyāṇamittatā) is the state of having good friends who are dwellers in loving-kindness. The pervasions of specific, non-specific, and directional should be understood in the grasping of loving-kindness thus: specificity (odissakatā) is with regard to oneself, a very dear person, a neutral person, and a hostile person; non-specificity (anodissakatā) is when the boundaries have been broken down; directional pervasion (disāpharaṇatā) is by way of pervading one direction, and so on. Alternatively, specific directional pervasion is by way of a monastery, a street, a village, etc. Non-specific directional pervasion is without designation of a monastery, etc., by way of the eastern direction, etc. Or, referring to the twofold grasping in this way, it is said 'specific and non-specific directional pervasion.' And the grasping should be understood as lasting up to access concentration. The cultivation (bhāvanā) is the repeated practice (āsevanā) of what has been grasped. Therein, it is fivefold by way of: all beings, all living things, all creatures, all persons, all those included in an individual existence. Since it proceeds in four ways for each one—'May they be free from enmity, free from ill will, free from trouble, may they maintain themselves in happiness'—the unspecified pervasion of loving-kindness is twentyfold. Proceeding by way of the seven types of beings—all women, all men, all noble ones, all non-noble ones, all devas, all humans, all those in states of deprivation—it is sevenfold, or twenty-eightfold. Proceeding by way of the ten directions, it is tenfold. Or, in each direction, the specified pervasion should be understood as having four hundred and eighty divisions based on the distinctions of beings, women, etc., and freedom from enmity, etc. 'For one who cultivates loving-kindness' means for one who develops the loving-kindness jhāna. The phrase 'You are angry with this one,' etc., is a demonstration of the method of reviewing. 'Like an unaccepted message' means like an unaccepted gift. 'He reflects' (paṭisaṅkhāneti) is in the sense of 'he investigates' (vīmaṃsati). Like the Elder Attagutta in the perilous forest.

18. Aṭṭhame [V 1.0076] kusaladhammasampaṭipattiyā paṭṭhapanasabhāvatāya tappaṭipakkhānaṃ visosanasabhāvatāya ca ārambhadhātuādito pavattavīriyanti āha – “paṭhamārambhavīriya”nti. Yasmā paṭhamārambhamattassa kosajjavidhamanaṃ thāmagamanañca natthi, tasmā vuttaṃ – “kosajjato nikkhantattā tato balavatara”nti. Yasmā pana aparāparuppattiyā laddhāsevanaṃ uparūpari visesaṃ āvahantaṃ ativiya thāmagatameva hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ – “paraṃ paraṃ ṭhānaṃ akkamanato tatopi balavatara”nti. Panūdanāyāti nīharaṇāya.
