Yathā mahato palighassa ugghāṭakajanassa mahanto ussāho icchitabbo, evamidhāpīti “nikkamo cetaso palighugghāṭanāyā”ti vuttaṃ. Mahāparakkamo eva parena kataṃ bandhanaṃ chindeyya, evamidhāpīti vuttaṃ – “parakkamo cetaso bandhanacchedanāyā”ti.

18. In the eighth: regarding the energy that arises from the element of initiative, etc., which has the nature of establishing the practice of wholesome qualities and the nature of drying up their opposites, it is said: 'initial-effort energy' (paṭhamārambhavīriya). Because mere initial effort possesses neither the dispelling of laziness nor the attainment of strength, it is said: 'stronger than that, due to having emerged from laziness.' But because, through successive arising, having attained repeated practice, it brings about higher and higher distinction and becomes exceedingly strong, it is said: 'even stronger than that, due to successively advancing to higher states.' 'For the purpose of driving away' (panūdanāya) means for the purpose of removing (nīharaṇāya). Just as great exertion is required of a person who is unfastening a great cross-bar, so too here; thus it is said: 'exertion (nikkamo) is for unfastening the mind's cross-bar.' Only one of great striving could sever a bond made by another, so too here; thus it is said: 'striving (parakkamo) is for severing the mind's bonds'.

Āraddhaṃ saṃsādhitaṃ paripūritaṃ vīriyaṃ etassāti āraddhavīriyo, nipphannavīriyo, āraddhaṃ paṭṭhapitaṃ vīriyaṃ etassāti āraddhavīriyo. Vīriyārambhappasutoti āha – “āraddhavīriyassāti paripuṇṇavīriyassaceva paggahitavīriyassa cā”ti. Catudosāpagatanti atilīnatādīhi catūhi dosehi apagataṃ. Catudosāpagatattameva vibhāveti “na ca atilīna”ntiādinā. Atilīnañhi bhāvanācittaṃ kosajjapakkhikaṃ siyā, atipaggahitañca uddhaccapakkhikaṃ. Bhāvanāvīthiṃ anajjhogāhetvā saṅkocāpatti atilīnatā. Ajjhogāhetvā antosaṅkoco ajjhattaṃ saṃkhittatā. Atipaggahitatā accāraddhavīriyatā. Bahiddhā vikkhittatā bahivisaṭavitakkānudhāvanā. Tadetaṃ vīriyaṃ caṅkamādikāyikappayogāvahaṃ kāyikaṃ, tadaññaṃ cetasikaṃ. Rattidivassa pañca koṭṭhāseti pubbaṇhasāyanhapaṭhamamajjhimapacchimayāmasaṅkhāte pañca koṭṭhāse. Tadubhayampīti kāyikaṃ cetasikañca vīriyaṃ. Milakkhatissattherassa mahāsīvattherassa ca vatthu heṭṭhā dassitameva.

One whose energy is initiated, accomplished, and fully developed is called 'āraddhavīriya' (one with initiated energy), one with perfected energy. One whose energy is initiated and established is called 'āraddhavīriya.' Regarding 'one who is devoted to the exertion of energy' (vīriyārambhappasuto), it is said: 'āraddhavīriyassa' means one whose energy is both complete and diligently applied. 'Free from the four faults' (catudosāpagataṃ) means free from the four faults such as being too slack, etc. He elaborates on being free from the four faults with the phrase 'neither too slack,' etc. Indeed, a mind that is too slack in meditation would belong to the side of sloth, while one overly exerted would belong to the side of restlessness. Not properly engaging in the path of meditation, the tendency to contract is 'too slackness' (atilīnatā). Engaging but contracting inwardly is 'internal constriction' (ajjhattaṃ saṃkhittatā). 'Overexertion' (atipaggahitatā) is excessively initiated energy. 'External distraction' (bahiddhā vikkhittatā) is the chasing after scattered thoughts. This energy, which brings about physical application such as walking, is bodily energy, while the other is mental energy. 'Five intervals of day and night' refers to the five periods counted as the forenoon, afternoon, and the first, middle, and last watches of the night. 'Both' refers to both bodily and mental energy. The stories of the Elder Milakkha-Tissa and the Great Elder Sīva have already been shown below.

Pītimallakattherassa [M 1.0086] vatthu pana evaṃ veditabbaṃ. So kira gihikāle mallayuddhāya āhiṇḍanto tīsu rajjesu paṭākaṃ gahetvā tambapaṇṇidīpaṃ āgamma rājānaṃ disvā raññā katānuggaho ekadivasaṃ kilañcakāsanasālādvārena gacchanto “rūpaṃ, bhikkhave, na tumhākaṃ, taṃ pajahatha, taṃ vo pahīnaṃ dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāya bhavissatī”ti (saṃ. ni. 3.33-34; 4.102; ma. ni. 1.247) natumhākavaggaṃ sutvā cintesi – “neva kira rūpaṃ attano, na vedanā”ti. So taṃyeva aṅkusaṃ katvā nikkhamitvā mahāvihāraṃ gantvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā pabbajito upasampanno dvemātikā paguṇaṃ katvā tiṃsa bhikkhū gahetvā avaravāliyaaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā samaṇadhammaṃ akāsi. Pādesu avahantesu jaṇṇukehi caṅkamati. Tamenaṃ [V 1.0077] rattiṃ eko migaluddako “migo”ti maññamāno pahari, satti vinivijjhitvā gatā. So taṃ sattiṃ harāpetvā pahāramukhāni tiṇavaṭṭiyā pūrāpetvā pāsāṇapiṭṭhiyaṃ attānaṃ nisīdāpetvā okāsaṃ kāretvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ patvā ukkāsitasaddena āgatānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ byākaritvā imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Now, the story of the Elder Pītimallaka should be understood thus. It is said that in his lay life, while wandering for wrestling matches, he took a banner in three kingdoms and came to the island of Tambapaṇṇi. Having seen the king and received his support, one day, while passing through the gate of the hall for the infirm, he heard the Natumhāka section: 'Monks, form is not yours, abandon it. That abandonment will be for your long-term welfare and happiness.' (SN 3.33-34; 4.102; MN 1.247) Reflecting, he thought: 'Indeed, neither form nor feeling belongs to oneself.' Making that very thought his goad, he left, went to the Great Monastery, requested ordination, and was ordained and fully ordained. Having mastered the two mātikās, he took thirty monks and went to the lower courtyard of the monastery, where he practiced the duties of a recluse. When his feet wore away, he walked on his knees. One night, a deer hunter, mistaking him for a deer, struck him. The spear pierced and went through. He had that spear removed, filled the wound openings with wads of grass, and seated himself on a stone slab. Creating an opportunity, he developed insight and, together with the analytical knowledges, attained arahantship. Then, responding to the monks who had come at the sound of his clearing his throat, he uttered this inspired utterance:

“Bhāsitaṃ buddhaseṭṭhassa, sabbalokaggavādino;

Na tumhākaṃ idaṃ rūpaṃ, taṃ jaheyyātha bhikkhavo. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.373; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.106);

Spoken by the Buddha, the foremost, the foremost speaker in all the world: 'This form is not yours; monks, you should abandon it.' (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.373; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.106)

“Aniccā vata saṅkhārā, uppādavayadhammino;

Uppajjitvā nirujjhanti, tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho”ti. (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.373; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.106; theragā. 1168);

Impermanent, alas, are formations; their nature is to arise and cease. Having arisen, they pass away; their stilling is bliss. (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.373; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.106; Theragā. 1168)

Kuṭumbiyaputtatissattherassapi vatthu evaṃ veditabbaṃ. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira tisso nāma kuṭumbiyaputto cattālīsa hiraññakoṭiyo pahāya pabbajitvā agāmake araññe viharati, tassa kaniṭṭhabhātubhariyā “gacchatha, naṃ jīvitā voropethā”ti pañcasate core pesesi, te gantvā theraṃ parivāretvā nisīdiṃsu. Thero āha – “kasmā āgatattha upāsakā”ti? Taṃ jīvitā voropessāmāti. Pāṭibhogaṃ me upāsakā gahetvā ajjekarattiṃ jīvitaṃ dethāti. Ko te, samaṇa, imasmiṃ ṭhāne pāṭibhogo bhavissatīti? Thero mahantaṃ pāsāṇaṃ gahetvā ūruṭṭhīni bhinditvā “vaṭṭati upāsakā pāṭibhogo”ti āha. Te apakkamitvā caṅkamanasīse aggiṃ katvā nipajjiṃsu. Therassa vedanaṃ vikkhambhetvā [M 1.0087] sīlaṃ paccavekkhato parisuddhasīlaṃ nissāya pītipāmojjaṃ uppajji. Tato anukkamena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento tiyāmarattiṃ samaṇadhammaṃ katvā aruṇuggamane arahattaṃ patto imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

The story of the Elder Tissa, the householder’s son, should also be understood thus. It is said that in Sāvatthī, there was a householder’s son named Tissa who, after abandoning forty crores of gold, went forth into homelessness and dwelt in a remote wilderness. His younger brother’s wife, thinking, 'Go, deprive him of his life,' sent five hundred robbers. They went, surrounded the Elder, and sat down. The Elder asked: 'Why have you come, lay followers?' 'We have come to deprive him of his life.' 'Then, lay followers, take a pledge from me and grant me life for just this one night.' 'What pledge will you have in this place, monk?' The Elder took a large stone, broke his thigh bones, and said: 'Is this pledge acceptable, lay followers?' They departed, made a fire at the head of his walking path, and lay down. The Elder, suppressing his pain and reflecting on his virtue, experienced joy and gladness based on his purified virtue. Then, gradually developing insight, he practiced the duties of a recluse for the three watches of the night. At the break of dawn, he attained arahantship and uttered this inspired utterance:

“Ubho pādāni bhinditvā, saññapessāmi vo ahaṃ;

Aṭṭiyāmi harāyāmi, sarāgamaraṇaṃ ahaṃ.

'Having broken both feet, I will make you understand; I am disgusted and despise this death with passion.'

“Evāhaṃ cintayitvāna, yathābhūtaṃ vipassisaṃ;

Sampatte aruṇuggamhi, arahattaṃ apāpuṇi”nti. (visuddhi. 1.20; dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.373; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.106);

'Having thought thus, I contemplated according to reality; at the arrival of dawn, I attained arahantship.' (Visuddhi. 1.20; Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.373; Ma. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.106)

Atibhojane [V 1.0078] nimittaggāhoti atibhojane thinamiddhassa nimittaggāho, “ettake bhutte taṃ bhojanaṃ thinamiddhassa kāraṇaṃ hoti, ettake na hotī”ti thinamiddhassa kāraṇākāraṇaggāho hotīti attho. Byatirekavasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā ettake bhutte taṃ bhojanaṃ thinamiddhassa kāraṇaṃ na hotīti bhojane mattaññutāva atthato dassitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha – “catupañca…pe… taṃ na hotī”ti. Divā sūriyālokanti divā gahitanimittaṃ sūriyālokaṃ rattiyaṃ manasikarontassapīti evamettha attho veditabbo. Dhutaṅgānaṃ vīriyanissitattā vuttaṃ – “dhutaṅganissitasappāyakathāyapī”ti.

Grasping at a sign in overeating means grasping at a sign of sloth and torpor due to overeating, thinking, 'Eating this much food causes sloth and torpor, but eating this much does not.' This is stated by way of contrast; therefore, it should be understood that moderation in eating is, in effect, shown here, meaning that eating this much does not cause sloth and torpor. Therefore, it is said: 'Four or five... that does not happen.' 'The sunlight during the day' means that the sign of sunlight grasped during the day should also be contemplated at night; this is how the meaning here should be understood. Because the ascetic practices depend on energy, it is said, 'Even in a discussion of what is suitable for one supported by ascetic practices.'

19. Navame jhānena vā vipassanāya vā vūpasamitacittassāti jhānena vā vipassanāya vā avūpasamakarakilesavigamanena vūpasamitacittassa. Kukkuccampi katākatānusocanavasena pavattamānaṃ cetaso avūpasamāvahatāya uddhaccena samānalakkhaṇanti ubhayassa pahānakāraṇaṃ abhinnaṃ katvā vuttaṃ. Bahussutassa ganthato atthato ca suttādīni vicārentassa tabbahulavihārino atthavedādippaṭilābhasambhavato vikkhepo na hoti. Yathā vidhippaṭipattiyā yathānurūpapattikārappavattiyā ca vikkhepo ca katākatānusocanañca na hotīti “bāhusaccenapi uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyatī”ti āha. Yadaggena bāhusaccena uddhaccakukkuccaṃ pahīyati, tadaggena paripucchakatāvinayappakataññutāhipi taṃ pahīyatīti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vuddhasevitā ca vuddhasīlitaṃ āvahatīti cetaso vūpasamakarattā “uddhaccakukkuccappahānakārī”ti vuttaṃ, vuddhataṃ pana anapekkhitvā kukkuccavinodakā vinayadharā kalyāṇamittāti vuttāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vikkhepo ca pabbajitānaṃ yebhuyyena [M 1.0088] kukkuccahetuko hotīti “kappiyākappiyaparipucchābahulassā”tiādinā vinayanayeneva paripucchakatādayo niddiṭṭhā.

19. In the ninth, the phrase 'of one with a pacified mind' means of one whose mind is pacified by jhāna or by insight, or by the removal of defilements that cause non-pacification. Remorse, too, arising from regretting what was done or left undone, leads to the mind’s lack of pacification, and thus shares the same characteristic as agitation; therefore, the cause for abandoning both is stated as being non-distinct. For one who is learned, reflecting on the meaning and on the texts, such as the suttas, and dwelling much on them, distraction does not arise due to the possibility of attaining understanding of meaning, etc. Because proper practice and suitable conduct prevent distraction and remorse over what was done or left undone, it is said, 'Agitation and remorse are abandoned through much learning.' To the extent that agitation and remorse are abandoned by great learning, it should be understood that they are also abandoned by frequent questioning and expertise in the Vinaya. Associating with the elders brings about the conduct of the elders, and because it pacifies the mind, it is said to be 'a means of abandoning agitation and remorse.' However, it should be understood that Vinaya masters who dispel remorse are called good friends, without regard for seniority. For the most part, distraction among monastics arises from remorse; hence, questioning and other qualities are explained in the Vinaya method, such as 'one who frequently inquires about what is allowable and what is not.'

20. Dasame bahussutānaṃ dhammasabhāvāvabodhasambhavato vicikicchā anavakāsā evāti āha – “bāhusaccenapi…pe… vicikicchā pahīyatī”ti. Kāmaṃ bāhusaccaparipucchakatāhi sabbāpi aṭṭhavatthukā vicikicchā pahīyati, tathāpi ratanattayavicikicchāmūlikā sesavicikicchāti āha – “tīṇi ratanāni ārabbha paripucchābahulassapī”ti. Ratanattayaguṇāvabodhehi “satthari kaṅkhatī”tiādivicikicchāya asambhavoti. Vinaye pakataññutā “sikkhāya kaṅkhatī”ti (dha. sa. 1008; vibha. 915) vuttāya vicikicchāya pahānaṃ karotīti āha – “vinaye ciṇṇavasībhāvassapī”ti. Okappaniyasaddhāsaṅkhātaadhimokkhabahulassāti saddheyyavatthuno anuppavisanasaddhāsaṅkhātaadhimokkhena adhimuccanabahulassa. Adhimuccanañca adhimokkhuppādanamevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Saddhāya vā taṃninnapoṇatā adhimutti adhimokkho[V 1.0079]. Nīvaraṇānaṃ paccayassa ceva paccayaghātassa ca vibhāvitattā vuttaṃ – “vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathita”nti.

20. In the tenth, for the learned, doubt has no opportunity because understanding of the nature of phenomena arises; thus it is said, 'Doubt is abandoned through much learning.' Indeed, all eight grounds for doubt are abandoned through much learning and frequent questioning, yet the remaining doubts are rooted in doubt about the Three Jewels; thus it is said, 'Even for one who frequently questions concerning the Three Jewels.' Through understanding the qualities of the Three Jewels, doubt such as 'one doubts the Teacher' does not arise. Expertise in the Vinaya causes the abandonment of the doubt spoken of as 'one doubts about the training'; thus it is said: 'Even for one who has practiced mastery in the Vinaya.' 'One who is abundant in determination known as trusting faith' means one who is abundant in resolving by means of determination, which is known as faith that penetrates a trustworthy object. And resolving should be seen as simply the arising of determination. Or, the inclination and tendency towards that object by means of faith is resolve and determination. Because the condition for the hindrances and the destruction of that condition have been explained, it is said, 'The round and the escape from the round have been taught.'

Nīvaraṇappahānavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Abandonment of the Hindrances is concluded.

3. Akammaniyavaggavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Akammaniya Chapter

21. Tatiyassa [V 1.0080] paṭhame abhāvitanti samathavipassanābhāvanāvasena na bhāvitaṃ tathā abhāvitattā. Tañhi “avaḍḍhita”nti vuccati paṭipakkhābhibhavena paribrūhanābhāvato. Tenāha bhagavā – “akammaniyaṃ hotī”ti.

21. In the first discourse of the third chapter, 'undeveloped' means not developed by way of the cultivation of serenity and insight, and thus being undeveloped in that way. For it is called 'undeveloped' due to the absence of augmentation, being overcome by opposing factors. Therefore, the Blessed One said: 'It becomes unfit for work.'

22. Dutiye vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Paṭhameti tatiyavaggassa paṭhamasutte. Vaṭṭavasenāti vipākavaṭṭavasena. Tebhūmakavaṭṭanti tebhūmakavipākavaṭṭaṃ. Vaṭṭapaṭilābhāya kammanti vipākavaṭṭassa paṭilābhāya upanissayabhūtaṃ kammaṃ, tassa sahāyabhūtaṃ kilesavaṭṭampi kammaggahaṇeneva saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Vivaṭṭapaṭilābhāya kammanti vivaṭṭādhigamassa upanissayabhūtaṃ kammaṃ. Yaṃ pana carimabhavanibbattakaṃ kammaṃ, taṃ vivaṭṭappaṭilābhāya kammaṃ hoti, na hotīti? Na hoti vaṭṭapādakabhāvato. Carimabhavapaṭisandhi [M 1.0089] viya pana vivaṭṭūpanissayoti sakkā viññātuṃ. Na hi kadāci tihetukapaṭisandhiyā vinā visesādhigamo sambhavati. Imesu suttesūti imesu pana paṭhamadutiyasuttesu yathākkamaṃ vaṭṭavivaṭṭameva kathitaṃ.

22. In the second discourse, the meaning should be understood in the reverse of what was stated. 'In the first' means in the first sutta of the third chapter. 'By way of the round' means by way of the round of result. 'The round of the three planes' means the round of result in the three planes. 'Action for the attainment of the round' means action that is a supporting condition for attaining the round of result; and it should be understood that the round of defilements that accompanies it is also included by the term 'action.' 'Action for the attainment of the escape from the round' means action that is a supporting condition for achieving the attainment of the escape from the round. But is the kamma that produces the final existence action for the attainment of the escape from the round or not? It is not, because it serves as a foundation for the round. However, like the rebirth-linking of the final existence, it can be understood as a supporting condition for the escape from the round, for a higher attainment is never possible without a three-rooted rebirth-linking. 'In these suttas' means that in this first and second sutta, the round and the escape from the round are explained in due order.

23. Tatiye abhāvitanti ettha bhāvanā nāma samādhibhāvanā. Sā yattha āsaṅkitabbā, taṃ kāmāvacarapaṭhamamahākusalacittādiabhāvitanti adhippetanti āha – “devamanussasampattiyo”tiādi.

23. In the third discourse, regarding 'undeveloped': here, 'development' means the development of concentration. Where that development is to be expected, that it is 'undeveloped' is intended to refer to the first great wholesome sense-sphere consciousness and so on; thus it is said: 'Heavenly and human attainments,' and so on.

24. Catutthe yasmā cittanti vivaṭṭavaseneva uppannacittaṃ adhippetaṃ, tasmā jātijarābyādhimaraṇasokādidukkhassa anibbattanato mahato atthāya saṃvattatīti yojanā veditabbā.

24. In the fourth discourse, 'because the mind' is intended to mean the mind that has arisen only by way of the escape from the round. Therefore, the connection should be understood thus: it conduces to great benefit through the non-production of the suffering of birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, and so on.

25-26. Pañcamachaṭṭhesu uppannanti avigatuppādādikhaṇattayampi abhāvitaṃ bhāvanārahitaṃ apātubhūtameva paṇḍitasammatassa uppannakiccassa asādhanato yathā “aputto”ti. So hi samattho hutvā pitu puttakiccaṃ asādhento aputtoti loke vuccati, evaṃ sampadamidaṃ. Tenāha – “kasmā”tiādi. Tesu dhammesūti lokuttarapādakajjhānādīsu. Thero pana matthakappattameva bhāvitaṃ cittaṃ dassento “maggacittamevā”ti āha.

25-26. In the fifth and sixth discourses, 'arisen' means that even though it possesses the three moments beginning with arising, which have not passed away, it is undeveloped, devoid of cultivation, and unmanifest, because it does not accomplish the duty of an arisen thing as approved by the wise, just as one is called 'sonless.' For a man, though capable, is called 'sonless' in the world for not accomplishing a son's duty for his father; such is this case. Hence it is said: 'Why?' and so on. 'In these states' means in the jhānas that are the basis for the supramundane, and so on. But the Elder, showing that the developed mind is only that which has reached the peak, said: 'It is only the path-consciousness.'

27-28. Sattamaṭṭhamesu [V 1.0081] punappunaṃ akatanti bhāvanābahulīkāravasena punappunaṃ na kataṃ. Imānipi dveti imesu dvīsu suttesu āgatāni imānipi dve cittāni.

27-28. In the seventh and eighth discourses, 'not done again and again' means not done repeatedly by way of making it abundant through cultivation. 'These two also' refers to these two minds mentioned in these two discourses.

29-30. Navame adhivahatīti āneti. Dukkhenāti kicchena. Duppesanatoti dukkhena pesetabbato. Matthakappattaṃ vipassanāsukhaṃ pākatikajjhānasukhato santatarapaṇītataramevāti āha – “jhānasukhato vipassanāsukha”nti. Tenāha bhagavā –

29-30. In the ninth discourse, 'adhivahati' means 'brings forth.' 'Dukkhena' means 'with difficulty.' 'Duppesanato' means 'because it is to be sent forth with difficulty.' The happiness of insight that has reached its peak is indeed more peaceful and sublime than the ordinary happiness of jhāna. Thus it is said: 'The happiness of insight is greater than the happiness of jhāna.' Therefore, the Blessed One said:

“Suññāgāraṃ paviṭṭhassa, santacittassa bhikkhuno;

Amānusī rati hoti, sammā dhammaṃ vipassato.

"For a monk who has entered an empty dwelling, whose mind is peaceful, there is a joy beyond the human for one rightly contemplating the Dhamma."

“Yato [M 1.0090] yato sammasati, khandhānaṃ udayabbayaṃ;

Labhatī pītipāmojjaṃ, amataṃ taṃ vijānata”nti. (dha. pa. 374);

"Whenever one discerns the rise and fall of the aggregates, one obtains joy and gladness. That is the Deathless for those who know."

Tañhi cittaṃ vissaṭṭhaindavajirasadisaṃ amoghabhāvato.

For that mind is like a released thunderbolt, because of its unfailing nature.

Akammaniyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Akammaniya Chapter is concluded.

4. Adantavaggavaṇṇanā

4. Commentary on the Adanta Chapter

31-36. Catutthassa [V 1.0082] paṭhame adantanti cittabhāvanāya vinā na dantaṃ. Tenāha – “satisaṃvararahita”nti. Catutthe tatiye vuttavipariyāyena attho veditabbo. Pañcamachaṭṭhesu purimasadisoyevāti tatiyacatutthasadiso eva.

31–36. In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, 'untamed' means not tamed without the cultivation of the mind. Hence it is said: 'lacking mindfulness and restraint.' In the third sutta of the fourth chapter, the meaning should be understood in the reverse way of what was stated. In the fifth and sixth suttas, it is just like the preceding ones, that is, just like the third and fourth.

37-38. Sattamaṭṭhamesu upamā panetthāti yathā paṭhamādīsu adantahatthiassādayo upamābhāvena gahitā, evamettha satthamaṭṭhamesu “asaṃvutagharadvārādivasena veditabbā”ti vuttaṃ.

37–38. In the seventh and eighth suttas, the simile here is this: just as in the first and other suttas, similes such as the untamed elephant and horse were taken, so here in the seventh and eighth suttas it is said, 'They should be understood by way of an unguarded house door, etc.'

39-40. Navamadasamesu catūhipi padehīti adantādīhi catūhi padehi yojetvā navamadasamāni suttāni vuttānīti yojanā.

39–40. In the ninth and tenth suttas, 'by the four terms' means that the ninth and tenth suttas are stated by connecting them with the four terms beginning with 'untamed'; this is the connection.

Adantavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Adanta Chapter is concluded.

5. Paṇihitaacchavaggavaṇṇanā

5. Commentary on the Paṇihitaaccha Chapter

41. Pañcamassa [V 1.0083] paṭhame upamāva opammaṃ, so eva attho, tasmiṃ opammatthe bodhetabbe nipāto. Seyyathāpīti yathāti attho. Ettha ca tatra bhagavā katthaci atthena upamaṃ parivāretvā dasseti vatthasutte viya, pāricchattakopama (a. ni. 7.69) aggikkhandhopamādi (a. ni. 7.72) suttesu viya ca. Katthaci upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā dasseti loṇambilasutte (a. ni. 3.101) viya, suvaṇṇakārasattasūriyopamādisuttesu [M 1.0091] (a. ni. 7.66) viya ca. Imasmiṃ pana sālisūkopame upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā dassento “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave”tiādimāhāti potthakesu likhanti, taṃ majjhimaṭṭhakathāya vatthasuttavaṇṇanāya (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.70) na sameti. Tattha hi idaṃ vuttaṃ –

41. In the first sutta of the fifth chapter, `upamā` is the same as `opamma`; that is the very meaning. The particle is for making known that meaning of comparison. 'Seyyathāpi' means 'just as.' And here, in some instances the Blessed One presents the simile by surrounding it with the meaning, as in the Vatthasutta, and as in the suttas on the Pāricchattaka simile, the simile of the mass of fire, and so on. In some instances, He presents the meaning by surrounding it with the simile, as in the Loṇambila Sutta, and as in the suttas on the simile of the goldsmith and the seven suns, and so on. But in this Sālisūkopama (simile of the rice stalk), while presenting the meaning by surrounding it with the simile, He says, 'Just as, monks,' and so on—so it is written in the books; but that does not agree with the commentary on the Vatthasutta in the Majjhima Aṭṭhakathā. For there, this is stated—

Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, vatthanti upamāvacanamevetaṃ. Upamaṃ karonto ca bhagavā katthaci paṭhamaṃyeva upamaṃ dassetvā pacchā atthaṃ dasseti, katthaci paṭhamaṃ atthaṃ dassetvā pacchā upamaṃ, katthaci upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā dasseti, katthaci atthena upamaṃ. Tathā hesa “seyyathāpissu, bhikkhave, dve agārā sadvārā, tattha cakkhumā puriso majjhe ṭhito passeyyā”ti sakalampi devadūtasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 3.261 ādayo) upamaṃ paṭhamaṃ dassetvā pacchā atthaṃ dassento āha. “Tirokuṭṭaṃ tiropākāraṃ tiropabbataṃ asajjamāno gacchati, seyyathāpi, ākāse”tiādinā pana nayena sakalampi iddhividhaṃ atthaṃ paṭhamaṃ dassetvā pacchā upamaṃ dassento āha. “Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇapuriso sāratthiko sāragavesī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.314) nayena sakalampi cūḷasāropamasuttaṃ upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā dassento āha. “Idha pana, bhikkhave, ekacce kulaputtā dhammaṃ pariyāpuṇanti suttaṃ…pe… seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso alagaddatthiko”tiādinā nayena sakalampi alagaddasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 1.238) mahāsāropamasuttanti evamādīni suttāni atthena upamaṃ parivāretvā dassento āha. Svāyaṃ idha paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ dassetvā pacchā atthaṃ dassetīti.

The phrase 'Just as, monks, a cloth' is merely an expression of comparison. When making a comparison, the Blessed One sometimes presents the simile first and then shows the meaning; sometimes presents the meaning first and then the simile; sometimes shows the meaning by surrounding it with the simile; and sometimes shows the simile by surrounding it with the meaning. Thus, for example, in the entire Devadūta Sutta (MN 130), he first presents the simile, saying: “Just as, monks, there might be two houses with doors, and a man with good eyes standing in the middle might see…” and then shows the meaning. But in the entire section on psychic powers, he first shows the meaning by the method: “He goes unimpeded through walls, through ramparts, through mountains, as if in space,” and then shows the simile. In the entire Cūḷasāropama Sutta (MN 29), he shows the meaning by surrounding it with the simile, by the method: “Just as, brahmin, a man needing heartwood, seeking heartwood…” In the entire Alagaddūpama Sutta (MN 22), the Mahāsāropama Sutta, and other suttas of this kind, he shows the simile by surrounding it with the meaning, by the method: “Here, monks, some sons of good families learn the Dhamma—discourses… Just as, monks, a man needing a water-snake…” So here, he first shows the simile and then shows the meaning.

Ettha hi cūḷasāropamādīsu (ma. ni. 1.312) paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ vatvā tadanantaraṃ upameyyatthaṃ vatvā puna upamaṃ vadanto upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā dassetīti vutto. Alagaddūpamasuttādīsu [V 1.0084] pana atthaṃ paṭhamaṃ vatvā tadanantaraṃ upamaṃ vatvā puna atthaṃ vadanto atthena upamaṃ parivāretvā dassetīti vutto. Tenevettha līnatthappakāsiniyaṃ vuttaṃ – “upameyyatthaṃ paṭhamaṃ vatvā tadanantaraṃ atthaṃ vatvā puna upamaṃ vadanto upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā [M 1.0092] dassetī”ti vutto. Atthena upamaṃ parivāretvāti etthāpi eseva nayoti. Idha pana katthaci atthena upamaṃ parivāretvā dasseti. “Vatthasutte viya pāricchattakopamaaggikkhandhopamādisuttesu viya cā”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha vatthasutte tāva “seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, vatthaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ malaggahitaṃ, tamenaṃ rajako yasmiṃ yasmiṃ raṅgajāte upasaṃhareyya. Yadi nīlakāya, yadi pītakāya, yadi lohitakāya, yadi mañjiṭṭhakāya, durattavaṇṇamevassa aparisuddhavaṇṇamevassa. Taṃ kissa hetu? Aparisuddhattā, bhikkhave, vatthassa. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, citte saṃkiliṭṭhe duggati pāṭikaṅkhā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.70) paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ dassetvā pacchā upameyyattho vutto, na pana paṭhamaṃ atthaṃ vatvā tadanantaraṃ upamaṃ dassetvā puna attho vutto. Yena katthaci atthena upamaṃ parivāretvā dasseti. Vatthasutte viyāti vadeyya.

Here, in the Cūḷasāropama Sutta and others (MN 1.312), by first stating the simile, then immediately after stating the meaning to be illustrated, and then again stating the simile, it is said that he shows the meaning by surrounding it with the simile. However, in the Alagaddūpama Sutta and others, by first stating the meaning, then immediately after stating the simile, and then again stating the meaning, it is said that he shows the simile by surrounding it with the meaning. Therefore, it is said in the Līnatthappakāsinī: “First stating the meaning to be illustrated, then immediately after stating the meaning, and again stating the simile, thus it is said that one shows the meaning by surrounding it with the simile.” For the case of showing the simile by surrounding it with the meaning, the method is the same. Here, however, it is stated that in some places he shows the simile by surrounding it with the meaning, “as in the Vatthasutta, and like the Pāricchattaka and Aggikkhandha similes and other suttas.” There, in the Vatthasutta, for example: “Just as, monks, a cloth is stained and soiled, and a dyer applies any dye to it—whether blue, yellow, red, or crimson—its color will be inferior and impure. Why is that? Because the cloth is not clean. In the same way, monks, when the mind is defiled, an unhappy destination is to be expected,” and so on (MN 1.70). Here, first the simile is shown, and afterward the meaning to be illustrated is stated; the meaning is not stated first, followed by the simile, and then the meaning again, which would justify the claim that 'in some places he shows the simile by surrounding it with the meaning, as in the Vatthasutta.'

Tathā pāricchattakopamepi “yasmiṃ, bhikkhave, samaye devānaṃ tāvatiṃsānaṃ pāricchattako koviḷāro paṇḍupalāso hoti, attamanā, bhikkhave, devā tāvatiṃsā, tasmiṃ samaye honti paṇḍupalāso dāni pāricchattako koviḷāro, na cirasseva dāni pannapalāso bhavissati…pe… evameva kho, bhikkhave, yasmiṃ samaye ariyasāvako agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajjāya ceteti. Paṇḍupalāso, bhikkhave, ariyasāvako tasmiṃ samaye hotī”tiādinā (a. ni. 7.69) paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ dassetvā pacchā attho vutto. Aggikkhandhopame “passatha no tumhe, bhikkhave, amuṃ mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ ādittaṃ sampajjalitaṃ sajotibhūtanti. Evaṃ, bhanteti. Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṃ nu kho varaṃ yaṃ amuṃ mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ ādittaṃ sampajjalitaṃ sajotibhūtaṃ āliṅgetvā upanisīdeyya vā upanipajjeyya vā, yaṃ khattiyakaññaṃ vā brāhmaṇakaññaṃ vā gahapatikaññaṃ vā mudutalunahatthapādaṃ āliṅgetvā upanisīdeyya vā upanipajjeyya vā”tiādinā (a. ni. 7.72) paṭhamaṃ upamaṃyeva dassetvā pacchā attho vutto, na pana paṭhamaṃ atthaṃ vatvā tadanantaraṃ upamaṃ dassetvā puna attho vutto, tasmā “katthaci atthena upamaṃ parivāretvā dasseti vatthasutte viya pāricchattakopamaaggikkhandhopamādisuttesu viya cā”ti na vattabbaṃ.

Similarly, in the Pāricchattaka simile: “Monks, at the time when the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree of the Tāvatiṃsa gods has yellow leaves, the Tāvatiṃsa gods are delighted, thinking, ‘Now the Pāricchattaka koviḷāra tree has yellow leaves; soon it will shed its leaves.’… In the same way, monks, at the time when a noble disciple resolves to go forth from the household life into homelessness, he is like a tree with yellow leaves,” and so on (AN 7.69). Here, first the simile is shown, and afterward the meaning is stated. In the Aggikkhandha simile: “Monks, do you see that great mass of fire, blazing, burning, and radiant?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “What do you think, monks? Which would be better—to embrace and sit or lie down beside that great mass of fire, blazing, burning, and radiant, or to embrace and sit or lie down beside a maiden of a noble, brahmin, or householder family, with soft and tender hands and feet?” and so on (AN 7.72). Here, first the simile is shown, and afterward the meaning is stated; the meaning is not stated first, followed by the simile, and then the meaning again. Therefore, it should not be said that “in some places he shows the simile by surrounding it with the meaning, as in the Vatthasutta, and like the Pāricchattaka and Aggikkhandha similes and other suttas.”

Keci [M 1.0093] panettha evaṃ vaṇṇayanti “atthaṃ paṭhamaṃ vatvā pacchā ca upamaṃ dassento atthena upamaṃ parivāretvā dasseti nāma, upamaṃ pana paṭhamaṃ vatvā pacchā atthaṃ dassento upamāya atthaṃ [V 1.0085] parivāretvā dasseti nāma, tadubhayassapi āgataṭṭhānaṃ nidassento ‘vatthasutte viyā’tiādimāhā”ti. Tampi “katthaci atthena upamaṃ parivāretvā dasseti vatthasutte viya pāricchattakopamaaggikkhandhopamādisuttesu viya cā”ti vattabbaṃ, evañca vuccamāne “katthaci upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā dasseti loṇambilasutte viyā”ti visuṃ na vattabbaṃ “aggikkhandhopamādisutte viyā”ti ettha ādisaddeneva saṅgahitattā. Loṇambilasuttepi hi –

Some, however, explain it thus: 'First stating the meaning and then showing the simile is called “showing the simile by surrounding it with the meaning.” On the other hand, first stating the simile and then showing the meaning is called “showing the meaning by surrounding it with the simile.” To provide examples for both, the text cites “as in the Vatthasutta, etc.”' That explanation, too, is flawed. For if it were correct, then the statement 'in some places he shows the simile by surrounding it with the meaning, as in the Vatthasutta, and like the Pāricchattaka and Aggikkhandha similes and other suttas' would have to be accepted. And if this were said, then 'in some places he shows the meaning by surrounding it with the simile, as in the Loṇambila Sutta' should not be stated separately, because it would already be included by the word 'etc.' in 'as in the Aggikkhandha simile and other suttas.' For in the Loṇambila Sutta too—

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo sūdo rājānaṃ vā rājamahāmattaṃ vā nānaccayehi sūpehi paccupaṭṭhito assa ambilaggehipi tittakaggehipi kaṭukaggehipi madhuraggehipi khārikehipi akhārikehipi loṇikehipi aloṇikehipi.

“Just as, monks, a wise, competent, and skilled cook might serve a king or a royal minister with various kinds of soups: predominantly sour, predominantly bitter, predominantly pungent, predominantly sweet, alkaline, non-alkaline, salty, and unsalty.

“Sa kho so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo sūdo sakassa bhattassa nimittaṃ uggaṇhāti ‘idaṃ vā me ajja bhattasūpeyyaṃ ruccati, imassa vā abhiharati, imassa vā bahuṃ gaṇhāti, imassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati. Ambilaggaṃ vā me ajja bhattasūpeyyaṃ ruccati, ambilaggassa vā abhiharati, ambilaggassa vā bahuṃ gaṇhāti, ambilaggassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsati…pe… aloṇikassa vā vaṇṇaṃ bhāsatī’ti. Sa kho so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo sūdo lābhī ceva hoti acchādanassa, lābhī vetanassa, lābhī abhihārānaṃ. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo sūdo sakassa bhattanimittaṃ uggaṇhāti. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, idhekacco paṇḍito byatto kusalo bhikkhu kāye kāyānupassī viharati…pe… vedanāsu…pe… citte…pe… dhammesu dhammānupassī viharati ātāpī sampajāno satimā vineyya loke abhijjhādomanassaṃ. Tassa dhammesu dhammānupassino viharato cittaṃ samādhiyati, upakkilesā pahīyanti, so taṃ nimittaṃ uggaṇhāti.

That wise, discerning, and skillful cook, monks, observes the signs of his master’s meal: ‘Today this curry pleased my master, or he reached for that, or he took much of this, or he spoke highly of that. Today the sour curry pleased my master, or he reached for the sour one, or he took much of the sour one, or he spoke highly of the sour one… or he spoke highly of the unsalted one.’ That wise, discerning, and skillful cook, monks, gains robes, wages, and bonuses. Why is that? Because, monks, that wise, discerning, and skillful cook observes the signs of his master’s meal. In the same way, monks, here a wise, discerning, and skillful monk dwells contemplating the body in the body… feelings in feelings… mind in mind… phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, mindful, having subdued covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. As he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, his mind becomes concentrated, his defilements are abandoned, and he grasps that sign.

“Sa [M 1.0094] kho, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo bhikkhu lābhī ceva hoti diṭṭheva dhamme sukhavihārānaṃ, lābhī hoti satisampajaññassa. Taṃ kissa hetu? Tathā hi so, bhikkhave, paṇḍito byatto kusalo bhikkhu sakassa cittassa nimittaṃ uggaṇhātī”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.374) –

That wise, discerning, and skillful monk, monks, gains pleasant abidings in this very life, and he gains mindfulness and clear comprehension. Why is that? Because, monks, that wise, discerning, and skillful monk observes the signs of his own mind.

Evaṃ paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ dassetvā pacchā attho vutto. “Suvaṇṇakārasūriyopamādisuttesu viya cā”ti [V 1.0086] idañca udāharaṇamattena saṅgahaṃ gacchati suvaṇṇakārasuttādīsu paṭhamaṃ upamāya adassitattā. Etesu hi suvaṇṇakāropamasutte (a. ni. 3.103) tāva –

Thus, the simile is first shown, and afterward the meaning is explained. "As in the Suttas on the Simile of the Goldsmith and the Sun, and so forth," and this is included merely as an example, since the simile is not shown first in the Suvaṇṇakārasuttas and others. Indeed, in the Suvaṇṇakāropamasutta (AN 3.103), for example—

“Adhicittamanuyuttena, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā tīṇi nimittāni kālena kālaṃ manasi kātabbāni, kālena kālaṃ samādhinimittaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ, kālena kālaṃ paggahanimittaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ, kālena kālaṃ upekkhānimittaṃ manasi kātabbaṃ. Sace, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu ekantaṃ samādhinimittaṃyeva manasi kareyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ cittaṃ kosajjāya saṃvatteyya. Sace, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu ekantaṃ paggahanimittaṃyeva manasi kareyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ cittaṃ uddhaccāya saṃvatteyya. Sace, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu ekantaṃ upekkhānimittaṃyeva manasi kareyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ cittaṃ na sammā samādhiyeyya āsavānaṃ khayāya. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyutto bhikkhu kālena kālaṃ samādhinimittaṃ…pe… paggahanimittaṃ…pe… upekkhānimittaṃ manasi karoti, taṃ hoti cittaṃ muduñca kammaniyañca pabhassarañca, na ca pabhaṅgu, sammā samādhiyati āsavānaṃ khayāya.

Monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind should attend to three signs from time to time: he should attend to the sign of concentration from time to time, he should attend to the sign of exertion from time to time, and he should attend to the sign of equanimity from time to time. If, monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind attends solely to the sign of concentration, it is possible that his mind will tend towards laziness. If, monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind attends solely to the sign of exertion, it is possible that his mind will tend towards restlessness. If, monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind attends solely to the sign of equanimity, it is possible that his mind will not be rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. But when, monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind attends to the sign of concentration from time to time… the sign of exertion… the sign of equanimity from time to time, his mind becomes pliable, workable, luminous, and not brittle, and it becomes rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints.

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā ukkaṃ bandheyya, ukkaṃ bandhitvā ukkāmukhaṃ ālimpeyya, ukkāmukhaṃ ālimpitvā saṇḍāsena jātarūpaṃ gahetvā ukkāmukhe pakkhipeyya, ukkāmukhe pakkhipitvā kālena kālaṃ abhidhamati, kālena kālaṃ udakena paripphoseti, kālena kālaṃ ajjhupekkhati. Sace, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ ekantaṃ abhidhameyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ jātarūpaṃ [M 1.0095] daheyya. Sace, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ ekantaṃ udakena paripphoseyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ jātarūpaṃ nibbāpeyya. Sace, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ ekantaṃ ajjhupekkheyya, ṭhānaṃ taṃ jātarūpaṃ na sammā paripākaṃ gaccheyya. Yato ca kho, bhikkhave, suvaṇṇakāro vā suvaṇṇakārantevāsī vā taṃ jātarūpaṃ kālena kālaṃ abhidhamati, kālena kālaṃ udakena paripphoseti, kālena kālaṃ ajjhupekkhati, taṃ hoti jātarūpaṃ muduñca kammaniyañca pabhassarañca, na ca pabhaṅgu, sammā upeti kammāya. Yassā yassā ca piḷandhanavikatiyā ākaṅkhati, yadi paṭṭikāya yadi kuṇḍalāya yadi gīveyyakena yadi suvaṇṇamālāya, tañcassa atthaṃ anubhoti.

Just as, monks, a goldsmith or a goldsmith’s apprentice would set up a furnace, having set up the furnace he would plaster its mouth, having plastered its mouth he would take gold with tongs and place it in the furnace’s mouth. Having placed it in the furnace’s mouth, from time to time he blows on it, from time to time he sprinkles water on it, and from time to time he just observes it. If, monks, the goldsmith or his apprentice were to blow on that gold exclusively, it is possible that the gold would burn. If, monks, the goldsmith or his apprentice were to sprinkle water on that gold exclusively, it is possible that the gold would be extinguished. If, monks, the goldsmith or his apprentice were to just observe that gold exclusively, it is possible that the gold would not reach proper refinement. But when, monks, the goldsmith or his apprentice blows on that gold from time to time, sprinkles water on that gold from time to time, and just observes that gold from time to time, that gold becomes soft, workable, luminous, and not brittle, and it is properly ready for work. For whatever kind of ornament he wishes, whether a frontlet, an earring, a necklace, or a golden garland, it serves his purpose.

“Evameva [V 1.0087] kho, bhikkhave, adhicittamanuyuttena bhikkhu…pe… sammā samādhiyati āsavānaṃ khayāya. Yassa yassa ca abhiññāsacchikaraṇīyassa dhammassa cittaṃ abhininnāmeti abhiññāsacchikiriyāya, tatra tatreva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇāti sati satiāyatane”ti (a. ni. 3.103) –

In the same way, monks, a monk devoted to the higher mind... is rightly concentrated for the destruction of the taints. And for whatever state realizable by direct knowledge he directs his mind for the purpose of realizing it by direct knowledge, he attains the capability of witnessing it in every case, whenever the basis is present.

Evaṃ paṭhamaṃ atthaṃ dassetvā tadatantaraṃ upamaṃ vatvā punapi attho evaṃ paṭhamaṃ atthaṃ dassetvā tadanantaraṃ upamaṃ vatvā punapi attho vutto.

Thus, having first shown the meaning, then having stated a simile, and again the meaning; in this way, having first shown the meaning, then having stated a simile, the meaning is stated again.

Sattasūriyopame ca –

And in the Simile of the Seven Suns:

“Aniccā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā, adhuvā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā, anassāsikā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā, yāvañcidaṃ, bhikkhave, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṃ alaṃ virajjituṃ alaṃ vimuccituṃ. Sineru, bhikkhave, pabbatarājā caturāsītiyojanasahassāni āyāmena, caturāsītiyojanasahassāni vitthārena, caturāsītiyojanasahassāni mahāsamudde ajjhogāḷho, caturāsītiyojanasahassāni mahāsamuddā accuggato. Hoti so kho, bhikkhave, samayo, yaṃ kadāci karahaci dīghassa addhuno accayena bahūni vassāni bahūni vassasatāni bahūni vassasahassāni bahūni vassasatasahassāni devo na vassati, deve [M 1.0096] kho pana, bhikkhave, avassante ye kecime bījagāmabhūtagāmā osadhitiṇavanappatayo, te ussussanti visussanti na bhavanti. Evaṃ aniccā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā, evaṃ adhuvā, bhikkhave, saṅkhārā”tiādinā (a. ni. 7.66) –

Impermanent, monks, are conditioned phenomena; unstable, monks, are conditioned phenomena; offering no security, monks, are conditioned phenomena. This is enough, monks, to become disenchanted with all conditioned phenomena, enough to become dispassionate, enough to be liberated. Monks, Sineru, the king of mountains, is eighty-four thousand yojanas in length, eighty-four thousand yojanas in width, eighty-four thousand yojanas sunk down into the great ocean, and eighty-four thousand yojanas rising above the great ocean. There comes a time, monks, when after the passing of a long period, for many years, many hundreds of years, many thousands of years, many hundreds of thousands of years, the deity does not rain. And when the deity does not rain, monks, whatever seed-life and plant-life, herbs, grasses, and great trees there are, they dry up, wither, and cease to be. So impermanent, monks, are conditioned phenomena; so unstable, monks, are conditioned phenomena,’ and so on.

Paṭhamaṃ atthaṃ dassetvā tadanantaraṃ upamaṃ vatvā punapi attho vutto. Atha vā “sūriyassa, bhikkhave, udayato etaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ etaṃ pubbanimittaṃ, yadidaṃ aruṇuggaṃ. Evameva kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhuno ariyassa aṭṭhaṅgikassa maggassa uppādāya etaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ etaṃ pubbanimittaṃ, yadidaṃ kalyāṇamittatā”ti yadetaṃ saṃyuttanikāye (saṃ. ni. 5.49) āgataṃ, taṃ idha sūriyopamasuttanti adhippetaṃ siyā. Tampi “katthaci upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā dassetī”ti iminā na sameti paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ vatvā tadanantaraṃ atthaṃ dassetvā puna upamāya avuttattā. Paṭhamameva hi tattha upamā dassitā, “imasmiṃ pana sālisūkopame upamāya atthaṃ parivāretvā dassento seyyathāpi, bhikkhaveti ādimāhā”ti. Idampi vacanamasaṅgahitaṃ vatthasuttassa imassa ca visesābhāvato. Ubhayatthāpi hi paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ dassetvā pacchā attho vutto[V 1.0088], tasmā evamettha pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ “tatra bhagavā katthaci paṭhamaṃyeva upamaṃ dassetvā pacchā atthaṃ dasseti vatthasutte viya pāricchattakopama- (a. ni. 7.69) aggikkhandhopamādisuttesu (a. ni. 7.72) viya ca, katthaci atthena upamaṃ parivāretvā dasseti suvaṇṇakārasattasūriyopamādisuttesu (a. ni. 7.66) viya, imasmiṃ pana sālisūkopame paṭhamaṃ upamaṃ dassetvā pacchā atthaṃ dassento seyyathāpi, bhikkhaveti ādimāhā”ti. Aññathā majjhimaṭṭhakathāya virujjhati. Idhāpi ca pubbenāparaṃ na sameti. Majjhimaṭṭhakathāya vuttanayeneva vā idhāpi pāṭho gahetabbo.

First, the meaning is shown, then the simile is given, and afterward, the meaning is stated again. Alternatively, as it is said in the Saṃyutta Nikāya (SN 5.49): “Monks, just as the rising of the dawn is the forerunner, the precursor of the sun’s rising, so too, monks, is noble friendship the forerunner, the precursor for the arising of the Noble Eightfold Path.” This might be intended as the Sūriyopamasutta here. However, this does not align with the statement, “Sometimes, he presents the meaning encompassed by a simile,” because the simile is given first, followed by the meaning, and the simile is not stated again. For in that case, the simile is presented first, whereas here, in the Sālisūkopama, it is said that he presents the meaning encompassed by the simile, beginning with, “Just as, monks…” This statement is also inconsistent, as there is no difference between the Vatthasutta and this one. In both cases, the simile is presented first, and afterward, the meaning is stated. Therefore, the reading here should be as follows: “In some places, the Blessed One first presents the simile and afterward explains the meaning, as in the Vatthasutta, the Pāricchattakopama (AN 7.69), and the Aggikkhandhopama (AN 7.72) suttas. In other places, he presents the simile encompassed by the meaning, as in the Suvaṇṇakāra and Sattasūriya (AN 7.66) suttas. But here, in the Sālisūkopama, having first presented the simile, he explains the meaning, beginning with, ‘Just as, monks…’” Otherwise, it contradicts the Majjhimaṭṭhakathā. Here too, the latter does not agree with the former. Alternatively, the reading here should be taken in accordance with the method stated in the Majjhimaṭṭhakathā.

Kaṇasadiso sāliphalassa tuṇḍe uppajjanakavālo sālisūkaṃ, tathā yavasūkaṃ. Sūkassa tanukabhāvato bhedavato bhedo nātimahā hotīti āha – “bhindissati, chaviṃ chindissatīti attho”ti. Yathā micchāṭhapitasālisūkādi akkantampi hatthādiṃ na bhindati bhindituṃ ayoggabhāvena ṭhitattā, evaṃ ācayagāmicittaṃ avijjaṃ na bhindati bhindituṃ [M 1.0097] ayoggabhāvena uppannattāti imamatthaṃ dasseti “micchāṭhapitenā”tiādinā. Aṭṭhasu ṭhānesūti “dukkhe aññāṇa”ntiādinā vuttesu dukkhādīsu catūsu saccesu pubbantādīsu catūsu cāti aṭṭhasu ṭhānesu. Ghanabahalanti cirakālaparibhāvanāya ativiya bahalaṃ. Mahāvisayatāya mahāpaṭipakkhatāya bahuparivāratāya bahudukkhatāya ca mahatī avijjāti mahāavijjā. Taṃ mahāavijjaṃ. Mahāsaddo hi bahubhāvatthopi hoti “mahājano”tiādīsu viya. Taṇhāvānato nikkhantabhāvenāti tattha taṇhāya abhāvameva vadati.

The awn of rice is the bristle that arises on the tip of the rice grain, similar to a particle of husk; likewise for the awn of barley. Because the awn is fine and has a piercing nature, the piercing is not very great—hence it is said, 'It will pierce, meaning, it will cut the skin.' Just as a wrongly placed rice awn or the like does not pierce the hand or other parts even when pressed upon, because it is positioned in a way unsuitable for piercing, so too, the mind that leads to accumulation does not pierce ignorance, because it has arisen in a way unsuitable for piercing—this meaning is shown by the phrase 'wrongly placed,' and so on. 'In the eight instances' refers to the eight instances stated as 'ignorance of suffering,' and so on, namely, in the four truths of suffering, etc., and in the four points concerning the past, etc. 'Dense and thick' means extremely thick through long cultivation. Because of its vast scope, its great opposition, its extensive retinue, and its immense suffering, ignorance is called 'great ignorance.' That is the great ignorance. Indeed, the term 'great' can also denote abundance, as in phrases like 'a great multitude of people.' 'By having emerged from the thicket of craving' simply states the absence of craving there.

42. Dutiye pādeneva avamaddite akkantanti vuccamāne hatthena avamadditaṃ akkantaṃ viya akkantanti ruḷhī hesāti āha – “akkantanteva vutta”nti. Ariyavohāroti ariyadesavāsīnaṃ vohāro. Mahantaṃ aggahetvā appamattakasseva gahaṇe payojanaṃ dassetuṃ – “kasmā panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tena “vivaṭṭūpanissayakusalaṃ nāma yoniso uppāditaṃ appaka”nti na cintetabbaṃ, anukkamena laddhapaccayaṃ hutvā vaḍḍhamānaṃ khuddakanadī viya pakkhandamahoghā samuddaṃ, anukkamena nibbānamahāsamuddameva purisaṃ pāpetīti dīpeti. Paccekabodhiṃ buddhabhūminti ca paccatte upayogavacanaṃ. Vaṭṭavivaṭṭaṃ kathitanti yathākkamena vuttaṃ.

42. In the second case, when 'trampled' is said of something crushed by the foot, this is a conventional expression, just as 'trampled' is used for something crushed by the hand. Thus, it is said, 'It is simply called "trampled." ' 'Noble usage' refers to the usage of those dwelling in the noble land. To illustrate the benefit of grasping just a little without grasping a great amount, the passage begins, 'But why?' Therefore, one should not think, 'A wholesome state that is a support for the rolling back of the cycle, when wisely generated, is small.' It is explained that, having gradually obtained conditions and growing, like a small river entering the ocean as a great flood, it gradually leads a person to the great ocean of Nibbāna. 'Individual enlightenment' and 'the stage of a Buddha' are terms of application in each respective case. 'The cycle and the rolling back of the cycle have been spoken of' means they have been spoken of in due order.

43. Tatiye dosena paduṭṭhacittanti sampayuttadhammānaṃ, yasmiṃ santāne uppajjati, tassa ca dūsanena visasaṃsaṭṭhapūtimuttasadisena dosena padūsitacittaṃ. Attano cittenāti attano cetopariyañāṇena sabbaññutaññāṇena vā sahitena cittena. Paricchinditvāti ñāṇena paricchinditvā[V 1.0089]. Iṭṭhākārena etīti ayo, sukhaṃ. Sabbaso apeto ayo etassa, etasmāti vā apāyo, kāyikassa cetasikassa ca dukkhassa gati pavattiṭṭhānanti duggati, kāraṇāvasena vividhaṃ vikārena ca nipātiyanti etthāti vinipāto, appakopi natthi ayo sukhaṃ etthāti nirayoti evamettha attho veditabbo.

43. In the third case, 'a mind corrupted by hatred' refers to a mind defiled by hatred—which is like poison mixed with putrid urine—through its corruption of the associated states and the continuum in which it arises. 'By one's own mind' means by a mind associated with one's own knowledge of the minds of others or with omniscient knowledge. 'Having discerned' means having discerned with knowledge. That which proceeds in a desirable manner is 'ayo,' happiness. 'Apāya' is so called because happiness (ayo) is completely departed (apeto) for this being, or from this place. 'Duggati' is a bad destination, the resort and abode of physical and mental suffering. 'Vinipāta' is so called because beings are cast down (nipātiyanti) there in various ways and with distortions due to their causes. 'Niraya' is so called because not even a little happiness (ayo) exists there—this is how the meaning should be understood here.

44. Catutthe saddhāpasādena pasannanti saddhāsaṅkhātena pasādena pasannaṃ, na indriyānaṃ avippasannatāya. Sukhassa gatinti sukhassa pavattiṭṭhānaṃ. Sukhamevettha gacchanti, na dukkhanti vā sugati. Manāpiyarūpāditāya saha aggehīti saggaṃ, lokaṃ.

44. In the fourth case, 'serene with the serenity of faith' means serene with the serenity called faith, not with the clarity of the sense faculties. 'A destination of happiness' means the place where happiness occurs. 'Sugati' (a good destination) is so called because they go only to happiness there, not to suffering. 'Sagga' (heaven), the world, is so called because of agreeable forms and so on, and because one is together with (saha) the excellent (aggehi).

45. Pañcame [M 1.0098] pariḷāhavūpasamakaro rahado etthāti rahado, udakapuṇṇo rahado udakarahado. Udakaṃ dahati dhāretīti udakadaho. Āviloti kalalabahulatāya ākulo. Tenāha – “avippasanno”ti. Luḷitoti vātena āloḷito. Tenāha – “aparisaṇṭhito”ti. Vātābhighātena vīcitaraṅgamalasamākulatāya hi parito na saṇṭhito vā aparisaṇṭhito. Vātābhighātena udakassa ca appabhāvena kalalībhūto kaddamabhāvappattoti āha – “kaddamībhūto”ti. Sippiyo muttasippiādayo. Sambukā saṅkhasalākavisesā. Carantampi tiṭṭhantampīti yathālābhavacanametaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tameva hi yathālābhavacanataṃ dassetuṃ – “etthā”tiādi āraddhaṃ.

45. In the fifth case, a lake (rahado) is a pool that calms fever (pariḷāha). A lake full of water is a water-lake (udakarahado). It is a water-pool (udakadaho) because it holds (dahati) water. 'Turbid' (āvilo) means agitated (ākulo) due to an abundance of mud. Therefore, it is said: 'not clear' (avippasanno). 'Stirred up' (luḷito) means agitated (āloḷito) by the wind. Therefore, it is said: 'unsettled' (aparisaṇṭhito). Because it is filled with waves, ripples, and impurities from the striking of the wind, it is not settled all around, thus 'unsettled.' Because it has become muddy and reached a state of mire due to the striking of the wind and the shallowness of the water, it is said: 'become muddy' (kaddamībhūto). 'Shells' (sippiyo) are pearl-oysters and the like. 'Snails' (sambukā) are a type of spiral shell. 'Moving or standing'—this should be seen as a statement of what might be there. To show this very nature of being a statement of what might be there, it begins with 'here,' and so on.

Pariyonaddhenāti paṭicchāditena. Tayidaṃ kāraṇena āvilabhāvassa dassanaṃ. Diṭṭhadhamme imasmiṃ attabhāve bhavo diṭṭhadhammiko, so pana lokiyopi hoti lokuttaropīti āha – “lokiyalokuttaramissako”ti. Pecca samparetabbato samparāyo, paraloko. Tenāha – “so hi parattha atthoti parattho”ti. Iti dvidhāpi sakasantatipariyāpanno eva gahitoti itarampi saṅgahetvā dassetuṃ – “apicā”tiādimāha. Ayanti kusalakammapathasaṅkhāto dasavidho dhammo. Satthantarakappāvasāneti idaṃ tassa āsannabhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yassa kassaci antarakappassāvasāneti veditabbaṃ. Ariyānaṃ yuttanti ariyānaṃ ariyabhāvāya yuttaṃ, tato eva ariyabhāvaṃ kātuṃ samatthaṃ. Ñāṇameva ñeyyassa paccakkhakaraṇaṭṭhena dassananti āha – “ñāṇameva hī”tiādi. Kiṃ pana tanti āha – “dibbacakkhū”tiādi.

'Covered over' means concealed. This is the showing of the state of turbidity along with its cause. The benefit pertaining to the visible-here-and-now (diṭṭhadhammiko) is the benefit in this present existence; this can be mundane or supramundane, hence it is said: 'a mixture of mundane and supramundane.' 'Samparāya' is the other world, because it is to be gone to after death (pecca). Therefore, it is said: 'Because it is for the other world (parattha), it is called 'parattho' (for the other world).' Thus, since in both ways only that which is included in one's own continuum is taken, in order to include the other as well, it is said: 'moreover,' and so on. 'This' refers to the tenfold path of wholesome courses of action. 'At the end of the sword-interval aeon' is said with reference to its imminence. It should be understood as 'at the end of any intermediate aeon.' 'Befitting the noble ones' means it is befitting for the state of a noble one, and is thus capable of producing the state of a noble one. 'Knowledge itself' is called vision because it directly reveals the knowable, hence it is said: 'for knowledge itself,' and so on. But what is that? It is said: 'the divine eye,' and so on.

46. Chaṭṭhe acchoti tanuko. Tanubhāvameva hi sandhāya “abahalo”ti vuttaṃ. Yasmā pasanno nāma accho na bahalo, tasmā “pasannotipi vaṭṭatī”ti vuttaṃ. Vippasannoti visesena pasanno[V 1.0090]. So pana sammā pasanno nāma hotīti āha – “suṭṭhu pasanno”ti. Anāviloti akaluso. Tenāha – “parisuddho”tiādi. Saṅkhanti khuddakasevālaṃ, yaṃ “tilabījaka”nti vuccati. Sevālanti kaṇṇikasevālaṃ. Paṇakanti udakamalaṃ. Cittassa āvilabhāvo nīvaraṇahetukoti āha – “anāvilenāti pañcanīvaraṇavimuttenā”ti.

46. In the sixth case, 'accho' means thin. For it is with reference to being thin that 'abahalo' (not thick) is said. Since what is serene is indeed clear and not thick, it is therefore said, 'serene is also suitable.' 'Vippasanno' means especially serene. But that is called truly serene, hence it is said, 'very serene.' 'Anāvilo' means unpolluted. Therefore, it is said, 'pure,' etc. 'Saṅkha' means small duckweed, which is called 'tilabījaka.' 'Sevāla' means kaṇṇika duckweed. 'Paṇaka' means water scum. The polluted state of the mind is caused by the hindrances; hence it is said, 'unpolluted means freed from the five hindrances.'

47. Sattame [M 1.0099] rukkhajātānīti ettha jātasaddena padavaḍḍhanameva kataṃ yathā “kosajāta”nti āha – “rukkhānamevetaṃ adhivacana”nti. Koci hi rukkho vaṇṇena aggo hoti yathā taṃ rattacandanādi. Koci gandhena yathā taṃ gosītacandanaṃ. Koci rasena khadirādi. Koci thaddhatāya campakādi. Maggaphalāvahatāya vipassanāvasena bhāvitampi gahitaṃ. “Tattha tattheva sakkhibhabbataṃ pāpuṇātī”ti (a. ni. 3.103) vacanato “abhiññāpādakacatutthajjhānacittameva, āvuso”ti phussamittatthero vadati.

47. In the seventh case, in 'rukkhajātāni,' the word 'jāta' is used merely for word embellishment, as in 'kosajāta'; it is said, 'this is just a designation for trees.' Some trees are foremost in color, such as red sandalwood and so on. Some are foremost in fragrance, such as gosītacandana. Some in taste, like acacia and so on. Some in hardness, like champak and so on. What is developed by way of insight, bringing forth the path and fruit, is also included. As it is said, 'In each case, one attains the capacity to witness' (AN 3.103), the Elder Phussamitta says, 'Friend, it is precisely the fourth jhāna consciousness that serves as the foundation for higher knowledge.'

48. Aṭṭhame cittassa parivattanaṃ uppādanirodhā evāti āha – “evaṃ lahuṃ uppajjitvā lahuṃ nirujjhanaka”nti. Adhimattapamāṇattheti atikkantapamāṇatthe, pamāṇātītatāyanti attho. Tenāha – “ativiya na sukarā”ti. Cakkhuviññāṇampi adhippetamevāti sabbassapi cittassa samānakhaṇattā vuttaṃ. Cittassa ativiya lahuparivattibhāvaṃ theravādena dīpetuṃ – “imasmiṃ panatthe”tiādi vuttaṃ. Cittasaṅkhārāti sasampayuttaṃ cittaṃ vadati. Vāhasatānaṃ kho, mahārāja, vīhīnanti potthakesu likhanti, “vāhasataṃ kho, mahārāja, vīhīna”nti pana pāṭhena bhavitabbaṃ. Milindapañhepi (mi. pa. 4.1.2) hi katthaci ayameva pāṭho dissati. “Vāhasatāna”nti vā paccatte sāmivacanaṃ byattayena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Aḍḍhacūḷanti thokena ūnaṃ upaḍḍhaṃ. Kassa pana upaḍḍhanti? Adhikārato vāhassāti viññāyati. “Aḍḍhacuddasa”nti keci. “Aḍḍhacatuttha”nti apare. Sādhikaṃ diyaḍḍhasataṃ vāhāti daḷhaṃ katvā vadanti, vīmaṃsitabbaṃ. Catunāḷiko tumbo. Pucchāya abhāvenāti “sakkā pana, bhante, upamaṃ kātu”nti evaṃ pavattāya pucchāya abhāvena na katā upamā. Dhammadesanāpariyosāneti sannipatitaparisāya yathāraddhadhammadesanāya pariyosāne.

48. In the eighth case, the change of mind is simply its arising and cessation; thus it is said: 'so quickly arising and quickly ceasing.' 'In the sense of excessive measure' means in the sense of surpassing measure; the meaning is that it is beyond measure. Therefore, it is said: 'exceedingly difficult.' Eye-consciousness is also intended, for it is said that all consciousness has the same momentariness. To explain the extremely rapid transformation of the mind with a teaching of the Elders, it is said, 'in this regard,' and so on. 'Mental formations' refers to the mind together with its associated states. 'O great king, they write in books, "a hundred vāhas of rice,"' but the reading should be 'a hundred vāhas of rice, O great king.' Indeed, in the Milindapañha (Mil. 96), this very reading is found in some places. Or 'vāhasatānaṃ' should be seen as a singular possessive stated irregularly. 'Aḍḍhacūḷa' means a half less a little. A half of what? From the context, it is understood as a half of a vāha. Some say 'aḍḍhacuddasa'; others, 'aḍḍhacatuttha.' They firmly declare, 'more than one hundred and fifty vāhas'—this should be examined. A gourd is four nāḷis. 'Due to the absence of a question' means because a question such as, 'But, venerable sir, is it possible to give a simile?' was not posed, no simile was given. 'At the conclusion of the Dhamma teaching' means at the end of the Dhamma discourse as it was delivered to the assembled gathering.

49. Navame pabhassaranti pariyodātaṃ sabhāvaparisuddhaṭṭhena. Tenāha – “paṇḍaraṃ parisuddha”nti. Pabhassaratādayo nāma vaṇṇadhātuyaṃ labbhanakavisesāti āha – “kiṃ pana cittassa vaṇṇo nāma atthī”ti? Itaro arūpatāya “natthī”ti paṭikkhipitvā pariyāyakathā ayaṃ tādisassa cittassa parisuddhabhāvanādīpanāyāti dassento “nīlādīna”ntiādimāha. Tathā [V 1.0091] hi “so evaṃ samāhite citte parisuddhe pariyodāte”ti (dī. ni. 1.243-244; ma. ni. 1.384-386, 431-433; pārā. 12-13) vuttaṃ[M 1.0100]. Tenevāha – “idampi nirupakkilesatāya parisuddhanti pabhassara”nti. Kiṃ pana bhavaṅgacittaṃ nirupakkilesanti? Āma sabhāvato nirupakkilesaṃ, āgantukaupakkilesavasena pana siyā upakkiliṭṭhaṃ. Tenāha – “tañca kho”tiādi. Tattha attano tesañca bhikkhūnaṃ paccakkhabhāvato pubbe “ida”nti vatvā idāni paccāmasanavasena “ta”nti āha. Ca-saddo atthūpanayane. Kho-saddo vacanālaṅkāre, avadhāraṇe vā. Vakkhamānassa atthassa nicchitabhāvato bhavaṅgacittena sahāvaṭṭhānābhāvato upakkilesānaṃ āgantukatāti āha – “asahajātehī”tiādi. Rāgādayo upecca cittasantānaṃ kilissanti vibādhenti upatāpenti cāti āha – “upakkilesehīti rāgādīhī”ti. Bhavaṅgacittassa nippariyāyato upakkilesehi upakkiliṭṭhatā nāma natthi asaṃsaṭṭhabhāvato, ekasantatipariyāpannatāya pana siyā upakkiliṭṭhatāpariyāyoti āha – “upakkiliṭṭhaṃ nāmāti vuccatī”ti. Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāya vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādimāha. Tena bhinnasantānagatāyapi nāma iriyāya loke gārayhatā dissati, pageva ekasantānagatāya iriyāyāti imaṃ visesaṃ dasseti. Tenāha – “javanakkhaṇe…pe… upakkiliṭṭhaṃ nāma hotī”ti.

49. In the ninth case, 'luminous' means thoroughly purified, in the sense of being pure by nature. Hence it is said: 'white and pure.' It is said that luminosity and so on are specific qualities found in the element of form. Thus, it is asked: 'But does the mind have a color?' The other, due to its formlessness, rejects this, saying, 'It does not.' Showing that this is a figurative expression for indicating the purity and development of such a mind, it is said, 'of blue, etc.' Similarly, it is said, 'So with the mind concentrated, purified, bright' (e.g., DN 2). Therefore, it is said: 'This too is luminous because it is pure, being free from defilements.' But is the life-continuum mind free from defilements? Yes, by nature it is free from defilements, but it can be defiled by adventitious defilements. Therefore, it is said: 'But that...' Here, having previously said 'this' because it was directly experienced by himself and those monks, he now says 'that' by way of reference. The particle 'ca' serves to introduce a point. The particle 'kho' is for embellishment of speech or for emphasis. Because the meaning to be stated is certain, and because defilements do not coexist with the life-continuum mind, their adventitious nature is indicated when it is said, 'by those not co-arisen,' and so on. It is said, 'by defilements, such as lust,' because lust and so on, having approached, defile, oppress, and torment the mental continuum. It is said, 'it is called defiled,' because the life-continuum mind is not literally defiled by defilements, as it is not associated with them; but it may be figuratively called defiled because it is included in a single continuity. Now, to clarify that meaning with a simile, it is said: 'Just as...' Thereby, he shows this distinction: even conduct belonging to a different continuum is seen as blameworthy in the world, how much more so conduct belonging to the same continuity. Hence it is said: 'At the moment of impulsion... it is called defiled.'

50. Dasame bhavaṅgacittameva cittanti “pabhassaramidaṃ, bhikkhave, citta”nti vuttaṃ bhavaṅgacittameva. Yadaggena bhavaṅgacittaṃ tādisapaccayasamavāye upakkiliṭṭhaṃ nāma vuccati, tadaggena tabbidhurapaccayasamavāye upakkilesato vimuttanti vuccati. Tenāha – “upakkilesehi vippamuttaṃ nāma hotī”ti. Sesamettha navamasutte vuttanayānusārena veditabbaṃ.

50. In the tenth case, the life-continuum mind is indeed the mind. Hence, when it is said, 'Monks, this mind is luminous,' it is the life-continuum mind that is meant. Insofar as the life-continuum mind is called defiled in a combination of such conditions, to that same extent, in a combination of conditions devoid of those, it is called liberated from defilements. Hence it is said: 'It is called liberated from defilements.' The rest here should be understood according to the method explained in the ninth discourse.

Paṇihitaacchavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter on the Directed and the Clear is concluded.

6. Accharāsaṅghātavaggavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Chapter of the Finger-snap.

51. Chaṭṭhassa [V 1.0092] paṭhame assutavāti ettha “sādhu paññāṇavā naro”tiādīsu (jā. 2.18.101) atthitāmattassa bodhako vā-saddo. “Sīlavā hoti kalyāṇadhammo”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 3.381) pasaṃsāvisiṭṭhāya atthitāya. “Paññavā hoti [M 1.0101] udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.317; ma. ni. 2.25) atisayatthavisiṭṭhāya atthitāya, tasmā yassa pasatthaṃ atisayena vā sutaṃ atthi, so sutavā, saṃkilesaviddhaṃsanasamatthaṃ pariyattidhammassavanaṃ, taṃ sutvā tathattāya paṭipatti ca “sutavā”ti iminā padena pakāsitā. Sotabbayuttaṃ sutvā kattabbanipphattivasena suṇīti vā sutavā, tappaṭikkhepena na sutavāti assutavā.

51. In the first discourse of the sixth chapter, regarding 'assutavā' (unlearned): here, the suffix '-vā' indicates mere existence, as in such cases as 'sādhu paññāṇavā naro' (good is a man who has wisdom) (Jā. 2.18.101). In cases such as 'sīlavā hoti kalyāṇadhammo' (he is virtuous, of good character) (MN 3.381), it indicates existence distinguished by praise. In cases such as 'paññavā hoti udayatthagāminiyā paññāya samannāgato' (he is wise, endowed with the wisdom that comprehends arising and passing away) (DN 3.317; MN 2.25), it signifies existence distinguished by excellence. Therefore, one who has heard what is praiseworthy or excellent is 'sutavā' (learned). By this word 'sutavā' is expressed both the hearing of the scriptural teaching capable of destroying defilements and, having heard it, the practice for its realization. Alternatively, 'sutavā' is one who hears in the sense of accomplishing what should be done after hearing what is fit to be heard. The negation of that is 'assutavā'.

Ayañhi akāro “ahetukā dhammā (dha. sa. 2 dukamātikā), abhikkhuko āvāso”tiādīsu (pāci. 1047) taṃsamāyoganivattiyaṃ diṭṭho. “Appaccayā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 7 dukamātikā) taṃsambandhibhāvanivattiyaṃ. Paccayuppannañhi paccayasambandhīti apaccayuppannattā ataṃsambandhitā ettha jotitā. “Anidassanā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 9 dukamātikā) taṃsabhāvanivattiyaṃ. Nidassanañhi ettha daṭṭhabbatā. Atha vā passatīti nidassanaṃ, cakkhuviññāṇaṃ. Taggahetabbatānivattiyaṃ, tathā “anāsavā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 15 dukamātikā). “Appaṭighā dhammā (dha. sa. 10 dukamātikā) anārammaṇā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 55 dukamātikā) taṃkiccanivattiyaṃ. “Arūpino dhammā acetasikādhammā”ti taṃsabhāvanivattiyaṃ. Tadaññatā hi idha pakāsitā. “Amanusso”ti tabbhāvamattanivattiyaṃ. Manussattamattaṃ natthi, aññaṃ taṃsadisanti. Sadisatā hi ettha sūcitā. “Assamaṇo samaṇapaṭiñño abrahmacārī brahmacāripaṭiñño”ti (a. ni. 3.13) ca taṃsambhāvanīyaguṇanivattiyaṃ. Garahā hi idha ñāyati. “Kacci bhoto anāmayaṃ (jā. 1.15.146; 2.20.129) anudarā kaññā”ti ca tadanappabhāvanivattiyaṃ. “Anuppannā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 17 tikamātikā) taṃsadisabhāvanivattiyaṃ. Atītānañhi uppannapubbattā uppādidhammānañca paccayekadesasiddhiyā āraddhuppādabhāvato kālavinimuttassa ca vijjamānattā uppannānukūlatā, pageva paccuppannānanti tabbidhuratā hettha viññāyati. “Asekkhā dhammā”ti (dha. sa. 11 tikamātikā) tadapariyosānanivattiyaṃ. Tanniṭṭhānañhettha pakāsitanti evaṃ anekesaṃ [V 1.0093] atthānaṃ jotako. Idha pana “arūpino dhammā (dha. sa. 11 dukamātikā), acetasikā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 57 dukamātikā) viya taṃsabhāvanivattiyaṃ daṭṭhabbo, aññattheti attho. Etenassa sutādiñāṇavirahaṃ dasseti. Tena vuttaṃ – “āgamādhigamābhāvā ñeyyo assutavā itī”ti.

This prefix 'a' is seen in contexts like 'ahetukā dhammā' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 2 Dukamātikā) and 'abhikkhuko āvāso' (Pācittiya 1047), where it negates association with that thing. In 'appaccayā dhammā' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 7 Dukamātikā), it negates the state of being connected with that. For what arises from a condition is connected to that condition, but here, since it does not arise from a condition, its non-connection is indicated. In 'anidassanā dhammā' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 9 Dukamātikā), it negates the intrinsic nature of being visible. Here, 'nidassana' means the state of being seeable. Alternatively, 'nidassana' means 'that which sees,' i.e., eye-consciousness; it negates the state of being an object of that. Similarly in 'anāsavā dhammā' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 15 Dukamātikā). In 'appaṭighā dhammā' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 10 Dukamātikā) and 'anārammaṇā dhammā' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 55 Dukamātikā), it negates their respective functions. In 'arūpino dhammā' and 'acetasikā dhammā,' it negates their intrinsic nature, for here their otherness is declared. In 'amanusso,' it negates merely the state of being human. There is no mere humanity, but something else similar to it; for similarity is indicated here. In 'assamaṇo samaṇapaṭiñño, abrahmacārī brahmacāripaṭiñño' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.13), it negates the qualities that should be conceived of as belonging to an ascetic or celibate, for censure is understood here. And in phrases like 'kacci bhoto anāmayaṃ' (Jātaka 1.15.146; 2.20.129) and 'anudarā kaññā,' it negates an excessive state. In 'anuppannā dhammā' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 17 Tikamātikā), it negates a state similar to the arisen. For past states, because they have previously arisen; for states liable to arise, because a part of their conditions is accomplished and their arising has begun; and for the timeless element, because it exists, there is a conformity with the 'arisen' state—and even more so for present states. Here, the lack of this conformity is to be understood. In 'asekkhā dhammā' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 11 Tikamātikā), it negates their non-completion, for their completion is declared here. Thus, it illuminates many meanings. Here, however, as in phrases like 'arūpino dhammā' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 11 Dukamātikā) and 'acetasikā dhammā' (Dhammasaṅgaṇī, 57 Dukamātikā), it should be understood as negating their intrinsic nature; the meaning is 'otherness'. This shows the absence of knowledge derived from learning and so on. Hence it is said: 'Due to the absence of learning and realization, he is to be known as unlearned (assutavā).'

Idāni [M 1.0102] tassatthaṃ vivaranto “yo hī”tiādimāha. Tattha yasmā khandhadhātādikosallenapi upakkilesaupakkiliṭṭhānaṃ jānanahetubhūtaṃ bāhusaccaṃ hoti. Yathāha – “kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, bahussuto hoti? Yato kho, bhikkhu, khandhakusalo hoti. Dhātu…pe… āyatana…pe… paṭiccasamuppādakusalo hoti. Ettāvatā kho, bhikkhu, bahussuto hotī”ti. Tasmā “yassa ca khandhadhātuāyatanapaccayākārasatipaṭṭhānādīsū”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha vācuggatakaraṇaṃ uggaho. Atthaparipucchanaṃ puripucchā. Kusalehi saha codanāpariharaṇavasena vinicchayakaraṇaṃ vinicchayo. Ācariye pana payirupāsitvā atthadhammānaṃ āgamanaṃ sutamayañāṇavasena avabujjhanaṃ āgamo. Maggaphalanibbānānaṃ sacchikiriyā adhigamo.

Now, explaining its meaning, the text begins with 'yo hī' (for whoever). Here, extensive learning, which includes skill regarding the aggregates, elements, and so on, is the cause of knowing the defilements and the defiled. As it is said: 'To what extent, venerable sir, is one considered learned? When, bhikkhu, one is skilled in the aggregates, skilled in the elements... skilled in the sense bases... skilled in dependent origination—to that extent, bhikkhu, one is considered learned.' Therefore, it is said: 'For whom in the aggregates, elements, sense bases, conditions, foundations of mindfulness, etc.' Here, making the words one's own is acquisition (uggaho). Questioning the meaning is interrogation (paripucchā). Making a decision by way of challenging and resolving with the skillful is judgment (vinicchayo). Then, having attended on a teacher, understanding the meaning and the Dhamma through knowledge born of learning is learning (āgamo). Realizing the path, fruits, and Nibbāna is attainment (adhigamo).

Bahūnaṃ nānappakārānaṃ sakkāyadiṭṭhādīnaṃ avihatattā tā janenti, tāhi vā janitāti puthujjanā. Avighātameva vā jana-saddo vadati. Puthu satthārānaṃ mukhullokikāti ettha puthū janā satthupaṭiññā etesanti puthujjanā. Sabbagatīhi avuṭṭhitāti ettha janetabbā, jāyanti vā ettha sattāti janā, gatiyo, tā puthū etesanti puthujjanā. Ito pare jāyanti etehīti janā, abhisaṅkhārādayo, te etesaṃ puthū vijjantīti puthujjanā. Abhisaṅkhārādiattho eva vā jana-saddo daṭṭhabbo. Oghā kāmoghādayo. Rāgaggiādayo santāpā. Te eva sabbepi vā kilesā pariḷāhā. Puthu pañcasu kāmaguṇesu rattāti ettha jāyatīti jano, rāgo gedhoti evamādiko, puthu jano etesanti puthujjanā. Puthūsu janā jātā rattāti evaṃ rāgādiattho eva vā jana-saddo daṭṭhabbo.

Because they generate, or are generated by, the many various kinds of identity view and so on, which have not been destroyed, they are called ordinary people (puthujjanā). Or, the word 'jana' itself means 'non-destruction'. Here, regarding 'those who look to the faces of various teachers,' it means that for them there are various persons who claim to be teachers, hence 'puthujjanā'. Here, regarding 'those not arisen from all destinies,' 'jana' means 'to be generated,' or 'beings are born here,' i.e., destinies (gatiyo); for them, these destinies are various (puthu), hence 'puthujjanā'. 'Jana' refers to that by which they are born hereafter, meaning volitional formations and so on; because these are various for them, they are called 'puthujjanā'. Alternatively, the word 'jana' should be understood as having the meaning of volitional formations and so on. The floods are the flood of sensuality, etc. The fevers are the fires of lust, etc. These, or all defilements, are the torments. Here, regarding 'variously attached to the five strands of sensual pleasure,' 'jana' means that which arises—lust, greed, and so on. For them, this 'jana' is various, hence 'puthujjanā'. Or, the word 'jana' should be understood as having the meaning of lust and so on, in the sense that 'people (janā) are born (jātā) and attached (rattā) in various ways (puthūsu).'

Rattāti vatthaṃ viya raṅgajātena cittassa vipariṇāmakarena chandarāgena rattā sārattā. Giddhāti abhikaṅkhanasabhāvena abhigijjhanena giddhā gedhaṃ āpannā. Gadhitāti ganthitā viya dummocanīyabhāvena tattha paṭibaddhā. Mucchitāti kilesavasena visaññibhūtā viya anaññakiccā mohamāpannā. Ajjhopannāti anaññasādhāraṇe viya katvā gilitvā pariniṭṭhāpetvā ṭhitā. Laggāti vaṅkakaṇṭake viya āsattā, mahāpalipe yāva nāsikaggā palipannapuriso viya uddharituṃ asakkuṇeyyabhāvena nimuggā[M 1.0103]. Laggitāti makkaṭālepe ālaggabhāvena [V 1.0094] sammasito viya makkaṭo pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ vasena ālaggitā. Palibuddhāti sambaddhā, upaddutā vā. Āvutāti āvaritā. Nivutāti nivāritā. Ovutāti paliguṇṭhitā, pariyonaddhā vā. Pihitāti pidahitā. Paṭicchannāti chāditā. Paṭikujjitāti heṭṭhāmukhajātā.

"Rattā" means dyed; like a cloth with a coloring agent, they are dyed and strongly attached by sensual lust, which causes the mind's alteration. "Giddhā" means greedy; having fallen into greed through intense longing, which has the nature of craving. "Gadhitā" means bound; bound there with the quality of being hard to release, as if tied. "Mucchitā" means infatuated; having fallen into delusion, unable to do anything else, as if having become unconscious through the power of defilements. "Ajjhopannā" means overcome; they stand having swallowed and finished it, having made it as if not common to others. "Laggā" means stuck; attached, like on a bent thorn, or immersed with the quality of being unable to pull oneself out, like a man sunk up to the tip of his nose in a great swamp. "Laggitā" means adhered; adhered by means of the five sense faculties, like a monkey touched by and stuck to monkey-lime. "Palibuddhā" means obstructed, or oppressed. "Āvutā" means covered. "Nivutā" means hindered. "Ovutā" means enveloped, or wrapped up. "Pihitā" means closed. "Paṭicchannā" means concealed. "Paṭikujjitā" means turned face downwards.

“Assutavā”ti etena avijjandhatā vuttāti āha – “andhaputhujjano vutto”ti. Cittaṭṭhiti cittapariggaho natthīti yāya paṭipattiyā cittassa upakkilesaṃ tato vippamuttiñca yathāsabhāvato jāneyya, sā cittabhāvanā cittaṭṭhiti. Ekārammaṇe suṭṭhu samādhānavasena avaṭṭhitiṃ pādakaṃ katvā pavattitā sampayuttadhammehi nissayārammaṇehi ca saddhiṃ cittassa pariggahasaññitā vipassanābhāvanāpi natthi, yāya vuttamatthaṃ yathāsabhāvato jāneyya.

By 'unlearned' (assutavā) is meant the blindness of ignorance; thus it is said, 'the blind ordinary person is meant.' There is no mental stability or mental grasp. That is, there is no practice by which one would know the mind’s defilements and liberation from them as they truly are; that is mental development, which is mental stability. There is also no insight development, designated as mental grasp, which, having made firm establishment on a single object by means of proper concentration its basis, proceeds together with associated states and support-objects, and by which one would know the stated meaning as it truly is.

52. Dutiye sutavāti padassa attho anantarasutte vuttoyeva. Ariyasāvakoti ettha catukkaṃ sambhavatīti taṃ dassetuṃ – “atthi ariyo”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Paccekaṃ saccāni buddhavantoti paccekabuddhā. Nanu sabbepi ariyā paccekameva saccāni paṭivijjhanti dhammassa paccattavedanīyabhāvato? Nayidamīdisaṃ paṭivedhaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Yathā pana sāvakā aññesaṃ nissayena saccāni paṭivijjhanti paratoghosena vinā tesaṃ dassanamaggassa anuppajjanato.
