Yathā ca sammāsambuddhā aññesaṃ nissayabhāvena saccāni abhisambujjhanti, na evamete, ete pana aparaneyyā hutvā aparanāyakabhāvena saccāni paṭivijjhanti. Tena vuttaṃ – “paccekaṃ saccāni buddhavantoti paccekabuddhā”ti.

52. In the second case, the meaning of the term 'learned' (sutavā) is as stated in the immediately preceding discourse. Here, to show that a fourfold classification is possible for 'noble disciple' (ariyasāvako), the text begins with 'there is the noble one,' and so on. By 'those who have understood the truths individually' (paccekaṃ saccāni buddhavanto) are meant Paccekabuddhas. But do not all noble ones penetrate the truths individually, since the Dhamma is to be personally experienced? This was not said in reference to this kind of penetration. For disciples penetrate the truths by relying on others, as their path of seeing does not arise without the voice of another. And just as the Perfectly Self-Enlightened Ones awaken to the truths by being a support for others, these are not like that; rather, being unled by another and without another guide, they penetrate the truths. Hence it is said, 'By "those who have understood the truths individually" are meant Paccekabuddhas.'

Atthi sāvako na ariyoti ettha pothujjanikāya saddhāya ratanattaye abhippasanno saddhopi gahito eva. Gihī anāgataphaloti idaṃ pana nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathāvuttapuggalo hi saraṇagamanato paṭṭhāya sotāpattiphalasacchikiriyāya paṭipannoicceva vattabbataṃ labhati. Svāyamattho dakkhiṇāvisuddhisuttena (ma. ni. 3.376 ādayo) dīpetabbo. Sutavāti ettha vuttaattho nāma attahitaparahitappaṭipatti, tassa vasena sutasampanno. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “so ca hoti sutena upapanno, appampi [M 1.0104] ce sahitaṃ bhāsamāno”ti ca ādi. Ariyasāvakoti veditabboti ariyassa bhagavato dhammassavanakicce yuttappayuttabhāvato vuttaṃ. Upakkilesehi vippamutti anupakkiliṭṭhatā, tassā yathāsabhāvajānanaṃ daḷhatarāya eva cittabhāvanāya sati hoti, na aññathāti “balavavipassanā kathitā”ti vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'there is a disciple who is not noble,' here even the faithful person who has profound confidence in the Triple Gem through mundane faith is included. The householder as one who has not yet attained the fruit—this should be seen merely as an example. For such a person, starting from taking refuge, is to be considered as one who has entered upon the practice for the realization of the fruit of stream-entry. This meaning should be clarified by the Dakkhiṇāvisuddhi Sutta (MN III 376ff.). The meaning stated here by 'learned' (sutavā) is the practice for one's own welfare and the welfare of others; by this one is accomplished in learning. With reference to this it was said: 'He is one who is endowed with learning; even if he speaks little, it is meaningful,' and so on. A noble disciple should be understood as such due to being engaged and diligent in the task of listening to the Dhamma of the Noble One, the Blessed One. Freedom from defilements is the state of being undefiled; knowing this in its true nature occurs only when there is a stronger mental development, and not otherwise. Hence, it is said, 'strong insight is spoken of.'

53. Tatiye aggikkhandhopamasuttantaaṭṭhuppattiyanti aggikkhandhopamasutte (a. ni. 7.72) desanāaṭṭhuppattiyaṃ[V 1.0095]. Taṃdesanāhetukañhi ekaccānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ micchāpaṭipattiṃ nimittaṃ katvā bhagavā imaṃ suttaṃ desesi. Avijahitameva hoti sabbakālaṃ suppatiṭṭhitasatisampajaññattā. Yasmā buddhānaṃ rūpakāyo bāhirabbhantarehi malehi anupakkiliṭṭho sudhotajātimaṇisadiso, tasmā vuttaṃ – “upaṭṭhākānuggahatthaṃ sarīraphāsukatthañcā”ti. Vītināmetvāti phalasamāpattīhi vītināmetvā. Kālaparicchedavasena vivittāsane vītināmanaṃ vivekaninnatāya ceva paresaṃ diṭṭhānugatiāpajjanatthañca. Nivāsetvāti vihāranivāsanaparivattanavasena nivāsetvā. Kadāci ekakassa, kadāci bhikkhusaṅghaparivutassa, kadāci pakatiyā, kadāci pāṭihāriyehi vattamānehi ca gāmappaveso tathā tathā vinetabbapuggalavasena. Upasaṃharitvāti himavantādīsu pupphitarukkhādito ānetvā. Oṇatuṇṇatāya bhūmiyā satthu padanikkhepasamaye samabhāvāpatti, sukhasamphassavikasitapadumasampaṭicchanañca suppatiṭṭhitapādatāya nissandaphalaṃ, na iddhinimmānaṃ. Nidassanamattañcetaṃ sakkharākaṭhalakaṇṭakasaṅkukalalādiapagamo sucibhāvāpattīti evamādīnampi tadā labbhanato.

53. In the third, regarding the origin of the Aggikkhandhopama Suttanta, it is the origin of the discourse in the Aggikkhandhopama Sutta (AN 7.72). The Blessed One taught this sutta by taking the wrong practice of certain monks as the occasion for that discourse. It is always unabandoned due to well-established mindfulness and clear comprehension. Because the Buddha's physical body is untainted by external or internal impurities, like a well-polished natural gem, it is said: 'for the support of attendants and for the comfort of the body.' By 'having passed the time' (vītināmetvā) is meant having passed the time with fruition attainments. Passing time in a secluded seat, according to the time allocation, is both due to an inclination towards solitude and for the sake of others following the example. By 'having robed' (nivāsetvā) is meant having robed in the manner of changing robes in the monastery. Sometimes the village entry is alone, sometimes surrounded by the monastic community, sometimes in a normal manner, sometimes with miraculous displays, thus according to the individuals to be trained in various ways. By 'having brought' (upasaṃharitvā) is meant having brought flowers and trees in bloom from places like the Himalayas. The ground becoming even from its unevenness, soft to the touch, and receiving his feet like a blooming lotus at the time of the Teacher’s foot placement, are the results of well-established feet, not a product of psychic power. This is merely an indication, for at that time the disappearance of gravel, potsherds, thorns, splinters, mud, and so on, and the attainment of a pure state, are also obtainable.

Indakhīlassa anto ṭhapitamatteti idaṃ yāvadeva veneyyajanavinayatthāya satthu pāṭihāriyaṃ pavattanti katvā vuttaṃ. Dakkhiṇapādeti idaṃ buddhānaṃ sabbapadakkhiṇatāya. “Chabbaṇṇarasmiyo”ti vatvāpi “suvaṇṇarasapiñjarāni viyā”ti idaṃ buddhānaṃ sarīre pītābhāya yebhuyyatāya vuttaṃ. Madhurenākārena saddaṃ karonti daṭṭhabbasārassa diṭṭhatāya. Bheriādīnaṃ pana saddāyanaṃ dhammatāva. Paṭimānentīti “sudullabhaṃ idaṃ ajja amhehi labbhati, ye mayaṃ īdisena paṇītena āhārena bhagavantaṃ upaṭṭhahāmā”ti patītamānasā mānenti pūjenti. Tesaṃ santānāni oloketvāti [M 1.0105] tesaṃ tathā upaṭṭhākānaṃ puggalānaṃ atīte etarahi ca pavattacittasantānāni oloketvā. Arahatte patiṭṭhahantīti sambandho. Tatthāti vihāre. Gandhamaṇḍalamāḷeti catujjātiyagandhena kataparibhaṇḍe maṇḍalamāḷe.

That the Indakhīla was placed inside is said to be merely for the sake of disciplining those to be trained, as a marvel of the Teacher that occurs. By 'with the right foot'—this is due to the Buddhas' custom of always keeping to the right. Even having said 'six-colored rays,' it is also stated 'like golden yellow,' referring to the predominance of the yellow radiance in the Buddhas' body. They produce sounds with a sweet tone due to the essence of what is to be seen having been seen. But the sounding of drums and the like is simply their nature. By 'they honor' (paṭimānenti) is meant that with delighted minds they honor and revere, thinking, 'Today we have obtained something very rare—that we may serve the Blessed One with such excellent food.' By 'having observed their mental continuums' (tesaṃ santānāni oloketvā) is meant having observed the past and present mental continuums of those individuals who serve in such a way. They will be 'established in arahantship'; this is the connection. By 'there' (tatthāti) is meant in the monastery. By 'the fragrant pavilion' (gandhamaṇḍalamāḷe) is meant a circular pavilion with furnishings made from four kinds of fragrant substances.

Dullabhā khaṇasampattīti satipi manussattappaṭilābhe patirūpadesavāsaindriyāvekallasaddhāpaṭilābhādayo guṇā dullabhāti attho. Cātumahārājika…pe… vasavattibhavanaṃ gacchantīti idaṃ tattha suññavimānāni sandhāya vuttaṃ. Bhagavā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā pacchābhattaṃ tayo bhāge katvā paṭhamabhāge sace ākaṅkhati, dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ kappeti. Sace ākaṅkhati, buddhāciṇṇaphalasamāpattiṃ samāpajjati. Atha yathākālaparicchedaṃ tato vuṭṭhahitvā dutiyabhāge pacchimayāme tatiyakoṭṭhāse viya lokaṃ voloketi veneyyānaṃ ñāṇaparipākaṃ passituṃ. Tenāha – “sace ākaṅkhatī”tiādi.

By 'rare is the attainment of favorable circumstances' (dullabhā khaṇasampattīti) is meant that even with the attainment of human birth, qualities such as residence in a suitable region, integrity of the senses, and acquisition of faith are rare. The realm of the Four Great Kings...up to the realm of the Vasavatti devas—this is said with reference to the empty celestial mansions there. The Blessed One, having entered the fragrant hut after the meal, divided the afternoon into three parts. In the first part, if he wished, he would lie down on his right side in the lion's posture. If he wished, he would enter the fruition attainment customary for the Buddhas. Then, rising from it according to the time allocation, in the second part he surveys the world to see the maturation of knowledge in those capable of being guided, just as in the third portion of the last watch. Hence it is said: 'if he wishes,' and so on.

Kālayuttanti [V 1.0096] pattakallaṃ, “imissā velāya imassa evaṃ vattabba”nti taṃkālānurūpaṃ. Samayayuttanti tasseva vevacanaṃ, aṭṭhuppattianurūpaṃ vā. Samayayuttanti vā ariyasamayasaṃyuttaṃ. Desakālānurūpameva hi buddhā bhagavanto dhammaṃ desenti, desentā ca ariyasammataṃ paṭiccasamuppādanayaṃ dīpentāva desenti. Atha vā samayayuttanti hetūdāharaṇasahitaṃ. Kālena sāpadesañhi bhagavā dhammaṃ deseti, kālaṃ viditvā parisaṃ uyyojeti, na yāva samandhakārā dhammaṃ deseti.

By 'timely' (kālayutta) is meant appropriate, that is, 'at this time, this should be said to this person,' in accordance with that time. By 'opportune' (samayutta) is meant a synonym for the same, or it means fitting the arising of circumstances. Or 'opportune' means connected with the noble occasion. Indeed, the Blessed Buddhas teach the Dhamma in accordance with place and time; and while teaching, they illuminate the noble-approved principle of dependent origination. Alternatively, 'opportune' means accompanied by reason and example. For the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma at the right time, with a purpose, knowing the time, and dismisses the assembly; he does not teach the Dhamma until deep darkness falls.

Utuṃ gaṇhāpeti, na pana malaṃ pakkhāletīti adhippāyo. Na hi bhagavato kāye rajojallaṃ upalimpatīti. Tato tatoti attano attano divāṭṭhānādito. Okāsaṃ labhamānāti purebhattapacchābhattapurimayāmesu okāsaṃ alabhitvā idāni majjhimayāme okāsaṃ labhamānā, bhagavatā vā katokāsatāya okāsaṃ labhamānā. Pacchābhattassa tīsu bhāgesu paṭhamabhāge sīhaseyyakappanaṃ ekantikaṃ na hotīti āha – “purebhattato paṭṭhāya nisajjāpīḷitassa sarīrassā”ti. Teneva hi tattha “sace ākaṅkhatī”ti tadā sīhaseyyakappanassa anibaddhatā vibhāvitā. Kilāsubhāvo parissamo[M 1.0106]. Sīhaseyyaṃ kappeti sarīrassa kilāsubhāvamocanatthanti yojetabbaṃ. Buddhacakkhunā lokaṃ voloketīti idaṃ pacchimayāme bhagavato bahulaṃ āciṇṇavasena vuttaṃ. Appekadā avasiṭṭhabalañāṇehi sabbaññutaññāṇeneva ca bhagavā tamatthaṃ sādhetīti.

He has the weather arranged, but does not wash away the dirt—this is the meaning. Indeed, dust and stains do not cling to the Blessed One’s body. From one’s own respective daytime dwelling place and so forth. Obtaining an opportunity—not having obtained an opportunity in the forenoon, the afternoon, or the first watch of the night, but now obtaining an opportunity in the middle watch; or, obtaining an opportunity because the Blessed One has made it possible. In the first of the three parts of the afternoon, the lion's posture is not absolute, thus it is said: 'From before the meal, the body is afflicted by sitting.' For this reason, the phrase 'if he wishes' indicates the non-obligatory nature of the lion's posture at that time. Weariness means fatigue. The lion's posture is to be understood as for the purpose of releasing the body's weariness. With the Buddha’s eye, he surveys the world—this is said with reference to the Blessed One’s frequent practice in the last watch of the night. Sometimes, the Blessed One accomplishes that purpose with the remaining powers and knowledges, or with the omniscient knowledge itself.

Imasmiṃyeva kicceti pacchimayāmakicce. Balavatā paccanutāpena saṃvaḍḍhamānena karajakāye mahāpariḷāho uppajjatīti āha – “nāmakāye santatte karajakāyo santatto”ti. Nidhānagatanti sannicitalohitaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Uṇhaṃ lohitaṃ mukhato uggañchīti lohitaṃ uṇhaṃ hutvā mukhato uggañchi. Ṭhānanti bhikkhupaṭiññaṃ. Taṃ pāpaṃ vaḍḍhamānanti bhikkhupaṭiññāya avijahitattā tathā pavaḍḍhamānapāpaṃ. Antimavatthuajjhāpannānampi upāyena pavattiyamāno yonisomanasikāro sātthako hotiyevāti dassento “jātasaṃvegā”tiādimāha. Aho sallekhitanti aho ativiya sallekhena itaṃ pavattaṃ. Kāsāvapajjototi bhikkhūnaṃ bahubhāvato ito cito ca vicarantānaṃ tesaṃ kāsāvajutiyā pajjotito. Isivātaparivātoti sīlakkhandhādīnaṃ nibbānassa ca esanato isīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ guṇagandhena ceva guṇagandhavāsitena sarīragandhena ca parito samantato vāyito.

In this very duty, that is, in the duty of the last watch. Because of the powerful remorse that grows, great distress arises in the body born of action—thus it is said: 'When the mental body is inflamed, the body born of action is inflamed.' 'Nidhānagata' is said with reference to accumulated blood. 'Hot blood gushed from the mouth' means the blood, being hot, gushed from the mouth. 'Ṭhāna' refers to the monk's vow. 'That evil grew' means the evil growing in that way because the monk's vow was not abandoned. To show that even for those who have fallen into the final offense, wise attention, arising through proper means, is indeed beneficial, he says, 'aroused by urgency,' and so on. 'Oh, how refined!' means 'Oh, this proceeded with great refinement.' 'The illumination of the saffron robes' means that due to the abundance of monks moving here and there, it was illuminated by the radiance of their saffron robes. 'The wind blowing around the sages' means that because of the seeking of the aggregates of virtue and so forth, and Nibbāna, by the sages, the monks, it was blown all around, perfumed by the fragrance of their virtues and by the fragrance of their bodies imbued with the fragrance of virtue.

Dhammasaṃvego uppajji anāvajjanena pubbe tassa atthassa asaṃviditattā. Dhammasaṃvegoti ca [V 1.0097] tādise atthe dhammatāvasena uppajjanakaṃ sahottappañāṇaṃ. Assāsaṭṭhānanti cittassāsakāraṇaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ. Sabbesaṃ kiccānaṃ pubbabhāgo sabbapubbabhāgo. “Sabbe sattā averā hontū”tiādinā hi cittassa paṭṭhānaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ hitapharaṇaṃ. Itaraṃ ito thokaṃ mahantanti katvā idaṃ “cūḷaccharāsaṅghātasutta”nti vuttaṃ. Accharāsaṅghāto vuccati aṅguliphoṭanakkhaṇo akkhinimisakālo, yo ekassa akkharassa uccāraṇakkhaṇo. Tenāha – “dve aṅguliyo paharitvā saddakaraṇamatta”nti. Sabbasattānaṃ hitapharaṇacittanti sabbesampi sattānaṃ sammadeva hitesitavasena pavattacittaṃ. Āvajjento āsevatīti hitesitavasena āvajjento. Āvajjanena ābhujantopi āsevati nāma ñāṇavippayuttena. Jānantoti tathā ñāṇamattaṃ uppādentopi. Passantoti tathā ñāṇacakkhunā paccakkhato viya vipassantopi. Paccavekkhantoti tamatthaṃ pati [M 1.0107] pati avekkhantopi. Saddhāya adhimuccantotiādi pañcannaṃ indriyānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Abhiññeyyantiādi catusaccavasena vuttaṃ. Sabbameva cetaṃ vitthārato, sāmaññena āsevanadassanamevāti idhādhippetameva āsevanatthaṃ dassetuṃ – “idha panā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

Spiritual urgency arose because, due to lack of attention, the significance of that matter had not been understood before. Spiritual urgency refers to the knowledge that arises together with moral dread, in accordance with the nature of such a thing. The basis of relief is the meditation subject that brings comfort to the mind. The preliminary part of all duties is the foremost preliminary. For indeed, by 'May all beings be free from enmity' and so forth, there is the establishing of the mind, its presence, and the pervading of welfare. Because the other differs from this slightly or greatly, this is called the 'Minor Discourse on the Snap of the Fingers.' The snap of the fingers is said to be the moment of snapping the fingers, the time it takes to blink an eye, which is the time taken to utter one syllable. Hence it is said: 'Merely the making of a sound by striking two fingers together.' The mind that pervades with welfare for all beings means the mind that proceeds rightly with the desire for the welfare of all beings. 'He cultivates by reflecting' means reflecting with the desire for welfare. Even bending the mind by reflection is called cultivation, though it be devoid of knowledge. 'Knowing' means even producing mere knowledge in that way. 'Seeing' means even seeing clearly in that way, as if directly, with the eye of knowledge, through insight. 'Reviewing' means even repeatedly examining that matter. 'Being resolved by faith,' and so forth, is stated in terms of the five faculties. 'What should be fully understood,' and so forth, is stated in terms of the four truths. All this is in detail, but here, to show that only the general meaning of cultivation and seeing is intended, it is said: 'Now here...' and so forth.

Arittajjhānoti avirahitajjhāno. Atucchajjhānoti jhānena atuccho. Cāgo vā vevacananti āha – “apariccattajjhāno”ti. Viharatīti padassa vibhaṅge (vibha. 540) āgatanayena atthaṃ dassento “viharatīti iriyatī”tiādimāha. Ayaṃ panettha saddattho – viharatīti ettha vi-saddo vicchedatthajotano. Haratīti neti, pavattetīti attho, vicchinditvā harati viharatīti vuttaṃ hoti. So hi ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā aparipatantaṃ attabhāvaṃ harati pavatteti, tasmā “viharatī”ti vuccati. Iriyatīti ṭhānanisajjādikiriyaṃ karonto pavattati. Pavattatīti ṭhānādisamaṅgī hutvā pavattati. Pāletīti ekaṃ iriyāpathabādhanaṃ iriyāpathantarehi rakkhanto pāleti. Yapeti yāpetīti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Ekañhi iriyāpathabādhanaṃ aññena iriyāpathena vicchinditvā aparipatantaṃ attabhāvaṃ pālento yapeti yāpetīti vuccati. Caratīti ṭhānanisajjādīsu aññatarasamaṅgī hutvā pavattati. Iminā padenāti “viharatī”ti iminā padena.

'Arittajjhāno' means meditation not devoid of jhāna. 'Atucchajjhāno' means not empty of jhāna. Or 'cāgo' is a synonym, thus he says 'apariccattajjhāno' (meditation not abandoned). Regarding 'viharatī,' in the analysis of the word (Vibhaṅga 540), showing its meaning according to the method presented there, it is said: 'Viharatī means he moves,' and so on. Here, however, the meaning of the word is this: In 'viharatī,' the prefix 'vi-' conveys the sense of separation. 'Harati' means he carries, he maintains; the meaning is that he carries by cutting off, thus it is said 'viharatī.' For he carries and maintains his being, preventing it from falling, by cutting off the discomfort of one posture with another posture; therefore, it is called 'viharatī.' 'Iriyati' means he proceeds performing actions such as standing, sitting, and so forth. 'Pavattati' means he proceeds, being endowed with standing and so forth. 'Pāleti' means he protects and maintains by guarding against the discomfort of one posture with other postures. 'Yapeti, yāpeti' are synonyms for this. For by cutting off the discomfort of one posture with another posture, while guarding it, he maintains his being, preventing it from falling; thus it is called 'yapeti, yāpeti.' 'Carati' means he proceeds, being endowed with one of the postures such as standing, sitting, and so forth. 'By this word' means by the word 'viharatī'.

Iriyāpathavihāroti ettha iriyanaṃ pavattanaṃ iriyā, kāyappayogo kāyikakiriyā. Tassā pavattanūpāyabhāvato iriyāya patho iriyāpatho, ṭhānanisajjādi. Na hi ṭhānanisajjādīhi avatthāhi vinā kiñci kāyikakiriyaṃ pavattetuṃ sakkā. Ṭhānasamaṅgī vā hi kāyena kiñci kareyya, gamanādīsu aññatarasamaṅgī vā. Viharaṇaṃ, viharati etenāti vā vihāro, iriyāpathova vihāro iriyāpathavihāro, so ca atthato ṭhānanisajjādiākārappavatto catusantatirūpappabandho [V 1.0098] eva. Ovādānusāsanīnaṃ ekānekavārādivisiṭṭhoyeva bhedo, na pana paramatthato tesaṃ nānākaraṇanti dassetuṃ – “paramatthato panā”tiādimāha. Tattha ese eke ekaṭṭhetiādīsu eso eko ekatthotiādinā attho veditabbo.

'Iriyāpathavihāra' (mode of deportment) means here: 'iriyā' is movement, proceeding; bodily application, bodily action. Because it is the means of its proceeding, the path of 'iriyā' is 'iriyāpatha', i.e., standing, sitting, and so forth. For without these states—standing, sitting, etc.—no bodily action can take place. For one would perform something with the body, being endowed with standing, or being endowed with one of the others such as walking. Dwelling, or that by which one dwells, is 'vihāra'. The mode of deportment itself is 'vihāra', hence 'iriyāpathavihāra'. And in essence, it is simply the continuous series of material phenomena of the four continuities, manifesting in the manner of standing, sitting, and so forth. The distinction of advice and instruction is only specific in terms of single or multiple instances and so forth, but to show that ultimately there is no difference in them, he says: 'But in the ultimate sense...' and so on. In this context, the meaning of phrases like 'ese eke ekaṭṭhe' should be understood as 'this is one, in one meaning,' and so forth.

Raṭṭhassa[M 1.0108], raṭṭhato vā laddho piṇḍo raṭṭhapiṇḍo. Tenāha – “ñātiparivaṭṭaṃ pahāyā”tiādi. Tattha “amhākamete”ti viññāyantīti ñātī, pitāmahapituputtādivasena parivaṭṭanaṭṭhena parivaṭṭo, ñātiyeva parivaṭṭo ñātiparivaṭṭo. Theyyaparibhogo nāma anarahassa paribhogo. Bhagavatā hi attano sāsane sīlavato paccayā anuññātā, na dussīlassa. Dāyakānampi sīlavato eva pariccāgo, na dussīlassa attano kārānaṃ mahapphalabhāvassa paccāsīsanato. Iti satthārā ananuññātattā dāyakehi ca apariccattattā saṅghamajjhepi nisīditvā paribhuñjantassa dussīlassa paribhogo theyyāya paribhogo theyyaparibhogo. Iṇavasena paribhogo iṇaparibhogo paṭiggāhakato dakkhiṇāvisuddhiyā abhāvato iṇaṃ gahetvā paribhogo viyāti attho.

Alms obtained from the state or from the countryside are called 'country alms.' Hence it is said, 'Having abandoned the circle of relatives,' and so on. Herein, 'relatives' means those who are recognized as 'these are ours'; 'parivaṭṭa' (circle) means a revolving cycle in the sense of grandfathers, fathers, sons, and so forth; 'ñātiparivaṭṭa' is simply the circle of relatives. Enjoyment by theft is enjoyment by one who is unworthy. For the Blessed One has permitted the use of requisites in his dispensation only for the virtuous, not for the immoral. And for donors, the offering is only for the virtuous, not for the immoral, because they expect their own actions to have great fruit. Thus, because it is not permitted by the Teacher and not given up by the donors, the enjoyment of an immoral person, even if he sits in the midst of the Sangha and enjoys, is enjoyment by theft, or theft-enjoyment. Enjoyment by way of debt is called 'debt-enjoyment'. Because there is no purity of the offering from the recipient's side, the meaning is that it is like enjoying after taking on debt.

Dātabbaṭṭhena dāyaṃ, taṃ ādiyantīti dāyādā, puttānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tesaṃ bhāvo dāyajjaṃ, dāyajjavasena paribhogo dāyajjaparibhogo, puttabhāvena paribhogoti vuttaṃ hoti. Sekkhā hi bhikkhū bhagavato orasaputtā, te pitu santakānaṃ dāyādā hutvā te paccaye paribhuñjanti. Kiṃ pana te bhagavato paccaye paribhuñjanti, udāhu gihīnanti? Gihīhi dinnāpi bhagavatā anuññātattā bhagavato santakā ananuññātesu sabbena sabbaṃ paribhogābhāvato, anuññātesuyeva ca paribhogasambhavato. Dhammadāyādasuttañcettha sādhakaṃ.

That which is to be given is 'dāya'; those who take it are 'dāyādā' (heirs), this is a designation for sons. Their state is 'dāyajja' (inheritance); enjoyment by way of inheritance is 'dāyajjaparibhoga', which means enjoyment by being sons. For the trainee monks are the Blessed One's legitimate sons; being heirs to their father's possessions, they enjoy those requisites. But do they enjoy the requisites belonging to the Blessed One, or those of householders? Even though given by householders, because they are permitted by the Blessed One, they belong to the Blessed One, since there is absolutely no enjoyment of what is not permitted, and enjoyment is possible only of what is permitted. Here, the Dhammadāyāda Sutta supports this.

Vītarāgā eva taṇhāya dāsabyaṃ atītattā sāmino hutvā paribhuñjantīti āha – “khīṇāsavassa paribhogo sāmiparibhogo nāmā”ti. Avītarāgānañhi taṇhāparavasatāya paccayaparibhoge sāmibhāvo natthi, tadabhāvena vītarāgānaṃ tattha sāmibhāvo yathāruciparibhogasambhavato. Tathā hi te paṭikūlampi appaṭikūlākārena, appaṭikūlampi paṭikūlākārena, tadubhayampi vajjetvā ajjhupekkhanākārena paccaye paribhuñjanti, dāyakānañca manorathaṃ pūrenti. Yo panāyaṃ sīlavato paccavekkhitaparibhogo, so iṇaparibhogassa paccanīkattā āṇaṇyaparibhogo nāma hoti. Yathā hi iṇāyiko attano ruciyā icchitaṃ desaṃ gantuṃ na labhati, evaṃ iṇaparibhogayutto lokato [M 1.0109] nissarituṃ na labhatīti tappaṭipakkhattā sīlavato paccavekkhitaparibhogo “āṇaṇyaparibhogo”ti vuccati, tasmā nippariyāyato catuparibhogavinimutto [V 1.0099] visuṃyevāyaṃ paribhogoti veditabbo. So idha visuṃ na vutto, dāyajjaparibhogeyeva vā saṅgahaṃ gacchati. Sīlavāpi hi imāya sikkhāya samannāgatattā “sekho”tveva vuccati. Imesu paribhogesu sāmiparibhogo dāyajjaparibhogo ca ariyānaṃ puthujjanānañca vaṭṭati, iṇaparibhogo na vaṭṭati. Theyyaparibhoge kathāyeva natthi. Kathaṃ panettha sāmiparibhogo dāyajjaparibhogo ca puthujjanānaṃ sambhavati? Upacāravasena. Yo hi puthujjanassapi sallekhappaṭipattiyaṃ ṭhitassa paccayagedhaṃ pahāya tattha anupalittena cittena paribhogo, so sāmiparibhogo viya hoti. Sīlavato pana paccavekkhitaparibhogo dāyajjaparibhogo viya hoti dāyakānaṃ manorathassa avirādhanato. Kalyāṇaputhujjanassa paribhoge vattabbameva natthi tassa sekkhasaṅgahato. Sekkhasuttaṃ (saṃ. ni. 5.13) hetassa atthassa sādhakaṃ.

Those free from lust, having transcended the slavery of craving, enjoy as masters. Thus it is said: "The enjoyment of one whose taints are destroyed is called 'master's enjoyment.'" For those not free from lust, there is no mastery in the enjoyment of requisites, being under the sway of craving. Due to its absence, those free from lust have mastery there, as enjoyment occurs according to their wishes. Indeed, they enjoy requisites by treating what is disagreeable as agreeable, what is agreeable as disagreeable, and by avoiding both through equanimity, thereby fulfilling the wishes of the donors. But the enjoyment with reflection of a virtuous one, being the opposite of debt-like enjoyment, is called "enjoyment free from debt." Just as a debtor cannot go to any place he wishes, so one bound by debt-like enjoyment cannot escape the world. Therefore, because it counteracts that, the enjoyment with reflection of a virtuous one is called "enjoyment free from debt." Thus, this should be understood directly as a distinct kind of enjoyment, separate from the four kinds of enjoyment. Here, it is not separately mentioned but is included under inherited enjoyment. For even a virtuous one, being endowed with this training, is called a "trainee." Among these enjoyments, master's enjoyment and inherited enjoyment apply to both noble ones and ordinary people, but debt-like enjoyment does not. Thieving enjoyment is not even worth discussing. But how do master's enjoyment and inherited enjoyment apply to ordinary people here? Figuratively. For an ordinary person established in the practice of effacement, if they abandon greed for requisites and enjoy them with an untainted mind, it is like master's enjoyment. And the enjoyment with reflection of a virtuous one is like inherited enjoyment because it does not violate the wishes of the donors. For a virtuous ordinary person, nothing more need be said, as they are included among the trainees. The "Discourse on the Trainee" (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.13) supports this meaning.

Imassa bhikkhunoti accharāsaṅghātamattampi kālaṃ mettacittaṃ āsevantassa bhikkhuno. Amogho raṭṭhapiṇḍaparibhogoti “ayaṃ pabbajito samaṇo bhikkhūti āmisaṃ dentānaṃ tāya mettāsevanāya attano santāne dosamalassa vā tadekaṭṭhānañca pāpadhammānaṃ pabbājanato vūpasamanato saṃsāre ca bhayassa sammāva ikkhaṇato ajjhāsayassa avisaṃvādanenassa amogho raṭṭhapiṇḍaparibhogo. Mahaṭṭhiyanti mahatthikaṃ mahāpayojanaṃ. Mahapphalanti vipulapphalaṃ. Mahānisaṃsanti mahānissandapphalaṃ. Mahājutikanti mahānubhāvaṃ. Mahāvipphāranti mahāvitthāraṃ. Ettha ca paṭhamaṃ kāraṇaṃ mettāsevanāya tassa bhikkhuno sāmiādibhāvena raṭṭhapiṇḍaparibhogārahatā, dutiyaṃ parehi dinnassa dānassa mahaṭṭhiyabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Ko pana vādoti mettāya āsevanamattampi evaṃmahānubhāvaṃ, ko pana vādo bahulīkāre, ettha vattabbameva natthī”ti attho.

“Of this monk” means of a monk who cultivates a mind of loving-kindness even for the time it takes to snap one's fingers. “The enjoyment of the country’s almsfood is not in vain” means that for those who give material support, believing, “This is a renunciant, a recluse, a bhikkhu,” the almsfood received by him is not in vain because, through that cultivation of loving-kindness, he expels the stain of aversion and associated evil qualities from his own mind, thereby calming them; and because he rightly perceives the danger in saṃsāra, and his aspiration is not false. “Of great benefit” (mahaṭṭhiya) means of great purpose, of great advantage. “Of great fruit” (mahapphala) means of abundant fruit. “Of great reward” (mahānisaṃsa) means of extensive resultant fruit. “Of great radiance” (mahājutika) means of great power. “Of great expansion” (mahāvipphāra) means of great pervasiveness. Here, the first reason is that the monk’s cultivation of loving-kindness makes him worthy of enjoying the country’s almsfood by way of being a master and so forth. The second reason is that it makes the gifts given by others of great benefit. “What more is to be said?” means that if even a mere cultivation of loving-kindness has such great power, what more is to be said of making it a frequent practice? On this point, there is nothing further to be said.

54. Catutthe uppādeti vaḍḍhetīti ettha bhāvanāsaddassa uppādanavaḍḍhanatthatā pubbe vuttā eva.

54. In the fourth case, the meaning of the word “bhāvanā” as “generates and increases” (uppādeti vaḍḍheti) has already been stated previously.

55. Pañcame [M 1.0110] imesu dvīsūti catutthapañcamesu. “Tatiye vuttanayeneva veditabba”nti vatvā tathā veditabbataṃ dassetuṃ – “yo hi āsevatī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tena āsevanābhāvanāmanasikārānaṃ atthavisesābhāvamāha. Yadi evaṃ suttantassa desanā kathanti āha – “sammāsambuddho panā”tiādi. Yāya dhammadhātuyāti sabbaññutaññāṇamāha. Tena hi dhammānaṃ ākārabhedaṃ ñatvā tadanurūpaṃ ekampi dhammaṃ tathā vibhajitvā bhagavā dasseti. Tīhi koṭṭhāsehīti [V 1.0100] āsevanābhāvanāmanasikārabhāgehi. Mettā hi sabbavatthuno mettāyanavasena ānītā sevanā āsevanā, tassā vaḍḍhanā bhāvanā, avissajjetvā manasi ṭhapanaṃ manasikāro.

55. In the fifth case, “among these two” refers to the fourth and fifth cases. Having stated, “It should be understood in the same way as explained in the third,” to show how it should be so understood, “for whoever cultivates,” etc., was said. Thereby, he indicates the absence of a difference in meaning between cultivation, development, and attention. If so, how is the discourse of the sutta taught? To this, it is said, “but the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One,” etc. “By which Dhamma-element” refers to the knowledge of omniscience. For, having known the distinctions in the characteristics of phenomena, the Blessed One analyzes even a single phenomenon accordingly and presents it. “By three divisions” means through the parts of cultivation, development, and attention. For loving-kindness, when brought to bear on all objects by way of directing loving-kindness, is “cultivation” (āsevanā); its increase is “development” (bhāvanā); and keeping it in mind without letting it go is “attention” (manasikāro).

56. Chaṭṭhe aniyamitavacanaṃ “ime nāmā”ti niyametvā avuttattā. Niyamitavacanaṃ “akusalā”ti sarūpeneva vuttattā. Asesato pariyādinnā honti appakassapi akusalabhāgassa aggahitassa abhāvato. Akusalaṃ bhajantīti akusalabhāgiyā. Akusalapakkhe bhavāti akusalapakkhikā. Tenāha – “akusalāyevā”tiādi. Paṭhamataraṃ gacchatīti paṭhamataraṃ pavattati, paṭhamo padhāno hutvā vattatīti attho. Ekuppādādivasena hi ekajjhaṃ pavattamānesu catūsu arūpakkhandhesu ayameva paṭhamaṃ uppajjatīti idaṃ natthi, lokuttaramaggesu viya pana paññindriyassa, lokiyadhammesu manindriyassa puretarassa bhāvo sātisayoti “sabbete manopubbaṅgamā”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi abhidhammepi (dha. sa. 1) “yasmiṃ samaye kāmāvacaraṃ kusalaṃ cittaṃ uppannaṃ hotī”ti cittaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ jeṭṭhaṃ katvā desanā pavattā. Suttesupi vuttaṃ – “manopubbaṅgamā dhammā (dha. pa. 1, 2), chadvārādhipati rājā”ti (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.buddhavaggo, erakapattanāgarājavatthu). Tenāha – “ete hī”tiādi. Tesaṃ mano uppādakoti ca yadaggena mano sampayuttadhammānaṃ jeṭṭhako hutvā pavattati, tadaggena te attānaṃ anuvattāpento te tathā uppādento nāma hotīti katvā vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana cittassa jeṭṭhakabhāvameva sandhāya rājagamanaññāyena sahuppattipi paṭhamuppatti viya katvā vuttāti ayamattho dassito. Anvadevāti eteneva cittassa khaṇavasena paṭhamuppattiyā abhāvo dīpitoti daṭṭhabbo. Tenevāha – “ekatoyevāti attho”ti.

56. In the sixth case, the indeterminate statement is so called because it is not stated with specification, as in “these are named.” The determinate statement is so called because it is stated in its own form, as in “unwholesome.” They are entirely included because not even a small part of the unwholesome is left ungoverned. Those who partake in the unwholesome are “unwholesome-partakers” (akusalabhāgiyā). Those who are on the side of the unwholesome are “of the unwholesome faction” (akusalapakkhikā). Therefore, it is said: “solely unwholesome,” etc. “Proceeds first” means it proceeds first; it occurs as the first and foremost—this is the meaning. For when the four immaterial aggregates arise together by way of a single arising, etc., it is not the case that “this one arises first.” However, just as with the wisdom faculty in supramundane paths, the preeminence of the mind faculty in mundane phenomena is superior. Hence, it is said: “All these are preceded by mind.” Indeed, in the Abhidhamma (Dhs. 1), the teaching proceeds by making mind the forerunner and chief, saying, “At whatever time a wholesome mind pertaining to the sensuous sphere arises.” In the Suttas, it is also said: “Phenomena are preceded by mind” (Dhp. 1-2), and “The king, ruler of the six doors.” Therefore, it is said: “For these,” etc. And “mind is their producer” is said because insofar as the mind, being the chief among associated phenomena, proceeds, to that extent it makes them follow itself, thus causing them to arise in that way. In the commentary, however, with reference to the mind's state of being the chief, this meaning is shown by stating that even simultaneous arising is like the first arising, in the manner of a king's procession. It should be understood that “Immediately following” (anvadeva) indicates by this very statement the absence of a first arising of mind by way of moments. Therefore, it is said: “Together—this is the meaning.”

57. Sattame [M 1.0111] catubhūmakāpi kusalā dhammā kathitāti “ye keci kusalā dhammā”ti anavasesapariyādānato vuttaṃ.

57. In the seventh case, because even wholesome states pertaining to the four planes are spoken of, it is said “whatever wholesome states there are” by way of including them all without remainder.

58. Aṭṭhame idanti liṅgavipallāsena niddeso, nipātapadaṃ vā etaṃ “yadida”ntiādīsu viyāti āha – “ayaṃ pamādoti attho”ti. Pamajjanākāroti pamādāpatti. Cittassa vossaggoti imesu ettakesu ṭhānesu satiyā aniggaṇhitvā cittassa vossajjanaṃ sativiraho. Vossaggānuppadānanti vossaggassa anu anu padānaṃ punappunaṃ vissajjanaṃ. Asakkaccakiriyatāti etesaṃ dānādīnaṃ kusaladhammānaṃ pavattane puggalassa vā deyyadhammassa vā asakkaccakiriyā. Satatabhāvo sātaccaṃ, sātaccena kiriyā sātaccakiriyā, sāyeva sātaccakiriyatā, na sātaccakiriyatā asātaccakiriyatā. Anaṭṭhitakiriyatāti [V 1.0101] aniṭṭhitakiriyatā nirantaraṃ na anuṭṭhitakiriyatā ca. Olīnavuttitāti nirantarakaraṇasaṅkhātassa vipphārassa abhāvena olīnavuttitā. Nikkhittachandatāti kusalakiriyāya vīriyachandassa nikkhittabhāvo. Nikkhittadhuratāti vīriyadhurassa oropanaṃ, osakkitamānasatāti attho. Anadhiṭṭhānanti kusalakaraṇe appatiṭṭhitabhāvo. Ananuyogoti ananuyuñjanaṃ. Kusaladhammesu āsevanādīnaṃ abhāvo anāsevanādayo. Pamādoti sarūpaniddeso. Pamajjanāti ākāraniddeso. Pamajjitattanti bhāvaniddeso. Parihāyantīti iminā pamādassa sāvajjataṃ dasseti. Tayidaṃ lokiyānaṃ vasena, na lokuttarānanti āha – “uppannā…pe… ida”ntiādi.

58. In the eighth case, 'idaṃ' is an explanation by distortion of gender, or it is a particle like 'yadidaṃ' and so on. Thus it is said: "This means negligence." "The way of being negligent" (pamajjanākāro) means incurring negligence (pamādāpatti). "The abandonment of the mind" (cittassa vossaggo) is the letting go of the mind in these many situations without restraint by mindfulness; it is the absence of mindfulness. "Repeated abandonment" (vossaggānuppadāna) is the repeated, continuous giving up of abandonment. "Careless action" (asakkaccakiriyatā) is the lack of carefulness in performing skillful actions such as giving and so forth, with respect to either the person or the thing to be given. Constant existence is continuity (sātacca); action with continuity is continuous action (sātaccakiriyā); that very continuity is continuous action (sātaccakiriyatā); its opposite is non-continuous action (asātaccakiriyatā). "Unfinished action" (anaṭṭhitakiriyatā) is both not completed and not continuously performed action. "Sluggish conduct" (olīnavuttitā) is sluggishness, due to the absence of vigor, which is characterized as continuous action. "Abandoned enthusiasm" (nikkhittachandatā) is the abandonment of enthusiasm for effort in skillful actions. "Abandoned burden" (nikkhittadhuratā) is the laying down of the burden of effort; it means a mind that has slipped back. "Non-resolution" (anadhiṭṭhāna) is the state of not being established in doing good. "Non-application" (ananuyoga) is not applying oneself. The absence of cultivation and so on in skillful qualities is non-cultivation and so forth (anāsevanādayo). "Negligence" (pamāda) is an explanation of its essence. "Being negligent" (pamajjanā) is an explanation of the mode. "The state of negligence" (pamajjitatta) is an explanation of the nature. "They decline" (parihāyanti) – this shows the faultiness of negligence. This is said with reference to worldly beings, not the transcendent. Thus it is said: "Arisen... this" and so on.

59. Navame na pamajjati etenāti appamādo, pamādassa paṭipakkho satiyā avippavāso. Atthato niccaṃ upaṭṭhitāya satiyā etaṃ nāmaṃ. Pamādo pana satiyā satisampajaññassa vā paṭipakkhabhūto akusalacittuppādo daṭṭhabbo. Tenāha – “pamādassa paṭipakkhavasena vitthārato veditabbo”ti.

59. In the ninth case, "one is not negligent by means of this" (na pamajjati etena) is diligence (appamāda), the opposite of negligence (pamāda), the non-absence of mindfulness (satiyā avippavāso). In meaning, this is a name for mindfulness that is constantly present. Negligence, however, should be seen as the arising of unwholesome consciousness, which is the opposite of mindfulness or of mindfulness and clear comprehension. Therefore, it is said: "It should be understood in detail by way of being the opposite of negligence."

60. Dasame kucchitaṃ sīdatīti kusīto da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā, tassa bhāvo kosajjaṃ, ālasiyanti attho.

60. In the tenth case, "he sinks into what is blameworthy" (kucchitaṃ sīdati) is kusīto (lazy), with the 'da' changed to 'ta'; its state is kosajja, meaning indolence.

Accharāsaṅghātavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Accharāsaṅghāta Chapter is concluded.

7. Vīriyārambhādivaggavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Chapter Beginning with the Commencement of Energy

61. Sattamassa [V 1.0102][M 1.0112] paṭhame vīrānaṃ kammanti vīriyaṃ, vidhinā vā īrayitabbaṃ pavattetabbanti vīriyaṃ, tadeva kusalakiriyāya padhānaṭṭhena ārambho vīriyārambho. Āraddhavīriyatā paggahitavīriyatā paripuṇṇavīriyatāti paccekaṃ vīriyatāsaddo yojetabbo.

61. In the first of the seventh, "the work of the heroes" is energy (vīriya); or what should be aroused and set in motion according to the rule is energy. That very energy, being the commencement in the sense that it is the principal factor for wholesome action, is the commencement of energy (vīriyārambha). Regarding "Āraddhavīriyatā (aroused energy), paggahitavīriyatā (exerted energy), paripuṇṇavīriyatā (perfected energy)"—the word 'vīriyatā' should be connected with each.

62. Dutiye mahatī icchā etassāti mahiccho, tassa bhāvo mahicchatā. Mahāvisayo lobho mahālobho mahantānaṃ vatthūnaṃ bahūnañca abhigijjhanato. Itarītarātiādinā pabbajitānaṃ uppajjanamahicchatā vuttā. Pañcahi kāmaguṇehītiādi gahaṭṭhānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ. Icchāti sabhāvaniddeso. Icchāgatāti icchāpavattā. Mahicchatāti mahāicchatā. Atthato panāyaṃ rāgo evāti vuttaṃ – “rāgo sārāgo”tiādi.

62. In the second, one who has great desire is called 'mahiccho,' and its state is 'mahicchatā.' Greed for vast objects is great greed (mahālobha), due to intensely craving great and numerous things. By 'itarītarāti' and so on, the great desire that arises among renunciants is stated. 'Pañcahi kāmaguṇehi' and so on is stated with reference to householders. 'Icchā' is a definition of its inherent nature. 'Icchāgatā' means 'proceeding according to desire.' 'Mahicchatā' means 'great desire.' But in meaning, this is simply lust, as stated: 'rāgo sārāgo,' and so on.

63. Tatiye appicchassāti ettha appa-saddo abhāvattho “appābādho hoti appātaṅko”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.304) viyāti āha – “anicchassā”ti. Loke pākaṭassa hi akkhirogakucchirogādibhedassa ābādhassa abhāvaṃ sandhāya “appābādho”ti vuttaṃ. Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ pākaṭataraṃ kātuṃ “ettha hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Byañjanaṃ sāvasesaṃ viya parittakepi appasaddassa dissamānattā. Attho pana niravaseso sabbaso paccayicchāya abhāvassa adhippetattā. Tenāha – “na hī”tiādi.

63. In the third, regarding 'appicchassa,' here the word 'appa' means 'absence,' just as in 'appābādho hoti appātaṅko' (MN 2.304) and so on; thus it is said: 'anicchassa' (without desire). Indeed, in the world, 'appābādho' is stated with reference to the absence of manifest ailments such as eye diseases and stomach diseases. Now, to make the meaning already stated even clearer, 'ettha hi' and so on is stated. The expression appears as if with a remainder, because the word 'appa' is also seen to mean 'a small amount.' But the meaning is complete, because the utter absence of desire for requisites is intended. Therefore, it is said: 'na hi' and so on.

Icchāya abhāveneva appiccho nāma hotīti imamatthaṃ pakārantarena dīpetuṃ – “apicā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atricchatā nāma atra atra icchā. Asantaguṇasambhāvanatāya pāpā lāmikā nihīnā icchā pāpicchatā. Yāya paccayuppādanatthaṃ attani vijjamānaguṇe sambhāveti, paccayānaṃ paṭiggahaṇe ca na mattaṃ jānāti, ayaṃ mahicchatā. Asantaguṇasambhāvanatāti attani avijjamānānaṃ guṇānaṃ vijjamānānaṃ viya paresaṃ pakāsanā. Santaguṇasambhāvanatāti icchācāre ṭhatvā attani vijjamānasīladhutadhammādiguṇavibhāvanā. Tādisassapi paṭiggahaṇe amattaññutāpi hoti, sāpi abhidhamme āgatāyevāti sambandho. Dussantappayoti duttappayo.

To explain this meaning—that one is called 'appiccho' precisely because of the absence of desire—in another way, 'apicā' and so on is stated. 'Atricchatā' means 'desire for this and that.' Pāpicchatā is evil, base, low desire, by way of displaying non-existent qualities. That by which one displays existing qualities in oneself for the sake of producing requisites, and does not know moderation in accepting requisites—this is mahicchatā. 'Asantaguṇasambhāvanatā' means 'declaring to others qualities that do not exist in oneself as if they existed.' 'Santaguṇasambhāvanatā' means 'making known one's own existing qualities, such as virtue and the qualities of the ascetic practices, while acting with desire.' Even for such a one, in acceptance there is also immoderation; that too is found in the Abhidhamma—this is the connection. 'Dussantappayo' means 'duttappayo' (difficult to please).

Atilūkhabhāvanti [M 1.0113] pattacīvaravasena ativiya lūkhabhāvaṃ. Tadassa disvā manussā “ayaṃ amaṅgaladivaso[V 1.0103], sumbhakasiniddhapattacīvaro ayyo pubbaṅgamo kātabbo”ti cintetvā, “bhante, thokaṃ bahi hothā”ti āhaṃsu. Ummujjīti manussānaṃ ajānantānaṃyeva pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā gaṇhantoyeva ummujji. Yadi thero “khīṇāsavabhāvaṃ jānantū”ti iccheyya, na naṃ manussā “bahi hothā”ti vadeyyuṃ, khīṇāsavānaṃ pana tathācittameva na uppajjeyya.

'Atilūkhabhāvaṃ' refers to extreme roughness with regard to bowl and robes. Seeing this, people thought, "Today is an inauspicious day; this venerable one with rough bowl and robes should be made to go first," and said, "Venerable sir, please stay outside for a while." 'Ummujji' means he emerged, having submerged into the earth and taken the requisites, without the people knowing. If the elder had wished, "Let them know my state as one whose taints are destroyed," people would not have told him, "Stay outside." But for those whose taints are destroyed, such a thought does not even arise.

Appicchatāpadhānaṃ puggalādhiṭṭhānaṃ catubbidhaicchāpabhedaṃ dassetvā punapi puggalādhiṭṭhānena catubbidhaṃ icchābhedaṃ dassento “aparopi catubbidho appiccho”tiādimāha. Paccayaappicchoti paccayesu icchārahito. Dhutaṅgaappicchoti dhutaguṇasambhāvanāya icchārahito. Pariyattiappicchoti bahussutasambhāvanāya icchārahito. Adhigamaappicchoti “ariyo”ti sambhāvanāya icchārahito. Dāyakassa vasanti appaṃ vā yaṃ dātukāmo bahuṃ vāti dāyakassa cittassa vasaṃ, ajjhāsayanti attho. Deyyadhammassa vasanti deyyadhammassa abahubhāvaṃ. Attano thāmanti attano pamāṇaṃ. Yattakena attā yāpeti, tattakasseva gahaṇaṃ. Yadi hītiādi saṅkhepato vuttassa atthassa vivaraṇaṃ. Pamāṇenevāti yāpanappamāṇeneva.

Having few desires is the principal matter. Having shown the fourfold division of desire based on the individual, it further shows a fourfold division of desire based on the individual, stating, "Again, another fourfold person of few desires" and so on. 'Paccayaappiccho' means 'one without desire for requisites.' 'Dhutaṅgaappiccho' means 'one without desire for the esteem of ascetic qualities.' 'Pariyattiappiccho' means 'one without desire for the esteem of being very learned.' 'Adhigamaappiccho' means 'one without desire for the esteem of being 'noble'.' 'Dāyakassa vasaṃ' means 'according to the donor's intention, whether he wishes to give little or much'; that is the meaning of 'ajjhāsayassa vasaṃ.' 'Deyyadhammassa vasaṃ' means 'the non-abundance of the gift.' 'Attano thāmaṃ' means 'one's own capacity.' Taking only as much as one sustains oneself with. 'Yadi hi' and so on is an explanation of the meaning stated in brief. 'Pamāṇeneva' means 'only by the measure for sustaining life'.

Ekabhikkhupi nāññāsīti sosānikavatte sammadeva vattitattā ekopi bhikkhu na aññāsi. Abbokiṇṇanti avicchedaṃ. Dutiyo maṃ jāneyyāti dutiyo sahāyabhūtopi yathā maṃ jānituṃ na sakkuṇeyya, tathā saṭṭhi vassāni nirantaraṃ susāne vasāmi, tasmā ahaṃ aho sosānikuttamo. Upakāro hutvāti uggahaparipucchādīhi pariyattidhammavasena upakāro hutvā. Dhammakathāya janapadaṃ khobhetvāti lomahaṃsanasādhukāradānacelukkhepādivasena sannipatitaṃ itarañca “kathaṃ nu kho appaṃ ayyassa santike dhammaṃ sossāmā”ti kolāhalavasena mahājanaṃ khobhetvā? Yadi thero bahussutabhāvaṃ jānāpetuṃ iccheyya, pubbeva janapadaṃ khobhento dhammaṃ katheyya. Gatoti “ayaṃ so, yena rattiyaṃ dhammakathā katā”ti jānanabhāvena pariyattiappicchatāya purāruṇāva gato.

'Not even a single monk knew' means 'not even one monk knew, because he properly maintained the practice of dwelling in a charnel ground.' 'Abbokiṇṇaṃ' means 'uninterrupted.' 'May a second not know me' means 'so that not even a second companion would be able to know me, thus I lived for sixty years without interruption in the charnel ground; therefore, ah, I am the foremost among those who dwell in charnel grounds.' 'Having been of help' means 'having been of help by means of learning, questioning, and so on, by way of the Dhamma of the scriptures.' 'By teaching the Dhamma, he stirred up the countryside' means 'having stirred up the great multitude—both those assembled, by means of hair-raising, applause, the throwing of cloths, and so on, and others—through the uproar, "How indeed shall we hear even a little Dhamma from the venerable one?"' If the elder had wished to make known his great learning, he would have taught the Dhamma, stirring up the countryside beforehand. 'Gone' means 'he had left before dawn, due to his fewness of wishes regarding his learning, so that people would not know, "This is the one who gave the Dhamma talk last night".'

Tayo [M 1.0114] kulaputtā viyāti pācīnavaṃsadāye sāmaggivāsaṃvuṭṭhā anuruddho, nandiyo, kimiloti ime tayo kulaputtā viya. Etesupi hi anuruddhattherena bhagavatā “atthi pana vo anuruddhā evaṃ appamattānaṃ ātāpīnaṃ pahitattānaṃ viharantānaṃ uttarimanussadhammo alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso adhigato phāsuvihāro”ti (ma. ni. 1.328) puṭṭhena “idha pana mayaṃ, bhante, yāvadeva ākaṅkhāma, vivicceva kāmehi vivicca akusalehi dhammehi savitakkaṃ savicāraṃ vivekajaṃ pītisukhaṃ paṭhamaṃ jhānaṃ upasampajja viharāmā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.328) anupubbavihārasamāpattīsu [V 1.0104] ārocitāsu itare therā na icchiṃsu. Tathā hi te pakkante bhagavati āyasmantaṃ anuruddhaṃ etadavocuṃ – “kinnu mayaṃ āyasmato anuruddhassa evamārocimha ‘imāsañca imāsañca vihārasamāpattīnaṃ mayaṃ lābhino’ti? Yaṃ no āyasmā anuruddho bhagavato sammukhāpi āsavānaṃ khayaṃ pakāsetī”ti? Ghaṭīkāropi attano ariyabhāve kikissa rañño bhagavatā ārocite na attamano ahosi? Tenāha – “ghaṭīkārakumbhakāro viyā”ti. Imasmiṃ panattheti “yathayidaṃ, bhikkhave, appicchatā”ti vutte appicchatāsaṅkhāte atthe. Balavaalobhenāti daḷhatarappavattikena alobhena.

'Like the three men of good family' means 'like these three men of good family, Anuruddha, Nandiya, and Kimbila, who had taken up residence in harmony in the eastern bamboo grove.' For indeed, among them, when the Venerable Anuruddha was asked by the Blessed One, "But have you, Anuruddhas, while dwelling thus diligent, ardent, and resolute, attained any superhuman state, a distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones, a pleasant abiding?" (MN 1.328), and when the successive meditative attainments were declared by him, beginning with, "Here, venerable sir, as long as we wish, we dwell having entered and abided in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, born of seclusion, filled with rapture and pleasure..." (MN 1.328), the other elders were not pleased. For when the Blessed One had departed, they said this to the Venerable Anuruddha: "Did we, venerable Anuruddha, declare to you, 'We are attainers of these and these meditative attainments,' that you have proclaimed the destruction of the taints in the presence of the Blessed One?" Was Ghaṭīkāra also not pleased when his noble state was revealed by the Blessed One to King Kikī? Therefore, it is said: "Like Ghaṭīkāra the potter." 'In this context' means 'in the meaning designated as fewness of wishes, when it was said, "Monks, this is fewness of wishes".' 'With strong non-greed' means 'with non-greed that proceeds very firmly.'

64. Catutthe natthi etassa santuṭṭhīti asantuṭṭhi, tassa bhāvo asantuṭṭhitā. Taṃ pana sarūpato dassento “asantuṭṭhe puggale…pe… lobho”ti āha. Sevantassātiādīni aññamaññavevacanāni.

64. In the fourth, "there is no contentment for him" is asantuṭṭhi (discontent); its state is asantuṭṭhitā (discontentment). But showing it in its essential nature, he says, "In a discontented person... greed." 'Sevantassa' and so on are synonyms for each other.

65-67. Pañcame tussanaṃ tuṭṭhi, samaṃ, sakena, santena vā tuṭṭhi etassāti santuṭṭhi, tassa bhāvo santuṭṭhitā. Yassa santosassa atthitāya bhikkhu “santuṭṭho”ti vuccati, taṃ dassento “itarītarapaccayasantosena samannāgatassā”ti āha – cīvarādike yattha katthaci kappiye paccaye santussanena samaṅgībhūtassāti attho. Atha vā itaraṃ vuccati hīnaṃ paṇītato aññattā, tathā paṇītampi itaraṃ hīnato aññattā. Apekkhāsiddhā hi itaratā. Iti yena dhammena hīnena vā paṇītena vā cīvarādipaccayena santussati, so tathā pavatto alobho itarītarapaccayasantoso, tena samannāgatassa[M 1.0115]. Yathālābhaṃ attano lābhānurūpaṃ santoso yathālābhasantoso. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Labbhatīti vā lābho, yo yo lābho yathālābho, tena santoso yathālābhasantoso. Balanti kāyabalaṃ. Sāruppanti bhikkhuno anucchavikatā.

65-67. In the fifth, 'tussanaṃ' is 'tuṭṭhi' (satisfaction); 'santuṭṭhi' is 'satisfaction with what is equal, with one's own, or with what is'; its state is 'santuṭṭhitā' (contentment). Showing that by reason of the existence of this contentment a monk is called 'santuṭṭho' (content), he says: 'endowed with contentment with whatever requisite'—meaning 'complete with contentment with any allowable requisite whatsoever, such as robes.' Or alternatively, 'itaraṃ' (other) is said of the inferior because it is different from the superior, and likewise, the superior is 'itaraṃ' because it is different from the inferior. For 'otherness' is established by relation. Thus, that non-greed, so arisen, by which one is content with any requisite such as robes, whether inferior or superior—that is 'contentment with whatever requisite' (itarītarapaccayasantoso); 'endowed with that' (tena samannāgatassa). 'Contentment with what is obtained' (yathālābhasantoso) is contentment in accordance with one's own gain. The same method applies to the remaining two terms. Or, 'gain' (lābho) is what is obtained (labbhati); whatever gain, that is 'as obtained' (yathālābho); contentment with that is 'contentment with what is obtained' (yathālābhasantoso). 'Balaṃ' means 'bodily strength.' 'Sāruppaṃ' means 'suitability for a monk'.

Yathāladdhato aññassa apatthanā nāma siyā appicchatāpi pavattiākāroti tato vinivecitameva santosassa sarūpaṃ dassento “labhantopi na gaṇhātī”ti āha. Taṃ parivattetvā pakatidubbalādīnaṃ garucīvaraṃ aphāsubhāvāvahaṃ sarīrakhedāvahañca hotīti payojanavasena na atricchatādivasena taṃ parivattetvā lahukacīvaraparibhogo santosavirodhi na hotīti āha – “lahukena yāpentopi santuṭṭhova hotī”ti. Mahagghacīvaraṃ bahūni vā cīvarāni labhitvā tāni vissajjetvā tadaññassa gahaṇaṃ yathāsāruppanaye ṭhitattā na santosavirodhīti āha – “tesaṃ…pe… dhārentopi santuṭṭhova hotī”ti. Evaṃ sesapaccayesupi yathāsāruppaniddese [V 1.0105] api-saddaggahaṇe adhippāyo veditabbo. Muttaharītakanti gomuttaparibhāvitaṃ, pūtibhāvena vā chaḍḍitaṃ harītakaṃ. Buddhādīhi vaṇṇitanti appicchatāsantuṭṭhīsu bhikkhū niyojetuṃ “pūtimuttabhesajjaṃ nissāya pabbajjā”tiādinā (mahāva. 73, 128) buddhādīhi pasatthaṃ. Paramasantuṭṭhova hoti paramena ukkaṃsagatena santosena samannāgatattā. Yathāsāruppasantosova aggoti tattha tattha bhikkhu sāruppaṃyeva nissāya santussanavasena pavattanato aggo. Chaṭṭhasattamesu natthi vattabbaṃ.

Since not desiring something other than what has been obtained is a characteristic of having few wishes, showing the nature of contentment as distinguished from that, it is said: "Even when obtaining, he does not accept." And if, for one who is naturally weak and so on, a heavy robe brings discomfort and bodily fatigue, then exchanging it for a light robe for a practical reason, not out of excessive desire, does not conflict with contentment; thus it is said: "Even while maintaining himself with a light one, he remains content." Having obtained an expensive robe or many robes, giving them away and taking another is not in conflict with contentment, because one stands in the method of what is suitable; thus it is said: "...even when wearing another suitable robe, he remains content." In this way, the intention of including the word 'api' in the explanation of what is suitable regarding the remaining requisites should also be understood. 'Muttaharītaka' means myrobalan steeped in cow urine, or myrobalan discarded because it is putrid. 'Praised by the Buddha and others' means praised by the Buddha and others in order to apply monks to fewness of wishes and contentment, as in: "The going forth relies on medicine of putrid urine," etc. (Mahāvagga 73, 128). 'He is supremely content' because he is endowed with supreme contentment that has reached the highest point. 'Contentment with what is suitable is supreme' means it is the highest because in every case a monk proceeds by way of contentment, relying only on what is suitable. There is nothing to be said about the sixth and seventh.

68-69. Aṭṭhamanavamesu na sampajānātīti asampajāno, tassa bhāvo asampajaññaṃ. Vuttappaṭipakkhena sampajaññaṃ veditabbaṃ.

68-69. In the eighth and ninth, 'one who does not fully comprehend' is asampajāno; the state of that is asampajañña. Sampajañña (full comprehension) should be understood by the opposite of what was stated.

70. Dasame pāpamittā devadattasadisā. Te hi hīnācāratāya, dukkhassa vā sampāpakatāya “pāpā”ti vuccanti. Tenākārena pavattānanti yo pāpamittassa khanti ruci adhimutti tanninnatātaṃsampavaṅkatādiākāro, tenākārena pavattānaṃ. Catunnaṃ khandhānamevetaṃ nāmanti catunnaṃ arūpakkhandhānaṃ [M 1.0116] “pāpamittatā”ti etaṃ nāmaṃ. Yasmā assaddhiyādipāpadhammasamannāgatā puggalā visesato pāpā puññadhammavimokkhatāya, te yassa mittā sahāyā, so pāpamitto, tassa bhāvo pāpamittatā. Tenāha – “ye te puggalā assaddhā”tiādi.

70. In the tenth, evil friends are like Devadatta. Indeed, they are called 'evil' because of their low conduct or because they lead to suffering. 'Those who behave in that manner' refers to the manner of tolerance, liking, inclination, tendency, association, etc., of an evil friend. 'This is merely a name for the four aggregates' means that this name 'evil friendship' applies to the four immaterial aggregates. Because individuals endowed with evil qualities such as lack of faith are especially evil due to their being devoid of wholesome qualities and liberation, whoever has them as friends or companions is an evil friend, and the state of being such is called 'evil friendship.' Therefore, it is said: 'Those individuals who are faithless...' and so on.

Vīriyārambhādivaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the chapter beginning with the Exertion of Energy is concluded.

8. Kalyāṇamittādivaggavaṇṇanā

8. Commentary on the Chapter beginning with Good Friendship.

71. Aṭṭhamassa [V 1.0106] paṭhame buddhā, sāriputtādayo vā kalyāṇamittā. Vuttapaṭipakkhanayenāti “pāpamittatā”ti pade vuttassa paṭipakkhanayena.

71. In the first of the eighth, the Buddhas, or Sāriputta and others, are good friends. 'By way of the opposite of what was stated' means by way of the opposite of what was stated in the term 'evil friendship'.

72-73. Dutiye yogoti samaṅgībhāvo. Payogoti payuñjanaṃ paṭipatti. Ayogoti asamaṅgībhāvo. Appayogoti appayuñjanaṃ appaṭipatti. Anuyogenāti anuyogahetu.

72-73. In the second, 'yoga' means being in harmony. 'Payoga' means applying, practice. 'Ayoga' means not being in harmony. 'Appayoga' means not applying, non-practice. 'Anuyogena' means because of application.

74. Catutthe bujjhanakasattassāti catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ paṭivijjhanakapuggalassa. Aṅgabhūtāti tasseva paṭivedhassa kāraṇabhūtā. Ettha ca cattāri ariyasaccāni bujjhati, aññāṇaniddāya vāpi bujjhatīti bodhīti laddhanāmo ariyasāvako bujjhanakasatto, tassa bujjhanakasattassa. Bodhiyāti tassā dhammasāmaggisaṅkhātāya bodhiyā. Bujjhanaṭṭhena bodhiyo, bodhiyo eva saccasampaṭibodhassa aṅgāti vuttaṃ. “Bujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā”ti. Vipassanādīnaṃ kāraṇānaṃ bujjhitabbānañca saccānaṃ anurūpaṃ bujjhanato anubujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, paṭimukhaṃ paccakkhabhāvena abhimukhaṃ bujjhanato paṭibujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā, sammā aviparītato bujjhanato sambujjhantīti bojjhaṅgāti evaṃ atthavisesadīpakehi upasaggehi anubujjhantītiādi vuttaṃ. Bodhisaddo sabbavisesayuttaṃ bujjhanasāmaññena saṅgaṇhāti. Bodhāya saṃvattantīti iminā tassā dhammasāmaggiyā bujjhanassa ekantakāraṇataṃ dasseti. Evaṃ panetaṃ padaṃ vibhattamevāti vuttappakārena etaṃ “bojjhaṅgā”ti (paṭi. ma. 2.17) padaṃ niddese paṭisambhidāmagge vibhattameva.

74. In the fourth, 'of the awakening-being' refers to the individual who penetrates the four noble truths. 'Factors' means they are causes of that very penetration. Here, the noble disciple is called an 'awakening-being' because he awakens to the four noble truths, or awakens from the slumber of ignorance, thus obtaining the name 'bodhi'; it is of that awakening-being. 'Of awakening' refers to that awakening which is designated as the harmony of the Dhamma. They are 'bodhi' (awakenings) in the sense of awakening; indeed, the 'bodhi' are factors for the full understanding of the truths, as it is said: 'They awaken, thus they are bojjhaṅgas.' Because they awaken in conformity with the causes, such as insight, and the truths to be awakened to, they awaken accordingly (anubujjhanti), thus they are bojjhaṅgas; because they awaken directly through personal experience, they awaken towards (paṭibujjhanti), thus they are bojjhaṅgas; because they awaken correctly without distortion, they awaken completely (sambujjhanti), thus they are bojjhaṅgas. In this way, 'they awaken accordingly,' etc., is said with prefixes that highlight distinctions in meaning. The term 'bodhi' encompasses all specific aspects under the general notion of awakening. 'They conduce to awakening'—by this, it shows that that harmony of the Dhamma is the exclusive cause of awakening. Thus this term is indeed analyzed; in the manner stated, this word 'bojjhaṅgas' (Paṭi. ma. 2.17) is indeed analyzed in the Niddesa in the Paṭisambhidāmagga.

75. Pañcame [M 1.0117] yāthāvasarasabhūmīti yāthāvato sakiccakaraṇabhūmi. Sāti yāthāvasarasabhūmi. Vipassanāti balavavipassanā. Keci “bhaṅgañāṇato paṭṭhāyā”ti vadanti. Vipassanāya pādakajjhāne ca satiādayo bojjhaṅgapakkhikā eva pariyāyabodhipakkhiyabhāvato. Tatthātiādi catubbidhānaṃ bojjhaṅgānaṃ bhūmivibhāgadassanaṃ.

75. In the fifth, 'the ground of suitable opportunity' means the ground for performing one's own task appropriately. That is the ground of suitable opportunity. 'Insight' means powerful insight. Some say, 'starting from the knowledge of dissolution.' When insight and the foundational jhāna are present, mindfulness and the others are indeed allied with the enlightenment factors, because they belong to the side of awakening indirectly. 'There,' etc., is the showing of the division of grounds for the four kinds of enlightenment factors.

76. Chaṭṭhe tesaṃ antareti tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ antare. Kāmaṃ saṅgītiāruḷhavasena appakamidaṃ suttapadaṃ, bhagavā panettha sannipatitaparisāya ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ vitthārikaṃ karotīti katvā idaṃ vuttaṃ – “mahatī desanā bhavissatī”ti. Gāmanigamādikathā natthīti tassā kathāya atiracchānakathābhāvamāhu[V 1.0107]. Tathā hi sā pubbe bahuñātikaṃ ahosi bahupakkhaṃ, idāni appañātikaṃ appapakkhanti aniccatāmukhena niyyānikapakkhikā jātā. Etāyāti yathāvuttāya parihāniyā. Patikiṭṭhanti nihīnaṃ. Mama sāsaneti idaṃ kammassakatajjhānapaññānampi visesanameva. Tadubhayampi hi bāhirakānaṃ tappaññādvayato sātisayameva sabbaññubuddhānaṃ desanāya laddhavisesato vivaṭṭūpanissayato ca.

76. In the sixth, 'among them' means among those bhikkhus. Although this Sutta passage is brief because it has been included in the council recitation, the Blessed One here elaborates extensively in accordance with the disposition of the assembled gathering, and for this reason it is said: 'There will be a great teaching.' There is no talk about villages, towns, etc.—they say this because that talk was not animal talk. For previously, it was well-known and had many supporters, but now it is little-known and has few supporters—thus, through the gateway of impermanence, it has become allied with what leads to liberation. 'By this' means by the aforesaid decline. 'Degraded' means inferior. 'In my dispensation'—this is a distinction even of the wisdom of ownership of kamma and of jhāna. For both of these are indeed superior to the two kinds of wisdom of outsiders, because of the distinction obtained from the teaching of the omniscient Buddhas and because it is a basis for turning away from the round of existence.

77. Sattame tesaṃ cittācāraṃ ñatvāti tathā kathentānaṃ tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tattha upagamanena attano desanāya bhājanabhūtaṃ cittappavattiṃ ñatvā. Kammassakatādīti ādisaddena jhānapaññādīnaṃ catunnampi paññānaṃ gahaṇaṃ.

77. In the seventh, 'having known their mental conduct' means having known the state of mind of those bhikkhus who were speaking thus, which had become a vessel for his teaching by their approaching that place. 'Ownership of kamma, etc.'—by the word 'etc.' the four kinds of wisdom, such as the wisdom of jhāna, are included.

78-80. Aṭṭhamādīsu heṭṭhā vuttanayenevāti “yā esa mama sāsane”tiādinā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

78-80. In the eighth and so on, it is by the method stated previously; that is, by the method stated previously, beginning with 'This which is in my dispensation…' The rest here is of obvious meaning.

Kalyāṇamittādivaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter Beginning with the Good Friend is concluded.

81-82. Navame vagge natthi vattabbaṃ.

81-82. In the ninth chapter, there is nothing to be said.

10. Dutiyapamādādivaggavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Second Chapter Beginning with Heedlessness.

98-115. Dasame [V 1.0108] vagge ajjhattasantāne bhavaṃ ajjhattikaṃ. Ajjhattasantānato bahiddhā bhavaṃ bāhiraṃ. Vuttapaṭipakkhanayenāti “avināsāyā”ti evamādinā attho gahetabbo. Catukkoṭiketi “anuyogo akusalānaṃ[M 1.0118], ananuyogo kusalānaṃ, anuyogo kusalānaṃ, ananuyogo akusalāna”nti (a. ni. 1.96) evaṃ pariyosānasutte āgatanayaṃ gahetvā “nāhaṃ, bhikkhave, aññaṃ ekadhammampi samanupassāmī”tiādinā (a. ni. 1.11) āgatasuttānaṃ samaññā jātā.

98-115. In the tenth chapter, 'internal' (ajjhattika) is what exists within one's own continuum. 'External' (bāhira) is what exists outside one's own continuum. 'By the method of the stated opposite' means the meaning should be understood as 'for non-decline,' and so on. The 'fourfold scheme' refers to this: having taken the method that comes in the concluding Sutta—'application to unwholesome states, non-application to wholesome states, application to wholesome states, non-application to unwholesome states' (AN 1.96)—the collective name for the Suttas that begin 'Bhikkhus, I do not perceive even one other thing...' (AN 1.11) has arisen.

130. Suttantanaye yathācodanā saṃkilesadhammānaṃ vipariyesanaṃ, taṃtaṃdhammakoṭṭhāsānañca ūnato adhikato ca pavedanaṃ adhammaṃ dhammoti dīpanaṃ. Tesaṃyeva pana aviparītato anūnādhikato ca pavedanaṃ dhammaṃ dhammoti dīpanaṃ. Evaṃ vinayappaṭipattiyā ayathāvidhippavedanaṃ adhammaṃ dhammoti dīpanaṃ. Yathāvidhippavedanaṃ dhammaṃ dhammoti dīpanaṃ. Suttantanayena pañcavidho saṃvaravinayo pahānavinayo ca vinayo, tappaṭipakkhena avinayo. Vinayanayena vatthusampadādinā yathāvidhippaṭipatti eva vinayo, tabbipariyāyena avinayo veditabbo. Tiṃsa nissaggiyā pācittiyāti ettha iti-saddo ādyattho. Tena dvenavuti pācittiyā, cattāro pāṭidesaniyā, satta adhikaraṇasamathāti imesaṃ saṅgaho. Ekatiṃsa nissaggiyāti ettha “tenavuti pācittiyā”tiādinā vattabbaṃ. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

130. According to the Suttanta method, the misrepresentation of defiling qualities as they are pointed out, and the declaration of those respective portions of the Dhamma as deficient or excessive, is the proclamation of non-Dhamma as Dhamma. But the declaration of those same qualities without misrepresentation, without deficiency or excess, is the proclamation of Dhamma as Dhamma. Similarly, regarding the practice of the Vinaya, the declaration of conduct not in accordance with the rule is the proclamation of non-Dhamma as Dhamma. The declaration of conduct in accordance with the rule is the proclamation of Dhamma as Dhamma. According to the Suttanta method, the fivefold discipline of restraint and the discipline of abandonment are 'discipline' (vinaya), while their opposite is 'non-discipline' (avinayo). According to the Vinaya method, practice in accordance with the rule, beginning with the fulfillment of the basis, is indeed 'discipline'; its opposite should be understood as 'non-discipline'. In 'thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiyas,' the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so on.' By this, the ninety-two Pācittiyas, four Pāṭidesanīyas, and seven Adhikaraṇasamathas are included. Regarding 'thirty-one Nissaggiyas,' it should be stated 'ninety-three Pācittiyas,' and so on. The rest here is easily understood.

Adhigantabbato adhigamo, maggaphalāni. Nibbānaṃ pana antaradhānābhāvato idha na gayhati. Paṭipajjanaṃ paṭipatti, sikkhattayasamāyogo. Paṭipajjitabbato vā paṭipatti. Pariyāpuṇitabbato pariyatti, piṭakattayaṃ. Maggaggahaṇena gahitāpi tatiyavijjāchaṭṭhābhiññā vijjābhiññāsāmaññato “tisso vijjā cha abhiññā”ti punapi gahitā. Tato paraṃ cha abhiññāti vassasahassato paraṃ cha abhiññā nibbattetuṃ sakkonti, na paṭisambhidāti adhippāyo. Tatoti abhiññākālato pacchā. Tāti abhiññāyo. Pubbabhāge jhānasinehābhāvena kevalāya vipassanāya ṭhatvā aggaphalappattā sukkhavipassakā nāma, maggakkhaṇe pana “jhānasineho natthī”ti na vattabbo “samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ bhāvetī”ti (a. ni. 4.170) vacanato. Pacchimakassāti sabbapacchimassa. Kiñcāpi ariyo aparihānadhammo[V 1.0109][M 1.0119], sotāpannassa pana uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā adhigatadhammo uppanno nāma natthi, paccayasāmaggiyā asati yāva uparivisesaṃ nibbattetuṃ na sakkonti, tāva adhigamassa asambhavo evāti āha – “sotāpannassa…pe… nāma hotī”ti. Tassidaṃ manussalokavasena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Attainment' (adhigama) is so called because it is to be attained; this refers to the paths and fruits. Nibbāna, however, is not included here because it does not disappear. 'Practice' (paṭipatti) is the act of practicing, the undertaking of the threefold training; or, 'practice' is so called because it is to be practiced. 'Learning' (pariyatti) is so called because it is to be learned; this refers to the three Piṭakas. Although the third knowledge and the sixth higher knowledge are included by the mention of the path, they are included again as 'the three knowledges and the six higher knowledges' due to the general terms 'knowledge' and 'higher knowledge'. After that, the six higher knowledges: the meaning is that after a thousand years, they are able to produce the six higher knowledges, but not the analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā). 'After that' means after the time of the higher knowledges. 'Those' means the higher knowledges. In the earlier period, those who attain the highest fruit by standing in bare insight, without affection for jhāna, are called 'dry-insight practitioners'. At the moment of the path, however, it should not be said that 'there is no affection for jhāna,' because of the statement 'one develops serenity and insight yoked together' (AN 4.170). 'Of the last one' means of the very last one. Although a noble one is of a nature not to decline, for a stream-enterer, beyond the end of life, no attained state arises. As long as there is an absence of the convergence of conditions and they are unable to produce a higher distinction, there is simply no possibility of attainment. Thus it is said: 'For a stream-enterer... it is called.' This should be understood as being stated with reference to the human world.

Na codentīti aññamaññasmiṃ vijjamānaṃ dosaṃ jānantāpi na codenti na sārenti. Akukkuccakā hontīti kukkuccaṃ na uppādenti. “Asakkaccakārino hontī”ti ca paṭhanti, sāthalikatāya sikkhāsu asakkaccakārino hontīti attho. Bhikkhūnaṃ satepi sahassepi dharamāneti idaṃ bāhullavasena vuttaṃ. Antimavatthuanajjhāpannesu katipayamattesupi bhikkhūsu dharantesu, ekasmiṃ vā dharante paṭipatti anantarahitā eva nāma hoti. Tenevāha – “pacchimakassa…pe… antarahitā hotī”ti.

'They do not blame' means that even knowing faults exist among themselves, they neither accuse nor remind. 'They are free from remorse' means they do not give rise to remorse. It is also read as 'they are without earnestness,' meaning they are without earnestness in the trainings due to laxity. Even if a hundred or a thousand monks are maintaining it, this is stated in terms of abundance. Even if only a few monks, or even one, maintains it among those who have not fallen into the final offense, the practice is indeed uninterrupted. Therefore he said: 'When the last one... it disappears.'

Antevāsike gahetunti antevāsike saṅgahetuṃ. Atthavasenāti aṭṭhakathāvasena. Matthakato paṭṭhāyāti uparito paṭṭhāya. Uposathakkhandhakamattanti vinayamātikāpāḷimāha. Āḷavakapañhādīnaṃ viya devesu pariyattiyā pavatti appamāṇanti āha – “manussesū”ti.

'To take the pupils' means to gather the pupils. 'For the sake of meaning' means according to the commentary. 'Starting from the culmination' means starting from above. 'Just the Uposatha Khandhaka' refers to the Vinaya-matrix text. He said 'among humans,' indicating that, like the Āḷavaka questions and others, the extent of the teaching's prevalence among the devas is immeasurable.

Oṭṭhaṭṭhivaṇṇanti oṭṭhānaṃ aṭṭhivaṇṇaṃ, dantakasāvaṃ ekaṃ vā dve vā vāre rajitvā dantavaṇṇaṃ katvā dhārentīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kesesu vā allīyāpentīti tena kāsāvakhaṇḍena kese bandhantā allīyāpenti. Bhikkhugottassa abhibhavanato vināsanato gotrabhuno. Atha vā gottaṃ vuccati sādhāraṇaṃ nāmaṃ, mattasaddo luttaniddiṭṭho, tasmā “samaṇā”ti gottamattaṃ anubhavanti dhārentīti gotrabhuno, nāmamattasamaṇāti attho. Kāsāvagatakaṇṭhatāya, kāsāvaggahaṇahetuuppajjanakasokatāya vā kāsāvakaṇṭhā. Saṅghagatanti saṅghaṃ uddissa dinnattā saṅghagataṃ. Taṃ sarīranti taṃ dhātusarīraṃ.

'The color of bones on the lips' means the bone-color of the lips. Having dyed them one or two times with yellow dye to make the teeth bone-colored, they wear it—this is what is meant. Or, 'they attach it to their hair' means that tying their hair with a piece of yellow robe, they attach it. Due to overpowering and destroying the lineage of the bhikkhu, it is 'gotrabhu' (lineage-destroying). Alternatively, 'gotta' (lineage) is said to be a common name; the word 'matta' (mere) is implicitly stated. Therefore, 'gotrabhu' means they experience or bear merely the designation 'ascetic,' meaning they are ascetics in name only. 'Yellow-robed around the neck' means having the yellow robe around the neck, or due to the sorrow arising from having taken the yellow robe. 'Belonging to the Sangha' means it belongs to the Sangha because it was given for the Sangha. 'That body' refers to that relic-containing body.

Tenevāti pariyattiantaradhānamūlakattā eva itaraantaradhānassa. Sakko devarājā chātakabhaye paratīragamanāya bhikkhū ussukkamakāsīti adhippāyo. Neti ubhayepi paṃsukūlikatthere dhammakathikatthere ca. Therāti tattha ṭhitā sakkhibhūtā therā. Dhammakathikattherā “yāva tiṭṭhanti [M 1.0120] suttantā…pe… yogakkhemā na dhaṃsatī”ti idaṃ suttaṃ āharitvā “suttante rakkhite sante, paṭipatti hoti rakkhitā”ti iminā vacanena paṃsukūlikatthere appaṭibhāne akaṃsu[V 1.0110]. Idāni pariyattiyā anantaradhānameva itaresaṃ anantaradhānahetūti imamatthaṃ byatirekato anvayato ca upamāhi vibhāvetuṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Taṃ suviññeyyameva.

'Thus' means that the disappearance of the teaching (pariyatti) is indeed the root cause of the disappearance of other things. The meaning is that Sakka, king of devas, urged the bhikkhus to go to the other shore out of fear of famine. 'No' refers to both the refuse-rag elders and the Dhamma-preaching elders. 'Elders' means the elders who were present there as witnesses. The Dhamma-preaching elders, bringing forward this sutta, 'as long as the suttantas remain...peace from bondage does not decay...', rendered the refuse-rag elders speechless with this statement: 'When the suttantas are protected, practice is protected.' Now, to explain this meaning—that the non-disappearance of the teaching is the cause of the non-disappearance of the others—by way of both negation and affirmation with similes, 'Just as...' and so on was said. That is easily understood.

Dutiyapamādādivaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Explanation of the Second Chapter Beginning with Heedlessness is completed.

140-150. Ekādasamadvādasamavaggā suviññeyyā eva.

140-150. The eleventh and twelfth chapters are easily understood.

13. Ekapuggalavaggavaṇṇanā

13. Commentary on the Chapter of the Single Person

170. Ekapuggalassāti [V 1.0111] ekapuggalavaggassa. Tenāha – “paṭhame”ti. Ekoti gaṇanaparicchedo, tato eva dutiyādipaṭikkhepattho. Padhānāsahāyatthopi ekasaddo hotīti tannivattanatthaṃ “gaṇanaparicchedo”ti āha. Sammutiyā desanā sammutidesanā. Paramatthassa desanā paramatthadesanā. Tatthāti sammutiparamatthadesanāsu, na sammutiparamatthesu. Tenāha – “evarūpā sammutidesanā, evarūpā paramatthadesanā”ti. Tatridaṃ sammutiparamatthānaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ – yasmiṃ bhinne, buddhiyā vā avayavavinibbhoge kate na taṃsamaññā, sā ghaṭapaṭādippabhedā sammuti, tabbipariyāyena paramatthā. Na hi kakkhaḷaphusanādisabhāve so nayo labbhati. Tattha rūpādidhammasamūhaṃ santānavasena pavattamānaṃ upādāya puggalavohāroti puggaloti sammutidesanā. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Uppādavayavanto sabhāvadhammā na niccāti aniccāti āha – “aniccanti paramatthadesanā”ti. Esa nayo sesapadesupi. Nanu khandhadesanāpi sammutidesanāva. Rāsaṭṭho vā hi khandhaṭṭho koṭṭhāsaṭṭho vāti? Saccametaṃ, ayaṃ pana khandhasamaññā phassādīsu pavattatajjāpaññatti viya paramatthasannissayā tassa āsannatarā, puggalasamaññādayo viya na dūreti paramatthasaṅgahā vuttā. Khandhasīsena vā tadupādānasabhāvadhammā eva gahitā. Nanu ca sabhāvadhammā sabbepi sammutimukheneva desanaṃ ārohanti, na samukhenāti sabbāpi desanā sammutidesanāva siyāti? Nayidamevaṃ, desetabbadhammavibhāgena desanāvibhāgassa adhippetattā. Na hi saddo kenaci pavattinimittena vinā atthaṃ pakāsetīti.

170. ‘Of a single person’ (ekapuggalassa) refers to the chapter on a single person (ekapuggalavagga). Therefore he says, ‘in the first’. ‘One’ (eka) is a numerical limit, and from that, the meaning is the rejection of the second and so on. The word ‘one’ can also mean ‘principal’ or ‘without a companion’; therefore, to exclude that, he says, ‘a numerical limit’. A teaching by way of convention is conventional teaching. A teaching of ultimate reality is ultimate teaching. There (tatthā) means in conventional and ultimate teachings, not in conventional and ultimate realities themselves. Therefore he says, ‘Such is conventional teaching, such is ultimate teaching’. Here is the characteristic of conventional and ultimate realities: When something is divided, or when its parts are mentally analyzed and separated, and the designation no longer applies—such as a pot, a cloth, and so on—that is conventional. In contrast, the ultimate is otherwise. For in the nature of hardness, contact, and so on, this reasoning is not found. There, the designation of a person (puggalavohāra) arises based on the continuum of aggregates like form and so on, which are continually occurring; thus, ‘person’ (puggala) is a conventional teaching. The same reasoning applies to the remaining terms. He says that phenomena with arising and passing away as their nature are impermanent, not permanent; thus, ‘impermanent’ (anicca) is an ultimate teaching. The same reasoning applies to the remaining terms. But isn’t the teaching of the aggregates also conventional? For is the meaning of ‘aggregate’ (khandha) that of a heap, a mass, or a collection of parts? Indeed, this is true.
