However, this designation ‘aggregate’ (khandha), like the designation of contact (phassa) and so on, which are applied to their respective realities, is closer to the ultimate, being dependent on ultimate reality, not far removed like the designations of a person and so on; thus, they are stated as included in the ultimate. Alternatively, under the heading of aggregates, the very intrinsic nature of the phenomena that are the objects of clinging is grasped. But don’t all intrinsic phenomena enter teaching through conventional means, not directly? Wouldn’t all teaching then be conventional? This is not so, because the division of teaching is intended based on the division of the phenomena to be taught. For a word does not reveal meaning without some basis for its usage.

Sammutivasena [M 1.0121] desanaṃ sutvāti “idhekacco puggalo attantapo hoti attaparitāpānuyogamanuyutto”tiādinā (pu. pa. 174) sammutimukhena pavattitadesanaṃ sutamayañāṇuppādavasena sutvā. Atthaṃ paṭivijjhitvāti tadanusārena catusaccasaṅkhātaṃ atthaṃ saha vipassanāya maggapaññāya paṭivijjhitvā. Mohaṃ pahāyāti tadekaṭṭhakilesehi saddhiṃ anavasesaṃ mohaṃ pajahitvā. Visesanti aggaphalanibbānasaṅkhātaṃ visesaṃ. Tesanti tādisānaṃ veneyyānaṃ. Paramatthavasenāti “pañcimāni, bhikkhave, indriyānī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 5.471-476 ādayo) paramatthadhammavasena. Sesaṃ anantaranaye vuttasadisameva.

‘Having heard the conventional teaching’ means having heard the teaching conveyed in conventional terms, such as ‘Here, some person is one who practices self-mortification, devoted to the pursuit of self-torment,’ and so on (Pug. 174), by way of the arising of knowledge by hearing. ‘Having penetrated the meaning’ means having penetrated the meaning designated as the Four Noble Truths, along with insight and path-wisdom, in accordance with that. ‘Having abandoned delusion’ means having completely relinquished delusion together with the defilements that have the same basis. ‘The distinction’ (visesa) refers to the supreme distinction, known as the highest fruit, Nibbāna. ‘For them’ (tesaṃ) means for such trainable beings. ‘By way of ultimate meaning’ (paramatthavasena) means by way of ultimate realities, as in ‘These, bhikkhus, are the five faculties,’ and so on (SN 5.471-476, etc.). The rest is similar to what was stated in the preceding method.

Tatrāti tassaṃ sammutivasena paramatthavasena ca desanāyaṃ. Desabhāsākusaloti nānādesabhāsāsu [V 1.0112] kusalo. Tiṇṇaṃ vedānanti nidassanamattaṃ, tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ sippuggahaṇaṭṭhānānampīti adhippāyo. Teneva sippuggahaṇaṃ parato vakkhati. Sippāni vā vijjāṭṭhānabhāvena vedantogadhāni katvā “tiṇṇaṃ vedāna”nti vuttaṃ. Kathetabbabhāvena ṭhitāni, na katthaci sannicitabhāvenāti vedānampi kathetabbabhāveneva ṭhānaṃ dīpento “guhā tīṇi nihitā na gayhantī”tiādimicchāvādaṃ paṭikkhipati. Nānāvidhā desabhāsā etesanti nānādesabhāsā.

‘There’ (tatra) means in that teaching, both in conventional terms and in ultimate terms. ‘Skilled in the dialects of various regions’ (desabhāsākusala) means skilled in the languages of various regions. ‘Of the three Vedas’ (tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ) is merely an example; the intention is also ‘of the places for acquiring arts and crafts relating to the three Vedas’. Therefore, he will explain the acquiring of crafts later. Alternatively, having made the crafts embedded in the Vedas as a place for learning sciences, it is said, ‘of the three Vedas’. They exist in a state of being spoken about, not in a state of being accumulated anywhere; thus, showing that the Vedas too have the state of being spoken about, he refutes the false doctrines beginning with ‘three things are placed in a cave; they are not grasped’. The term `nānādesabhāsā` is a compound referring to various regional languages.

Paramo uttamo attho paramattho, dhammānaṃ yathābhūtasabhāvo. Lokasaṅketamattasiddhā sammuti. Yadi evaṃ kathaṃ sammutikathāya saccatāti āha – “lokasammutikāraṇā”ti, lokasamaññaṃ nissāya pavattanatoti attho. Lokasamaññā hi abhinivesena viññeyyā, nāññāpanā ekaccassa sutassa sāvanā viya na musā anatidhāvitabbato tassā. Tenāha bhagavā – “janapadaniruttiṃ nābhiniveseyya, samaññaṃ nātidhāvaye”ti. Dhammānanti sabhāvadhammānaṃ. Bhūtakāraṇāti yathābhūtakāraṇā yathābhūtaṃ nissāya pavattanato. Sammutiṃ voharantassāti “puggalo, satto”tiādinā lokasamaññaṃ kathentassa.

The ultimate, supreme meaning is ultimate reality (paramattha), the true nature of phenomena as they are. Conventional reality (sammuti) is established merely by worldly agreement. If this is so, how can there be truth in conventional speech? It is said, ‘because of worldly convention’ (lokasammutikāraṇā), meaning it proceeds dependent on worldly designation. Worldly designations, indeed, are to be understood through acceptance, not through instruction, like the mere hearing of something taught to someone; for it is not false, as it should not be transgressed. Therefore, the Blessed One said: ‘One should not be attached to local language; one should not transgress common usage.’ ‘Of phenomena’ (dhammānaṃ) refers to phenomena with intrinsic nature. ‘By true cause’ (bhūtakāraṇā) means by a cause in accordance with reality, because it proceeds dependent on reality. ‘One who speaks conventionally’ (sammutiṃ voharantassa) refers to someone who utters worldly designations like ‘person,’ ‘being,’ and so on.

Hirottappadīpanatthanti lokapālanakicce hirottappadhamme kiccato pakāsetuṃ. Tesañhi kiccaṃ sattasantāne eva pākaṭaṃ hotīti puggalādhiṭṭhānāya kathāya taṃ vattabbaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Yasmiñhi [M 1.0122] cittuppāde kammaṃ uppannaṃ, taṃsantāne eva tassa phalassa uppatti kammassakatā. Evañhi kataviññāṇanāso akatāgamo ca natthīti sā puggalādhiṭṭhānāya eva desanāya dīpetabbā. Tehi sattehi kātabbapuññakiriyā paccattapurisakāro. Sopi santānavasena niṭṭhapetabbato puggalādhiṭṭhānāya eva kathāya dīpetabbo. Ānantariyadīpanatthanti cutianantaraṃ phalaṃ anantaraṃ nāma, tasmiṃ anantare niyuttāni taṃnibbattanena anantarakaraṇasīlāni, anantarakaraṇapayojanāni vāti ānantariyāni, mātughātādīni, tesaṃ dīpanatthaṃ. Tānipi hi santānavasena niṭṭhapetabbato “mātaraṃ jīvitā voropetī”tiādinā (paṭṭhā. 1.1.423) puggalādhiṭṭhānāya eva kathāya dīpetabbāni, tathā “so mettāsahagatena cetasā ekaṃ disaṃ pharitvā viharatī”tiādinā (dī. ni. 1.556; 3.308; ma. ni. 1.77; 2.309; 3.230; vibha. 642-643) “so anekavihitaṃ pubbenivāsaṃ anussarati ekampi jāti”ntiādinā (dī. ni. 1.244-245; ma. ni. 1.148, 384, 431; pārā. 12), “atthi dakkhiṇā dāyakato visujjhati, no paṭiggāhakato”tiādinā (ma. ni. 3.381) ca pavattā brahmavihārapubbenivāsadakkhiṇāvisuddhikathā puggalādhiṭṭhānā [V 1.0113] eva katvā dīpetabbā sattasantānavisayattā. “Aṭṭha purisapuggalā (saṃ. ni. 1.249) na samayavimutto puggalo”tiādinā (pu. pa. 2) ca paramatthakathaṃ kathentopi lokasammutiyā appahānatthaṃ puggalakathaṃ katheti. Etena vuttāvasesāya kathāya puggalādhiṭṭhānabhāve payojanaṃ sāmaññavasena saṅgahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Kāmañcetaṃ sabbaṃ apariññātavatthukānaṃ vasena vuttaṃ, pariññātavatthukānampi pana evaṃ desanā sukhāvahā hoti.

‘For the purpose of explaining shame and fear of wrongdoing’ (hirottappadīpanatthaṃ) means to clarify, by way of their function, the qualities of shame and fear of wrongdoing in their role as world protectors. For their function is evident only in the continuity of a being; thus, this should be stated in a discussion based on the individual. This same method applies to the rest. For in whatever mental state an action arises, the manifestation of its result in that very continuity is the ownership of action. For in this way, there is no destruction of a deed done nor arrival of what was not done; this must be explained by a teaching based on the individual. The meritorious deeds to be performed by those beings are the personal efforts of individuals. Since these too must be established through the continuity of a being, they should also be explained in a discussion based on the individual. ‘For the purpose of explaining the immediate karmas’ (ānantariyadīpanatthaṃ) means that the result immediately following death is called ‘immediate’ (anantara); those actions connected to it—which by their nature produce an immediate result or have an immediate purpose—are the immediate karmas (ānantariya), such as matricide; this is for the purpose of explaining them. For these too must be established through the continuity of a being, and thus should be explained in a discussion based on the individual, as in ‘one who deprives one’s mother of life’ (Paṭṭhāna 1.1.423) and so on. Similarly, the discussions on the divine abodes, recollection of past lives, and the purification of offerings, which proceed with passages such as ‘he dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness’ (Dīgha Nikāya 1.556; 3.308; Majjhima Nikāya 1.77; 2.309; 3.230; Vibhaṅga 642–643), ‘he recollects his manifold past lives, even a single birth’ (Dīgha Nikāya 1.244–245; Majjhima Nikāya 1.148, 384, 431; Pārājika 12), and ‘an offering is purified by the giver, not by the recipient’ (Majjhima Nikāya 3.381), should be explained by taking the individual as the basis, since they pertain to the domain of a being’s continuity. Even when giving a discourse on the ultimate reality, such as ‘the eight types of noble individuals’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.249) or ‘the individual who is not liberated at the proper time’ (Puggalapaññatti 2), one speaks of the individual in order not to abandon worldly convention. By this, it should be understood that the purpose for the remaining discussions being based on the individual is included in a general sense. And although all this is stated for the sake of those for whom the subject matter is not fully understood, even for those for whom it is fully understood, such a teaching brings ease.

Ekapuggaloti visiṭṭhasamācārāpassayavirahito ekapuggalo. Buddhānañhi sīlādiguṇena sadevake loke visiṭṭho nāma koci natthi, tathā sadisopi samānakāle. Tenāha – “na imasmiṃ loke parasmiṃ vā pana buddhena seṭṭho sadiso ca vijjatī”ti (vi. va. 1047; kathā. 799), tasmā sadisopi koci natthi. Hīnopi apassayabhūto nattheva. Tena vuttaṃ – “visiṭṭhasamācārāpassayavirahito ekapuggalo”ti. Ye [M 1.0123] ca sīlādiguṇehi natthi etesaṃ samāti asamā, purimakā sammāsambuddhā. Tehi samo majjhe bhinnasuvaṇṇanekkhaṃ viya nibbisiṭṭhoti asamasamaṭṭhenapi ekapuggalo aññassa tādisassa abhāvā. Tena vuttaṃ – “asadisaṭṭhenā”tiādi.

‘A unique individual’ (ekapuggala) means a single person who is without a superior, an equal in conduct, or one to lean upon. For the Buddha, in the world with its gods, there is no one superior in virtues such as morality, nor is there an equal at the same time. Therefore, it is said: ‘Neither in this world nor in the next is there found one superior or equal to the Buddha’ (Vv 83.21; Kv 18.5). Thus, there is no one equal either. Nor is there any inferior who could serve as a support. Hence, it is said: ‘a single person who is without a superior, an equal in conduct, or one to lean upon.’ Those for whom there is no equal in virtues such as morality are the ‘unequalled’ (asamā), namely, the former Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas. He is equal to them, yet distinct, like a broken gold ornament among others; therefore, also by the meaning of ‘equal to the unequalled’ (asamasama), he is a unique individual due to the absence of another like him. Hence, it is said: ‘by the meaning of being incomparable’ (asadisaṭṭhena), and so on.

Sattaloko adhippeto sattanikāye uppajjanato. Manussaloke eva uppajjati devabrahmalokānaṃ buddhānaṃ uppattiyā anokāsabhāvato. Kāmadevaloke tāva nuppajjati brahmacariyavāsassa aṭṭhānabhāvato tathā anacchariyabhāvato. Acchariyadhammā hi buddhā bhagavanto. Tesaṃ sā acchariyadhammatā devattabhāve ṭhitānaṃ loke na pākaṭā hoti yathā manussabhūtānaṃ. Devabhūte hi sammāsambuddhe dissamānaṃ buddhānubhāvaṃ devānubhāvatova loke dahati, na buddhānubhāvato. Tathā sati “ayaṃ sammāsambuddho”ti nādhimuccati na sampasīdati, issarakuttaggāhaṃ na vissajjeti, devattabhāvassa ca cirakālāvaṭṭhānato ekaccasassatavādato na parimuccati. Brahmaloke nuppajjatīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Sattānaṃ tādisaggāhavinimocanatthañhi buddhā bhagavanto manussasugatiyaṃyeva uppajjanti, na devasugatiyaṃ. Yasmā imaṃ cakkavāḷaṃ majjhe katvā iminā saddhiṃ cakkavāḷānaṃ dasasahassasseva jātikkhettabhāvo dīpito ito aññassa buddhānaṃ uppattiṭṭhānassa tepiṭake buddhavacane āgataṭṭhānassa abhāvato. Tasmā vuttaṃ – “imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷe uppajjatī”ti.

The world of beings is intended, because they arise in the abode of beings. They arise only in the human world, because the realms of devas and brahmas are not a suitable place for the arising of Buddhas. They do not arise in the desire-realm deva world, because it is not a place for living the holy life and also because of the lack of the extraordinary. For the Blessed Buddhas are possessors of extraordinary qualities. That extraordinary nature of theirs is not as evident in the world when they exist in the state of a deva as it is when they are in human form. For when a Perfectly Enlightened One is seen in the form of a deva, the world considers the Buddha’s power to be merely the power of a deva, not the power of a Buddha. In that case, one is not convinced and does not gain faith that “this is a Perfectly Enlightened One,” one does not abandon the grasping at a creator god, and, due to the long duration of existence in the deva state, one is not freed from certain eternalist views. They do not arise in the brahma world—here too, the same method applies. It is for the purpose of liberating beings from such grasping that the Blessed Buddhas arise only in the good destiny of the human world, not in the good destiny of the deva world. Because, with this world-system as the center, the birth-field is shown to be ten thousand world-systems, and because no other place for the arising of Buddhas is found in the Buddha’s word in the Tipiṭaka, it is therefore said: “They arise only in this world-system.”

Idha uppajjantopi kasmā jambudīpe eva uppajjati, na sesadīpesūti? Keci tāva āhu – “yasmā pathaviyā nābhibhūtā buddhabhāvasahā acalaṭṭhānabhūtā bodhimaṇḍabhūmi jambudīpe eva[V 1.0114], tasmā jambudīpe eva uppajjatī”ti. Eteneva “tattha majjhimadese eva uppajjatī”ti etampi saṃvaṇṇitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ tathā itaresampi avijahitaṭṭhānānaṃ tattheva labbhanato. Yasmā purimabuddhānaṃ mahābodhisattānaṃ paccekabuddhānañca nibbattiyā sāvakabodhisattānaṃ sāvakabodhiyā abhinīhāro sāvakapāramiyā sambharaṇaparipācanañca buddhakkhettabhūte imasmiṃyeva cakkavāḷe jambudīpe eva ijjhati, na aññattha. Veneyyajanavinayanattho ca buddhuppādo, tasmā aggasāvakamahāsāvakādiveneyyavisesāpekkhāya imasmiṃ jambudīpe eva buddhā nibbattanti, na sesadīpesu. Ayañca nayo sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇasamāciṇṇoti tesaṃ uttamapurisānaṃ [M 1.0124] tattheva uppatti sampatticakkānaṃ viya aññamaññūpanissayatāya daṭṭhabbā. Tena vuttaṃ – aṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tīsu dīpesu buddhā na nibbattanti, jambudīpe eva nibbattantīti dīpaṃ passī”ti (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 2.17; bu. vaṃ. aṭṭha. 27 avidūrenidānakathā).

Even when arising in this world, why do they arise only in Jambudīpa and not in the other continents? Some say: “Because the ground of the Bodhi-seat in Jambudīpa is not overcome by the earth, is able to bear the state of a Buddha, and is an unshakeable place, therefore they arise only in Jambudīpa.” By this it should be understood that the statement “they arise only in the Middle Country there” is also explained, and also because the other unabandoned places are found there. Because the birth of the Great Bodhisattas of former Buddhas and of Paccekabuddhas, the aspiration for disciple-enlightenment by disciple-bodhisattvas, and the accumulation and maturation of the disciple-perfections—all these succeed only in this very world-sphere, which is the Buddha-field, in Jambudīpa, and nowhere else. Moreover, the purpose of a Buddha’s arising is the training of those who can be trained; therefore, with regard to exceptional disciples such as the chief disciples and great disciples, Buddhas are born only in this Jambudīpa, not in the other continents. And this is the method practiced and well-practiced by all Buddhas. The arising of these supreme persons in that very place should be seen as mutually supportive, like the wheels of attainment. Thus, it is said in the commentary: “Buddhas are not born in the three continents; they are born only in Jambudīpa. He saw the continent.” (Dī. Ni. Aṭṭha. 2.17; Bu. Vaṃ. Aṭṭha. 27, Avidūrenidānakathā).

Ubhayampidaṃ vippakatavacanameva uppādakiriyāya vattamānakālikattā. Uppajjamānoti vā uppajjituṃ samattho. Sattiattho cāyaṃ māna-saddo. Yāvatā hi sāmatthiyena mahābodhisattānaṃ carimabhave uppatti icchitabbā, tatthakena bodhisambhārasambhūtena paripuṇṇena samannāgatoti attho. Bhedoti viseso. Tameva hi tividhaṃ visesaṃ dassetuṃ – “esa hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatassa mahābhinīhārassa siddhakālato paṭṭhāya mahābodhisatto buddhabhāvāya niyatabhāvappattatāya bodhisambhārapaṭipadaṃ paṭipajjamāno yathāvuttasāmatthiyayogena uppajjamāno nāmāti attho uppādassa ekantikattā. Pariyesantoti vicinanto. Paripakkagate ñāṇeti iminā tato pubbe ñāṇassa aparipakkatāya eva laddhāvasarāya kammapilotiyā vasena bodhisatto tathā mahāpadhānaṃ padahīti dasseti. Arahattaphalakkhaṇe uppanno nāma “uppanno hotī”ti vattabbattā. Āgatova nāma hetusampadāya sammadeva nipphannattā.

Both of these are indeed incomplete statements, being in the present tense regarding the act of arising. Or, 'arising' means capable of arising, and this word 'māna' has the meaning of capability. Inasmuch as the arising of the Great Bodhisattas in their final existence is to be expected through a certain capability, the meaning is that they are endowed with that complete capability, which is born from the accumulation of the provisions for enlightenment. 'Difference' means distinction. To show this threefold distinction, it is indeed said: "For this reason," etc. From the time of the fulfillment of the eightfold great aspiration onward, the Great Bodhisatta, having attained a fixed state for Buddhahood and practicing the path of accumulating the requisites for enlightenment, is called "one arising" due to the certainty of arising, through the application of the aforementioned capability. 'Seeking' means investigating. By the phrase "with knowledge that has fully matured," it is shown that before that time, due to his knowledge not being fully mature, the Bodhisatta, having seized the opportunity through the cloak of action, exerted great effort accordingly. He is said to have "arisen" at the moment of attaining the fruit of Arahantship because it can be said that "he has arisen." 'Indeed come' means that, due to the perfection of causes, he has been rightly and perfectly produced.

Hitatthāyāti lokiyalokuttarassa hitassa siddhiyā. Sukhatthāyāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tassāti tassa sattalokassa. So panāyaṃ sattaloko yena anukkamena dhammābhisamayaṃ pāpuṇi, taṃ teneva anukkamena dassento “mahābodhimaṇḍe”tiādimāha. Yāvajjadivasāti ettha ajja-saddena sāsanassa avaṭṭhānakālaṃ vadati. Devamanussānanti ukkaṭṭhaniddesoti dassetuṃ – “na kevala”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Etesampīti nāgasupaṇṇādīnampi.

'For the welfare' means for the accomplishment of worldly and supramundane welfare. 'For the happiness,' the same principle applies here as well. 'Of that' refers to that world of beings. And showing that world of beings in the very same sequence by which it attained the realization of the Dhamma, he said, 'at the great Bodhi-maṇḍa,' and so on. 'Until this very day': here, the word 'today' refers to the time of the Dispensation's duration. 'Devas and humans'—this is stated to indicate the highest designation, as shown by "not only" and so on. 'For these too' refers to nāgas, supaṇṇas, and so on.

Ayaṃ pucchāti iminā “katamo”ti padassa sāmaññato pucchābhāvo dassito, na visesatoti tassa pucchāvisesabhāvañāpanatthaṃ mahāniddese (mahāni. 150) āgatā sabbāpi pucchā [V 1.0115] atthuddhāranayena dasseti “pucchā ca nāmesā”tiādinā. Adiṭṭhaṃ jotīyati etāyāti adiṭṭhajotanā. Diṭṭhaṃ saṃsandīyati etāyāti diṭṭhasaṃsandanā. Saṃsandanañca sākacchāvasena [M 1.0125] vinicchayakaraṇaṃ. Vimatiṃ chindati etāyāti vimaticchedanā. Anumatiyā pucchā anumatipucchā. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave”tiādi pucchāya “kā tumhākaṃ anumatī”ti anumati pucchitā hoti. Kathetukamyatāpucchāti kathetukamyatāya pucchā. Lakkhaṇanti ñātuṃ icchito yo koci sabhāvo. Aññātanti yena kenaci ñāṇena aññātabhāvamāha. Adiṭṭhanti dassanabhūtena ñāṇena paccakkhaṃ viya adiṭṭhataṃ. Atulitanti “ettakaṃ eta”nti tulābhūtena atulitataṃ. Atīritanti tīraṇabhūtena akatañāṇakiriyāsamāpanataṃ. Avibhūtanti ñāṇassa apākaṭabhāvaṃ. Avibhāvitanti ñāṇena apākaṭakatabhāvaṃ.

'This is a question': by this, the general nature of the question is shown by the word "what," not its specific aspect. To clarify the specific nature of the question, the Mahāniddesa presents all questions, extracting their meaning, beginning with, "This is indeed a question." What is unseen is illuminated by it—thus, it is the illumination of the unseen. What is seen is scrutinized by it—thus, it is the scrutinization of the seen. And scrutinization is the act of determining through discussion. It cuts through doubt—thus, it is the cutting of doubt. A question based on approval is an approval-based question. Through questions like, "What do you think, monks?" approval is sought by asking, "What is your approval?" 'A question arising from the desire to speak' is a question motivated by the desire to speak. 'A characteristic' is any condition one wishes to know. 'The unknown' refers to a state of being unknown by any kind of knowledge. 'The unseen' refers to a state of being unseen, as if by direct knowledge. 'The unmeasured' refers to a state of being unmeasured, as if by a balance. 'The unexamined' refers to the non-completion of the act of knowing by means of investigation. 'The unrevealed' refers to the unmanifested state of knowledge. 'The unclarified' refers to what has not been made clear by knowledge.

Yehi guṇavisesehi nimittabhūtehi bhagavati “tathāgato”ti ayaṃ samaññā pavattā, taṃdassanatthaṃ “aṭṭhahi kāraṇehi bhagavā tathāgato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Guṇavisesanemittikāneva hi bhagavato sabbāni nāmāni. Yathāha –

To show by which distinctive qualities, serving as signs, this designation "Tathāgata" arose for the Blessed One, it is said, "The Blessed One is a Tathāgata for eight reasons," and so on. Indeed, all the Blessed One's names are based on distinctive qualities as their cause. As it is said—

“Asaṅkhyeyyāni nāmāni, saguṇena mahesino;

Guṇena nāmamuddheyyaṃ, api nāmasahassato”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1313; udā. aṭṭha. 53; paṭi. ma. aṭṭha. 1.1.76);

"Countless are the names of the Great Sage, endowed with virtues. A name based on a quality should be uttered, rather than a thousand names."

Tathā āgatoti ettha ākāraniyamanavasena opammasampaṭipādanattho tathā-saddo. Sāmaññajotanāpi hi visese avatiṭṭhatīti. Paṭipadāgamanattho āgata-saddo, na ñāṇagamanattho “tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato”tiādīsu (dī. ni. aṭṭha. 1.7; ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.12; saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 2.3.78; a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.170; udā. aṭṭha. 18) viya, nāpi kāyagamanattho “āgato kho mahāsamaṇo, magadhānaṃ giribbaja”ntiādīsu (mahāva. 63) viya. Tattha yadākāraniyamanavasena opammasampaṭipādanattho tathā-saddo, taṃkaruṇāpadhānattā mahākaruṇāmukhena purimabuddhānaṃ āgamanappaṭipadaṃ udāharaṇavasena sāmaññato dassento yaṃ-taṃ-saddānaṃ ekantasambandhabhāvato “yathā sabbaloka…pe… āgatā”ti sādhāraṇato vatvā puna taṃ paṭipadaṃ mahāpadhānasuttādīsu (dī. ni. 2.1 ādayo) sambahulaniddesena supākaṭānaṃ āsannānañca vipassiādīnaṃ channaṃ sammāsambuddhānaṃ vasena nidassento “yathā vipassī bhagavā”tiādimāha. Tattha yena abhinīhārenāti manussattaliṅgasampattihetusatthudassanapabbajjāabhiññādiguṇasampattiadhikāracchandānaṃ vasena aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatena [M 1.0126] mahāpaṇidhānena. Sabbesañhi [V 1.0116] buddhānaṃ kāyappaṇidhānaṃ imināva abhinīhārena samijjhatīti. Evaṃ mahābhinīhāravisesena “tathāgato”ti padassa atthaṃ dassetvā idāni pāramipūraṇavasena dassetuṃ – “yathā vipassī bhagavā…pe… kassapo bhagavā dānapāramiṃ pūretvā”tiādimāha.

"Thus come" (tathā āgato): Here, the word "tathā" conveys the meaning of illustrating a simile by way of stipulating a likeness. For even a general denotation is established in specifics. The word "āgata" signifies the meaning of arrival by way of a course of practice, not the meaning of arrival by way of knowledge, as in phrases like "he has come to suchness" (tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato), etc., nor does it mean physical arrival, as in phrases like "the Great Ascetic has come to the mountain stronghold of the Magadhans" (āgato kho mahāsamaṇo, magadhānaṃ giribbajaṃ), etc. Here, when the word "tathā" conveys the meaning of illustrating a simile by way of stipulating a likeness, he shows in a general way the path of arrival of the previous Buddhas through the gateway of great compassion, as compassion is primary. Due to the invariable connection of the words "yaṃ" and "taṃ," it is stated generally as "just as all the world... has come." Then, again, pointing out that very path by means of the six Perfectly Self-Enlightened Buddhas, beginning with Vipassī, who are well-known and recent, with extensive exposition in suttas such as the Mahāpadhāna Sutta, he says, "just as the Blessed One Vipassī," etc. Here, "through which aspiration" (yena abhinīhārena) refers to the great aspiration endowed with eight factors: human birth, perfection of gender, the necessary cause, seeing a Teacher, going forth, the attainment of qualities such as the higher knowledges, a deed of service, and strong desire. For the bodily aspiration of all Buddhas is accomplished precisely through this aspiration. Having thus explained the meaning of the word "Tathāgata" through the distinction of the great aspiration, now to explain it through the fulfillment of the perfections, he says: "Just as the Blessed One Vipassī... Kassapa the Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfection of generosity," etc.

Ettha ca suttantikānaṃ mahābodhippaṭipadāya kosallajananatthaṃ kā panetā pāramiyo, kenaṭṭhena pāramiyo, katividhā cetā, ko tāsaṃ kamo, kāni lakkhaṇarasapaccupaṭṭhānapadaṭṭhānāni, ko paccayo, ko saṃkileso, kiṃ vodānaṃ, ko paṭipakkho, kā paṭipatti, ko vibhāgo, ko saṅgaho, ko sampādanūpāyo, kittakena kālena sampādanaṃ, ko ānisaṃso, kiñcetāsaṃ phalanti pāramīsu ayaṃ vitthārakathā veditabbā. Sā panesā icchantena dīghāgamaṭīkāyaṃ (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7) vuttanayeneva veditabbā, na idha dassitā. Yathāvuttāya paṭipadāya yathāvuttavibhāgānaṃ pāramīnaṃ pūritabhāvaṃ sandhāyāha – “samatiṃsa pāramiyo pūretvā”ti.

Here, for suttanta-followers, to generate skill in the path to supreme enlightenment, this detailed discussion about the perfections—what are these perfections? By what meaning are they perfections? Of how many kinds are they? What is their order? What are their characteristics, function, manifestation, and proximate cause? What is their condition? What is their defilement? What is their cleansing? What is their opponent? What is their practice? What is their division? What is their collection? What is the way to accomplish them? In how much time is their accomplishment? What is their benefit? What is their fruit?—should be understood. But this, for one who wishes, should be understood according to the method stated in the subcommentary to the Dīgha Nikāya (Dī. Ni. Ṭī. 1.7); it is not presented here. Referring to the fulfillment of the perfections with their divisions as stated in the aforementioned path, it is said: "Having fulfilled the thirty perfections."

Satipi mahāpariccāgānaṃ dānapāramibhāve pariccāgavisesabhāvadassanatthañceva sudukkarabhāvadassanatthañca mahāpariccāgehi visuṃ gahaṇaṃ. Tatoyeva ca aṅgapariccāgato visuṃ nayanapariccāgaggahaṇaṃ, pariccāgabhāvasāmaññepi dhanarajjapariccāgato puttadārapariccāgaggahaṇañca kataṃ. Gatapaccāgatikavattasaṅkhātāya pubbabhāgappaṭipadāya saddhiṃ abhiññāsamāpattinipphādanaṃ pubbayogo. Dānādīsuyeva sātisayappaṭipattinipphādanaṃ pubbacariyā, yā vā cariyāpiṭakasaṅgahitā. “Abhinīhāro pubbayogo, dānādippaṭipatti vā kāyavivekavasena ekacariyā vā pubbacariyā”ti keci. Dānādīnañceva appicchatādīnañca saṃsāranibbānesu ādīnavānisaṃsānañca vibhāvanavasena sattānaṃ bodhittaye patiṭṭhāpanaparipācanavasena ca pavattā kathā dhammakkhānaṃ. Ñātīnaṃ atthacariyā ñātatthacariyā. Sāpi karuṇāyanavaseneva. Ādi-saddena lokatthacariyādayo saṅgaṇhāti. Kammassakatañāṇavasena anavajjakammāyatanasippāyatanavijjāṭṭhānaparicayavasena khandhāyatanādiparicayavasena lakkhaṇattayatīraṇavasena ca ñāṇacāro buddhicariyā. Sā pana atthato paññāpāramīyeva, ñāṇasambhāradassanatthaṃ visuṃ [M 1.0127] gahaṇaṃ. Koṭīti pariyanto, ukkaṃsoti attho. Cattāro satipaṭṭhāne bhāvetvāti sambandho. Tattha bhāvetvāti uppādetvā. Brūhetvāti vaḍḍhetvā. Satipaṭṭhānādiggahaṇena āgamanappaṭipadaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetvā dasseti. Vipassanāsahagatā eva vā satipaṭṭhānādayo daṭṭhabbā. Ettha ca “yena abhinīhārenā”tiādinā āgamanappaṭipadāya ādiṃ dasseti, “dānapārami”ntiādinā majjhaṃ, “cattāro satipaṭṭhāne”tiādinā pariyosānanti veditabbaṃ.

Even though great sacrifices are part of the perfection of giving, they are mentioned separately to show their special nature as sacrifices and their extreme difficulty. For that very reason, the sacrifice of eyes is mentioned separately from the sacrifice of limbs; and although the nature of sacrifice is common, the sacrifice of children and wives is mentioned separately from the sacrifice of wealth and kingdom. The preliminary endeavor is the production of the attainments of higher knowledge together with the preliminary practice known as the practice of not returning. The preliminary conduct is the production of extraordinary practice in giving and so forth, or that conduct included in the Cariyāpiṭaka. Some say: "The aspiration is the preliminary endeavor; the practice of giving and so forth, or solitary conduct by way of bodily seclusion, is the preliminary conduct." The Dhamma-discourse is the talk that proceeds by way of explaining the dangers and benefits in saṃsāra and Nibbāna regarding giving and so forth, and fewness of wishes and so on, and by way of establishing and maturing beings in the threefold enlightenment. Ñātatthacariyā is conduct for the welfare of relatives. That too is solely by way of compassion. The word 'etc.' includes conduct for the welfare of the world and so forth. The conduct of an Awakened One is the range of knowledge, by way of knowledge of kamma as one's own, by way of familiarity with blameless fields of action, fields of craft, and fields of knowledge, by way of familiarity with aggregates, sense bases, etc., and by way of discerning the three characteristics. But in essence, it is just the perfection of wisdom; it is mentioned separately to show the accumulation of knowledge. 'Koṭi' means 'end'; the meaning is 'supreme.' The connection is 'having developed the four foundations of mindfulness.' Here, 'having developed' means having produced. 'Having cultivated' means having increased. By the inclusion of the foundations of mindfulness, etc., it shows that the path of approach has been brought to its culmination. Or the foundations of mindfulness, etc., should be seen as accompanied by insight. Here, it should be understood that the beginning of the path of approach is shown by 'by which aspiration,' etc., the middle by 'the perfection of giving,' etc., and the end by 'the four foundations of mindfulness,' etc.

Sampatijātoti [V 1.0117] muhuttajāto nikkhantamatto. Nikkhantamattañhi mahāsattaṃ paṭhamaṃ brahmāno suvaṇṇajālena paṭiggaṇhiṃsu, tesaṃ hatthato cattāro mahārājāno ajinappaveṇiyā, tesaṃ hatthato manussā dukūlacumbaṭakena paṭiggaṇhiṃsu, manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhito. Yathāhātiādinā mahāpadānadesanāya vuttavacanaṃ nidasseti. Setamhi chatteti dibbasetacchatte. Anudhāriyamāneti dhāriyamāne. Ettha ca chattaggahaṇeneva khaggādīni pañca kakudhabhaṇḍāni vuttānevāti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Khaggatālavaṇṭamorahatthakavālabījaniuṇhīsapaṭṭāpi hi chattena saha tadā upaṭṭhitā ahesuṃ. Chattādīniyeva ca tadā paññāyiṃsu, na chattādiggāhakā. Sabbā ca disāti dasa disā, nayidaṃ sabbadisāvilokanaṃ sattapadavītihāruttarakālaṃ. Mahāsatto hi manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā puratthimaṃ disaṃ olokesi, tattha devamanussā gandhamālādīhi pūjayamānā, “mahāpurisa, idha tumhehi sadisopi natthi, kuto uttaritaro”ti āhaṃsu. Evaṃ catasso disā catasso anudisā heṭṭhā uparīti sabbā disā anuviloketvā sabbattha attanā sadisaṃ adisvā “ayaṃ uttarā disā”ti sattapadavītihārena agamāsi. Āsabhinti uttamaṃ. Aggoti sabbapaṭhamo. Jeṭṭhoti seṭṭhoti ca tasseva vevacanaṃ. Ayamantimā jāti, natthi dāni punabbhavoti imasmiṃ attabhāve pattabbaṃ arahattaṃ byākāsi. “Anekesaṃ visesādhigamānaṃ pubbanimittabhāvenā”ti saṃkhittena vuttamatthaṃ “yañhī”tiādinā vitthārato dasseti. Tattha etthāti –

'Just born' means born a moment ago, just emerged. For as soon as the Great Being emerged, the Brahmās first received him with a golden net; from their hands, the Four Great Kings received him with a deerskin cloth; from their hands, humans received him with a roll of fine cloth; from the hands of humans, he descended and stood on the ground. By 'as it is said,' etc., he illustrates the words spoken in the Mahāpadāna discourse. 'Under a white parasol' refers to the divine white parasol. 'Being carried along' means being borne. Here, it should be understood that by the mention of the parasol alone, the five royal emblems, such as the sword, are also stated. For at that time, the sword, the palm-leaf fan, the peacock-tail whisk, the yak-tail whisk, and the turban-band were present along with the parasol. Only the parasol and other emblems were evident then, not their bearers. 'All directions' means the ten directions. This surveying of all directions did not occur after the seven steps were taken. For the Great Being, after descending from the hands of humans, looked toward the eastern direction. There, gods and humans honored him with perfumes and garlands, saying, "O Great Man, here there is none equal to you—how much less superior!" Thus, having surveyed the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, below, and above—all directions—and seeing no one equal to himself anywhere, he declared, 'This is the supreme direction,' and took seven steps. 'Āsabhaṃ' means supreme. 'Agga' means foremost. 'Jeṭṭha' and 'seṭṭha' are synonyms for the same. 'This is the last birth; there is now no more renewed existence'—thus he proclaimed the arahantship to be attained in this very existence. The briefly stated meaning—'as a precursor to the attainment of many distinctions'—is elaborated in detail with phrases like 'for indeed.' Here, in this context—

“Anekasākhañca [M 1.0128] sahassamaṇḍalaṃ,

Chattaṃ marū dhārayumantalikkhe;

Suvaṇṇadaṇḍā vītipatanti cāmarā,

Na dissare cāmarachattagāhakā”ti. (su. ni. 693) –

"With many branches and a thousand circles, The parasol was held by the gods in the sky. Golden-handled chowries were waving to and fro, But the bearers of the chowries and parasol were unseen."

Imissā gāthāya. Sabbaññutaññāṇameva sabbattha appaṭihatacāratāya anāvaraṇañāṇanti āha – “sabbaññutānāvaraṇañāṇapaṭilābhassā”ti. Tathā ayaṃ bhagavāpi gato…pe… pubbanimittabhāvenāti etena abhijātiyaṃ dhammatāvasena uppajjanakavisesā sabbabodhisattānaṃ sādhāraṇāti dasseti. Pāramitānissandā hi teti.

By this verse, he says that omniscient knowledge itself is unobstructed knowledge due to its unimpeded range everywhere, referring to 'the attainment of omniscient, unobstructed knowledge.' Likewise, by 'this Blessed One has gone... (etc.)... by way of being a preliminary sign,' he shows that the specific distinctions that arise by way of natural law at birth are common to all Bodhisattas. For they are indeed the outflow of the perfections.

Vikkamīti agamāsi. Marūti devā. Samāti vilokanasamatāya samā sadisiyo. Mahāpuriso hi yathā ekaṃ disaṃ vilokesi, evaṃ sesadisāpi, na katthaci vilokane vibandho tassa [V 1.0118] ahosīti. Samāti vā viloketuṃ yuttāti attho. Na hi tadā bodhisattassa virūpabībhacchavisamarūpāni viloketuṃ ayuttāni disāsu upaṭṭhahantīti.

'Vikkamī' means he went. 'Marū' means devas (gods). 'Samā' means equal, similar, by way of the evenness of his gaze. Indeed, just as the Great Being looked in one direction, so too in all other directions—there was no hindrance to his gaze anywhere. Or 'samā' means fit to look. For at that time, no deformed, repulsive, or uneven forms appeared in the directions that were unfit for the Bodhisatta to behold.

“Evaṃ tathā gato”ti kāyagamanaṭṭhena gatasaddena tathāgatasaddaṃ niddisitvā idāni ñāṇagamanaṭṭhena taṃ dassetuṃ – “atha vā”tiādimāha. Tattha nekkhammenāti alobhappadhānena kusalacittuppādena. Kusalā hi dhammā idha nekkhammaṃ, na pabbajjādayo. “Paṭhamajjhānenā”ti ca vadanti. Pahāyāti pajahitvā. Gato adhigato, paṭipanno uttarivisesanti attho. Pahāyāti vā pahānahetu, pahānalakkhaṇaṃ vā. Hetulakkhaṇattho hi ayaṃ pahāyasaddo. Kāmacchandādippahānahetukañhi “gato”ti ettha vuttaṃ gamanaṃ avabodho, paṭipatti eva vā kāmacchandādippahānena ca lakkhīyati. Esa nayo padāletvātiādīsupi. Abyāpādenāti mettāya. Ālokasaññāyāti vibhūtaṃ katvā manasikaraṇena upaṭṭhitaālokasañjānanena. Avikkhepenāti samādhinā. Dhammavavatthānenāti kusalādidhammānaṃ yāthāvanicchayena. “Sappaccayanāmarūpavavatthānenā”tipi vadanti. Evaṃ kāmacchandādinīvaraṇappahānena “abhijjhaṃ loke pahāyā”tiādinā (vibha. 508) vuttāya paṭhamajjhānassa pubbabhāgappaṭipadāya bhagavato tathāgatabhāvaṃ dassetvā idāni saha upāyena aṭṭhahi [M 1.0129] samāpattīhi aṭṭhārasahi ca mahāvipassanāhi taṃ dassetuṃ – “ñāṇenā”tiādimāha. Nāmarūpapariggahakaṅkhāvitaraṇānañhi vibandhabhūtassa mohassa dūrīkaraṇena ñātapariññāyaṃ ṭhitassa aniccasaññādayo sijjhanti, tathā jhānasamāpattīsu abhiratinimittena pāmojjena tattha anabhiratiyā vinoditāya jhānādīnaṃ samadhigamoti samāpattivipassanānaṃ arativinodanaavijjāpadālanādiupāyo, uppaṭipāṭiniddeso pana nīvaraṇasabhāvāya avijjāya heṭṭhā nīvaraṇesupi saṅgahadassanatthanti daṭṭhabbo. Samāpattivihārappavesavibandhanena nīvaraṇāni kavāṭasadisānīti āha – “nīvaraṇakavāṭaṃ ugghāṭetvā”ti.

Having indicated the word 'Tathāgata' by the word 'gone' in the sense of bodily going, he now says 'or else,' etc., to show it in the sense of going by knowledge. Herein, nekkhammena means by the arising of wholesome consciousness with non-greed as predominant. For here, wholesome states are nekkhamma, not renunciation and so on. And they say, 'by the first jhāna.' Pahāya means having abandoned. Gato means attained, entered upon the path to a higher distinction—this is the meaning. Or pahāya means the cause of abandoning, or the characteristic of abandoning. For this word pahāya has the meaning of cause and characteristic. For the going mentioned here as 'gone' is understanding, which is caused by the abandoning of sensual desire, etc., or it is practice, which is characterized by the abandoning of sensual desire, etc. This method applies also to 'having broken open,' etc. Abyāpādena means by loving-kindness. Ālokasaññāya means by knowing the arisen light through attention that has made it manifest. Avikkhepena means by concentration. Dhammavavatthānena means by the accurate discernment of wholesome and other states. Some say, 'by the discernment of name-and-form with its causes.' Thus, having shown the Blessed One's state of being a Tathāgata by the preliminary practice for the first jhāna, as stated in 'having abandoned covetousness in the world,' etc. (Vibh. 508), through abandoning the hindrances of sensual desire, etc., he now says 'by knowledge,' etc., to show it with the means of the eight attainments and the eighteen great insights. For by dispelling delusion, which is an impediment to overcoming doubt regarding the comprehension of name-and-form, the perceptions of impermanence, etc., succeed for one who stands in full understanding by knowing. Likewise, the attainment of jhānas and so on is achieved by dispelling discontent with them through the delight that is the sign of fondness for the jhāna attainments; this is the means for the attainments and insight, namely, dispelling discontent, breaking ignorance, and so on. The inverted order of enumeration, however, should be understood as for the purpose of showing the inclusion of ignorance, which is of the nature of a hindrance, even among the hindrances below. Because the hindrances are like closed doors, obstructing entry into the abidings in the attainments, he says, 'having opened the door of the hindrances.'

“Rattiṃ vitakketvā vicāretvā divā kammante payojetī”ti (ma. ni. 1.251) vuttaṭṭhāne vitakkavicārā dhūmāyanā adhippetāti āha – “vitakkavicāradhūma”nti. Kiñcāpi paṭhamajjhānūpacāreyeva dukkhaṃ, catutthajjhānopacāreyeva ca sukhaṃ pahīyati, atisayappahānaṃ pana sandhāyāha – “catutthajjhānena sukhadukkhaṃ pahāyā”ti. Rūpasaññāti saññāsīsena rūpāvacarajjhānāni ceva tadārammaṇāni ca vuttāni. Rūpāvacarajjhānampi hi “rūpa”nti vuccati uttarapadalopena “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīsu (ma. ni. 2.248; 3.312; dha. sa. 248; paṭi. ma. 1.209). Tassa ārammaṇampi kasiṇarūpaṃ “rūpa”nti vuccati [V 1.0119] purimapadalopena “bahiddhā rūpāni passati suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 2.173-174; ma. ni. 2.249; dha. sa. 244-245). Tasmā idha rūpe rūpajjhāne taṃsahagatasaññā rūpasaññāti evaṃ saññāsīsena rūpāvacarajjhānāni vuttāni. Rūpaṃ saññā assāti rūpasaññaṃ, rūpassa nāmanti vuttaṃ hoti. Evaṃ pathavīkasiṇādibhedassa tadārammaṇassa cetaṃ adhivacananti veditabbaṃ. Paṭighasaññāti cakkhādīnaṃ vatthūnaṃ rūpādīnaṃ ārammaṇānañca paṭighātena paṭihananena visayivisayasamodhāne samuppannā dvipañcaviññāṇasahagatā saññā paṭighasaññā. Nānattasaññāyoti nānatte gocare pavattā saññā, nānattā vā saññā nānattasaññā, aṭṭha kāmāvacarakusalasaññā, dvādasa akusalasaññā, ekādasa kāmāvacarakusalavipākasaññā, dve akusalavipākasaññā, ekādasa kāmāvacarakiriyasaññāti etāsaṃ catucattālīsasaññānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Etā hi yasmā rūpasaññādibhede nānatte [M 1.0130] nānāsabhāve gocare pavattanti, yasmā ca nānattā nānāsabhāvā aññamaññaṃ asadisā, tasmā “nānattasaññā”ti vuccanti.

In the place where it is said, 'Having thought and examined at night, one applies oneself to work by day' (MN 1.251), thought and examination are intended as a smouldering, hence it is said: 'the smouldering of thought and examination.' Although pain is abandoned even in the access to the first jhāna, and pleasure even in the access to the fourth jhāna, it is with reference to the surpassing abandonment that it is said: 'by the fourth jhāna, having abandoned pleasure and pain.' By perception of form (rūpasaññā), by way of the heading of perception, the fine-material sphere jhānas and their objects are referred to. For even a fine-material sphere jhāna is called 'form' (rūpa) by the omission of the latter word, as in 'one with form sees forms' (MN 2.248; 3.312; Dhs. 248; Paṭis. 1.209). Its object, the kasiṇa-form, is also called 'form' (rūpa) by the omission of the first word, as in 'one sees external forms, beautiful and ugly' (DN 2.173-174; MN 2.249; Dhs. 244-245). Therefore, here, the perception associated with form, with the form-jhāna, is perception of form (rūpasaññā); thus, by way of the heading of perception, the fine-material sphere jhānas are referred to. Rūpasañña is perception of form; it is said to be a name for form. Thus, this should be understood as a designation for its object, which is differentiated as the earth kasiṇa, etc. Perception of impingement (paṭighasaññā) is the perception that arises with the two sets of fivefold consciousness from the impingement, the striking, of the bases such as the eye with the objects such as forms, when subject and object meet. By perception of diversity (nānattasaññā) is meant perception that occurs in diverse objects, or diverse perceptions. This is a designation for these forty-four perceptions: eight wholesome sense-sphere perceptions, twelve unwholesome perceptions, eleven wholesome resultant sense-sphere perceptions, two unwholesome resultant perceptions, and eleven functional sense-sphere perceptions. For since these perceptions occur in diverse objects, diverse in nature, such as the perception of form, etc., and since they are diverse, dissimilar in nature, and unlike one another, they are called 'perceptions of diversity'.

Aniccassa, aniccanti vā anupassanā aniccānupassanā, tebhūmakadhammānaṃ aniccataṃ gahetvā pavattāya anupassanāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Niccasaññanti saṅkhatadhamme “niccā sassatā”ti pavattaṃ micchāsaññaṃ. Saññāsīsena diṭṭhicittānampi gahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Esa nayo ito paresupi. Nibbidānupassanāyāti saṅkhāresu nibbijjanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Nandinti sappītikataṇhaṃ. Virāgānupassanāyāti saṅkhāresu virajjanākārena pavattāya anupassanāya. Nirodhānupassanāyāti saṅkhārānaṃ nirodhassa anupassanāya. “Te saṅkhārā nirujjhantiyeva, āyatiṃ samudayavasena na uppajjantī”ti evaṃ vā anupassanā nirodhānupassanā. Tenevāha – “nirodhānupassanāya nirodheti, no samudetī”ti. Muccitukamyatā hi ayaṃ balappattāti. Paṭinissajjanākārena pavattā anupassanā paṭinissaggānupassanā. Paṭisaṅkhā santiṭṭhanā hi ayaṃ. Ādānanti niccādivasena gahaṇaṃ. Santatisamūhakiccārammaṇānaṃ vasena ekattaggahaṇaṃ ghanasaññā. Āyūhanaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇaṃ. Avatthāvisesāpatti vipariṇāmo. Dhuvasaññanti thirabhāvaggahaṇaṃ. Nimittanti samūhādighanavasena sakiccaparicchedatāya ca saṅkhārānaṃ saviggahaggahaṇaṃ. Paṇidhinti rāgādipaṇidhiṃ. Sā panatthato taṇhāvasena saṅkhāresu nanditā. Abhinivesanti attānudiṭṭhiṃ.

Contemplation of impermanence (aniccānupassanā) is the contemplation of the impermanent, or of what is 'impermanent.' This is a name for the contemplation that occurs by grasping the impermanence of phenomena in the three realms. Perception of permanence (niccasaññā) is the wrong perception that occurs regarding conditioned phenomena as 'permanent, eternal.' It should be understood that by the heading of perception, views and their associated states of consciousness are also included. This method applies to the rest as well. Contemplation of revulsion (nibbidānupassanā) is the contemplation that occurs in the manner of being revolted by formations. Delight (nandi) is craving accompanied by joy. Contemplation of dispassion (virāgānupassanā) is the contemplation that occurs in the manner of becoming dispassionate towards formations. Contemplation of cessation (nirodhānupassanā) is the contemplation of the cessation of formations. Or, the contemplation, 'Those formations are simply ceasing; in the future they do not arise by way of origination,' is the contemplation of cessation. Therefore it was said, 'Through the contemplation of cessation, one brings to cessation, one does not cause to originate.' For this is the desire to be freed that has attained strength. The contemplation that occurs in the manner of relinquishment is the contemplation of relinquishment (paṭinissaggānupassanā). This is indeed reflective discernment. Grasping (ādāna) is the taking up in terms of permanence, etc. Perception of solidity (ghanasaññā) is the grasping of oneness by way of continuity, aggregation, function, and object. Accumulation (āyūhana) is volitional formation. Transformation (vipariṇāmo) is the undergoing of a different state. Perception of stability (dhuvasaññā) is the grasping of a lasting condition. The sign (nimitta) is the grasping of formations as a concrete thing due to aggregation, etc., and by the delimitation of their own function. Longing (paṇidhi) is longing rooted in lust, etc. But in essence, it is delight in formations by way of craving. Adherence (abhinivesa) is the view of self.

Aniccadukkhādivasena sabbadhammatīraṇaṃ adhipaññādhammavipassanā. Sārādānābhinivesanti asāre sāraggahaṇavipallāsaṃ. Issarakuttādivasena loko samuppannoti abhiniveso sammohābhiniveso[V 1.0120]. Keci pana “ahosiṃ nu kho ahamatītamaddhānantiādinā pavattasaṃsayāpatti sammohābhiniveso”ti vadanti. Saṅkhāresu leṇatāṇabhāvaggahaṇaṃ ālayābhiniveso. “Ālayaratā ālayasammuditā”ti (dī. ni. 2.64; ma. ni. 1.281; 2.337; saṃ. ni. 1.172; mahāva. 7) vacanato ālayo taṇhā, sāyeva cakkhādīsu rūpādīsu ca abhinivesavasena pavattiyā ālayābhinivesoti keci. “Evaṃvidhā saṅkhārā paṭinissajjīyantī”ti pavattaṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭisaṅkhānupassanā. Vaṭṭato vigatattā vivaṭṭaṃ, nibbānaṃ. Tattha ārammaṇakaraṇasaṅkhātena anupassanena pavattiyā vivaṭṭānupassanā, gotrabhū. Saṃyogābhinivesanti saṃyujjanavasena saṅkhāresu [M 1.0131] abhinivisanaṃ. Diṭṭhekaṭṭheti diṭṭhiyā sahajātekaṭṭhe pahānekaṭṭhe ca. Oḷāriketi uparimaggavajjhe kilese apekkhitvā vuttaṃ, aññathā dassanapahātabbāpi dutiyamaggavajjhehi oḷārikāti. Aṇusahagateti aṇubhūte. Idaṃ heṭṭhimamaggavajjhe apekkhitvā vuttaṃ. Sabbakileseti avasiṭṭhasabbakilese. Na hi paṭhamādimaggehipi pahīnā kilesā puna pahīyantīti.

Examining all phenomena in terms of impermanence, suffering, and so forth is insight into phenomena as higher wisdom (adhipaññā-dhamma-vipassanā). Adherence to taking what is essential (sārādānābhinivesa) is the perversion of grasping the non-essential as essential. The adherence that the world arises through a creator, etc., is the adherence of delusion (sammohābhinivesa). Some, however, say that the arising of doubt, such as 'Did I exist in the past?' and so on, is the adherence of delusion. Taking the formations as a shelter or refuge is the adherence to clinging (ālayābhinivesa). Because of the statement, 'Delighting in clinging, rejoicing in clinging,' clinging is craving; some say that that same craving, arising through adherence in the sense of attachment to the eye, etc., and to forms, etc., is adherence to clinging. The knowledge that arises thus: 'Such formations are to be relinquished'—this is contemplation as reflection (paṭisaṅkhānupassanā). Freedom from the round of rebirth is the unrolling (vivaṭṭa), Nibbāna. There, the contemplation of the unrolling arises through the act of making it an object of observation—this is the change-of-lineage (gotrabhū). Adherence to fetters (saṃyogābhinivesa) is clinging to formations in the manner of fetters. Oneness in view (diṭṭhekaṭṭha) refers to oneness co-arising with view and oneness in abandoning. Coarse (oḷārika) is said with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the higher paths. Otherwise, even defilements to be abandoned by insight would be coarse compared to those to be abandoned by the second path. Subtly accompanied (aṇusahagata) refers to the subtle. This is said with reference to the defilements to be abandoned by the lower paths. All defilements (sabbakilesa) means all remaining defilements. For defilements abandoned by the first path and so on are not abandoned again.

Kakkhaḷattaṃ kathinabhāvo. Paggharaṇaṃ dravabhāvo. Lokiyavāyunā bhastāya viya yena taṃtaṃkalāpassa uddhumāyanaṃ, thaddhabhāvo vā, taṃ vitthambhanaṃ. Vijjamānepi kalāpantarabhūtānaṃ kalāpantarabhūtehi phuṭṭhabhāve taṃtaṃbhūtavivittatā rūpapariyanto ākāsoti yesaṃ yo paricchedo, tehi so asamphuṭṭhova, aññathā bhūtānaṃ paricchedabhāvo na siyā byāpitabhāvāpattito. Yasmiṃ kalāpe bhūtānaṃ paricchedo, tehi asamphuṭṭhabhāvo asamphuṭṭhalakkhaṇaṃ. Tenāha – bhagavā ākāsadhātuniddese (dha. sa. 637) “asamphuṭṭho catūhi mahābhūtehī”ti.

Hardness (kakkhaḷatta) is the state of being solid. Flowing (paggharaṇa) is the state of being liquid. Distension (vitthambhana) is the swelling of particular material qualities within their respective groups, or the state of rigidity, just as a bellows is inflated by worldly wind. Even when there is contact between elements of one group and elements of another group, the distinctness of those respective elements, which is the delimitation of form, is space. Whatever delimitation there is for these elements, by them, space is indeed uncontacted; otherwise, there would be no delimitation of the elements, as they would become pervasive. In whatever group of qualities there is delimitation of the elements, their uncontactedness is the characteristic of uncontactedness. Therefore, the Blessed One said in the exposition of the space element (Dh. Sa. 637): 'Uncontacted by the four great elements.'

Virodhipaccayasannipāte visadisuppatti ruppanaṃ. Cetanāpadhānattā saṅkhārakkhandhadhammānaṃ cetanāvasenetaṃ vuttaṃ – “saṅkhārānaṃ abhisaṅkharaṇalakkhaṇa”nti. Tathā hi suttantabhājanīye saṅkhārakkhandhavibhaṅge (vibha. 92) “cakkhusamphassajā cetanā”tiādinā cetanāva vibhattā. Abhisaṅkharalakkhaṇā ca cetanā. Yathāha – “tattha katamo puññābhisaṅkhāro, kusalā cetanā kāmāvacarā”tiādi. Pharaṇaṃ savipphārikatā. Assaddhiyeti assaddhiyahetu. Nimittatthe bhummaṃ. Esa nayo kosajjetiādīsu. Vūpasamalakkhaṇanti kāyacittapariḷāhūpasamalakkhaṇaṃ. Līnuddhaccarahite adhicitte pavattamāne paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu abyāvaṭatāya ajjhupekkhanaṃ paṭisaṅkhānaṃ pakkhapātupacchedato.

Agitation (ruppana) is the dissimilar occurrence that arises when opposing conditions come together. Due to the dominance of volition, the phenomena of the volitional formations aggregate are spoken of in terms of volition—thus it is said: 'The characteristic of formations is active conditioning.' Indeed, in the Suttanta classification's analysis of the formations aggregate (Vibh. 92), volition is distinguished by phrases such as 'volition born of eye-contact,' and so on. And volition has the characteristic of active conditioning, as stated: 'Here, what is a meritorious active conditioning? It is wholesome volition pertaining to the sensuous sphere,' and so forth. Pervasion (pharaṇa) means being fully diffused. By 'through lack of faith' (assaddhiye) is meant 'due to lack of faith.' The locative case is used in the sense of a cause. This method applies to 'through laziness' (kosajje), etc. The characteristic of calming (vūpasamalakkhaṇa) is the characteristic of calming bodily and mental disturbance. When the higher mind operates free from sluggishness and restlessness, there is equanimous reflection due to non-interference in exertion, restraint, and encouragement, and due to cutting off partiality.

Musāvādādīnaṃ visaṃvādanādikiccatāya lūkhānaṃ apariggāhakānaṃ paṭipakkhabhāvato pariggāhakasabhāvā [V 1.0121] sammāvācā, siniddhabhāvato sampayuttadhamme sammāvācāpaccayasubhāsitānaṃ sotārañca puggalaṃ pariggaṇhātīti sā pariggahalakkhaṇā. Kāyikakiriyā kiñci kattabbaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, sayañca samuṭṭhahanaṃ ghaṭanaṃ hotīti sammākammantasaṅkhātā viratīpi [M 1.0132] samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇā daṭṭhabbā, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā ukkhipanaṃ samuṭṭhāpanaṃ kāyikakiriyāya bhārukkhipanaṃ viya. Jīvamānassa sattassa, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā jīvitindriyapavattiyā, ājīvasseva vā suddhi vodānaṃ. “Saṅkhārā”ti idha cetanā adhippetāti vuttaṃ – “saṅkhārānaṃ cetanālakkhaṇa”nti. Namanaṃ ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvo. Āyatanaṃ pavattanaṃ. Āyatanavasena hi āyasaṅkhātānaṃ cittacetasikānaṃ pavatti. Taṇhāya hetulakkhaṇanti vaṭṭassa janakahetubhāvo, maggassa pana nibbānasampāpakattanti ayametesaṃ viseso.

Right speech has the characteristic of embracing (pariggaha), because it is the opposite of harsh and unprotective actions like false speech, whose function is deception, etc., and because, due to its gentle nature, it embraces the associated phenomena and the person who listens to well-spoken words supported by right speech. Right action, as a form of abstinence, should be understood as having the characteristic of initiating, for bodily action initiates something that needs to be done, and the initiating itself is an exertion. Alternatively, it is the uplifting, the initiating of associated phenomena, like the lifting of a burden by bodily action. Purification is the continuation of the life faculty of a living being or of associated phenomena, or it is the purity of livelihood itself. Here, 'formations' (saṅkhārā) is intended as volition (cetanā)—thus it is said: 'Formations have volition as their characteristic.' Bending (namana) is the inclination toward an object. The sense base (āyatana) is the condition for occurrence. For through the sense bases, the mind and mental factors, which are designated as 'sources' or 'comings-forth,' arise. Craving has the characteristic of being a cause—it is the generative cause of the cycle, while the path has the characteristic of leading to Nibbāna. This is the distinction between them.

Tathalakkhaṇaṃ aviparītasabhāvo. Ekaraso aññamaññanātivattanaṃ anūnādhikabhāvo. Yuganaddhā samathavipassanāva. “Saddhāpaññā paggahāvikkhepā”tipi vadanti. Khayoti kilesakkhayo maggo. Anuppādapariyosānatāya anuppādo phalaṃ. Passaddhi kilesavūpasamo. Chandassāti kattukāmatāchandassa. Mūlalakkhaṇaṃ patiṭṭhābhāvo. Samuṭṭhānalakkhaṇaṃ ārammaṇappaṭipādakatāya sampayuttadhammānaṃ uppattihetutā. Samodhānaṃ visayādisannipātena gahetabbākāro, yā saṅgatīti vuccati. Samaṃ, saha odahanti anena sampayuttadhammāti vā samodhānaṃ, phasso. Samosaranti sannipatanti etthāti samosaraṇaṃ. Vedanāya vinā appavattamānā sampayuttadhammā vedanānubhavananimittaṃ samosaṭā viya hontīti evaṃ vuttaṃ. Gopānasīnaṃ kūṭaṃ viya sampayuttānaṃ pāmokkhabhāvo pamukhalakkhaṇaṃ. Tato, tesaṃ vā sampayuttadhammānaṃ uttari padhānanti tatuttari. Paññuttarā hi kusalā dhammā. Vimuttiyāti phalassa. Tañhi sīlādiguṇasārassa paramukkaṃsabhāvena sāraṃ. Ayañca lakkhaṇavibhāgo chadhātupañcajhānaṅgādivasena taṃtaṃsuttapadānusārena porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ āgatanayena ca katoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā hi pubbe vuttopi koci dhammo pariyāyantarappakāsanatthaṃ puna dassito, tato eva ca “chandamūlakā kusalā dhammā manasikārasamuṭṭhānā phassasamodhānā vedanāsamosaraṇā”ti, “paññuttarā kusalā dhammā”ti, “vimuttisāramidaṃ brahmacariya”nti, “nibbānogadhañhi, āvuso, brahmacariyaṃ nibbānapariyosāna”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.512) ca suttapadānaṃ vasena “chandassa mūlalakkhaṇa”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

The characteristic of suchness (tathalakkhaṇa) is its unperverted nature. It has a single taste, not surpassing one another, being neither deficient nor excessive. Paired practice (yuganaddha) is serenity and insight. Some also say 'faith and wisdom, exertion and non-distraction'. Destruction (khaya) is the destruction of defilements, namely, the path. Non-arising (anuppāda) is the fruit, due to its culmination in non-arising. Tranquility (passaddhi) is the calming of defilements. Desire (chanda) is the desire to do, the desire to act. The root characteristic is the nature of being a foundation. The characteristic of origination is being the cause for the arising of associated states by providing the object. Combination (samodhāna) is the mode to be grasped by the coming together of objects, etc., which is called association. Or, combination (samodhāna) is contact (phassa), because associated states evenly or together establish something through it. They converge and meet here—thus, convergence (samosaraṇa). Without feeling, the associated states do not function; they are, on account of being the cause for the experiencing of feeling, as if converging together—thus it is said. Like the peak of a gabled roof, the foremost state of the associated states is the characteristic of leadership. Beyond that, or further dominant among those associated states, thus, 'further beyond' (tatuttari). Indeed, wholesome states are surpassed by wisdom. As for liberation (vimutti), it is the fruit. For it is the essence of the virtues beginning with morality, being the supreme excellence of its essence. This analysis of characteristics should be seen as done according to the six elements, the five jhāna factors, etc., following the wording of the suttas and according to the method that has come down in the ancient commentaries. Thus, even a previously stated teaching is shown again for the purpose of explaining another aspect. Hence, it is said: 'Wholesome states are rooted in desire, originate from attention, combined with contact, converging upon feeling,' 'wholesome states are surpassed by wisdom,' 'the essence of this holy life is liberation,' 'for, friend, the holy life is immersed in Nibbāna, culminating in Nibbāna' (Saṃ. Ni. 5.512). Thus, based on the wording of these suttas, 'the root characteristic of desire,' etc., is stated.

Tathadhammā [M 1.0133] nāma cattāri ariyasaccāni aviparītasabhāvattā. Tathāni taṃsabhāvattā, avitathāni amusāsabhāvattā, anaññathāni aññākārarahitattā. Jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭhoti [V 1.0122] jātipaccayā sambhūtaṃ hutvā sahitassa attano paccayānurūpassa uddhaṃ uddhaṃ āgatabhāvo, anupavattatthoti attho. Atha vā sambhūtaṭṭho ca samudāgataṭṭho ca sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho, na jātito jarāmaraṇaṃ na hoti, na ca jātiṃ vinā aññato hotīti jātipaccayasambhūtaṭṭho, itthañca jātito samudāgacchatīti jātipaccayasamudāgataṭṭho. Yā yā jāti yathā yathā paccayo hoti, tadanurūpaṃ pātubhāvoti attho. Avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭhoti etthāpi na avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo na hoti, na ca avijjaṃ vinā saṅkhārā uppajjanti. Yā yā avijjā yesaṃ yesaṃ saṅkhārānaṃ yathā yathā paccayo hoti, ayaṃ avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho, paccayabhāvoti attho.

The four noble truths are called 'realities' (tathadhammā) because they are of an unperverted nature. They are 'real' (tathāni) because they are of such a nature; 'not deceptive' (avitathāni) because they are of a non-false nature; and 'not otherwise' (anaññathāni) because they are devoid of a different form. The meaning of 'born from and arisen from birth as condition' (jātipaccayasambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho) is the state of having arisen successively, in accordance with its own conditions, for that which has come to be from birth as condition; this is the meaning of 'continuation'. Alternatively, 'the meaning of being born' (sambhūtaṭṭho) and 'the meaning of having arisen' (samudāgataṭṭho) together mean 'the meaning of being born and having arisen' (sambhūtasamudāgataṭṭho): ageing and death do not exist without birth, nor do they arise from anything other than birth—this is the meaning of 'being born from birth as condition' (jātipaccayasambhūtaṭṭho); and in this way, it arises from birth—this is the meaning of 'having arisen from birth as condition' (jātipaccayasamudāgataṭṭho). Whatever birth, in whatever way, becomes a condition, its corresponding manifestation occurs—this is the meaning. The meaning of 'ignorance as a condition for formations' (avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho): here too, it is not that ignorance is not a condition for formations, nor do formations arise without ignorance. Whatever ignorance, in whatever way, becomes a condition for whichever formations—this is the meaning of 'ignorance as a condition for formations' (avijjāya saṅkhārānaṃ paccayaṭṭho), that is, the state of being a condition.

Bhagavā taṃ jānāti passatīti sambandho. Tenāti bhagavatā. Taṃ vibhajjamānanti yojetabbaṃ. Tanti rūpāyatanaṃ. Iṭṭhāniṭṭhādīti ādi-saddena majjhattaṃ saṅgaṇhāti, tathā atītānāgatapaccuppannaparittaajjhattabahiddhātadubhayādibhedaṃ. Labbhamānakapadavasenāti “rūpāyatanaṃ diṭṭhaṃ, saddāyatanaṃ sutaṃ, gandhāyatanaṃ rasāyatanaṃ phoṭṭhabbāyatanaṃ mutaṃ, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ manasā viññāta”nti (dha. sa. 966) vacanato diṭṭhapadañca viññātapadañca rūpārammaṇe labbhati. Anekehi nāmehīti “rūpārammaṇaṃ iṭṭhaṃ aniṭṭhaṃ majjhattaṃ parittaṃ atītaṃ anāgataṃ paccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ bahiddhā diṭṭhaṃ viññātaṃ rūpaṃ rūpāyatanaṃ rūpadhātu vaṇṇanibhā sanidassanaṃ sappaṭighaṃ nīlaṃ pītaka”nti evamādīhi anekehi nāmehi. Terasahi vārehīti rūpakaṇḍe āgate terasa niddesavāre sandhāyāha. Dvepaññāsāya nayehīti ekekasmiṃ vāre catunnaṃ catunnaṃ vavatthāpananayānaṃ vasena dvipaññāsāya nayehi. Tathamevāti aviparītadassitāya appaṭivattiyadesanatāya ca tathameva hoti. Jānāmi abbhaññāsinti vattamānātītakālesu ñāṇappavattidassanena anāgatepi ñāṇappavatti vuttāyevāti daṭṭhabbā. Vidita-saddo anāmaṭṭhakālaviseso veditabbo “diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ muta”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.188; ma. ni. 1.7-8; saṃ. ni. 3.208; a. ni. 4.23) viya. Na upaṭṭhāsīti attattaniyavasena na upagañchi[M 1.0134]. Yathā rūpārammaṇādayo dhammā yaṃsabhāvā yaṃpakārā ca, tathā ne passati jānāti gacchatīti tathāgatoti evaṃ padasambhavo veditabbo. Keci pana “niruttinayena pisodarādipakkhepena vā dassīsaddassa lopaṃ, āgata-saddassa cāgamaṃ katvā tathāgato”ti vaṇṇenti.

The connection is: 'The Blessed One knows it, sees it.' `By him` (tena) means by the Blessed One. `That being analyzed` should be construed. `That` refers to the form base. `Pleasant, unpleasant, etc.` (iṭṭhāniṭṭhādīti): by the word 'etc.,' the neutral is included, as well as distinctions such as past, future, present, limited, internal, external, and both. By way of the obtainable terms (labbhamānakapadavasena), from the statement: 'The form base is seen, the sound base is heard, the smell base, the taste base, the touch base is sensed, all form is cognized by the mind' (Dhs. 966), the terms 'seen' and 'cognized' are obtainable in relation to form as an object. `By many names` (anekehi nāmehi)—such as: 'Form as an object is pleasant, unpleasant, neutral, limited, past, future, present, internal, external, seen, cognized, form, form base, form element, color, appearance, visible, resistant, blue, yellow,' etc., by these many names. `By thirteen occasions` (terasahi vārehi)—referring to the thirteen expositions that appear in the section on form. `By fifty-two modes` (dvepaññāsāya nayehi)—by the four applications of establishing (vavatthāpana) in each occasion, making fifty-two modes. `Just so` (tathameva)—it is just so due to the teaching being shown without perversion and being irreversible. `I know, I fully know` (jānāmi abbhaññāsi): by showing the occurrence of knowledge in the present and past, it should be understood that the occurrence of knowledge in the future is also stated. The term `known` (vidita) should be understood as without a specified time, as in 'seen, heard, sensed,' etc. (Dī. Ni. 3.188; Ma. Ni. 1.7-8; Saṃ. Ni. 3.208; A. Ni. 4.23). `Did not attend to` (na upaṭṭhāsi)—did not approach in the sense of self or what pertains to self. Just as form objects and other phenomena are of such a nature and such characteristics, so too does he see, know, and go—thus should the origin of the word `Tathāgata` be understood. Some, however, explain it by saying: 'Through etymological method, by the elision of the word `dassī` and the augment of the word `āgata`, as in the case of `pisodara` and so on, it becomes `Tathāgata`.'

Yaṃ rattinti yassaṃ rattiyaṃ. Accantasaṃyoge cetaṃ upayogavacanaṃ. Tiṇṇaṃ mārānanti kilesābhisaṅkhāradevaputtasaṅkhātānaṃ tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ. Anupavajjanti niddosatāya na upavajjaṃ. Anūnanti pakkhipitabbābhāvena na ūnaṃ. Anadhikanti apanetabbābhāvena na adhikaṃ. Sabbākāraparipuṇṇanti [V 1.0123] atthabyañjanādisampattiyā sabbākārena paripuṇṇaṃ. No aññathāti “tathevā”ti vuttamevatthaṃ byatirekena sampādeti. Tena yadatthaṃ bhāsitaṃ, tadatthanipphādanato yathā bhāsitaṃ bhagavatā, tathevāti aviparītadesanataṃ dasseti. Gadatthoti etena tathaṃ gadatīti tathāgatoti da-kārassa ta-kāraṃ katvā niruttinayena vuttanti dasseti. Tathā gatamassāti tathāgato. Gatanti ca kāyassa vācāya vā pavattīti attho. Tathāti ca vutte yaṃ-taṃ-saddānaṃ abyabhicāritasambandhatāya yathāti ayamattho upaṭṭhitoyeva hoti. Kāyavācākiriyānañca aññamaññānulomena vacanicchāyaṃ kāyassa vācā, vācāya ca kāyo sambandhabhāvena upatiṭṭhatīti imamatthaṃ dassento āha – “bhagavato hī”tiādi. Imasmiṃ pana atthe tathāvāditāya tathāgatoti ayampi attho siddho hoti. So pana pubbe pakārantarena dassitoti āha – “evaṃ tathākāritāya tathāgato”ti.

`On which night` (yaṃ rattiṃ) means in which night. This is a term of usage in the context of continuous connection. `Of the three Māras` (tiṇṇaṃ mārānaṃ) refers to the three Māras known as defilements, formations, and the son of a deity. `Not blameworthy` (anupavajja) means not blameworthy due to faultlessness. `Not deficient` (anūna) means not deficient due to the absence of anything to be added. `Not excessive` (anadhika) means not excessive due to the absence of anything to be removed. `Complete in all aspects` (sabbākāraparipuṇṇa) means fully complete in all respects, by the accomplishment of meaning, phrasing, and so on. `Not otherwise` (no aññathā) establishes, by way of exclusion, the very meaning stated as 'just so' (tatheva). Thus, because the purpose for which it was spoken is fulfilled, it shows that the teaching is not perverted, being just as the Blessed One spoke it, 'just so' (tatheva). By this, it shows that because he speaks what is real (tathaṃ gadati), he is called `Tathāgata`, with the 'da' being made into a 'ta' according to etymological method. His going is thus (tathā gatamassa), so he is a `Tathāgata`. `Going` (gata) means the activity of body or speech. And when `thus` (tathā) is said, due to the invariable connection of the words `yaṃ` and `taṃ`, the meaning `just as` is immediately present. To show that the actions of body and speech mutually conform, and that in the desire to speak, the body is related to speech and speech to the body, he says: 'For the Blessed One,' etc. In this sense, the meaning of `Tathāgata` as 'one who speaks in accordance with reality' is also established. But since this was previously shown in another way, he says: 'Thus, due to acting in accordance with reality, he is the `Tathāgata`.'

Tiriyaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsūti etena yadeke “tiriyaṃ viya upari adho ca santi lokadhātuyo”ti vadanti, taṃ paṭisedheti. Desanāvilāsoyeva desanāvilāsamayo yathā “puññamayaṃ dānamaya”ntiādīsu (dī. ni. 3.305; itivu. 60; netti. 33). Nipātānaṃ vācakasaddasannidhāne tadatthajotanabhāvena pavattanato gata-saddoyeva avagatatthaṃ atītatthañca vadatīti āha – “gatoti avagato atīto”ti. Atha vā abhinīhārato paṭṭhāya yāva [M 1.0135] sambodhi, etthantare mahābodhiyānapaṭipattiyā hānaṭṭhānasaṃkilesanivattīnaṃ abhāvato yathā paṇidhānaṃ, tathā gato abhinīhārānurūpaṃ paṭipannoti tathāgato. Atha vā mahiddhikatāya paṭisambhidānaṃ ukkaṃsādhigamena anāvaraṇañāṇatāya ca katthacipi paṭighātābhāvato yathā ruci, tathā kāyavācācittānaṃ gatāni gamanāni pavattiyo etassāti tathāgato. Yasmā ca loke vidhayuttagatapakārasaddā samānatthā dissanti, tasmā yathāvidhā vipassiādayo bhagavanto, ayampi bhagavā tathāvidhoti tathāgato. Yathā yuttā ca te bhagavanto, ayampi bhagavā tathā yuttoti tathāgato. Atha vā yasmā saccaṃ tatvaṃ tacchaṃ tathanti ñāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ, tasmā tathena ñāṇena āgatoti tathāgatoti evampi tathāgatasaddassa attho veditabbo.

`Horizontally in the immeasurable world-systems` (tiriyaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu): this refutes those who say, 'Just as there are world-systems horizontally, so too are there world-systems above and below.' `The display of the teaching` (desanāvilāsa) is itself made of the display of the teaching, as in 'made of merit, made of giving,' etc. (Dī. Ni. 3.305; Itivu. 60; Netti. 33). Because particles, when near words expressing meaning, function to illuminate that meaning, the word `gata` (gone) conveys both the understood meaning and the past meaning—thus it is said, '`gata` means understood and past.' Alternatively, starting from the initial aspiration up until enlightenment, in this interval, because there is no falling away, stagnation, or defilement in the practice of the great vehicle to enlightenment, he has gone according to his aspiration, having practiced in conformity with his aspiration—thus, he is `Tathāgata`. Or, due to great psychic power, the supreme attainment of the analytical knowledges, and unobstructed knowledge, and because there is no obstruction anywhere, the goings, movements, and activities of his body, speech, and mind proceed as he wishes—thus, he is `Tathāgata`. And because in the world, words denoting kind, propriety, going, and mode are seen to have similar meanings, therefore, just as the Blessed Ones like Vipassī were of such a kind, this Blessed One is also of such a kind—thus, `Tathāgata`. Just as those Blessed Ones were rightly endowed, this Blessed One is also rightly endowed—thus, `Tathāgata`. Or, because 'true', 'reality', 'factual', and 'real' (tathaṃ) are designations for knowledge, therefore, he has come by that real knowledge—thus, `Tathāgata`. In this way also, the meaning of the word `Tathāgata` should be understood.

“Pahāya kāmādimale yathā gatā,

Samādhiñāṇehi vipassiādayo;

Mahesino sakyamunī jutindharo,

Tathāgato tena tathāgato mato.

“Just as the great seers, Vipassī and others, went, having abandoned stains such as sensual desires and being endowed with concentration and wisdom, so too has the radiant Sakyan sage, the great seer, gone. For that reason, he is considered a Tathāgata.”

“Tathañca [V 1.0124] dhātāyatanādilakkhaṇaṃ,

Sabhāvasāmaññavibhāgabhedato;

Sayambhuñāṇena jinoyamāgato,

Tathāgato vuccati sakyapuṅgavo.

“And because this Victor, the Sakyan Bull, has come with self-originated knowledge to the real characteristics of elements, bases, and so forth, distinguished by their specific nature, general nature, and division, he is called the Tathāgata.”

“Tathāni saccāni samantacakkhunā,

Tathā idappaccayatā ca sabbaso;

Anaññaneyyena yato vibhāvitā,

Yāthāvato tena jino tathāgato.

“The truths are real, realized by the All-Seeing One, and specific conditionality is likewise real in every way; since these have been made manifest by him, who is not led by another, just as they are in reality, therefore the Victor is a Tathāgata.”

“Anekabhedāsupi lokadhātusu,

Jinassa rupāyatanādigocare;

Vicittabhede tathameva dassanaṃ,

Tathāgato tena samantalocano.

Even in world-systems of many kinds, in the Conqueror’s domain of the form sense-base and so forth; though there is diverse variety, his seeing is just the same; therefore, the Tathāgata is one with eyes on all sides.

“Yato [M 1.0136] ca dhammaṃ tathameva bhāsati,

Karoti vācāyanulomamattano;

Guṇehi lokaṃ abhibhuyyirīyati,

Tathāgato tenapi lokanāyako.

Since he speaks the Dhamma just as it is, and acts in accordance with his words; he surpasses the world with virtues; therefore, the Tathāgata is also a leader of the world.

“Yathābhinīhāramato yathāruci,

Pavattavācā tanucittabhāvato;

Yathāvidhā yena purā mahesino,

Tathāvidho tena jino tathāgato”ti. (dī. ni. ṭī. 1.7) –

According to his aspiration and thought, according to his liking, his speech proceeds from a mind subtle in nature; just as was the manner of the great sages of old, so is the manner of the Victor, the Tathāgata.

Saṅgahagāthā mukhamattameva, kasmā? Appamādapadaṃ viya sakalakusaladhammasampaṭipattiyā sabbabuddhaguṇānaṃ saṅgāhakattā. Tenevāha – “sabbākārenā”tiādi. Sesamettha uttānatthameva.

The summary verse is merely the introduction. Why? Because, like the state of diligence, it is a summary of all the qualities of the Buddhas for the attainment of all wholesome qualities. Therefore, it is said: “In every way,” and so forth. The rest here is clear in meaning.

171. Dutiye uppattīti paṭhamāya jātiyā nibbattiṃ vatvā ariyāya jātiyā nibbattiṃ dassetuṃ – “nipphattī”ti āha. Tadā hissa buddhabhāvanipphattīti. “Dullabho”tiādiṃ [V 1.0125] vatvā kāraṇassa dūrasambhārabhāvato tattha kāraṇaṃ dassento “ekavāra”ntiādimāha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – tattha vāragaṇanā nāma māsasaṃvaccharakappagaṇanādikā, kappānaṃ ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ dve asaṅkhyeyyāni tīṇi asaṅkhyeyyānipi pāramiyo pūretvāpi buddhena bhavituṃ na sakkā, heṭṭhimakoṭiyā pana cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca nirantaraṃ dasa pāramiyo pūretvā buddhabhāvaṃ pattuṃ sakkā, na ito aññathāti iminā kāraṇena dullabho pātubhāvo buddhānanti.

171. In the second instance, “arising” means that having spoken of birth in the first instance, in order to show the arising of the noble birth, it is said: “accomplishment.” For then is meant his accomplishment of Buddhahood. Having stated “difficult to obtain,” and so forth, to show the reason for its difficulty due to the remoteness of the accumulation of causes, it is said: “once,” and so forth. This means: there, the reckoning of periods is by months, years, eons, and so on. Even after fulfilling the perfections for one, two, or three incalculable eons, one cannot become a Buddha. However, at the lower limit, by fulfilling the ten perfections uninterruptedly for four incalculable and one hundred thousand eons, one can attain Buddhahood—not otherwise. For this reason, the manifestation of Buddhas is difficult to obtain.

172. Tatiye niccaṃ na hotīti abhiṇhappavattikaṃ na hoti kadācideva sambhavato. Yebhuyyena manussā acchariyaṃ disvā accharaṃ paharanti, taṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ – “accharaṃ paharitvā passitabbo”ti. Samannāgatattāti etena acchariyā guṇadhammā etasmiṃ santīti acchariyoti dasseti. Apica ādito pabhuti abhinīhārāvaho, tato parampi anaññasādhāraṇe guṇadhamme āciṇṇavāti acchariyoti āha – “āciṇṇamanussotipi acchariyamanusso”tiādi. Mahābodhiñāṇameva maṇḍabhūtaṃ mahābodhimaṇḍo. Sabbaññutaññāṇapadaṭṭhānañhi maggañāṇaṃ, maggañāṇapadaṭṭhānañca sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ [M 1.0137] “mahābodhī”ti vuccati. Anivattakenāti bodhiyā niyatabhāvāpattiyā mahābodhisattabhāvato anivattanasabhāvena. Buddhakārakadhammānaṃ pūraṇampi na aññassa kassaci āciṇṇantiādinā hetuavatthāya phalāvatthāya sattānaṃ upakārāvatthāya cāti tīsupi avatthāsu lokanātho anaññasādhāraṇānaṃ guṇadhammānaṃ āciṇṇatāya acchariyamanusso vuttoti dasseti.

172. In the third, “not constant” means it does not occur frequently but arises only occasionally. Generally, people, upon seeing a marvel, snap their fingers. With reference to this, it is said: “he is to be observed after snapping the fingers.” “Endowed with” shows that because marvelous qualities are present in him, he is marvelous. Moreover, from the very beginning, he brings about aspiration, and thereafter, he is accustomed to unparalleled qualities. Therefore, it is said: “even a practiced person is a marvelous person,” and so forth. The great knowledge of enlightenment itself, being the essence, is the Great Bodhi-maṇḍa. For the knowledge of the path is the foundation for omniscient knowledge, and omniscient knowledge is the foundation for the knowledge of the path—this is called “the Great Enlightenment.” “By the irreversible one” means that due to having attained the state of certainty regarding enlightenment, he is by nature irreversible from the state of a great bodhisattva. The fulfillment of the qualities that make a Buddha is not practiced by anyone else. Thus it is shown that in all three stages—the stage of the cause, the stage of the fruit, and the stage of benefiting beings—the Lord of the World is called a marvelous person on account of having practiced unparalleled qualities.

173. Catutthe kāle kiriyāti kālakiriyā. Katarasmiṃ kāle kīdisī kiriyā. Sāmaññajotanā hi visese avatiṭṭhati, visesatthinā ca viseso anuppayojitabboti āha – “ekasmiṃ kāle pākaṭā kiriyā”ti. Katarasmiṃ pana ekasmiṃ kāle, kathañca pākaṭāti? Kappānaṃ satasahassādhikāni anekāni asaṅkhyeyyāni abhikkamitvā yathādhippetamanorathapāripūrivasena samupaladdhe ekasmiṃ kāle, sadevaloke ativiya acchariyamanussassa parinibbānanti accantapākaṭā. Anutāpakarāti cetodukkhāvahā. Dasasahassacakkavāḷesūti vuttaṃ tassa buddhakkhettabhāvena paricchinnattā, tadaññesañca avisayattā.

173. In the fourth, “action at the time” is kālakiriyā. At what time and what kind of action? A general indication rests on the particular, and a particular should be supplied by one who seeks the particular—thus he said, “At one time the action is manifest.” But at what single time, and how is it manifest? After many incalculable and more than a hundred thousand eons have passed, at one time, attained through the fulfillment of the desired aspiration, the final passing away of such a very marvelous person is exceedingly manifest in the world with its deities. It causes remorse, bringing mental pain. “In ten thousand world-systems”—this is said because it is defined by being his Buddha-field, and because it is beyond the domain of others.

174. Pañcame dutiyassa buddhassāti dutiyassa sabbaññubuddhassa abhāvā. Sutabuddho nāma sutamayena ñāṇena bujjhitabbassa buddhattā. Catusaccabuddho nāma catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ anavasesato buddhattā. Paccekabuddho nāma paccekaṃ attanoyeva yathā catusaccasambodho hoti, evaṃ [V 1.0126] buddhattā. Sammāsambuddho eva hi yathā sadevakassa lokassa catusaccasambodho hoti, evaṃ saccāni abhisambujjhati. Cattāri vā aṭṭha vā soḷasa vāti idaṃ katamahābhinīhārānaṃ mahābodhisattānaṃ paññādhikasaddhādhikavīriyādhikavibhāgavasena vuttaṃ. “Paññādhikānañhi saddhā mandā hoti, paññā tikkhā.
