Saddhādhikānaṃ paññā majjhimā hoti. Vīriyādhikānaṃ paññā mandā, paññānubhāvena ca sammāsambodhi adhigantabbā”ti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Avisesena pana vimuttiparipācanīyadhammānaṃ tikkhamajjhimamudubhāvena tayopete bhedā yuttāti vadanti. Tividhā hi bodhisattā abhinīhārakkhaṇe bhavanti ugghaṭitaññuvipañcitaññuneyyabhedena. Tesu [M 1.0138] ugghaṭitaññū sammāsambuddhassa sammukhā cātuppadikaṃ gāthaṃ suṇanto tatiyapade apariyositeyeva chahi abhiññāhi saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pattuṃ samatthūpanissayo hoti. Dutiyo satthu sammukhā ekaṃ gāthaṃ suṇanto apariyositeyeva catutthapade chahi abhiññāhi arahattaṃ pattuṃ samatthūpanissayo hoti. Itaro bhagavato sammukhā cātuppadikagāthaṃ sutvā pariyositāya gāthāya chahi abhiññāhi arahattaṃ pattuṃ samatthūpanissayo hoti. Tayopete vinā kālabhedena katābhinīhārā laddhabyākaraṇā pāramiyo pūrento yathākkamaṃ yathāvuttabhedena kālena sammāsambodhiṃ pāpuṇanti, tesu tesu pana kālabhedesu aparipuṇṇesu te te mahāsattā divase divase vessantaradānasadisaṃ dānaṃ dentāpi tadanurūpaṃ sīlādisesapāramidhamme ācinantāpi antarā buddhā bhavissantīti akāraṇametaṃ. Kasmā? Ñāṇassa aparipaccanato. Paricchinnakālanipphāditaṃ viya hi sassaṃ paricchinnakāle nipphāditā sammāsambodhi tadantarā sabbussāhena vāyamantenapi na sakkā pāpuṇitunti pāramipūrī yathāvuttakālavisesena sampajjatīti veditabbaṃ. Saddhinti samānakāle.

174. In the fifth, “of a second Buddha” refers to the absence of a second all-knowing Buddha. A “Sutabuddha” is so called because of being a Buddha with respect to what is to be understood through knowledge based on hearing. A “Catusaccabuddha” is so named because of fully awakening to the four noble truths without remainder. A “Paccekabuddha” is one who awakens individually, for himself alone, just as there is the awakening to the four truths. Only a “Sammāsambuddha” truly awakens to the truths in such a way that the world, including its gods, awakens to the four truths. The “four, eight, or sixteen” refers to the division of great bodhisattvas who have made the great aspiration, based on whether they are dominant in wisdom, faith, or energy. The commentary states: “For those dominant in wisdom, faith is weak, but wisdom is sharp. For those dominant in faith, wisdom is moderate. For those dominant in energy, wisdom is weak, yet through the power of wisdom, perfect enlightenment is to be attained.” Generally, however, they say that these three divisions are suitable because of the sharp, moderate, and soft nature of the qualities that ripen for liberation. Indeed, bodhisattvas at the moment of aspiration are of three kinds: those with quick understanding, those requiring detailed explanation, and those to be guided. Among them, the one with quick understanding, upon hearing a four-line verse in the presence of a Sammāsambuddha, has the supporting condition to attain arahantship with the six higher knowledges and analytical insights even before the third line is completed. The second type, hearing a single verse in the Teacher’s presence, has the supporting condition to attain arahantship with the six higher knowledges before the fourth line is completed. The third type, hearing a four-line verse from the Blessed One, has the supporting condition to attain arahantship with the six higher knowledges only after the verse is completed. These three, having made their aspirations without a difference in time, having received predictions, and fulfilling the perfections in due order, attain perfect enlightenment at the appropriate times as described. However, if those great beings are not complete in those respective time divisions, even if they give gifts like Vessantara daily or accumulate virtues such as morality, they will not become Buddhas in the interim; this is not a possibility. Why? Because their knowledge has not fully matured. Just as a crop ripens only at its fixed time, so too does perfect enlightenment—it cannot be attained before its fixed time, no matter how much effort is exerted. It should be understood that the fulfillment of the perfections is accomplished only at the designated time and special period mentioned. “Saddhiṃ” means at the same time.

Asahāyoti nippariyāyato vuttaṃ. Sahaayanaṭṭho hi sahāyaṭṭho. Paṭipattivasena bhagavatā saha samaṃ ayanaṃ nāma kassacipi nattheva. Hatthādiavayavato paṭi paṭi minitabbato paṭimā vuccati attabhāvo. Samattho nāma natthīti devo vā māro vā brahmā vā koci natthi. Paṭisamoti paṭinidhibhāvena samo. Paṭibhāgaṃ dātunti “cattāro satipaṭṭhānā”tiādinā vuttassa dhammabhāgassa dhammakoṭṭhāsassa paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ katvā bhāgaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ paṭivacanaṃ dātuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Natthi etassa sīlādiguṇehi paṭibimbabhūto puggaloti appaṭipuggalo. Tenāha – “añño kocī”tiādi. Tisahassimahāsahassīnaṃ vibhāgo parato āvi bhavissati. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

“Without a companion” is said unequivocally. The meaning of “companion” is indeed “one whose going is together.” In terms of practice, no one at all has a going equal to that of the Blessed One. The individual self (attabhāvo) is called an “image” (paṭimā) because it is to be measured part by part, such as by the hands and other limbs. “None is capable” means there is no one—whether a god, Māra, or Brahmā. “Equal in return” (paṭisamo) means equal in the sense of a substitute. “To give a comparable portion” means there is no one capable of giving a portion, a section, as a counter-portion or response to the portion of the Dhamma spoken of as “the four foundations of mindfulness,” and so forth. He is without a counterpart person (appaṭipuggalo), meaning there is no person who is a reflection of his virtues, such as moral conduct. Therefore, it is said: “No other whatsoever,” and so forth. The division of the three-thousand-great-thousand world system will become clear later. The rest here is easily understood.

175. Chaṭṭhādīsu tasmiṃ puggaleti sammāsambuddhe. Tanti paññācakkhu. Pātubhūtameva hoti tassa [V 1.0127] sahassa uppajjanato. Uppattīti uppajjanaṃ. Nipphattīti parivuddhi. Kīvarūpassāti kīdisassa. Sāvakavisayeva hatthagataṃ paññācakkhu nāma dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃyevāti āha – “sāriputtattherassā”tiādi. Samādhipaññāti samādhisahagatā paññā. “Samādhisaṃvattanikā [M 1.0139] khippanisantiādivisesāvahā paññā”ti keci. Ālokoti paññāāloko eva. Tathā obhāso. Tīṇipīti tīṇipi suttāni. Lokiyalokuttaramissakānīti pubbabhāgapaññāya adhippetattā vuttaṃ.

175. In the sixth, etc., "in that person" refers to the Perfectly Enlightened One. "That" means the eye of wisdom. "Has appeared" means it has manifested from the moment of its arising. "Arising" refers to origination. "Maturity" means full growth. "Of what kind" asks about its nature. The eye of wisdom, attainable by disciples, is specifically at hand for the two chief disciples—thus it is said, "of the Venerable Sāriputta," etc. "Wisdom associated with concentration" is the meaning of samādhipaññā. Some say, "It is wisdom that conduces to concentration, brings quick penetration, and bestows special qualities." "Light" is indeed the light of wisdom. Similarly, "illumination." "All three" means all three discourses. "Mixed with mundane and supramundane" is said because it is intended as preliminary wisdom.

Uttamadhammānanti attano uttaritarassa abhāvena seṭṭhadhammānaṃ. Daṭṭhabbato dassanaṃ, bhagavato rūpakāyo. Tatthapi visesato rūpāyatanaṃ. Tenāha – “cakkhuviññāṇena daṭṭhuṃ labhatī”ti. Natthi ito uttaranti anuttaraṃ, tadeva anuttariyaṃ, dassanañca taṃ anuttariyañcāti dassanānuttariyaṃ. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ pana padaviseso – suyyatīti savanaṃ, bhagavato vacanaṃ. Labbhatīti lābho, bhagavati saddhā. Sikkhitabbato sikkhā. Sīlasamādhipaññāparicaraṇaṃ pāricariyā, upaṭṭhānaṃ. Anussaraṇaṃ anussati, satthu guṇānussaraṇaṃ. Imesanti yathāvuttānaṃ channaṃ anuttariyānaṃ. Pātubhāvo hotīti tathāgatassa pātubhāvā tappaṭibaddhattā tabbisayattā ca pātubhāvo hoti. “Dassanānuttariya”nti ca sadevake loke uttaritarassa bhagavato rūpassa na dassanamattaṃ adhippetaṃ, atha kho tassa rūpadassanamukhena aveccappasādena buddhaguṇe okappetvā ogāhetvā dassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tenāha – “āyasmā hī”tiādi. Idampi dassanānuttariyanti pubbe vuttato nibbisesattā vuttaṃ. Dasabalaṃ dassanāya labhitvāti ānandatthero viya pasādabhattimettāpubbakaṃ dasabalaṃ dassanāya labhitvā. Dassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvāti dassanamukhena pavattaṃ vipassanācāraṃ vaḍḍhetvā. Dassanamukhena yāva anulomañāṇaṃ vipassanācāraṃ vaḍḍhetvā tadanantaraṃ aṭṭhamakamahābhūmiṃ okkamanto dassanaṃ sotāpattimaggaṃ pāpeti nāma. Idha parato pavattaṃ dassanaṃ dassanameva nāma, mūladassanaṃ pana saccadassanassapi kāraṇabhāvato dassanānuttariyaṃ nāma. Esa nayo sesānuttariyesupi.

"Of the highest qualities" refers to the supreme qualities, due to the absence of anything superior to them. It is 'seeing' because it is to be seen; this refers to the physical form of the Blessed One. Therein, specifically, the visible sense-sphere. Therefore, it is said: "One can see with eye-consciousness." "There is nothing superior to this" means the unsurpassed; that itself is the unsurpassable. Both the seeing and that unsurpassable state are called "the unsurpassable seeing." The same principle applies to the remaining terms. Here, however, is a distinction in phrasing: It is 'hearing' because it is to be heard; this refers to the speech of the Blessed One. It is 'gain' because it is to be obtained; this refers to faith in the Blessed One. It is 'training' because it is to be trained in. Service (pāricariyā) is the practice of virtue, concentration, and wisdom; it means attendance. Recollection (anussati) is the act of recollecting, the recollection of the Teacher’s virtues. "Of these" refers to the six unsurpassable states as previously mentioned. "The manifestation occurs" means that due to the appearance of the Tathāgata, the manifestation occurs, being connected to it and within its domain. "The unsurpassable seeing" is not merely the sight of the Blessed One’s form, which is supreme in the world with its gods, but rather the seeing should be understood as that which involves placing trust in and immersing oneself in the Buddha’s qualities through unwavering faith, by means of seeing his form. Therefore, it is said: "The venerable one," and so forth. This too is called "the unsurpassable seeing" because it is no different from what was stated before. "Having gained the vision of the Ten-Powered One" means, like the Venerable Ānanda, having first developed faith, devotion, and loving-kindness, one attains the vision of the Ten-Powered One. "Having developed the seeing" means having developed the insight practice that proceeds by means of the seeing. Having developed the insight practice by means of the seeing up to the knowledge of adaptation, immediately afterward, one who enters the stage of the eighth person is said to bring the seeing to the stream-entry path. Here, the seeing that proceeds from that is simply called "seeing," but the root seeing, because it serves as the cause for seeing the truths, is called "the unsurpassable seeing." The same principle applies to the remaining unsurpassable states.

Dasabale saddhaṃ paṭilabhatīti sammāsambuddhe bhagavati saddhaṃ paṭilabhati. Tisso sikkhā sikkhitvāti tisso pubbabhāgasikkhā sikkhitvā. Paricaratīti upaṭṭhānaṃ karoti. “Itipi so bhagavā”tiādinā buddhānussativasena anussatijjhānaṃ uppādetvā taṃ padaṭṭhānaṃ katvā vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhento “anussatiṃ vaḍḍhetvā”ti vutto.

"He gains faith in the Ten-Powered One" means he gains faith in the Blessed One, the Perfectly Enlightened One. "Having trained in the three trainings" means having trained in the three preliminary trainings. "He serves" means he renders service. By recollecting in the manner of recollection of the Buddha, beginning with 'Indeed, the Blessed One is so,' he arouses meditative absorption based on recollection and, making that the foundation, develops insight—thus, he is said to have 'developed recollection.'

Sacchikiriyā [M 1.0140] hotīti paccakkhakaraṇaṃ hoti. Maggakkhaṇe hi labbhamānā paṭisambhidā phalakkhaṇe [V 1.0128] sacchikatā nāma hoti tato paraṃ atthādīsu yathicchitaṃ viniyogakkhamabhāvato. Catassoti gaṇanaparicchedo. Paṭisambhidāti pabhedā. Kassa pana pabhedāti? “Atthe ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā”tiādivacanato (vibha. 718-721) ñāṇassetā pabhedā. Tasmā catasso paṭisambhidāti cattāro ñāṇappabhedāti attho. Atthapaṭisambhidāti atthe paṭisambhidā, atthapabhedassa salakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ atthe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇanti attho. Tathā dhammapabhedassa salakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ dhamme pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā. Niruttipabhedassa salakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ niruttābhilāpe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā. Paṭibhānapabhedassa salakkhaṇavibhāvanavavatthānakaraṇasamatthaṃ paṭibhāne pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā.

"Realization" means the act of directly experiencing. For, the analytical knowledges obtainable at the path moment are called "realized" at the fruition moment, because thereafter they are capable of being applied as desired in regard to meanings and so forth. "Four" is a numerical determination. "Analytical knowledges" (paṭisambhidā) means distinctions. But distinctions of what? From the statement, "Knowledge of meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning," and so forth, it is understood that these are distinctions of knowledge. Therefore, "the four analytical knowledges" means the four distinctions of knowledge. "The analytical knowledge of meaning" (atthapaṭisambhidā) means the analytical knowledge in meaning; that is, the knowledge concerning the analysis of meaning, which is capable of clarifying and determining the specific characteristics of that analysis of meaning. Similarly, "the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma" (dhammapaṭisambhidā) is the knowledge concerning the analysis of the Dhamma, which is capable of clarifying and determining the specific characteristics of that analysis of the Dhamma. "The analytical knowledge of language" (niruttipaṭisambhidā) is the knowledge concerning the analysis of language and expression, which is capable of clarifying and determining the specific characteristics of that analysis of language. "The analytical knowledge of intuition" (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā) is the knowledge concerning the analysis of intuition, which is capable of clarifying and determining the specific characteristics of that analysis of intuition.

Atthesu ñāṇantiādīsu atthoti saṅkhepato hetuphalaṃ. Tañhi hetuvasena araṇīyaṃ gantabbaṃ pattabbaṃ, tasmā “attho”ti vuccati. Pabhedato pana yaṃ kiñci paccayuppannaṃ, nibbānaṃ, bhāsitattho, vipāko, kiriyāti ime pañca dhammā “attho”ti veditabbā. Taṃ atthaṃ paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ atthapaṭisambhidā. Dhammoti saṅkhepato paccayo. So hi yasmā tanti dahati vidahati pavatteti ceva pāpeti ca ṭhapeti ca, tasmā “dhammo”ti vuccati. Pabhedato pana yo koci phalanibbattako hetu ariyamaggo bhāsitaṃ kusalaṃ akusalanti pañcavidhoti veditabbo, taṃ dhammaṃ paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ dhamme pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ dhammapaṭisambhidā.

In such phrases as "knowledge in meanings," "meaning" (attha), in brief, is cause and effect. For it is to be gone to, reached, and attained by way of a cause; therefore, it is called "meaning." In detail, however, these five things are to be understood as "meaning": whatever is conditionally arisen, Nibbāna, the meaning of what is spoken, resultant consciousness, and functional consciousness. For one who reviews that meaning, the knowledge that has penetrated its analysis is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā). "Dhamma," in brief, is the condition. For since it places, arranges, sets in motion, causes to reach, and establishes, therefore it is called "dhamma." In detail, however, it should be understood as fivefold: any cause that produces a result, the Noble Path, what is spoken, the wholesome, and the unwholesome. For one who reviews that dhamma, the knowledge that has penetrated its analysis is the analytical knowledge of dhamma (dhammapaṭisambhidā).

Atthadhammaniruttābhilāpe ñāṇanti tasmiṃ atthe ca dhamme ca sabhāvaniruttisaddaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa tasmiṃ sabhāvaniruttiabhilāpe pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ. Evamayaṃ niruttipaṭisambhidā saddārammaṇā nāma jātā, na paññattiārammaṇā. Kasmā? Yasmā saddaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ sabhāvanirutti, ayaṃ na sabhāvaniruttī”ti pajānāti. Paṭisambhidāpatto hi “phasso”ti vutte “ayaṃ sabhāvaniruttī”ti jānāti, “phassā”ti vā “phassa”nti vā vutte “ayaṃ na sabhāvaniruttī”ti jānāti. Vedanādīsupi eseva nayo. Ayaṃ panesa [M 1.0141] nāmākhyātopasaggābyayapadampi jānātiyeva sabhāvaniruttiyā yāthāvato jānanato. Ñāṇesu ñāṇanti sabbatthakañāṇaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā paccavekkhantassa pabhedagataṃ ñāṇaṃ.

Knowledge in the expression of language concerning meaning and phenomena means the knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions in that natural linguistic expression, arising in one who reviews, having taken as object the sound of the natural expression concerning that meaning and phenomenon. Thus, this analytical knowledge of language has sound as its object, not concepts. Why? Because upon hearing a sound, one understands: 'This is a natural expression; this is not a natural expression.' For one who has attained analytical knowledge, when 'contact' (phasso) is said, they know: 'This is a natural expression.' But when 'contacts' (phassā) or 'contact' (phassaṃ) is said, they know: 'This is not a natural expression.' The same method applies to feeling and so on. Moreover, this one also knows nouns, verbs, prefixes, and indeclinable particles as they really are, due to knowing the natural expression as it really is. Knowledge in knowledges means the knowledge that has penetrated the distinctions, arising in one who reviews, having taken as object the all-pervading knowledge.

Imā pana catasso paṭisambhidā sekkhabhūmiyaṃ asekkhabhūmiyanti dvīsu ṭhānesu pabhedaṃ gacchanti. Adhigamo pariyatti savanaṃ paripucchā pubbayogoti imehi pañcahi kāraṇehi visadā [V 1.0129] honti. Adhigamo nāma saccappaṭivedho. Pariyatti nāma buddhavacanaṃ. Tañhi gaṇhantassa paṭisambhidā visadā honti. Savanaṃ nāma dhammassavanaṃ. Sakkaccaṃ dhammaṃ suṇantassapi hi paṭisambhidā visadā honti. Paripucchā nāma aṭṭhakathā. Uggahitapāḷiyā atthaṃ kathentassapi hi paṭisambhidā visadā honti. Pubbayogo nāma pubbayogāvacaratā. Haraṇapaccāharaṇanayena paṭipākaṭakammaṭṭhānassapi paṭisambhidā visadā hontīti. Lokiyalokuttarā vāti ettha tisso paṭisambhidā lokiyā, atthapaṭisambhidā siyā lokiyā, siyā lokuttarāti evaṃ vibhajitvā attho veditabbo.

These four analytical knowledges are distinguished on two grounds: the ground of the trainee and the ground of the adept. They become clear through five causes: attainment, study, listening, inquiry, and prior practice. Attainment means the penetration of the truths. Study means the word of the Buddha; for one who grasps it, the analytical knowledges become clear. Listening means hearing the Dhamma; for one who listens to the Dhamma attentively, the analytical knowledges also become clear. Inquiry means the commentaries; for one who explains the meaning of the Pāli text they have learned, the analytical knowledges become clear. Prior practice means engagement in prior practice; the analytical knowledges also become clear for one whose meditation subject has become manifest through the method of application and withdrawal. Regarding whether they are mundane or supramundane: three analytical knowledges are mundane, while the analytical knowledge of meaning may be either mundane or supramundane. The meaning should be understood by distinguishing it thus.

Buddhuppādeyevāti avadhāraṇena buddhuppāde eva labbhanato, abuddhuppāde alabbhanato anaññasādhāraṇo paṭivedho adhippeto. Evañca katvā “mahato cakkhussā”tiādīsu paññāmahattādikampi anaññasādhāraṇameva adhippetanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tathā vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyādayopi paresaṃ tabbhāvāvahā daṭṭhabbā. Yā kāci dhātuyo lokiyā lokuttarā vā, sabbā tā imāheva saṅgahitā, ettheva antogadhāti vuttaṃ – “imāva aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo nānāsabhāvato nānādhātuyo”ti. Svāyamattho anekadhātunānādhātuñāṇavibhaṅgena (vibha. 751) dīpetabbo. “Sacchikiriyā”ti vuttattā “vijjāti phale ñāṇa”nti vuttaṃ.

Regarding 'Only upon the arising of a Buddha,' by this emphasis (eva), a penetration that is not common to others is intended, because it is attainable only when a Buddha arises and unattainable when a Buddha does not arise. And so, it should be seen that in phrases like 'of the great eye,' the greatness of wisdom and other qualities are also intended to be not common to others. Similarly, the realization of the fruit of knowledge and liberation, and so on, should be understood as bringing about that state for others. Whatever elements there are, mundane or supramundane, they are all included here, encompassed within this. Thus, it is said: 'These eighteen elements are diverse elements because of their diverse individual natures.' This meaning should be clarified by the analysis of the knowledge of the many and diverse elements (Vibhaṅga 751). Since 'realization' is mentioned, it is said: 'Knowledge means the knowledge in the fruit.'

187. Yasmā cakkati aparāparaṃ parivattatīti cakkaṃ, tasmā iriyāpathāpi aparāparaṃ parivattanaṭṭhena cakkasadisattā cakkanti vuttā, tathā patirūpadesavāsādisampattiyo. Tato paṭṭhāya dhammacakkaṃ abhinīharati nāmāti ettha tadā mahāsatto attānaṃ abhinīhārayogaṃ karonto “dhammacakkaṃ abhinīharati nāmā”ti vutto tato paṭṭhāya dhammacakkābhinīhāravibandhakaradhammānuppajjanato. Abhinīhaṭaṃ nāmāti etthapi ayameva [M 1.0142] nayo. Arahattamaggaṃ paṭivijjhantopi dhammacakkaṃ uppādetiyeva nāma tadatthaṃ ñāṇaṃ paripācetīti katvā. Arahattaphalakkhaṇe dhammacakkaṃ uppāditaṃ nāma tasmiṃ khaṇe dhammacakkassa uppādanāya kātabbakiccassa kassaci abhāvā. Paṭivedhañāṇañhi idha “dhammacakka”nti adhippetaṃ. Idāni desanāñāṇavasena dhammacakkaṃ dassetuṃ – “kadā pavatteti nāmā”tiādimāha. Na kevalaṃ therasseva, atha kho sabbesampi sāsanikānaṃ dhammakathā bhagavato dhammadesanā catunnaṃ ariyasaccānaṃ catunnañca ekattādinayānaṃ avirādhanatoti dassetuṃ – “yo hi koci bhikkhu vā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

187. Because it turns and revolves continuously, it is called a wheel (cakka). For that reason, the postures are also called a wheel, due to their nature of continuously changing, resembling a wheel; and so too are attainments such as residence in a suitable place. 'From that point onward, he sets forth the Wheel of the Dhamma' means that at that time the Great Being, making the application of his aspiration, is said to 'set forth the Wheel of the Dhamma' because from that point onward no phenomena obstructing the setting forth of the Wheel of the Dhamma arise. Here, regarding 'has been set forth,' this same method applies. Even when penetrating the path of arahantship, one is indeed said to generate the Wheel of Dhamma, on the grounds that one matures the knowledge for that purpose. At the moment of the fruit of arahantship, the Wheel of Dhamma is said to have been generated, because at that moment there is no further duty to be performed for the generation of the Wheel of Dhamma. For here, 'knowledge of penetration' is what is meant by 'Wheel of the Dhamma.' Now, to explain the Wheel of Dhamma by way of the knowledge of teaching, it begins, 'When does he set it rolling?' and so on. To show that the Dhamma talk of not only the Elder, but indeed of all those in the Dispensation, is the Blessed One's teaching of the Dhamma, as long as it does not contradict the four noble truths and the four methods such as unity, it begins, 'For whatever monk...' and so on. The rest is easily understood.

Ekapuggalavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Chapter of the Single Person is concluded.

14. Etadaggavaggo

14. The Chapter of the Foremost

(14) 1. Paṭhamaetadaggavaggo

(14) 1. The First Chapter of the Foremost

Etadaggapadavaṇṇanā

Commentary on the Term 'Etadagga'

188. Etadaggesu [V 1.0130] paṭhamavaggassa paṭhame ādimhi dissatīti ettha aggasaddoti ānetvā yojetabbaṃ. Ajjataggeti ajjadivasaṃ ādiṃ katvāti attho. Aṅgulaggenāti aṅgulikoṭiyā. Ambilagganti ambilakoṭṭhāso. Koṭibhūtāti paramakoṭibhūtā tasmiṃ ṭhāne tādisānaṃ aññesaṃ abhāvato. Tato eva seṭṭhabhūtātipi aggā. Etadaggasannikkhepoti etadagge ṭhapanaṃ aṭṭhuppattiādīhi catūhipi kāraṇehi. Mahāpaññatāya therena etadaggaṭṭhānassa laddhabhāvaṃ vitthārato dassetuṃ – “katha”ntiādimāha. Dve padantarānīti kaṇḍambamūle yugandharapabbateti dvīsu ṭhānesu dve padāni dassetvā. Muṇḍapīṭhakanti yaṃ sattaṅgaṃ pañcaṅgaṃ vā na hoti, kevalaṃ muṇḍakapīṭhaṃ, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Avattharitvā nisīdīti buddhānubhāvena ajjhottharitvā nisīdi. Tenāha – “evaṃ nisīdanto”tiādi. Kāyasakkhiṃ katvāti nāmakāyena desanāya sampaṭicchanavasena sakkhibhūtaṃ katvā. Kusalā dhammā akusalā dhammā abyākatā dhammāti iti-saddo ādyattho, tena sabbaṃ abhidhammadesanaṃ saṅgaṇhāti.

188. In the first sutta of the first chapter on the foremost, because it is seen at the beginning, here the word 'agga' should be supplied and connected. 'Ajjatagge' means 'taking today as the starting point.' 'Aṅgulaggena' means 'by the fingertip.' 'Ambilagganti' means 'the sour part.' 'Koṭibhūtā' means 'having become the peak,' that is, the ultimate peak, because of the absence of any others like them in that position; for that very reason, they are also 'foremost' (aggā), having become the best. 'Etadaggasannikkhepo' means the placing in the foremost position by means of the four causes, beginning with the occasion of its arising. To show in detail how the foremost position was obtained by the Elder because of his great wisdom, it begins with 'How?' and so on. 'Dve padantarāni' means having shown two different words in two places: 'at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree' and 'on Mount Yugandhara.' 'Muṇḍapīṭhaka' refers to that which is not a seven-limbed or five-limbed seat, but merely a bare stool; this is said in reference to that. 'He sat down without spreading anything out' means he sat down having been pervaded by the Buddha’s power. For that reason, it is said, 'Thus sitting down...' and so on. 'Kāyasakkhiṃ katvā' means having made himself a personal witness by way of receiving the teaching with the mental body. 'Wholesome phenomena, unwholesome phenomena, indeterminate phenomena'—here the word 'iti' has the meaning of 'and so on,' thereby encompassing the entire Abhidhamma teaching.

Pāṭihāriyaṭṭhāneti yamakapāṭihāriyassa kataṭṭhāne. Passathāti tesaṃ bahubhāvaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Assāti manussasamūhassa ekabhāvaṃ. Ākappanti [M 1.0143] ākāraṃ. Mahājanoti sadevake loke sabbo mahājano. Yathā nirayadassanaṃ saṃvegajananatthaṃ, evaṃ devalokadassanampi saṃvegajananatthameva “anupubbikathāyaṃ saggakathā viya evaṃ sabbasampattisamupetopi saggo anicco addhuvo cavanadhammo”ti. Sajjetvāti samapaṇṇāsāya mucchanāhi yathā kāmena nivādetuṃ sakkā, evaṃ sajjetvā.

'At the place of the miracle' means at the place where the twin miracle was performed. 'Behold' is said with reference to their great number. 'Assa' refers to the single group of the human multitude. 'Ākappa' means appearance. 'The great multitude' means the entire great multitude in the world with its devas. Just as seeing hell is for the purpose of generating spiritual urgency, so too is seeing the deva world for the purpose of generating spiritual urgency, as in the gradual discourse, like the talk on heaven: 'Thus even heaven, endowed with all prosperity, is impermanent, not lasting, and subject to passing away.' 'Sajjetvā' means having prepared it so that one is able to play it as one wishes with the fifty modulations.

Puthujjanapañcakaṃ pañhanti puthujjanapañhaṃ ādiṃ katvā pavattitaṃ khīṇāsavapañhapariyantaṃ pañhapañcakaṃ. Paṭhamaṃ…pe… pucchīti puthujjanavisaye pañhaṃ pucchi. Paṭisambhidā yathābhinīhāraṃ [V 1.0131] yathāsakaṃ vipassanābhinīhārena paṭhamabhūmiyādayo viya pavattitavisayāti vuttaṃ – “te attano attano paṭisambhidāvisaye ṭhatvā kathayiṃsū”ti. Buddhavisaye pañhaṃ pucchīti –

'The pentad of questions' means the group of five questions that proceeds beginning with the question on the worldling and ending with the question on the one whose cankers are destroyed. 'The first... he asked' means he asked a question concerning the domain of the worldling. The analytical knowledges have their domains of operation according to their aspiration, that is, according to their respective aspiration for insight, like the first stage and so on. Thus it is said: 'They spoke, each standing in their own domain of analytical knowledge.' 'He asked a question concerning the domain of the Buddha' means—

“Ye ca saṅkhātadhammāse, ye ca sekhā puthū idha;

Tesaṃ me nipako iriyaṃ, puṭṭho pabrūhi mārisā”ti. (su. ni. 1044) –

"Those here who have comprehended the Dhamma, and the many trainees—O venerable sir, you who are discerning, having been asked, please declare to me their conduct."

Idaṃ pañhaṃ pucchi. Tattha saṅkhātadhammāti saṅkhātā ñātā catusaccadhammā, ye ca saṅkhātadhammā catūhi maggehi paṭividdhacatusaccadhammāti attho. Iminā asekkhā kathitā. Puthu-saddo ubhayatthapi yojetabbo “ye puthū saṅkhātadhammā, ye ca puthū sekhā”ti. Tesanti tesaṃ dvinnaṃ sekkhāsekkhapuggalānaṃ me puṭṭhoti yojetabbaṃ, mayā puṭṭhoti attho. Iriyanti sekkhāsekkhabhūmiyā āgamanappaṭipadaṃ. Iriyati gacchati sekkhabhūmiṃ asekkhabhūmiñca etāyāti iriyā, taṃ tesaṃ iriyaṃ āgamanappaṭipadaṃ mayā puṭṭho pabrūhi kathehīti attho. Evaṃ bhagavā buddhavisaye pañhaṃ pucchitvā “imassa nu kho, sāriputta, saṃkhittena bhāsitassa kathaṃ vitthārena attho daṭṭhabbo”ti āha. Thero pañhaṃ oloketvā “satthā maṃ sekkhāsekkhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ āgamanappaṭipadaṃ pucchatī”ti pañhe nikkaṅkho hutvā “āgamanappaṭipadā nāma khandhādivasena bahūhipi mukhehi sakkā kathetuṃ, katarākārena nu kho kathento satthu ajjhāsayaṃ gaṇhituṃ sakkhissāmī”ti ajjhāsaye kaṅkhi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “dhammasenāpati…pe… na sakkotī”ti. Pucchitapañhaṃ vissajjetuṃ paṭibhāne asati disāvilokanaṃ sattānaṃ sabhāvoti dassento, “puratthima…pe... nāsakkhī”ti āha. Tattha pañhuppattiṭṭhānanti pañhuppattikāraṇaṃ.

This question was asked. Here, “comprehended things” (saṅkhātadhammā) means the four noble truths that are comprehended and known; and “comprehended things” are the four noble truths penetrated by the four paths—this is the meaning. By this, the non-trainee (asekkha) is spoken of. The word “puthu” should be applied in both places: “those who are variously comprehended things, and those who are variously trainees.” “Tesanti” should be construed as “asked by me of those two—trainees and non-trainees”; the meaning is “asked by me.” “Iriyanti” means the path of approach to the state of trainees and non-trainees. “Iriyati” means “goes”; that by which one goes to the state of trainees and non-trainees is called “iriyā.” That conduct of theirs, the path of approach, when asked by me, 'explain it, speak of it'—this is the meaning. Thus, having asked the question concerning the domain of the Buddha, the Blessed One said, “Now, Sāriputta, how should the detailed meaning of this brief statement be understood?” The Elder, considering the question, and having become free of doubt regarding the question, thought, “The Teacher is asking me about the path of approach of the bhikkhus who are trainees and non-trainees.” “The path of approach can be spoken of in many ways, such as through the aggregates, etc. But in what way, indeed, speaking, shall I be able to grasp the Teacher's intention?”—he was uncertain regarding the intention. This is what is meant by “the general of the Dhamma... was unable.” Showing that looking in the directions is the nature of beings when there was no ready wit to answer the asked question, he said, “eastern... was unable.” Here, “the basis for the arising of the question” (pañhuppattiṭṭhāna) means the cause for the arising of the question.

Therassa [M 1.0144] kilamanabhāvaṃ jānitvāti “sāriputto pañhe nikkaṅkho, ajjhāsaye me kaṅkhamāno kilamatī”ti therassa kilamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā. Catumahābhūtikakāyapariggahanti etena khandhamukhena nāmarūpapariggaho vutto. “Bhūtamidanti, sāriputta, samanupassasī”ti hi vadantena bhagavatā khandhavasena nāmarūpapariggaho dassito. Evaṃ kirassa bhagavato ahosi “sāriputto mayā naye adinne kathetuṃ na sakkhissati, dinne pana naye mamajjhāsayaṃ gahetvā khandhavasena kathessatī”ti. Therassa saha nayadānena so pañho nayasatena nayasahassena upaṭṭhāsi. Tenāha – “aññātaṃ bhagavā, aññātaṃ sugatā”ti.

Knowing the Elder's state of weariness, thinking, “Sāriputta is free from doubt regarding the question, but being doubtful about my intention, he grows weary,”—thus knowing the Elder's state of weariness. The comprehension of the body composed of the four great elements—by this, the comprehension of name-and-form is stated by way of the aggregates. For when the Blessed One says, “Do you regard this as what has come to be, Sāriputta?”, the comprehension of name-and-form is shown by the Blessed One by way of the aggregates. Thus, it seems, the Blessed One thought: “Sāriputta will not be able to speak if a method is not given by me, but if a method is given, having grasped my intention, he will speak by way of the aggregates.” With the giving of the method to the Elder, that question became clear to him in a hundred ways, in a thousand ways. Therefore, he said: “It is known, Blessed One, it is known, Sugata.”

Arūpāvacare paṭisandhi nāma na hotīti bodhisambhārasambharaṇassa anokāsabhāvato vuttaṃ. Tenāha – “abhabbaṭṭhānattā”ti, laddhabyākaraṇānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ uppattiyā abhabbadesattāti attho[V 1.0132]. Rūpāvacare nibbattīti kammavasitāsambhavato arūpāvacare anibbattitvā rūpāvacare nibbatti.

In the formless realm, rebirth-linking does not occur, it is said, due to the absence of opportunity for accumulating the requisites of enlightenment. Therefore, it is said: “Because it is an impossible state”—the meaning is that it is an impossible place for the arising of Bodhisattvas who have received a prediction. Rebirth occurs in the form realm; due to the possibility of mastery over kamma, one is not reborn in the formless realm but in the form realm.

Parosahassantiādinā parosahassajātakaṃ dasseti. Tattha parosahassampīti atirekasahassampi. Samāgatānanti sannipatitānaṃ bhāsitassa atthaṃ jānituṃ asakkontānaṃ bālānaṃ. Kandeyyuṃ te vassasataṃ apaññāti te evaṃ samāgatā apaññā ime bālattā sasā viya vassasatampi vassasahassampi rodeyyuṃ parideveyyuṃ. Rodamānāpi pana atthaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ vā neva jāneyyunti dīpeti. Ekova seyyo puriso sapaññoti evarūpānaṃ bālānaṃ parosahassatopi eko paṇḍitapurisova seyyo varataroti attho. Kīdiso sapaññoti āha – “yo bhāsitassa vijānāti attha”nti, ayaṃ jeṭṭhantevāsiko viya yo bhāsitassa atthaṃ jānāti, so tādiso sapañño varataroti attho. Dutiye parosatajātake jhāyeyyunti yāthāvato atthaṃ jānituṃ samāhitā hutvā cinteyyuṃ. Sesamettha vuttanayameva.

By the term 'parosahassa' and so on, the Parosahassa Jātaka is shown. There, 'parosahassampi' means even more than a thousand. 'Samāgatānaṃ' refers to the fools who, having gathered, are unable to understand the meaning of what was spoken. 'They would weep for a hundred years without wisdom'—these very fools, assembled in such a way, lacking wisdom, would cry and lament for a hundred years or even a thousand years, like hares, due to their foolishness. But even while crying, they would not know the meaning or the reason—this is explained. 'One wise man is better'—even more than a thousand such fools, one wise man is better, superior—this is the meaning. 'What kind of wise man?' He says: 'One who understands the meaning of what is spoken'—this means that one who knows the meaning of what is spoken, like the chief disciple, such a wise man is superior. In the second Parosata Jātaka, 'they would meditate' means they would reflect, having become composed, to understand the meaning as it really is. The rest here follows the same method as previously stated.

Tatiyajātake ye saññinoti ṭhapetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanalābhino avasesacittakasatte dasseti. Tepi duggatāti tassā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattiyā alābhato tepi duggatā dukkhaṃ upagatā saññībhave. “Saññā rogo saññā gaṇḍo saññā salla”nti [M 1.0145] (ma. ni. 3.24) hi te saññāya ādīnavadassino. Yepi asaññinoti asaññībhave nibbatte acittakasatte dasseti. Tepi imissāyeva samāpattiyā alābhato duggatāyeva. Jhānasukhaṃ anaṅgaṇaṃ niddosaṃ yathāvuttadosābhāvato. Balavacittekaggatāsabhāvenapi taṃ anaṅgaṇaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Nevasaññī nāsaññīti āhāti atīte kira bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto araññāyatane kālaṃ karonto antevāsikehi puṭṭho “nevasaññī nāsaññī”ti āha. Purimajātake vuttanayeneva tāpasā jeṭṭhantevāsikassa kathaṃ na gaṇhiṃsu. Bodhisatto ābhassarato āgantvā ākāse ṭhatvā imaṃ gāthamāha. Tena vuttaṃ – “sesaṃ vuttanayeneva veditabba”nti.

In the Third Jātaka, “those with perception” refers to the remaining conscious beings, excluding those who have attained the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. They too are miserable because they fail to attain that meditative attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; they are miserable, having undergone suffering, in the realm of perception. Indeed, those who see the danger in perception say: “Perception is a disease, perception is a boil, perception is a dart.” And “those who are without perception” refers to the non-conscious beings reborn in the non-perceptive state. They too are miserable because they fail to attain this same meditative attainment. The bliss of jhāna is stainless and faultless, due to the absence of the aforementioned flaws. By its nature of strong one-pointedness of mind, it is also called stainless. “Neither perceiving nor not perceiving”—so he spoke. It is said that in the past, while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta, nearing death in a forest hermitage, was asked by his disciples and replied, “Neither perceiving nor not perceiving.” Just as in the previous Jātaka, the ascetics did not heed the senior disciple’s words. The Bodhisatta, coming from the Ābhassara realm, stood in the sky and spoke this verse. Therefore, it is said: “The rest should be understood in the same way.”

Catutthajātake (jā. 1.1.135) candassa viya ābhā etassāti candābhaṃ, odātakasiṇaṃ. Sūriyābhanti sūriyassa viya ābhā etassāti sūriyābhaṃ, pītakasiṇaṃ. Yodha paññāya gādhatīti yo puggalo idha sattaloke idaṃ kasiṇadvayaṃ paññāya gādhati, ārammaṇaṃ katvā anuppavisati, tattha vā patiṭṭhahati. Avitakkena dutiyajjhānena ābhassarūpago hotīti so puggalo tathā katvā paṭiladdhena dutiyena jhānena ābhassarabrahmalokūpago hoti. Sesaṃ purimanayeneva [V 1.0133] veditabbanti iminā imaṃ dasseti (jā. aṭṭha. 1.1.135 candābhajātakavaṇṇanā) – atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto araññāyatane kālaṃ karonto antevāsikehi pucchito “candābhaṃ sūriyābha”nti vatvā ābhassare nibbatto. Tāpasā jeṭṭhantevāsikassa na saddahiṃsu. Bodhisatto āgantvā ākāse ṭhito imaṃ gāthaṃ abhāsi.

In the Fourth Jātaka (Jā. 1.1.135), “candābhaṃ” means “like the radiance of the moon,” referring to the white kasiṇa. “Sūriyābhaṃ” means “like the radiance of the sun,” referring to the yellow kasiṇa. “Yodha paññāya gādhati” (who here penetrates with wisdom) means that the person who, in this world of beings, penetrates these two kasiṇas with wisdom, making them an object of meditation, enters into them or becomes established therein. “Avitakkena dutiyajjhānena ābhassarūpago hoti” (by the second jhāna without initial thought goes to the Ābhassara realm) means that the person, having done so and having attained the second jhāna which is without initial thought, goes to the Ābhassara Brahma realm. The rest should be understood in the same way as before. This illustrates (Jā. Aṭṭha. 1.1.135, Candābha Jātaka Commentary): In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, nearing death in a forest hermitage, was asked by his disciples, and he replied, “Candābhaṃ, sūriyābhaṃ,” and was reborn in the Ābhassara realm. The ascetics did not believe the senior disciple. The Bodhisatta, having returned, stood in the sky and spoke this verse.

Pañcamajātake āsīsethevāti āsācchedaṃ akatvā attano kammesu āsaṃ kareyyeva. Na nibbindeyyāti na nibbedaṃ uppādeyya, na ukkaṇṭheyyāti attho. Voti nipātamattaṃ. Yathā icchinti ahañhi saṭṭhihatthā narakā uṭṭhānaṃ icchiṃ, somhi tatheva jāto, tato uṭṭhitoyevāti dīpeti.

In the Fifth Jātaka, “āsīsetheva” (he should indeed hope) means that without cutting off hope, one should indeed place hope in one’s own actions. “Na nibbindeyya” (he should not become disgusted) means one should not give rise to disgust, one should not be repelled—this is the meaning. “Voti” is merely a particle. “Yathā icchi” (as he desired)—for I indeed desired to rise from a sixty-cubit hell, and I became just so, and from there I have indeed arisen—thus it is explained.

Atīte (jā. aṭṭha. 4.13.sarabhamigajātakavaṇṇanā) kira bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sarabhamigayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā araññe paṭivasati. Rājā migavittako ahosi [M 1.0146] thāmasampanno. Ekadivasaṃ gantvā amacce āha – “yassa passena migo palāyati, teneva so dātabbo”ti. Athekadivasaṃ sarabhamigo uṭṭhāya rañño ṭhitaṭṭhānena palāyi. Atha naṃ amaccā uppaṇḍesuṃ. Rājā cintesi – “ime maṃ parihāsanti, mama pamāṇaṃ na jānantī”ti gāḷhaṃ nivāsetvā pattikova khaggaṃ ādāya “sarabhaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti vegena pakkhandi. Atha naṃ disvā tīṇi yojanāni anubandhi. Sarabho araññaṃ pāvisi. Rājāpi pāvisiyeva. Tattha sarabhamigassa gamanamagge saṭṭhihatthamatto mahāpūtipātanarakaāvāṭo atthi, so tiṃsahatthamattaṃ udakena puṇṇo tiṇehi ca paṭicchanno. Sarabho udakagandhaṃ ghāyitvāva āvāṭabhāvaṃ ñatvā thokaṃ osakkitvā gato. Rājā pana ujukameva āgacchanto tasmiṃ pati.

It is said that in the past (Jā. Aṭṭha. 4.13. Sarabhamiga Jātaka Commentary), while Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a sarabha deer and lived in the forest. The king was a passionate hunter, endowed with strength. One day, he went and told his ministers: “Whosoever's post a deer flees past, he shall be fined.” Then one day, the sarabha deer, rising up, fled past the place where the king was standing. Thereupon the ministers mocked him. The king thought: “These men are ridiculing me; they do not know my strength.” Tightening his clothes firmly, he went on foot, and taking his sword, he rushed forward swiftly, thinking, “I will catch the sarabha!” Seeing it, he pursued it for three leagues. The sarabha entered the forest, and the king also entered. Now, along the path of the sarabha deer, there was a great hell-pit of putrid filth, sixty cubits deep, filled with water up to thirty cubits and covered over with grass. The sarabha, smelling the scent of the water and thus knowing it was a pit, retreated slightly and went around it. But the king, coming straight on, fell into it.

Sarabho tassa padasaddaṃ asuṇanto nivattitvā taṃ apassanto “narakaāvāṭe patito bhavissatī”ti ñatvā āgantvā olokento taṃ gambhīre udake appatiṭṭhe kilamantaṃ disvā tena katāparādhaṃ hadaye akatvā sañjātakāruñño “mā mayi passante varāko nassatu, imamhā taṃ dukkhā mocessāmī”ti āvāṭatīre ṭhito “mā bhāyi, mahārāja, ahaṃ taṃ dukkhā mocessāmī”ti vatvā attano piyaputtaṃ uddharituṃ ussāhaṃ karonto viya tassuddharaṇatthāya silāya yoggaṃ katvā “vijjhissāmī”ti āgataṃ rājānaṃ saṭṭhihatthā narakā uddharitvā assāsetvā piṭṭhiṃ āropetvā araññā nīharitvā senāya avidūre otāretvā ovādamassa datvā [V 1.0134] pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi. Rājā senaṅgaparivuto nagaraṃ gantvā “ito paṭṭhāya sakalaraṭṭhavāsino pañca sīlāni rakkhantū”ti dhammabheriṃ carāpesi. Mahāsattena pana attano kataguṇaṃ kassaci akathetvā sāyaṃ nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā alaṅkatasayane sayitvā paccūsakāle mahāsattassa guṇaṃ saritvā uṭṭhāya sayanapiṭṭhe pallaṅkena nisīditvā pītipuṇṇena hadayena udānaṃ udānento “āsīsetheva puriso”tiādinā imā cha gāthā abhāsi.

Not hearing the sound of his footsteps, the sarabha turned back and, not seeing him, knew, “He must have fallen into the hell-pit.” He came back and looked, and seeing him struggling in the deep water where he could find no footing, he did not take to heart the offense committed against him. With compassion arisen, he thought: “Let not this poor man perish while I am watching. I shall free him from this suffering.” Standing at the edge of the pit, he said: “Do not fear, great king, I shall free you from this suffering.” Then, as if striving to rescue his own beloved son, he made an effort with a rock for his rescue. He lifted the king—who had come thinking, “I shall strike him”—out of the sixty-cubit-deep pit, comforted him, placed him on his back, and carried him out of the forest. He set him down not far from the army, gave him advice, and established him in the five precepts. The king, surrounded by his troops, returned to the city and had the drum of the Dhamma sounded, proclaiming: “From now on, let all inhabitants of the land observe the five precepts.” The king, however, not speaking to anyone of the good deed done for him, ate a meal of various excellent flavors in the evening and lay down on an adorned bed. At dawn, remembering the virtue of the Great Being, he arose, sat cross-legged upon the bed, and with a heart full of joy, uttered an inspired utterance, reciting these six verses beginning, “A man should indeed hope…”

Tattha ahitā hitā cāti dukkhaphassā sukhaphassā ca, maraṇaphassā, jīvitaphassātipi attho. Sattānañhi maraṇaphasso ahito, jīvitaphasso hito. Tesaṃ acintito maraṇaphasso āgacchatīti dasseti[M 1.0147]. Acintitampīti mayā “āvāṭe patissāmī”ti na cintitaṃ, “sarabhaṃ māressāmī”ti cintitaṃ. Idāni pana me cintitaṃ naṭṭhaṃ, acintitameva jātanti udānavasena vadati. Bhogāti yasaparivārā, ete cintāmayā na honti. Tasmā ñāṇavatā vīriyameva kātabbanti vadati. Vīriyavato hi acintitampi hotiyeva.

There, “ahitā hitā ca” (harmful and beneficial) means painful contact and pleasant contact, or even death-contact and life-contact. For beings, death-contact is harmful, and life-contact is beneficial. It shows that death-contact comes without being thought of. “Acintitampi” (even unthought of) means: “I did not think, ‘I will fall into a pit,’ but I did think, ‘I will kill the sarabha.’ Now, however, my thought has failed, and only what was unthought of has arisen”—thus he speaks by way of an inspired utterance. “Bhogā” (wealth) means fame and retinue; these are not born of thought. Therefore, he says, one with wisdom should make effort. For the energetic, even what is unthought of comes to pass.

Tassetaṃ udānaṃ udānentasseva aruṇaṃ uṭṭhahi. Purohito pātova sukhaseyyapucchanatthaṃ āgantvā dvāre ṭhito tassa udānagītasaddaṃ sutvā cintesi – “rājā hiyyo migavaṃ agamāsi, tattha sarabhamigaṃ viddho bhavissati, tena maññe udānaṃ udānetī”ti. Evaṃ brāhmaṇassa rañño paripuṇṇabyañjanaṃ udānaṃ sutvā sumajjite ādāse mukhaṃ olokentassa chāyā viya raññā ca sarabhena ca katakāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ ahosi, so nakhaggena dvāraṃ ākoṭesi. Rājā “ko eso”ti pucchi. Ahaṃ, deva, purohitoti. Athassa dvāraṃ vivaritvā “ito ehācariyā”ti āha. So pavisitvā rājānaṃ jayāpetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito “ahaṃ, mahārāja, tayā araññe katakāraṇaṃ jānāmi, tvaṃ ekaṃ sarabhamigaṃ anubandhanto narake patito, atha naṃ so sarabho silāya yoggaṃ katvā narakato uddhari, so tvaṃ tassa guṇaṃ saritvā udānaṃ udānesī”ti vatvā “sarabhaṃ giriduggasmi”ntiādinā dve gāthā abhāsi.

Then, as he was uttering that inspired utterance, dawn broke. The royal priest, coming early to inquire about the king's comfortable sleep, stood at the door. Hearing the sound of his inspired song, he thought: “Yesterday the king went hunting. There, he must have shot a sarabha deer. That is why, I suppose, he is uttering this inspired utterance.” Thus, when the brahmin heard the king’s inspired utterance, complete in every aspect, the deed done by the king and the sarabha became as clear to him as the reflection of a face in a well-polished mirror. He tapped on the door with his fingernail. The king asked: “Who is that?” “It is I, sire, the royal priest,” he replied. Then, opening the door for him, the king said: “Come in, teacher.” Entering, he greeted the king and stood to one side. “Great king,” he said, “I know the deed you performed in the forest. You, while pursuing a sarabha deer, fell into a pit. Then that sarabha, making an effort with a rock, lifted you out of the pit. Remembering its virtue, you uttered this inspired utterance.” Having said this, he recited two verses beginning with, “The sarabha in the mountain gorge…”

Tattha anusarīti anubandhi. Vikkantanti uddharaṇatthāya kataparakkamaṃ. Anujīvasīti upajīvasi, tassānubhāvena tayā jīvitaṃ laddhanti attho. Samuddharīti uddharaṇaṃ akāsi. Silāya yoggaṃ sarabho karitvāti silāya sopānasadisāya narakato uddharaṇayoggataṃ karitvā. Alīnacittanti saṅkocaṃ appattacittaṃ. Ta migaṃ vadesīti suvaṇṇasarabhamigaṃ idha sirisayane nipanno vaṇṇesi. Taṃ sutvā rājā, “ayaṃ mayā saddhiṃ na migavaṃ āgato, sabbañca pavattiṃ jānāti, kathaṃ nu kho jānāti, pucchissāmi na”nti cintetvā – “kiṃ tvaṃ nu tatthevā”ti navamagāthamāha[V 1.0135]. Tattha bhiṃsarūpanti kiṃ nu te ñāṇaṃ balavajātikaṃ, tenetaṃ jānāsīti vadati. Brāhmaṇo “nāhaṃ sabbaññubuddho, byañjanaṃ amakkhetvā tayā kathitagāthāya pana mayhaṃ attho upaṭṭhātī”ti dīpento “na cevaha”nti dasamagāthamāha[M 1.0148]. Tattha subhāsitānanti byañjanaṃ amakkhetvā suṭṭhu bhāsitānaṃ. Atthaṃ tadānentīti yo tesaṃ attho, taṃ ānenti upadhārentīti attho. Tadā purohito dhammasenāpati ahosi. Tenevāha – “atītepī”tiādi. Sesaṃ uttānatthameva.

There, 'anusarī' means 'he pursued.' 'Vikkantaṃ' means 'the effort made for the sake of rescue.' 'Anujīvasi' means 'you live on,' the meaning being 'life was obtained by you through its power.' 'Samuddhari' means 'he performed the rescue.' 'Silāya yoggaṃ sarabho karitvā' means 'the sarabha, having made a rock suitable for rescue from the pit, like a staircase.' 'Alīnacittaṃ' means 'a mind that has not shrunk back,' a mind free from hesitation. 'Taṃ migaṃ vadesi' means 'you praise that deer, that golden sarabha, while lying here on this royal couch.' Hearing this, the king thought, 'This man did not come with me on the hunt, yet he knows everything that happened. How can he know? I will ask him,' and then spoke the ninth verse: 'Were you there then?' There, 'bhiṃsarūpaṃ' means 'what kind of powerful knowledge do you possess, that you know this?' The brahmin, explaining, 'I am not an omniscient Buddha, but without distorting the letter, the meaning of the verse spoken by you has become clear to me,' spoke the tenth verse: 'I was not indeed...' There, 'subhāsitānaṃ' means 'of things well-spoken, without distorting the letter.' 'Atthaṃ tadānenti' means 'they bring that meaning,' that is, 'they make it understood.' At that time, the royal priest was the General of the Dhamma. Therefore it was said: 'In the past also…' and so on. The rest has a clear meaning.

Aññāsikoṇḍaññattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña

Aññāsikoṇḍaññattherādayotiādīsu pana yāthāvasarasaguṇavasenāti yathāsabhāvaguṇavasena. Pabbajjāvasena paṭivedhavasena suciraṃ sunipuṇaṃ rattindivaparicchedajānanavasena ca rattaññutā veditabbāti taṃ dassento “ṭhapetvā hi sammāsambuddha”ntiādimāha. Pākaṭova hotīti satipaññāvepullappattiko pākaṭo vibhūto hoti. Aññāsikoṇḍaññoti sāvakesu sabbapaṭhamaṃ cattāri ariyasaccāni ñātakoṇḍañño. Sabbesupi etadaggesūti sabbesupi etadaggasuttesu, sabbesu vā etadaggaṭṭhapanesu.

In the case of the Elder Aññāsikoṇḍañña and others, 'yāthāvasarasaguṇavasenāti' means 'according to the quality of the occasion,' that is, 'according to the quality of their own nature.' The state of being of long standing (rattaññutā) should be understood by way of ordination, by way of penetration of the truth, and by way of knowing the division of night and day for a long time and with subtlety. To illustrate this, he said, 'except for the Perfectly Enlightened One…' and so on. 'Pākaṭova hoti' means 'he becomes manifest,' that is, 'one who has attained the abundance of mindfulness and wisdom becomes manifest, evident.' 'Aññāsikoṇḍañña' means 'Koṇḍañña who understood,' who was the first among the disciples to understand the Four Noble Truths. 'Sabbesupi etadaggesūti' means 'in all these foremost instances,' that is, 'in all the suttas on the foremost, or in all the appointments to the position of foremost.'

Dhurapattānīti pattānaṃ pamukhabhūtāni bāhirapattāni. Navutihatthānīti majjhimapurisassa hatthena navutiratanāni. Padumeneva taṃ taṃ padesaṃ uttarati atikkamatīti padumuttaro, bhagavā. Gandhadāmamālādāmādīhīti ādisaddena pattadāmādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Tattha gandhadāmehi katamālā gandhadāmaṃ. Lavaṅgatakkolajātipupphādīhi katamālā mālādāmaṃ. Tamālapattādīhi katamālā pattadāmaṃ. Vaṅgapaṭṭeti vaṅgadese uppannaghanasukhumavatthe. Uttamasukhumavatthanti kāsikavatthamāha.

Dhurapattānīti means 'the foremost of bowls,' that is, the principal external bowls. Navutihatthānīti means 'ninety cubits,' that is, ninety spans of a middle-sized man's hand. Padumuttaro, the Blessed One, means 'he crosses over and transcends each region like a lotus.' Gandhadāmamālādāmādīhi means 'with garlands of fragrance and floral garlands, etc.,' and here the term 'etc.' includes garlands of leaves, and the like. Among these, a garland made with fragrant substances is a garland of fragrance. A garland made with flowers such as cloves, cubebs, and jasmine is a floral garland. A garland made with leaves such as tamāla leaves is a garland of leaves. Vaṅgapaṭṭeti means 'fine cloth from Bengal,' that is, thick, fine cloth produced in the Bengal region. Uttamasukhumavatthanti means 'the finest fine cloth,' referring to cloth from Kāsi.

Teparivaṭṭadhammacakkappavattanasuttantapariyosāneti ettha “idaṃ dukkhaṃ ariyasacca”ntiādinā saccavasena, “dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pariññeyya”ntiādinā kiccavasena, “dukkhaṃ ariyasaccaṃ pariññāta”ntiādinā katavasena ca tīhi ākārehi parivaṭṭetvā catunnaṃ saccānaṃ desitattā tayo parivaṭṭā etassa atthīti tiparivaṭṭaṃ, tiparivaṭṭameva teparivaṭṭaṃ, teparivaṭṭañca taṃ dhammacakkappavattanañcāti teparivaṭṭadhammacakkappavattanaṃ, tadeva suttantaṃ, tassa pariyosāneti attho.

Teparivaṭṭadhammacakkappavattanasuttantapariyosāneti: Here, because the four truths are taught with three aspects—namely, with regard to the truth as 'This is suffering, a noble truth,' etc.; with regard to the function as 'Suffering, a noble truth, is to be fully understood,' etc.; and with regard to the accomplishment as 'Suffering, a noble truth, has been fully understood,' etc.—there are three turnings; hence, tiparivaṭṭaṃ (three turnings). Tiparivaṭṭaṃ itself is teparivaṭṭaṃ (threefold turning). And teparivaṭṭaṃ and the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma together is teparivaṭṭadhammacakkappavattanaṃ (threefold turning of the Wheel of Dhamma). The meaning is: at the conclusion of that very discourse.

Sāligabbhaṃ phāletvā ādāyāti sāligabbhaṃ phāletvā tattha labbhamānaṃ sālikhīrarasaṃ ādāya. Anucchavikanti buddhānaṃ anucchavikaṃ khīrapāyasaṃ pacāpema. Veṇiyo purisabhāvavasena bandhitvā [V 1.0136] kalāpakaraṇe [M 1.0149] kalāpaggaṃ. Khale kalāpānaṃ ṭhapanadivase khalaggaṃ. Madditvā vīhīnaṃ rāsikaraṇadivase khalabhaṇḍaggaṃ. Koṭṭhesu hi dhaññassa pakkhipanadivase koṭṭhaggaṃ.

Sāligabbhaṃ phāletvā ādāya means 'having split the young rice grain and taken it,' that is, having split the young rice grain and taken the rice-milk sap found there. Anucchavikanti means 'suitable for the Buddhas,' that is, 'we shall have rice-milk porridge prepared that is suitable for the Buddhas.' Kalāpaggaṃ is the first portion taken when making sheaves by binding them. Khalaggaṃ is the first portion from the threshing floor on the day the sheaves are placed there. Khalabhaṇḍaggaṃ is the first portion from the heap of goods on the threshing floor on the day a heap of paddy is made after threshing. Koṭṭhaggaṃ is the first portion from the granary on the day the grain is deposited therein.

Dve gatiyoti dve eva nipphattiyo, dve niṭṭhāti attho. Tasmiṃ kumāre sabbaññutaṃ patteti koṇḍaññamāṇavasseva laddhiyaṃ ṭhatvā itarepi cha janā putte anusāsiṃsu. Bodhirukkhamūle pācīnapassaṃ acalaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, yaṃ “vajirāsana”ntipi vuccati. Mahataṃ mahatiyo vahatīti “pācīnamukho”ti avatvā “pācīnalokadhātuabhimukho”ti vuttaṃ. Maṃsacakkhupi lokanāthassa appaṭighātaṃ mahāvisayañcāti. Caturaṅgasamannāgatanti “kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca, aṭṭhi ca avasissatū”tiādinā (ma. ni. 2.184; saṃ. ni. 2.22, 237; a. ni. 2.5; mahāni. 196) vuttacaturaṅgasamannāgataṃ.

Dve gatiyo means 'two destinies,' that is, two attainments, two ends. Standing firm in the view of the young Koṇḍañña that 'this prince will attain omniscience,' the other six men also instructed their sons. At the foot of the Bodhi tree, the eastern side is the immovable spot, which is also called the 'Diamond Throne' (Vajirāsana). Because it bears the great and mighty, it is said 'facing the eastern world-system' instead of 'facing east.' Even the physical eye of the Lord of the World is unobstructed and has a great range. Caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ means 'endowed with four factors,' referring to the four factors mentioned in the phrase, 'Let only skin, sinews, and bones remain,' etc. (MN 2.184; SN 2.22, 237; AN 2.5; Mahāni. 196).

Idaṃ pana sabbamevāti “kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ desessāmī”tiādinayappavattaṃ (ma. ni. 1.284; 2.341; mahāva. 10) sabbameva. Parivitakkamattameva tathā atthasiddhiyā abhāvato. Pupphitaphalitaṃ katvāti abhiññāpaṭisambhidāhi sabbapāliphullaṃ, maggaphalehi sabbaso phalabhārabharitañca karonto pupphitaṃ phalitaṃ katvā. Apakkamitukāmo hutvāti dvepi aggasāvake attano nipaccakāraṃ karonte disvā tesaṃ guṇātirekataṃ bahu maññanto buddhānaṃ santikā apakkamitukāmo hutvā. Tatthevāti chaddantadahatīreyeva.

Idaṃ pana sabbameva means 'Now, all this,' referring to the entire preceding narrative that proceeds in the manner of 'To whom shall I first teach the Dhamma?' and so on (MN 1.284; 2.341; Mahāva. 10). It was merely a deliberation, as there was no actual accomplishment in that way. Pupphitaphalitaṃ katvā means 'having made it bloom and bear fruit,' that is, making it fully blossomed with the super-knowledge and analytical insights, and completely laden with the burden of the fruits of the path and fruition. Apakkamitukāmo hutvā means 'wishing to depart,' that is, seeing both chief disciples showing deference to him, and greatly esteeming their surpassing virtues, he wished to depart from the presence of the Buddhas. Tattheva means 'right there,' that is, right at the bank of the Chaddanta Lake.

Sāriputta-moggallānattheravatthu

The Story of the Venerable Sāriputta and Moggallāna

189-190. Dutiyatatiyesu iddhimantānanti ettha manta-saddo atisayatthavisayoti therassa atisayikaiddhitaṃ dassetuṃ – “iddhiyā sampannāna”nti vuttaṃ. Saha paṃsūhi kīḷiṃsūti sahapaṃsukīḷitā. Idhalokattabhāvamevāti diṭṭhadhammikaattabhāvameva. Soḷasa paññā paṭivijjhitvā ṭhitoti majjhimanikāye anupadasuttantadesanāya “mahāpañño, bhikkhave, sāriputto, puthupañño, bhikkhave, sāriputto, hāsapañño, bhikkhave, sāriputto, javanapañño, bhikkhave, sāriputto, tikkhapañño, bhikkhave, sāriputto, nibbedhikapañño, bhikkhave, sāriputto”ti (ma. ni. 3.93) evamāgatā [M 1.0150] mahāpaññādikā cha, tasmiṃyeva sutte āgatā navānupubbavihārasamāpattipaññā, arahattamaggapaññāti imā soḷasavidhā paññā paṭivijjhitvā sacchikatvā ṭhito.

In the second and third instances, regarding 'iddhimantānaṃ' (of those with psychic powers): here, the word 'manta' refers to the sphere of surpassing excellence. Thus, to show the elder's extraordinary psychic power, it is said, 'endowed with psychic powers.' Regarding 'saha paṃsūhi kīḷiṃsu' (they played together in the dust): they were those who played together in the dust. Regarding 'idhalokattabhāvameva' (only this state of existence in this world): it means merely the state of existence pertaining to this visible world. Regarding 'soḷasa paññā paṭivijjhitvā ṭhito' (having penetrated and realized the sixteen kinds of wisdom, he stood firm): in the Middle Length Discourses, in the teaching of the Anupada Sutta, it is said: 'Monks, Sāriputta is of great wisdom; monks, Sāriputta is of broad wisdom; monks, Sāriputta is of joyous wisdom; monks, Sāriputta is of swift wisdom; monks, Sāriputta is of sharp wisdom; monks, Sāriputta is of penetrative wisdom' (MN 3.93). Thus, these six kinds of wisdom—great wisdom and so on—are mentioned. In that same discourse, the wisdom of the nine progressive dwelling attainments and the wisdom of the path of arahantship are mentioned. Having penetrated and realized these sixteen kinds of wisdom, he stood firm.

Pañhasākacchanti [V 1.0137] pañhassa pucchanavasena vissajjanavasena ca sākacchaṃ karoti. Atthikehi upaññātaṃ magganti etaṃ anubandhanassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Idañhi vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ bhikkhuṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandheyyaṃ. Kasmā? Yasmā idaṃ piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhanaṃ nāma atthikehi upaññātaṃ maggaṃ, ñāto ceva upagato ca maggoti attho. Atha vā atthikehi amhehi maraṇe sati amatenapi bhavitabbanti evaṃ kevalaṃ atthīti upaññātaṃ, anumānañāṇena upagantvā ñātaṃ nibbānaṃ nāma atthi, taṃ magganto pariyesantoti evampettha attho daṭṭhabbo.

Pañhasākacchanti means they engage in discussion by way of asking and answering questions. Atthikehi upaññātaṃ maggaṃ means 'the path pointed out by those who seek': this is the reason for following. Indeed, this is said: 'What if I were to follow this monk closely?' Why? Because this following closely is known as the path pointed out by those who seek—the path is known and approached; this is the meaning. Alternatively, it is pointed out by those who seek: 'Since we are subject to death, there must also be the deathless.' Thus, it is known simply as something that exists, known by approaching with inferential knowledge: 'There exists something called Nibbāna,' and they seek it—thus the meaning should be understood here.

Nesaṃ parisāyāti dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ parivārabhūtaparisāya. Dve aggasāvaketi sāriputtamoggallāne dve mahānubhāve sāvake. Ṭhānantareti aggasāvakattasaññite ṭhānantare ṭhapesi. Kasmā panettha “aggasāvake”ti avatvā “mahāsāvake”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi aññepi mahātherā abhiññātādiguṇavisesayogena “mahāsāvakā”ti vattabbataṃ labhanti, imeyeva pana sāvakesu anaññasādhāraṇabhūtā visesato “mahāsāvakā”ti vattabbāti dassanatthaṃ “dvepi mahāsāvake”ti vuttaṃ.

Nesaṃ parisāya means 'in their assembly': this refers to the assembly that was the retinue of the two chief disciples. Dve aggasāvake means 'the two chief disciples': these are Sāriputta and Moggallāna, two disciples of great power. Ṭhānantare means 'in that position': it means he established them in the position recognized as that of the chief disciples. But why, in this context, is it said 'great disciples' and not 'chief disciples'? If other great elders also attain the designation of 'great disciples' by virtue of special qualities such as higher knowledges, then these two alone, being uniquely distinguished among the disciples, deserve especially to be spoken of as 'great disciples.' To show this, it is said, 'the two great disciples.'

Mahākassapattheravatthu

The Story of the Venerable Mahākassapa

191. Catutthe yasmā dhutavādadhutadhammadhutaṅgāni dhutamūlakāni, tasmā “dhuto veditabbo”ti āraddhaṃ, tattha kilese dhuni dhutavāti dhuto, dhutakileso puggalo, kilesadhunano vā dhammo, kilesadhunano dhammoti ca sapubbabhāgo ariyamaggo daṭṭhabbo. Taṃ dhutasaññitaṃ kilesadhunanadhammaṃ vadati, pare tattha patiṭṭhāpetīti dhutavādo. Catukkañcettha sambhavatīti taṃ dassetuṃ – “ettha panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Tayidanti nipāto, tassa so ayanti attho. Dhutabhūtassa dhutabhūtā dhammā dhutadhammā. Appicchatā santuṭṭhitā heṭṭhā vuttā eva[M 1.0151]. Kilese sammā likhati tacchatīti sallekho, kilesajegucchī, tassa bhāvo sallekhatā. Dvīhipi kāmehi viviccatīti paviveko, yonisomanasikārabahulo puggalo, tassa bhāvo pavivekatā. Iminā sarīraṭṭhapanamattena atthīti idamaṭṭhi ttha-kārassa ṭṭha-kāraṃ katvā, tassa bhāvo idamaṭṭhitā, imehi vā kusaladhammehi atthi idamaṭṭhi, yena ñāṇena “pabbajitena nāma paṃsukūlikaṅgādīsu patiṭṭhitena bhavitabba”nti yathānusiṭṭhaṃ dhutaguṇe samādiyati ceva pariharati ca, taṃ ñāṇaṃ idamaṭṭhitā. Tenāha – “idamaṭṭhitā ñāṇamevā”ti. Dhutadhammā nāmāti dhutaṅgasevanāya paṭipakkhabhūtānaṃ pāpadhammānaṃ dhunanavasena pavattiyā dhutoti laddhanāmāya dhutaṅgacetanāya upakārakā dhammāti katvā dhutadhammā nāma[V 1.0138]. Anupatantīti tadantogadhā tappariyāpannā honti tadubhayasseva pavattivisesabhāvato. Paṭikkhepavatthūsūti dhutaṅgasevanāya paṭikkhipitabbavatthūsu pahātabbavatthūsu.

191. In the fourth case, since the advocacy of asceticism (dhutavāda), the ascetic qualities (dhutadhamma), and the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) are rooted in 'dhuta' (shaking off), it begins with 'one should be known as dhuta.' Here, 'dhuto' means one who has shaken off defilements; it is an individual whose defilements have been shaken off. Or, it is the Dhamma that shakes off defilements; and the Dhamma that shakes off defilements should be understood as the Noble Path together with its preliminary part. One who speaks that Dhamma designated as 'dhuta,' which shakes off defilements, and establishes others therein, is called a 'dhutavāda.' Since a fourfold distinction is possible here, to show this, the passage beginning with 'ettha panā' is introduced. The word 'tayidaṃ' is a particle, and its meaning is 'that is this.' Qualities that are 'dhuta' for one who has become 'dhuta' are 'dhutadhammā.' Fewness of wishes (appicchatā) and contentment (santuṭṭhitā) have already been stated above. 'Sallekho' (effacement) is rightly scraping away and carving defilements; 'sallekhatā' is the state of one disgusted with defilements. 'Paviveko' (seclusion) is being secluded from both kinds of sensual pleasures; 'pavivekatā' is the state of one who abounds in wise attention. Regarding idamaṭṭhitā: from the phrase 'by this mere establishment of the body, there is this' (iminā sarīraṭṭhapanamattena atthīti idamaṭṭhi), changing the 'tha' to 'ṭṭha', its state is idamaṭṭhitā. Or, 'there is this' through these wholesome qualities. The knowledge by which one who has gone forth, being established in the practice of wearing rag-robes and so on, undertakes and maintains the ascetic qualities according to the instruction—that knowledge is idamaṭṭhitā. Hence it is said, 'idamaṭṭhitā is indeed knowledge.' Regarding 'dhutadhammā nāma' (ascetic qualities): they are so called because they are helpful to the volition (cetanā) for the ascetic practices, a volition which has gained the name 'dhuta' because it proceeds by way of shaking off the evil qualities opposed to the cultivation of the ascetic practices. Regarding 'anupatanti' (they follow): they are included within and comprised in that, because they are a specific mode of occurrence of both of those. Regarding 'paṭikkhepavatthūsu' (in the grounds for rejection): in the things to be rejected, the things to be abandoned.

Paṃsukūlikaṅgaṃ…pe… nesajjikaṅganti uddesopi peyyālanayena dassito. Yadettha vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.22 ādayo) vitthārato vuttaṃ. Dhutavādaggahaṇeneva therassa dhutabhāvopi gahito hotīti “dhutavādāna”nteva vuttaṃ. Ayaṃ mahāti abhinīhārādimahantatāyapi sāsanassa upakāritāyapi ayaṃ thero mahā, guṇamahantatāya pasaṃsāvacanameva vā etaṃ therassa yadidaṃ mahākassapoti yathā “mahāmoggallāno”ti.

The practice of wearing rag-robes... and so on, up to the practice of not lying down: the enumeration of these has also been shown by way of abbreviation. Whatever needs to be said about this has been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 1.22 ff.). By the mention of 'dhutavāda' (advocate of asceticism), the elder's ascetic nature is also grasped; thus it is simply said, 'among those who advocate the ascetic practices.' Regarding 'ayaṃ mahā' (this great one): this elder is great both by virtue of his greatness in terms of his aspirations and so on, and by his helpfulness to the Dispensation. Or, this 'Mahākassapa' is simply a term of praise for the elder's greatness of virtue, just as it is said 'Mahāmoggallāna'.

Satthu dhammadesanāya vatthuttaye sañjātappasādatāya upāsakabhāve ṭhitattā vuttaṃ – “uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāyā”tiādi. Etassa aggabhāvassāti yojetabbaṃ. Saccakāroti saccabhāvāvaho kāro, avisaṃvādanavasena vā tadatthasādhanoti attho. Kolāhalanti kutūhalavipphāro. Satthā sattame sattame saṃvacchare dhammaṃ kathento sattānaṃ savanayoggaṃ kālaṃ sallakkhento divā sāyanhasamayaṃ katheti, rattiyaṃ sakalayāmaṃ. Tenāha – “brāhmaṇo brāhmaṇe āha – ‘bhoti kiṃ rattiṃ dhammaṃ suṇissasi divā’”ti. Vissāsikoti vissāsikabhāvo. “Tato paṭṭhāya so”ti vā pāṭho.

Because faith arose in the Triple Gem through the Teacher's exposition of the Dhamma, and because he stood in the state of a lay disciple, it was said: 'Having undertaken the Uposatha observances,' and so on. This should be connected to 'its supreme state.' Regarding 'saccakāro' (act of truth): it means an act that brings about truthfulness, or it accomplishes that purpose by not deceiving; that is the meaning. Regarding 'kolāhala' (commotion): it means a flurry of excitement. The Teacher, teaching the Dhamma every seventh year, discerning the time suitable for beings to listen, teaches during the day in the evening and at night throughout the entire watch. Hence it is said: 'The brahmin said to the brahmin woman, "Madam, will you listen to the Dhamma by night or by day?"' Regarding 'vissāsika' (trustworthy): it means trustworthiness. Alternatively, the reading is 'tato paṭṭhāya so' (from then on, he).

Dve [M 1.0152] asaṅkhyeyyāni pūritapāramissāti idaṃ sā paramparāya sotapatitaṃ atthaṃ gahetvā āha. Adinnavipākassāti avipakkavipākassa. Bhaddake kāleti yutte kāle. Nakkhattanti nakkhattena lakkhitaṃ chaṇaṃ. Tasmiṃ tasmiñhi nakkhatte anubhavitabbachaṇāni nakkhattāni nāma, itarāni pana chaṇāni nāma. Sammāpatitadukkhato vimocanena tato niyyānāvahatāya icchitatthassa labhāpanato ca niyyānikaṃ. Tesanti suvaṇṇapadumānaṃ. Olambakāti suvaṇṇaratanavicittā ratanadāmā. Puññaniyāmenāti puññānubhāvasiddhena niyāmena. Svassa bārāṇasirajjaṃ dātuṃ katokāso. Phussarathanti maṅgalarathaṃ. Setacchattauṇhīsavālabījanikhaggamaṇipādukāni pañcavidhaṃ rājakakudhabhaṇḍanti vadanti. Idha pana setacchattaṃ visuṃ gahitanti sīhāsanaṃ pañcamaṃ katvā vadanti. Pārupanakaṇṇanti pārupanavatthassa dasantaṃ. Dibbavatthadāyipuññānubhāvacodito “nanu tātā thūla”nti āha. Aho tapassīti aho kapaṇo ahaṃ rājāti attho. Buddhānaṃ saddahitvāti buddhānaṃ sāsanaṃ saddahitvā. Caṅkamanasatānīti iti-saddo ādyattho. Tena hi aggisālādīni pabbajitasāruppāni ṭhānāni saṅgaṇhāti.

Regarding 'dve asaṅkhyeyyāni pūritapāramissā' (two incalculable aeons filled with perfections): this was said by her, having grasped the meaning that had come down through tradition. Regarding 'adinnavipākassa' (of that whose result has not yet been given): it means of that whose result has not yet ripened. Regarding 'bhaddake kāle' (at a good time): it means at a suitable time. Regarding 'nakkhatta' (constellation/festival): it means a festival marked by a constellation. For in each constellation, there are festivals to be experienced called 'nakkhattāni', while others are simply called 'chaṇāni' (festivals). Because it liberates from suffering that has occurred, leads to deliverance from it, and brings about the attainment of the desired goal, it is called 'niyyānika' (leading to deliverance). Regarding 'tesaṃ' (of them): it refers to the golden lotuses. Regarding 'olambakā' (hanging down): it means jeweled garlands adorned with gold and various gems. Regarding 'puññaniyāmena' (by the rule of merit): it means by the rule established through the power of merit. He was given the opportunity to give his kingdom of Bārāṇasī. Regarding 'phussaratha' (auspicious chariot): it means the auspicious chariot. The white parasol, turban, yak-tail fan, sword, and jeweled sandals are said to be the five royal regalia. Here, however, the white parasol is taken separately, and they say the lion throne is the fifth. Regarding 'pārupanakaṇṇa' (edge of the covering cloth): it means the hem of the covering cloth. Urged on by the power of the merit from giving a divine cloth, he said, 'Father, is it not too thick?' Regarding 'aho tapassī' (alas, an ascetic!): it means 'Alas, I, the king, am wretched!' Regarding 'buddhānaṃ saddahitvā' (having faith in the Buddhas): it means having faith in the Buddhas' dispensation. Regarding 'caṅkamanasatāni' (hundreds of walking paths): the word 'iti' here has the meaning of 'and so on.' Therefore, it includes places suitable for those who have gone forth, such as fire halls.

Sādhukīḷitanti [V 1.0139] ariyānaṃ parinibbutaṭṭhāne kātabbasakkāraṃ vadati. Nappamajji, nirogā ayyāti pucchitākāradassanaṃ. Parinibbutā devāti devī paṭivacanaṃ adāsi. Paṭiyādetvāti niyyātetvā. Samaṇakapabbajjanti samitapāpehi ariyehi anuṭṭhātabbapabbajjaṃ. So hi rājā paccekabuddhānaṃ vesassa diṭṭhattā “idameva bhaddaka”nti tādisaṃyeva liṅgaṃ gaṇhi. Tatthevāti brahmaloke eva. Vīsatime vasse sampatteti āharitvā sambandho. Brahmalokato cavitvā nibbattattā, brahmacariyādhikārassa ca cirakālasambhūtattā “evarūpaṃ kathaṃ mā kathethā”ti āha. Vīsati dharaṇāni nikkhanti vadanti, pañcapalaṃ nikkhanti apare. Itthākaroti itthiratanassa uppattiṭṭhānaṃ. Ayyadhītāti amhākaṃ ayyassa dhītā, bhaddakāpilānīti attho. Samānapaṇṇanti sadisapaṇṇaṃ sadisalekhaṃ kumārassa kumārikāya ca yuttaṃ paṇṇalekhaṃ. Te purisā samāgataṭṭhānato magadharaṭṭhe mahātitthagāmaṃ maddaraṭṭhe sāgalanagarañca uddissa apakkamantā aññamaññaṃ vissajjantā nāma hontīti “ito ca etto ca pesesu”nti vuttā.

‘The well-played festival’ refers to the honor that should be shown at the place of the noble ones' final Nibbāna. ‘Do not be heedless, Venerables, are you free from illness?’—this shows the manner of questioning. ‘The deities have attained final Nibbāna’—the queen gave this reply. ‘Having prepared’ means having dispatched. ‘The going forth of a recluse’ refers to the going forth to be undertaken by the noble ones who have quelled evil. That king, having seen the guise of the Paccekabuddhas, thought, ‘This alone is excellent,’ and adopted that very same appearance. ‘Right there’ means in the Brahma-world itself. The connection is made by supplying the words, ‘having reached the twentieth year.’ Having passed away from the Brahma-world and been reborn, and because the qualification for the holy life had arisen after a long time, he said, ‘Do not speak in such a way!’ Some say a nikkha is twenty dharaṇas; others, five palas. ‘The woman-mine’ refers to the place of origin of the woman-gem. ‘The master's daughter’ means the daughter of our master, that is, Bhaddakāpilānī. ‘An equal letter’ means a similar letter, a suitable written letter for the prince and the princess. Those men, departing from the meeting place and heading towards the great ferry village in the Magadha country and the city of Sāgala in the Madda country, were dismissing one another; thus it is said, ‘messengers from here and from there.’

Pupphadāmanti hatthihatthappamāṇaṃ pupphadāmaṃ. Tānīti tāni ubhohi ganthāpitāni dve pupphadāmāni. Teti ubho bhaddā ceva pippalikumāro ca[M 1.0153]. Lokāmisenāti kāmassādena. Asaṃsaṭṭhāti na saṃyuttā ghaṭe jalantena viya padīpena ajjhāsaye samujjalantena vimokkhabījena samussāhitacittattā. Yantabaddhānīti sassasampādanatthaṃ tattha tattha dvārakavāṭayojanavasena baddhāni nikkhamanatumbāni. Kammantoti kasikammakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ. Dāsikagāmāti dāsānaṃ vasanagāmā. Osāretvāti pakkhipitvā. Ākappakuttavasenāti ākāravasena kiriyāvasena. Ananucchavikanti pabbajitabhāvassa ananurūpaṃ. Tassa matthaketi dvedhāpathassa dvidhābhūtaṭṭhāne. Etesaṃ saṅgahaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatīti nisīdatīti sambandho. Sā pana tattha satthu nisajjā edisīti dassetuṃ – “nisīdanto panā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha yā buddhānaṃ aparimitakālasambhūtācinteyyāpariññeyyapuññasambhārūpacayanibbattā rūpappabhāvabuddhaguṇavijjotitā dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇaasītianubyañjanasamujjalitā byāmappabhāketumālālaṅkatā sabhāvasiddhitāya akittimā rūpakāyasirī, taṃyeva mahākassapassa adiṭṭhapubbappasādasaṃvaddhanatthaṃ aniggūhitvā nisinno bhagavā “buddhavesaṃ gahetvā…pe… nisīdī”ti vutto. Asītihatthappadesaṃ byāpetvā pavattiyā asītihatthāti vuttā. Satasākhoti bahusākho anekasākho. Suvaṇṇavaṇṇova ahosi nirantaraṃ buddharasmīhi samantato samokiṇṇabhāvato.

‘The flower garland’ means a garland of flowers as long as an elephant’s trunk. ‘Those’ refers to the two flower garlands tied by both. ‘The two’ refers to both Bhaddā and Pippalikumāra. ‘With the allurement of worldly pleasures’ means with the taste of sensual pleasures. ‘Unattached’ means not connected, like a lamp blazing in a pot, because their minds were aroused by the seed of liberation blazing in their hearts. ‘Bound by devices’ refers to the exit-valves fastened here and there by means of door-bar arrangements for the purpose of producing crops. ‘Workplace’ means the place for agricultural work. ‘Servants’ village’ means the village where servants reside. ‘Having placed’ means having inserted. ‘By appearance and gesture’ means by appearance and action. ‘Unfitting’ means unsuitable for the life of a renunciate. ‘At its head’ means at the divided place of the crossroads. The connection is that it is proper to gather them, and so he sits. To show that the Teacher’s sitting there was of such a kind, it is said: ‘While sitting, however…’ There, the Buddha’s physical radiance—born from immeasurable eons of accumulated merit, inconceivable and unfathomable, adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, shining with the Buddha’s virtues and knowledge and the radiance of his form, wreathed in a fathom-long net of rays, naturally perfect and flawless physical splendor—that very radiance, to increase the faith of Mahākassapa, who had never seen it before, the Blessed One sat without concealing it. It is said that he sat ‘assuming the Buddha’s appearance…’. ‘Eighty cubits’ means spreading over an area of eighty cubits. ‘With a hundred branches’ means many-branched, with numerous branches. ‘Golden in color’ means it appeared entirely golden because it was completely surrounded by the Buddha’s rays.

Tīsu ṭhānesūti dūrato nātidūre āsanneti tīsu ṭhānesu. Tīhi ovādehīti “tasmātiha te, kassapa, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘tibbaṃ me hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ bhavissati theresu navesu [V 1.0140] majjhimesū’ti. Evañhi te, kassapa, sikkhitabbaṃ. Tasmātiha te, kassapa, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘yaṃ kiñci dhammaṃ suṇissāmi kusalūpasaṃhitaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ aṭṭhiṃ katvā manasi karitvā sabbaṃ cetasā samannāharitvā ohitasoto dhammaṃ suṇissāmī’ti, evañhi te, kassapa, sikkhitabbaṃ. Tasmātiha te, kassapa, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘sātasahagatā ca me kāyagatāsati na vijahissatī’ti, evañhi te, kassapa, sikkhitabba”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.154) imehi tīhi ovādehi. Ettha hi bhagavā paṭhamaṃ ovādaṃ therassa brāhmaṇajātikattā jātimānappahānatthamabhāsi, dutiyaṃ bāhusaccaṃ nissāya uppajjanakaahaṃkārappahānatthaṃ, tatiyaṃ upadhisampattiṃ nissāya uppajjanakaattasinehappahānatthaṃ[M 1.0154]. Mudukā kho tyāyanti mudukā kho te ayaṃ. Kasmā pana bhagavā evamāha? Therena saha cīvaraṃ parivattetukāmatāya. Kasmā parivattetukāmo jātoti? Theraṃ attano ṭhāne ṭhapetukāmatāya. Kiṃ sāriputtamoggallānā natthīti? Atthi, evaṃ panassa ahosi “imena ciraṃ ṭhassanti, kassapo pana vīsativassasatāyuko, so mayi parinibbute sattapaṇṇiguhāyaṃ vasitvā dhammavinayasaṅgahaṃ katvā mama sāsanaṃ pañcavassasahassaparimāṇakālappavattanakaṃ karissatīti attano ṭhāne ṭhapesi. Evaṃ bhikkhū kassapassa sussūsitabbaṃ maññissantī”ti. Tasmā evamāha.
