‘In three places,’ means from afar, not too far, and near—in these three places. ‘With three admonitions’—‘Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: “Intense moral shame and moral dread shall be ever present in me toward elders, those newly ordained, and those of middle standing.” Thus, Kassapa, should you train yourself. ‘Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: “Whatever Dhamma associated with the wholesome I hear, I will make it the essence, bring it to mind, apply all my awareness to it, and listen to the Dhamma with an attentive ear.” Thus, Kassapa, should you train yourself. ‘Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: “Mindfulness of the body accompanied by pleasure will not be neglected by me.” Thus, Kassapa, should you train yourself.’ (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.154) These are the three admonitions. Here, the Blessed One gave the first admonition to the elder because he was born a brahmin, for the sake of abandoning pride of birth. The second was given relying on extensive learning, for the sake of abandoning the conceit that arises from it. The third was given relying on the accomplishment of requisites, for the sake of abandoning the self-love that arises from it. ‘Gentle are yours,’ meaning ‘These of yours are indeed soft.’ But why did the Blessed One say this? Because he wished to exchange robes with the elder. Why did he wish to exchange? To establish the elder in his own place. ‘What, are Sāriputta and Moggallāna not there?’ They are, but he thought: ‘These two will not remain for long. But Kassapa, who has a lifespan of one hundred and twenty years, after my passing will dwell in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, compile the Dhamma and Vinaya, and ensure my Dispensation lasts for five thousand years.’ Thus, he established him in his own place. ‘Therefore, the monks will think they should attend to Kassapa.’ That is why he spoke thus.

Candūpamoti candasadiso hutvā. Kiṃ parimaṇḍalatāya? No, apica kho yathā cando gaganatalaṃ pakkhandamāno na kenaci saddhiṃ santhavaṃ vā sinehaṃ vā ālayaṃ vā karoti, na ca na hoti mahājanassa piyo manāpo, ayampi evaṃ kenaci saddhiṃ santhavādīnaṃ akaraṇena bahujanassa piyo manāpo candūpamo hutvā khattiyakulādīni cattāri kulāni upasaṅkamatīti attho. Apakasseva kāyaṃ apakassa cittanti teneva santhavādīnaṃ akaraṇena kāyañca cittañca apakaḍḍhitvā, apanetvāti attho. Niccaṃ navoti niccanavakova, āgantukasadiso hutvāti attho. Āgantuko hi paṭipāṭiyā sampattagehaṃ pavisitvā sace naṃ gharasāmikā disvā “amhākampi puttabhātaro vippavāsaṃ gantvā evaṃ vicariṃsū”ti anukampamānā nisīdāpetvā bhojenti, bhuttamattoyeva “tumhākaṃ bhājanaṃ gaṇhathā”ti uṭṭhāya pakkamati, na tehi saddhiṃ santhavaṃ vā karoti, kiccakaraṇīyāni vā saṃvidahati, evamayampi paṭipāṭiyā sampattaṃ gharaṃ pavisitvā yaṃ iriyāpathe pasannā manussā denti, taṃ gahetvā chinnasanthavo tesaṃ kiccakaraṇīye abyāvaṭo hutvā nikkhamatīti dīpeti.

‘Like the moon’ means being like the moon. ‘Is it by being perfectly round?’ ‘No, rather, just as the moon, ascending into the sky, does not form familiarity, affection, or attachment with anyone, yet is dear and pleasing to the multitude, so too, by not forming familiarity and so on with anyone, he becomes moon-like, loved and pleasing to the many, approaching the four families—the warrior clans and others—this is the meaning. ‘Drawing back the body, drawing back the mind’—by not forming familiarity and so on with anyone, he withdraws and removes both body and mind—this is the meaning. ‘Always new’—he is ever new, like a guest—this is the meaning. For a guest, arriving in due order at a household, if the householders see him and, thinking, ‘Our sons and brothers, having gone away, wander like this,’ out of compassion, they seat him and offer food. As soon as he has eaten, he simply says, ‘Take your dishes,’ rises, and departs. He does not form familiarity with them or arrange tasks with them. Similarly, this one, arriving in due order at a household, takes what people give because they are pleased with his conduct and, having severed familiarity, departs without involving himself in their affairs—this is explained.

Appagabbhoti nappagabbho, aṭṭhaṭṭhānena kāyapāgabbhiyena, catuṭṭhānena vacīpāgabbhiyena, anekaṭṭhānena manopāgabbhiyena ca virahitoti attho. Aṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ kāyapāgabbhiyaṃ nāma saṅghagaṇapuggalabhojanasālajantāgharanahānatitthabhikkhācāramaggesu [V 1.0141] antaragharapavesane ca kāyena appatirūpakaraṇaṃ. Catuṭṭhānaṃ vacīpāgabbhiyaṃ nāma saṅghagaṇapuggalaantaragharesu appatirūpavācānicchāraṇaṃ. Anekaṭṭhānaṃ manopāgabbhiyaṃ nāma tesu tesu [M 1.0155] ṭhānesu kāyavācāhi ajjhācāraṃ anāpajjitvāpi manasā kāmavitakkādīnaṃ vitakkanaṃ. Sabbesampi imesaṃ pāgabbhiyānaṃ abhāvena appagabbho hutvā kulāni upasaṅkamatīti attho. Kassapasaṃyuttena ca candūpamappaṭipadāditherassa dhutavādesu aggabhāvassa bodhitattā vuttaṃ “etadeva kassapasaṃyuttaṃ aṭṭhuppattiṃ katvā”ti.

‘Not bold’—he is not bold, devoid of bodily impudence in eight respects, verbal impudence in four respects, and mental impudence in many respects—this is the meaning. The eight respects of bodily impudence are improper bodily actions in the Saṅgha, the group, toward an individual, in the dining hall, the hot-room, the bathing place, the ford, and on the alms-round routes, as well as entering an inner house. The four respects of verbal impudence are uttering improper speech in the Saṅgha, the group, toward an individual, and in the inner house. The many respects of mental impudence are, in those various situations, even without committing transgression with body or speech, mentally thinking thoughts of sensual desire, etc. By the absence of all these kinds of impudence, he approaches families without impudence—this is the meaning. And because the Elder’s preeminence in the ascetic observances, beginning with the practice of the moon simile, was made known, it is said, ‘having made this very Kassapa Saṃyutta the occasion.’

Anuruddhattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Anuruddha

192. Pañcame bhojanapapañcamattanti gocaragāme piṇḍāya caraṇāhāraparibhogasaññitaṃ bhojanapapañcamattaṃ. Dīparukkhānanti lohadantakaṭṭhamayānaṃ mahantānaṃ dīparukkhānaṃ. Lohamayesupi hi tesu dīpādhāresu dīparukkhakāti ruḷhiresā daṭṭhabbā. Olambakadīpamaṇḍaladīpasañcaraṇadīpādikā sesadīpā.

192. In the fifth, 'the mere proliferation of food' refers to the proliferation of food associated with the partaking of almsfood while wandering for alms in a village, which is one's feeding-ground. 'Lamp-trees' refers to large lamp-trees made of iron, ivory, or wood. Even in those made of iron, the term 'lamp-tree' should be understood as a conventional usage for lamp-holders. The remaining lamps are hanging lamps, circular lamps, wandering lamps, and so forth.

Anupariyāyi padakkhiṇakaraṇavasena. Ahaṃ tenāti yena tuyhaṃ attho, ahaṃ tena pavāremi, tasmā taṃ āharāpetvā gaṇhāti attho. Suvaṇṇapātiyaṃyevassa bhattaṃ uppajjīti devatānubhāvena uppajji, na kiñci pacanakiccaṃ atthi. Satta mahāpurisavitakke vitakkesīti “appicchassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo mahicchassā”tiādike satta mahāpurisavitakke vitakkesi. Aṭṭhameti “nippapañcārāmassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo papañcārāmassā”ti etasmiṃ purisavitakke.

'Circling around' means performing a circumambulation. 'I by that' means, 'Whatever you need, I offer it by that,' so the meaning is to have it brought and taken. 'Food appeared in the golden bowl' means it appeared through the power of the deities; there was no need for any cooking. 'He considered the seven thoughts of a great man' refers to considering the seven thoughts of a great man beginning with, 'This Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of many desires.' The eighth is the thought, 'This Dhamma is for one who delights in non-proliferation, not for one who delights in proliferation.'

Mama saṅkappamaññāyāti “appicchassāyaṃ dhammo, nāyaṃ dhammo mahicchassā”tiādinā (dī. ni. 3.358; a. ni. 8.30) mahāpurisavitakkavasena āraddhamattaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetuṃ asamatthabhāvena ṭhitaṃ mama saṅkappaṃ jānitvā. Manomayenāti manomayena viya manasā nimmitasadisena, pariṇāmitenāti attho. Iddhiyāti “ayaṃ kāyo idaṃ cittaṃ viya hotū”ti evaṃ pavattāya adhiṭṭhāniddhiyā.

'Knowing my intention' means knowing my intention, which, based on the thoughts of a great man, such as 'This Dhamma is for one of few desires, not for one of many desires,' was begun but remained unable to reach completion. 'Mind-made' means like something created by the mind, similar to something mentally fashioned; the meaning is 'transformed.' 'By psychic power' refers to the power of resolve, functioning as, 'May this body be like this mind.'

Yadā me ahu saṅkappoti yasmiṃ kāle mayhaṃ “kīdiso nu kho aṭṭhamo mahāpurisavitakko”ti parivitakko ahosi, yadā me ahu saṅkappo, tato mama saṅkappamaññāya [V 1.0142] iddhiyā upasaṅkami, uttari desayīti yojanā. Uttari desayīti “nippapañcārāmassāyaṃ dhammo nippapañcaratino[M 1.0156], nāyaṃ dhammo papañcārāmassa papañcaratino”ti (dī. ni. 3.358; a. ni. 8.30) imaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ mahāpurisavitakkaṃ pūrento upari desayi. Taṃ pana desitaṃ dassento āha – “nippapañcarato buddho, nippapañcamadesayī”ti, papañcā nāma rāgādayo kilesā, tesaṃ vūpasamanatāya tadabhāvato ca lokuttaradhammā nippapañcā nāma. Yathā taṃ pāpuṇāti, tathā dhammaṃ desesi, sāmukkaṃsikaṃ catusaccadesanaṃ adesayīti attho.

'When I had the thought' means at the time when I had the pondering, 'What now is the eighth thought of a great man?'—when I had that thought, then, knowing my intention, he approached by psychic power and further taught. This is the connection. 'Further taught' means completing and teaching the eighth thought of a great man: 'This Dhamma is for one who delights in and is fond of non-proliferation, not for one who delights in and is fond of proliferation.' To show what was taught, he said: 'The Buddha delights in non-proliferation; he taught non-proliferation.' Proliferations are defilements such as lust; because of their pacification and absence, the supramundane states are called non-proliferation. He taught the Dhamma so that one might attain it, meaning he gave the exalted teaching of the four truths.

Tassāhaṃ dhammamaññāyāti tassa satthu desanādhammaṃ jānitvā. Vihāsinti yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjanto vihariṃ. Sāsane ratoti sikkhattayasaṅgahe sāsane abhirato. Tisso vijjā anuppattāti pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ, dibbacakkhuñāṇaṃ, āsavakkhayañāṇanti imā tisso vijjā mayā anuppattā sacchikatā. Tato eva kataṃ buddhassa sāsanaṃ, anusiṭṭhi ovādo anuṭṭhitoti attho.

'Having understood the Dhamma from him' means having known the Teacher's teaching. 'I lived' means I lived practicing as instructed. 'Delighting in the Dispensation' means delighting in the Dispensation which includes the threefold training. 'The three knowledges were attained' means the knowledge of past lives, the divine eye, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints—these three knowledges were attained and realized by me. Thus, the Buddha's Dispensation has been fulfilled; the instruction and advice has been carried out—this is the meaning.

Bhaddiyattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Bhaddiya

193. Chaṭṭhe ucca-saddena samānattho uccā-saddoti āha – “uccākulikānanti ucce kule jātāna”nti. Kāḷī sā devīti kāḷavaṇṇatāya kāḷī sā devī. Kulānukkamena rajjānuppatti mahākulinassevāti vuttaṃ – “soyeva cā”tiādi.

193. In the sixth, he said that the word `uccā` has the same meaning as the word `ucca` (high); 'of high families' (`uccākulikānaṃ`) means 'of those born in a high family.' 'That goddess Kāḷī' (`Kāḷī sā devī`) means that goddess was Kāḷī because of her dark complexion. It is said, 'Succession to the kingdom by family lineage is for one of a great family only,' as indicated by the passage beginning 'and he alone' (`soyeva cā'ti`).

Lakuṇḍakabhaddiyattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Bhaddiya the Dwarf

194. Sattame rittakoti deyyavatthurahito. Guṇe āvajjetvāti bhagavato rūpaguṇe ceva ākappasampadādiguṇe ca attano adhippāyaṃ ñatvā ambapakkassa paṭiggahaṇaṃ paribhuñjananti evamādike yathāupaṭṭhite guṇe āvajjetvā.

194. In the seventh, 'empty' (`rittako`) means devoid of things to be given. 'Reflecting on the qualities' means reflecting on the qualities as they arose, such as: the qualities of the Blessed One—the beauty of his form and his accomplished deportment—and, having known one's own intention, the acceptance and consumption of the ripe mango, and so on.

Piṇḍolabhāradvājattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja

195. Aṭṭhame abhītanādabhāvena sīhassa viya nādo sīhanādo, so etesaṃ atthīti sīhanādikā, tesaṃ sīhanādikānaṃ. Garahitabbapasaṃsitabbadhamme yāthāvato jānantasseva garahā pasaṃsā [V 1.0143][M 1.0157] ca yuttarūpāti āha – “buddhā ca nāmā”tiādi. Khīṇā jātītiādīhi paccavekkhaṇañāṇassa bhūmiṃ dasseti. Tena hi ñāṇena ariyasāvako paccavekkhanto “khīṇā jātī”tiādiṃ pajānāti. Katamā panassa jāti khīṇā, kathañca pajānātīti? Na tāvassa atītā khīṇā pubbeva khīṇattā, na anāgatā anāgate vāyāmābhāvato, na paccuppannā vijjamānattā. Yā pana maggassa abhāvitattā uppajjeyya ekacatupañcavokārabhavesu ekacatupañcakkhandhappabhedā jāti, sā maggassa bhāvitattā anuppādadhammataṃ āpajjanena khīṇā. Taṃ so maggabhāvanāya pahīnakilese paccavekkhitvā “kilesābhāve vijjamānampi kammaṃ āyatiṃ appaṭisandhikaṃ hotī”ti jānanto pajānāti.

195. In the eighth, a lion's roar (`sīhanāda`) is a roar like a lion's due to its fearlessness. Those who possess it are called possessors of the lion's roar (`sīhanādikā`); of those possessors of the lion's roar. He said, 'The Buddhas indeed...' and so on, because blame and praise are appropriate only for one who knows blameworthy and praiseworthy things as they actually are. With 'Destroyed is birth' and so on, he shows the basis of the knowledge of reviewing. For with that knowledge, the noble disciple, reviewing, understands 'Destroyed is birth' and so on. But what birth of his is destroyed, and how does he understand it? Not his past birth, since it was already destroyed; not the future birth, because there is no striving for it in the future; not the present birth, because it still exists. But that birth which, due to the undeveloped state of the path, would arise in one-, four-, or five-constituent existences as a division of one, four, or five aggregates, is destroyed through the development of the path by reaching the state of non-arising. Having reviewed the defilements abandoned by the development of the path, he understands, knowing, 'Even though karma exists, in the absence of defilements it does not lead to renewed existence in the future.'

Vusitanti vuṭṭhaṃ parivuṭṭhaṃ, kataṃ caritaṃ niṭṭhitanti attho. Brahmacariyanti maggabrahmacariyaṃ. Puthujjanakalyāṇakena hi saddhiṃ satta sekkhā maggabrahmacariyaṃ vasanti nāma, khīṇāsavo vuṭṭhavāso. Tasmā ariyasāvako attano brahmacariyavāsaṃ paccavekkhanto “vusitaṃ brahmacariya”nti pajānāti. Kataṃ karaṇīyanti catūsu saccesu catūhi maggehi pariññāpahānasacchikiriyābhāvanābhisamayavasena soḷasavidhaṃ kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpitanti attho. Puthujjanakalyāṇakādayo hi taṃ kiccaṃ karonti, khīṇāsavo katakaraṇīyo. Tasmā ariyasāvako attano karaṇīyaṃ paccavekkhanto “kataṃ karaṇīya”nti pajānāti. Nāparaṃ itthattāyāti idāni puna itthabhāvāya evaṃ soḷasavidhakiccabhāvāya, kilesakkhayāya vā maggabhāvanāya kiccaṃ me natthīti pajānāti. Atha vā itthattāyāti itthabhāvato imasmā evaṃpakārā idāni vattamānakkhandhasantānā aparaṃ khandhasantānaṃ mayhaṃ natthi, ime pana pañcakkhandhā pariññātā tiṭṭhanti chinnamūlakā rukkhā viya, te carimakaviññāṇanirodhena anupādāno viya jātavedo nibbāyissantīti pajānāti.

'Lived' means dwelt, fully dwelt; the meaning is that the practice has been done and is finished. 'The holy life' means the holy life of the path. For the virtuous worldling along with the seven trainees live the holy life of the path, whereas the one whose taints are destroyed has completed the living of it. Therefore, the noble disciple, reviewing his own living of the holy life, understands, 'The holy life has been lived.' 'What had to be done has been done' means that the sixteenfold task regarding the four truths—by means of the four paths, through the full understanding, abandoning, realization, and development of them—has been finished. For the virtuous worldling and others are doing that task, whereas the one whose taints are destroyed has done what was to be done. Therefore, the noble disciple, reviewing his own task, understands, 'What had to be done has been done.' 'There is no more for this state of being' means he understands: 'Now there is no further task for me for this state of being, for this sixteenfold task, or for the destruction of defilements through the development of the path.' Alternatively, 'for this state of being' means he understands: 'From this state of being, from this present continuity of aggregates of this kind, there is no further continuity of aggregates for me. These five aggregates, however, remain fully understood, like a tree cut at the root. With the cessation of the final consciousness, they will be extinguished like a fire without fuel.'

Mantāṇiputtapuṇṇattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta

196. Navame aṭṭhārasasupi vijjāṭṭhānesu nipphattiṃ gatattā “sabbasippesu kovido hutvā”ti vuttaṃ. Abhidayāabbhaññāvahasseva dhammassa tattha upalabbhanato “mokkhadhammaṃ adisvā”ti vuttaṃ. Tenāha – “idaṃ vedattayaṃ nāmā”tiādi[M 1.0158]. Tathā hi anena duggatiparimuccanampi dullabhaṃ, abhiññāparivārānaṃ aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ lābhitāya sayaṃ ekadesena upasanto paramukkaṃsagataṃ uttamadamathasamathaṃ anaññasādhāraṇaṃ bhagavantaṃ sambhāvento “ayaṃ puriso”tiādimāha. Piṭakāni gahetvā āgacchantīti phalabhājanāni gahetvā assāmikāya [V 1.0144] āgacchanti. Buddhānanti gāravavasena bahuvacananiddeso kato. Paribhuñjīti devatāhi pakkhittadibbojaṃ vanamūlaphalāphalaṃ paribhuñji. Patte patiṭṭhāpitasamanantarameva hi devatā tattha dibbojaṃ pakkhipiṃsu. Sammasitvāti paccavekkhitvā, parivattetvāti ca vadanti. Arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsūti mahādevattherassa anumodanakathāya anupubbikathāsakkhikāya suvisodhitacittasantānā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

196. In the ninth (section), having attained accomplishment in the eighteen fields of knowledge, it is said, 'he became skilled in all crafts.' Since the Dhamma that brings about higher and direct knowledge is found there, it is said, 'not seeing the liberating Dhamma.' Therefore, he said, 'this is called the threefold Veda,' and so on. Indeed, by this, even liberation from a woeful state is difficult to obtain. Having attained the eight attainments which have direct knowledge as their retinue, being himself partially calmed, he praised the Blessed One—who had attained the highest excellence, the supreme taming and calm, unique among all—saying, 'this person,' and so on. 'Taking the baskets, they came' means they came carrying fruit vessels without an owner. 'Of the Buddhas'—this is expressed in the plural out of reverence. 'He partook'—he partook of the divine nutriment placed by the deities, the roots and fruits of the forest. For immediately after the bowl was placed, the deities placed divine nutriment there. 'Having comprehended' means having reflected upon; and they say it means 'having turned over.' 'They attained arahantship' means that through the Elder Mahādeva's discourse of appreciation, which had the gradual teaching as its witness, their mental continuities being thoroughly purified, they attained arahantship.

Dasahi kathāvatthūhīti appicchakathā santuṭṭhikathā pavivekakathā asaṃsaggakathā vīriyārambhakathā sīlasampadākathā samādhisampadākathā paññāsampadākathā vimuttisampadākathā vimuttiñāṇadassanasampadākathāti imehi dasahi kathāvatthūhi. Jātibhūmiraṭṭhavāsinoti jātibhūmivantadesavāsino, satthu jātadesavāsinoti attho. Sīsānulokikoti purato gacchantassa sīsaṃ anu anu passanto. Okāsaṃ sallakkhetvāti sākacchāya avasaraṃ sallakkhetvā. Sattavisuddhikkamaṃ pucchīti “kiṃ nu kho, āvuso, sīlavisuddhatthaṃ bhagavati brahmacariyaṃ vussatī”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.257) satta visuddhiyo pucchi. Dhammakathikānaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi savisesena dasakathāvatthulābhitāya.

'By the ten topics of discussion' means by these ten topics of discussion: talk on having few desires, talk on contentment, talk on seclusion, talk on non-association, talk on arousing energy, talk on the accomplishment of virtue, talk on the accomplishment of concentration, talk on the accomplishment of wisdom, talk on the accomplishment of liberation, and talk on the accomplishment of the knowledge and vision of liberation. 'Residents of the country of his native land' means those living in the country of the Teacher's birthplace; that is, residents of the Teacher’s native land. 'Sīsānulokika' means looking closely at the head of one going ahead. 'Having assessed the opportunity' means having assessed the occasion for discussion. 'He asked about the seven purifications' means he asked, 'Friend, is the holy life lived under the Blessed One for the sake of the purification of virtue?' and so on, inquiring about the seven purifications. He placed him in the foremost position among Dhamma speakers because he had especially attained the ten topics of discussion.

Mahākaccānattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Mahākaccāna

197. Dasame saṃkhittena kathitadhammassāti madhupiṇḍikasuttantadesanāsu viya saṅkhepena desitadhammassa. Taṃ desanaṃ vitthāretvāti taṃ saṅkhepadesanaṃ āyatanādivasena vitthāretvā. Atthaṃ vibhajamānānanti tassā saṅkhepadesanāya atthaṃ vibhajitvā kathentānaṃ. Atthavasena vāti “ettakā etassa atthā”ti atthavasena vā desanaṃ pūretuṃ sakkonti. Byañjanavasena vāti “ettakāni ettha byañjanāni desanāvasena vattabbānī”ti byañjanavasena vā pūretuṃ sakkonti. Ayaṃ pana mahākaccānatthero ubhayavasenapi sakkoti tassa saṅkhepena uddiṭṭhassa vitthārena satthu ajjhāsayānurūpaṃ [M 1.0159] desanato, tasmā tattha aggoti vutto. Vuttanayenevāti “pātova subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāyā”tiādinā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva. Aññehīti aññāsaṃ itthīnaṃ kesehi ativiya dīghā. Na kevalañca dīghā eva, atha kho siniddhanīlamudukañcikā ca. Nikkesīti appakesī yathā “anudarā kaññā”ti.

197. In the tenth, 'of the Dhamma spoken in brief' refers to the teaching of the Dhamma in brief, as in the Madhupiṇḍika Sutta. 'Expounding that teaching in detail' means elaborating on that brief teaching by way of the sense bases and so on. 'Of those who analyze the meaning' means of those who, having analyzed the meaning of that brief teaching, explain it. 'By way of meaning' means they are able to complete the teaching, saying, 'This much is its meaning.' 'By way of phrasing' means they are able to complete it, saying, 'This much is the phrasing to be spoken in the teaching here.' However, this Elder Mahākaccāna was capable in both ways, by expounding in detail, in accordance with the Teacher's intention, what was stated briefly. Therefore, he was declared foremost in that regard. 'In the manner already stated' refers to the way previously mentioned below, such as, 'having eaten excellent food in the morning and undertaken the Uposatha observances.' 'Than others' means much longer than the hair of other women. Not only was it long, but it was also glossy, dark-blue, soft, and curly at the ends. 'Without hair' means with very little hair, like 'a maiden with a slender waist.'

Paṇiyanti vikketabbabhaṇḍaṃ. Āvajjetvāti upanissayaṃ kesānaṃ pakatibhāvāpattiñca āvajjetvā. Gāravenāti muṇḍasīsāpi there gāravena ekavacaneneva āgantvā. Nimantetvāti svātanāya [V 1.0145] nimantetvā. Imissā itthiyāti yathāvuttaseṭṭhidhītaramāha. Diṭṭhadhammikovāti avadhāraṇaṃ aṭṭhānapayuttaṃ, diṭṭhadhammiko yasapaṭilābhova ahosīti attho. Yasapaṭilābhoti ca bhavasampattipaṭilābho. Sattasu hi javanacetanāsu paṭhamā diṭṭhadhammavedanīyaphalā, pacchimā upapajjavedanīyaphalā, majjhe pañca aparāpariyavedanīyaphalā, tasmā paṭhamaṃ ekaṃ cetanaṃ ṭhapetvā sesā yathāsakaṃ paripuṇṇaphaladāyino honti, paṭhamacetanāya pana diṭṭhadhammiko yasapaṭilābhova ahosi.

'Merchandise' means goods to be sold. 'Having considered' means having reflected on the supporting condition for the hair and its return to its natural state. 'With respect' means that even with a shaven head, she approached the elder with respect and with but a single word. 'Having invited' means having invited for the next day’s meal. 'Of this woman' refers to the merchant’s daughter as previously mentioned. 'Visible in this very life'—the emphasis is inappropriately applied; the meaning is that the attainment of fame was indeed visible in this very life. 'Attainment of fame' also means the attainment of worldly prosperity. For among the seven moments of impulsion-consciousness, the first yields a result to be experienced in this very life, the last yields a result to be experienced in the next life, and the middle five yield results to be experienced in subsequent lives. Therefore, setting aside the first consciousness, the rest give their full results in due course. But from the first consciousness, only the attainment of fame was visible in this very life.

Paṭhamaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the first chapter, 'The Foremost,' is completed.

(14) 2. Dutiyaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā

(14) 2. Commentary on the Second Etadagga Chapter

Cūḷapanthakattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Cūḷapanthaka

198-200. Dutiyassa [V 1.0146] paṭhame manena nibbattitanti abhiññāmanena uppāditaṃ. Manena katakāyoti abhiññācittena desantaraṃ pattakāyo. Manena nibbattitakāyoti abhiññāmanasā nimmitakāyo “aññaṃ kāyaṃ abhinimminātī”tiādīsu (dī. ni. 1.236-237; paṭi. ma. 3.14) viya. Ekasadiseyevāti attasadiseyeva. Ekavidhamevāti attanā katappakārameva. Etapparamo hi yebhuyyena sāvakānaṃ iddhinimmānavidhi. Aggo nāma jāto ekadesena satthu iddhinimmānānuvidhānato.

In the first of the second chapter, 'produced by the mind' means produced by the mind of direct knowledge. 'A body made by the mind' means a body that has reached another place by means of the mind of direct knowledge. 'A body produced by the mind' means a body created by the mind of direct knowledge, as in 'he creates another body' and so on. 'Of one and the same likeness' means just like oneself. 'Of one and the same kind' means of the same type as made by oneself. For this, for the most part, is the highest extent of the method of psychic creation for disciples. He became known as foremost because he followed, in some measure, the Teacher's method of psychic creation.

Lābhitāyāti [M 1.0160] ettha lābhīti īkāro atisayattho. Tena therassa catunnaṃ rūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ atisayena savisesalābhitaṃ dasseti. Arūpāvacarajjhānānaṃ lābhitāyāti etthāpi eseva nayo. Na kevalañcetā cetosaññāvivaṭṭakusalatā rūpārūpajjhānalābhitāya eva, atha kho imehipi kāraṇehīti dassetuṃ – “cūḷapanthako cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Cetoti cettha cittasīsena samādhi vutto, tasmā cetaso samādhissa vivaṭṭanaṃ cetovivaṭṭo, ekasmiṃyevārammaṇe samādhicittaṃ vivaṭṭetvā heṭṭhimassa heṭṭhimassa uparūpari hāpanato rūpāvacarajjhānalābhī cetovivaṭṭakusalo nāma. “Sabbaso rūpasaññāna”ntiādinā (dha. sa. 265) vuttasaññā atikkamitvā “ākāsānañcāyatanasaññāsahagataṃ…pe… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasaññāsahagata”nti (dha. sa. 265-268) saññāsīsena vuttajjhānānaṃ vivaṭṭakusalo, tathā itthipurisādisaññā niccasaññādito cittaṃ vivaṭṭetvā kevale rūpārūpadhammamatte asaṅkhate nibbāne ca visesato vaṭṭanato ca suññatānupassanābahulo saññāvivaṭṭakusalo. Samādhikusalatāya cetovivaṭṭakusalatā tabbahulavihāritāya. Tathā vipassanākusalatāya saññāvivaṭṭakusalatā. Ekoti cūḷapanthakattheraṃ vadati. Samādhilakkhaṇeti savitakkasavicārādisamādhisabhāve. Puna ekoti mahāpanthakattheramāha. Vipassanālakkhaṇeti sattaanupassanā aṭṭhārasamahāvipassanādivipassanāsabhāve. Samādhigāḷhoti samādhismiṃ ogāḷhacitto subhāvitabhāvanatā. Aṅgasaṃkhitteti [V 1.0147] caturaṅgikativaṅgikādivasena jhānaṅgānaṃ saṅkhipane. Ārammaṇasaṃkhitteti kasiṇugghāṭimākāsādinibbattanena kasiṇādiārammaṇānaṃ saṃkhipane. Aṅgavavatthāpaneti vitakkādīnaṃ jhānaṅgānaṃ vavatthāpane. Ārammaṇavavatthāpaneti pathavīkasiṇādijjhānārammaṇānaṃ vavatthāpane.

Here, in `Lābhitāya`, the `ī` in `lābhī` conveys a sense of exceeding. Thus, it indicates that the elder possessed the four rūpāvacara jhānas in an exceptional and special manner. Regarding the attainment of the arūpāvacara jhānas, the same principle applies. Not only was this skill in the turning of mind and perception a reason for the attainment of rūpa and arūpa jhānas, but these other qualities are also reasons—as illustrated by the phrase 'And Cūḷapanthaka,' and so on. Here, `ceto` refers to concentration (samādhi) as the chief aspect of the mind. Therefore, the turning of the mind's concentration is called `cetovivaṭṭa`. By turning the concentrated mind on a single object, abandoning each lower state for the one above it, one who attains the rūpāvacara jhānas is called 'skilled in the turning of mind.' Having transcended the perceptions spoken of in the passage beginning 'with the complete transcendence of perceptions of form' (Dhs. 265), he became skilled in the turning of the jhānas spoken of under the heading of perception, associated with the perception of the base of infinite space up to the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (Dhs. 265–268). Similarly, by turning the mind away from perceptions of men, women, etc., and from the perception of permanence, and focusing solely on rūpa and arūpa phenomena—and especially applying himself to the unconditioned Nibbāna—and being frequently engaged in emptiness contemplation, he became skilled in the turning of perceptions. Through proficiency in concentration, there is skill in the turning of mind by dwelling frequently in it. Likewise, through proficiency in insight, there is skill in the turning of perceptions. The word `eko` refers to the Elder Cūḷapanthaka. `Samādhilakkhaṇa` signifies the nature of concentration, including initial and sustained application. Again, `eko` refers to the Elder Mahāpanthaka. `Vipassanālakkhaṇa` signifies the nature of insight, such as the seven contemplations and the eighteen great insights. `Samādhigāḷho` means with mind immersed in concentration, due to well-cultivated practice. `Aṅgasaṃkhitta` refers to the condensing of jhāna factors, such as by way of the fourfold or threefold jhāna. `Ārammaṇasaṃkhitta` denotes the condensing of meditation objects, by producing such things as the space revealed by removing the kasiṇa device. `Aṅgavavatthāpana` means the determining of jhāna factors like initial application. `Ārammaṇavavatthāpana` refers to the determining of jhāna objects, such as the earth kasiṇa.

Jhānaṅgehīti rūpāvacarajjhānaṅgehi, jhānaṅgāneva jhānaṃ. Puna jhānaṅgehīti arūpāvacarajjhānaṅgehi. Bhātāti jeṭṭhabhātā. Assāti kuṭumbiyassa. Suvaṇṇapūjanti sovaṇṇamayaṃ pupphapūjaṃ katvā. Devapureti tāvatiṃsabhavane sudassanamahānagare. Aggadvārenāti tasmiṃ divase aggaṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ vivaṭena nagaradvārena nikkhamitvā.

With the factors of jhāna means with the factors of form-sphere jhāna; the factors themselves are jhāna. Again, with the factors of jhāna means with the factors of formless-sphere jhāna. Brother means the elder brother. `Assa` means of the householder. Golden offering means having made a floral offering of gold. In the city of the gods means in the great city of Sudassana in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven. Through the chief gate means on that day, having exited through the foremost city gate, which was opened first of all.

Kokanadanti [M 1.0161] padumavisesanaṃ yathā “kokāsaka”nti. Taṃ kira bahupattaṃ vaṇṇasampannaṃ atisugandhañca hoti. “Kokanadaṃ nāma setapaduma”ntipi vadanti. Pātoti pageva. Ayañhettha attho – yathā kokanadasaṅkhātaṃ padumaṃ pāto sūriyuggamanavelāyaṃ phullaṃ vikasitaṃ avītagandhaṃ siyā virocamānaṃ, evaṃ sarīragandhena guṇagandhena ca sugandhaṃ saradakāle antalikkhe ādiccamiva attano tejasā tapantaṃ aṅgehi niccharaṇakajutiyā aṅgīrasaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ passāti.

`Kokanada` is a special type of lotus, like the 'kokāsaka.' It is said to have many petals, be rich in color, and be extremely fragrant. Some also say, 'Kokanada is the name for the white lotus.' `Pāto` means early morning. The meaning here is this: just as the lotus known as Kokanada blooms at sunrise in the early morning, fully open, its fragrance not yet faded, shining brightly, so too, see Aṅgīrasa, the Perfectly Enlightened One, fragrant with the scent of his body and the fragrance of his virtues, shining with his own radiance like the sun in the autumn sky, with the lustre issuing from his limbs.

Cūḷapanthako kira kassapasammāsambuddhakāle pabbajitvā paññavā hutvā aññatarassa dandhabhikkhuno uddesagahaṇakāle parihāsakeḷiṃ akāsi. So bhikkhu tena parihāsena lajjito neva uddesaṃ gaṇhi, na sajjhāyamakāsi. Tena kammenāyaṃ pabbajitvāva dandho jāto, tasmā gahitagahitapadaṃ upariuparipadaṃ gaṇhantassa nassati. Iddhiyā abhisaṅkharitvā suddhaṃ coḷakhaṇḍaṃ adāsīti tassa pubbahetuṃ disvā tadanurūpe kammaṭṭhāne niyojento suddhaṃ coḷakhaṇḍaṃ adāsi. So kira pubbe rājā hutvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto nalāṭato sede muccante parisuddhena sāṭakena nalāṭaṃ puñchi, sāṭako kiliṭṭho ahosi. So “imaṃ sarīraṃ nissāya evarūpo parisuddhasāṭako pakatiṃ jahitvā kiliṭṭho jāto, aniccā vata saṅkhārā”ti aniccasaññaṃ paṭilabhi. Tena kāraṇenassa rajoharaṇameva paccayo jāto.

It is said that Cūḷapanthaka, in the time of Kassapa the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha, having gone forth as a monk and become wise, made a jest while a certain slow monk was receiving instruction. That monk, ashamed by the mockery, neither grasped the instruction nor made recitation. By that deed, this one, having gone forth, was born slow-witted; therefore, as he grasped the next word, the word he had just grasped was lost. The statement that the Buddha gave him a pure piece of cloth, having created it by psychic power, means that having seen Cūḷapanthaka's past cause, and assigning him to a meditation subject appropriate to it, he gave him a pure piece of cloth. It is said that formerly, having been a king, while circumambulating the city, as sweat flowed from his forehead, he wiped his forehead with a pure cloth, and the cloth became soiled. He reflected, 'Relying on this body, such a pure cloth has abandoned its nature and become soiled. Truly, conditioned things are impermanent!' He obtained the perception of impermanence. For that reason, the removal of dust itself became a condition for him.

Lomānīti coḷakhaṇḍatantagataaṃsuke vadati. “Kiliṭṭhadhātukānī”ti kiliṭṭhasabhāvāni. Evaṃgatikamevāti idaṃ cittampi bhavaṅgavasena pakatiyā paṇḍaraṃ parisuddhaṃ rāgādisampayuttadhammavasena saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ jātanti dasseti. Nakkhattaṃ samānetvāti nakkhattaṃ samannāharitvā, āvajjetvāti attho[V 1.0148]. Biḷārassatthāyāti biḷārassa gocaratthāya. Jalapathakammikenāti samuddakammikena. Cārinti khāditabbatiṇaṃ. Saccakāranti saccabhāvāvahaṃ kāraṃ, “attanā gahite bhaṇḍe aññesaṃ na dātabba”nti vatvā dātabbalañjanti vuttaṃ hoti. Tatiyena paṭihārenāti tatiyena sāsanena. Pattikā hutvāti sāmino hutvā.

`Lomāni` refers to the fibres of the cloth. `Kiliṭṭhadhātukāni` means things having a defiled nature. This shows that this mind too, though naturally bright and pure in its bhavaṅga aspect, becomes defiled when associated with lust and other defiling elements. `Nakkhattaṃ samānetvā` means having brought the constellation to mind, that is, having adverted to it. `Biḷārassatthāya` means for the sake of the cat's food. `Jalapathakammikena` means by a seafarer. `Cārin` means grass to be eaten. `Saccakāraṃ` means an act that brings about truthfulness; it is said to be a pledge to be given, with the words, 'Goods taken by oneself should not be given to others.' `Tatiyena paṭihārena` means with the third message. `Pattikā hutvā` means having become masters.

Appakenapīti thokenapi parittenapi. Medhāvīti paññavā. Pābhatenāti bhaṇḍamūlena. Vicakkhaṇoti vohārakusalo. Samuṭṭhāpeti attānanti mahantaṃ dhanaṃ yasañca uppādetvā tattha attānaṃ saṇṭhapeti patiṭṭhāpeti[M 1.0162]. Yathā kiṃ? Aṇuṃ aggiṃva sandhamaṃ, yathā paṇḍito puriso parittakaṃ aggiṃ anukkamena gomayacuṇṇādīni pakkhipitvā mukhavātena dhamento samuṭṭhāpeti vaḍḍheti, mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ karoti, evameva paṇḍito thokampi pābhataṃ labhitvā nānāupāyehi payojetvā dhanañca yasañca vaḍḍheti, vaḍḍhetvā puna tattha attānaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti. Tāya eva vā pana dhanassa mahantatāya attānaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, abhiññātaṃ pākaṭaṃ karotīti attho.

`Appakenapi` means even with a little, even with a small amount. `Medhāvī` means one endowed with wisdom. `Pābhatena` refers to capital. `Vicakkhaṇo` means adept in worldly dealings. `Samuṭṭhāpeti attānaṃ` means having generated great wealth and fame, one settles and establishes oneself therein. Like what? Like fanning a tiny spark of fire. Just as a wise person, gradually adding cow dung powder and the like to a small fire, fans it with their breath, nurtures, and grows it into a great mass of fire, so too does a wise person, having obtained even a small amount of capital, employ various means to increase wealth and fame, and having increased them, establishes oneself therein. Or, by the very greatness of that wealth, one establishes oneself, making oneself well-known and evident—this is the meaning.

Subhūtittheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Subhūti

201-202. Tatiye raṇāti hi rāgādayo kilesā vuccantīti “saraṇā dhammā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 100 dukamātikā) rāgādayo kilesā “raṇā”ti vuccanti. Raṇanti etehīti raṇā. Yehi abhibhūtā sattā nānappakārena kandanti paridevanti, tasmā te rāgādayo “raṇā”ti vuttā. Desitaniyāmato anokkamitvāti desitānokkamanato anupagantvā deseti, satthārā desitaniyāmeneva anodissakaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desetīti vuttaṃ hoti. Evanti evaṃ mettājhānato vuṭṭhāya bhikkhāgahaṇe sati. Bhikkhādāyakānaṃ mahapphalaṃ bhavissatīti idaṃ cūḷaccharāsaṅghātasuttena (a. ni. 1.51 ādayo) dīpetabbaṃ. Accharāsaṅghātamattampi hi kālaṃ mettacittaṃ āsevantassa bhikkhuno dinnadānaṃ mahapphalaṃ hoti mahānisaṃsaṃ, tena ca so amoghaṃ raṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ bhuñjatīti ayamattho tattha āgatoyeva. Nimittaṃ gaṇhitvāti ākāraṃ sallakkhetvā.

201-202. In the third, by ‘strife’ is meant defilements such as lust, for in such passages as ‘phenomena with strife’ (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 100, Dukamātikā), defilements like lust are called ‘strife.’ They are called ‘strife’ because beings, overcome by them, lament and grieve in various ways; therefore, these defilements like lust are called ‘strife.’ ‘Without deviating from the prescribed rule’ means that one teaches without going beyond what has been taught; it means that one teaches the Dhamma according to the rule prescribed by the Teacher, without making it specific to anyone. ‘Thus’ means in this way, upon receiving alms after arising from the meditation on loving-kindness. ‘It will be of great fruit to the almsgivers’—this should be illustrated by the Cūḷaccharāsaṅghāta Sutta (AN 1.51, etc.). For even for the time it takes to snap one’s fingers, if a monk cultivates a mind of loving-kindness, the alms given to him are of great fruit and great benefit, and thus he partakes of the country’s alms-food not in vain—this meaning is indeed found there. ‘Taking the sign’ means discerning the characteristic.

Khadiravaniyarevatattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Revata of the Acacia Wood

203. Pañcame vanasabhāganti sabhāgaṃ vanaṃ, sabhāganti ca sappāyanti attho. Yañhi pakativiruddhaṃ [V 1.0149] byādhiviruddhañca na hoti, taṃ “sabhāga”nti vuccati. Udakasabhāgantiādīsupi imināva nayena attho veditabbo. Kalyāṇakammāyūhanakkhaṇoti kalyāṇakammūpacayassa okāso. Tiṇṇaṃ bhātikānanti upatisso, cundo, upasenoti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ jeṭṭhabhātikānaṃ. Tissannañca bhaginīnanti cālā, upacālā, sīsupacālāti imesaṃ tissannaṃ jeṭṭhabhaginīnaṃ. Ettha ca sāriputtatthero sayaṃ pabbajitvā [M 1.0163] cālā, upacālā, sīsupacālāti tisso bhaginiyo, cundo upasenoti ime bhātaro pabbājesi, revatakumāro ekova gehe avasissati. Tena vuttaṃ – “amhākaṃ…pe… pabbājentī”ti. Mahallakatarāti vuddhatarā. Idañca kumārikāya cirajīvitaṃ abhikaṅkhamānā āhaṃsu. Sā kira tassa ayyikā vīsativassasatikā khaṇḍadantā palitakesā valittacā tilakāhatagattā gopānasivaṅkā ahosi. Vidhāvanikanti vidhāvanakīḷikaṃ. Tissannaṃ sampattīnanti anussavavasena manussadevamokkhasampattiyo sandhāya vadati, manussadevabrahmasampattiyo vā. Sīvalissa puññaṃ vīmaṃsissāmāti “sīvalinā katapuññassa vipākadānaṭṭhānamida”nti ñatvā evamāha. Sabhāgaṭṭhānanti samaṃ desaṃ.

203. In the fifth, ‘a suitable forest’ means a forest that is suitable; and ‘suitable’ means agreeable. For what is not naturally adverse or adverse to one's health is called ‘suitable.’ The meaning should be understood in the same way for ‘suitable water,’ and so on. ‘The opportunity for accumulating wholesome deeds’ means the occasion for the accumulation of wholesome actions. ‘The three brothers’ refers to Upatissa, Cunda, and Upasena—these three elder brothers. ‘And the three sisters’ refers to Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsupacālā—these three elder sisters. Here, the Elder Sāriputta himself, having gone forth, then ordained his three sisters—Cālā, Upacālā, and Sīsupacālā—and his brothers Cunda and Upasena, leaving only the boy Revata at home. Hence it is said, ‘Our… ordaining.’ ‘More elderly’ means older. And this was said by those who wished for the girl’s long life. It is said that his grandmother was one hundred and twenty years old, with broken teeth, gray hair, wrinkled skin, a body marked with moles, and bent like a roof-rafter. ‘A game of chase’ means a sport of running about. ‘The three attainments’ refers to the attainments of humans, devas, and liberation, spoken of by way of tradition, or the attainments of humans, devas, and Brahmās. ‘We will examine Sīvali’s merit’—knowing that “this is the place for the fruition of merit made by Sīvali,” they spoke thus. ‘A suitable place’ means a level place.

Taṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyakanti kiñcāpi arahanto gāmante kāyavivekaṃ na labhanti, cittavivekaṃ pana labhanteva. Tesañhi dibbappaṭibhāgānipi ārammaṇāni cittaṃ cāletuṃ na sakkonti, tasmā gāmo vā hotu araññādīnaṃ vā aññataraṃ, ‘yattha arahanto viharanti, taṃ bhūmirāmaṇeyyakaṃ’, so bhūmippadeso ramaṇīyo evāti attho.

‘That land is delightful’—although arahants do not find physical seclusion in a village, they do indeed find mental seclusion. For even objects comparable to the divine cannot shake their minds. Therefore, whether it be a village or a forest or the like, ‘where arahants dwell, that land is delightful’—meaning that region of land is indeed pleasing.

Kaṅkhārevatattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Kaṅkhārevata

204. Chaṭṭhe akappiyo, āvuso, guḷoti ekadivasaṃ thero antarāmagge guḷakaraṇaṃ okkamitvā guḷe piṭṭhampi chārikampi pakkhitte disvāna “akappiyo guḷo, sāmiso na kappati guḷo vikāle paribhuñjitu”nti kukkuccāyanto evamāha. Akappiyā muggāti ekadivasaṃ antarāmagge vacce muggaṃ jātaṃ disvā “akappiyā muggā, pakkāpi muggā jāyantī”ti kukkuccāyanto evamāha. Sesamettha sabbaṃ uttānameva.

204. In the sixth, “Unallowable, friend, is the molasses”—one day, the elder, while on the road, came upon molasses being made and saw that flour and ashes had been put into it. Feeling scrupulous, he said, “The molasses is unallowable; molasses with additives is not permitted to be consumed at the wrong time.” “Unallowable are the mung beans”—one day, while on the road, he saw mung beans that had sprouted on the path and, feeling scrupulous, said, “The mung beans are unallowable; even ripe mung beans sprout.” The rest here is all straightforward.

Soṇakoḷivisattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Soṇa Koḷivisa

205. Sattame hāpetabbameva ahosi accāraddhavīriyattā. Udakena samupabyūḷheti udakena thalaṃ ussāretvā tattha tattha rāsikate. Haritūpalittāyāti gomayaparibhaṇḍakatāya. Tividhena udakena [V 1.0150] posentīti khīrodakaṃ gandhodakaṃ kevalodakanti evaṃ tividhena udakena posenti paripālenti. Parissāvetvāti parisodhetvā gahite taṇḍuleti yojetabbaṃ. Devo maññeti devo viya[M 1.0164]. Vīṇovādenāti “taṃ kiṃ maññasi, soṇa, yadā te vīṇāya tantiyo accāyatā honti, api nu te vīṇā tasmiṃ samaye saravatī vā hoti kammaññā vāti? No hetaṃ, bhanteti. Evameva kho, soṇa, accāraddhavīriyaṃ uddhaccāya saṃvattati, atisithilavīriyaṃ kosajjāya saṃvattati. Tasmātiha tvaṃ, soṇa, vīriyasamataṃ adhiṭṭhaha, indriyānañca samataṃ paṭivijjhā”ti (mahāva. 243) evaṃ vīṇaṃ upamaṃ katvā pavattitena vīṇopamovādena. Vīriyasamathayojanatthāyāti vīriyassa samathena yojanatthāya.

205. In the seventh, due to excessively aroused energy, it had to be given up. ‘Piled up with water’ means having raised the dry land with water and made it into heaps here and there. ‘Smeared with green’ refers to being thoroughly covered with cow dung. ‘Nourishing with three kinds of water’ means nourishing and protecting with milk-water, scented water, and plain water—thus with three kinds of water. ‘Having strained’ should be connected with ‘the taken rice grains,’ meaning having purified them. ‘Like a god’ means like a deity. By ‘the advice on the lute’ is meant the advice given using the lute as an analogy: “What do you think, Soṇa? When the strings of your lute are too tight, is your lute then tuneful and playable?” “No, venerable sir.” “In the same way, Soṇa, excessively aroused energy leads to restlessness, and too slack energy leads to laziness. Therefore, Soṇa, you should resolve on balanced energy and penetrate the balance of the faculties.” (Mahāvagga 243). ‘For the purpose of yoking with balanced energy’ means for the purpose of yoking energy with serenity.

Soṇakuṭikaṇṇattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Soṇa Kuṭikaṇṇa

206. Aṭṭhame kuṭikaṇṇoti vuccatīti “koṭikaṇṇo”ti vattabbe “kuṭikaṇṇo”ti voharīyati. Kulaghare bhavā kulagharikā. Sā kira avantiraṭṭhe kulaghare mahāvibhavassa seṭṭhissa bhariyā. Dasabalassa dhammakathaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya cintesīti idaṃ aṅguttarabhāṇakānaṃ matena vuttaṃ. Suttanipātaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “sapariso bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamma dhammadesanaṃ assosi, na ca kañci visesaṃ adhigañchi. Kasmā? So hi dhammaṃ suṇanto hemavataṃ anussaritvā ‘āgato nu kho me sahāyako, no’ti disādisaṃ oloketvā taṃ apassanto ‘vañcito me sahāyo, yo evaṃ vicittappaṭibhānaṃ bhagavato desanaṃ na suṇātī’ti vikkhittacitto ahosī”ti vuttaṃ.

206. In the eighth, he is called ‘Kuṭikaṇṇa’; though ‘Koṭikaṇṇa’ should be said, ‘Kuṭikaṇṇa’ is the usage. ‘Kulagharikā’ means one born in a good family. She, it is said, was the wife of a very wealthy merchant in a good family in the Avanti country. ‘Having heard the Dhamma talk of the Ten-Powered One, she became established in the fruit of stream-entry and reflected’—this is stated according to the view of the Aṅguttara reciters. In the Suttanipāta commentary, however, it is said: ‘He approached the Blessed One with his retinue and listened to the Dhamma teaching but did not attain any distinction. Why? For he, while listening to the Dhamma, recollected Hemavata and, looking around in all directions, thinking, “Has my friend come or not?” and not seeing him, he became distracted, thinking, “My friend has been cheated, who does not hear the Blessed One’s teaching of such varied brilliance.”’

Yasmā paṭisandhijātiabhinikkhamanabodhiparinibbānesveva dvattiṃsa pubbanimittāni hutvāva paṭivigacchanti, na ciraṭṭhitikāni honti, dhammacakkappavattane (saṃ. ni. 5.1081; paṭi. ma. 2.30) pana tāni savisesāni hutvā cirataraṃ ṭhatvā nirujjhanti, tasmā vuttaṃ – “tiyojanasahassaṃ himavantaṃ akālapupphitaṃ disvā”tiādi. Aggabalakāyāti sabbapurato gacchantā balakāyā. Kena pupphitabhāvaṃ jānāsīti kena kāraṇena himavantassa pupphitabhāvaṃ jānāsīti, yena kāraṇena imaṃ akālapupphapāṭihāriyaṃ jātaṃ, taṃ jānāsīti vuttaṃ hoti. Tassa pavattitabhāvanti tassa dhammacakkassa bhagavatā pavattitabhāvaṃ. Sadde nimittaṃ gaṇhīti sadde ākāraṃ sallakkhesi. Tatoti “ahaṃ ‘etaṃ amatadhammaṃ tampi [M 1.0165] jānāpessāmī’ti tava santikaṃ āgatosmī”ti yaṃ vuttaṃ, tadanantaranti attho.

Since the thirty-two preliminary signs, having appeared only at the moments of conception, birth, renunciation, enlightenment, and final Nibbāna, vanish and do not last long—but during the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma (SN 5.1081; Paṭis I 30), they appear with distinction, last for a longer time, and then cease—therefore it is said: ‘Having seen the Himalayas in full bloom out of season across three thousand yojanas,’ and so on. ‘The foremost host of the strong’ means the hosts of the strong going before all. ‘By what do you know it is in bloom?’ means: ‘By what reason do you know the Himalayas are in bloom?’ That is to say, ‘Do you know the reason by which this miraculous out-of-season flowering has occurred?’ ‘The state of its being set in motion’ refers to the state of that Wheel of Dhamma being set in motion by the Blessed One. ‘He took the sign in the sound’ means he discerned the characteristic in the sound. ‘From that’ means immediately after what was said: ‘I have come to you thinking, “This Deathless Dhamma, I shall make it known to him as well.”’

Sātāgiro [V 1.0151] hemavatassa buddhuppādaṃ kathetvā taṃ bhagavato santikaṃ ānetukāmo “ajja pannaraso”tiādigāthamāha. Tattha (su. ni. aṭṭha. 1.153) ajjāti ayaṃ rattindivo pakkhagaṇanato pannaraso, upavasitabbato uposatho. Tīsu vā uposathesu ajja pannaraso uposatho, na cātuddasiuposatho, na sāmaggīuposatho. Divi bhavāni dibbāni, dibbāni ettha atthīti dibbāni. Kāni tāni? Rūpāni. Tañhi rattiṃ devānaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuto sannipatitānaṃ sarīravatthābharaṇavimānappabhāhi abbhādiupakkilesavirahitāya candappabhāya ca sakalajambudīpo alaṅkato ahosīti ativiya alaṅkato ca parivisuddhidevassa bhagavato sarīrappabhāya. Tenāha – “dibbā ratti upaṭṭhitā”ti.

Sātāgira, having spoken of the Buddha's arising to Hemavata and wishing to bring him to the Blessed One, spoke the verse beginning with, “Today is the fifteenth.” Herein, “today” refers to this day and night, the fifteenth by the counting of fortnights; and because it is to be observed, it is the Uposatha. Of the three Uposathas, today is the fifteenth Uposatha, not the fourteenth Uposatha, nor the Uposatha of concord. “Divine” means existing in heaven; divine things exist here. What are those? Forms. For on that night, when the gods from the ten-thousandfold world-system had gathered, the entire Jambudīpa was adorned with the radiance of their bodies, clothing, ornaments, and celestial mansions, free from the impurities of clouds and the like, and also with the light of the moon. Thus, it was exceedingly adorned, and also by the bodily radiance of the Blessed One, the exceedingly pure deva. Therefore, he said, “The divine night has arrived.”

Evaṃ rattiguṇavaṇṇanāpadesenapi sahāyassa cittaṃ pasādaṃ janento buddhuppādaṃ kathetvā āha – “anomanāmaṃ satthāraṃ, handa passāma gotama”nti. Tattha anomehi alāmakehi sabbākāraparipūrehi guṇehi nāmaṃ assāti anomanāmo. Tathā hissa “bujjhitā saccānīti buddho, bodhetā pajāyāti buddho”tiādinā (mahāni. 192; cūḷani. pārāyanatthutigāthāniddeso 97; paṭi. ma. 1.162) nayena buddhoti anomehi guṇehi nāmaṃ. “Bhaggarāgoti bhagavā, bhaggadosoti bhagavā”tiādinā (mahāni. 84) nayena bhagavāti anomehi guṇehi nāmaṃ. Esa nayo “arahaṃ sammāsambuddho vijjācaraṇasampanno”tiādīsu. Diṭṭhadhammikādiatthehi devamanusse anusāsati “imaṃ pajahatha, imaṃ samādāya vattathā”ti satthā. Taṃ anomanāmaṃ satthāraṃ. Handāti vacasāyatthe nipāto. Passāmāti tena attānaṃ saha saṅgahetvā paccuppannabahuvacanaṃ. Gotamanti gotamagottaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – “satthā, na satthā”ti mā vimatiṃ akāsi, ekantabyavasito hutvāva ehi passāma gotamanti.

Thus, by using the description of the qualities of the night as a pretext, arousing confidence in his companion’s mind, he spoke of the Buddha’s arising, saying: “The Teacher of peerless name—come, let us see Gotama!” Herein, ‘of peerless name’ (anomanāmo) means his name is endowed with peerless (anoma), flawless (alāmaka), and perfectly complete qualities. For indeed, by the method such as, “He is Buddha because he has awakened to the truths; he is Buddha because he enlightens the populace,” his name is ‘Buddha’ because of peerless qualities. By the method such as, “He is Bhagavā because he has broken lust; he is Bhagavā because he has broken hatred,” his name is ‘Bhagavā’ because of peerless qualities. This same method applies to “Arahant, Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, endowed with knowledge and conduct,” and so forth. He is the Teacher (satthā) because he instructs gods and humans regarding benefits pertaining to this life and beyond, saying, “Abandon this; undertake this and practice.” That is the Teacher of peerless name. ‘Handa’ is a particle conveying the sense of urging. ‘Let us see’ (passāma) is the present plural, including oneself with the other. ‘Gotama’ refers to the Gotama clan. This is what is said: “Do not have any doubt as to whether he is ‘a teacher’ or ‘not a teacher’—being fully resolved, come, let us see Gotama!”

Evaṃ vutte hemavato “ayaṃ sātāgiro ‘anomanāmaṃ satthāra’nti bhaṇanto tassa sabbaññutaṃ pakāseti, sabbaññuno ca dullabhā loke, sabbaññupaṭiññehi pūraṇādisadiseheva loko upadduto. So pana yadi sabbaññū, addhā tādilakkhaṇaṃ patto bhavissati, tena evaṃ gahessāmī”ti [M 1.0166] cintetvā tādilakkhaṇaṃ pucchanto āha – “kacci mano”tiādi. Tattha kaccīti pucchā. Manoti cittaṃ. Supaṇihitoti suṭṭhu ṭhapito acalo asampavedhī. Sabbesu bhūtesu sabbabhūtesu. Tādinoti tādilakkhaṇaṃ pattasseva sato. Pucchā eva vā ayaṃ “so tava satthā sabbabhūtesu tādī, udāhu no”ti. Iṭṭhe aniṭṭhecāti evarūpe ārammaṇe. Saṅkappāti vitakkā. Vasīkatāti vasaṃ gamitā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yaṃ taṃ satthāraṃ vadasi, tassa te satthuno [V 1.0152] kacci tādilakkhaṇaṃ sampattassa sato sabbabhūtesu mano supaṇihito, udāhu yāva paccayaṃ na labhati, tāva supaṇihito viya khāyati. So vā te satthā kacci sabbabhūtesu sattesu tādī, udāhu no, ye ca iṭṭhāniṭṭhesu ārammaṇesu rāgadosavasena saṅkappā uppajjeyyuṃ, tyāssa kacci vasīkatā, udāhu kadāci tesampi vasena vattatīti.

When this was said, Hemavata thought: “This Sātāgira, by saying ‘the Teacher of peerless name,’ proclaims his omniscience. But omniscient ones are rare in the world, and the world is troubled by those who claim omniscience, such as Pūraṇa and others. If he is truly omniscient, he must certainly have attained such a nature. Therefore, I will test him thus.” Reflecting in this way, he asked about that nature, saying, “Is the mind…?” and so on. Herein, ‘kacci’ is an interrogative particle. ‘Mano’ means the mind, the citta. ‘Supaṇihito’ means well-established, immovable, unperturbed. ‘Sabbesu bhūtesu’ means toward all beings. ‘Tādino’ means of one who has attained such a nature. Or, this is simply the question: “Is your Teacher ‘such’ toward all beings, or not?” ‘In the liked and disliked’ means in such objects. ‘Saṅkappā’ means thoughts, vitakkas. ‘Vasīkatā’ means brought under control. This is what is said: “Regarding the Teacher of whom you speak—has his mind, having attained such a nature, become well-established toward all beings? Or does it only appear to be well-established so long as it does not encounter a condition? And is your Teacher ‘such’ toward all beings, or not? And when thoughts arise concerning agreeable and disagreeable objects due to lust and hatred, are they mastered by him? Or does he sometimes act under their influence?”

Tīṇi vassānīti soṇassa pabbajitadivasato paṭṭhāya tīṇi vassāni. Tadā kira bhikkhū yebhuyyena majjhimadeseyeva vasiṃsu, tasmā tattha katipayā eva ahesuṃ. Te ca ekasmiṃ nigame eko dveti evaṃ visuṃ visuṃ vasiṃsu, therānañca katipaye bhikkhū ānetvā aññesu ānīyamānesu pubbaṃ ānītā kenacideva karaṇīyena pakkamiṃsu, kañci kālaṃ āgametvā puna tesu ānīyamānesu itare pakkamiṃsu, evaṃ punappunaṃ ānayanena sannipāto cireneva ahosi, thero ca tadā ekavihārī ahosi. Tena vuttaṃ – “tīṇi vassāni gaṇaṃ pariyesitvā”ti. Tīṇi vassānīti ca accantasaṃyoge upayogavacanaṃ. Satthu adhippāyaṃ ñatvāti attano āṇāpaneneva “iminā saddhiṃ ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vasitukāmo bhagavā”ti satthu adhippāyaṃ jānitvā. Bhagavā kira yena saddhiṃ ekagandhakuṭiyaṃ vasitukāmo, tassa senāsanapaññattiyaṃ ānandattheraṃ āṇāpeti.

For three years: that is, three years from the day Soṇa went forth. At that time, it is said, the monks mostly lived in the Middle Country, so there were only a few there. And they lived separately, one or two in a single market town. And for the elder, when some monks had been brought, and while others were being brought, those who had been brought earlier departed on some business. After waiting for some time, when those others were being brought again, the first group departed. In this way, due to repeatedly bringing them, the assembly was formed only after a long time. The elder, at that time, was dwelling alone. Therefore, it is said: “For three years, having sought a community.” And the phrase “for three years” is a usage in the accusative case indicating continuous duration. Knowing the Teacher’s intention: this means knowing the Teacher’s intention from his own command, “The Blessed One wishes to dwell in a single perfumed chamber with this one.” It is said that when the Blessed One wished to dwell in a single perfumed chamber with someone, he would instruct the Elder Ānanda regarding the preparation of the lodging.

Ajjhokāse vītināmetvāti ajjhokāse nisajjāya vītināmetvā. Yasmā bhagavā āyasmato soṇassa samāpattisamāpajjanena paṭisanthāraṃ karonto sāvakasādhāraṇā sabbā samāpattiyo anulomappaṭilomaṃ samāpajjanto bahudeva rattiṃ ajjhokāse nisajjāya vītināmetvā pāde pakkhāletvā vihāraṃ pāvisi, tasmā āyasmāpi soṇo bhagavato adhippāyaṃ ñatvā tadanurūpaṃ sabbā tā samāpattiyo [M 1.0167] samāpajjanto bahudeva rattiṃ ajjhokāse nisajjāya vītināmetvā pāde pakkhāletvā vihāraṃ pāvisīti vadanti. Pavisitvā ca bhagavatā anuññāto cīvaratirokaraṇiyaṃ katvā bhagavato pādapasse nisajjāya vītināmesi. Ajjhesīti āṇāpesi. Paṭibhātu taṃ bhikkhu dhammo bhāsitunti bhikkhu tuyhaṃ dhammo bhāsituṃ upaṭṭhātu, ñāṇamukhaṃ āgacchatu, yathāsutaṃ yathāpariyattaṃ dhammaṃ bhaṇāhīti attho. Aṭṭhakavaggiyānīti aṭṭhakavaggabhūtāni kāmasuttādisoḷasasuttāni (mahāni. 1). Suggahitoti sammā uggahito. Sabbe vare yācīti vinayadharapañcamena gaṇena upasampadā dhuvanhānaṃ cammattharaṇaṃ gaṇaṅgaṇūpāhanaṃ cīvaravippavāsoti ime pañca vare yāci. Sutte āgatamevāti udānapāḷiyaṃ āgatasuttaṃ sandhāya vadati.

Having spent the night outdoors: this means having spent it sitting outdoors. Because the Blessed One, while extending a welcome to the Venerable Soṇa by entering attainments, spent much of the night sitting outdoors, entering and emerging in forward and reverse order from all the attainments common to disciples, and then, having washed his feet, he entered the dwelling. Therefore, they say that the Venerable Soṇa, understanding the Blessed One’s intention, accordingly entered all those same attainments, spent much of the night sitting outdoors, washed his feet, and entered the dwelling. After entering, having been given permission by the Blessed One, he made a screen of his robe and spent the night sitting at the Blessed One’s feet. He requested (ajjhesi): this means he commanded. Let the Dhamma occur to you, monk, to be spoken: this means, “Monk, may the Dhamma present itself to you to be spoken, may it come to the forefront of your knowledge; speak the Dhamma as you have heard it, as you have learned it.” The Aṭṭhakavagga verses: this refers to the sixteen suttas belonging to the Aṭṭhakavagga, beginning with the Kāma Sutta. Well-memorized (suggahito): this means properly learned. He asked for all the boons: he asked for these five boons: (1) higher ordination by a quorum of five monks with an expert in the Vinaya as the fifth; (2) constant bathing; (3) the use of ground-coverings made of hide; (4) the use of multi-layered sandals; and (5) permission to be away from one’s robes. It is found in the Sutta: this is said with reference to the sutta found in the Udāna Pāḷi.

Sīvalittheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Sīvali

207. Navame [V 1.0153] sākacchitvā sākacchitvāti raññā saddhiṃ paṭivirujjhanavasena punappunaṃ sākacchaṃ katvā. Guḷadadhinti patthinnaṃ guḷasadisaṃ kaṭhinadadhiṃ. Atiañchitunti ativiya ākaḍḍhituṃ. Kañjiyaṃ vāhetvāti dadhimatthuṃ pavāhetvā, parissāvetvāti attho. “Dadhito kañjiyaṃ gahetvā”tipi pāṭho. Nanti suppavāsaṃ. Bījapacchiṃ phusāpentīti iminā sambandho. Yāva na ukkaḍḍhantīti yāva dāne na ukkaḍḍhanti, dātukāmāva hontīti adhippāyo mahādukkhaṃ anubhosīti pasavanibandhanaṃ mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhosi. Sāmikaṃ āmantetvāti sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhā tibbāhi kharāhi dukkhavedanāhi phuṭṭhā “sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā, yo imassa evarūpassa dukkhassa pahānāya dhammaṃ deseti. Suppaṭipanno vata tassa bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, yo imassa evarūpassa dukkhassa pahānāya paṭipanno. Susukhaṃ vata nibbānaṃ, yatthidaṃ evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ na saṃvijjatī”ti (udā. 18) imehi tīhi vitakkehi taṃ dukkhaṃ adhivāsentī satthu santikaṃ pesetukāmatāya sāmikaṃ āmantetvā. Pure maraṇāti maraṇato puretarameva. Iṅgitanti ākāraṃ. Jīvitabhattanti jīvitasaṃsaye dātabbabhattaṃ. Sabbakammakkhamo ahosīti sattavassikehi dārakehi kātabbaṃ yaṃ kiñci kammaṃ kātuṃ samatthatāya sabbassa kammassa khamo ahosi. Teneva so sattāhaṃ mahādāne [M 1.0168] dīyamāne jātadivasato paṭṭhāya dhammakaraṇaṃ ādāya saṅghassa udakaṃ parissāvetvā adāsi.

207. In the ninth, sākacchitvā sākacchitvā means having repeatedly engaged in discussion with the king in order to oppose him. Guḷadadhi means hard curd, similar to molasses, which was desired. Atiañchituṃ means to pull out excessively. Kañjiyaṃ vāhetvā means having poured off the curd-whey, that is, having strained it. Another reading is: “Having taken the whey from the curds.” Nāṃ refers to Suppavāsā. Bījapacchiṃ phusāpentī connects with this, meaning causing the seed-basket to touch. Yāva na ukkaḍḍanti means until they do not hold back from giving, the intention being that they remain desirous to give. Mahādukkhaṃ anubhosi means she experienced great suffering related to childbirth. Sāmikaṃ āmantetvā means, being in a difficult pregnancy for seven days, afflicted by intense, sharp pains, she thought: “Truly, the Blessed One is a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, who teaches the Dhamma for the abandonment of this kind of suffering. Truly, the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples is practicing well, who are practicing for the abandonment of this kind of suffering. Truly, Nibbāna is blissful, where this kind of suffering does not exist.” Enduring that suffering with these three thoughts, desiring to send someone to the Teacher, she called her husband. Pure maraṇā means even before death. Iṅgita means a sign. Jīvitabhatta means food to be given when life is in danger. Sabbakammakkhamo ahosi means he was capable of performing any task that seven-year-old boys could do, being able to do all tasks. For this reason, during the seven-day great offering, from the day of his birth, taking up the water-strainer, he strained water for the Saṅgha and gave it.

Yomantiādigāthāya “yo bhikkhu imaṃ rāgapalipathañceva kilesaduggañca saṃsāravaṭṭañca catunnaṃ saccānaṃ appaṭivijjhanakamohañca atīto cattāro oghe tiṇṇo hutvā pāraṃ anuppatto, duvidhena jhānena jhāyī, taṇhāya abhāvena anejo, kathaṃkathāya abhāvena akathaṃkathī, upādānānaṃ abhāvena anupādiyitvā kilesanibbānena nibbuto, tamahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmī”ti attho.

By the verse beginning Yo’maṃ, the meaning is: ‘The monk who has overcome this mire of lust, the difficult terrain of defilements, the cycle of saṃsāra, and the delusion of not penetrating the four truths; who, having crossed the four floods, has reached the far shore; who meditates with the twofold jhāna; who is unshaken due to the absence of craving; who is without doubt due to the absence of perplexity; who, not clinging due to the absence of attachments, is extinguished by the extinction of defilements—him I call a brahmin.’

Sabbesaṃyeva pana kesānaṃ oropanañca arahattasacchikiriyā ca apacchāapurimā ahosīti iminā therassa khuraggeyeva arahattuppatti dīpitā. Ekacce pana ācariyā evaṃ vadanti “heṭṭhā vuttanayena dhammasenāpatinā ovāde dinne ‘yaṃ mayā kātuṃ sakkā, tamahaṃ jānissāmī’ti pabbajitvā vipassanākammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā taṃ divasaṃyeva aññataraṃ vicittaṃ kuṭikaṃ disvā pavisitvā mātukucchiyaṃ satta vassāni attanā anubhūtadukkhaṃ anussaritvā tadanusārena atītānāgate ñāṇaṃ nentassa ādittā viya tayo bhavā upaṭṭhahiṃsu. Ñāṇassa paripākaṃ gatattā [V 1.0154] vipassanāvīthiṃ otaritvā tāvadeva maggappaṭipāṭiyā sabbepi āsave khepento arahattaṃ pāpuṇī”ti. Ubhayathāpi therassa arahattuppattiyeva pakāsitā, thero pana pabhinnappaṭisambhido chaḷabhiñño ahosi.

However, the shaving of all his hair and the realization of arahantship occurred simultaneously, neither before nor after the other. By this, it is shown that the elder’s attainment of arahantship occurred right at the razor’s edge. Some teachers, however, say this: “When the General of the Dhamma gave him the advice as mentioned above, he thought, ‘What I am capable of doing, that I shall know.’ Having gone forth, he took up the meditation subject of insight. That very day, seeing a certain beautiful hut, he entered it and recollected the suffering he had endured in his mother’s womb for seven years. In accordance with that, as he extended his knowledge to the past and the future, the three realms of existence appeared to him as if on fire. As his knowledge had reached maturity, he entered the path of insight and, right then, following the sequence of the path and eradicating all the taints, he attained arahantship.” In both accounts, the elder’s attainment of arahantship is made clear. The elder, however, attained the analytical knowledges and possessed the six supernormal knowledges.

Vakkalittheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Vakkali

208. Dasame āhārakaraṇavelanti bhojanakiccavelaṃ. Adhigacche padaṃ santanti saṅkhārūpasamaṃ sukhanti laddhanāmaṃ santaṃ padaṃ nibbānaṃ adhigaccheyya. Paṭhamapādena pabbate ṭhitoyevāti paṭhamena pādena gijjhakūṭe pabbate ṭhitoyeva. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

208. In the tenth, āhārakaraṇavelā means the time for the task of eating. Adhigacche padaṃ santaṃ means one might attain the peaceful state, Nibbāna, which has received the name ‘the stilling of formations, happiness.’ Paṭhamapādena pabbate ṭhitoyeva means standing on Mount Vulture Peak with the first foot only. The rest here is easily understood.

Dutiyaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Second Chapter of the Foremost is Concluded.

(14) 3. Tatiyaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā

(14) 3. The Commentary on the Third Chapter of the Foremost

Rāhula-raṭṭhapālattheravatthu

The Story of the Elders Rāhula and Raṭṭhapāla

209-210. Tatiyassa [V 1.0155][M 1.0169] paṭhamadutiyesu tisso sikkhāti adhisīlaadhicittaadhipaññāsaṅkhātā tisso sikkhā. Cuddasa bhattacchede katvāti sattāhaṃ nirāhāratāya ekekasmiṃ divase dvinnaṃ bhattacchedānaṃ vasena cuddasa bhattacchede katvā.

209-210. In the first and second of the third, tisso sikkhā means the three trainings designated as higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom. Cuddasa bhattacchede katvā means having made fourteen breaks in meals by way of being without food for seven days, with two breaks in meals on each day.

Tesanti tesaṃ tāpasānaṃ. Lābubhājanādiparikkhāraṃ saṃvidhāyāti lābubhājanāditāpasaparikkhāraṃ saṃvidahitvā. Sapariḷāhakāyadhātukoti ussannapittatāya sapariḷāhakāyasabhāvo. Satasahassāti satasahassaparimāṇā. Satasahassaṃ parimāṇaṃ etesanti satasahassā uttarapadalopena yathā “rūpabhavo rūpa”nti, atthiatthe vā akārapaccayo daṭṭhabbo. Pāṇātipātādiakusaladhammasamudācārasaṅkhāto āmagandho kuṇapagandho natthi etesanti nirāmagandhā, yathāvuttakilesasamudācārarahitāti attho. Kilesasamudācāro hettha “āmagandho”ti vutto. Kiṃkāraṇā? Amanuññattā, kilesaasucimissattā, sabbhi jigucchitattā, paramaduggandhabhāvavahattā ca. Tathā hi ye ye ussannakilesā sattā, te te atiduggandhā honti. Teneva nikkilesānaṃ matasarīrampi duggandhaṃ na hoti. Dānaggaparivahanaketi dānaggadhuravahanake. Māpakoti divase divase parimitaparibbayadānavasena dhaññamāpako.

Tesaṃ means ‘of those ascetics.’ Lābubhājanādiparikkhāraṃ saṃvidhāya means having arranged the ascetics’ requisites, such as gourd-bowls. Sapariḷāhakāyadhātuko means having a bodily nature full of heat due to an excess of bile. Satasahassā means numbering a hundred thousand. Satasahassaṃ, a hundred thousand, is their measure, thus satasahassā; it is formed by the elision of the latter word, as in rūpabhavo becoming rūpa. Or, the suffix ‘a’ should be seen in the sense of ‘possessing.’ Nirāmagandhā means they are without the raw stench, that is, the raw stench—the stench of a corpse—which is designated as the practice of unwholesome states such as the taking of life, is not found in them; the meaning is that they are without the practice of defilements as described. Here, the practice of defilements is called ‘raw stench.’ For what reason? Because it is unpleasant, mixed with the impurity of defilements, despised by the good, and because it carries a supremely foul nature. For indeed, whatever beings have an excess of defilements, they are extremely foul-smelling. For that reason, even the dead body of one without defilements is not foul-smelling. Dānaggaparivahanake means carrying the yoke of the foremost offering. Māpako means a measurer of grain, by way of giving a limited expenditure daily.

Pāḷiyanti vinayapāḷiyaṃ. Migajātakaṃ āharitvā kathesīti atīte kira bodhisatto migayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā migagaṇaparivuto araññe vasati. Athassa bhaginī attano puttakaṃ upanetvā “bhātika imaṃ bhāgineyyaṃ migamāyaṃ sikkhāpehī”ti āha. Bodhisatto “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā “gaccha tāta, asukavelāyaṃ nāma āgantvā sikkheyyāsī”ti āha. So mātulena vuttavelaṃ anatikkamitvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā migamāyaṃ sikkhi. So ekadivasaṃ vane vicaranto pāsena baddho baddharavaṃ viravi. Migagaṇo palāyitvā “putto te pāsena baddho”ti tassa mātuyā ārocesi. Sā bhātu santikaṃ gantvā “bhātika bhāgineyyo [M 1.0170] te migamāyaṃ sikkhāpito”ti [V 1.0156] pucchi. Bodhisatto “mā tvaṃ puttassa kiñci pāpakaṃ āsaṅki, suggahitā tena migamāyā, idāni taṃ hāsayamāno āgacchissatī”ti vatvā “migaṃ tipallattha”ntiādimāha.

Pāḷiyaṃ means in the Vinaya Pāḷi. He related the Migajātaka, thus: It is said that in the past the Bodhisatta was reborn in the deer realm and lived in the forest surrounded by a herd of deer. Then his sister brought her young one to him and said, “Brother, teach this nephew the deer’s tricks.” The Bodhisatta consented, saying, “Good,” and then said, “Go, dear one, come at such and such a time and you should learn.” That nephew, not missing the time appointed by his maternal uncle, approached him and learned the deer’s tricks. One day, while wandering in the forest, he was caught in a snare and cried out the cry of the captured. The herd of deer fled and informed his mother, saying, “Your son is caught in a snare.” She went to her brother and asked, “Brother, was your nephew taught the deer’s tricks?” The Bodhisatta said, “Do not suspect any harm for your son; the deer’s tricks have been well-grasped by him. Now he will come, causing you to rejoice.” Having said this, he spoke the verse beginning, “The deer, the threefold feint…”

Tattha miganti bhāgineyyamigaṃ. Tipallatthaṃ vuccati sayanaṃ, ubhohi passehi ujukameva ca nipannakavasena tīhākārehi pallatthaṃ assa, tīṇi vā pallatthāni assāti tipallattho, taṃ tipallatthaṃ. Anekamāyanti bahumāyaṃ bahuvañcanaṃ. Aṭṭhakkhuranti ekekasmiṃ pāde dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ vasena aṭṭhahi khurehi samannāgataṃ. Aḍḍharattāpapāyinti purimayāmaṃ atikkamitvā majjhimayāme araññato āgamma pānīyassa pivanato aḍḍharatte āpaṃ pivatīti aḍḍharattāpapāyī. “Aḍḍharatte āpapāyi”ntipi pāṭho. Mama bhāgineyyaṃ migaṃ ahaṃ sādhukaṃ migamāyaṃ uggaṇhāpesiṃ. Kathaṃ? Yathā ekena sotena chamāyaṃ assasanto chahi kalāhi atibhoti bhāgineyyo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ayañhi tava puttaṃ tathā uggaṇhāpesiṃ, yathā ekasmiṃ uparimanāsikāsote vātaṃ sannirumbhitvā pathaviyaṃ allīnena ekena heṭṭhimanāsikāsotena tatheva chamāyaṃ assasanto chahi kalāhi luddakaṃ atibhoti, chahi koṭṭhāsehi ajjhottharati vañcetīti attho. Katamehi chahi? Cattāro pāde pasāretvā ekena passena seyyāya, khurehi tiṇapaṃsukhaṇanena, jivhāninnāmanena, udarassa uddhumātabhāvakaraṇena, uccārapassāvavissajjanena, vātassa nirumbhanenāti. Atha vā tathā naṃ uggaṇhāpesiṃ, yathā ekena sotena chamāyaṃ assasanto. Chahīti heṭṭhā vuttehi chahi kāraṇehi. Kalāhīti kalāyissati, luddakaṃ vañcessatīti attho. Bhotīti bhaginiṃ ālapati. Bhāgineyyoti evaṃ chahi kāraṇehi vañcakaṃ bhāgineyyaṃ niddisati.

There, `miga` refers to the nephew deer. `Tipallattha` is called a lying posture, meaning that it is a lying posture in three ways: lying straight on both sides, or having three lying postures. `Anekamāya` means full of deceit, much trickery. `Aṭṭhakkhura` means endowed with eight hooves, two on each foot. `Aḍḍharattāpapāyī` means one who drinks water at midnight, having come from the forest in the middle watch after passing the first watch, to drink water. The reading ‘aḍḍharatte āpapāyī’ is also found. I thoroughly taught my nephew deer the deer's art. How? So that with one nostril breathing on the ground, he surpasses the hunter with six arts. This is what is said: I taught your son in such a way that, by blocking the wind in one upper nostril and with one lower nostril pressed to the ground, he breathes in the same manner on the ground and surpasses the hunter with six arts, meaning he overwhelms and deceives him with six parts. What are the six? Lying on one side with the four legs stretched out, digging grass and dust with the hooves, letting the tongue hang out, puffing up the belly, releasing excrement and urine, and holding the breath. Or, I taught him so that with one nostril breathing on the ground, he surpasses. `Chahi` refers to the six reasons mentioned above. `Kalāhi` means he will trick, he will deceive the hunter—this is the meaning. `Bhoti` addresses the sister. `Bhāgineyya` thus points out the deceitful nephew with these six reasons.

Evaṃ bodhisatto bhāgineyyassa migamāyaṃ sādhukaṃ uggahitabhāvaṃ vadanto bhaginiṃ samassāsesi. Sopi migapotako pāse baddho anibandhitvāyeva bhūmiyaṃ mahāphāsukapassena pāde pasāretvā nipanno pādānaṃ āsannaṭṭhāne khurehi eva paharitvā paṃsuñca tiṇāni ca uppāṭetvā uccārapassāvaṃ vissajjetvā sīsaṃ pātetvā jivhaṃ ninnāmetvā sarīraṃ kheḷakilinnaṃ katvā vātaggahaṇena udaraṃ uddhumātakaṃ katvā akkhīni parivattetvā heṭṭhānāsikāsotena vātaṃ sañcarāpento uparimanāsikāsotena [M 1.0171] vātaṃ sannirumbhitvā sakalasarīraṃ thaddhabhāvaṃ gāhāpetvā matakākāraṃ dassesi, nīlamakkhikāpi naṃ samparivāresuṃ, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne kākā nilīyiṃsu. Luddo āgantvā udare hatthena paharitvā “pātova baddho bhavissati, pūtiko jāto”ti tassa bandhanarajjuṃ mocetvā “ettheva dāni naṃ ukkantitvā maṃsaṃ ādāya gamissāmī”ti [V 1.0157] nirāsaṅko hutvā sākhāpalāsaṃ gahetuṃ āraddho. Migapotakopi uṭṭhāya catūhi pādehi ṭhatvā kāyaṃ vidhunitvā gīvaṃ pasāretvā mahāvātena chinnavalāhako viya vegena mātu santikaṃ agamāsi. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, rāhulo idāneva sikkhākāmo, pubbepi sikkhākāmoyevā”ti evaṃ migajātakaṃ āharitvā kathesi.

Thus the Bodhisatta, speaking of how his nephew had thoroughly learned the deer's art, comforted his sister. That young deer, caught in the snare, lay on the ground as if untroubled by the bonds, stretching its legs on its very comfortable side. It struck the ground near its feet with its hooves, tearing up dust and grass, then released its excrement and urine. It let its head droop, let its tongue hang out, made its body wet with saliva, and by taking in air, its belly swelled up. It rolled its eyes, let the wind pass through its lower nostrils while blocking the upper ones, and making its whole body stiff, it showed the appearance of being dead. Blue flies swarmed around it, and crows perched here and there. The hunter, arriving, struck its belly with his hand and said, 'It must have been caught early in the morning; it has become putrid.' He loosened the binding rope and, free from suspicion, began to gather branches and leaves, thinking, 'I will cut it up right here and take the meat away.' The young deer, rising up, stood on all fours, shook its body, stretched its neck, and swiftly ran to its mother like a cloud torn apart by a strong wind. The Teacher said, 'Bhikkhus, Rāhula is not desirous of training only now; he was desirous of training in the past as well.' Thus, having brought forth this Deer Jātaka, he related it.

Ambalaṭṭhiyarāhulovādaṃ desesīti “passasi no tvaṃ, rāhula, imaṃ parittaṃ udakāvasesaṃ udakādāne ṭhapitanti? Evaṃ, bhante. Evaṃ parittakaṃ kho, rāhula, tesaṃ sāmaññaṃ, yesaṃ natthi sampajānamusāvāde lajjā”ti evamādinā ambalaṭṭhiyarāhulovādaṃ (ma. ni. 2.107 ādayo) kathesi. Gehasitaṃ vitakkaṃ vitakkentassāti āyasmā kira rāhulo bhagavato piṭṭhito piṭṭhito gacchantova pādatalato yāva upari kesantā tathāgataṃ olokesi, so bhagavato buddhavesavilāsaṃ disvā “sobhati bhagavā dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇavicittasarīro byāmappabhāparikkhittatāya vippakiṇṇasuvaṇṇacuṇṇamajjhagato viya vijjulatāparikkhitto kanakapabbato viya yantasamākaḍḍhitaratanavicittasuvaṇṇaagghikaṃ viya paṃsukūlacīvarappaṭicchannopi rattakambalaparikkhittakanakapabbato viya pavāḷalatāpaṭimaṇḍitasuvaṇṇaghaṭikaṃ viya cīnapiṭṭhacuṇṇapūjitasuvaṇṇacetiyaṃ viya lākhārasānulitto kanakathūpo viya rattavalāhakantaragato taṅkhaṇamuggatapuṇṇacando viya aho samatiṃsapāramitānubhāvena sajjitassa attabhāvassa sirisampattī”ti cintesi. Tato attānampi oloketvā “ahampi sobhāmi, sace bhagavā catūsu mahādīpesu cakkavattirajjaṃ akarissa, mayhaṃ pariṇāyakaṭṭhānantaramadassa, evaṃ sante ativiya jambudīpatalaṃ atisobhissā”ti attabhāvaṃ nissāya gehasitaṃ chandarāgaṃ uppādesi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “satthu ceva attano ca rūpasampattiṃ disvā gehasitaṃ vitakkaṃ vitakkentassā”ti.

He taught the Ambalaṭṭhika-Rāhulovāda Discourse: 'Do you see, Rāhula, this small amount of water left in the water vessel?' 'Yes, venerable sir.' 'Just so little, Rāhula, is the recluseship of those who have no shame in deliberate lying.' Thus, with such words, he taught the Ambalaṭṭhika-Rāhulovāda Discourse (Majjhima Nikāya 2.107, etc.). 'One who entertains thoughts connected with the household'—it is said that the Venerable Rāhula, while walking right behind the Blessed One, gazed at the Tathāgata from the soles of his feet up to the tips of his hair. Seeing the Buddha's majestic appearance, he thought: 'The Blessed One shines brilliantly, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, surrounded by a fathom-long radiance, as if in the midst of scattered gold dust, like a golden mountain surrounded by lightning, like a golden vase adorned with jewels and drawn by a machine, even though covered by a rag-robe, like a golden mountain enveloped in a red blanket, like a golden jar adorned with coral vines, like a golden shrine worshipped with Chinese flour, like a golden stupa smeared with lac resin, like the full moon just risen from within a red cloud. Oh, the glorious fortune of an existence fashioned by the power of the thirty perfections!' Then, looking at himself, he thought: 'I too am splendid. If the Blessed One were to exercise the rule of a wheel-turning monarch over the four great continents, he would grant me the position of his successor. In that case, the surface of Jambudīpa would be exceedingly splendid!' Thus, based on his own person, he gave rise to sensual desire connected with the household. With reference to that, this was said: 'Seeing the perfection of form of both the Teacher and himself, he entertained thoughts connected with the household.'

Bhagavāpi [M 1.0172] purato gacchantova cintesi – “paripuṇṇacchavimaṃsalohito dāni rāhulassa attabhāvo, rajanīyesu rūpārammaṇādīsu cittassa pakkhandanakālo jāto, nipphalatāya nu kho rāhulo vītināmetī”ti.
