Atha sahāvajjaneneva pasanne udake macchaṃ viya parisuddhe ādāsamaṇḍale mukhanimittaṃ viya ca tassa taṃ cittuppādaṃ addasa, disvā ca “ayaṃ rāhulo mayhaṃ atrajo hutvā mama pacchato āgacchanto ‘ahaṃ sobhāmi, mayhaṃ vaṇṇāyatanaṃ pasanna’nti attabhāvaṃ nissāya gehasitaṃ chandarāgaṃ uppādeti, atitthe pakkhando, uppathaṃ paṭipanno, agocare carati, disāmūḷhaaddhiko viya agantabbaṃ disaṃ gacchati, ayaṃ kho panassa kileso abbhantare vaḍḍhanto attatthampi yathābhūtaṃ passituṃ na dassissati paratthampi ubhayatthampi, tato [V 1.0158] nirayepi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhāpessati, tiracchānayoniyampi pettivisayepi asurakāyepi sambādhepi mātukucchisminti anamatagge saṃsāravaṭṭe paripātessati. Yathā kho pana anekaratanapūrā mahānāvā bhinnaphalakantarena udakaṃ ādiyamānā muhuttampi na ajjhupekkhitabbā hoti, vegena vegenassā vivaraṃ pidahituṃ vaṭṭati, evameva ayampi na ajjhupekkhitabbo. Yāvassa ayaṃ kileso abbhantare sīlaratanādīni na vināseti, tāvadeva naṃ niggaṇhissāmī”ti ajjhāsayaṃ akāsi. Tato rāhulaṃ āmantetvā “yaṃ kiñci, rāhula, rūpaṃ atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ ajjhattaṃ vā bahiddhā vā oḷārikaṃ vā sukhumaṃ vā hīnaṃ vā paṇītaṃ vā yaṃ dūre santike vā, sabbaṃ rūpaṃ ‘netaṃ mama, nesohamasmi, na meso attā’ti evametaṃ yathābhūtaṃ sammappaññāya daṭṭhabbanti. Rūpameva nu kho bhagavā rūpameva nu kho sugatāti. Rūpampi rāhula, vedanāpi rāhula, saññāpi rāhula, saṅkhārāpi rāhula, viññāṇampi rāhulā”ti mahārāhulovādasuttaṃ (ma. ni. 2.113 ādayo) abhāsi. Taṃ dassetuṃ – “yaṃ kiñci rāhula…pe… kathesī”ti vuttaṃ.

The Blessed One, while walking ahead, thought: "Now Rāhula's body is full of skin, flesh, and blood; the time has come for his mind to leap towards enticing forms and other objects. Is Rāhula passing his time fruitlessly?" Then, just as one sees a fish in clear water or a reflection in a spotless mirror, so too did he perceive the arising of that thought in Rāhula's mind. Seeing this, he reflected: "This Rāhula, being my own son, follows behind me thinking, 'I am radiant, my appearance is pleasing,' and thus, relying on his body, he gives rise to household-bound sensual desire. His leap is misplaced, his path is wrong, he wanders where he should not, like a traveler lost in the wilderness, heading in the wrong direction. Moreover, this defilement growing within him will prevent him from seeing his own good, others' good, or both as they truly are. It will lead him to rebirth in hell, the animal realm, the ghost realm, the demon realm, or even the cramped womb—thus spinning him endlessly in the beginningless cycle of existence. Just as a great ship filled with various jewels, taking in water through a cracked plank, cannot be ignored even for a moment—one must quickly plug the leak—so too must this not be ignored. As long as this defilement does not destroy the jewels of virtue within him, I will restrain him now." Then, calling Rāhula, he said: "Whatever form, Rāhula—past, future, or present, internal or external, gross or subtle, inferior or superior, far or near—all form should be seen with right wisdom as it truly is: 'This is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.'" "Is it only form, Blessed One? Is it only form, Sugata?" "Form too, Rāhula, feeling too, Rāhula, perception too, Rāhula, formations too, Rāhula, and consciousness too, Rāhula." Thus, the Blessed One taught the Great Discourse of Advice to Rāhula (Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, Majjhima Nikāya 2.113 ff.). To explain this, it is said: "Whatever, Rāhula… he taught."

Saṃyuttake pana rāhulovādoti rāhulasaṃyutte vuttarāhulovādaṃ sandhāya vadanti. Tattha “sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā saṃkhittena dhammaṃ desetu, yamahaṃ, bhante, bhagavato dhammaṃ sutvā eko vūpakaṭṭho appamatto ātāpī pahitatto vihareyya”nti therena yācito “taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rāhula, cakkhu niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vāti? Aniccaṃ, bhante. Yaṃ panāniccaṃ[M 1.0173], dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vāti? Dukkhaṃ, bhante. Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”tiādinā rāhulovādaṃ (saṃ. ni. 2.188 ādayo) ārabhi. Therassa vipassanācāroyeva, na pana mahārāhulovādo viya vitakkūpacchedāya vuttoti adhippāyo.

In the Saṃyutta Nikāya, however, it is called the "Rāhulovāda," referring to the Rāhulovāda mentioned in the Rāhulasaṃyutta. There, when the elder requested, "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I may dwell alone, secluded, diligent, ardent, and resolute," the Buddha began the Rāhulovāda (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.188 ff.) with the question, "What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?"—"Impermanent, venerable sir."—"And what is impermanent, is that suffering or happiness?"—"Suffering, venerable sir."—"And what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it proper to regard it as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?" and so on. The intention here is that it was taught to the elder as the practice of insight meditation, not like the Mahārāhulovāda, which was taught to cut off discursive thinking.

Athassa satthā ñāṇaparipākaṃ ñatvātiādīsu bhagavato kira rahogatassa paṭisallīnassa evaṃ cetaso parivitakko udapādi “paripakkā kho rāhulassa vimuttiparipācanīyā dhammā, yannūnāhaṃ rāhulaṃ uttari āsavānaṃ khaye vineyya”nti? Athassa bhagavā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto āyasmantaṃ rāhulaṃ āmantesi – “gaṇhāhi, rāhula, nisīdanaṃ, yena andhavanaṃ tenupasaṅkamissāma divāvihārāyā”ti. “Evaṃ, bhante”ti kho āyasmā rāhulo bhagavato paṭissutvā nisīdanaṃ ādāya bhagavato piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhi. Tena kho pana samayena anekāni devatāsahassāni bhagavantaṃ abhivanditvā anubandhitā honti “ajja bhagavā āyasmantaṃ rāhulaṃ [V 1.0159] uttari āsavānaṃ khaye vinessatī”ti. Atha kho bhagavā andhavanaṃ ajjhogāhetvā aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle paññatte āsane nisīdi. Āyasmāpi rāhulo bhagavantaṃ abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Atha āyasmantaṃ rāhulaṃ āmantetvā “taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rāhula, cakkhu niccaṃ vā aniccaṃ vāti? Aniccaṃ, bhante. Yaṃ panāniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ vā taṃ sukhaṃ vāti? Dukkhaṃ, bhante. Yaṃ panāniccaṃ dukkhaṃ vipariṇāmadhammaṃ, kallaṃ nu taṃ samanupassituṃ ‘etaṃ mama, esohamasmi, eso me attā’”tiādinā rāhulovādaṃ (saṃ. ni. 4.121) adāsi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “andhavane nisinno cūḷarāhulovādaṃ kathesī”ti.

Then, knowing the maturity of his knowledge, it is said that while the Blessed One was in seclusion, this thought arose in his mind: "The qualities conducive to Rāhula’s liberation have matured. Suppose I were to instruct Rāhula further in the destruction of the taints?" Then, the Blessed One, having dressed in the morning, took his bowl and robe, entered Sāvatthī for alms, and after the meal, on his return from the alms round, addressed Venerable Rāhula: "Take a sitting cloth, Rāhula, let us go to Andhavana for the day’s abiding."—"Yes, venerable sir," replied Venerable Rāhula, and taking a sitting cloth, he followed close behind the Blessed One. At that time, many thousands of deities, having paid homage to the Blessed One, followed him, thinking, "Today the Blessed One will instruct Venerable Rāhula further in the destruction of the taints." Then, the Blessed One entered Andhavana and sat down on a prepared seat at the foot of a tree. Venerable Rāhula also paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Then, addressing Venerable Rāhula, the Blessed One gave the Rāhulovāda (Saṃyutta Nikāya 4.121), beginning with the question, "What do you think, Rāhula, is the eye permanent or impermanent?"—"Impermanent, venerable sir."—"And what is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?"—"Suffering, venerable sir."—"And what is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change, is it proper to regard it as ‘This is mine, this I am, this is my self’?" and so on. With reference to this, it is said: "Seated in Andhavana, he taught the Cūḷarāhulovāda."

Koṭisatasahassadevatāhīti āyasmatā rāhulena padumuttarassa bhagavato pādamūle pathavindhararājakāle patthanaṃ ṭhapentena saddhiṃ patthanaṃ ṭhapitadevatāyevetā. Tāsu pana kāci bhūmaṭṭhadevatā, kāci antalikkhaṭṭhakā, kāci cātumahārājikādidevaloke, kāci brahmaloke nibbattā, imasmiṃ pana divase sabbā ekaṭṭhāne andhavanasmiṃyeva sannipatitā.

The phrase 'by a hundred thousand crores of deities' (koṭisatasahassadevatāhi) refers to those very deities who, along with Venerable Rāhula, had made an aspiration at the feet of the Blessed Padumuttara during the time of King Pathavindhara. Among them, some were earth-dwelling deities, some were dwelling in the sky, some were born in the Cātumahārājika and other deva-worlds, and some were reborn in the Brahma-world. On this day, however, all of them gathered together in one place, right in the Andhavana.

Ābhidosikanti [M 1.0174] pārivāsikaṃ ekarattātikkantaṃ pūtibhūtaṃ. Ekarattātikkantasseva hi nāmasaññā esā, yadidaṃ ābhidosikoti. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho – pūtibhāvadosena abhibhūtoti abhidoso, abhidosoyeva ābhidosiko. Kummāsanti yavakummāsaṃ. Adhivāsetvāti “tena hi, tāta raṭṭhapāla, adhivāsehi svātanāya bhatta”nti pitarā nimantito svātanāya bhikkhaṃ adhivāsetvā. Ettha ca thero pakatiyā ukkaṭṭhasapadānacāriko svātanāya bhikkhaṃ nāma nādhivāseti, mātu anuggahena pana adhivāseti. Mātu kirassa theraṃ anussaritvā anussaritvā mahāsoko uppajjati, rodaneneva dukkhī viya jātā, tasmā thero “sacāhaṃ taṃ apassitvā gamissāmi, hadayampissā phaleyyā”ti anuggahena adhivāsesi. Paṇḍitā hi bhikkhū mātāpitūnaṃ ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ vā kātabbaṃ anuggahaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā dhutaṅgasuddhikā na bhavanti.

Ābhidosika refers to food that has been left overnight and become spoiled. This term denotes food that has passed beyond a single night; hence the name 'ābhidosika.' The meaning here is this: overcome by the fault of spoilage, it is called abhidosa, and abhidosa itself is ābhidosika. 'Kummāsa' refers to barley gruel. 'Having accepted' means that when his father invited him, saying, 'Well then, dear Raṭṭhapāla, accept the meal for tomorrow,' he agreed to receive alms the next day. Here, the elder, who was naturally accustomed to the strict practice of going for alms from house to house in sequence, would not ordinarily accept an invitation for the next day’s meal. However, out of compassion for his mother, he accepted. For whenever his mother remembered the elder, great sorrow arose, and she would weep as if afflicted by suffering. Therefore, the elder thought, 'If I were to leave without seeing her, her heart might break,' and so he accepted out of compassion. For wise monks do not achieve purity in their ascetic practices by neglecting the compassion that should be shown to their parents, teachers, or preceptors.

Alaṅkatapaṭiyatte itthijaneti pitarā uyyojite itthijane. Pitā kirassa dutiyadivase sakanivesane mahantaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇassa puñjaṃ kārāpetvā kilañjehi paṭicchādāpetvā āyasmato raṭṭhapālassa purāṇadutiyikāyo “etha tumhe vadhū, yena alaṅkārena alaṅkatā pubbe raṭṭhapālassa kulaputtassa piyā hotha manāpā, tena alaṅkārena alaṅkarothā”ti āṇāpetvā paṇītaṃ khādanīyaṃ bhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādāpetvā kāle ārocite āgantvā paññatte āsane nisinnaṃ “idaṃ te, raṭṭhapāla, mattikaṃ dhanaṃ, aññaṃ pettikaṃ, aññaṃ pitāmahaṃ; sakkā, tāta raṭṭhapāla, bhoge [V 1.0160] ca bhuñjituṃ, puññāni ca kātuṃ? Ehi tvaṃ, tāta raṭṭhapāla, sikkhaṃ paccakkhāya hīnāyāvattitvā bhoge ca bhuñjassu, puññāni ca karohī”ti yācitvā tena paṭikkhipitvā dhamme desite “ahaṃ imaṃ uppabbājessāmī”ti ānayiṃ, so “dāni me dhammakathaṃ kātuṃ āraddho, alaṃ me vacanaṃ na karissatī”ti uṭṭhāya gantvā tassa orodhānaṃ dvāraṃ vivarāpetvā “ayaṃ vo sāmiko, gacchatha, yaṃ kiñci katvāna gaṇhituṃ vāyamathā”ti uyyojesi. Tīsu vayesu ṭhitā nāṭakitthiyo theraṃ parivārayiṃsu. Tāsu ayaṃ asubhasaññaṃ uppādesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “alaṅkatapaṭiyatte itthijane asubhasaññaṃ uppādetvā”ti.

The phrase 'the adorned and prepared women' refers to the women sent by his father. Indeed, on the second day, the father had a great heap of gold and silver prepared in his own residence and covered with mats. He commanded the former wives of the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, saying, 'Come, you brides, adorn yourselves with the same ornaments with which you were formerly adorned, when you were dear and pleasing to the young man Raṭṭhapāla.' Having prepared fine food and drink, when the time was announced, he approached the Venerable Raṭṭhapāla, who was seated on the appointed seat, and entreated him, 'Here, Raṭṭhapāla, is your maternal wealth, other is paternal, and other is from your grandfather. Surely, dear Raṭṭhapāla, you can both enjoy wealth and perform meritorious deeds. Come, dear Raṭṭhapāla, renounce the training, return to the lower life, enjoy wealth, and perform meritorious deeds.' When he was thus entreated, Raṭṭhapāla refused and taught the Dhamma. The father, thinking, 'I will make him disrobe,' had brought them. But then, thinking, 'Now he has started to give me a Dhamma talk; he will not heed my word,' he rose, went, and had the door of the women's quarters opened, sending them forth with the words, 'Here is your master; go, and by whatever means, strive to win him over.' The dancing women, standing in three age groups, surrounded the elder. Towards them, he aroused the perception of foulness. Hence it is said: 'having aroused the perception of foulness in the adorned and prepared women.'

Ṭhitakova [M 1.0175] dhammaṃ desetvāti –

This refers to his having taught the Dhamma while standing.

“Passa cittakataṃ bimbaṃ, arukāyaṃ samussitaṃ;

Āturaṃ bahusaṅkappaṃ, yassa natthi dhuvaṃ ṭhiti.

“See this painted image, a body of wounds, built up, diseased, of many thoughts, for which there is no lasting stability.”

“Passa cittakataṃ rūpaṃ, maṇinā kuṇḍalena ca;

Aṭṭhiṃ tacena onaddhaṃ, saha vatthehi sobhati.

“Behold this painted form, with jewels and earrings; a bone covered with skin, it shines with its clothes.”

“Alattakakatā pādā, mukhaṃ cuṇṇakamakkhitaṃ;

Alaṃ bālassa mohāya, no ca pāragavesino.

“Feet reddened with lac, a face smeared with powder— enough to delude a fool, but not one seeking the further shore.”

“Aṭṭhāpadakatā kesā, nettā añjanamakkhitā;

Alaṃ bālassa mohāya, no ca pāragavesino.

“Hair plaited in eight-fold braids, eyes smeared with collyrium— enough to delude a fool, but not one seeking the further shore.”

“Añjanīvaṇṇavā cittā, pūtikāyo alaṅkato;

Alaṃ bālassa mohāya, no ca pāragavesino.

“Like a painted collyrium-pot, this foul body is adorned— enough to delude a fool, but not one seeking the further shore.”

“Odahi migavo pāsaṃ, nāsadā vāguraṃ migo;

Bhutvā nivāpaṃ gacchāmi, kandante migabandhake”ti. (ma. ni. 2.302; theragā. 769-774) –

“The hunter set the snare, but the deer did not approach the trap. Having eaten the bait, I depart, while the deer-trapper laments.”

Imāhi gāthāhi dhammaṃ desetvā.

Having taught the Dhamma with these stanzas.

Ākāsaṃ [V 1.0161] uppatitvāti ākāsaṃ pakkhanditvā. Kasmā pana thero ākāsena gato? Pitā kirassa seṭṭhi sattasu dvārakoṭṭhakesu aggaḷāni dāpetvā malle āṇāpesi “sace nikkhamitvā gacchati, hatthapādesu naṃ gahetvā kāsāyāni haritvā gihivesaṃ gaṇhāpethā”ti. Tasmā thero “ete mādisaṃ mahākhīṇāsavaṃ hatthe vā pāde vā gahetvā apuññaṃ pasaveyyuṃ, taṃ nesaṃ mā ahosī”ti cintetvā ākāsena agamāsi. Migacīranti evaṃnāmakaṃ uyyānaṃ. Catupārijuññapaṭimaṇḍitanti jarāpārijuññaṃ, byādhipārijuññaṃ, bhogapārijuññaṃ, ñātipārijuññanti imehi catūhi pārijuññehi paṭimaṇḍitaṃ. Pārijuññanti ca parihānīti attho. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

The phrase 'having risen into the sky' means 'having leapt into the sky.' But why did the elder go by way of the sky? It is said his father, the merchant, had bolts placed on the seven gate-towers and commanded the wrestlers, 'If he goes out, seize him by the hands and feet, take away his ochre robes, and make him put on layman's clothes.' Therefore, the elder thought, 'Lest these people, by seizing someone like me, a great one whose taints are destroyed, by the hand or foot, should generate demerit, may that not happen to them,' and so he went by way of the sky. Migacīra is a park of that name. The phrase 'adorned with four kinds of decay' refers to its being adorned with these four decays: the decay of old age, the decay of illness, the decay of wealth, and the decay of relatives. And 'pārijuñña' means decline. The rest here is easily understood.

Kuṇḍadhānattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Kuṇḍadhāna

211. Tatiye salākaṃ gaṇhantīti salākagāhakā. Sunāparantajanapadaṃ gacchantepi paṭhamameva salākaṃ gaṇhīti sambandho. Chabbassantareti channaṃ [M 1.0176] vassānaṃ abbhantare. Mettīti mittabhāvo. Bhedake satīti bhedakaraṇe sati. Gumbasabhāgatoti gumbasamīpato, ayameva vā pāṭho. Itthī hutvāti itthī viya hutvā, manussitthivaṇṇaṃ māpetvāti attho. Dīgharattānugatoti dīghakālaṃ anubandho. Ettakaṃ addhānanti ettakaṃ kālaṃ. Handāvusoti gaṇhāvuso. Atthaṃ gahetvāti bhūtatthaṃ gahetvā, ayameva vā pāṭho. Koṇḍo jātoti dhutto jāto.

211. In the third verse, `salākagāhakā` means those who take the voting-tickets. The connection is that he took the voting-ticket first even when going to the Sunāparanta country. `Chabbassantare` means within six years. `Mettī` means friendliness, the state of being a friend. `Bhedake sati` means when there is a cause for division. `Gumbasabhāgato` means from the vicinity of the thicket, or this is the reading itself. `Itthī hutvā` means having become like a woman; that is, having magically created the appearance of a human woman. `Dīgharattānugato` means followed for a long time. `Ettakaṃ addhānaṃ` means for such a duration. `Handāvusoti` means 'Take it, friend!' `Atthaṃ gahetvā` means having grasped the true meaning, or this is the reading itself. `Koṇḍo jāto` means a rogue was born.

Māvoca pharusaṃ kañcīti kañci ekapuggalaṃ pharusaṃ mā avoca. Vuttā paṭivadeyyu tanti tayā pare dussīlāti vuttā tampi tatheva paṭivadeyyuṃ. Dukkhā hi sārambhakathāti esā kāraṇuttarā yugaggāhakathā nāma dukkhā. Paṭidaṇḍā phuseyyu tanti kāyadaṇḍādīhi paraṃ paharantassa tādisāva paṭidaṇḍā tava matthake pateyyuṃ.

`Māvoca pharusaṃ kañci` means: 'Do not speak harshly to any single individual.' `Vuttā paṭivadeyyuṃ taṃ` means: those spoken to would retort to you; those you call 'immoral' would retort to you in the same way. `Dukkhā hi sārambhakathā` means: this contentious talk, which is retaliatory and quarrelsome, is indeed painful. `Paṭidaṇḍā phuseyyuṃ taṃ` means: counter-punishments would touch you; for one who strikes another with bodily punishment and so on, similar counter-punishments would fall upon your head.

Sace neresi attānanti sace attānaṃ niccalaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissasi. Kaṃso upahato yathāti mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ chinditvā talamattaṃ katvā ṭhapitaṃ kaṃsatālaṃ viya. Tādisañhi hatthehi pādehi daṇḍena vā pahatampi saddaṃ na karoti. Esa pattosi nibbānanti sace evarūpo bhavituṃ sakkhissasi, imaṃ paṭipadaṃ pūrayamāno eso tvaṃ idāni appattopi nibbānaṃ pattosi nāma. Sārambho te na vijjatīti “evañca sati tvaṃ dussīlo, ahaṃ susīlo”ti evamādiko uttarikaraṇavācālakkhaṇo sārambho te na vijjati, na bhavissatiyevāti attho. Parikkilesenāti saṃkilesahetunā.

`Sace neresi attānaṃ` means: 'If you can make yourself still.' `Kaṃso upahato yathā` means: like a bronze cymbal that has had its rim cut off, leaving only the base. For such a thing, even when struck with hands, feet, or a stick, makes no sound. `Esa pattosi nibbānaṃ` means: if you can become like this, fulfilling this practice, then although you have not yet attained it, you are said to have attained Nibbāna. `Sārambho te na vijjatīti` means: the contentiousness characterized by escalating speech such as, 'In that case you are immoral, and I am moral,' will not exist for you; the meaning is, it will certainly not arise. `Parikkilesena` means: by the cause of defilement.

Vaṅgīsattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Vaṅgīsa

212. Catutthe [V 1.0162] sampannapaṭibhānānanti paripuṇṇapaṭibhānānaṃ. Cutiṃ yo vedi…pe… sabbasoti yo sattānaṃ cutiñca paṭisandhiñca sabbākārena pākaṭaṃ katvā jānāti, taṃ ahaṃ alagganatāya asattaṃ, paṭipattiyā suṭṭhu gatattā sugataṃ, catunnaṃ saccānaṃ sambuddhattā buddhaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho. Yassa gatinti yassete devādayo gatiṃ na jānanti, tamahaṃ āsavānaṃ khīṇatāya khīṇāsavaṃ, kilesehi ārakattā arahantaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

212. In the fourth verse, `sampannapaṭibhānānaṃ` means: of those fully accomplished in eloquence. `Cutiṃ yo vedi…pe… sabbaso` means: he who knows the passing away and rebirth of beings in every way, having made it manifest. The meaning is: him I call a brahmin: 'unattached' (`asattaṃ`) because of non-attachment; 'well-gone' (`sugataṃ`) because he has gone well in practice; 'awakened' (`buddhaṃ`) because he has fully awakened to the four truths. `Yassa gatiṃ` means: whose destination the gods and others do not know. The meaning is: him I call a brahmin: 'one whose taints are destroyed' (`khīṇāsavaṃ`) because his taints are destroyed; 'an arahant' (`arahantaṃ`) because he is far from defilements.

Upasenavaṅgantaputtattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Upasena Vaṅgantaputta

213. Pañcame [M 1.0177] sabbapāsādikānanti sabbaso pasādaṃ janentānaṃ. Kintāyanti kiṃ te ayaṃ. Atilahunti atisīghaṃ. Yassa tasmiṃ attabhāve uppajjanārahānaṃ maggaphalānaṃ upanissayo natthi, taṃ buddhā “moghapuriso”ti vadanti ariṭṭhalāḷudāyiādike viya. Upanissaye satipi tasmiṃ khaṇe magge vā phale vā asati “moghapurisā”ti vadantiyeva dhaniyattherādike viya. Imassapi tasmiṃ khaṇe maggaphalānaṃ abhāvato “moghapurisā”ti āha, tucchamanussāti attho. Bāhullāyāti parisabāhullāya. Anekapariyāyenāti anekakāraṇena.

213. In the fifth verse, `sabbapāsādikānaṃ` means of those who entirely inspire confidence. `Kintāyaṃ` means 'What is this to you?' `Atilahuṃ` means very swiftly. One in whom there is no supporting condition for the arising of the path and its fruits in that existence—the Buddhas call such a one a 'vain person' (`moghapuriso`), like Ariṭṭha, Lāludāyi, and others. Even if there is a supporting condition, if at that moment the path or fruit is absent, they still call them 'vain persons' (`moghapurisā`), like the Elder Dhaniya and others. Because at that moment this one also lacked the path and its fruits, he called him a 'vain person,' meaning a worthless person. `Bāhullāya` means because of the abundance of the assembly. `Anekapariyāyena` means for many reasons.

Icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhaveti bhagavā kira taṃ addhamāsaṃ na kañci bodhaneyyasattaṃ addasa, tasmā evamāha, evaṃ santepi tantivasena dhammadesanā kattabbā siyā. Yasmā panassa etadahosi – “mayi okāsaṃ kāretvā paṭisallīne bhikkhū adhammikaṃ katikavattaṃ karissanti, taṃ upaseno bhindissati, ahaṃ tassa pasīditvā bhikkhūnaṃ dassanaṃ anujānissāmi. Tato maṃ passitukāmā bahū bhikkhū dhutaṅgāni samādiyissanti, ahañca tehi ujjhitasanthatapaccayā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapessāmī”ti, tasmā evamāha. Therassāti upasenattherassa. Manāpāni te bhikkhu paṃsukūlānīti “bhikkhu tava imāni paṃsukūlāni manāpāni attano ruciyā khantiyā gahitānī”ti pucchati. Na kho me, bhante, manāpāni paṃsukūlānīti, bhante, na mayā attano ruciyā khantiyā gahitāni, galaggāhena viya matthakatāḷanena viya ca gāhito mayāti dasseti. Pāḷiyaṃ āgatamevāti vinayapāḷiṃ sandhāya vadati.

Icchāmahaṃ, bhikkhavo means the Blessed One, it is said, did not see any being fit to be taught for half a month; therefore, he spoke thus. Even so, the teaching of the Dhamma should be done according to tradition. But he thought: 'When I provide an opportunity and the bhikkhus go into seclusion, they will make improper disciplinary agreements. Upasena will break them, and I, pleased with him, will grant the bhikkhus an audience. Then, many bhikkhus, desiring to see me, will undertake ascetic practices, and I will lay down a training rule because of a rejected mat-requisite'—therefore, he spoke thus. Therassa means of Venerable Upasena. Manāpāni te bhikkhu paṃsukūlāni means he asks, 'Bhikkhu, are these rag-robes pleasing to you, taken according to your own liking and tolerance?' Na kho me, bhante, manāpāni paṃsukūlāni means he shows that they were not taken according to his own liking and tolerance, but as if seized by the throat or struck on the crown of the head. Pāḷiyaṃ āgatamevāti means he speaks referring to the Vinaya text.

Dabbattheravatthu

The Story of Venerable Dabba

214. Chaṭṭhe [V 1.0163] aṭṭhārasasu mahāvihāresūti rājagahassa samantato ṭhitesu aṭṭhārasasu mahāvihāresu. Upavijaññāti āsannapasūtikālā. Rahogatoti rahasi gato. Saṅghassa veyyāvaccakaraṇe kāyaṃ yojetukāmo cintesīti thero kira attano katakiccabhāvaṃ disvā “ahaṃ imaṃ sarīraṃ dhāremi, tañca kho vātamukhe ṭhitapadīpo viya aniccatāmukhe ṭhitaṃ nacirasseva nibbāyanadhammaṃ yāva [M 1.0178] na nibbāyati, tāva kiṃ nu kho ahaṃ saṅghassa veyyāvaccaṃ kareyya”nti cintento iti paṭisañcikkhati “tiroraṭṭhesu bahū kulaputtā bhagavantaṃ adisvāva pabbajanti, te ‘bhagavantaṃ passissāma ceva vandissāmā’ti ca dūratopi āgacchanti, tatra yesaṃ senāsanaṃ nappahoti, te silāpattakepi seyyaṃ kappenti. Pahomi kho panāhaṃ attano ānubhāvena tesaṃ tesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ icchāvasena pāsādavihāraaḍḍhayogādīni mañcapīṭhattharaṇāni nimminitvā dātuṃ? Punadivase cettha ekacce ativiya kilantarūpā honti, te gāravena bhikkhūnaṃ purato ṭhatvā bhattānipi na uddisāpenti, ahaṃ kho pana tesaṃ bhattānipi uddisituṃ pahomī”ti. Iti paṭisañcikkhanto “yaṃnūnāhaṃ saṅghassa senāsanañca paññapeyyaṃ, bhattāni ca uddiseyya”nti cintesi. Sabhāgasabhāgānanti suttantikādiguṇavasena sabhāgānaṃ, na mittasanthavavasena. Thero hi yāvatikā suttantikā honti, te uccinitvā uccinitvā ekato tesaṃ anurūpameva senāsanaṃ paññapeti. Venayikābhidhammikakammaṭṭhānikakāyadaḷhibahulesupi eseva nayo. Teneva pāḷiyaṃ (pārā. 380) vuttaṃ – “yete bhikkhū suttantikā, tesaṃ ekajjhaṃ senāsanaṃ paññapetī”tiādi.

214. Sixth, in the eighteen great monasteries—meaning in the eighteen great monasteries situated around Rājagaha. Upavijaññā—meaning near the time of giving birth. Rahogata—meaning gone privately. Desiring to apply himself to doing service for the Saṅgha—the elder, seeing that he had fulfilled his duties, thought: “I maintain this body, but it stands like a lamp in the wind, situated at the mouth of impermanence, destined to be extinguished before long. Before it is extinguished, what service should I perform for the Saṅgha?” Thus reflecting, he pondered: “Many young men from outlying districts go forth without even seeing the Blessed One. They come from afar thinking, ‘We will see and pay homage to the Blessed One.’ Those who cannot find accommodation even prepare beds on stone slabs. But by my power, could I not create mansions, monasteries, half-gabled dwellings, etc., and provide beds, chairs, and mats according to the wishes of those young men? Moreover, the next day some become extremely weary. Out of respect, they stand before the bhikkhus without even being able to have food allocated. But I am capable of allocating food for them.” Reflecting thus, he thought: “Why shouldn’t I arrange lodging and allocate meals for the Saṅgha?” Sabhāgasabhāgāna—meaning according to shared qualities such as those versed in the Suttas, not according to friendship or familiarity. For the elder would select those who were versed in the Suttas and assign suitable lodgings to them together. The same method applies to those versed in Vinaya, Abhidhamma, skilled in meditation practice, or those who are physically strong. Therefore, in the Pāli (Pārā. 380) it is said: “For those bhikkhus who are versed in the Suttas, he allocates lodging together,” and so on.

Aṅguliyā jalamānāyāti tejokasiṇacatutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya abhiññāñāṇena aṅgulijalanaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā teneva tejodhātusamāpattijanitena aggijālena aṅguliyā jalamānāya. Ayaṃ mañcotiādīsu pana there “ayaṃ mañco”tiādiṃ vadante nimmitāpi attano attano gataṭṭhāne “ayaṃ mañco”tiādiṃ vadanti. Ayañhi nimmitānaṃ dhammatā.

Aṅguliyā jalamānāya—meaning when the finger is burning, having attained the fourth jhāna based on the fire kasiṇa and emerged, one determines the burning of the finger through the knowledge of higher powers, and thus the finger burns with the flame of fire produced by that attainment of the fire element. But in the case of “This is a couch,” etc., when the elder says “This is a couch,” etc., even the created things themselves say “This is a couch,” etc., in their respective places. For this is the nature of created things.

“Ekasmiṃ bhāsamānasmiṃ, sabbe bhāsanti nimmitā;

Ekasmiṃ tuṇhimāsine, sabbe tuṇhī bhavanti te”ti. (dī. ni. 2.286);

“When one speaks, all the created ones speak; When one sits silent, all of them become silent.” (Dī. Ni. 2.286)

Yasmiṃ pana vihāre mañcapīṭhādīni na paripūrenti, tattha attano ānubhāvena pūrenti, tena nimmitānaṃ avatthukaṃ vacanaṃ na hoti sabbattha mañcapīṭhādīnaṃ sabbhāvato. Sabbavihāresu ca [V 1.0164] gamanamagge samappamāṇe katvā adhiṭṭhāti. Katikasaṇṭhānādīnaṃ pana nānappakārattā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ vihāre katikavattāni visuṃ visuṃ kathāpetīti veditabbaṃ. Aniyametvā [M 1.0179] nimmitānañhi “ekasmiṃ bhāsamānasmi”ntiādidhammatā vuttā. Tathā hi ye vaṇṇavayasarīrāvayavaparikkhārakiriyāvisesādīhi niyamaṃ akatvā nimmitā honti, te aniyametvā nimmitattā iddhimatā sadisāva honti. Ṭhānanisajjādīsu bhāsitatuṇhībhāvādīsu vā yaṃ yaṃ iddhimā karoti, taṃ tadeva karonti. Sace pana nānappakāre kātukāmo hoti, keci paṭhamavaye, keci majjhimavaye, keci pacchimavaye, tathā dīghakese upaḍḍhamuṇḍe missakakese upaḍḍharattacīvare paṇḍukacīvare, padabhāṇadhammakathāsarabhaññapañhapucchanapañhavissajjanarajanapacanacīvarasibbanadhovanādīni karonte, aparepi vā nānappakāre kātukāmo hoti, tena pādakajjhānato vuṭṭhāya “ettakā bhikkhū paṭhamavayā hontū”tiādinā nayena parikammaṃ katvā puna samāpajjitvā vuṭṭhāya adhiṭṭhite adhiṭṭhānacittena saddhiṃ icchiticchitappakārāyeva honti. Puna attano vasanaṭṭhānameva āgacchatīti tehi saddhiṃ janapadakathaṃ kathento anisīditvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ veḷuvanameva paccāgacchati. Pāḷiyanti vinayapāḷiyaṃ.

In a monastery where beds, chairs, etc., are not fully provided, one fulfills them through one’s own power. Therefore, the statement that those created things lack substance is not true, since beds, chairs, etc., exist in their true nature everywhere. And in all monasteries, having made the paths of movement of equal size, one resolves upon them. However, due to the various kinds of agreements, it should be understood that the agreed-upon duties are announced separately in each respective monastery. For those created without restriction, the nature of “When one speaks,” etc., is stated. Indeed, those created without any fixed condition—such as in complexion, age, bodily features, requisites, or special actions—are just like those possessed of psychic power because they are created without restriction. Whatever a psychic power-holder does in terms of standing, sitting, speaking, or remaining silent, they do exactly that. But if one wishes to create various forms—some in early youth, some in middle age, some in old age; likewise with long hair, half-shaven heads, mixed hair, half-red robes, pale-yellow robes; or if one wishes them to perform various actions like reciting texts, teaching Dhamma, chanting, questioning, answering questions, dyeing robes, cooking, sewing robes, washing, etc.—then, having emerged from the base of absorption, one performs the preliminary work in this way: “Let so many bhikkhus be of early youth,” etc. Having performed the preliminary work, one re-enters absorption and, upon emerging, resolves. Then, together with the resolving mind, they appear exactly as desired. Again, one returns to one’s own dwelling place. Thus, while conversing with them on worldly talk, without sitting down, one returns to one’s own dwelling place, the Bamboo Grove. Pāḷiyanti—meaning in the Vinaya Pāli.

Pilindavacchattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Pilindavaccha

215. Sattame piyānanti piyāyitabbānaṃ. Manāpānanti manavaḍḍhanakānaṃ. Pilindoti panassa gottaṃ, vacchoti nāmanti ettha vuttavipariyāyenapi vadanti “pilindoti nāmaṃ, vacchoti gotta”nti. Teneva ācariyadhammapālattherena theragāthāsaṃvaṇṇanāya (theragā. aṭṭha. 1.8 pilindavacchattheragāthāvaṇṇanā) vuttaṃ – “pilindotissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu, vacchoti pana gottaṃ. Tena so aparabhāge pilindavacchoti paññāyitthā”ti. Saṃsandetvāti ekato katvā.

215. In the seventh story, piyānanti means of those who are to be loved. Manāpānanti means of those who increase satisfaction. As for “Pilinda,” it is his clan name, and “Vaccha” is his personal name—though here some say the opposite: “Pilinda is the name, Vaccha is the clan.” Thus, the Elder Teacher Dhammapāla stated in the commentary on the Theragāthā (Theragāthā Commentary 1.8, commentary on the verses of the Elder Pilindavaccha): “They gave him the name Pilinda, but his clan was Vaccha. Therefore, later he became known as Pilindavaccha.” Saṃsandetvāti means having brought together.

Satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā paṭiladdhasaddho pabbajitvāti idaṃ aṅguttarabhāṇakānaṃ kathāmaggena vuttaṃ. Apare pana bhaṇanti – anuppanneyeva amhākaṃ bhagavati sāvatthiyaṃ brāhmaṇagehe nibbattitvā pilindavacchoti paññāto saṃsāre saṃvegabahulatāya paribbājakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā cūḷagandhāraṃ nāma vijjaṃ sādhetvā ākāsacārī paracittavidū ca hutvā rājagahe lābhaggayasaggappatto paṭivasati. Atha yadā amhākaṃ bhagavā abhisambuddho hutvā anukkamena rājagahaṃ upagato, tato paṭṭhāya buddhānubhāvena [M 1.0180] tassa sā vijjā na sampajjati, atthakiccaṃ na sādheti. So cintesi – “sutaṃ kho pana metaṃ ‘ācariyapācariyānaṃ bhāsamānānaṃ yattha mahāgandhāravijjā dharati, tattha cūḷagandhāravijjā na sampajjatī’ti. Samaṇassa pana gotamassa āgatakālato [V 1.0165] paṭṭhāya nāyaṃ mama vijjā sampajjati, nissaṃsayaṃ samaṇo gotamo mahāgandhāravijjaṃ jānāti, yannūnāhaṃ taṃ payirupāsitvā tassa santike vijjaṃ pariyāpuṇeyya”nti. So bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā etadavoca – “ahaṃ, mahāsamaṇa, tava santike ekaṃ vijjaṃ pariyāpuṇitukāmo, okāsaṃ me karohī”ti. Bhagavā “tena hi pabbajā”ti āha. So “vijjāya parikammaṃ pabbajjā”ti maññamāno pabbajīti. Paravambhanavasenāti paresaṃ garahanavasena.

“Having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he gained faith and went forth”—this is the account given by the Aṅguttara reciters. Others, however, say: “Even before our Blessed One arose, having been born in a brahmin household in Sāvatthī, he was known as Pilindavaccha. Due to his great sense of urgency regarding saṃsāra, he went forth into the wanderer’s life and mastered a knowledge called Cūḷagandhāra. Becoming one who could travel through the air and know others’ thoughts, he resided in Rājagaha, having attained the highest gains and renown. Then, when our Blessed One had become fully enlightened and gradually arrived at Rājagaha, from that time onward, due to the Buddha’s power, that knowledge of his no longer succeeded, nor did it accomplish its purpose. He thought: ‘I have heard it said by teachers and their teachers that where the great Gandhāra knowledge prevails, the lesser Gandhāra knowledge does not succeed. Since the ascetic Gotama’s arrival, this knowledge of mine has not succeeded. Undoubtedly, the ascetic Gotama knows the great Gandhāra knowledge. Why don’t I attend upon him and learn that knowledge from him?’ So he approached the Blessed One and said: ‘Great ascetic, I wish to learn a knowledge from you—please grant me the opportunity.’ The Blessed One said: ‘Then go forth.’ Thinking, ‘Going forth is the preparation for the knowledge,’ he went forth. ‘Paravambhanavasena’ means by way of disparaging others, that is, by way of criticizing others.

Akakkasanti apharusaṃ. Viññāpaninti atthaviññāpaniṃ. Saccanti bhūtatthaṃ. Nābhisajeti yāya girāya aññaṃ kujjhāpanavasena na lagāpeyya, khīṇāsavo nāma evarūpameva giraṃ na bhāseyya, tasmā tamahaṃ brūmi brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

“Akakkasa” means not harsh, that is, not rough. “Viññāpanī” means explanatory, that is, making the meaning clear. “Sacca” means truthful, that is, factual. “Nābhisajeti” means does not offend, that is, with speech by which one would not provoke another to anger. One whose taints are destroyed would not speak such speech. Therefore, I say of him, “I call him a brahmin”—this is the meaning.

Anuvicinitvāti anuvicāretvā. Caṇḍikataṃ gacchantanti sīghagatiyā gacchantaṃ.

“Anuvicinitvā” means having investigated, that is, having examined. “Caṇḍikataṃ gacchantaṃ” means moving fiercely, that is, going with quick speed.

Bāhiyadārucīriyattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Bāhiya Dārucīriya.

216. Aṭṭhame ekarattivāsena gantvāti devatānubhāvena gantvā. “Buddhānubhāvenā”tipi vadanti. Evaṃ gato ca vihāraṃ pavisitvā sambahule bhikkhū bhuttapātarāse kāyālasiyavimocanatthāya abbhokāse caṅkamante disvā “kahaṃ etarahi satthā”ti pucchi. Bhikkhū “sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭho”ti vatvā taṃ pucchiṃsu – “tvaṃ pana kuto āgato”ti? Suppārakā āgatomhīti. Kadā nikkhantosīti? Hiyyo sāyaṃ nikkhantomhīti. Dūrato āgato, tava pāde dhovitvā telena makkhetvā thokaṃ vissamāhi, āgatakāle satthāraṃ dakkhissatīti. Ahaṃ, bhante, satthu vā attano vā jīvitantarāyaṃ na jānāmi, ekarattenevamhi katthaci aṭṭhatvā anisīditvā vīsayojanasatikaṃ maggaṃ āgato, satthāraṃ passitvāva vissamissāmīti. So evaṃ vatvā taramānarūpo sāvatthiṃ pavisitvā bhagavantaṃ anopamāya buddhasiriyā piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā [M 1.0181] “cirassaṃ vata me diṭṭho sammāsambuddho”ti diṭṭhaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya oṇatasarīro gantvā antaravīthiyameva pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā gopphakesu daḷhaṃ gahetvā evamāha – “desetu me, bhante, bhagavā dhammaṃ, desetu me sugato dhammaṃ, yaṃ mamassa dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti.

216. In the eighth (story), “having traveled in one night” means having traveled by the power of devas. Some also say, “by the power of the Buddha.” Having gone thus, he entered the monastery and saw many monks walking in the open air after their morning meal to relieve bodily stiffness. He asked, “Where is the Teacher now?” The monks replied, “He has entered Sāvatthī for alms.” Then they asked him, “But where have you come from?” “I have come from Suppāraka,” he said. “When did you depart?” “Yesterday evening.” “You have come from afar. Wash your feet, anoint them with oil, and rest awhile. You will see the Teacher when he returns.” “Venerable sirs, I do not know of any danger to the Teacher's life or my own. In a single night, I have traveled a hundred and twenty yojanas without stopping or sitting down anywhere. I will rest only after seeing the Teacher.” Saying this, he hurried into Sāvatthī and saw the Blessed One walking for alms with incomparable Buddha-splendor. “After so long, I see the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One!” he exclaimed. From the moment he saw him, he went forward with his body bent low. Right there in the middle of the street, he prostrated with five points touching the ground, firmly grasped the Blessed One’s ankles, and said, “Teach me the Dhamma, Blessed One! Teach me the Dhamma, Sublime One, for my long-term welfare and happiness!”

Atha naṃ satthā “akālo kho tāva, bāhiya, antaragharaṃ paviṭṭhomhi piṇḍāyā”ti paṭikkhipi[V 1.0166]. Taṃ sutvā bāhiyo, “bhante, saṃsāre saṃsarantena kabaḷīkārāhāro na no laddhapubbo, tumhākaṃ vā mayhaṃ vā jīvitantarāyaṃ na jānāmi, desetha me dhamma”nti. Satthā dutiyampi paṭikkhipiyeva. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “imassa maṃ diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya sakalasarīraṃ pītiyā nirantaraṃ ajjhotthaṭaṃ hoti, balavapītivegena dhammaṃ sutvāpi na sakkhissati paṭivijjhituṃ, majjhattupekkhā tāva tiṭṭhatu, ekaratteneva vīsayojanasataṃ maggaṃ āgatattā darathopissa balavā, sopi tāva paṭippassambhatū”ti. Tasmā dvikkhattuṃ paṭikkhipitvā tatiyaṃ yācito antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhitova “tasmātiha te, bāhiya, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ diṭṭhe diṭṭhamattaṃ bhavissatī”tiādinā (udā. 10) nayena dhammaṃ deseti. Imamatthaṃ saṃkhipitvā dassento “satthāraṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭha”ntiādimāha. Tattha antaraghareti antaravīthiyaṃ.

Then the Teacher declined him, saying, “Now is not the time, Bāhiya, I have entered the village for alms.” Hearing this, Bāhiya said, “Venerable sir, as we wander in saṃsāra, this coarse food has not been obtained by us before, and I do not know of any danger to your life or my own. Teach me the Dhamma!” The Teacher declined a second time. It seems he thought, “From the moment he saw me, his entire body has been continuously overwhelmed by joy. Due to the strong force of joy, even if he hears the Dhamma, he will not be able to penetrate it. Let equanimity first be established. Having traveled a hundred and twenty yojanas in a single night, his fatigue is also strong. Let that too subside first.” Thus, after declining twice, when asked a third time, the Teacher, standing right there in the middle of the street, taught him the Dhamma, saying, “Therefore, Bāhiya, you should train thus: ‘In the seen, there will be only the seen…’” (Udāna 1.10). Summarizing this meaning, the text says, “The Teacher had entered for alms…” Here, “in the village” (antaragharaṃ) means “in the middle of the street” (antaravīthiyaṃ).

Aparipuṇṇapattacīvaratāya pattacīvaraṃ pariyesantoti so kira vīsativassasahassāni samaṇadhammaṃ karonto “bhikkhunā nāma attano paccaye labhitvā aññaṃ anoloketvā sayameva bhuñjituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ekabhikkhussapi pattena vā cīvarena vā saṅgahaṃ nākāsi. Tenassa “iddhimayapattacīvaraṃ na uppajjissatī”ti ñatvā ehibhikkhubhāvena pabbajjaṃ na adāsi. Tāvadeva ca pabbajjaṃ yācito “paripuṇṇaṃ te pattacīvara”nti pucchitvā “aparipuṇṇa”nti vutte “tena hi pattacīvaraṃ pariyesāhī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Tasmā so pattacīvaraṃ pariyesanto saṅkāraṭṭhānato coḷakhaṇḍāni saṃkaḍḍhati.

“Because he sought a bowl and robe due to the incompleteness of his own,” means that for twenty thousand years he practiced the ascetic life, thinking, “A monk, having obtained his own requisites, should not look to others, but should use them himself.” Thus, he did not help even a single monk with a bowl or robe. Knowing that “a bowl and robe of miraculous power will not arise for him,” he did not grant ordination by the “Come, monk” formula. When he was asked for ordination right then, he asked, “Is your bowl and robe complete?” Upon being told “It is incomplete,” he said, “Then go and seek a bowl and robe,” and departed. Therefore, he, seeking a bowl and robe, gathered scraps of cloth from a rubbish heap.

Sahassamapīti paricchedavacanaṃ. Ekasahassaṃ dvesahassānīti evaṃ sahassena ce paricchinnā gāthā honti, tā ca anatthapadasaṃhitā ākāsavaṇṇapabbatavaṇṇādīni pakāsakehi anibbānadīpakehi anatthakehi padehi saṃhitā yāva bahukā honti, tāva pāpikā evāti attho[M 1.0182]. Ekaṃ gāthāpadaṃ seyyoti “appamādo amatapadaṃ…pe… yathā matā”ti (dha. pa. 21) evarūpā ekagāthāpi seyyoti attho.

“Even a thousand” (sahassamapi) is a term denoting limitation. Whether one thousand, two thousand, or thus measured by thousands, if verses are defined by such numbers, yet are composed of meaningless words—descriptions of the color of the sky, the color of mountains, and the like—expressing pointless things and not illuminating Nibbāna, they are truly evil for as long as they are numerous—this is the meaning. “A single verse is better” means that even one verse such as “Heedfulness is the path to the Deathless… as are the dead” (Dhp. 21) is superior—this is the meaning.

Kumārakassapattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Kumāra Kassapa.

217. Navame ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ sampattiṃ anubhavamānoti sāvakabodhiyā niyatatāya puññasambhārassa ca sātisayattā vinipātaṃ agantvā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ devesu ca manussesu ca sampattiṃ anubhavamāno. “Ekissā kuladārikāya kucchimhi uppanno”ti vatvā tamevassa uppannabhāvaṃ [V 1.0167] mūlato paṭṭhāya dassetuṃ – “sā cā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha sāti kuladārikā. Ca-saddo byatirekattho. Tena vuccamānaṃ visesaṃ jotayati. Kulagharanti patikulagehaṃ. Gabbhanimittanti gabbhassa saṇṭhitabhāvaviggahaṃ. Satipi visākhāya sāvatthivāsikulapariyāpannatte tassā tattha padhānabhāvadassanatthaṃ “visākhañcā”tiādi vuttaṃ yathā “brāhmaṇā āgatā, vāsiṭṭhopi āgato”ti. Bhagavatā evaṃ gahitanāmattāti yojanā. Yasmā rājaputtā loke “kumārā”ti voharīyanti, ayañca rañño kittimaputto, tasmā āha – “rañño…pe… sañjāniṃsū”ti.

217. In the ninth [story], 'experiencing prosperity for one buddha-interval' means that due to the certainty of enlightenment as a disciple and the excellence of his accumulation of merit, without going to a lower realm, he experienced prosperity among gods and humans for one buddha-interval. To show his birth from the very beginning, after saying, 'He was born in the womb of a certain maiden of good family,' it is said, 'And she...' and so on. Therein, 'sā' refers to the maiden of good family. The word 'ca' has the meaning of distinction; thus, it illuminates the specific point being mentioned. 'Kulaghara' means the husband's family home. 'Gabbhanimitta' refers to the form indicating the established state of pregnancy. Although Visākhā was included among the families residing in Sāvatthī, to show her prominence there, it is said, 'Visākhā and...'—just as it is said, 'Brahmins have come, and Vāsiṭṭha has also come.' The construction is: 'because her name was thus taken by the Blessed One.' Since princes in the world are called 'kumāras,' and this was the king’s adopted son, therefore it is said, 'The king’s... they recognized.'

Pañcadasa pañhe abhisaṅkharitvāti “bhikkhu, bhikkhu, ayaṃ vammiko rattiṃ dhūpāyati, divā pajjalatī”tiādinā vammikasutte (ma. ni. 1.249) āgatanayena pañcadasa pañhe abhisaṅkharitvā. Pāyāsiraññoti “natthi paraloko, natthi sattā opapātikā, natthi sukatadukkaṭānaṃ kammānaṃ phalaṃ vipāko”ti (dī. ni. 2.410, 412) evaṃladdhikassa pāyāsirājassa. Rājā hi tadā anabhisitto hutvā pasenadinā kosalena dinnasetabyanagaraṃ ajjhāvasanto imaṃ diṭṭhiṃ gaṇhi. Pañcadasahi pañhehi paṭimaṇḍetvāti “taṃ kiṃ maññasi, rājañña, ime candimasūriyā imasmiṃ vā loke parasmiṃ vā devā vā te manussā”ti evamādīhi (dī. ni. 2.411) pañcadasahi pañhehi paṭimaṇḍitaṃ katvā. Suttanteti pāyāsisuttante (dī. ni. 2.406 ādayo).

'Having prepared fifteen questions' means having prepared fifteen questions in the manner that appears in the Vammika Sutta (Majjhima Nikāya 1.249), beginning with, 'Monk, monk, this ant-hill smokes by night and blazes by day.' 'Of King Pāyāsi' means of King Pāyāsi, who held such a doctrine as, 'There is no other world, there are no spontaneously reborn beings, there is no fruit or result of good and bad deeds' (Dīgha Nikāya 2.410, 412). For at that time, the king, not yet consecrated, was dwelling in the city of Setavyā, which had been given by Pasenadi Kosala, and had adopted this view. 'Having embellished with fifteen questions' means having made it embellished with fifteen questions, such as, 'What do you think, noble king, these moon and sun, are they in this world or another? Are they gods or humans?' and so on (Dīgha Nikāya 2.411). 'In the Suttanta' means in the Pāyāsi Suttanta (Dīgha Nikāya 2.406 ff.).

Mahākoṭṭhikattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Mahākoṭṭhika

218. Dasamaṃ uttānatthameva.

218. The tenth is of obvious meaning.

Tatiyaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Third Chapter on the Foremost is completed.

(14) 4. Catutthaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā

(14) 4. Commentary on the Fourth Chapter on the Foremost

Ānandattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Ānanda

219-223. Catutthavaggassa [V 1.0168][M 1.0183] paṭhame heṭṭhā vuttappamāṇanti heṭṭhā koṇḍaññattherassa vatthumhi “tassa dhurapattāni navutihatthāni honti, kesaraṃ tiṃsahatthaṃ, kaṇṇikā dvādasahatthā, pādena patiṭṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ ekādasahattha”nti evaṃ vuttappamāṇaṃ. Rañño pesesīti paccantassa kupitabhāvaṃ ārocetvā pesesi. Theragāthāsaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ (theragā. aṭṭha. 2.1016 ānandattheragāthāvaṇṇanā) pana “paccantassa kupitabhāvaṃ rañño anārocetvā sayameva taṃ vūpasamesi, taṃ sutvā rājā tuṭṭhamānaso puttaṃ pakkosāpetvā ‘varaṃ te, sumana, dammi, gaṇhāhī’ti āhā”ti vuttaṃ. Na metaṃ cittaṃ atthīti mama evarūpaṃ cittaṃ natthi. Avañjhanti atucchaṃ. Aññaṃ varehīti aññaṃ patthehi, aññaṃ gaṇhāhīti vuttaṃ hoti. Udakaṃ adhiṭṭhāyāti “udakaṃ hotū”ti adhiṭṭhahitvā. Gatenāti gamanena. Na āmisacakkhukāti cīvarādipaccayasaṅkhātaṃ āmisaṃ na olokenti.

219-223. In the first [story] of the fourth chapter, 'the measurements stated below' means the measurements stated as follows in the story of the Elder Koṇḍañña below: 'His yoke was ninety hands long, the mane thirty hands, the central knob twelve hands, and the place where it stood on its base eleven hands.' 'He sent to the king' means he sent [a messenger] to the king after reporting the angered state of the border region. However, in the commentary on the Theragāthā (Theragāthā Aṭṭhakathā 2.1016, the commentary on the Elder Ānanda's verses), it is said: 'Without reporting the angered state of the border region to the king, he himself pacified it. Hearing this, the king, with a pleased mind, had his son summoned and said, “Sumana, I grant you a boon, take it.”' 'That thought is not mine' means 'I do not have such a thought.' 'Not futile' means 'not empty.' 'Choose another' means 'desire another, take another,' it is said. 'Having resolved on water' means having resolved, 'Let there be water.' 'By going' means by the act of going. 'Not with an eye for material things' means they do not look for material things, reckoned as robes and other requisites.

Vasanaṭṭhānasabhāgeyevāti vasanaṭṭhānasamīpeyeva. Ekantavallabhoti upaṭṭhākaṭṭhāne ekantena vallabho. Etassevāti etasseva bhikkhussa. Dvejjhakathā na hontīti dvidhābhūtakathā na honti, anekantikakathā na hontīti vuttaṃ hoti. Anibaddhāti aniyatā. Lohitena galantenāti itthambhūtakkhāne karaṇavacanaṃ, galantena lohitena yuttoti attho. Anvāsattoti anugato. Uṭṭhehi, āvuso ānanda, uṭṭhehi, āvuso ānandāti turite idamāmeḍitavacanaṃ. Duvidhena udakenāti sītudakena uṇhudakena ca. Tividhena dantakaṭṭhenāti khuddakaṃ mahantaṃ majjhimanti evaṃ tippakārena dantakaṭṭhena. Nava vāre anupariyāyatīti satthari pakkosante paṭivacanadānāya thinamiddhavinodanatthaṃ navakkhattuṃ anupariyāyati. Tenevāha – “evañhissa ahosī”tiādi. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

'In the very region of the dwelling place' means in the very proximity of the dwelling place. 'Exceedingly beloved' means exceedingly beloved in the position of attendant. 'Of this very one' means of this very monk. 'There are no ambiguous talks' means there are no talks that are twofold, that is, there are no inconclusive talks, it is said. 'Unbound' means 'unfixed.' 'With dripping blood' is an instrumental case denoting circumstance; the meaning is 'endowed with dripping blood.' 'Followed' means 'gone along with.' 'Arise, friend Ānanda, arise, friend Ānanda' is a repeated expression spoken urgently. 'With two kinds of water' means with cold water and with hot water. 'With three kinds of tooth-sticks' means with small, large, and medium, thus with three sorts of tooth-sticks. 'He circles nine times' means that when the Teacher summons him, he circles nine times in order to give a reply and to dispel sloth and torpor. Therefore, it is said: 'Thus it was for him,' and so on. The remainder here is easily understood.

Uruvelakassapattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Uruvelakassapa

224. Dutiye [V 1.0169] yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ vitthārato vinayapāḷiyaṃ āgatameva.

224. In the second [story], what should be said has already come in detail in the Vinaya Pāḷi.

Kāḷudāyittheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Kāḷudāyī

225. Tatiye [M 1.0184] gamanākappanti gamanākāraṃ. Sesamettha uttānameva.

225. In the third [story], 'gamanākappaṃ' means the manner of going. The rest here is obvious.

Bākulattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Bākula

226. Catutthe nirābādhānanti ābādharahitānaṃ. Yathā “dvāvīsati dvattiṃsā”tiādimhi vattabbe “bāvīsati bāttiṃsā”tiādīni vuccanti, evamevaṃ dve kulāni assāti dvikulo, dvekuloti vā vattabbe bākuloti vuttanti āha – “bākuloti dvīsu kulesu vaḍḍhitattā evaṃladdhanāmo”ti. Upayogenāti ānubhāvena. Phāsukakāleti arogakāle. Gadduhanamattampīti goduhanamattampi kālaṃ. Idha pana na sakalo goduhanakkhaṇo adhippeto, atha kho gāviṃ thane gahetvā ekakhīrabinduduhanakālamattaṃ adhippetaṃ. Ārogyasālanti āturānaṃ arogabhāvakaraṇatthāya katasālaṃ.

226. In the fourth [story], 'of the unafflicted' means 'of those without affliction.' Just as when 'dvāvīsati dvattiṃsā' (twenty-two, thirty-two) and so forth should be said, 'bāvīsati bāttiṃsā' (twenty-two, thirty-two) and so forth are said, so too, what should be said as 'dvikulo' or 'dvekulo' (meaning 'of two families') is said as 'Bākulo.' Thus it is said: 'He was named Bākula because he was raised in two families.' 'By application' means 'by his power.' 'At a comfortable time' means 'at a time of health.' 'Even for the time of milking' means 'even for the time it takes to milk a cow.' Here, however, not the entire duration of milking a cow is intended, but rather the time it takes to grasp a cow's udder and milk a single drop of milk. 'A hall of health' means 'a hall built for the purpose of making the sick healthy.'

Nimujjanummujjanavasenāti jāṇuppamāṇe udake thokaṃyeva nimujjanummujjanavasena. Chaḍḍetvā palāyīti macchassa mukhasamīpeyeva chaḍḍetvā palāyi. Dārakassa tejenāti dārakassa puññatejena. Māriyamānāva marantīti daṇḍādīhi pothetvā māriyamānāva maranti, na jālena baddhatāmattena amāriyamānā. Nīhaṭamattova matoti nīhaṭakkhaṇeyeva mato. Tenassa māraṇatthaṃ upakkamo na kato, yena upakkamena dārakassa ābādho siyā. Tanti macchaṃ. Sakalamevāti avikalameva paripuṇṇāvayavameva. Na keḷāyatīti na nandati, kismiñci na maññati. Piṭṭhito phālentīti dārakassa puññatejena piṭṭhito phālentī. Bheriṃ carāpetvāti “puttaṃ labhi”nti ugghosanavasena bheriṃ carāpetvā. Pakatiṃ ācikkhīti attano puttabhāvaṃ kathesi. Kucchiyā dhāritattā amātā kātuṃ na sakkāti jananībhāvato amātā kātuṃ na sakkā. Macchaṃ gaṇhantāpīti macchaṃ vikkiṇitvā gaṇhantāpi. Tathā gaṇhantā ca tappariyāpannaṃ sabbaṃ gaṇhanti nāmāti āha – “vakkayakanādīni bahi katvā gaṇhantā nāma natthī”ti. Ayampi amātā kātuṃ na sakkāti dinnaputtabhāvato na sakkā.

'By way of sinking and emerging' means by way of sinking and emerging just a little in knee-deep water. 'Having thrown, she fled' means having thrown him right near the fish's mouth, she fled. 'By the boy's power' means by the boy's power of merit. 'They die only when being killed' means they die only when being killed by being beaten with sticks and the like, not while not being killed merely by being caught in a net. 'Dead as soon as it was taken out' means dead at the very moment it was taken out. Therefore, no attempt was made to kill it, by which attempt the boy might have been harmed. 'It' means the fish. 'Whole' means not defective, with all its parts complete. 'Does not play' means does not rejoice, is not conceited about anything. 'They split it from the back' means due to the boy's power of merit, they split it from the back. 'Having had a drum beaten' means having had a drum beaten by way of an announcement, 'A son has been obtained!' 'She told the true state of affairs' means she spoke of his being her son. 'Because she had carried him in her womb, she cannot be made a non-mother' means because of her motherhood, she cannot be made a non-mother. 'Even those who take the fish' means even those who take it by buying the fish. And those who take it thus take everything pertaining to it; thus it is said: 'There are none who take it after putting the guts and so on outside.' 'This one too cannot be made a non-mother' means she cannot because of her status as the adoptive mother.

Sobhitattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Sobhita

227. Pañcamaṃ [V 1.0170][M 1.0185] uttānatthameva.

227. The fifth is of obvious meaning.

Upālittheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Upāli

228. Chaṭṭhe bhārukacchakavatthunti aññataro kira bhārukacchadesavāsī bhikkhu supinante purāṇadutiyikāya methunaṃ dhammaṃ paṭisevitvā “assamaṇo ahaṃ vibbhamissāmī”ti bhārukacchaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge āyasmantaṃ upāliṃ passitvā etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Āyasmā upāli, evamāha – “anāpatti, āvuso, supinantenā”ti. Yasmā supinante avisayattā evaṃ hoti. Tasmā upālitthero bhagavatā avinicchitapubbampi imaṃ vatthuṃ nayaggāhena evaṃ vinicchini. Gahapatino dve dārakā honti putto ca bhāgineyyo ca. Atha so gahapati gilāno hutvā āyasmantaṃ ajjukaṃ etadavoca – “imaṃ, bhante, okāsaṃ yo imesaṃ dārakānaṃ saddho hoti pasanno, tassa ācikkheyyāsī”ti. Tena ca samayena tassa ca gahapatino bhāgineyyo saddho hoti pasanno. Athāyasmā ajjuko taṃ okāsaṃ tassa dārakassa ācikkhi. So tena sāpateyyena kuṭumbañca saṇṭhapesi, dānañca paṭṭhapesi. Atha tassa gahapatino putto āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “ko nu kho, bhante ānanda, pituno dāyajjo putto vā bhāgineyyo vā”ti. Putto kho, āvuso, pituno dāyajjoti. Āyasmā, bhante, ayyo ajjuko amhākaṃ sāpateyyaṃ amhākaṃ methunakassa ācikkhīti. Assamaṇo, āvuso, so ajjukoti. Athāyasmā ajjuko āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “dehi me, āvuso ānanda, vinicchaya”nti. Te ubhopi upālittherassa santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Athāyasmā upāli, āyasmantaṃ ānandaṃ etadavoca – “yo nu kho, āvuso ānanda, sāmikena ‘imaṃ okāsaṃ itthannāmassa ācikkhā’ti vutto, tassa ācikkhati, kiṃ so āpajjatī”ti? Na, bhante, kiñci āpajjati antamaso dukkaṭamatthampīti. Ayaṃ, āvuso, āyasmā ajjuko sāmikena “imaṃ okāsaṃ itthannāmassa ācikkhā”ti vutto tassa ācikkhati, anāpatti, āvuso, āyasmato ajjukassāti. Bhagavā taṃ sutvā “sukathitaṃ, bhikkhave, upālinā”ti vatvā [M 1.0186] sādhukāramadāsi, taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Kumārakassapavatthu (a. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.217) pana heṭṭhā āgatameva.

228. In the sixth, the story of the one from Bhārukaccha: It is said that a certain monk residing in the Bhārukaccha region, while dreaming, engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife. Thinking, 'I am no longer an ascetic, I will disrobe,' he was going to Bhārukaccha and on the way saw Venerable Upāli and told him about this matter. Venerable Upāli said, 'Friend, there is no offense in a dream.' This is because in a dream, it is not within one's sphere of control. Therefore, even though the Blessed One had not previously decided this case, the Elder Upāli decided it by grasping the principle. A householder had two boys: a son and a nephew. Then that householder, having fallen ill, said this to Venerable Ajjuka: 'Venerable sir, to whichever of these boys is faithful and confident, you should point out this location.' At that time, the householder's nephew was faithful and confident. So Venerable Ajjuka pointed out that location to that boy. With that property, he established the household and instituted charitable giving. Then the householder’s son said this to Venerable Ānanda: 'Venerable Ānanda, who is the father's heir, the son or the nephew?' 'Friend, the son is the father's heir.' 'Venerable sir, the venerable Ajjuka has pointed out our property to our kinsman!' 'Friend, that Ajjuka is no ascetic.' Then Venerable Ajjuka said to Venerable Ānanda, 'Friend Ānanda, give me a judgment.' Both of them went to the Elder Upāli. Then the Elder Upāli said to Venerable Ānanda, 'Friend Ānanda, if someone is told by the owner, "Point out this location to so-and-so," and he points it out to him, what offense does he commit?' 'Venerable sir, he commits no offense, not even a dukkaṭa.' 'Friend, this Venerable Ajjuka was told by the owner, "Point out this location to so-and-so," and he pointed it out to him. There is no offense for Venerable Ajjuka.' Having heard that, the Blessed One said, 'Well spoken, monks, by Upāli,' and gave his approval. This was said with reference to that. The story of Kumārakassapa (A. Ni. Aṭṭha. 1.1.217), however, has already been presented below.

Channaṃ khattiyānanti bhaddiyo sakyarājā anuruddho ānando bhagu kimilo devadattoti imesaṃ [V 1.0171] channaṃ khattiyānaṃ. Pasādhakoti maṇḍayitā. Pāḷiyanti saṅghabhedakkhandhakapāḷiyanti (cūḷava. 330 ādayo).

'Of the six khattiyas' refers to these six khattiyas: Bhaddiya the Sakyan king, Anuruddha, Ānanda, Bhagu, Kimila, and Devadatta. 'Pasādhako' means an adorner. 'Pāḷiyaṃ' refers to the Pāli text of the Saṅghabhedakkhandhaka (Chapter on Schism in the Saṅgha) in the Cūḷavagga (beginning at 330, etc.).

Nandakattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Nandaka

229. Sattame ekasamodhāneti ekasmiṃ samodhāne, ekasmiṃ sannipāteti attho. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

229. In the seventh, 'ekasamodhāne' means in a single gathering, in a single assembly—this is the meaning. The rest is easily understood.

Nandattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Nanda

230. Aṭṭhame na taṃ catusampajaññavasena aparicchinditvā oloketīti sātthakasappāyagocaraasammohasampajaññasaṅkhātānaṃ catunnaṃ sampajaññānaṃ vasena aparicchinditvā taṃ disaṃ na oloketi. So hi āyasmā “yamevāhaṃ indriyesu aguttadvārataṃ nissāya sāsane anabhiratiādivippakārappatto, tameva suṭṭhu niggahessāmī”ti ussāhajāto balavahirottappo, tattha ca katādhikārattā indriyasaṃvaro ukkaṃsapāramippatto catusampajaññaṃ amuñcitvāva sabbadisaṃ āloketi. Vuttañcetaṃ bhagavatā –

230. In the eighth, 'he does not look without determining it by means of the fourfold clear comprehension' means he does not look in that direction without first determining it through the four kinds of clear comprehension, which are known as purpose, suitability, domain, and non-delusion. For that venerable one, stirred by effort and possessing strong moral shame and fear of wrongdoing, thought thus: 'Whatever harm I have incurred due to unguarded sense-doors—such as dissatisfaction with the teaching—I will thoroughly restrain that very thing.' Having devoted himself diligently to that and attained the perfection of sense restraint, he surveys all directions without abandoning the fourfold clear comprehension. This was said by the Blessed One:

“Sace, bhikkhave, nandassa puratthimā disā āloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā nando puratthimaṃ disaṃ āloketi ‘evaṃ me puratthimaṃ disaṃ ālokayato nābhijjhādomanassā pāpakā akusalā dhammā anvāsavissantī’ti. Itiha tattha sampajāno hoti. Sace, bhikkhave, nandassa pacchimā disā, uttarā disā, dakkhiṇā disā, uddhaṃ, adho, anudisā anuviloketabbā hoti, sabbaṃ cetaso samannāharitvā nando anudisaṃ anuviloketi ‘evaṃ me anudisaṃ anuvilokayato…pe… sampajāno hotī’”ti (a. ni. 8.9).

"Monks, if Nanda should look toward the eastern direction, he does so with his mind fully collected, thinking: 'As I look toward the eastern direction, no covetousness or displeasure, no evil, unwholesome qualities will flow in.' Thus he is clearly comprehending in that matter. If, monks, Nanda should look toward the western direction, the northern direction, the southern direction, upward, downward, or the intermediate directions, he surveys the intermediate directions with his mind fully collected, thinking: 'As I survey the intermediate directions in this way… he is clearly comprehending.'" (A.N. 8.9)

Abhisekagehapavesanaāvāhamaṅgalesu [M 1.0187] vattamānesūti idha tīṇi maṅgalāni vuttāni, vinayaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “taṃ divasameva nandakumārassa kesavissajjanaṃ, paṭṭabandho, gharamaṅgalaṃ, chattamaṅgalaṃ, āvāhamaṅgalanti pañca maṅgalāni hontī”ti vuttaṃ. Tattha kulamariyādavasena kesoropanaṃ kesavissajjanaṃ. Yuvarājapaṭṭabandhanaṃ paṭṭabandho. Abhinavagharappavesanamaho gharamaṅgalaṃ. Vivāhakaraṇamaho āvāhamaṅgalaṃ. Yuvarājachattamaho chattamaṅgalaṃ.

Regarding 'while the consecration, house-entering, and marriage ceremonies were occurring'—here, three auspicious ceremonies are mentioned. However, in the Vinaya commentary, it is said: 'On that very day, there were five auspicious ceremonies for Prince Nanda: the hair-cutting, the head-binding, the house-warming ceremony, the parasol ceremony, and the marriage ceremony.' Among these: the shaving of hair according to family tradition is the hair-cutting. The tying of the crown prince’s diadem is the head-binding. The grand festival of entering the new house is the house-warming ceremony. The grand marriage celebration is the marriage ceremony. The grand ceremony of the crown prince's parasol is the parasol ceremony.

Nandakumāraṃ [V 1.0172] abhisekamaṅgalaṃ na tathā pīḷesi, yathā janapadakalyāṇiyā vuttavacananti ajjhāharitabbaṃ. Tadeva pana vacanaṃ sarūpato dassetuṃ – “pattaṃ ādāya gamanakāle”tiādi vuttaṃ. Janapadakalyāṇīti janapadamhi kalyāṇī uttamā cha sarīradosarahitā pañca kalyāṇasamannāgatā. Sā hi yasmā nātidīghā nātirassā nātikisā nātithūlā nātikāḷī nāccodātāti atikkantā mānusavaṇṇaṃ, asampattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ, tasmā cha sarīradosarahitā. Chavikalyāṇaṃ maṃsakalyāṇaṃ nhārukalyāṇaṃ aṭṭhikalyāṇaṃ vayakalyāṇanti imehi pana kalyāṇehi samannāgatattā pañca kalyāṇasamannāgatā nāma. Tassā hi āgantukobhāsakiccaṃ natthi, attano sarīrobhāseneva dvādasahatthe ṭhāne ālokaṃ karoti, piyaṅgusāmā vā hoti suvaṇṇasāmā vā, ayamassā chavikalyāṇatā. Cattāro panassā hatthapādā mukhapariyosānañca lākhārasaparikammakataṃ viya rattapavāḷarattakambalasadisaṃ hoti, ayamassā maṃsakalyāṇatā. Vīsati pana nakhapattāni maṃsato amuttaṭṭhāne lākhārasapūritāni viya, muttaṭṭhāne khīradhārāsadisāni honti, ayamassā nhārukalyāṇatā. Dvattiṃsa dantā suphusitā sudhotavajirapanti viya khāyanti, ayamassā aṭṭhikalyāṇatā. Vīsaṃvassasatikāpi samānā soḷasavassuddesikā viya hoti nippalitena, ayamassā vayakalyāṇatā. Iti imehi pañcahi kalyāṇehi samannāgatattā “janapadakalyāṇī”ti vuccati. Tuvaṭanti sīghaṃ.

It should be supplied that the consecration ceremony for Prince Nanda did not trouble him as much as the words spoken by the Beauty of the Land. But to present that very statement in its exact form, it was said, "Taking the bowl at the time of departure," etc. "Beauty of the Land" means the most excellent woman in the region, free from six bodily defects and endowed with five beauties. For she was neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too fat, neither too dark nor too fair—thus surpassing human complexion yet not attaining divine complexion. Therefore, she was free from the six bodily defects. And because she was endowed with five beauties—beauty of skin, flesh, sinews, bones, and youth—she was called "endowed with five beauties." For her, there was no need for an external light; her own body radiated light up to a distance of twelve cubits. She was either the color of a priyangu flower or like refined gold—this was her beauty of skin. Her four limbs and the area around her mouth were as if treated with lacquer, like red coral or red blankets—this was her beauty of flesh. Her twenty nail-plates were as if filled with lacquer where they did not emerge from the flesh, and where they emerged, they resembled streams of milk—this was her beauty of sinews. Her thirty-two teeth were perfectly set and shone like a row of well-washed diamonds—this was her beauty of bones. Even at the age of one hundred and twenty years, she appeared like a girl of sixteen, without gray hairs—this was her beauty of youth. Thus, because she was endowed with these five beauties, she was called "the Beauty of the Land." 'Tuvaṭaṃ' means quickly.

Imasmiṃ ṭhāne nivattessati, imasmiṃ ṭhāne nivattessatīti cintentamevāti so kira tathāgate gāravavasena “pattaṃ vo, bhante, gaṇhathā”ti vattuṃ avisahanto evaṃ cintesi – “sopānasīse pattaṃ gaṇhissatī”ti[M 1.0188]. Satthā tasmimpi ṭhāne na gaṇhi. Itaro “sopānapādamūle gaṇhissatī”ti cintesi. Satthā tatthāpi na gaṇhi. Itaro “rājaṅgaṇe gaṇhissatī”ti cintesi. Satthā tatthāpi na gaṇhi. Evaṃ “idha gaṇhissati, ettha gaṇhissatī”ti cintentameva satthā vihāraṃ netvā pabbājesi.

“In this place he will turn back, in this place he will turn back”—thinking thus, it is said that out of respect for the Tathāgata, he could not bring himself to say, “Take your bowl, venerable sir,” and instead thought, “He will take the bowl at the top of the staircase.” The Teacher did not take it there either. The other thought, “He will take it at the foot of the staircase.” The Teacher did not take it there either. The other thought, “He will take it in the royal courtyard.” The Teacher did not take it there either. Thus, while he kept thinking, “Here he will take it, here he will take it,” the Teacher led him to the monastery and gave him the going forth.

Mahākappinattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Mahākappina

231. Navame sutavittakoti dhammassavanapiyo. Paṭihārakassāti dovārikassa. Saccakārenāti saccakiriyāya. Satthā “uppalavaṇṇā āgacchatū”ti cintesi. Therī āgantvā sabbā pabbājetvā bhikkhunīupassayaṃ gatāti idaṃ aṅguttarabhāṇakānaṃ kathāmaggaṃ dassentena vuttaṃ. Teneva dhammapadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.mahākappinattheravatthu) vuttaṃ –

231. In the ninth story, ‘sutavitta’ means one who delights in hearing the Dhamma. ‘Paṭihārakassa’ means ‘of the gatekeeper.’ ‘Saccakārena’ means ‘by an act of truth.’ The Teacher thought, ‘Let Uppalavaṇṇā come.’ This, that the elder nun came, ordained them all, and went to the bhikkhunī monastery, was stated by the reciters of the Aṅguttara Nikāya to show the course of the story. Therefore, it is stated in the Dhammapada Commentary (Dhammapada Aṭṭhakathā, Mahākappinattheravatthu):

“Tā [V 1.0173] satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsu. Evaṃ kira vutte satthā uppalavaṇṇāya āgamanaṃ cintesīti ekacce vadanti. Satthā pana tā upāsikāyo āha – ‘sāvatthiṃ gantvā bhikkhunīupassaye pabbājethā’ti. Tā anupubbena janapadacārikaṃ caramānā antarāmagge mahājanena abhihaṭasakkārasammānā padasāva vīsayojanasatikaṃ maggaṃ gantvā bhikkhunīupassaye pabbajitvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsū”ti.

“Having paid homage to the Teacher, they stood to one side and requested ordination. When this was said, it is said the Teacher thought of Uppalavaṇṇā’s arrival—so some say. But the Teacher told those laywomen, ‘Go to Sāvatthī and be ordained in the bhikkhunī monastery.’ Traveling gradually through the countryside, honored and revered by the people along the way, they walked on foot the one hundred and twenty yojana path to the bhikkhunī monastery, where they were ordained and attained arahantship.”

Dhammapītīti dhammapāyako, dhammaṃ pivantoti attho. Dhammo ca nāmesa na sakkā bhājanena yāguādīni viya pātuṃ, navavidhaṃ pana lokuttaradhammaṃ nāmakāyena phusanto ārammaṇato sacchikaronto pariññābhisamayādīhi dukkhādīni ariyasaccāni paṭivijjhanto dhammaṃ pivati nāma. Sukhaṃ setīti desanāmattametaṃ, catūhipi iriyāpathehi sukhaṃ viharatīti attho. Vippasannenāti anāvilena nirupakkilesena. Ariyappavediteti buddhādīhi ariyehi pavedite satipaṭṭhānādibhede bodhipakkhiyadhamme. Sadā ramatīti evarūpo dhammapīti vippasannena cetasā viharanto paṇḍiccena samannāgato sadā ramati abhiramati. Bāhitapāpattā “brāhmaṇā”ti theraṃ ālapati.

‘Dhammapīti’ means one who drinks the Dhamma—that is, one who imbibes the Dhamma. This Dhamma cannot be drunk from a vessel like gruel and other things; rather, one is said to ‘drink’ the Dhamma by contacting the ninefold supramundane Dhamma with the mental body, by realizing it as an object, and by penetrating the noble truths such as suffering through full understanding, realization, and so on. ‘Sukhaṃ seti’ (dwells happily) is merely an expression; the meaning is that one abides happily in all four postures. ‘Vippasannena’ (with a serene mind) means with an unclouded and undefiled mind. ‘Ariyappavedite’ (proclaimed by the noble ones) refers to the factors of enlightenment, such as the various kinds of foundations of mindfulness, proclaimed by the noble ones like the Buddha. ‘Sadā ramati’ (always delights) means such a one who delights in the Dhamma, dwelling with a serene mind and endowed with wisdom, always rejoices and delights. Because he has cast out evil, he addresses the elder as ‘brāhmaṇa.’”

Sāgatattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Sāgata

232. Dasame [M 1.0189] chabbaggiyānaṃ vacanenāti kosambikā kira upāsakā āyasmantaṃ sāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā abhivādetvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā evamāhaṃsu – “kiṃ, bhante, ayyānaṃ dullabhañca manāpañca, kiṃ paṭiyādemā”ti? Evaṃ vutte chabbaggiyā bhikkhū kosambike upāsake etadavocuṃ – “atthāvuso kāpotikā, nāma pasannā bhikkhūnaṃ dullabhā ca manāpā ca, taṃ paṭiyādethā”ti. Atha kosambikā upāsakā ghare ghare kāpotikaṃ pasannaṃ paṭiyādetvā āyasmantaṃ sāgataṃ piṇḍāya carantaṃ disvā etadavocuṃ – “pivatu, bhante, ayyo sāgato kāpotikaṃ pasannaṃ, pivatu, bhante, ayyo sāgato kāpotikaṃ pasanna”nti. Athāyasmā sāgato ghare ghare kāpotikaṃ pasannaṃ pivitvā nagaramhā nikkhamanto nagaradvāre pati. Tena vuttaṃ – “chabbaggiyānaṃ vacanena sabbagehesu kāpotikaṃ pasannaṃ paṭiyādetvā”tiādi. Tattha kāpotikā nāma kapotapādasamānavaṇṇā rattobhāsā. Pasannāti surāmaṇḍassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vinaye samuṭṭhitanti surāpānasikkhāpade (pāci. 326 ādayo) āgataṃ.

232. In the tenth story, regarding the statement of the monks of the group of six: It is said that the lay followers of Kosambī approached the Venerable Sāgata, paid homage, stood to one side, and said: “What, venerable sir, is difficult to obtain and agreeable to the venerable ones? What should we prepare?” When this was said, the monks of the group of six addressed the lay followers of Kosambī: “Friends, there is a clear liquor called kāpotikā, which is difficult to obtain and agreeable to the monks. Prepare that.” Then the lay followers of Kosambī prepared kāpotikā clear liquor in every house and, seeing the Venerable Sāgata walking for alms, said: “Venerable Sāgata, please drink the kāpotikā clear liquor. Venerable Sāgata, please drink the kāpotikā clear liquor.” Then the Venerable Sāgata drank the kāpotikā clear liquor in every house and, upon leaving the city, collapsed at the city gate. Hence it is said: “At the word of the monks of the group of six, they prepared kāpotikā clear liquor in all the houses,” and so on. Here, kāpotikā refers to a drink with a reddish hue, the color of a pigeon’s foot. Pasannā is a term for the clear essence of fermented liquor. This originates in the Vinaya, in the training rule against drinking alcohol (Pācittiya 51).

Rādhattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Rādha

233. Ekādasame [V 1.0174] satthā sāriputtattherassa saññaṃ adāsīti brāhmaṇaṃ pabbājetuṃ saññaṃ adāsi, āṇāpesīti vuttaṃ hoti. Bhagavā kira taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ pabbajjaṃ alabhitvā kisaṃ lūkhaṃ dubbaṇṇaṃ uppaṇḍuppaṇḍukajātaṃ disvā bhikkhū āmantesi – “ko, bhikkhave, tassa brāhmaṇassa adhikāraṃ saratī”ti. Evaṃ vutte āyasmā sāriputto bhagavantaṃ etadavoca – “ahaṃ kho, bhante, tassa brāhmaṇassa adhikāraṃ sarāmī”ti. Kiṃ pana tvaṃ, sāriputta, brāhmaṇassa adhikāraṃ sarasīti. Idha me, bhante, so brāhmaṇo rājagahe piṇḍāya carantassa kaṭacchubhikkhaṃ dāpesi, imaṃ kho ahaṃ, bhante, tassa brāhmaṇassa adhikāraṃ sarāmī”ti. Sādhu sādhu, sāriputta. Kataññuno hi, sāriputta, sappurisā katavedino, tena hi tvaṃ, sāriputta, taṃ brāhmaṇaṃ pabbājehi upasampādehīti. Aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ āgatoti alīnacittajātakassa (jā. 1.2.11-12) aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ (jā. aṭṭha. 2.2.alīnacittajātakavaṇṇanā) āgato.

233. In the eleventh story, ‘the Teacher gave a sign to the Elder Sāriputta’ means he gave a sign to ordain the brahmin; that is to say, he commanded him. It is said that the Blessed One, seeing that brahmin—who had not obtained ordination—thin, wretched, of poor complexion, and pale, addressed the monks: “Monks, who remembers a service done by that brahmin?” When this was said, the Venerable Sāriputta said to the Blessed One: “I, venerable sir, remember a service done by that brahmin.” “What service do you remember, Sāriputta?” “Here, venerable sir, that brahmin had a ladleful of almsfood given to me while I was wandering for alms in Rājagaha. This, venerable sir, is the service I remember.” “Good, good, Sāriputta. Truly, Sāriputta, good people are grateful and acknowledge what has been done for them. Therefore, Sāriputta, you should give that brahmin the going forth and the higher ordination.” ‘This is found in the origin story’ means it is found in the origin story of the Alīnacitta Jātaka (Jā 1.2.11–12; Jā-a 2.2, Alīnacittajātakavaṇṇanā).

Nidhīnanti [M 1.0190] tattha tattha nidahitvā ṭhapitānaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇādipūrānaṃ nidhikumbhīnaṃ. Pavattāranti kicchajīvike duggatamanusse anukampaṃ katvā “ehi, te sukhena jīvanupāyaṃ dassessāmī”ti nidhiṭṭhānaṃ netvā hatthaṃ pasāretvā “imaṃ gahetvā sukhaṃ jīvā”ti ācikkhitāraṃ viya. Vajjadassinanti dve vajjadassino “iminā naṃ asāruppena vā khalitena vā saṅghamajjhe niggaṇhissāmī”ti randhagavesako ca, anaññātaṃ ñāpanatthāya ñātaṃ anuggaṇhanatthāya sīlādīnamassa vuddhikāmatāya taṃ taṃ vajjaṃ olokanena ullumpanasabhāvasaṇṭhito ca. Ayaṃ idha adhippeto. Yathā hi duggatamanusso “imaṃ gaṇhāhī”ti tajjetvāpi pothetvāpi nidhiṃ dassente kopaṃ na karoti, pamuditova hoti, evamevaṃ evarūpe puggale asāruppaṃ vā khalitaṃ vā disvā ācikkhante kopo na kātabbo, tuṭṭheneva bhavitabbaṃ. “Bhante, mahantaṃ vo kammaṃ kataṃ mayhaṃ ācariyupajjhāyaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā ovadantehi, punapi maṃ vadeyyāthā”ti pavāretabbameva.

‘Nidhīnaṃ’ (of treasures) refers to pots of hidden treasure filled with gold, silver, and so on, stored here and there. ‘Pavattāraṃ’ (a revealer) is like one who, having compassion for poor and struggling people, says, “Come, I will show you a means to live comfortably,” then leads them to the site of the treasure, extends his hand, and says, “Take this and live happily.” ‘Vajjadassinaṃ’ (one who sees faults) refers to two kinds of fault-seers: one who looks for openings to rebuke another in the midst of the Saṅgha for some impropriety or mistake; and another who, for the purpose of making the unknown known and of supporting the known, and out of a desire for the growth of another’s virtues such as moral conduct, is by nature disposed to uplift by observing and pointing out those faults. This latter one is intended here. For just as a poor person does not become angry but rejoices when shown a hidden treasure, even if threatened or struck, so too, one should not be angry but should be pleased when such a person, seeing an impropriety or a mistake, points it out. One should indeed invite correction, saying: “Venerable sirs, you have done me a great service by standing in the place of a teacher and preceptor to advise me. Please speak to me again.”

Niggayhavādinti ekacco hi saddhivihārikādīnaṃ asāruppaṃ vā khalitaṃ vā disvā “ayaṃ me mukhodakadānādīhi sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahati, sace naṃ vakkhāmi, na maṃ upaṭṭhahissati, evaṃ me parihāni bhavissatī”ti taṃ vattuṃ avisahanto na niggayhavādī nāma hoti, so imasmiṃ sāsane kacavaraṃ ākirati. Yo pana tathārūpaṃ vajjaṃ disvā vajjānurūpaṃ tajjento paṇāmento daṇḍakammaṃ karonto vihārā nīharanto sikkhāpeti, ayaṃ niggayhavādī nāma seyyathāpi, sammāsambuddho. Vuttañhetaṃ – “niggayha niggayhāhaṃ, ānanda, vakkhāmi, pavayha pavayha[V 1.0175], ānanda, vakkhāmi, yo sāro, so ṭhassatī”ti (ma. ni. 3.196). Medhāvinti dhammojapaññāya samannāgataṃ. Tādisanti evarūpaṃ paṇḍitaṃ bhajeyya payirupāseyya. Tādisañhi ācariyaṃ bhajamānassa antevāsikassa seyyo hoti na pāpiyo, vaḍḍhiyeva hoti, no parihānīti.

'Niggayhavādī' (a reprover) means that if someone, upon seeing unsuitable or faulty behavior in a co-resident and so on, thinks, 'This person serves me diligently with offerings of water for the mouth and so on. If I reprove him, he will no longer serve me, and thus I will suffer loss,' and being unable to speak that reproof, such a person is not called a reprover; he scatters rubbish in this Dispensation. But one who, seeing such a fault, reproves according to the fault, admonishes, imposes a penalty, expels from the monastery, and trains him—such a one is called a reprover, just like the Perfectly Enlightened One. For it is said: 'Reproving, reproving, Ānanda, I will speak; sifting, sifting, Ānanda, I will speak. What is essential will remain' (MN 3.196). 'Medhāvī' (wise) means endowed with wisdom that is the essence of the Dhamma. 'Tādisaṃ' (such a one) means one should associate with and attend upon such a wise person. For a resident pupil who associates with such a teacher, there is what is better, not what is worse; there is only growth, not decline.

Mogharājattheravatthu

The Story of the Elder Mogharāja

234. Dvādasame kaṭṭhavāhananagareti kaṭṭhavāhanena gahitattā evaṃladdhanāmake nagare. Atīte kira bārāṇasivāsī eko rukkhavaḍḍhakī sake ācariyake adutiyo. Tassa soḷasa sissā ekamekassa sahassaṃ antevāsikā. Evaṃ te sattarasādhikā soḷasa sahassā ācariyantevāsikā [M 1.0191] sabbepi bārāṇasiṃ upanissāya jīvikaṃ kappentā pabbatasamīpaṃ gantvā rukkhe gahetvā tattheva nānāpāsādavikatiyo niṭṭhāpetvā kullaṃ bandhitvā gaṅgāya bārāṇasiṃ ānetvā sace rājā atthiko hoti, rañño ekabhūmakaṃ vā sattabhūmakaṃ vā pāsādaṃ yojetvā denti. No ce, aññesampi vikkiṇitvā puttadāraṃ posenti.
