Atha nesaṃ ekadivasaṃ ācariyo “na sakkā vaḍḍhakikammena niccaṃ jīvituṃ, dukkarañhi jarākāle etaṃ kamma”nti cintetvā antevāsike āmantesi – “tātā, udumbarādayo appasārarukkhe ānethā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā ānayiṃsu. So tehi kaṭṭhasakuṇaṃ katvā tassabbhantaraṃ pavisitvā vātena yantaṃ pūresi. Kaṭṭhasakuṇo suvaṇṇahaṃsarājā viya ākāse laṅghitvā vanassa upari caritvā antevāsīnaṃ purato oruhi.

234. In the twelfth story: in the city named Kaṭṭhavāhananagara because it was seized by Kaṭṭhavāhana. In the past, it is said, there was a carpenter living in Bārāṇasī, second to none in his craft. He had sixteen pupils, and each had a thousand resident pupils. Thus, these sixteen thousand and seventeen masters and pupils, all making a living depending on Bārāṇasī, would go near a mountain, get trees, and right there finish various kinds of palace structures. They would then bind them into a raft, bring them to Bārāṇasī by the Ganges, and if the king was in need, they would assemble and give the king a one-storey or a seven-storey palace. If not, they would sell them to others and support their children and wives. Then one day their master thought, 'It is not possible to live forever by the craft of carpentry; this work is indeed difficult in old age.' He then addressed his resident pupils: 'Dears, bring udumbara and other trees with little heartwood.' They agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and brought them. He made a wooden bird from them, entered inside it, and filled the mechanism with wind. The wooden bird, like a golden swan-king, leapt into the sky, moved above the forest, and descended in front of the resident pupils.

Athācariyo sisse āha – “tātā īdisāni kaṭṭhavāhanāni katvā sakkā sakalajambudīpe rajje gahetuṃ, tumhepi tātā etāni karotha, rajjaṃ gahetvā jīvissāma, dukkaraṃ vaḍḍhakisippena jīvitu”nti. Te tathā katvā ācariyassa paṭivedesuṃ. Tato ne ācariyo āha – “katamaṃ tātā rajjaṃ gaṇhāmā”ti? Bārāṇasirajjaṃ ācariyāti. Alaṃ tātā, mā etaṃ rucittha, mayañhi taṃ gahetvāpi “vaḍḍhakirājā, vaḍḍhakiyuvarājā”ti vaḍḍhakivādā na muccissāma, mahanto jambudīpo, aññattha gacchāmāti. Tato saputtadārakā kaṭṭhavāhanāni abhiruhitvā sajjāvudhā hutvā himavantābhimukhā gantvā himavati aññataraṃ nagaraṃ pavisitvā rañño nivesaneyeva paccuṭṭhaṃsu. Te tattha rajjaṃ gahetvā ācariyaṃ rajje abhisiñciṃsu. So “kaṭṭhavāhano rājā”ti pākaṭo ahosi, taṃ nagaraṃ tena gahitattā “kaṭṭhavāhananagara”nteva nāmaṃ labhi.

Then the teacher said to his pupils: 'Dears, by making such wooden vehicles, it is possible to seize kingdoms in the entire Jambudīpa. You too, dears, make these, and we shall live by seizing a kingdom. It is hard to live by the carpenter’s craft.' They did so and informed the teacher. Then the teacher said to them: 'Which kingdom shall we seize, dears?' 'The kingdom of Bārāṇasī, teacher.' 'Enough, dears, do not desire that. Even if we take it, we will not be freed from being called ‘the carpenter king, the carpenter crown prince’—from such talk of carpenters. Jambudīpa is vast; let us go elsewhere.' Then, with their wives and children, they mounted the wooden vehicles, became fully armed, and set out toward the Himālaya. Entering a certain city in the Himālaya, they descended upon the king’s residence itself. There, they seized the kingdom and consecrated the teacher as king. He became known as 'King Kaṭṭhavāhana' (the Wooden-Vehicle King), and because it was seized by him, that city obtained the name 'Kaṭṭhavāhananagara'.

Tapacāranti [V 1.0176] tapacaraṇaṃ. Pāsāṇacetiye piṭṭhipāsāṇe nisīdīti pāsāṇakacetiyanti laddhavohāre piṭṭhipāsāṇe sakkena māpite mahāmaṇḍape nisīdi. Tattha kira mahato pāsāṇassa upari pubbe devaṭṭhānaṃ ahosi, uppanne pana bhagavati vihāro jāto, so teneva purimavohārena “pāsāṇacetiya”nti vuccati.

'Tapacāraṃ' means the practice of austerities. 'At the Pāsāṇacetiya, he sat on the flat rock' means he sat in the great pavilion created by Sakka on the flat rock that was known by the designation 'Pāsāṇakacetiya'. It is said that formerly there was a shrine for deities on top of a great rock there, but when the Blessed One arose, a monastery came to be, so it is called 'Pāsāṇacetiya' by that same former designation.

Tena [M 1.0192] pucchite dutiyo hutvā satthāraṃ pañhaṃ pucchīti –

When asked by him, being the second one, he asked the Teacher a question:

“Muddhaṃ muddhādhipātañca, bāvarī paripucchati;

Taṃ byākarohi bhagavā, kaṅkhaṃ vinaya no ise”ti. (su. ni. 1031) –

‘The head and the falling of the head—Bāvarī asks. Explain that, O Blessed One; dispel our doubt, O Seer.’ (Snp 1031)

Evaṃ tena pañhe pucchite bhagavatā ca –

When the question was thus asked by him, the Blessed One replied:

“Avijjā muddhāti jānāhi, vijjā muddhādhipātinī;

Saddhāsatisamādhīhi, chandavīriyena saṃyutā”ti. (su. ni. 1032) –

‘Know that ignorance is the head; knowledge is what makes the head fall, when it is conjoined with faith, mindfulness, and concentration, with zeal and energy.’ (Snp 1032)

Pañhe vissajjite dutiyo hutvā pañhaṃ pucchi.

When the question was answered, being the second one, he asked a question.

Athassa…pe… pañhaṃ kathesīti –

Then to him… he stated the question:

“Kathaṃ lokaṃ avekkhantaṃ, maccurājā na passatī”ti. (su. ni. 1124) –

‘How should one look upon the world so that the King of Death does not see one?’ (Snp 1124)

Tena pañhe pucchite –

When the question was asked by him:

“Suññato lokaṃ avekkhassu, mogharāja sadā sato;

Attānudiṭṭhiṃ ūhacca, evaṃ maccutaro siyā;

Evaṃ lokaṃ avekkhantaṃ, maccurājā na passatī”ti. (su. ni. 1125) –

‘Look upon the world as empty, Mogharāja, always mindful; having uprooted the view of self, thus one may cross beyond death. The King of Death does not see one who looks upon the world thus.’ (Snp 1125)

Pañhaṃ vissajjesi.

He answered the question.

Sesajanāti tasmiṃ samāgame sannipatitā sesajanā. Na kathīyantīti “ettakā sotāpannā”tiādinā [V 1.0177] na vuccanti. Evaṃ pārāyane vatthu samuṭṭhitanti pārāyanavagge idaṃ vatthu samuṭṭhitaṃ.

'The remaining people' means the other people who had gathered in that assembly. 'They are not spoken of' means it is not said, 'So many became stream-enterers,' and so on. 'Thus the account arose in the Pārāyana' means this account arose in the Pārāyanavagga.

Catutthaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Fourth Chapter on the Foremost is concluded.

Therapāḷisaṃvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Pāli text concerning the Elders is concluded.

(14) 5. Pañcamaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā

(14) 5. Commentary on the Fifth Chapter on the Foremost

Mahāpajāpatigotamītherīvatthu

The Story of the Elder Nun Mahāpajāpatī Gotamī

235. Theripāḷisaṃvaṇṇanāya [V 1.0178] paṭhame yadidaṃ mahāgotamīti ettha “yadidaṃ mahāpajāpati gotamī”ti ca paṭhanti. Tattha gotamīti gottaṃ. Nāmakaraṇadivase [M 1.0193] panassā laddhasakkārā brāhmaṇā lakkhaṇasampattiṃ disvā “sace ayaṃ dhītaraṃ labhissati, cakkavattirañño mahesī bhavissati. Sace puttaṃ labhissati, cakkavattirājā bhavissatī”ti ubhayathāpi “mahatīyevassā pajā bhavissatī”ti byākariṃsu, tasmā puttapajāya ceva dhītupajāya ca mahantatāya “mahāpajāpatī”ti vohariṃsu. Tadubhayaṃ pana saṃsandetvā “mahāpajāpatigotamī”ti vuttaṃ. Vārabhikkhanti vārena dātabbaṃ bhikkhaṃ. Nāmaṃ akaṃsūti gottaṃyeva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Mātucchanti cūḷamātaraṃ. Mātubhaginī hi mātucchāti vuccati. Kalahavivādasuttapariyosāneti “kutopahūtā kalahā vivādā”tiādinā suttanipāte āgatassa kalahavivādasuttassa (su. ni. 868 ādayo) pariyosāne. Idañca aṅguttarabhāṇakānaṃ kathāmaggānusārena vuttaṃ. Apare pana “tasmiṃyeva suttanipāte ‘attadaṇḍābhayaṃ jāta’ntiādinā āgatassa attadaṇḍasuttassa (su. ni. 941 ādayo) pariyosāne”ti vadanti. Nikkhamitvā pabbajitānanti ettha ehibhikkhupabbajjāya ete pabbajitāti vadanti. Teneva suttanipāte attadaṇḍasuttasaṃvaṇṇanāya (su. ni. aṭṭha. 2.942 ādayo) vuttaṃ – “desanāpariyosāne pañcasatā sākiyakumārā koḷiyakumārā ca ehibhikkhupabbajjāya pabbajitā. Te gahetvā bhagavā mahāvanaṃ pāvisī”ti. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

235. In the commentary on the Therīpāḷi, concerning the first passage, yadidaṃ mahāgotamī, some also read yadidaṃ mahāpajāpati gotamī. Here, Gotamī is her clan name. On her naming day, the brahmins who had received honor, seeing the excellence of her marks, declared: “If she has a daughter, she will become the chief queen of a wheel-turning monarch. If she has a son, he will become a wheel-turning monarch.” In both cases, they predicted, “Great indeed will be her progeny.” Therefore, due to the greatness of both her son’s and daughter’s progeny, she was called “Mahāpajāpatī.” Combining both, she was referred to as “Mahāpajāpatigotamī.” Vārabhikkhaṃ means alms to be given in turn. Nāmaṃ akaṃsu means they made the clan name itself her name. Mātucchā means the younger mother, for a mother’s sister is called mātucchā. Kalahavivādasuttapariyosāne refers to the conclusion of the Kalahavivāda Sutta, which begins with kutopahūtā kalahā vivādā in the Sutta Nipāta (Sn 868 ff.). This is stated according to the tradition of the Aṅguttara reciters. Others, however, say it refers to the conclusion of the Attadaṇḍa Sutta, which begins with attadaṇḍābhayaṃ jātaṃ in the same Sutta Nipāta (Sn 941 ff.). Concerning Nikkhamitvā pabbajitānaṃ, here they say that they went forth with the ehi bhikkhu ordination. Accordingly, in the commentary on the Attadaṇḍa Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta (SnA 2.942 ff.), it is said: “At the end of the discourse, five hundred Sakyan and Koliyan youths went forth with the ‘ehi bhikkhu’ ordination. Taking them, the Blessed One entered the Great Wood.” The rest here is easily understood.

Khemātherīvatthu

The Story of Khemā the Elder Nun.

236. Dutiye parapariyāpannā hutvāti paresaṃ dāsī hutvā. Suvaṇṇarasapiñjaro ahosīti suvaṇṇarasapiñjaro viya ahosi.

236. In the second passage, parapariyāpannā hutvā means 'having become a slave to others.' Suvaṇṇarasapiñjaro ahosi means 'he was as if golden-hued.'

Makkaṭakova [V 1.0179] jālanti yathā nāma makkaṭako suttajālaṃ katvā majjhaṭṭhāne nābhimaṇḍale nipanno pariyante patitaṃ paṭaṅgaṃ vā makkhikaṃ vā vegena gantvā vijjhitvā tassa rasaṃ pivitvā punāgantvā tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne nipajjati, evameva ye sattā rāgarattā dosapaduṭṭhā mohamūḷhā sayaṃkataṃ taṇhāsotaṃ anupatanti, te taṃ samatikkamituṃ na sakkonti, evaṃ duratikkamaṃ. Etampi chetvāna vajanti dhīrāti paṇḍitā etaṃ bandhanaṃ chinditvā anapekkhino nirālayā hutvā arahattamaggena sabbaṃ dukkhaṃ pahāya vajanti gacchantīti attho.

Makkaṭakova jālaṃ means: Just as a spider, having made a web, lies in the middle at the center, and when an insect or a fly falls at the edge, it swiftly goes, pierces it, drinks its juice, and then returns to lie in the same spot—even so, those beings who are obsessed with lust, corrupted by hatred, and deluded by ignorance, follow the self-made stream of craving, and they are not able to cross beyond it; thus, it is hard to overcome. Etampi chetvāna vajanti dhīrā means: The wise sever this bond and, free from longing, without attachment, having abandoned all suffering by the path to arahantship, go forth—this is the meaning.

Uppalavaṇṇātherīvatthu

The Story of Uppalavaṇṇā the Elder Nun.

237. Tatiyaṃ [M 1.0194] uttānatthameva.

237. The third passage is simply explicit in meaning.

Paṭācārātherīvatthu

The Story of Paṭācārā the Elder Nun.

238. Catutthe paṭihārasatenapīti dvārasatenapi. Paṭihārasaddo hi dvāre dovārike ca dissati. Kulasabhāganti attano gehasamīpaṃ.

238. In the fourth passage, paṭihārasatenapi means 'even with a hundred doors.' The word paṭihāra is indeed seen to refer to both doors and doorkeepers. Kulasabhāgaṃ means 'near one's own house.'

Tāṇāyāti tāṇabhāvāya patiṭṭhānatthāya. Bandhavāti putte ca pitaro ca ṭhapetvā avasesā ñātisuhajjā. Antakenādhipannassāti maraṇena abhibhūtassa. Pavattiyañhi puttādayo annapānādidānena ceva uppannakiccanittharaṇena ca tāṇā hutvāpi maraṇakāle kenaci upāyena maraṇaṃ paṭibāhituṃ asamatthatāya tāṇatthāya leṇatthāya na santi nāma. Teneva vuttaṃ – “natthi ñātīsu tāṇatā”ti.

Tāṇāya means 'for the sake of protection and support.' Bandhavā means 'friends and kin, excluding sons and fathers.' Antakenādhipannassa means 'overwhelmed by death.' Indeed, even though sons and others may provide shelter by giving food and drink and fulfilling arising duties, at the time of death, they are unable by any means to ward off death—thus, they are not truly a shelter or refuge. Therefore, it is said: “There is no shelter among relatives.”

Etamatthavasanti etaṃ tesaṃ aññamaññassa tāṇaṃ bhavituṃ asamatthabhāvasaṅkhātaṃ kāraṇaṃ jānitvā paṇḍito catupārisuddhisīlena saṃvuto rakkhitagopito hutvā nibbānagamanaṃ aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ sīghaṃ sodheyyāti attho.

Etamatthavasaṃ means: Knowing this reason, namely their inability to provide mutual protection, the wise person, restrained by virtue purified in four ways, being protected and guarded, should quickly purify the eightfold path that leads to Nibbāna. This is the meaning.

Dhammadinnātherīvatthu

The Story of Dhammadinnā the Elder Nun.

239. Pañcame parāyattaṭṭhāneti paresaṃ dāsiṭṭhāne. Sujātattherassa adhikārakammaṃ katvāti sā kira attano kese vikkiṇitvā sujātattherassa nāma aggasāvakassa dānaṃ datvā patthanaṃ akāsi[V 1.0180]. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ. Hatthe pasāriteti tassa hatthāvalambanatthaṃ pubbāciṇṇavasena hatthe pasārite. So kira anāgāmī hutvā gehaṃ āgacchanto yathā aññesu divasesu ito cito ca olokento sitaṃ kurumāno hasamāno āgacchati, evaṃ anāgantvā santindriyo santamānaso hutvā agamāsi. Dhammadinnā sīhapañjaraṃ ugghāṭetvā vīthiṃ olokayamānā tassa āgamanākāraṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho eta”nti cintetvā tassa paccuggamanaṃ kurumānā sopānasīse ṭhatvā olambanatthaṃ hatthaṃ pasāresi. Upāsako attano hatthaṃ samiñjesi. Sā [M 1.0195] “pātarāsabhojanakāle jānissāmī”ti cintesi. Upāsako pubbe tāya saddhiṃ ekato bhuñjati. Taṃ divasaṃ pana taṃ anapaloketvā yogāvacarabhikkhu viya ekakova bhuñji. Tenāha – “bhuñjamānopi imaṃ detha, imaṃ harathāti na byāharī”ti. Tattha imaṃ dethāti imaṃ khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā detha. Imaṃ harathāti imaṃ khādanīyaṃ vā bhojanīyaṃ vā apaharatha. Santhavavasenāti kilesasanthavavasena. Cirakālaparibhāvitāya ghaṭadīpajālāya viya abbhantare dibbamānāya hetusampattiyā codiyamānā āha – “evaṃ sante…pe… mayhaṃ pabbajjaṃ anujānāthā”ti.

239. In the fifth passage, parāyattaṭṭhāne means 'in the position of being a slave to others.' Sujātattherassa adhikārakammaṃ katvā refers to her having performed an action of merit for Sujāta Thera; it is said that she sold her own hair, gave an offering to the chief disciple named Sujāta Thera, and then made an aspiration. This is what is being referred to. Hatthe pasārite means she stretched out her hand to offer him support, as was her previous habit. It is said that he, having become a non-returner, did not come home as on other days—looking around here and there, smiling and laughing—but instead arrived with calm senses and a peaceful mind. Dhammadinnā, having opened the lion-barred window and looking down the street, saw his manner of arrival and wondered, “What is this?” She went to meet him and, standing at the top of the stairs, stretched out her hand to offer him support. The layman withdrew his own hand. She thought, “I will find out at breakfast time.” Previously, the layman used to eat together with her. But that day, without even glancing at her, he ate alone like a meditating monk. Therefore, it is said: “Even while eating, he did not say, ‘Give this’ or ‘Take this away.’” Here, imaṃ detha means 'give this food or meal.' Imaṃ haratha means 'remove this food or meal.' Santhavavasena means 'by way of the intimacy of defilements.' Prompted by the perfection of her causal conditions, which shone within her like the flame of a pot-lamp tended for a long time, she said: “If this is so... please grant me permission to go forth.”

Ayaṃ tāva seṭṭhi gharamajjhe ṭhitova dukkhassantaṃ akāsīti sā kira “dhammadinne tuyhaṃ doso natthi, ahaṃ pana ajja paṭṭhāya santhavavasena…pe… kulagharaṃ gacchā”ti vutte evaṃ cintesi – “pakatipuriso evaṃ vattā nāma natthi, addhā etena lokuttaradhammo nāma paṭividdho”ti. Tenassā ayaṃ saṅkappo ahosi “ayaṃ tāva seṭṭhi gharamajjhe ṭhitova dukkhassantaṃ akāsī”ti. Majjhimanikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ (ma. ni. aṭṭha. 1.460) pana “atha kasmā mayā saddhiṃ yathāpakatiyā ālāpasallāpamattampi na karothāti so cintesi – ‘ayaṃ lokuttaradhammo nāma garu bhāriyo na pakāsetabbo; sace kho panāhaṃ na kathessāmi, ayaṃ hadayaṃ phāletvā ettheva kālaṃ kareyyā’ti tassā anuggahatthāya kathesi – ‘dhammadinne ahaṃ satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā lokuttaradhammaṃ nāma adhigato, taṃ adhigatassa evarūpā lokiyakiriyā na vaṭṭatī’”ti vuttaṃ.

Ayaṃ tāva seṭṭhi gharamajjhe ṭhitova dukkhassantaṃ akāsi means: It is said that when she was told, “Dhammadinnā, there is no fault in you, but from today onwards, because of intimacy... I will no longer visit your family’s house,” she thought, “No ordinary man speaks like this—surely he has realized the supramundane Dhamma.” Thus, this thought arose in her: “This merchant, while standing right in the middle of the house, has indeed made an end of suffering.” In the Majjhima Nikāya commentary (MN-a 1.460), however, it is said: “Then, why do you not even exchange the slightest casual talk with me as before?” He reflected, “This supramundane Dhamma is weighty and profound—it should not be revealed. But if I do not speak, she may break her heart and die right here.” Out of compassion for her, he explained, “Dhammadinnā, having heard the Dhamma taught by the Teacher, I have attained the supramundane Dhamma. For one who has attained it, such worldly activities are no longer fitting.”

Pañcakkhandhādivasena pañhe pucchīti “sakkāyo sakkāyoti ayye vuccati, katamo nu kho ayye sakkāyo vutto bhagavatā”tiādinā cūḷavedallasutte (ma. ni. 1.460 ādayo) āgatanayena pucchi. Pucchitaṃ pucchitaṃ vissajjesīti “pañca kho ime, āvuso visākha, upādānakkhandhā sakkāyo vutto bhagavatā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.460 ādayo) tattheva āgatanayena vissajjesi. Sūrabhāvanti tikkhabhāvaṃ. Anadhigataarahattamaggassa uggahena [V 1.0181] vinā tattha pañho na upaṭṭhātīti āha – “uggahavasena arahattamaggepi pucchī”ti. Taṃ nivattentīti “vimuttiyā panāyye kiṃ paṭibhāgo”ti pucchite “vimuttiyā kho, āvuso visākha, nibbānaṃ paṭibhāgo”ti (ma. ni. 1.466) vutte “nibbānassa, panāyye, kiṃ paṭibhāgo”ti puna pucchite taṃ nivattentī “accasarāvuso [M 1.0196] visākhā”tiādimāha. Tattha accasarāti apucchitabbaṃ pucchanto pañhaṃ atikkāmitā ahosīti attho. Nāsakkhi pañhānaṃ pariyantaṃ gahetunti pañhānaṃ paricchedappamāṇaṃ gahetuṃ nāsakkhi. Pañhānañhi paricchedaṃ gahetuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne aṭṭhatvā tato paraṃ pucchanto nāsakkhi pañhānaṃ pariyantaṃ gahetuṃ. Appaṭibhāgadhammassa ca paṭibhāgaṃ pucchi. Nibbānaṃ nāmetaṃ appaṭibhāgaṃ, na sakkā nīlaṃ vā pītakaṃ vāti kenaci dhammena saddhiṃ paṭibhāgaṃ katvā dassetuṃ, tañca tvaṃ iminā adhippāyena pucchasīti attho. Nibbānogadhanti nibbānaṃ ogāhetvā ṭhitaṃ, nibbānantogadhaṃ nibbānaṃ anuppaviṭṭhanti attho. Nibbānaparāyaṇanti nibbānaṃ paraṃ ayanamassa parāgati, na tato paraṃ gacchatīti attho. Nibbānaṃ pariyosānaṃ avasānaṃ assāti nibbānapariyosānaṃ.

She asked a question in terms of the five aggregates and so on, saying: “Venerable, it is called ‘identity’; what, venerable, is the identity spoken of by the Blessed One?” and so on, according to the method found in the Cūḷavedalla Sutta (MN 1.460ff.). Whatever was asked, she answered, saying: “Friend Visākha, these five aggregates subject to clinging are what the Blessed One calls identity,” and so on, according to the method found in that same text. ‘Sūrabhāva’ means sharpness. Because for one who has not attained the path to arahantship the question does not arise without learning, it is said: “She asked even about the path to arahantship by way of learning.” She turned him back: when asked, “But, venerable, what is the counterpart to liberation?” and it was said, “Friend Visākha, nibbāna is the counterpart to liberation,” and then asked again, “But, venerable, what is the counterpart to nibbāna?”—she turned him back, saying, “You have gone too far, friend Visākha,” and so on. Herein, ‘accasarā’ means that by asking what should not be asked, he had overstepped the question. ‘He was unable to grasp the limit of the questions’ means he could not determine the extent or boundary of the questions. For by asking beyond the proper point, without stopping where one should, he was unable to grasp the limit of the questions. And he asked for a counterpart to that which has no counterpart. Nibbāna, indeed, is without a counterpart; it cannot be shown to have a counterpart in relation to any phenomenon, such as blue or yellow. The meaning is: “And you ask this with that intention.” ‘Nibbānogadha’ means plunged into and established in nibbāna; the meaning is that it has entered into nibbāna. ‘Nibbānaparāyaṇa’ means that for which nibbāna is the ultimate recourse, the final destiny; the meaning is that it does not go beyond that. ‘Nibbānapariyosāna’ means that for which nibbāna is the final end, the conclusion.

Pureti atītesu khandhesu. Pacchāti anāgatesu khandhesu. Majjheti paccuppannesu khandhesu. Akiñcananti yassa etesu tīsu taṇhāgāhasaṅkhātaṃ kiñcanaṃ natthi, tamahaṃ rāgakiñcanādīhi akiñcanaṃ kassaci gahaṇassa abhāvena anādānaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ vadāmīti attho.

‘Pureti’ refers to the past aggregates. ‘Pacchāti’ refers to the future aggregates. ‘Majjheti’ refers to the present aggregates. ‘Akiñcana’ means: one who has no impediment—that is, the grip of craving—in these three, such a one I call a brahmin, who is without impediments such as lust, and who is without grasping due to the absence of any taking. This is the meaning.

Paṇḍitāti dhātuāyatanādikusalatāsaṅkhātena paṇḍiccena samannāgatā. Vuttañhetaṃ –

‘Wise’ means endowed with wisdom, characterized by skill regarding elements, sense bases, and so on. For this was said:

“Kittāvatā nu kho, bhante, paṇḍito hoti? Yato kho, ānanda, bhikkhu dhātukusalo ca hoti āyatanakusalo ca paṭiccasamuppādakusalo ca ṭhānāṭṭhānakusalo ca, ettāvatā kho, ānanda, bhikkhu paṇḍito hotī”ti.

“To what extent, venerable sir, is one wise? When, Ānanda, a monk is skilled in the elements, skilled in the sense bases, skilled in dependent origination, and skilled in what is possible and impossible, to that extent, Ānanda, a monk is wise.”

Mahāpaññāti mahante atthe mahante dhamme mahantā niruttiyo mahantāni paṭibhānāni pariggahaṇe samatthāya paññāya samannāgatā. Imissā hi theriyā asekkhappaṭisambhidāppattatāya paṭisambhidāyo pūretvā ṭhitatāya paññāmahattaṃ. Yathā taṃ dhammadinnāyāti yathā dhammadinnāya bhikkhuniyā byākataṃ, ahaṃ evameva byākareyyanti attho. Tanti nipātamatthaṃ.

‘Of great wisdom’ means endowed with a wisdom capable of grasping great meanings, great teachings, great expressions, and great insights. For this elder nun, the greatness of her wisdom is due to her having attained the analytical knowledges of an adept and her standing with the analytical knowledges fulfilled. ‘Just as it was by Dhammadinnā’ means: ‘Just as it was explained by the bhikkhunī Dhammadinnā, so too would I explain it.’ The word ‘taṃ’ is merely a particle.

Nandātherīvatthu

The Story of the Elder Nun Nandā

240. Chaṭṭhe [V 1.0182][M 1.0197] aññaṃ maggaṃ apassantīti aññaṃ upāyaṃ apassantī. Vissatthāti nirāsaṅkā. Itthinimittanti itthiyā subhanimittaṃ, subhākāranti vuttaṃ hoti. Dhammapade gāthaṃ vatvāti –

240. In the sixth story, ‘not seeing another path’ means not seeing another means. ‘Vissatthā’ means without apprehension. ‘The mark of a woman’ means the beautiful sign of a woman; that is to say, her lovely form. Having spoken a verse from the Dhammapada:

“Aṭṭhīnaṃ nagaraṃ kataṃ, maṃsalohitalepanaṃ;

Yattha jarā ca maccu ca, māno makkho ca ohito”ti. (dha. pa. 150) –

“A city is made of bones, plastered with flesh and blood, where aging and death, conceit and contempt are deposited.” (Dhp. 150)

Imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā. Tatrāyamadhippāyo – yatheva hi pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇādīnaṃ odahanatthāya kaṭṭhāni ussāpetvā vallīhi bandhitvā mattikāya vilimpitvā nagarasaṅkhātaṃ bahiddhā gehaṃ karonti, evamidaṃ ajjhattikampi tīṇi aṭṭhisatāni ussāpetvā nhāruvinaddhaṃ maṃsalohitalepanaṃ tacapaṭicchannaṃ jīraṇalakkhaṇāya jarāya maraṇalakkhaṇassa maccuno ārogyasampadādīni paṭicca uppajjanalakkhaṇassa mānassa sukatakāraṇavināsanalakkhaṇassa makkhassa ca odahanatthāya nagaraṃ kataṃ. Evarūpo eva hi ettha kāyikacetasiko ābādho ohito, ito uddhaṃ kiñci gayhūpagaṃ natthīti.

Having spoken this verse. Here, the intended meaning is this: Just as people, for the purpose of depositing early and late grains and other things, build an outer house called a city by raising up logs, binding them with vines, and plastering them with clay, so too this internal body is constructed by raising up the three hundred bones, bound by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood, and covered with skin—a city made for the purpose of depositing aging, which is characterized by decay; death, which is characterized by mortality; conceit, which is characterized by arising in dependence on health and prosperity; and contempt, which is characterized by destroying the cause of good deeds. Indeed, such bodily and mental afflictions are deposited here; beyond this, there is nothing fit to be grasped.

Suttaṃ abhāsīti –

She spoke this Sutta:

“Caraṃ vā yadi vā tiṭṭhaṃ, nisinno uda vā sayaṃ;

Samiñjeti pasāreti, esā kāyassa iñjanā.

“Whether walking or standing, sitting or else lying down; one bends, one stretches—this is the body’s motion.

“Aṭṭhinahārusaṃyutto, tacamaṃsāvalepano;

Chaviyā kāyo paṭicchanno, yathābhūtaṃ na dissatī”ti. (su. ni. 195-196) –

“Connected with bones and sinews, plastered with skin and flesh; the body is covered with hide, not seen as it really is.” (Snp. 195–196)

Ādinā suttamabhāsi.

She spoke the sutta beginning with this.

Soṇātherīvatthu

The Story of the Elder Nun Soṇā

241. Sattame [V 1.0183] sabbepi visuṃ visuṃ gharāvāse patiṭṭhāpesīti ettha sabbepi visuṃ visuṃ gharāvāse patiṭṭhāpetvā “puttāva maṃ paṭijaggissanti, kiṃ me visuṃ kuṭumbenā”ti sabbaṃ sāpateyyampi vibhajitvā adāsīti veditabbaṃ. Teneva hi tato paṭṭhāya “ayaṃ amhākaṃ kiṃ karissatī”ti attano santikaṃ āgataṃ “mātā”ti saññampi na kariṃsu. Tathā hi naṃ katipāhaccayena jeṭṭhaputtassa bhariyā “aho amhākaṃ ayaṃ jeṭṭheputto [M 1.0198] meti dve koṭṭhāse datvā viya imameva gehaṃ āgacchatī”ti āha. Sesaputtānaṃ bhariyāyopi evamevaṃ vadiṃsu. Jeṭṭhadhītaraṃ ādiṃ katvā tāsaṃ gehaṃ gatakāle tāpi naṃ evameva vadiṃsu. Sā avamānappattā hutvā “kiṃ me imesaṃ santike vutthena, bhikkhunī hutvā jīvissāmī”ti bhikkhunīupassayaṃ gantvā pabbajjaṃ yāci, tā naṃ pabbājesuṃ. Imameva vatthuṃ dassento “bahuputtikasoṇā tesaṃ attani agāravabhāvaṃ ñatvā ‘gharāvāsena kiṃ karissāmī’ti nikkhamitvā pabbajī”ti āha.

241. In the seventh story, regarding ‘established all of them separately in households,’ it should be understood that after establishing all of them separately in households, thinking, ‘My children will look after me, what need have I for a separate household?’ she divided and gave away all her property. For that very reason, from then on, when she came to them, they did not even acknowledge her as ‘mother,’ thinking, ‘What will this one do for us?’ Thus, after a few days, the wife of the eldest son said, ‘Oh, this one comes to our very house as if, thinking, “This is my eldest son,” she had given us a double portion.’ The wives of the other sons also spoke in the same way. When she went to the houses of her daughters, beginning with the eldest, they too spoke to her in the same way. Having been subjected to humiliation, she thought, ‘What is the use of my living near them? I will become a nun and live that life.’ She went to the nuns’ residence and requested the going-forth, and they gave her the going-forth. Illustrating this very story, it is said: ‘Soṇā of Many Children, realizing their lack of respect toward her, thought, “What shall I do with household life?” and went forth and was ordained.’

Vihāraṃ gacchantiyoti bhikkhuvihāraṃ gacchantiyo. Dhammamuttamanti navavidhalokuttaradhammaṃ. So hi uttamadhammo nāma yo hi taṃ na passati, tassa vassasatampi jīvanato taṃ dhammaṃ passantassa paṭivijjhantassa ekāhampi ekakkhaṇampi jīvitaṃ seyyo. Āgantukajanoti vihāragataṃ bhikkhunījanaṃ sandhāya vadati. Anupadhāretvāti asallakkhetvā.

‘Going to the monastery’ means the bhikkhunīs going to the monks’ monastery. ‘The supreme Dhamma’ means the ninefold supramundane Dhamma. For that is indeed called the supreme Dhamma; for one who does not see it, a life of a hundred years is not as good as a single day, a single moment, of life for one who sees and penetrates that Dhamma. ‘Visitors’ refers to the group of nuns who had come to the monastery. ‘Without noticing’ means without considering.

Bakulātherīvatthu

The Story of the Elder Nun Bakulā

242. Aṭṭhamaṃ uttānatthameva.

242. The eighth story is clear in meaning.

Kuṇḍalakesātherīvatthu

The Story of the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesā

243. Navame catukketi vīthicatukke. Catunnaṃ samāhāro catukkaṃ. Cārakatoti bandhanāgārato. Ubbaṭṭetvāti uddharitvā.

243. In the ninth story, ‘at the four-way’ means at the crossroads. A collection of four is a ‘four-way.’ ‘From the prison’ means from the jail. ‘Having rescued’ means having lifted out.

Muhuttamapi cintayeti muhuttaṃ taṅkhaṇampi ṭhānuppattikapaññāya taṅkhaṇānurūpaṃ atthaṃ cintituṃ sakkuṇeyya. Sahassamapi ce gāthā, anatthapadasaṃhitāti ayaṃ gāthā dārucīriyattherassa bhagavatā bhāsitā, idhāpi ca sāyeva gāthā dassitā. Therigāthāsaṃvaṇṇanāyaṃ ācariyadhammapālattherenapi kuṇḍalakesittheriyā [V 1.0184] vatthumhi ayameva gāthā vuttā. Dhammapadaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana kuṇḍalakesittheriyā vatthumhi –

Regarding 'even for a moment, if one thinks,' it means that even for a brief moment, for that instant, one would be able to contemplate the meaning appropriate to that instant with wisdom arising on the spot. Regarding 'Though a thousand verses be spoken, if they are full of meaningless words,' this verse was spoken by the Blessed One regarding the Elder Dārucīriya, and here too the same verse is shown. In the commentary on the Therīgāthā, the venerable teacher Dhammapāla also cited this verse in the story of the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesī. However, in the Dhammapada commentary, regarding the story of the Elder Nun Kuṇḍalakesī –

“Yo ca gāthāsataṃ bhāse, anatthapadasaṃhitā;

Ekaṃ dhammapadaṃ seyyo, yaṃ sutvā upasammatī”ti. (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 1.102) –

‘Though one should recite a hundred verses full of meaningless words, better is one verse of the Dhamma, hearing which one is pacified.’

Ayaṃ gāthā āgatā. Taṃtaṃbhāṇakānaṃ kathāmaggānusārena tattha tattha tathā vuttanti na idha ācariyassa pubbāparavirodho saṅkitabbo.

This verse has come down. According to the narrative tradition of the reciters of the texts, it is stated here and there in such a way, and therefore no contradiction between the earlier and later statements of the teacher should be suspected here.

Bhaddākāpilānītherī-bhaddākaccānātherīvatthu

The Story of the Elder Nun Bhaddā Kāpilānī and the Elder Nun Bhaddā Kaccānā

244-245. Dasamaṃ [M 1.0199] ekādasamañca uttānatthameva.

244-245. The tenth and eleventh sections are simply clear in meaning.

Kisāgotamītherīvatthu

The Story of the Elder Nun Kisāgotamī

246. Dvādasame tīhi lūkhehīti vatthalūkhasuttalūkharajanalūkhasaṅkhātehi tīhi lūkhehi. Siddhatthakanti sāsapabījaṃ.

246. In the twelfth story, 'with three wretched things' refers to the three wretched things enumerated as wretched cloth, wretched thread, and wretched dye. 'Siddhatthaka' means a mustard seed.

Taṃ puttapasusammattanti taṃ rūpabalādisampanne putte ca pasū ca labhitvā “mama puttā abhirūpā balasampannā paṇḍitā sabbakiccasamatthā, mama goṇo arogo abhirūpo mahābhāravaho, mama gāvī bahukhīrā”ti evaṃ puttehi ca pasūhi ca sammattaṃ naraṃ. Byāsattamanasanti cakkhuviññeyyādīsu ārammaṇesu hiraññasuvaṇṇādīsu pattacīvarādīsu vā yaṃ yaṃ laddhaṃ hoti, tattha tattheva lagganāya sattamānasaṃ. Suttaṃ gāmanti niddaṃ upagataṃ sattakāyaṃ. Mahoghovāti yathā evarūpaṃ gāmaṃ gambhīrato vitthārato ca mahanto mahānadiogho antamaso sunakhampi asesetvā sabbaṃ ādāya gacchati, evaṃ vuttappakāraṃ naraṃ maccu ādāya gacchatīti attho. Amataṃ padanti maraṇarahitaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ, amataṃ mahānibbānanti attho. Sesamettha uttānameva.

Regarding 'infatuated with children and cattle,' this refers to a man who, having obtained children endowed with beauty, strength, and so on, and cattle, becomes infatuated with his children and cattle, thinking, 'My sons are handsome, strong, wise, and capable of all tasks; my bull is healthy, handsome, and can carry great loads; my cow gives much milk.' Regarding 'with mind attached,' this means a mind that clings to whatever object is obtained, whether it be visible objects and so on, gold and silver and so on, or bowls and robes and so on. Regarding 'the sleeping village,' this means the group of beings that has fallen asleep. Regarding 'like a great flood,' just as a great river flood, great in depth and breadth, carries away everything in such a village, leaving not even a dog behind, so too does death carry away such a person. Regarding 'the deathless state,' this means the portion free from death, that is, the great Nibbāna. The rest here is clear in meaning.

Siṅgālakamātātherīvatthu

The Story of the Elder Nun Siṅgālakamātā

247. Terasamaṃ [V 1.0185] uttānatthameva.

247. The thirteenth story is simply clear in meaning.

(Pañcamaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.)

(The Commentary on the Fifth Etadagga Section is concluded.)

Theripāḷisaṃvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Therīpāḷi is concluded.

(14) 6. Chaṭṭhaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā

(14) 6. The Commentary on the Sixth Etadagga Section

Tapussa-bhallikavatthu

The Story of Tapussa and Bhallika

248. Upāsakapāḷisaṃvaṇṇanāya [V 1.0186][M 1.0200] paṭhame sabbapaṭhamaṃ saraṇaṃ gacchantānanti sabbesaṃ paṭhamaṃ hutvā saraṇaṃ gacchantānaṃ. Ito paranti sattasattāhato paraṃ. Gamanūpacchedaṃ akāsīti gamanavicchedaṃ akāsi. Yathā te goṇā dhuraṃ chaḍḍetvā pothiyamānāpi na gacchanti, tathā akāsīti attho. Tesanti tapussabhallikānaṃ. Adhimuccitvāti āvisitvā. Yakkhassa āvaṭṭo yakkhāvaṭṭo. Evaṃ sesesupi. Atītabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇaṃ olokesīti atītabuddhā kena bhājanena paṭiggaṇhiṃsūti buddhāciṇṇaṃ olokesi. Dvevācike saraṇe patiṭṭhāyāti saṅghassa anuppannattā buddhadhammavasena dvevācike saraṇe patiṭṭhahitvā. Cetiyanti pūjanīyavatthuṃ. Jīvakesadhātuyāti jīvamānassa bhagavato kesadhātuyā.

248. In the first story of the commentary on the Upāsakapāḷi, regarding 'those who go for refuge first of all,' it means those who, being the first of all, go for refuge. Regarding 'after this,' it means after seven weeks. Regarding 'he made an end to their journey,' it means he interrupted their journey. The meaning is that he acted in such a way that their oxen, having thrown off the yoke, would not proceed even when beaten. Regarding 'their,' it refers to Tapussa and Bhallika. Regarding 'having been possessed,' it means having been entered. 'Yakkhāvaṭṭo' means 'yakkhassa āvaṭṭo' (the yakkha's turning back). The same applies to the rest. Regarding 'he looked for the practice of past Buddhas,' it means he considered with what kind of vessel past Buddhas had accepted alms. Regarding 'having been established in the twofold refuge,' it means having been established in the twofold refuge of the Buddha and the Dhamma, since the Saṅgha had not yet arisen. Regarding 'cetiya,' it means a venerable object. Regarding 'the hair relic of the living one,' it means the hair relic of the Blessed One while he was alive.

Anāthapiṇḍikaseṭṭhivatthu

The Story of the Merchant Anāthapiṇḍika

249. Dutiye teneva guṇenāti teneva dāyakabhāvasaṅkhātena guṇena. So hi sabbakāmasamiddhatāya vigatamaccheratāya karuṇādiguṇasamaṅgitāya ca niccakālaṃ anāthānaṃ piṇḍamadāsi. Tena sabbakālaṃ upaṭṭhito anāthānaṃ piṇḍo etassa atthīti anāthapiṇḍikoti saṅkhaṃ gato. Yojanikavihāre kāretvāti yojane yojane ekamekaṃ vihāraṃ kāretvā. “Evarūpaṃ dānaṃ pavattesī”ti vatvā tameva dānaṃ vibhajitvā dassento “devasikaṃ pañca salākabhattāni hontī”tiādimāha. Tattha salākāya gāhetabbaṃ bhattaṃ salākabhattaṃ. Ekasmiṃ pakkhe ekadivasaṃ dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ pakkhikabhattaṃ. Dhuragehe ṭhapetvā dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ dhurabhattaṃ. Āgantukānaṃ dātabbaṃ bhattaṃ āgantukabhattaṃ. Evaṃ sesesupi. Pañca āsanasatāni gehe niccapaññattāneva hontīti gehe nisīdāpetvā bhuñjantānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ pañca āsanasatāni niccapaññattāni honti.

249. In the second story, regarding 'by that very quality,' it means by that very quality known as being a donor. For he, due to his complete fulfillment of all desires, his freedom from stinginess, and his possession of qualities such as compassion, constantly gave alms to the destitute. Therefore, because alms for the destitute were always provided by him, he came to be known as Anāthapiṇḍika. Regarding 'having had monasteries built at every yojana,' it means having had one monastery built at each yojana. Having said, 'He maintained such giving,' and then analyzing that very giving, he said, 'There were five daily ticket-foods,' and so on. Therein, 'ticket-food' is food to be received by a ticket. 'Fortnightly food' is food to be given on one day in a fortnight. 'Regular food' is food to be given that is set aside in the main house. 'Food for visitors' is food to be given to visitors. The same applies to the rest. Regarding 'five hundred seats were always prepared in the house,' it means that for the five hundred monks who were made to sit and eat in the house, five hundred seats were always prepared.

Cittagahapativatthu

The Story of the Householder Citta

250. Tatiye [V 1.0187] migā eva migarūpāni. Bhikkhaṃ samādāpetvāti, “bhante, mayhaṃ anuggahaṃ karotha, idha nisīditvā bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti bhikkhāgahaṇatthaṃ samādāpetvā[M 1.0201]. Vivaṭṭaṃ uddissa upacitaṃ nibbedhabhāgiyakusalaṃ upanissayo. Saḷāyatanavibhattimeva desesīti saḷāyatanavibhāgappaṭisaṃyuttameva dhammakathaṃ kathesi. Therenāti tattha sannihitānaṃ sabbesaṃ jeṭṭhena mahātherena. Pañhaṃ vissajjetuṃ asakkontenāti cittena gahapatinā “yā imā, bhante thera, anekavihitā diṭṭhiyo loke uppajjanti, ‘sassato loko’ti vā, ‘asassato loko’ti vā, ‘antavā loko’ti vā, ‘anantavā loko’ti vā, ‘taṃ jīvaṃ taṃ sarīra’nti vā, ‘aññaṃ jīvaṃ aññaṃ sarīra’nti vā, ‘hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘hoti ca na hoti ca tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā, ‘neva hoti na na hoti tathāgato paraṃ maraṇā’ti vā yāni cimāni dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni brahmajāle gaṇitāni, imā nu kho, bhante, diṭṭhiyo kismiṃ sati honti, kismiṃ asati na hontī”ti evamādinā (saṃ. ni. 4.345) pañhe puṭṭhe taṃ pañhaṃ vissajjetuṃ asakkontena. Imaṃ kira pañhaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ puṭṭho mahāthero tuṇhī ahosi. Atha isidattatthero cintesi – “ayaṃ thero neva attanā byākaroti, na aññaṃ ajjhesati, upāsako ca bhikkhusaṅghaṃ vihesati, ahametaṃ byākaritvā phāsuvihāraṃ katvā dassāmī”ti. Evaṃ cintetvā ca āsanato vuṭṭhāya therassa santikaṃ gantvā “byākaromahaṃ, bhante, cittassa gahapatino etaṃ pañha”nti (saṃ. ni. 4.345) āha. Evaṃ vutte thero “byākarohi tvaṃ, āvuso isidatta, cittassa gahapatino etaṃ pañha”nti isidattaṃ ajjhesi. Tena vuttaṃ – “pañhaṃ vissajjetuṃ asakkontena ajjhiṭṭho”ti.

250. In the third story, the deer were simply forms of deer. Regarding 'having persuaded them to accept alms,' it means persuading them to accept alms by saying, 'Venerable sirs, do me a favor; sit here and accept alms.' The wholesome qualities conducive to penetration, accumulated with a view to release from the round of existence, were a decisive support. Regarding 'he taught only the analysis of the six sense bases,' it means he gave a Dhamma talk connected only with the analysis of the six sense bases. Regarding 'by the elder,' it means by the great elder who was the most senior of all those assembled there. Regarding 'being unable to answer the question,' this refers to his being unable to answer the question when asked by the householder Citta in this way: 'Venerable elder, these various views that arise in the world—such as “the world is eternal,” or “the world is not eternal,” or “the world is finite,” or “the world is infinite,” or “the soul and the body are the same,” or “the soul and the body are different,” or “the Tathāgata exists after death,” or “the Tathāgata does not exist after death,” or “the Tathāgata both exists and does not exist after death,” or “the Tathāgata neither exists nor does not exist after death,” and these sixty-two views enumerated in the Brahmajāla—venerable sir, when what exists do these views come to be, and when what does not exist do they not come to be?' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.345). When this question was asked up to the third time, the great elder, it seems, remained silent. Then the Elder Isidatta thought: 'This elder neither answers himself nor requests another, and the lay follower is troubling the community of monks. I will answer this and provide a comfortable situation.' Having thought thus, he rose from his seat, went to the elder, and said: 'Venerable sir, I will answer this question of the householder Citta' (Saṃ. Ni. 4.345). When this was said, the elder requested Isidatta: 'Friend Isidatta, you answer this question of the householder Citta.' Therefore it was said: 'being unable to answer the question, he was requested.'

Pañhaṃ vissajjetvāti “yā imā, gahapati, anekavihitā diṭṭhiyo loke uppajjanti ‘sassato loko’ti vā, ‘asassato loko’ti vā…pe… yāni cimāni dvāsaṭṭhi diṭṭhigatāni brahmajāle gaṇitāni, imā kho, gahapati, diṭṭhiyo sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā sati honti, sakkāyadiṭṭhiyā asati na hontī”tiādinā nayena pañhaṃ vissajjetvā. Gihisahāyakabhāve ñāteti therassa gihisahāyakabhāve cittena gahapatinā ñāte. Citto kira, gahapati, tassa pañhaveyyākaraṇe tuṭṭho “kuto, bhante, ayyo isidatto āgacchatī”ti vatvā “avantiyā kho ahaṃ, gahapati, āgacchāmī”ti vutto “atthi, bhante, avantiyā [M 1.0202] isidatto nāma kulaputto amhākaṃ adiṭṭhasahāyo pabbajito, diṭṭho so āyasmatā”ti pucchi. Thero ca “evaṃ, gahapatī”ti vatvā “kahaṃ nu kho, bhante, so āyasmā etarahi viharatī”ti puna puṭṭho [V 1.0188] tuṇhī ahosi. Atha citto gahapati “ayyo no, bhante, isidatto”ti pucchitvā “evaṃ, gahapatī”ti vutte attano gihisahāyabhāvaṃ aññāsi.

Having answered the question thus: "Householder, these various views that arise in the world—'the world is eternal' or 'the world is not eternal'... and so on... these sixty-two views enumerated in the Brahmajāla—these views, householder, exist when there is identity-view; when there is no identity-view, they do not exist," he answered the question in this manner. The fact that the Elder had been a friend of the householder in his previous lay life was known through Citta the householder realizing it. Citta the householder, pleased with his explanation of the question, said, "Venerable sir, from where does the venerable Isidatta come?" When told, "I come from Avanti, householder," he asked, "Venerable sir, is there in Avanti a clansman named Isidatta, an unseen friend of ours, who has gone forth? Has the venerable one seen him?" The Elder replied, "Yes, householder." When asked further, "But where, venerable sir, does that venerable one dwell now?" the Elder remained silent. Then Citta the householder, asking, "Venerable sir, are you our Isidatta?" and hearing, "Yes, householder," recognized that they had been friends in their former lay lives.

Tejosamāpattipāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvāti ekasmiṃ kira divase citto gahapati “sādhu me, bhante, ayyo uttarimanussadhammā iddhipāṭihāriyaṃ dassetū”ti mahātheraṃ yāci. Thero “tena hi tvaṃ, gahapati, āḷinde uttarāsaṅgaṃ paññāpetvā tattha tiṇakalāpaṃ okirā”ti vatvā tena ca tathā kate sayaṃ vihāraṃ pavisitvā ca ghaṭikaṃ datvā tathārūpaṃ iddhābhisaṅkhāraṃ abhisaṅkhāresi, yathā tāḷacchiggaḷena ca aggaḷantarikāya ca acci nikkhamitvā tiṇāni jhāpeti, uttarāsaṅgaṃ na jhāpeti. Atha citto gahapati uttarāsaṅgaṃ papphoṭetvā saṃviggo lomahaṭṭhajāto ekamantaṃ ṭhito theraṃ bahi nikkhamantaṃ disvā “abhiramatu, bhante, ayyo macchikāsaṇḍe, ramaṇīyaṃ ambāṭakavanaṃ, ahaṃ ayyassa ussukkaṃ karissāmi cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārāna”nti āha. Tato thero “na dāni idha vasituṃ sakkā”ti tamhā vihārā pakkāmi. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “tejosamāpatti pāṭihāriyaṃ dassetvā ‘idāni idha vasituṃ na yutta’nti yathāsukhaṃ pakkāmī”ti. Dve aggasāvakātiādīsu yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ vitthārato vinayapāḷiyaṃ āgatameva.

Having displayed the fire-element concentration miracle, it is said that one day Citta the householder requested the great elder, saying, "Venerable sir, may the noble one show me a superhuman state, a miracle of psychic power." The elder replied, "Well then, householder, spread an upper robe on the terrace and scatter a bundle of grass there." When this was done, the elder entered his dwelling, locked the door, and performed such a feat of psychic power that flames issued forth from the keyhole and the space between the bolt, burning the grass but not the upper robe. Then Citta the householder, having shaken off the upper robe, agitated, his hair standing on end, stood aside. Seeing the elder coming out, he said, "May the noble one find delightful pleasure, venerable sir, in Macchikāsaṇḍa, the lovely ambāṭaka grove. I will attend to the noble one's needs—robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal requisites." Then the elder, thinking, "It is no longer possible to stay here," departed from that monastery. With this in mind, it was said: "Having displayed the fire-element concentration miracle, thinking 'Now it is not proper to stay here,' he departed as he pleased." In the case of the two chief disciples and so forth, what should be said is already detailed in the Vinaya Piṭaka.

Saddhoti lokiyalokuttarāya saddhāya samannāgato. Sīlenāti agāriyasīlaṃ anagāriyasīlanti duvidhaṃ sīlaṃ, tesu idha agāriyaṃ sīlaṃ adhippetaṃ, tena samannāgatoti attho. Yasobhogasamappitoti yādiso anāthapiṇḍikādīnaṃ pañcaupāsakasataparivārasaṅkhāto agāriyo yaso, tādiseneva yasena, yo ca dhanadhaññādiko ceva sattavidhaariyadhanasaṅkhāto cāti duvidho bhogo, tena ca samannāgatoti attho. Yaṃ yaṃ padesanti puratthimādīsu disāsu evarūpo kulaputto yaṃ yaṃ padesaṃ bhajati, tattha tattha evarūpena lābhasakkārena pūjitova hotīti attho.

`Faithful` means endowed with faith, both mundane and supramundane. `Virtuous` refers to two kinds of virtue: the virtue of a householder and the virtue of one gone forth. Here, the virtue of a householder is intended, meaning he is endowed with it. `Endowed with fame and wealth` means possessing fame like that of Anāthapiṇḍika and others, reckoned as a retinue of five hundred lay followers, as well as wealth of two kinds: material wealth such as money and grain, and the seven kinds of noble wealth. `Whatever region` means that to whatever region in the directions, east and so on, such a clansman resorts, there he is honored with gain and respect.

Hatthakaāḷavakavatthu

The Story of Hatthaka of Āḷavī

251. Catutthe [M 1.0203] catubbidhena saṅgahavatthunāti dānapiyavacanaatthacariyāsamānattatāsaṅkhātena catubbidhena saṅgahavatthunā. “Sve bhattacāṭiyā saddhiṃ āḷavakassa pesetabbo ahosī”ti vuttamatthaṃ pākaṭaṃ katvā dassetuṃ – “tatrāyaṃ anupubbikathā”tiādimāha. Migavatthāya araññaṃ gantvāti āḷavako rājā vividhanāṭakūpabhogaṃ chaḍḍetvā corappaṭibāhanatthañca paṭirājanisedhanatthañca byāyāmakaraṇatthañca sattame sattame divase migavaṃ gacchanto ekadivasaṃ balakāyena saddhiṃ “yassa passena [V 1.0189] migo palāyati, tasseva so bhāro”ti katakatikavatto migavatthāya araññaṃ gantvā. Ekaṃ miganti attano ṭhitaṭṭhānena palātaṃ eṇimigaṃ. Anubandhitvāti tiyojanamaggaṃ ekakova anubandhitvā. Javasampanno hi rājā dhanuṃ gahetvā pattikova tiyojanaṃ taṃ migamanubandhi. Ghātetvāti yasmā eṇimigā tiyojanavegā eva honti, tasmā parikkhiṇajavaṃ taṃ migaṃ udakaṃ pavisitvā ṭhitaṃ ghātetvā. Dvidhā chetvā dhanukoṭiyaṃ lagetvā nivattetvā āgacchantoti anatthikopi maṃsena “nāsakkhi migaṃ gahetu”nti apavādamocanatthaṃ dvidhā chinnaṃ dhanukoṭiyaṃ lagetvā āgacchanto. Sandacchāyanti ghanacchāyaṃ bahalapattapalāsaṃ.

251. In the fourth verse, `by the four bases of beneficence` refers to the fourfold means of beneficence: giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality. To clarify the meaning stated earlier—"Tomorrow, he was to be sent to Āḷavaka with a food bowl"—the text begins, "Here, this is the gradual account," and so on. `Having gone to the forest for hunting` means King Āḷavaka, having abandoned various theatrical enjoyments and gone hunting every seventh day with his army to ward off thieves, prevent rival kings, and exert himself, set a rule: "Whichever side the deer flees toward, that person bears the responsibility." Having gone to the forest for hunting, he pursued a deer that fled from his own position. `Having followed` means he alone pursued it for three leagues. The king, swift as he was, took his bow and chased the deer on foot for three leagues. `Having killed` refers to the deer, whose speed was exhausted after running for three leagues, entering water and standing still, where he killed it. `Having cut it in two, hung it on the end of his bow, and returned` means that even though he had no need for the meat, to avoid the blame of 'He could not catch the deer,' he cut it in two, hung it on the end of his bow, and returned. `Dense shade` means thick shade with abundant leaves and foliage.

Rukkhe adhivatthā devatāti āḷavakaṃ yakkhaṃ sandhāya vadati. So hi mahārājūnaṃ santikā varaṃ labhitvā majjhanhikasamaye tassa rukkhassa chāyāya phuṭṭhokāsaṃ paviṭṭhe pāṇino khādanto tattha paṭivasati. Āḷavakassa nisīdanapallaṅke nisīdīti yattha abhilakkhitesu maṅgaladivasādīsu āḷavako nisīditvā siriṃ anubhoti, tasmiṃyeva dibbaratanapallaṅke nisīdi. Attano gamane asampajjamāne “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti āvajjentāti tadā kira sātāgirahemavatā bhagavantaṃ jetavaneyeva vanditvā “yakkhasamāgamaṃ gamissāmā”ti saparivārā nānāyānehi ākāsena gacchanti, ākāse ca yakkhānaṃ na sabbattha maggo atthi, ākāsaṭṭhāni vimānāni pariharitvā maggaṭṭhāneneva maggo hoti, āḷavakassa pana vimānaṃ bhūmaṭṭhaṃ suguttaṃ pākāraparikkhittaṃ susaṃvihitadvāraṭṭālakagopuraṃ upari kaṃsajālasañchannamañjūsāsadisaṃ tiyojanaṃ ubbedhena, tassa upari maggo hoti, te taṃ padesamāgamma gantumasamatthā [M 1.0204] ahesuṃ. Buddhānañhi nisinnokāsassa uparibhāgena yāva bhavaggā koci gantumasamattho, tasmā attano gamane asampajjamāne “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti āvajjesuṃ. Tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā cintesīti yasmā assaddhassa saddhākathā dukkathā hoti dussīlādīnaṃ sīlakathādayo viya, tasmā tesaṃ yakkhānaṃ santikā bhagavato pasaṃsaṃ sutvā eva aggimhi pakkhittaloṇasakkharā viya abbhantare uppannakopena paṭapaṭāyamānahadayo hutvā cintesi. Pabbatakūṭanti kelāsapabbatakūṭaṃ.

`The deity dwelling in the tree` refers to the yakkha Āḷavaka. Indeed, having obtained a boon from the great kings, he dwells there, devouring beings who enter the space touched by the shade of that tree at midday. `He sat on Āḷavaka's sitting couch` means he sat on that very divine jeweled couch where, on auspicious days and other such marked occasions, Āḷavaka sits and enjoys his splendor. `When their movement was not proceeding, they considered, "What could be the reason?"` refers to the following: At that time, it is said, Sātāgira and Hemavata, having paid homage to the Blessed One in Jetavana, set out with their retinues in various vehicles through the sky, thinking, "We will go to the gathering of yakkhas." In the sky, yakkhas do not have paths everywhere; their path is only through designated routes, avoiding celestial mansions. But Āḷavaka’s mansion was on the ground, well-guarded, surrounded by walls, with well-arranged gates, watchtowers, and gatehouses, covered above with a bronze net like a jeweled casket, three yojanas in height. Above it was the path. Reaching that spot, they were unable to proceed. For no one is capable of passing over the place where a Buddha is seated, up to the summit of existence. Thus, when their movement was not proceeding, they wondered, "What could be the reason?" `Hearing their discussion, he thought` means the following: because for the faithless, talk of faith is difficult to hear, just as talk of virtue is to the immoral and so on, therefore, upon hearing the praise of the Blessed One from those yakkhas, his heart crackled with anger that had arisen internally, like salt and sugar thrown into a fire, and he thought. `The mountain peak` refers to the peak of Mount Kelāsa.

Ito paṭṭhāya āḷavakayuddhaṃ vitthāretabbanti so kira manosilātale vāmapādena ṭhatvā “passatha dāni tumhākaṃ vā satthā mahānubhāvo, ahaṃ vā”ti dakkhiṇapādena saṭṭhiyojanamattaṃ kelāsakūṭapabbataṃ akkami, taṃ ayokūṭappahato viya niddhantaayapiṇḍo papaṭikāyo muñci. So tatra ṭhatvā “ahaṃ āḷavako”ti ugghosesi, sakalajambudīpaṃ saddo phari. Tiyojanasahassavitthatahimavāpi sampakampi yakkhassānubhāvena. So vātamaṇḍalaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi “eteneva samaṇaṃ [V 1.0190] palāpessāmī”ti. Te puratthimādibhedā vātā samuṭṭhahitvā aḍḍhayojanayojanadviyojanatiyojanappamāṇāni pabbatakūṭāni padāletvā vanagaccharukkhādīni ummūletvā āḷavinagaraṃ pakkhandā jiṇṇahatthisālādīni cuṇṇentā chadaniṭṭhakā ākāse bhamentā. Bhagavā “mā kassaci uparodho hotū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Te vātā dasabalaṃ patvā cīvarakaṇṇamattampi cāletuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Tato mahāvassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi “udakena ajjhottharitvā samaṇaṃ māressāmī”ti. Tassānubhāvena uparūpari satapaṭalasahassapaṭalādibhedā valāhakā uṭṭhahitvā pavassiṃsu. Vuṭṭhidhārāvegena pathavī chiddā ahosi. Vanarukkhādīnaṃ upari mahogho āgantvā dasabalassa cīvare ussāvabindumattampi temetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tato pāsāṇavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Mahantāni mahantāni pabbatakūṭāni dhūmāyantāni pajjalantāni ākāsenāgantvā dasabalaṃ patvā dibbamālāguḷāni sampajjiṃsu. Tato paharaṇavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Ekatodhārā ubhatodhārā asisattikhurappādayo dhūmāyantā pajjalantā ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle dibbapupphāni ahesuṃ.

From that point onward, the battle with Āḷavaka should be elaborated in detail. It is said that he stood on the Manosilā plateau with his left foot and said, “Now see for yourselves whether your teacher is of great power, or I am!” Then, with his right foot, he stepped on the Kelāsakūṭa mountain, sixty yojanas in size, causing it to burst apart like a mass of iron struck by an iron hammer, scattering fragments in all directions. Standing there, he roared, “I am Āḷavaka!” His voice spread throughout the entire Jambudīpa. The Himavā, stretching three thousand yojanas, also trembled due to the yakkha’s power. He then raised a whirlwind, thinking, “With this, I will drive away the ascetic!” Winds arose from the east and other directions, splitting mountain peaks measuring half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and three yojanas, uprooting trees and forests, and rushing toward the city of Āḷavī, crushing old elephant stables and scattering roof tiles into the sky. The Blessed One resolved, “May no harm come to anyone.” When the winds reached the Ten-Powered One, they could not even stir the edge of his robe. Next, he summoned a great rainstorm, thinking, “I will kill the ascetic by overwhelming him with water!” By his power, clouds arose in layers—hundreds and thousands of them—and poured down rain. The force of the downpour pierced the earth. A great flood rose over the forests and trees, but it could not moisten even a dewdrop on the Ten-Powered One’s robe. Then he summoned a shower of stones. Massive mountain peaks, smoking and blazing, came from the sky toward the Ten-Powered One but turned into divine flower garlands upon reaching him. Next, he unleashed a rain of weapons. Single-edged and double-edged swords, spears, razors, and other weapons, smoking and blazing, came from the sky, but at the feet of the Ten-Powered One, they became divine flowers.

Tato [M 1.0205] aṅgāravassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Kiṃsukavaṇṇā aṅgārā ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle dibbapupphāni hutvā vikiriṃsu. Tato kukkuḷavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Accuṇho kukkuḷo ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle candanacuṇṇaṃ hutvā nipati. Tato vālikavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Atisukhumā vālikā dhūmāyantā pajjalantā ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle dibbapupphāni hutvā nipatiṃsu. Tato kalalavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Taṃ dhūmāyantaṃ pajjalantaṃ ākāsenāgantvā dasabalassa pādamūle dibbagandhaṃ hutvā nipati. Tato andhakāraṃ samuṭṭhāpesi “bhiṃsetvā samaṇaṃ palāpessāmī”ti. Caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ andhakārasadisaṃ hutvā dasabalaṃ patvā sūriyappabhāvihatamivandhakāraṃ antaradhāyi. Evaṃ yakkho imāhi navahi vātavassapāsāṇapaharaṇaṅgārakukkuḷavālikakalalandhakāravuṭṭhīhi bhagavantaṃ palāpetumasakkonto nānāvidhappaharaṇahatthaanekappakārarūpabhūtagaṇasamākulāya caturaṅginiyā senāya sayameva bhagavantaṃ abhigato. Te bhūtagaṇā anekappakāravikāre katvā “gaṇhatha hanathā”ti bhagavato upari āgacchantā viya ca honti. Apica kho niddhantalohapiṇḍaṃ viya makkhikā bhagavantaṃ allīyitumasamatthā eva ahesuṃ.

Then he created a shower of embers. Embers the color of the Kiṃsuka flower came down from the sky and, turning into divine flowers, scattered at the feet of the Ten-Powered One. Then he created a shower of hot ashes. Extremely hot ashes descended from the sky and, turning into sandalwood powder, fell at the feet of the Ten-Powered One. Then he created a shower of sand. Extremely fine sand, smoking and blazing, came down from the sky and, turning into divine flowers, fell at the feet of the Ten-Powered One. Then he created a shower of mud. That smoking, blazing mud descended from the sky and, turning into divine fragrance, fell at the feet of the Ten-Powered One. Then he created darkness, thinking, “I will terrify the ascetic and make him flee.” The darkness, like one endowed with four constituents, reached the Ten-Powered One but vanished like darkness dispelled by the sun’s radiance. Thus, the yakkha, unable to drive away the Blessed One with these nine showers—of wind, rain, stones, weapons, embers, hot ashes, sand, mud, and darkness—himself approached the Blessed One with a fourfold army teeming with a host of spirits wielding various weapons and assuming many terrifying forms. Those spirit hordes, though they made many frightful transformations and seemed to advance upon the Blessed One shouting, “Seize him! Strike him!”—yet they were as powerless to cling to the Blessed One as flies to a heated iron ball.

Evaṃ sabbarattiṃ anekappakāravibhiṃsākāradassanenapi bhagavantaṃ cāletumasakkonto āḷavako cintesi – “yaṃnūnāhaṃ kenaci ajeyyaṃ dussāvudhaṃ muñceyya”nti. Sace hi so duṭṭho ākāse taṃ dussāvudhaṃ muñceyya, dvādasa vassāni devo na vasseyya. Sace pathaviyaṃ muñceyya[V 1.0191], sabbarukkhatiṇādīni sussitvā dvādasavassantaraṃ na puna ruheyyuṃ. Sace samudde muñceyya, tattakapāle udakabindu viya sabbaṃ susseyya. Sace sinerupabbate muñceyya, khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ hutvā vikireyya. So evaṃmahānubhāvaṃ dussāvudhaṃ uttarisāṭakaṃ muñcitvā aggahesi. Yebhuyyena dasasahassilokadhātudevatā vegena sannipatiṃsu “ajja bhagavā āḷavakaṃ damessati, tattha dhammaṃ sossāmā”ti. Yuddhadassanakāmāpi devatā sannipatiṃsu. Evaṃ sakalampi ākāsaṃ devatāhi paripuṇṇaṃ ahosi. Athāḷavako bhagavato samīpe uparūpari vicaritvā vatthāvudhaṃ muñci[M 1.0206]. Taṃ asanicakkaṃ viya ākāse bheravasaddaṃ karontaṃ dhūmāyantaṃ pajjalantaṃ bhagavantaṃ patvā yakkhassa mānamaddanatthaṃ pādapuñchanacoḷaṃ hutvā pādamūle nipati. Āḷavako taṃ disvā chinnavisāṇo viya usabho, uddhaṭadāṭho viya sappo nittejo nimmado nipātitamānaddhajo ahosi. Evamidaṃ āḷavakayuddhaṃ vitthāretabbaṃ.

All night long, Āḷavaka tried by displaying various terrifying forms to shake the Blessed One, but he could not. Then he thought, “What if I were to release my dreadful weapon, which no one can withstand?” For if that wicked one were to release that dreadful weapon into the sky, no rain would fall for twelve years. If he were to release it upon the earth, all trees and grass would wither and not grow again for twelve years. If he were to release it into the ocean, the entire body of water would dry up like a drop of water on a hot pan. If he were to release it upon Mount Sineru, it would shatter into fragments and scatter. He took off his upper garment, which was a dreadful weapon of such great power, and grasped it. Most of the deities from the ten-thousandfold world-system swiftly gathered, thinking, “Today the Blessed One will subdue Āḷavaka, and we will hear the Dhamma there.” Deities desiring to witness the battle also assembled. Thus, the entire sky was filled with deities. Then Āḷavaka, after circling above the Blessed One, released his cloth weapon. Like a thunderbolt, it roared terrifyingly through the sky, smoking and blazing as it approached the Blessed One. To crush the yakkha’s pride, it became a foot-wiping cloth and fell at his feet. Seeing this, Āḷavaka became like a bull with broken horns, a snake with extracted fangs—devoid of power and pride, his banner of arrogance struck down. Thus this battle with Āḷavaka should be elaborated.

Aṭṭha pañhe pucchīti –

He asked eight questions:

“Kiṃ sūdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭhaṃ,

Kiṃ su suciṇṇaṃ sukhamāvahāti;

Kiṃ su have sādutaraṃ rasānaṃ,

Kathaṃ jīviṃ jīvitamāhu seṭṭha”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 183) –

“What here is the best wealth for a person? What well-practiced brings happiness? What, indeed, is the sweetest of flavors? How lived is life said to be the best?”

Ādinā aṭṭha pañhe pucchi. Satthā vissajjesīti –

With this as the first, he asked eight questions. The Teacher answered:

“Saddhīdha vittaṃ purisassa seṭṭhaṃ,

Dhammo suciṇṇo sukhamāvahāti;

Saccaṃ have sādutaraṃ rasānaṃ,

Paññājīviṃ jīvitamāhu seṭṭha”nti. (saṃ. ni. 1.246; su. ni. 184) –

“Faith here is the best wealth for a person, Dhamma well-practiced brings happiness; Truth, indeed, is the sweetest of flavors, A life lived by wisdom is said to be the best.”

Ādinā vissajjesi. Vikkandamānāyāti accantaṃ paridevamānāya.

He answered beginning with this. ‘Vikkandamānāya’ means ‘while lamenting excessively’.

Mahānāmasakkavatthu

The Story of Mahānāma the Sakyan

252. Pañcame [V 1.0192] satthā tato paraṃ paṭiññaṃ nādāsīti saṃvaccharato paraṃ sikkhāpadapaññattiyā paccayappavāraṇāsādiyanassa vāritattā “paṭiññaṃ nādāsī”ti vuttaṃ. Tathā hi bhagavā tatiyavārepi mahānāmena sakkena “icchāmahaṃ, bhante, saṅghaṃ yāvajīvaṃ bhesajjena pavāretu”nti (pāci. 304-305) vutte “sādhu sādhu, mahānāma, tena hi tvaṃ, mahānāma, saṅghaṃ yāvajīvaṃ bhesajjena pavārehī”ti paṭiññaṃ adāsiyeva. Evaṃ paṭiññaṃ datvā pacchā chabbaggiyehi bhikkhūhi mahānāmassa sakkassa viheṭhitabhāvaṃ sutvā chabbaggiye bhikkhū vigarahitvā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi “agilānena bhikkhunā cātumāsappaccayapavāraṇā sāditabbā aññatra punappavāraṇāya aññatra niccappavāraṇāya. Tato ce uttari sādiyeyya, pācittiya”nti. Tasmā paṭhamaṃ anujānitvāpi pacchā sikkhāpadabandhanena vāritattā “paṭiññaṃ nādāsī”ti vuttaṃ.

252. In the fifth story, the phrase “the Teacher did not give a promise thereafter” is stated because after one year, the acceptance of an invitation for requisites was forbidden by the laying down of a training rule. For indeed, when Mahānāma the Sakyan requested for the third time, “Venerable sir, I wish to invite the Saṅgha with medicine for life,” the Blessed One did give a promise, saying, “Good, good, Mahānāma. Therefore, Mahānāma, you may invite the Saṅgha with medicine for life.” Having given this promise, he later heard that Mahānāma the Sakyan had been harassed by the group-of-six monks. After rebuking those monks, he laid down a training rule: “A four-month invitation for requisites may be accepted by a monk who is not ill, except for a renewed invitation or a permanent invitation. If he should accept beyond that, it is an offense requiring expiation.” Therefore, although it was initially allowed, it was later forbidden by the binding of the training rule; hence it is said, “He did not give a promise.”

Uggagahapatyādivatthu

The Story of Ugga the Householder and Others

253-256. Chaṭṭhasattamaaṭṭhamanavamāni [M 1.0207] suviññeyyāneva.

253-256. The sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth are quite easy to understand.

Nakulapitugahapativatthu

The Story of Nakulapitar the Householder

257. Dasame susumāragirinagareti evaṃnāmake nagare. Tassa kira nagarassa vatthupariggahadivase avidūre udakarahade susumāro saddamakāsi, giraṃ nicchāresi. Atha nagare anantarāyena māpite tameva susumāragirakaraṇaṃ subhanimittaṃ katvā “susumāragirī”tvevassa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Keci pana “susumārasaṇṭhānattā susumāro nāma eko giri, so tassa nagarassa samīpe, tasmā taṃ susumāragiri etassa atthīti susumāragirīti vuccatī”ti vadanti. Bhesakaḷāvaneti bhesakaḷānāmake vane. “Bhesakalāvane”tipi pāṭho. Kathaṃ pana bhagavati nesaṃ puttasaññā patiṭṭhāsīti āha – “ayaṃ kirā”tiādi. Daharasseva daharā ānītāti me daharasseva sato daharā ānītāti attho. Aticaritāti atikkamitvā caranto.

257. In the tenth story, at Susumāragirinagara, a city of that name. It is said that on the day the site for that city was being determined, a crocodile in a lake not far away made a sound, emitting a roar. Then, because the city was built without obstruction, taking that very roar of the crocodile as a good omen, they gave it the name 'Susumāragiri.' Some, however, say: 'There is a mountain named Susumāra due to its crocodile-like shape, and it is near that city; therefore, the city is called Susumāragiri, meaning 'it has the Susumāra mountain.'' ‘Bhesakaḷāvana’ means ‘in a forest named Bhesakaḷāvana.’ The reading ‘Bhesakalāvane’ also occurs. How, indeed, was the perception of him as a son established for them with regard to the Blessed One? He says, 'This indeed...' etc. ‘Daharasseva daharā ānītā’ means ‘young ones were brought while I was still young.’ ‘Aticaritā’ means ‘transgressing’.

(Chaṭṭhaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.)

(The commentary on the sixth Etadagga chapter is concluded.)

Upāsakapāḷisaṃvaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Upāsaka Pāḷi is concluded.

(14) 7. Sattamaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā

(14) 7. Commentary on the Seventh Chapter on the Foremost

Sujātāvatthu

The Story of Sujātā

258. Upāsikāpāḷisaṃvaṇṇanāya [V 1.0193] paṭhamaṃ suviññeyyameva.

258. The first part of the commentary on the Upāsikā Pāḷi is indeed easily understood.

Visākhāvatthu

The Story of Visākhā

259. Dutiye mahālatāpasādhanassāti mahālatāpiḷandhanassa. Tasmiñca piḷandhane catasso vajiranāḷiyo upayogaṃ agamaṃsu. Muttānaṃ ekādasa nāḷiyo, pavāḷassa dvāvīsati nāḷiyo, padumarāgamaṇīnaṃ tettiṃsa nāḷiyo. Iti etehi ca aññehi ca indanīlādīhi nīlapītalohitodātamañjiṭṭhasāmakabaravaṇṇavasena sattavaṇṇehi vararatanehi niṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi, taṃ sīse paṭimukkaṃ yāva pādapiṭṭhiyā bhassati, pañcannaṃ [M 1.0208] hatthīnaṃ balaṃ dhārayamānāva naṃ itthī dhāretuṃ sakkoti. Antoaggi bahi na nīharitabbotiādīnaṃ attho upari āvi bhavissati. Sesamettha suviññeyyameva.

259. In the second story, ‘of the great creeper adornment’ means of the great creeper ornament. In that ornament, four tubes of diamond were used, eleven tubes of pearls, twenty-two tubes of coral, and thirty-three tubes of ruby. Thus, with these and other excellent jewels of seven colors—namely blue, yellow, red, white, crimson, dark, and variegated, such as sapphire and so on—it was completed. When fastened on the head, it hangs down to the top of the feet. Only a woman possessing the strength of five elephants is able to wear it. The meaning of 'internal fire should not be brought out,' and so on, will become clear later. The rest here is indeed easily understood.

Khujjuttarā-sāmāvatīvatthu

The Story of Khujjuttarā and Sāmāvatī

260-261. Tatiyacatutthesu pāyāsassāti bahalatarassa pāyāsassa. Taṃ pāyāsaṃ bhuñjantesūti taṃ bahalataraṃ garusiniddhaṃ pāyāsaṃ bhuñjantesu. Jīrāpetuṃ asakkontoti antarāmagge appāhāratāya mandagahaṇikattā jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto. Vāḷamigaṭṭhāneti vāḷamigehi adhiṭṭhitaṭṭhāne. Anuvijjantoti vicārento. Sālāti naḷakārasālā. Mudhā na karissatīti mūlyaṃ vinā na karissati. Ālimpesīti aggiṃ adāsi, aggiṃ jālesīti attho. Pekkhāti āgamehi. Upadhisampadāti sarīrasampatti. Vaṭarukkhaṃ patvāti nigrodharukkhaṃ patvā. Suvaṇṇakaṭaketi suvaṇṇavalaye. Abbhuṃ meti me avaḍḍhīti attho. Anto asodhetvāti paṇṇasālāya [V 1.0194] anto kassaci atthibhāvaṃ vā natthibhāvaṃ vā anupadhāretvā. Sesaṃ suviññeyyameva.

260-261. In the third and fourth stories, ‘of the rice porridge’ means of the very thick rice porridge. ‘While eating that rice porridge’ means while eating that very thick, heavy, and rich rice porridge. ‘Being unable to digest it’ means being unable to digest it along the way due to having little food and a weak digestion. ‘A place of wild beasts’ means a place inhabited by wild beasts. ‘Investigating’ means considering. ‘Hall’ means a reed-worker's hall. ‘He will not do it for nothing’ means he will not do it without payment. ‘He kindled’ means he gave fire, that is, he lit a fire. ‘Pekkhā’ means expectations. ‘Perfection of the substrata’ means bodily perfection. ‘Having reached the banyan tree’ means having reached the banyan tree. ‘Golden bracelets’ means gold bangles. ‘It has increased for me’ means ‘it has grown for me.’ ‘Without investigating inside’ means without ascertaining whether anyone was inside the leaf-hut or not. The rest is indeed easily understood.

Uttarānandamātāvatthu

The Story of Uttarā, Nanda's Mother

262. Pañcame upanissayaṃ disvāti iminā yathā visesādhigamassa satipi paccuppannapaccayasamavāye avassaṃ upanissayasampadā icchitabbā, evaṃ diṭṭhadhammavedanīyabhāvena vipaccanakassa kammassapi paccuppannasamavāyo viya upanissayasampadāpi savisesā icchitabbāti dasseti. Tathā hi ukkaṃsagatasappurisūpanissayayonisomanasikāresu labbhamānesupi upanissayarahitassa visesādhigamo na sampajjatevāti. Kappiyaṃ katvāti yathā kappiyaṃ hoti, tathā katvā. Patte patiṭṭhapeyyāti āhāraṃ dānamukhe vissajjeyya. Tīhi cetanāhīti pubbabhāgamuñcaanumodanācetanāhi. Vuttañhetaṃ –

262. In the fifth story, by ‘having seen the supporting condition,’ this is shown: just as for the attainment of distinction, even when there is a conjunction of present conditions, the perfection of a supporting condition is certainly to be wished for, so too for karma that ripens to be experienced in this very life, just like the conjunction of present conditions, a special perfection of a supporting condition is also to be wished for. For, even when excellent supporting conditions from virtuous persons and wise attention are available, the attainment of distinction does not succeed for one who is without a supporting condition. ‘Having made it suitable’ means having acted in such a way that it becomes suitable. ‘One should place it in the bowl’ means one should release the food as an act of giving. ‘With three volitions’ means with the volitions of the preliminary stage, the act of giving, and subsequent rejoicing. For it has been said:

“Pubbeva dānā sumano, dadaṃ cittaṃ pasādaye;

Datvā attamano hoti, esā puññassa sampadā”ti. (a. ni. 6.37; pe. va. 305);

“Before giving, one is joyful; while giving, one makes the mind serene; after giving, one is gratified—this is the accomplishment of merit.”

Tava [M 1.0209] manaṃ sandhārehīti “ajja bhattaṃ cirāyita”nti kodhato tava cittaṃ sandhārehi, mā kujjhīti attho. Olokitolokitaṭṭhānaṃ…pe… samparikiṇṇaṃ viya ahosīti tena kasitaṭṭhānaṃ sabbaṃ suvaṇṇabhāvāpattiyā mahākosātakipupphehi sañchannaṃ viya ahosi. Tādiseti tayā sadise. Na kopemīti na vināsemi, jātiyā na hīḷemi. Pūjaṃ karotīti sammāsambuddhassa pūjaṃ karoti. Antaravatthunti gehaṅgaṇaṃ. Bhoti sambodhane nipāto. Jeti avaññālapanaṃ. Sayaṃ ariyasāvikābhāvato satthuvasena “sapitikā dhītā”ti vatvā satthu sammukhā dhammassavanena tassā visesādhigamaṃ paccāsīsantī “dasabale khamanteyeva khamissāmī”ti āha. Kadariyanti thaddhamacchariṃ.

‘Restrain your mind’ means: because ‘today the meal is late,’ restrain your mind from anger; the meaning is, do not be angry. ‘The place wherever one looked… was as if completely strewn’ means that the entire plowed field, having attained a state of gold, appeared as if covered with great kosātaki blossoms. ‘In one such as that’ means in one similar to you. ‘I do not disturb’ means I do not destroy, I do not disparage by birth. ‘He offers worship’ means he offers worship to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. ‘The inner ground’ means the house-yard. ‘Bhoti’ is a particle used in addressing. ‘Je’ is a contemptuous form of address. Being herself a noble female disciple, and speaking of herself as ‘a daughter with her father’ in relation to the Teacher, she, hoping for the other's attainment of distinction through hearing the Dhamma in the Teacher’s presence, said, ‘I will forgive only when the Ten-Powered One forgives.’ ‘Kadariya’ means an obstinate miser.

Suppavāsāvatthu

The Story of Suppavāsā

263. Chaṭṭhe paṇītadāyikānanti paṇītarasavatthūnaṃ dāyikānaṃ. Āyuno ṭhitihetuṃ bhojanaṃ dentī āyuṃ deti nāma. Esa nayo vaṇṇaṃ detītiādīsu. Tenāha – “pañca ṭhānānī”ti. Kammasarikkhakañcetaṃ [V 1.0195] phalanti dassento “āyuṃ kho pana datvā”tiādimāha. Tattha datvāti dānahetu. Bhāginīti bhāgavatī laddhuṃ bhabbā.

263. In the sixth story, ‘of the givers of excellent things’ means of the givers of items with excellent flavors. One who gives food, which is the cause for the continuation of life, is said to give life. This is the principle in such cases as ‘one gives beauty,’ and so on. Therefore, he said, ‘five things.’ Showing that this fruit corresponds to the action, he said, ‘Having given life…,’ and so on. Therein, ‘having given’ is because of the gift. ‘A partaker’ means one who has a share, one who is fit to receive.

Suppiyāvatthu

The Story of Suppiyā

264. Sattame ūrumaṃsaṃ chinditvā dāsiyā adāsīti āgataphalā viññātasāsanā ariyasāvikā attano sarīradukkhaṃ acintetvā tassa bhikkhuno rogavūpasamameva paccāsīsantī attano ūrumaṃsaṃ chinditvā dāsiyā adāsi. Satthāpi tassā tathāpavattaṃ ajjhāsayasampattiṃ disvā “mama sammukhībhāvūpagamanenevassā vaṇo ruhitvā sañchavi jāyati, phāsubhāvo hotī”ti ca disvā “pakkosatha na”nti āha. Sā cintesīti “sabbalokassa hitānukampako satthā na maṃ dukkhāpetuṃ pakkosati, atthettha kāraṇa”nti cintesi. Attanā katakāraṇaṃ sabbaṃ kathesīti buddhānubhāvavibhāvanatthaṃ kathesi, na attano daḷhajjhāsayatāya vibhāvanatthaṃ. Gilānupaṭṭhākīnaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesīti agaṇitattadukkhā gilānānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ gelaññavūpasamane yuttappayuttāti gilānupaṭṭhākīnaṃ aggaṭṭhāne ṭhapesīti.

264. In the seventh story, regarding the phrase ‘having cut the flesh of her thigh, she gave it to the slave woman’: the noble female disciple, who had attained the fruit and understood the teaching, not considering her own bodily suffering and hoping only for the alleviation of that monk’s illness, cut the flesh of her own thigh and gave it to the slave woman. The Teacher, seeing the perfection of her disposition that had occurred in this way, and seeing that ‘just by her coming into my presence, her wound will heal, new skin will form, and she will be well,’ said, ‘Summon her.’ ‘She thought’ means she thought: ‘The Teacher, compassionate for the welfare of the entire world, does not summon me to cause me suffering; there must be a reason for this.’ ‘She recounted everything she had done’ means she spoke for the purpose of demonstrating the Buddha’s power, not for the purpose of demonstrating her own firm resolve. ‘He placed her in the foremost position among attendants of the sick’ means that because, disregarding her own suffering, she was diligently engaged in alleviating the illness of sick monks, he placed her in the foremost position among attendants of the sick.

Kātiyānīvatthu

The Story of Kātyāyanī

265. Aṭṭhame [M 1.0210] aveccappasannānanti ratanattayaguṇe yāthāvato ñatvā pasannānaṃ, so panassa pasādo maggenāgatattā kenaci akampanīyo. Adhigatenāti maggādhigameneva adhigatena. “Avigatenā”ti vā pāṭho, tassattho “kadāci avigacchantenā”ti. So appadhaṃsiyo ca hoti, tasmā vuttaṃ – “adhigatena acalappasādenā”ti. Tattha kāyasakkhiṃ katvāti pamukhaṃ katvā, vacanatthato pana nāmakāyena desanāya sampaṭicchanavasena sakkhibhūtaṃ katvāti attho. Ummaggaṃ khanitvāti gharasandhicchedanena antopavisanamaggaṃ khanitvā. Dullabhassavananti dullabhasaddhammassavanaṃ. Mahāpathavī pavisitabbā bhaveyyāti avīcippavesanaṃ vadati.

265. In the eighth, 'aveccappasannānaṃ' means of those with unwavering faith in the qualities of the Three Jewels, having truly understood them as they are. That faith, being attained through the path, is unshakable by anything. 'Adhigatena' means attained precisely through the attainment of the path. Alternatively, the reading is 'avigatena,' meaning 'never disappearing.' It is indestructible; therefore, it is said, 'with attained, unshakable faith.' Here, 'kāyasakkhiṃ katvā' means having made it foremost. But in terms of the meaning of the expression, it means having made the mental body a witness by way of receiving the teaching. 'Ummaggaṃ khanitvā' means digging a tunnel, having dug a passage through a house-wall to enter inside. 'Dullabhassavanaṃ' means hearing the Dhamma that is difficult to hear. 'Mahāpathavī pavisitabbā bhaveyyā' speaks of entering Avīci.

Nakulamātāvatthu

The Story of Nakula's Mother

266. Navame vissāsakathaneneva nakulamātā nakulapitā ca satthuvissāsikā nāma jātāti vuttaṃ – “vissāsikānanti vissāsakathaṃ kathentīnaṃ upāsikāna”nti. Gahapatānīti gehasāminī. Vuttamevāti upāsakapāḷiyaṃ nakulapitukathāyaṃ vuttanayameva.

266. In the ninth, it is said that by merely speaking words of trust, Nakula's mother and Nakula's father became known as confidants of the Teacher. Thus it is stated: 'vissāsikānaṃ' means of female lay disciples who speak words of trust. 'Gahapatānī' means a female householder. 'Vuttameva' refers to the method already explained in the story of Nakula's father in the text on laymen.

Kāḷīkuraragharikāvatthu

The Story of Kāḷī of Kuraraghara

267. Dasame [V 1.0196] anussavenevāti paccakkhato rūpadassanena satthu sammukhā dhammassavanena ca vinā kevalaṃ anussavaneneva parassa vacanaṃ anugatassavaneneva uppannena pasādena. Anussavikappasādanti anussavato āgatappasādaṃ.

267. In the tenth, 'anussaveneva' means with faith that has arisen only by hearsay, from following the words of another, without directly seeing a form or hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher. 'Anussavikappasādaṃ' refers to faith that comes from hearsay.

(Sattamaetadaggavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.)

The commentary on the Etadaggavagga, the seventh chapter, is completed.

Upāsikāpāḷisaṃvaṇṇanā samattā.

The commentary on the text on female lay disciples is complete.

Niṭṭhitā ca manorathapūraṇiyā

And the Manorathapūraṇī is completed.

Aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Of the commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

Etadaggavaggavaṇṇanāya anuttānatthadīpanā.

The explanation of the abstruse meaning in the commentary on the Etadaggavagga.

15. Aṭṭhānapāḷi (paṭhamavagga)

15. The Text on Impossibilities (First Chapter)

(15) 1. Aṭṭhānapāḷi-paṭhamavaggavaṇṇanā

(15) 1. Commentary on the First Chapter of the Text on Impossibilities

268. Aṭṭhānapāḷivaṇṇanāyaṃ [V 1.0197][M 1.0211] avijjamānaṃ ṭhānaṃ aṭṭhānaṃ, natthi ṭhānanti vā aṭṭhānaṃ. Anavakāsoti etthāpi eseva nayo. Tadatthanigamanameva hi “netaṃ ṭhānaṃ vijjatī”ti vacananti. Tenāha – “ubhayenapī”tiādi. Yanti kāraṇatthe paccattavacanaṃ. Hetuattho cettha kāraṇatthoti āha – “yanti yena kāraṇenā”ti. Ukkaṭṭhaniddesenettha diṭṭhisampatti veditabbāti vuttaṃ – “maggadiṭṭhiyā sampanno”ti. Kuto panāyamattho labbhatīti? Liṅgato, liṅgaṃ cetassa niccato upagamanappaṭikkhepo. Catubhūmakesūti idaṃ catutthabhūmakasaṅkhārānaṃ ariyasāvakassa visayabhāvūpagamanato vuttaṃ, na pana te ārabbha niccato upagamanasabbhāvato. Vakkhati hi “tadabhāve catutthabhūmakasaṅkhārā panā”tiādinā. Abhisaṅkhatasaṅkhāraabhisaṅkharaṇakasaṅkhārānaṃ sappadesattā nippadesasaṅkhāraggahaṇatthaṃ “saṅkhatasaṅkhāresū”ti vuttaṃ, lokuttarasaṅkhārānaṃ pana nivattane kāraṇaṃ sayameva vakkhati. Etaṃ kāraṇaṃ natthīti tathā upagamane setughāto natthi. Tejussadattāti saṃkilesavidhamanatejassa adhikabhāvato. Tathā hi te gambhīrabhāvena duddasā akusalānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ na hontīti. Idaṃ pana pakaraṇavasena vuttaṃ. Appahīnavipallāsānañhi santānesu kusaladhammānampi te ārammaṇaṃ na honti.
