“Those who, having adopted their doctrine, sit reciting and pondering by night or by day—for them, on that object, wrong mindfulness is established: ‘For the one who acts, no evil is done; there is no cause, no condition; the dead are annihilated.’ Their mind becomes one-pointed, and impulsions impel. In the first impulsion, they are remediable; likewise in the second and so on. By the seventh, even for Buddhas they are beyond remedy, irreversible, like a calamitous thorn. There, some enter upon one view, some two, some even three. Even having entered upon one, two, or three, they are of fixed wrong view. They have attained an obstruction to the path to heaven, and an obstruction to the path to liberation. They are incapable of going to heaven immediately after that existence, much less to liberation. Such a being is called a ‘stump of the cycle, a guardian of the earth.’ For the most part, there is no emergence from such an existence.”

Piṭṭhicakkavāḷeti jhāyamānacakkavāḷassa parato ekasmiṃ okāse. Yaṃ jhāyamānānaṃ ajjhāyamānānañca cakkavāḷānamantaraṃ, yattha lokantarikanirayasamaññā, tādise ekasmiṃ okāse. Paccatiyevāti cakkavāḷe jhāyamāne ajjhāyamānepi attano kammabalena paccatiyeva.

“Piṭṭhicakkavāḷa” refers to a location beyond the burning world-sphere. It is the space between burning and non-burning world-spheres, which is known as the world-interstice hell. In such a place, even when a world-sphere is burning or not burning, one is still tormented due to the power of one’s own kamma.

311. Catutthe “mā khalī”ti vacanaṃ upādāya evaṃladdhanāmoti taṃ kira sakaddamāya bhūmiyā telaghaṭaṃ gahetvā gacchantaṃ, “tāta, mā khalī”ti sāmiko āha. So pamādena khalitvā patitvā sāmikassa bhayena palāyituṃ āraddho. Sāmiko upadhāvitvā sāṭakakaṇṇe aggahesi. So sāṭakaṃ chaḍḍetvā acelako hutvā palāto paṇṇena vā tiṇena vā paṭicchādetumpi ajānanto jātarūpeneva ekaṃ gāmaṃ [M 1.0229] pāvisi. Manussā taṃ disvā “ayaṃ samaṇo arahā appiccho, natthi iminā sadiso”ti pūvabhattādīni gahetvā upasaṅkamitvā “mayhaṃ sāṭakaṃ anivatthabhāvena idaṃ uppanna”nti tato paṭṭhāya sāṭakaṃ labhitvāpi na nivāsesi, tadeva ca pabbajjaṃ aggahesi. Tassa santike aññepi aññepīti pañcasatā manussā pabbajiṃsu. Taṃ sandhāyetaṃ vuttaṃ – “mā khalīti vacanaṃ upādāya evaṃladdhanāmo titthakaro”ti.

311. In the fourth case, he was named thus based on the words “mā khalī” (don’t slip). It is said that while he was walking on muddy ground holding a pot of oil, his master said, “My dear, don’t slip.” But due to carelessness, he slipped and fell. Fearing his master, he started to flee. The master ran after him and grabbed the corner of his cloth. He discarded the cloth and, becoming naked, fled, not knowing how to cover himself even with leaves or grass. He entered a village in his birth-form. People saw him and thought, “This ascetic is an arahant, of few wishes—there is no one like him.” Bringing cakes, cooked rice, and so on, they approached him. Thinking, “This has arisen for me because of my state of not wearing a cloth,” from then on, even when he obtained a cloth, he did not wear it. He took up that very state as his going forth. In his presence, others and others—five hundred people—went forth. With reference to this it was said: “The sectarian teacher named ‘Mā Khalī’ was so called based on the words ‘Don’t slip.’”

Samāgataṭṭhāneti dvinnaṃ nadīnaṃ udakappavāhassa sannipātaṭṭhāne. Dvinnaṃ udakānanti dvinnaṃ udakappavāhānaṃ. Yathāvuttaṭṭhāne macchaggahaṇatthaṃ khipitabbato khippaṃ, kuminaṃ, tadeva idha khippanti vuttaṃ. Tenāha – “kumina”nti. Ucchūhīti udakaucchūhi. Tucchapuriso ariyadhammābhāvato. Jhānamattampi [V 1.0216] hi tassa nattheva, kuto ariyamaggo. Manussakhippaṃ maññeti manussā patitvā byasanappattiatthaṃ oṭṭitaṃ kuminaṃ viya. Tenāha – “mahājanassā”tiādi.

“At the place of meeting” means at the place where the water-flow of two rivers converges. “Of two waters” means of two streams of water. A `khippaṃ` is a `kumina` (fish-trap), so called because it is to be cast in the aforementioned place to catch fish. That very thing is here called `khippaṃ`. Therefore, it is said, “a fish-trap.” “Ucchūhi” means with water-reeds. A worthless person is so because of the absence of noble qualities. For such a person, even mere absorption is absent, so how much more the noble path? He thinks it is a “human-trap” (manussakhippaṃ), like a fish-trap laid for humans to fall into and meet with disaster. Therefore it is said: “of the great multitude,” and so on.

312. Pañcamādīsu bāhirakasāsananti avisesena vuttaṃ – tassa sabbassapi aniyyānikattā satthupaṭiññassapi asabbaññubhāvato. Tenāha – “tattha hī”tiādi. Gaṇoti sāvakagaṇo. Tathābhāvāyāti ācariyena vuttākāratāya samaṅgibhāvatthaṃ. Jaṅghasatanti bahū aneke satte. Samakameva akusalaṃ pāpuṇātīti tesaṃ sabbesaṃ ekajjhaṃ samādapanepi tesaṃ akusalena samakameva akusalaṃ pāpuṇāti ekajjhaṃ bahūnaṃ samādapanepi tathā ussahanassa balavabhāvato. Visuṃ visuṃ samādapane vattabbameva natthi. Yathā hi dhammacariyāyaṃ samakamevāti vattabbā kalyāṇamittatā, evaṃ adhammacariyāyaṃ akalyāṇamittatāti.

312. In the fifth case and so on, the term “external teaching” is stated without distinction—because all of them are non-leading-out and because one who claims to be a teacher is not omniscient. Hence it is said: “For there indeed,” and so on. “Group” means the group of disciples. “For that state” means for the purpose of being endowed with the manner stated by the teacher. “Hundreds of beings” means many, numerous beings. Regarding “he reaches the unwholesome equally”: even when encouraging all of them together, he reaches an unwholesome state equal to their unwholesome state; this is because, even when encouraging many together, the effort is powerful. There is nothing to be said about encouraging them individually. For just as in the practice of the Dhamma, good friendship should be said to be equally beneficial, so too in unrighteous conduct is bad friendship equally unbeneficial.

313. Suṭṭhu akkhāteti ekantato niyyānikabhāvena akkhāte. Satthā ca sabbaññū hotīti asabbaññuno niyyānikabhāvena kathetuṃ asakkuṇeyyattā. Dhammo ca svākkhāto sammāsambuddhappaveditattā. Gaṇo ca suppaṭipanno satthārā suvinītattā. Samādapako hītiādi suppaṭipattiyā nidassanaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.

313. “Well proclaimed” means proclaimed as unfailingly leading out. And the Teacher is omniscient, because a non-omniscient one would be unable to teach in a way that leads out. The Dhamma is well proclaimed because it is taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One. The Sangha is practicing well because it is well-trained by the Teacher. “He is an encourager,” and so on, should be seen as an example of good practice.

314. Pamāṇaṃ jānitabbanti “ayaṃ ettakena yāpeti, imassa ettakaṃ dātuṃ yutta”nti evaṃ pamāṇaṃ jānitabbaṃ. Atireke…pe… nibbānasampatti vā natthi durakkhātattā dhammassa. Tassāti paṭiggāhakassa. Appicchapaṭipadā nāma natthi durakkhāte dhammavinayeti adhippāyo.

314. “The measure should be known”: the measure should be known thus: “This person can sustain himself on this much; it is appropriate to give this much to him.” If there is excess... the attainment of Nibbāna is not possible because the Dhamma is poorly proclaimed. “For him” means for the receiver. The practice of contentment is not possible when the Dhamma and Discipline are poorly proclaimed—this is the meaning.

315. Dāyakassa [M 1.0230] vaso nāma uḷāruḷāratābhedo ajjhāsayo. Deyyadhammassa pana thokabahutāva deyyadhammassa vaso nāma. Attano thāmoti yāpanappamāṇaṃ. Yadi hītiādi “katha”ntiādinā saṅkhepato vuttassa atthassa vivaraṇaṃ. Anuppannassāti anuppanno assa puggalassa. Cakkhubhūto hotīti mahājanassa cakkhu viya hoti. Sāsanaṃ ciraṭṭhititaṃ karotīti anuppannalābhuppādanena mahājanassa pasāduppādanena ca ciraṭṭhitikaṃ karoti.

315. The term “the donor’s power” refers to the inclination, distinguished as noble or very noble. The term “the power of the gift,” however, refers to the quantity of the gift, whether small or large. “One’s own strength” means the measure of sustenance. The phrase “if indeed” and so on, up to “how,” is an explanation of the meaning stated briefly. “Of the unarisen” means for a person for whom [gain] has not arisen. “He becomes the eye” means he becomes like an eye for the multitude. “He makes the Dispensation long-lasting” means he makes it long-lasting by generating gain that has not yet arisen and by generating faith in the multitude.

Kuṭumbariyavihāreti kuṭumbariyagāmasannissitavihāre. Bhuñjanatthāyāti tasmiṃyeva gehe nisīditvā bhuñjanatthāya. Gahetvā gamanatthāyāti gehato bahi gahetvā gamanatthāya. Dhurabhattānīti niccabhattāni. Cūḷupaṭṭhākanti veyyāvaccakaraṃ. Vīmaṃsitvāti yathā uddissa kataṃ na hoti, evaṃ vīmaṃsitvā[V 1.0217]. Mahājano appiccho bhavituṃ maññatīti mahājano sayaṃ appiccho bhavituṃ maññati diṭṭhānugatiṃ āpajjanena. Mahājanassāti bahujanassa. Avattharitvāti vitthārikaṃ katvā.

“In the Kuṭumbariya monastery” means in the monastery dependent on the village of Kuṭumbariya. “For the purpose of eating” means for the purpose of eating, having sat down in that very house. “For the purpose of taking and going” means for the purpose of taking it from the house and going outside. “Constant provisions” means regular meals. “A junior attendant” means one who performs services. “Having investigated” means having investigated so that it is not something made specifically for one. “The great multitude thinks of becoming of few wishes” means the great multitude itself thinks of becoming of few wishes by following the example seen. “Of the great multitude” means of many people. “Having spread out” means having made it widespread.

316. Pañcātapatappanaṃ catūsu passesu aggisantāpassa upari sūriyasantāpassa ca tappanaṃ, tañca kho gimhakāle. Chinnappapātapabbatasikharato patanaṃ maruppapātapatanaṃ. Pubbaṇhādīsu ādiccābhimukhāvaṭṭanaṃ ādiccānuparivattanaṃ.

316. The torment of fivefold heat is being tormented by the heat of fire on four sides and by the heat of the sun above, and that too in the hot season. Falling from a broken-off precipice or mountain peak is falling from a precipice in a desert. Facing the sun in the morning and so on is turning to follow the sun.

317. Ayampīti svākkhāte dhammavinaye kusītopi. Sāmaññanti tapacaraṇaṃ. Dupparāmaṭṭhanti micchācaritaṃ saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ. Nirayāyupakaḍḍhatīti nirayadukkhāya naṃ kaḍḍhati.

317. “This one also” means even one who is lazy in the well-proclaimed Dhamma and Vinaya. “Recluseship” means the practice of austerity. “Wrongly grasped” means wrong conduct, which is defiled. “It drags one to hell” means it drags one to the suffering of hell.

318. Vuttappakāreti pañcātapatappanādike vuttappakāre.

318. “Of the kind described” means of the kind described, such as the fivefold heat-torment and so on.

319. Evanti vuttappakārāya cittappasādavhayasuppaṭipattiyā. Tena samaṇadhammakaraṇasukhañca saṅgaṇhāti.

319. “Thus” means by the well-practiced conduct of the kind described, called confidence of mind. Thereby he also grasps the happiness of performing the duties of a recluse.

320. Navakanipāteti imasmiṃyeva aṅguttaranikāye vakkhamānaṃ navakanipātaṃ sandhāyāha. Nava puggalāti sattakkhattuparamakolaṃkolādayo nava puggalā. Sabbatthāti imasmiṃ sutte vuttāvasiṭṭhesu sabbesu suttesu.

320. “In the Book of the Nines”: this is said referring to the Book of the Nines that will be spoken of in this very Aṅguttara Nikāya. “Nine persons” means the nine persons, such as the one who is at most seven-times, the family-to-family attainer, and so on. “Everywhere” means in all the remaining suttas spoken of in this sutta.

Tatiyavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the third chapter is finished.

16. Ekadhammapāḷi

16. The Text on One Thing

(16) 4. Ekadhammapāḷi-catutthavaggavaṇṇanā

(16) 4. Commentary on the Fourth Chapter of the Text on One Thing

322. Catutthassa [V 1.0218][M 1.0231] paṭhame saññāṇabhūtāti upalakkhaṇabhūtā. Pañcadasayojanāvaṭṭakkhandhāti pañcadasayojanakkhandhaparikkhepā. Yathā cāti ca-saddena kadambarukkhādīnaṃ kappaṭṭhāyibhāvaṃ viya yojanasatubbedhādibhāvaṃ samuccinoti, na pana jambuyā jambudīpassa viya tehi aparagoyānādīnaṃ saññāṇabhāvaṃ. Rāmaṇeyyakanti ramaṇīyabhāvaṃ. Sesapadesūti vanarāmaṇeyyakādipadesu. Uggataṃ kūlaṃ ussitabhāvo etassāti ukkūlaṃ, vigataṃ apagataṃ kūlaṃ etassāti vikūlanti āha – “unnataṭṭhānaṃ ninnaṭṭhāna”nti ca. Nandiyāvaṭṭamacchapiṭṭhenevāti kujjakakulisakamacchasaṅghātapiṭṭheneva.

322. In the first of the fourth, “being a sign” means being an indication. “A round mass of fifteen yojanas” means a mass with a circumference of fifteen yojanas. “And just as”: by the word “ca” (and), it includes the state of lasting for an aeon, like the kadamba tree and so on, or the state of being a hundred yojanas in height and so on, but not their being a sign for Aparagoyāna and the other continents, as the rose-apple tree is for Jambudīpa. “Delightfulness” means the state of being delightful. “In the remaining places” means in places such as delightful groves and so on. “High bank” (`ukkūlaṃ`): it has a “risen bank” (`uggataṃ kūlaṃ`); “low bank” (`vikūlaṃ`): it has a “departed bank” (`vigataṃ kūlaṃ`). Thus it is said: “a high place and a low place.” “Like the back of a Nandiyāvaṭṭa fish” means like the back of a cluster of hunchbacked and `kulisaka` fish.

323. Dutiyādīsu cattāro apāyā aññatra manussehīti adhippetā, na devā aññatra manussehīti hīnāya jātiyā adhippetattā. Upādāyupādāyāpi majjhimadeso labbhati, yattha gati bhikkhūnaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ upāsakānaṃ upāsikānaṃ aññesampi kammavādikiriyavādiviññujātikānaṃ, yo patirūpadesoti vuccati. Tenāha – “sakalopi hī”tiādi.

323. In the second and following, by “other than humans” the four woeful states are intended, not the gods, because an inferior birth is intended. Even gradually, the middle country is obtained, where the destination of monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, and other wise people who hold to the doctrine of kamma and the doctrine of action is found; this is called a suitable country. Therefore it is said: “For the whole…” and so on.

324. Eḷāti doso. Tenāha – “niddosamukhāti attho”ti.

324. “Eḷā” means a fault. Therefore it is said: “The meaning is ‘with a faultless mouth.’”

326. Tathāgatassa guṇe jānitvā cakkhunāpi dassanaṃ dassanameva, ajānitvā pana dassanaṃ tiracchānagatānampi hotiyevāti āha – “ye tathāgatassa guṇe jānitvā”tiādi.

326. Knowing the virtues of the Tathāgata, even seeing with the eye is truly seeing; but seeing without knowing occurs even among animals. Thus it is said: “Those who, knowing the virtues of the Tathāgata…” and so on.

327. Pakāsetvā kathitanti saccāni pakāsetvā kathitaṃ.

327. “Having made clear, it is spoken” means having made clear the truths, it is spoken.

328. Sutānaṃ dhammānaṃ asammoso dhāraṇanti āha – “dhārentīti na pammussantī”ti.

328. Retention is the non-forgetting of the teachings that have been heard. Thus it is said: “They retain” means “they do not forget.”

329. Atthānatthaṃ upaparikkhantīti “ayaṃ imissā pāḷiyā attho, ayaṃ na attho”ti [V 1.0219] atthānatthaṃ upaparikkhanti. Anatthaparihārena hi atthaggahaṇaṃ yathā adhammaparivajjanena dhammappaṭipatti.

329. “They examine the meaning and non-meaning” means they scrutinize, “This is the meaning of this Pāli text; this is not the meaning,” thus examining the meaning and non-meaning. For grasping the meaning by avoiding the non-meaning is like practicing the Dhamma by avoiding what is not the Dhamma.

330. Anulomapaṭipadanti nibbānassa anulomikaṃ paṭipadaṃ.

330. “The conforming practice” means the practice that is in conformity with Nibbāna.

331. Saṃvegajanakesu [M 1.0232] kāraṇesūti saṃvegajanakesu jātiādīsu kāraṇesu. Saṃvejanīyesu ṭhānesu sahottappañāṇaṃ saṃvego.

331. “In causes that give rise to spiritual urgency” means in causes such as birth and so on that give rise to spiritual urgency. Spiritual urgency is knowledge together with moral dread in places that cause spiritual urgency.

332. Upāyenāti yena upāyena vaṭṭūpacchedo, tena upāyena. Padhānavīriyaṃ karontīti sammappadhānasaṅkhātaṃ vīriyaṃ karonti uppādenti.

332. “By a means” means by that means by which there is the cutting off of the round of existence. “They make an effort” means they make, they produce, the effort called “right exertion.”

333. Vavassajīyanti vissajjīyanti ettha saṅkhārāti vavassaggo, asaṅkhatā dhātūti āha – “vavassaggo vuccati nibbāna”nti.

333. “Relinquishment” (`vavassaggo`): it is “relinquishment” because formations are relinquished in it. It is the unconditioned element. Thus it is said: “Relinquishment is called Nibbāna.”

334. Uttamannānanti uttamānaṃ pañcannaṃ bhojanānaṃ. Uttamarasānanti uttamānaṃ rasānaṃ. Uñchācārenāti uñchācariyāya kassaci apariggahabhūtassa kiñci ayācitvā gahaṇaṃ uñchācāro. Ettha cātiādinā annādīnaṃ aggabhāvo nāma manāpaparamo icchitakkhaṇalābho, na tesaṃ lābhitāmattanti dasseti. Paṭilabhantīti denti paṇītabhāvena. Bhattassa ekapātīti ekapātipūraṃ bhattaṃ. Idaṃ kiṃ nāmāti “idaṃ annaggarasaggaṃ nāma hoti, na hotī”ti pucchati. Uñchena kapālābhatenāti missakabhattena. Yāpenteti yāpanasīsena yāpanahetuṃ bhattaṃ vadati. Upādāya aggarasaṃ nāmāti taṃ taṃ upādāyupādāya annaggarasaggaṃ daṭṭhabbanti dasseti. Cakkavattiāhārato hi cātumahārājikānaṃ āhāro aggoti evaṃ yāva paranimmitavasavattidevā netabbaṃ.

334. “Of the best foods” means of the five best foods. “Of the best flavors” means of the best flavors. “By the practice of gleaning”: the practice of gleaning is the taking of something by one who is unattached to anyone, without asking. Here, by “and so on,” it is shown that the excellence of food and so on is its supreme pleasantness and being obtained at the desired moment, not the mere fact of obtaining it. “They obtain” means they give because of its fine quality. “One bowl of food” means a bowl-full of food. “What is this called?” means one asks, “Is this called the best of food and flavor, or not?” “By what is gleaned and brought in the bowl” means by mixed food. “They sustain themselves”: one speaks of food as a cause of sustenance, for the sake of sustenance. “The best flavor in relation to”: this shows that the best food and flavor should be seen in relation to this and that. For the food of the Four Great Kings is excellent compared to the food of a wheel-turning monarch; thus it should be understood up to the Paranimmitavasavattī devas.

335. Attharaso nāma cattāri sāmaññaphalāni “ariyamaggānaṃ phalabhūto raso”ti katvā. Dhammaraso nāma cattāro maggā “sāmaññaphalassa hetubhūto raso”ti katvā vimuttiraso nāma amataṃ nibbānaṃ “sabbasaṅkhārasamatho”ti katvā.

335. The flavor of the goal is the four fruits of recluseship, taking it as “the flavor that is the fruit of the noble paths.” The flavor of the Dhamma is the four paths, taking it as “the flavor that is the cause of the fruit of recluseship.” The flavor of liberation is the deathless Nibbāna, taking it as “the stilling of all formations.”

Catutthavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the fourth chapter is finished.

Jambudīpapeyyālo niṭṭhito.

The Jambudīpa repetition series is finished.

17. Pasādakaradhammavaggavaṇṇanā

17. Commentary on the Chapter on Qualities that Inspire Confidence

366. Addhamidanti [V 1.0220] sandhivasena pāḷiyaṃ rassaṃ katvā vuttaṃ, ma-kāro padasandhikaroti āha – “addhā ida”nti. Ekaṃso esāti ekaṃso hetu [M 1.0233] esa lābhānaṃ. Pāpakaṃ nāmāti appakampi pāpaṃ nāma byattaṃ ekaṃsena na karoti. Tathassāti tathā sammāpaṭipajjamānassa assa. Āraññikattaṃ…pe… tecīvarikattanti imesaṃ dhutadhammānaṃ gahaṇeneva itaresampi taṃsabhāgānaṃ gahitabhāvo daṭṭhabbo. Thāvarappattabhāvoti sāsane thirabhāvappatti therabhāvo. Ākappassa sampattīti “añño me ākappo karaṇīyo”ti evaṃ vuttassa ākappassa sampatti. Kolaputtīti kolaputtiyanti āha – “kulaputtabhāvo”ti. Sampannarūpatāti upadhisampadā. Vacanakiriyāyāti vacanappayogassa madhurabhāvo mañjussaratā. Tenassa lābho uppajjatīti idaṃ na lābhuppādanūpāyadassanaparaṃ, atha kho evaṃ sammāpaṭipajjamānassa anicchantasseva lābho uppajjatīti lābhassa abyabhicārahetudassanaparaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Yathāha –

366. “Addhamidaṃ” is said in the Pāli, having been made short for the sake of euphonic conjunction; the letter “m” makes the word-conjunction, it is said, meaning “addhā idaṃ” (indeed this). “This is certain” means “this is a certain cause of gains.” “Evil” means one does not do even a little evil, which is manifest, with certainty. “Of such a one” means “of one who is practicing rightly thus.” “Being a forest-dweller… being a triple-robe-wearer”: by the taking up of these ascetic practices, it should be understood that other similar ones are also taken up. “The state of having attained firmness” means the attainment of a firm state in the Dispensation, the state of an elder. “Perfection of demeanor” means the perfection of demeanor spoken of thus: “another demeanor should be adopted by me.” “Being of good family” is explained as “the state of being a son of good family.” “Perfection of form” means perfection of the physical basis. “Action of speech” means the sweetness, the pleasantness of voice, in the use of speech. The phrase “gain arises for him” is not for the purpose of showing a means of producing gain, but rather it should be seen as showing the unfailing cause of gain, in that gain arises for one practicing rightly thus even without his wishing for it. As it is said:

“Ākaṅkheyya ce, bhikkhave, bhikkhu lābhī assaṃ cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānappaccayabhesajjaparikkhārānanti, sīlesvevassa paripūrakārī”ti (ma. ni. 1.65).

“If a monk, O monks, should wish: ‘May I be one who obtains robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick,’ let him be one who fulfills the precepts.”

Pasādakaradhammavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Section of Things That Cause Serenity is concluded.

18. Aparaaccharāsaṅghātavaggavaṇṇanā

18. Commentary on the Chapter on the Other Snap of the Fingers

382. Idampi [V 1.0221] suttanti ettha pi-saddo heṭṭhā vuttacūḷaccharāsaṅghātasuttaṃ sampiṇḍeti. Cūḷaccharāsaṅghātasutte appanaṃ appattāya mettāya tāvamahanto vipāko dassito, kimaṅgaṃ pana imissā appanāppattāya mettāyāti dassetuṃ – “appanāppattāya hī”tiādimāha. Vipākakathāyeva natthīti vipāke kathāyeva natthi, ayameva vā pāṭho. Gaṇanānupubbatāti gaṇanānupubbatāya. Paṭhamaṃ uppannantipi paṭhamaṃ, paṭhamaṃ samāpajjatīti idaṃ pana na ekantalakkhaṇaṃ. Ciṇṇavasībhāvo hi aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī ādito paṭṭhāya matthakaṃ pāpentopi samāpajjituṃ sakkoti, matthakato paṭṭhāya ādiṃ pāpentopi, antarantarā okkantopi samāpajjituṃ sakkoti eva. Pubbuppattiyaṭṭhena pana paṭhamaṃ nāma hoti. Vibhaṅgeti jhānavibhaṅge. Vipassanaṃ kayiramānaṃ lakkhaṇūpanijjhānakiccaṃ maggena sijjhati taggatasammohaviddhaṃsanato[M 1.0234]. Apica vipassanāya lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ maggena uppannena sijjhati itarathā parivattanato, tasmā maggo lakkhaṇūpanijjhānaṃ, na aniccādilakkhaṇānaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇato. Yathā phalaṃ nibbānassa asaṅkhatalakkhaṇaṃ ārammaṇakaraṇavasena upanijjhāyati, evaṃ maggopi. Evampissa lakkhaṇūpanijjhānataṃ veditabbaṃ. Vattabbameva natthi arittajjhānatāya. Sesaṃ visesaṃ, arittajjhānā evāti attho.

382. ‘Idampi sutta’—here the word ‘pi’ connects it with the Cūḷaccharāsaṅghātasutta mentioned earlier. In the Cūḷaccharāsaṅghātasutta, such a great result of loving-kindness not attained to absorption was shown; how much more then for this loving-kindness attained to absorption—thus it is said, ‘for one attained to absorption,’ etc. ‘Vipākakathāyeva natthi’ means ‘there is no discussion of the result’; or, this is the reading. ‘Gaṇanānupubbatā’ means ‘in the order of enumeration’. ‘Paṭhamaṃ uppanna’ is first, but ‘first entering upon’ is not an absolute characteristic. For one who has practiced mastery, even one who has attained the eight attainments, from the beginning up to the peak can enter absorption, or from the peak down to the beginning, or entering in between. But by the reason of prior arising, it is called first. ‘Vibhaṅgeti’ means ‘in the analysis of jhāna’. While insight is being practiced, the function of scrutinizing characteristics is accomplished by the path as it dispels delusion related to that. Moreover, the characteristic scrutiny of insight is accomplished by the path when it arises, otherwise it would be reversal. Therefore, the path is the characteristic scrutiny, not because it takes impermanence, etc., as objects. Just as the fruit contemplates the unconditioned characteristic of Nibbāna as its object, so too does the path. Thus, its characteristic scrutiny should be understood. ‘Vattabbameva natthi’ means ‘there is nothing to be said’—because of the non-interrupted jhāna. The rest is a distinction—meaning, they are indeed non-interrupted jhānas.

386-387. Hitapharaṇanti sattesu hitānurūpaṃ jhānassa pharitvā pavattanaṃ. Cetopaṭipakkhato vimuccati etāyāti cetovimutti, appanāppattā mettā. Tenāha – “idhā”tiādi. Eseva nayoti iminā karuṇādīnampi appanāppattataṃ atidisati. Vaṭṭaṃ honti kammavaṭṭabhāvato. Vaṭṭapādā hontīti vipākavaṭṭassa kāraṇaṃ honti.

386-387. ‘Hitapharaṇa’ means ‘the spreading and maintaining of jhāna in a manner corresponding to benefit for beings’. ‘Cetovimutti’ means ‘liberation of mind’ because ‘one is freed through this’; it is loving-kindness attained to absorption. Hence it is said, ‘here,’ etc. ‘Eseva nayo’ means ‘by this same method’—thus he also indicates the attainment to absorption of compassion, etc. ‘Vaṭṭaṃ honti’ means ‘they are rounds’—because they are states of the round of kamma. ‘Vaṭṭapādā honti’ means ‘they are the basis of the round’—they are causes of the round of result.

390. Ajjhattaparikammavasenāti attano kesādīsu parikammakaraṇavasena. Aṭṭhārasavidheti aṭṭhārasappabhede. Kāyeti rūpakāye. Rūpakāyo hi idha aṅgapaccaṅgānaṃ kesādīnañca dhammānaṃ samūhaṭṭhena hatthikāyarathakāyādayo viya kāyoti adhippeto. Samūhavisayatāya cassa kāyasaddassa samudāyūpādanatāya ca asubhākārassa “kāye”ti ekavacanaṃ. Tathā ārammaṇādivibhāgena anekabhedabhinnampi cittaṃ cittabhāvasāmaññena ekajjhaṃ gahetvā “citte”ti ekavacanaṃ kataṃ. Kāyānupassīti imassa atthaṃ dassetuṃ – “tameva kāyaṃ paññāya anupassanto”ti āha. Tameva kāyanti ca [V 1.0222] avadhāraṇena vedanādianupassanaṃ nivatteti. Tena ca puna kāyaggahaṇassa payojanaṃ sūcitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. “Kāye”ti hi vatvāpi puna “kāyānupassī”ti dutiyaṃ kāyaggahaṇaṃ asammissato vavatthānaghanavinibbhogādidassanatthaṃ kataṃ. Tena vedanādayopi ettha sitā, ettha paṭibaddhāti kāyavedanādianupassanappasaṅgepi āpanne na kāye vedanānupassī cittānupassī dhammānupassī vā. Atha kho kāyānupassīyevāti kāyasaṅkhātavatthusmiṃ kāyānupassanākārasseva dassanena asammissato vavatthānaṃ dassitaṃ hoti. Tathā na kāye aṅgapaccaṅgavinimuttaekadhammānupassī, nāpi kesalomādivinimuttaitthipurisānupassī. Yopi cettha kesalomādiko bhūtupādāyasamūhasaṅkhāto kāyo, katthapi na bhūtupādāyavinimuttaekadhammānupassī, atha kho rathasambhārānupassako viya aṅgapaccaṅgasamūhānupassī[M 1.0235], nāgarāvayavānupassako viya kesalomādisamūhānupassī, kadalikkhandhapattavaṭṭivinibbhujjako rittamuṭṭhiviniveṭhako viya ca bhūtupādāyasamūhānupassīyevāti nānappakārato samūhavaseneva kāyasaṅkhātassa vatthuno dassanena ghanavinibbhogo dassito hoti. Na hettha yathāvuttasamūhavinimutto kāyo vā itthī vā puriso vā añño vā koci dhammo dissati, yathāvuttadhammasamūhamatteyeva pana tathā tathā sattā micchābhinivesaṃ karonti.

390. ‘Ajjhattaparikammavasena’ means ‘by way of making preparation regarding one’s own hair and so on’. ‘Aṭṭhārasavidha’ means ‘having eighteen varieties’. ‘Kāye’ means ‘in the material body’. For here, the material body is intended as ‘body’ in the sense of a collection of limbs and parts, and of phenomena like hair, etc., just as an elephant’s body, a chariot’s body, and so on are called ‘body’ because they are collections. And because the word ‘body’ refers to a collective object, and because it is used to denote an aggregate, and because of the aspect of foulness, the singular form ‘in the body’ is used. Similarly, though the mind is divided into many types by distinctions such as object, etc., it is referred to in the singular as ‘in the mind’ by taking it as a single entity due to the common characteristic of the state of mind. To show the meaning of ‘kāyānupassī’ (one who contemplates the body), it is said: ‘contemplating that very body with wisdom’. And by the emphatic particle in ‘that very body,’ the contemplation of feelings, etc., is excluded. And thereby the purpose of mentioning ‘body’ again is indicated; this should be understood. For though ‘in the body’ is stated, the second mention of ‘kāyānupassī’ (one who contemplates the body) is made to show distinction without mixing, the dismantling of solidity, and so on. Thus, even when feelings, etc., are situated here, are bound here, one does not contemplate feelings in the body, nor the mind, nor phenomena. Rather, by seeing only the mode of contemplating the body in the object designated as the body, distinction without mixing is shown, meaning one is solely a contemplator of the body. Similarly, one does not contemplate a single phenomenon in the body separate from limbs and parts, nor a woman or man separate from hair, etc. Even the body here, which is designated as a collection of the great elements and derived matter, is nowhere contemplated as a single phenomenon separate from the great elements and derived matter; instead, just as one who contemplates a chariot’s parts contemplates the collection of limbs, or one who contemplates the parts of an elephant contemplates the collection of hair, etc., or like one who peels off a banana trunk layer by layer or unwraps an empty fist, one contemplates only the collection of the great elements and derived matter. Thus, by seeing the object designated as ‘body’ as a mere collection in various ways, the dismantling of solidity is shown. For here, no body, woman, man, or any other phenomenon is seen apart from the aforementioned collection of phenomena. Yet, beings wrongly fixate on these very collections in various ways.

Aṭṭhārasavidhenāti aṭṭhārasavidhā. Satipaṭṭhānabhāvakassāti satipaṭṭhānabhāvaṃ bhāventassa. Tīsu bhavesu kilese ātapetīti ātāpo, vīriyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Yadipi hi kilesānaṃ pahānaṃ ātāpananti, taṃ sammādiṭṭhiādīnampi attheva. Ātapasaddo viya pana ātāpasaddopi vīriyeva niruḷho. Atha vā paṭipakkhappahāne sampayuttadhammānaṃ abbhussahanavasena pavattamānassa vīriyassa sātisayaṃ tadātāpananti vīriyameva tathā vuccati, na aññadhammā, tasmā ātāpoti vīriyassa nāmaṃ, so assa atthīti ātāpī. Ayañca īkāro pasaṃsāya atisayassa vā dīpakoti ātāpiggahaṇena sammappadhānasamaṅgitaṃ dasseti. Tenevāha – “ātāpīti…pe… vīriyena vīriyavā”ti. Sampajānoti sampajaññasaṅkhātena ñāṇena samannāgato. Tenāha – “aṭṭhārasavidhena…pe… sammā pajānanto”ti. Ayaṃ panettha vacanattho – sammā samantato sāmañca pajānanto sampajāno, asammissato vavatthāne aññadhammānupassitābhāvena sammā aviparītaṃ sabbākārappajānena samantato uparūparivisesāvahabhāvena pavattiyā sammā pajānantoti attho.

‘Aṭṭhārasavidhena’ means ‘of eighteen kinds’. ‘Satipaṭṭhānabhāvakassa’ means ‘for one cultivating the development of mindfulness’. ‘Ātāpo’ means ‘it burns up defilements in the three realms’; this is a name for energy. Indeed, even the abandoning of defilements is called ‘ātāpana’, and this applies to right view and other factors as well. However, just as the word ‘ātāpa’ (heat) is established in its literal sense, so too is the word ‘ātāpa’ (ardor) established in the sense of energy. Alternatively, because energy arises with an excess of effort in abandoning opposing states and generating associated phenomena, that very ‘ātāpana’ is called energy—not any other factor. Therefore, ‘ātāpa’ is a name for energy, and one who possesses it is called ‘ātāpī’. And this suffix ‘-ī’ indicates praise or an excess; thus, by the term ‘ātāpī,’ it shows the endowment with right efforts. Hence it is said: ‘Ātāpī… possessing energy with energy’. ‘Sampajāno’ means ‘endowed with knowledge known as clear comprehension’. Therefore, it is said: ‘Eighteenfold… rightly comprehending’. Here, the meaning of the statement is: ‘Sammā pajānanto’ (rightly comprehending) means comprehending thoroughly and completely, without confusion, distinguishing correctly with no observing of other phenomena, comprehending rightly and without distortion in all aspects, and producing successive distinctions in the course of practice—this is the meaning.

Kāyo ca idha lujjanappalujjanaṭṭhena lokoti adhippetoti āha – “tasmiṃyeva kāyasaṅkhāte loke”ti. Pañcakāmaguṇikataṇhanti rūpādīsu pañcasu kāmaguṇesu pavattamānaṃ taṇhaṃ[V 1.0223]. Yasmā panettha abhijjhāgahaṇena kāmacchando, domanassaggahaṇena byāpādo saṅgahaṃ gacchati, tasmā nīvaraṇapariyāpannabalavadhammadvayadassanena nīvaraṇappahānaṃ vuttaṃ hotīti veditabbaṃ. Visesena cettha abhijjhāvinayena kāyasampattimūlakassa anurodhassa, domanassavinayena kāyavipattimūlakassa virodhassa, abhijjhāvinayena ca kāye abhiratiyā, domanassavinayena kāyabhāvanāya anabhiratiyā, abhijjhāvinayena kāye abhūtānaṃ [M 1.0236] subhasukhabhāvādīnaṃ pakkhepassa, domanassavinayena kāye bhūtānaṃ asubhāsukhabhāvādīnaṃ apanayanassa ca pahānaṃ vuttaṃ. Tena yogāvacarassa yogānubhāvo yogasamatthatā ca dīpitā hoti. Yogānubhāvo hi esa, yadidaṃ anurodhavirodhavippamutto aratiratisaho abhūtapakkhepabhūtāpanayanavirahito ca hoti. Anurodhavirodhavippamutto cesa aratiratisaho abhūtaṃ apakkhipanto bhūtañca anapanento yogasamattho hotīti. Suddharūpasammasanameva kathitanti kevalaṃ kāyānupassanābhāvato vuttaṃ.

The body here is intended as the world in the sense of crumbling and disintegrating, as stated: “in that very body designated as the world.” The craving for the five strands of sensual pleasure refers to the craving that arises in relation to the five sense objects—forms and so on. Moreover, since in this context, sensual desire is included by the term 'covetousness' and ill will by the term 'displeasure', it should be understood that the abandonment of the hindrances is taught by showing the two strong factors included within the hindrances. Specifically, here, through the removal of covetousness, the attraction rooted in bodily prosperity is abandoned; through the removal of displeasure, the aversion rooted in bodily misfortune is abandoned. Through the removal of covetousness, delight in the body is abandoned; through the removal of displeasure, discontent with the development of the body is abandoned. Through the removal of covetousness, the projection of unreal qualities—such as beauty and pleasure—onto the body is abandoned; through the removal of displeasure, the elimination of real qualities—such as ugliness and displeasure—from the body is abandoned. Thus, the meditator’s meditative power and capability in meditation are demonstrated. For this meditative power is indeed freedom from attraction and aversion, the overcoming of discontent and delight, and the absence of projecting the unreal and eliminating the real. Being free from attraction and aversion, overcoming discontent and delight, neither projecting the unreal nor eliminating the real—this is capability in meditation. It is said that only the contemplation of pure form is discussed, because it is purely the contemplation of the body.

Sukhādibhedāsu vedanāsūti sukhadukkhaadukkhamasukhasāmisanirāmisabhedāsu vedanāsu. Tattha sukhayatīti sukhā, sampayuttadhamme kāyañca laddhassāde karotīti attho. Suṭṭhu vā khādati, khanati vā kāyikaṃ cetasikañca ābādhanti sukhā, sukaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etissāti vā sukhā. Dukkhayatīti dukkhā, sampayuttadhamme kāyañca pīḷeti vibādhatīti attho. Duṭṭhu vā khādati, khanati vā kāyikaṃ cetasikañca sātanti dukkhā, dukkaraṃ okāsadānaṃ etissāti vā dukkhā. Dukkhasukhappaṭikkhepena adukkhamasukhāti upekkhā vuttā. Vediyati ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavatīti vedanā. Vediyamānoti anubhavamāno. Sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyāmīti pajānātīti kāyikaṃ vā cetasikaṃ vā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamāno “ahaṃ sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyāmī”ti pajānātīti attho. Tattha kāmaṃ uttānaseyyakāpi dārakā thaññapivanādikāle sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamānā “sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyāmā”ti pajānanti, na panetaṃ evarūpaṃ pajānanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ. Evarūpañhi jānanaṃ sattupaladdhiṃ na jahati, attasaññaṃ na ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vā satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā vā na hoti. Imassa pana bhikkhuno jānanaṃ sattupaladdhiṃ jahati, attasaññaṃ ugghāṭeti, kammaṭṭhānañceva satipaṭṭhānabhāvanā ca hoti. Idañhi “ko vediyati, tassa vedanā, kiṃ kāraṇā vedanā”ti evaṃ sampajānantassa vediyanaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ.

In the classification of feelings such as pleasant, etc., feelings are divided into pleasant, painful, neither-painful-nor-pleasant, sensual, and non-sensual. Herein, what is called 'pleasant' (sukhā) is that which delights or gives satisfaction to the associated states and the body—this is the meaning. Or, it thoroughly consumes or digs up bodily and mental affliction—this is pleasant. Alternatively, it is called pleasant because it easily provides opportunity. What is called 'painful' (dukkhā) is that which oppresses or harasses the associated states and the body—this is the meaning. Or, it poorly consumes or digs up bodily and mental ease—this is painful. Alternatively, it is called painful because it hardly provides opportunity. By the exclusion of both pain and pleasure, what is called 'neither-painful-nor-pleasant' (adukkhamasukhā) is equanimity. 'Feeling' (vedanā) is that which experiences the taste of an object. 'One who feels' is one who is experiencing. 'He knows, "I feel a pleasant feeling"'—whether bodily or mental—one experiencing a pleasant feeling knows, 'I feel a pleasant feeling.' This is the meaning. Herein, even infants lying on their backs, while suckling milk, etc., experience pleasant feelings and know, 'I feel a pleasant feeling,' but this is not the kind of knowing being referred to here. For such knowing does not abandon the perception of a being, does not uproot the notion of self, and is neither a meditation subject nor the development of mindfulness. But this monk’s knowing abandons the perception of a being, uproots the notion of self, and is both a meditation subject and the development of mindfulness. This is said with reference to the feeling of one who comprehends thus: 'Who feels? Whose feeling is it? What is the cause of the feeling?'

Tattha ko vediyatīti? Na koci satto vā puggalo vā vediyati. Kassa vedanāti? Na kassaci sattassa vā puggalassa vā vedanā. Kiṃ kāraṇā vedanāti? Vatthuārammaṇā ca panassa vedanāti. Tasmā esa evaṃ pajānāti “taṃ taṃ sukhādīnaṃ vatthubhūtaṃ rūpādiṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva [M 1.0237] vediyati, taṃ pana vedanāpavattiṃ upādāya ‘ahaṃ vediyāmī’ti [V 1.0224] vohāramattaṃ hotī”ti. Evaṃ “sukhādīnaṃ vatthubhūtaṃ rūpādiṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā vedanāva vediyatī”ti sallakkhento esa “sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyāmī”ti pajānātīti veditabbo.

Here, who feels? No being or person feels. Whose is the feeling? It is not the feeling of any being or person. What is the cause of feeling? Feeling has a basis and an object. Therefore, one understands thus: "Feeling itself feels by taking as its object that very form, etc., which is the basis for pleasure, etc. But regarding the occurrence of that feeling, it is merely a conventional expression to say, 'I feel.'" Thus, it should be understood that when one considers, "Feeling itself feels by taking as its object that very form, etc., which is the basis for pleasure, etc.," one thereby understands, "I feel a pleasant feeling."

Atha vā sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyāmīti pajānātīti sukhavedanākkhaṇe dukkhāya vedanāya abhāvato sukhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyamāno “sukhaṃ vedanaṃyeva vediyāmī”ti pajānāti. Tena yā pubbe bhūtapubbā dukkhā vedanā, tassā idāni abhāvato imissā ca sukhāya vedanāya ito paraṃ paṭhamaṃ abhāvato “vedanā nāma aniccā addhuvā vipariṇāmadhammā”ti itiha tattha sampajāno hoti. Dukkhaṃ vedanaṃ vediyāmīti pajānātītiādīsupi eseva nayo.

Alternatively, one understands, 'I feel a pleasant feeling.' That is, in the moment of a pleasant feeling, because of the absence of a painful feeling, one experiencing the pleasant feeling understands, 'I am experiencing only a pleasant feeling.' Because of the absence now of any painful feeling that existed previously, and because this pleasant feeling will also be absent in the future, just as it was previously, one is clearly aware right there: 'Feelings are impermanent, unstable, subject to change.' The same principle applies to understanding, 'I am experiencing a painful feeling,' and so on.

Sāmisaṃ vā sukhantiādīsu yasmā kilesehi āmasitabbato āmisā nāma pañca kāmaguṇā. Ārammaṇakaraṇavasena saha āmisehīti sāmisā, tasmā sāmisā sukhā nāma pañcakāmaguṇāmisanissitā chasu dvāresu uppannā chagehassitā somanassavedanā. Sāmisā dukkhā nāma chagehassitā domanassavedanā. Sā ca chasu dvāresu “iṭṭhārammaṇaṃ nānubhavissāmi nānubhavāmī”ti vitakkayato uppannā kāmaguṇanissitā domanassavedanā veditabbā. Nirāmisā sukhā nāma chanekkhammassitā somanassavedanā. Sā ca chasu dvāresu iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate aniccādivasena vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā ussukkāpetuṃ sakkontassa “ussakkitā me vipassanā”ti somanassajātassa uppannā somanassavedanā daṭṭhabbā.

In the phrase 'sensual pleasure' (sāmisaṃ vā sukhaṃ) and so on, the five strands of sensual pleasure are called 'āmisa' because they are to be touched by defilements. Those that are accompanied by sensual objects, in the manner of being an object, are called 'sāmisa.' Therefore, 'sensual pleasant feeling' (sāmisā sukhā) refers to a joyful feeling dependent on the five strands of sensual pleasure, arising in the six sense doors and rooted in the six sense abodes. 'Sensual painful feeling' (sāmisā dukkhā) refers to a sorrowful feeling rooted in the six sense abodes. And this should be understood as the sorrowful feeling dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure, arising in the six sense doors when one thinks, 'I will not experience the desired object' or 'I am not experiencing it.' 'Non-sensual pleasant feeling' (nirāmisā sukhā) refers to a joyful feeling rooted in the six kinds of renunciation. And this should be seen as the joyful feeling arising in one who, when a desired object appears in the six sense doors, establishes insight into impermanence and so forth, and is capable of arousing effort, thinking, 'My insight is aroused.'

Nirāmisā dukkhā nāma chanekkhammassitā domanassavedanā. Sā pana chasu dvāresu iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate anuttaravimokkhasaṅkhātaariyaphaladhammesu pihaṃ paṭṭhapetvā tadadhigamāya aniccādivasena vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapetvā ussukkāpetuṃ asakkontassa “imampi pakkhaṃ imampi māsaṃ imampi saṃvaccharaṃ vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā ariyabhūmiṃ pāpuṇituṃ nāsakkhi”nti anusocato uppannā domanassavedanā.

Non-sensual painful feeling is the sorrowful feeling rooted in the six kinds of renunciation. It is the sorrowful feeling that arises in one who, when a desirable object appears at the six sense doors, establishes longing for the noble fruition states, known as unsurpassed liberation; but being unable to earnestly cultivate insight into impermanence and so forth for its attainment, laments, "Even after earnestly cultivating insight for this fortnight, this month, or this year, I could not attain the noble state."

Sāmisā adukkhamasukhā nāma chagehassitā upekkhāvedanā. Sā ca chasu dvāresu iṭṭhārammaṇe āpāthagate guḷapiṇḍake nilīnamakkhikā viya rūpādīni anuvattamānā tattheva laggā laggitā hutvā uppannā kāmaguṇanissitā [M 1.0238] upekkhāvedanā. Nirāmisā adukkhamasukhā nāma chanekkhammassitā upekkhāvedanā. Sā pana chasu dvāresu iṭṭhādiārammaṇe āpāthagate iṭṭhe arajjantassa, aniṭṭhe adussantassa, asamapekkhanena amuyhantassa uppannā vipassanāñāṇasampayuttā [V 1.0225] upekkhāvedanā. Evaṃ vuttanti mahāsatipaṭṭhānasutte vuttaṃ. Sāva vedanā veditabbāti lujjanappalujjanaṭṭhena sā vedanā “loko”ti veditabbā.

Sensual neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the feeling of equanimity rooted in the six sense abodes. It is the feeling of equanimity dependent on the strands of sensual pleasure, which arises when, an agreeable object having appeared at the six sense doors, it follows after forms and so on, clinging and sticking right there like a fly hidden in a lump of molasses. Non-sensual neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the feeling of equanimity rooted in the six kinds of renunciation. It is the feeling of equanimity associated with insight knowledge that arises in one who does not delight in the agreeable, does not resent the disagreeable, and is not confused through impartial observation, when an agreeable or other object appears at the six sense doors. As it is said in the Great Discourse on the Foundations of Mindfulness, that very feeling is to be understood. By way of its nature of crumbling and disintegrating, that feeling should be understood as 'the world.'

Evaṃ vitthāriteti “sarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ sarāgaṃ cittanti pajānāti, vītarāgaṃ vā cittaṃ…pe… sadosaṃ vā cittaṃ, vītadosaṃ vā cittaṃ, samohaṃ vā cittaṃ, vītamohaṃ vā cittaṃ, saṃkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ, vikkhittaṃ vā cittaṃ, mahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ, amahaggataṃ vā cittaṃ, sauttaraṃ vā cittaṃ, anuttaraṃ vā cittaṃ, samāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ, asamāhitaṃ vā cittaṃ, vimuttaṃ vā cittaṃ, avimuttaṃ vā cittanti pajānātī”ti evaṃ satipaṭṭhānasutte (dī. ni. 2.381; ma. ni. 1.114) vitthāretvā dassite soḷasavidhe citte.

Thus, it is explained in detail: "One understands a mind with lust as 'a mind with lust,' a mind without lust as 'a mind without lust'... a mind with hatred as 'a mind with hatred,' a mind without hatred as 'a mind without hatred,' a mind with delusion as 'a mind with delusion,' a mind without delusion as 'a mind without delusion,' a contracted mind as 'a contracted mind,' a distracted mind as 'a distracted mind,' a developed mind as 'a developed mind,' an undeveloped mind as 'an undeveloped mind,' a surpassable mind as 'a surpassable mind,' an unsurpassed mind as 'an unsurpassed mind,' a concentrated mind as 'a concentrated mind,' an unconcentrated mind as 'an unconcentrated mind,' a liberated mind as 'a liberated mind,' an unliberated mind as 'an unliberated mind.'" In this way, the sixteen kinds of mind are shown in detail in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta (Dī. Ni. 2.381; Ma. Ni. 1.114).

Tattha sarāganti aṭṭhavidhaṃ lobhasahagataṃ. Vītarāganti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Idaṃ pana yasmā sammasanaṃ na dhammasamodhānaṃ, tasmā idha ekapadepi lokuttaraṃ na labbhati. Sesāni cattāri akusalacittāni neva purimapadaṃ, na pacchimapadaṃ bhajanti. Sadosanti duvidhaṃ domanassasahagataṃ. Vītadosanti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ. Sesāni dasa akusalacittāni neva purimapadaṃ, na pacchimapadaṃ bhajanti. Samohanti vicikicchāsahagatañceva uddhaccasahagatañcāti duvidhaṃ. Yasmā pana moho sabbākusalesu uppajjati, tasmā sesānipi idha vattantiyeva. Imasmiññeva hi duke dvādasākusalacittāni pariyādinnānīti. Vītamohanti lokiyakusalābyākataṃ.

Here, 'with lust' refers to the eight types associated with greed. 'Without lust' refers to worldly wholesome and indeterminate states. However, because this is contemplation and not the convergence of phenomena, here not even a single supramundane state is obtained. The remaining four unwholesome consciousnesses do not belong to either the first or the last category. 'With hatred' refers to the two types associated with displeasure. 'Without hatred' refers to worldly wholesome and indeterminate states. The remaining ten unwholesome consciousnesses do not belong to either the first or the last category. 'With delusion' refers to the two types associated with doubt and restlessness. Since delusion arises in all unwholesome states, the remaining ones are also included here. Indeed, in this pair, the twelve unwholesome consciousnesses are fully accounted for. 'Without delusion' refers to worldly wholesome and indeterminate states.

Saṃkhittanti thinamiddhānupatitaṃ. Etañhi saṅkucitacittaṃ nāma ārammaṇe saṅkocavasena pavattanato. Vikkhittanti uddhaccasahagataṃ. Etañhi pasaṭacittaṃ nāma ārammaṇe savisesaṃ vikkhepavasena visaṭabhāvena pavattanato. Mahaggatanti rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacarañca. Amahaggatanti kāmāvacaraṃ. Sauttaranti kāmāvacaraṃ. Anuttaranti rūpāvacaraṃ arūpāvacarañca. Tatrāpi sauttaraṃ rūpāvacaraṃ, anuttaraṃ arūpāvacarameva. Samāhitanti yassa appanāsamādhi vā upacārasamādhi vā atthi. Asamāhitanti ubhayasamādhivirahitaṃ. Vimuttanti [M 1.0239] tadaṅgavikkhambhanavimuttīhi vimuttaṃ. Avimuttanti ubhayavimuttirahitaṃ. Samucchedappaṭippassaddhinissaraṇavimuttīnaṃ pana idha okāsova natthi, okāsābhāvo ca sammasanacārassa adhippetattā veditabbo.

'Contracted' means overcome by sloth and torpor. This is called a contracted mind because it operates by way of contracting towards its object. 'Distracted' means accompanied by restlessness. This is called a scattered mind because it operates by way of dispersing and scattering with distinction over its object. 'Developed' means the form sphere and the formless sphere. 'Undeveloped' means the sense-sphere. 'Surpassable' means the sense-sphere. 'Unsurpassable' means the form sphere and the formless sphere. Even there, the form sphere is surpassable; the formless sphere alone is unsurpassable. 'Concentrated' means that which has either absorption concentration or access concentration. 'Unconcentrated' means devoid of both concentrations. 'Liberated' means liberated by substitution of opposites or by suppression. 'Unliberated' means devoid of both liberations. But there is no scope here for liberation by eradication, by tranquilization, and by escape; and this absence of scope should be understood as intended for the course of contemplation.

Upādānassa khandhā upādānakkhandhā, upādānassa paccayabhūtā dhammapuñjā dhammarāsayoti attho. Upādānehi ārammaṇakaraṇādivasena upādātabbā vā khandhā upādānakkhandhā. Cha ajjhattikabāhirāyatanānīti [V 1.0226] cakkhu sotaṃ ghānaṃ jivhā kāyo manoti imāni cha ajjhattikāyatanāni ceva, rūpaṃ saddo gandho raso phoṭṭhabbo dhammāti imāni cha bāhirāyatanāni ca. Ettha pana lokuttaradhammā na gahetabbā sammasanacārassa adhippetattā. Satta sambojjhaṅgāti satisambojjhaṅgādayo satta sambojjhaṅgā. Satiādayo hi sambodhissa, sambodhiyā vā aṅgāti sambojjhaṅgā. Tathā hi sambujjhati āraddhavipassakato paṭṭhāya yogāvacaroti sambodhi, yāya vā so satiādikāya sattadhammasāmaggiyā sambujjhati, kilesaniddāto uṭṭhāti, saccāni vā paṭivijjhati, sā dhammasāmaggī sambodhi, tassa sambodhissa, tassā vā sambodhiyā aṅgāti sambojjhaṅgā.

The aggregates of clinging are the clinging-aggregates; they are a heap of phenomena, a mass of phenomena, that serve as conditions for clinging—this is the meaning. Or, the aggregates that are to be clung to by clinging by means of being objects, etc., are the clinging-aggregates. The six internal and external sense bases are: the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these are the six internal sense bases; and form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena—these are the six external sense bases. Here, however, supramundane phenomena are not to be included, as the course of contemplation is intended. The seven factors of enlightenment are the seven factors of enlightenment beginning with mindfulness. For mindfulness and the others are limbs of enlightenment or for enlightenment, thus they are enlightenment factors. Indeed, enlightenment is when a meditator, starting from initiated insight, awakens. Or, it is the harmony of these seven factors—mindfulness and the rest—through which one awakens, rises from the slumber of defilements, or penetrates the truths. This harmony of phenomena is enlightenment. The limbs of that enlightenment, or the limbs for that enlightenment, are the factors of enlightenment.

Cattāri ariyasaccānīti “dukkhaṃ dukkhasamudayo dukkhanirodho dukkhanirodhagāminipaṭipadā”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.1071-1072) evaṃ vuttāni cattāri ariyasaccāni. Tattha purimāni dve saccāni vaṭṭaṃ pavattihetubhāvato. Pacchimāni vivaṭṭaṃ nivaṭṭatadadhigamūpāyabhāvato. Tesu bhikkhuno vaṭṭe kammaṭṭhānābhiniveso hoti sarūpato pariggahasambhavato. Vivaṭṭe natthi abhiniveso avisayattā avisayatte ca payojanābhāvato. Pañcadhā vuttesūti satipaṭṭhānasutte vuttesu. Suddhaarūpasammasanamevāti rūpena amissitattā kevalaṃ arūpasammasanameva. Khandhāyatanasaccakoṭṭhāsānaṃ pañcakkhandhasaṅgahato “rūpārūpasammasana”nti vuttaṃ. Pubbabhāgiyānampi satipaṭṭhānānaṃ saṅgahitattā “lokiyalokuttaramissakāneva kathitānī”ti āha.

The Four Noble Truths are the four noble truths stated thus: "Suffering, the origin of suffering, the cessation of suffering, and the path leading to the cessation of suffering" (Saṃ. Ni. 5.1071-1072). Among them, the first two truths pertain to the round of existence because they are the cause for its continuation. The latter two pertain to the end of the round because they are the means to its cessation and attainment. For a monk, there is application to a meditation subject in the round of existence, because of the possibility of grasping its intrinsic nature. In the end of the round, there is no such application, as it is not an object, and since it is not an object, it serves no purpose. 'When spoken of in fivefold terms' means as spoken of in the Satipaṭṭhāna Sutta. 'Only the pure contemplation of the immaterial' means that because it is unmixed with the material, it is solely the contemplation of the immaterial. Because the divisions of aggregates, sense bases, and truths are comprised in the five aggregates, 'contemplation of both material and immaterial' is mentioned. Because the preliminary stages of the foundations of mindfulness are also included, it is said that 'they are spoken of as mixed with both the mundane and the supramundane.'

394. Anibbattānanti ajātānaṃ. Payogaṃ parakkamanti ettha bhusaṃ yogo payogo, payogova parakkamo, payogasaṅkhātaṃ parakkamanti attho. Cittaṃ ukkhipatīti kosajjapakkhe patituṃ apadānavasena ukkhipati. Padhānavīriyanti [M 1.0240] sammappadhānalakkhaṇappattavīriyaṃ. Lokiyāti lokiyasammappadhānakathā. Sabbapubbabhāgeti sabbamaggānaṃ pubbabhāge. Kassapasaṃyuttapariyāyenāti kassapasaṃyutte āgatasuttena “uppannā me pāpakā akusalā dhammā appahīyamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyu”nti (saṃ. ni. 2.145) āgatattā. Sā lokiyāti veditabbā.

394. 'Of the unproduced' means of the unarisen. Regarding 'application' and 'striving': here, strong application is exertion; exertion itself is striving; the meaning is striving designated as application. 'Lifts up the mind' means that on the side of laziness, it lifts up the mind by way of not allowing it to fall. 'Energy of striving' is energy that has attained the characteristic of right striving. 'Worldly' refers to the discourse on worldly right striving. 'In all preliminary parts' means in the preliminary part of all paths. 'In the manner of the Kassapa Saṃyutta' means because in the Kassapa Saṃyutta it is stated in a sutta: 'Evil unwholesome states that have arisen in me, if not abandoned, would lead to harm' (Saṃyutta Nikāya 2.145). That is to be understood as worldly.

Samathavipassanāvāti avadhāraṇena maggaṃ nivattetvā tassa nivattane kāraṇaṃ dassento, “maggo panā”tiādimāha. Sakiṃ uppajjitvāti idaṃ bhūtakathanamattaṃ. Niruddhassa puna anuppajjanato “na koci guṇo”ti āsaṅkeyyāti āha – “so hī”tiādi. Anantarameva yathā phalaṃ uppajjati, tathā pavattiyevassa paccayadānaṃ. Purimasmimpīti “anuppannā me kusalā dhammā uppajjamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyu”nti etthapi. Vuttanti porāṇaṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Taṃ pana tathāvuttavacanaṃ [V 1.0227] na yuttaṃ dutiyasmiṃ viya purimasmiṃ maggassa aggahaṇe kāraṇābhāvato. Purimasmiṃ aggahite magge anuppajjamāno maggo anatthāya saṃvatteyyāti āpajjeyya, na cetaṃ yuttaṃ āpajjamāne tasmiṃ padhānatthasambhavato. Catukiccasādhanavasenāti anuppannākusalānuppādanādicatukiccasādhanavasena.

Regarding 'serenity and insight,' by way of emphasis, having excluded the path and showing the reason for that exclusion, he says, 'But the path,' etc. 'Having arisen once'—this is merely a statement of what has occurred. Because what has ceased does not arise again, one might suspect, 'There is no benefit,' so he says, 'For it,' etc. Its very process is the giving of a condition for the fruit to arise immediately after. 'In the former as well'—this applies here too: 'Unarisen wholesome states arising in me might lead to harm.' 'It has been said'—in the ancient commentary. But that statement is not appropriate, because unlike in the second case, in the former there is no reason for not including the path. If the path were not included in the former case, it would follow that the path, by not arising, would lead to harm; and this is not proper, for if that were the case, the purpose of striving would still be possible. 'By accomplishing the fourfold task' means by accomplishing the fourfold task beginning with the non-arising of unarisen unwholesome states, etc.

Vuttanayenāti “asamudācāravasena vā ananubhūtārammaṇavasena vā”tiādinā vuttanayena. Vijjamānāti dharamānasabhāvā. Khaṇattayapariyāpannattā uppādādisamaṅgino vattamānabhāvena uppannaṃ vattamānuppannaṃ. Tañhi uppādato paṭṭhāya yāva bhaṅgā uddhaṃ pannaṃ pattanti nippariyāyato “uppanna”nti vuccati. Anubhavitvā bhavitvā ca vigataṃ bhutvāvigataṃ. Anubhavanabhavanāni hi bhavanasāmaññena bhutvā-saddena vuttāni. Sāmaññameva hi upasaggena visesīyati. Idha vipākānubhavanavasena tadārammaṇaṃ avipakkavipākassa sabbathā avigatattā bhavitvāvigatamattavasena kammañca “bhutvāvigatuppanna”nti vuttaṃ. Na aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ viya rajjanādivasena anubhūtāpagataṃ javanaṃ uppajjitvā niruddhatāvasena bhūtāpagatañca saṅkhataṃ bhūtāpagatuppannanti. Tasmā idha okāsakatuppannaṃ vipākameva vadati, na tattha viya kammampi. Aṭṭhasāliniyañhi bhūtāvigatuppannaṃ okāsakatuppannañca aññathā dassitaṃ. Vuttañhi tattha (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 kāmāvacarakusalapadabhājanīya) –

By the stated method: by the method stated as, 'either due to the absence of misconduct or due to the absence of an experienced object,' and so forth. 'Existing' means possessing an existing nature. Because it is included in the three moments, being endowed with arising and so forth, it is called 'presently arisen' by virtue of having arisen in the present. For from its arising until its dissolution, it is called 'arisen' without qualification. 'Having been and gone' is that which has departed after having been experienced and having existed. For experiencing and existing are referred to by the general term 'having been' (bhutvā). The general term itself is specified by the prefix. Here, both its object (the result), by way of experiencing the result, and the kamma, merely by way of having been and gone—because the unripened result has not at all departed—are called 'having been and gone, arisen.' It is not as in the Aṭṭhasālinī, where the impulsion (javana), which is 'experienced and departed' due to delighting, etc., and the conditioned, which is 'having been and departed' by way of having arisen and ceased, are called 'having been and gone, arisen.' Therefore, here it speaks only of the result that is 'opportunity-arisen,' not of the kamma as in that case. For in the Aṭṭhasālinī, 'having been and gone, arisen' and 'opportunity-arisen' are shown differently. As stated there (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Aṭṭhakathā 1, Kāmāvacarakusalapadabhājanīya) –

“Ārammaṇarasaṃ [M 1.0241] anubhavitvā niruddhaṃ anubhūtāpagatasaṅkhātaṃ kusalākusalaṃ, upādādittayaṃ anuppatvā niruddhaṃ bhūtāpagatasaṅkhātaṃ sesasaṅkhatañca bhūtāpagatuppannaṃ nāma. ‘Yānissa tāni pubbe katāni kammānī’ti evamādinā nayena vuttaṃ kammaṃ atītampi samānaṃ aññaṃ vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassokāsaṃ katvā ṭhitattā, tathākatokāsañca vipākaṃ anuppannampi samānaṃ evaṃ kate okāse ekantena uppajjanato okāsakatuppannaṃ nāmā”ti.

The wholesome and unwholesome kamma that has ceased after experiencing the savour of the object is designated 'experienced and departed.' The remaining conditioned phenomena that have ceased after reaching the triad of arising, etc., are designated 'having been and departed.' These are called 'having been and departed, arisen.' As stated in the passage beginning 'Whatever deeds he has done before,' kamma, even though past, stands, having obstructed other results and having made an opportunity for its own result. And the result for which an opportunity has been so made, even though not yet arisen, is called 'opportunity-made-arisen' because it inevitably arises when such an opportunity has been made.

Idha pana sammohavinodaniyaṃ vuttanayeneva bhutvāvigatuppannaṃ okāsakatuppannañca dassitaṃ. Vuttañhi, sammohavinodaniyaṃ (vibha. aṭṭha. 406) –

Here, however, 'having been and gone, arisen' and 'opportunity-arisen' are shown in accordance with the method stated in the Sammohavinodanī. For it is said in the Sammohavinodanī (Vibh. Aṭṭha. 406):

“Kamme pana jahite ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavitvā niruddho vipāko bhutvāvigataṃ nāma. Kammaṃ uppajjitvā niruddhaṃ bhutvāvigataṃ nāma. Tadubhayampi bhutvāvigatuppannanti saṅkhyaṃ gacchati. Kusalākusalaṃ kammaṃ aññakammassa vipākaṃ paṭibāhitvā attano vipākassa [V 1.0228] okāsaṃ karoti. Evaṃ kate okāse vipāko uppajjamāno okāsakaraṇato paṭṭhāya uppannoti vuccati. Idaṃ okāsakatuppannaṃ nāmā”ti.

The result that has ceased after experiencing the savour of the object is called 'having been and gone.' Kamma that has arisen and ceased is called 'having been and gone.' Both are reckoned as 'having been and gone, arisen.' A wholesome or unwholesome kamma, having obstructed the result of another kamma, creates an opportunity for its own result. When such an opportunity has been made, the arising result is said to have arisen from the making of the opportunity. This is called 'opportunity-made-arisen.'

Tattha aṭṭhasāliniyā ayamadhippāyo – “satipi sabbesampi cittuppādānaṃ saṃvedayitasabhāvā ārammaṇānubhavane savipallāse pana santāne cittābhisaṅkhāravasena pavattito abyākatehi visiṭṭho kusalākusalānaṃ sātisayo visayānubhavanākāro. Yathā vikappaggāhavasena rāgādīhi tabbipakkhehi ca akusalaṃ kusalañca nippariyāyato ārammaṇarasaṃ anubhavati, na tathā vipāko kammavegakkhittattā, nāpi kiriyā ahetukānaṃ atidubbalatāya, sahetukānañca khīṇakilesassa chaḷaṅgupekkhāvato uppajjamānānaṃ atisantavuttittā, tasmā rajjanādivasena ārammaṇarasānubhavanaṃ sātisayanti akusalaṃ kusalañca uppajjitvā niruddhatāsāmaññena sesasaṅkhatañca bhūtāpagata”nti vuttaṃ. Sammohavinodaniyā pana vipākānubhavanavasena tadārammaṇaṃ avipakkapākassa sabbathā avigatattā bhavitvāvigatamattavasena kammañca bhutvāpagatanti [M 1.0242] vuttaṃ. Teneva tattha okāsakatuppannanti vipākamevāha, na kammampi, tasmā idhāpi sammohavinodaniyaṃ vuttanayeneva bhutvāpagatuppannaṃ okāsakatuppannañca vibhattanti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

In this regard, the intention of the Aṭṭhasālinī is as follows: "Although all mental states have the nature of experiencing objects, in a continuum with distortion, the manner of experiencing an object by wholesome and unwholesome states—proceeding by way of mental formations—is superior to and distinct from that of indeterminate states. Just as unwholesome and wholesome states directly experience the savour of an object through conceptual grasping, influenced by lust and the like or their opposites, the resultant (vipāka) does not do so, because it is propelled by the force of kamma; nor does the functional (kiriyā), due to the extreme weakness of rootless states, and for those with roots, due to the exceedingly peaceful occurrence for one who has destroyed the defilements and possesses six-limbed equanimity. Therefore, it is said that wholesome and unwholesome states are 'having been and departed' because their experiencing of the object's savour by way of delighting and so forth is superior; and the remaining conditioned phenomena are also 'having been and departed' by the commonality of having arisen and ceased." In the Sammohavinodanī, however, it is said that that object, by way of experiencing the result, and the kamma, are 'having been and departed' merely by way of having occurred and ceased, because the unripened result has not entirely departed. For that reason, in that text, only the result (vipāka) is referred to as 'opportunity-arisen,' not the kamma. Thus, here too, it should be understood that 'having been and departed, arisen' and 'opportunity-arisen' are distinguished in accordance with the method stated in the Sammohavinodanī.

Pañcakkhandhā pana vipassanāya bhūmi nāmāti sammasanassa ṭhānabhāvato vuttaṃ. Tesūti atītādibhedesu. Anusayitakilesāti appahīnā maggena pahātabbā adhippetā. Tenāha – “atītā vā…pe… na vattabbā”ti. Hontu tāva “atītā”ti vā “paccuppannā”ti vā na vattabbā, “anāgatā”ti pana kasmā na vattabbā, nanu kāraṇalābhe uppajjanārahā appahīnaṭṭhena thāmagatā kilesā anusayāti vuccantīti? Saccametaṃ, anāgatabhāvopi nesaṃ na paricchinno itarānāgatakkhandhānaṃ viyāti “anāgatā vāti na vattabbā”ti vuttaṃ. Yadi hi nesaṃ paricchinno anāgatabhāvo siyā, tato “paccuppannā, atītā”ti ca vattabbā siyuṃ, paccayasamavāye pana uppajjanārahataṃ upādāya anāgatavohāro tattha veditabbo.

The five aggregates, however, are called the ground for insight because they are the basis for comprehension. "Among these" refers to the divisions of past, etc. "Latent defilements" means those not yet abandoned, intended to be abandoned by the path. Therefore, it is said, "Whether past… or not to be spoken of." For now, let it be that they are "not to be spoken of" as "past" or "present," but why are they "not to be spoken of" as "future"? Surely, defilements capable of arising when the occasion arises, being strong in the sense of being unabandoned, are called latent? This is true, but even their future state is not precisely defined, like that of other future aggregates. Therefore, it is said, "or future—not to be spoken of." If their future state were precisely defined, then they could also be spoken of as "present" or "past." However, with reference to their capability of arising when a confluence of conditions occurs, the designation "future" should be understood there.

Idaṃ bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāmāti idaṃ yathāvuttaṃ kilesajātaṃ appahīnaṭṭhena bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāma kāraṇalābhe sati vijjamānakiccakaraṇato. Tāsu tāsu bhūmisūti manussadevādiattabhāvasaṅkhātesu upādānakkhandhesu. Ārammaṇakaraṇavasena hi bhavanti ettha kilesāti bhūmiyo, upādānakkhandhā. Asamugghātagatāti tasmiṃ tasmiṃ santāne anuppattidhammataṃ anāpāditatāya samugghātaṃ samucchedaṃ na gatāti asamugghātagatā. Bhūmiladdhuppannaṃ nāmāti ettha laddhabhūmikaṃ [V 1.0229] bhūmiladdhanti vuttaṃ aggiāhito viya. Okāsakatuppannasaddepi ca aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 kāmāvacarakusalapadabhājanīya) āgatanayena okāso kato etena kusalākusalakammena, okāso kato etassa vipākassāti ca duvidhatthepi evameva katasaddassa paranipāto veditabbo. Idha pana okāsakatuppannasaddena vipākasseva gahitattā “okāso kato etassa vipākassā”ti evaṃ viggaho daṭṭhabbo.

This is called 'arisen having obtained a ground': this group of defilements, as described, is called 'arisen having obtained a ground' because, not having been abandoned, it performs its function when the cause is obtained and it is present. 'In those various grounds' means in the aggregates of clinging designated as human, divine, and other states of existence. For defilements exist here by way of making them objects, thus the aggregates of clinging are 'grounds.' 'Not yet eradicated' means that in a given continuum they have not gone to eradication, to complete destruction, because the state of non-arising has not been brought about. In the phrase 'arisen having obtained a ground,' that which has obtained a ground is called 'ground-obtained,' similar to the term aggihita (one who has set up a fire). Also, in the case of the term 'opportunity-made-arisen,' according to the method found in the Aṭṭhasālinī (Dhammasaṅgaṇī Commentary, section on wholesome states of the sense sphere), the post-position of the past participle 'made' should be understood in two senses: 'an opportunity was made by this wholesome or unwholesome kamma,' and 'an opportunity was made for this result.' Here, however, since the term 'opportunity-made-arisen' is taken to refer only to the result, the analysis should be understood as: 'an opportunity was made for this result.'

Khaṇattayasamaṅgitāya samudācārappattaṃ samudācāruppannaṃ. Tenāha – “sampati vattamānaṃyevā”ti. Ārammaṇaṃ adhiggayha daḷhaṃ gahetvā pavattaṃ ārammaṇādhiggahituppannaṃ. Vikkhambhanappahānavasena appahīnā avikkhambhitā. Samucchedappahānavasena appahīnā asamugghātitā. Nimittaggāhavasena ārammaṇassa adhiggahitattā [M 1.0243] taṃ ārammaṇaṃ anussaritānussaritakkhaṇe kilesuppattihetubhāvena upatiṭṭhanato adhiggahitameva nāmaṃ hotīti āha – “ārammaṇassa adhiggahitattā”ti. Ettha ca āhaṭakhīrarukkho viya nimittaggāhavasena adhiggahitaṃ ārammaṇaṃ, anāhaṭakhīrarukkho viya avikkhambhitatāya antogatakilesaārammaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Nimittaggāhikā avikkhambhitakilesā vā puggalā vā āhaṭānāhaṭakhīrarukkhasadisā. Purimanayenevāti avikkhambhituppanne vuttanayeneva. Vitthāretabbanti “imasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne nuppajjissantī”ti na vattabbā. Kasmā? Asamugghātitattā. Yathā kiṃ? Yathā sace khīrarukkhaṃ kuṭhāriyā āhaneyyuṃ, imasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne khīraṃ na nikkhameyyāti na vattabbaṃ, evaṃ. Idaṃ asamugghātituppannaṃ nāmāti evaṃ yojetvā vitthāretabbaṃ.

By being endowed with the three moments, it is attained in occurrence and arisen in occurrence. Hence it is said: 'It occurs as presently happening.' Having firmly grasped the object and proceeded, it is arisen as having firmly grasped the object. Not abandoned by suppression, they are unsuppressed. Not abandoned by eradication, they are unuprooted. Because the object is grasped by taking up the sign, and because that object, when repeatedly recollected, is present as a cause for the arising of defilements, it is indeed called 'grasped.' Therefore, it is said: 'Because the object has been grasped.' Here, the object grasped by taking up the sign is like a tapped milk-tree, while the object with defilements remaining internally due to being unsuppressed is like an untapped milk-tree. Those who grasp signs, or persons with unsuppressed defilements, are comparable to tapped and untapped milk-trees. As in the previous method—that is, by the method stated for the unsuppressed arisen. It should be elaborated thus: 'In such and such a place, they will not arise'—this cannot be said. Why? Because they are unuprooted. To what can this be compared? Just as if one were to strike a milk-tree with an axe, one could not say, 'In this very spot, milk will not flow out'—so it is. This is what is called 'the unuprooted arisen.' It should be elaborated by construing it thus.

Imesu uppannesūti yathāvuttesu aṭṭhasu uppannesu. Idaṃ na maggavajjhaṃ appahātabbavatthuttā. Maggavajjhaṃ maggena paheyyavatthuttā. Rattoti rāgena samannāgato. Esa nayo duṭṭho mūḷhoti etthāpi. Vinibaddhoti mānasaṃyojanena virūpaṃ nibandhito. Parāmaṭṭhoti diṭṭhiparāmāsena dhammasabhāvaṃ atikkamma parato āmaṭṭho. Aniṭṭhaṅgatoti niṭṭhaṃ agato, saṃsayāpannoti attho. Thāmagatoti anusayavasena daḷhataṃ upagato. Yuganaddhāti pahātabbappahāyakayuge naddhā viya vattanakā ekakālikattā. Saṃkilesikāti saṃkilesadhammasahitā.

'In these arisen states' means in the eight arisen states as mentioned above. This is not to be abandoned by the path because it is not an object to be abandoned. It is to be abandoned by the path because it is an object to be abandoned by the path. 'Ratto' means one endowed with lust. This same method applies here also to 'duṭṭho' and 'mūḷho'. 'Vinibaddho' means bound in a distorted way by the fetter of conceit. 'Parāmaṭṭho' means having grasped wrongly, having transgressed the true nature of things through the misapprehension of views. 'Aniṭṭhaṅgato' means not having reached a conclusion; the meaning is 'fallen into doubt'. 'Thāmagato' means having become firm through underlying tendencies. 'Yuganaddhā' means bound together like a pair—that which is to be abandoned and that which abandons—because they occur simultaneously. 'Saṃkilesikā' means accompanied by defiling states.

Pāḷiyanti paṭisambhidāpāḷiyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 3.21). Tikālikesupi kilesesu vāyāmābhāvadassanatthaṃ ajātaphalataruṇarukkho pāḷiyaṃ nidassito, aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana jāto satto asamudāhaṭakileso nāma natthīti “jātaphalarukkhena dīpetabba”nti vatvā tamatthaṃ vivarituṃ “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Atha vā maggena pahīnakilesānameva atītādibhedena tidhā [V 1.0230] navattabbataṃ pākaṭaṃ kātuṃ ajātaphalarukkho upamāvasena pāḷiyaṃ ābhato, atītādīnaṃ appahīnatādassanatthampi “jātaphalarukkhena dīpetabba”nti aṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttaṃ. Tattha yathā acchinne rukkhe nibbattanārahāni phalāni chinne anuppajjamānāni kadāci sasabhāvāni ahesuṃ, honti, bhavissanti vāti atītādibhāvena na vattabbāni, evaṃ maggena pahīnakilesā ca daṭṭhabbā magge anuppanne uppattirahānaṃ uppanne sabbena sabbaṃ abhāvato[M 1.0244]. Yathā ca chede asati phalāni uppajjissantīti chedanassa sātthakatā, evaṃ maggabhāvanāya ca sātthakatā yojetabbā. Nāpi na pajahatīti uppajjanārahānaṃ pajahanato vuttaṃ. Uppajjitvāti lakkhaṇe tvā-saddo. Maggassa uppajjanakiriyāya hi samudayappahānanibbānasachikaraṇakiriyā viya khandhānaṃ parijānanakiriyā lakkhīyati.

'In the Pāḷi' refers to the Pāḷi text of the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 3.21). To show the absence of striving regarding defilements in the three times, a young tree that has not yet borne fruit is given as an example in the Pāḷi. However, in the commentary, it is said, 'There is no such thing as a born being with unmanifested defilements,' and thus 'it should be illustrated by a fruit-bearing tree.' Then, to explain this meaning, the passage beginning 'just as...' is stated. Alternatively, to make clear that defilements abandoned by the path are not to be spoken of in three ways—distinguished as past, etc.—the example of a tree that has not yet borne fruit is given in the Pāḷi as a simile. To also show that past, etc., have not been abandoned, the commentary states, 'It should be illustrated by a fruit-bearing tree.' There, just as fruits that are capable of arising on an uncut tree, but do not arise when it is cut, cannot be spoken of in terms of past, present, or future, as having existed, existing, or going to exist in their own nature, so too should the defilements abandoned by the path be understood; for when the path has not arisen, those capable of arising do so, but when it has arisen, they are completely absent. And just as the cutting is purposeful because fruits would arise if there were no cutting, so too should the purposefulness of developing the path be construed. 'Nor does one not abandon' is said because of the abandoning of what is capable of arising. 'Having arisen' (uppajjitvā): the suffix '-tvā' is in the sense of a characteristic. For by the action of the path's arising, the action of fully understanding the aggregates is characterized, just as are the actions of abandoning the origin and realizing Nibbāna.

Tepi pajahatiyevāti ye tehi kilesehi janetabbā upādinnakkhandhā, tepi pajahatiyeva tannimittassa abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhanato. Tenāha – “vuttampi ceta”ntiādi. Abhisaṅkhāraviññāṇassa nirodhenāti kammaviññāṇassa anuppattidhammatāpādanena. Etthāti etasmiṃ sotāpattimaggañāṇe hetubhūte. Eteti nāmarūpasaññitā saṅkhārā. Sabbabhavehi vuṭṭhātiyevātipi vadantīti arahattamaggo sabbabhavehi vuṭṭhātiyevāti vadanti taduppattito uddhaṃ bhavūpapattiyā kilesassapi abhāvato.

'He abandons even those' means that even those appropriated aggregates to be produced by those defilements are abandoned, due to the cessation of the formational consciousness that is their cause. Therefore, it is said: 'And this was also stated,' etc. 'By the cessation of formational consciousness' means by bringing about the state of non-arising for kamma-consciousness. 'Here' means in this knowledge of the path of stream-entry, which serves as the cause. 'These' means the formations designated as name-and-form. 'Some also say, "He indeed emerges from all states of existence"' means: they say that the path of Arahantship indeed emerges from all states of existence, because from its arising onwards, there is an absence of defilements for rebirth in a state of existence.

Ekacittakkhaṇikattā maggassāti adhippāyena “kathaṃ anuppannānaṃ…pe… ṭhitiyā bhāvanā hotī”ti pucchati. Maggappavattiyāyeva ubhayakiccasiddhito āha – “maggappavattiyāyevā”ti. Maggo hītiādinā tamatthaṃ vivarati. Anuppanno nāma vuccati, tasmā tassa bhāvanā anuppannānaṃ uppādāya bhāvanā vuttāti yojetabbā. Vattuṃ vaṭṭatīti yāvatā maggassa pavattiyeva ṭhiti, tattakāneva nibbattitalokuttarāni.

With the intention, 'Because the path lasts for a single mind-moment,' the question is asked: 'How is there development of the unarisen... for the sake of stability?' Because both functions are accomplished by the very occurrence of the path, it is answered: 'By the very occurrence of the path.' The meaning is explained with the words beginning, 'For the path...' It is called 'unarisen'; therefore, its development should be construed thus: 'the development for the arising of the unarisen is spoken of.' It is proper to say that to the extent that the path's occurrence is stability, the supramundane states are produced to that same extent.

398-401. Kattukamyatāchandaṃ adhipatiṃ karitvā paṭiladdhasamādhi chandasamādhīti āha – “chandaṃ nissāya pavatto samādhi chandasamādhī”ti padhānasaṅkhārāti catukiccasādhakassa sammappadhānavīriyassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tenāha – “padhānabhūtā saṅkhārā padhānasaṅkhārā”ti. Tattha padhānabhūtāti vīriyabhūtā. Saṅkhatasaṅkhārādinivattanatthaṃ padhānaggahaṇanti. Atha vā taṃ taṃ visesaṃ saṅkharotīti saṅkhāro, sabbaṃ vīriyaṃ. Tattha catukiccasādhakato sesanivattanatthaṃ padhānaggahaṇanti, padhānabhūtā seṭṭhabhūtāti attho. Catubbidhassa pana vīriyassa adhippetattā bahuvacananiddeso kato. Tehi dhammehīti chandasamādhinā padhānasaṅkhārehi ca. Iddhipādanti ettha ijjhatīti iddhi, samijjhati [V 1.0231] nipphajjatīti attho. Ijjhanti vā etāya sattā iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontītipi iddhi. Paṭhamenatthena iddhi eva pādo [M 1.0245] iddhipādo, iddhikoṭṭhāsoti attho. Dutiyenatthena iddhiyā pādoti iddhipādo, pādoti patiṭṭhā, adhigamūpāyoti attho. Tena hi yasmā uparūparivisesasaṅkhātaṃ iddhiṃ pajjanti pāpuṇanti, tasmā pādoti vuccati. Tenāha – “iddhiyā pādaṃ, iddhibhūtaṃ vā pādaṃ iddhipāda”nti.

398-401. Having made the desire-to-act (kattukamyatāchanda) the dominant factor, the concentration attained is called 'desire-concentration'; thus it is said: 'The concentration that arises depending on desire is desire-concentration.' 'Striving formations' is a designation for the energy of right striving (sammappadhānavīriya) that accomplishes the four tasks. Hence, it is said: 'Formations that are striving are striving formations.' Here, 'that are striving' means that are energy. The term 'striving' is included to exclude conditioned formations and so forth. Alternatively, because it forms this or that distinction, it is a 'formation' (saṅkhāra); this refers to all energy. Here, the term 'striving' is included to exclude the rest apart from that which accomplishes the four tasks; the meaning is that 'that which is striving' is 'that which is supreme.' But since fourfold energy is intended, the plural designation is used. 'By those states' means by desire-concentration and by the striving formations. Regarding 'basis of power' (iddhipāda): here, 'power' (iddhi) is so called because 'it succeeds' (ijjhati); the meaning is it is accomplished, it is brought to fruition. Or, it is 'power' because by means of it beings succeed, prosper, and attain excellence. In the first sense, power itself is the basis (pāda), hence 'basis of power'; the meaning is 'a constituent of power.' In the second sense, it is the basis of power, hence 'basis of power'; 'basis' means foundation, the means of attainment. Therefore, because by means of it they go to and attain the power designated as successively higher distinctions, it is called a 'basis.' Hence, it is said: 'The basis of power, or the basis that is power—is the basis of power.'

Atha vā iddhipādanti nipphattipariyāyena ijjhanaṭṭhena, ijjhanti etāya sattā iddhā vuddhā ukkaṃsagatā hontīti iminā vā pariyāyena iddhīti saṅkhaṃ gatānaṃ upacārajjhānādikusalacittasampayuttānaṃ chandasamādhipadhānasaṅkhārānaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṭṭhena pādabhūtaṃ sesacittacetasikarāsinti attho.
