Teneva iddhipādavibhaṅge (vibha. 434-437) “iddhipādoti tathābhūtassa vedanākkhandho…pe… viññāṇakkhandho”ti vuttaṃ. Sā eva ca tathāvuttā iddhi yasmā heṭṭhimā heṭṭhimā uparimāya uparimāya tayo chandasamādhippadhānasaṅkhārā pādabhūtā adhiṭṭhānabhūtā, tasmā vuttaṃ “iddhibhūtaṃ vā pāda”nti. Tathā heṭṭhā dhammā iddhipi honti iddhipādāpi, sesā pana sampayuttakā cattāro khandhā iddhipādāyeva. Vīriyacittavīmaṃsāsamādhippadhānasaṅkhārasaṅkhātāpi tayo tayo dhammā iddhipi honti iddhipādāpi, sesā pana sampayuttakā cattāro khandhā iddhipādāyeva.

Alternatively, the term 'basis of psychic power' (iddhipāda) signifies accomplishment in the sense of fruition, in the sense of succeeding. Or, in the sense that beings succeed, grow, and attain excellence by means of it—this is the meaning. Alternatively, by this meaning, it is the remaining mass of consciousness and mental factors that serves as the foot (pāda) in the sense of being the foundation (adhiṭṭhāna) for the formations of striving with concentration on desire, which are associated with access-jhāna and other wholesome states of mind, and which are reckoned as iddhi. Thus, in the Iddhipādavibhaṅga (Vibh. 434-437), it is said: 'The basis of psychic power is the aggregate of feeling... the aggregate of consciousness,' etc. And for this very iddhi, as described, because the lower three factors—desire, concentration, and striving formations—are the basis (pāda) and foundation (adhiṭṭhāna) for the successively higher ones, it is therefore said: 'or the foot that is iddhi.' Similarly, the lower states are both iddhi and iddhipāda, while the remaining associated four aggregates are solely iddhipāda. Likewise, the three states designated as the formations of striving with concentration on energy, mind, and investigation are also both iddhi and iddhipāda, whereas the remaining associated four aggregates are solely iddhipāda.

Apica pubbabhāgo pubbabhāgo iddhipādo nāma, paṭilābho paṭilābho iddhi nāmāti veditabbā. Ayamattho upacārena vā vipassanāya vā dīpetabbo. Paṭhamajjhānaparikammañhi iddhipādo nāma, paṭhamajjhānaṃ iddhi nāma. Dutiyajhāna… tatiyajhāna… catutthajhāna… ākāsānañcāyatana… viññāṇañcāyatana… ākiñcaññāyatana… nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaparikammaṃ iddhipādo nāma, nevasaññānāsaññāyatanaṃ iddhi nāma. Sotāpattimaggassa vipassanā iddhipādo nāma, sotāpattimaggo iddhi nāma. Sakadāgāmi-anāgāmi-arahattamaggassa vipassanā iddhipādo nāma, arahattamaggo iddhi nāma. Paṭilābhenapi dīpetuṃ vaṭṭatiyeva. Paṭhamajjhānañhi iddhipādo nāma, dutiyajjhānaṃ iddhi nāma. Dutiyajjhānaṃ iddhipādo nāma, tatiyajjhānaṃ iddhi nāma…pe… anāgāmimaggo iddhipādo nāma, arahattamaggo iddhi nāma.

Moreover, each preliminary stage is called the basis of psychic power, and each attainment is called psychic power—this should be understood. This meaning should be explained either by way of access or by insight. For the preparatory work for the first jhāna is called the basis of psychic power, and the first jhāna is called psychic power. The second jhāna... the third jhāna... the fourth jhāna... the base of infinite space... the base of infinite consciousness... the base of nothingness... the preparatory work for the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called the basis of psychic power, and the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is called psychic power. The insight (vipassanā) for the path of stream-entry is called the basis of psychic power, and the path of stream-entry is called psychic power. The insight (vipassanā) for the paths of once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship is called the basis of psychic power, and the path of arahantship is called psychic power. It is also appropriate to explain by way of attainment. For the first jhāna is called the basis of psychic power, and the second jhāna is called psychic power. The second jhāna is called the basis of psychic power, and the third jhāna is called psychic power...pe... the path of non-returning is called the basis of psychic power, and the path of arahantship is called psychic power.

Sesesupīti vīriyasamādhiādīsupi. Tattha hi vīriyaṃ, cittaṃ, vīmaṃsaṃ adhipatiṃ karitvā paṭiladdhasamādhi vīriyasamādhi, cittasamādhi, vīmaṃsāsamādhīti [M 1.0246] attho veditabbo. Chandādīsu ekanti [V 1.0232] chandādīsu catūsu ādito vuttattā ādibhūtaṃ ekaṃ padhānaṃ chandanti adhippāyo. Tenevāha – “tadāssa paṭhamiddhipādo”ti. Evaṃ sesāpīti etena vīriyaṃ cittaṃ vīmaṃsaṃ nissāya vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇantānaṃ vasena dutiyavīriyiddhipādādayo yojetabbāti dasseti. Iminā hi suttantena catunnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ matthakappattaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ dassitaṃ. Eko hi bhikkhu chandaṃ avassayati, kattukamyatākusaladhammacchandena atthanipphattiyaṃ sati “ahaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattessāmi, natthi mayhaṃ etassa nibbattane bhāro”ti chandaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ chandaṃ dhuraṃ chandaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbatteti. Eko vīriyaṃ avassayati, eko cittaṃ, eko paññaṃ avassayati, paññāya atthanipphattiyaṃ sati “ahaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattessāmi, natthi mayhaṃ etassa nibbattane bhāro”ti paññaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ paññaṃ dhuraṃ paññaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbatteti.

Regarding 'also in the others' (sesesupi): this means also in the others, such as energy-concentration and so on. Herein, it should be understood that having made energy, mind, and investigation the dominant factors, the concentration attained is energy-concentration, mind-concentration, and investigation-concentration. Regarding 'one among desire and the rest' (chandādīsu ekaṃ): since it is stated first among the four beginning with desire, the intention is that desire is the initial, foremost one. Therefore, it is said: 'That is his first basis of psychic power.' In this way, by 'also in the others,' it is shown that the second basis of psychic power beginning with energy and so on should be applied in the case of those who, relying on energy, mind, and investigation, develop insight and attain arahantship. Indeed, by this discourse, the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) that reaches its peak for four monks is shown. One monk relies on desire—when there is accomplishment of the goal through the desire to act for wholesome states, thinking, 'I will bring forth the supramundane Dhamma; there is no burden for me in bringing it forth,' he makes desire the chief, the burden, the forerunner, and thus brings forth the supramundane Dhamma. Another relies on energy, another on mind, another on wisdom—when there is accomplishment of the goal through wisdom, thinking, 'I will bring forth the supramundane Dhamma; there is no burden for me in bringing it forth,' he makes wisdom the chief, the burden, the forerunner, and thus brings forth the supramundane Dhamma.

Kathaṃ? Yathā hi catūsu amaccaputtesu ṭhānantaraṃ patthetvā vicarantesu eko upaṭṭhānaṃ avassayati, eko sūrabhāvaṃ, eko jātiṃ, eko mantaṃ. Kathaṃ? Tesu hi paṭhamo upaṭṭhāne appamādakāritāya atthanipphattiyā sati labbhamānaṃ “lacchāmetaṃ ṭhānantara”nti upaṭṭhānaṃ avassayati. Dutiyo upaṭṭhāne appamattopi “ekacco saṅgāme paccupaṭṭhite saṇṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, avassaṃ pana rañño paccanto kuppissati, tasmiṃ kuppite rathassa purato kammaṃ katvā rājānaṃ ārādhetvā āharāpessāmetaṃ ṭhānantara”nti sūrabhāvaṃ avassayati. Tatiyo “sūrabhāvepi sati ekacco hīnajātiko hoti, jātiṃ sodhetvā ṭhānantaraṃ dento mayhaṃ dassatī”ti jātiṃ avassayati. Catuttho “jātimāpi eko amantanīyo hoti, mantena kattabbakicce uppanne āharāpessāmetaṃ ṭhānantara”nti mantaṃ avassayati. Te sabbepi attano attano avassayabalena ṭhānantarāni pāpuṇiṃsu.

How? Just as among four ministers' sons seeking a position, one relies on attendance, another on valor, another on birth, and another on counsel. How? Among them, the first, when there is accomplishment of the goal through diligence in attendance, relies on attendance, thinking, 'We will obtain this position.' The second, even if diligent in attendance, thinks, 'Someone might not be able to stand firm when battle arises; but the king's border will surely be disturbed. When that is disturbed, having performed deeds at the forefront of the chariot, having pleased the king, we will obtain this position,' and so relies on valor. The third thinks, 'Even with valor, someone might be of low birth; when granting a position after scrutinizing birth, he will give it to me,' and so relies on birth. The fourth thinks, 'Even one of high birth might be unworthy of counsel; when a task needing counsel arises, we will obtain this position,' and so relies on counsel. All of them attained their positions through the strength of what each relied upon.

Tattha upaṭṭhāne appamatto hutvā ṭhānantaraṃ patto viya chandaṃ avassāya kattukamyatākusaladhammacchandena “atthanipphattiyaṃ sati ahaṃ lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattessāmi, natthi mayhaṃ etassa nibbattane sāro”ti chandaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ chandaṃ dhuraṃ chandaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā lokuttaradhammanibbattako [V 1.0233] daṭṭhabbo [M 1.0247] raṭṭhapālatthero (ma. ni. 2.293 ādayo) viya. So hi āyasmā “chande sati kathaṃ nānujānissantī”ti sattāhampi bhattāni abhuñjitvā mātāpitaro anujānāpetvā pabbajitvā chandameva avassāya lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattesi. Sūrabhāvena rājānaṃ ārādhetvā ṭhānantaraṃ patto viya vīriyaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ vīriyaṃ dhuraṃ vīriyaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā lokuttaradhammanibbattako daṭṭhabbo soṇatthero (mahāva. 243 ādayo) viya. So hi āyasmā vīriyaṃ dhuraṃ katvā lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattesi.

There, like one who attained a position by being diligent in attendance, one should regard the one who brings forth the supramundane Dhamma as relying on desire, by the desire to act for wholesome states, thinking, 'When there is accomplishment of the goal, I will bring forth the supramundane Dhamma; there is no burden for me in bringing it forth,' making desire the chief, the burden, the forerunner, like the Elder Raṭṭhapāla (MN 2.293 ff.). For that venerable one, thinking, 'When there is desire, how will they not give permission?' even without eating meals for seven days, having obtained permission from his parents, went forth, and relying on desire alone, brought forth the supramundane Dhamma. Like one who attained a position by means of valor, having pleased the king, one should regard the one who brings forth the supramundane Dhamma as making energy the chief, the burden, the forerunner, like the Elder Soṇa (Mahāva. 243 ff.). For that venerable one, making energy the burden, brought forth the supramundane Dhamma.

Jātisampattiyā ṭhānantaraṃ pattoviya cittaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ cittaṃ dhuraṃ cittaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā lokuttaradhammanibbattako daṭṭhabbo sambhūtatthero (theragā. aṭṭha. 2 sambhūtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā) viya. So hi āyasmā cittaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ cittaṃ dhuraṃ cittaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattesi. Mantaṃ avassāya ṭhānantaraṃ patto viya vīmaṃsaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ vīmaṃsaṃ dhuraṃ vīmaṃsaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā lokuttaradhammanibbattako daṭṭhabbo thero mogharājā (su. ni. 1122 ādayo; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddeso 85) viya. So hi āyasmā vīmaṃsaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ vīmaṃsaṃ dhuraṃ vīmaṃsaṃ pubbaṅgamaṃ katvā lokuttaradhammaṃ nibbattesi. Tassa hi bhagavā “suññato lokaṃ avekkhassū”ti (su. ni. 1125; cūḷani. mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddeso 88) suññatākathaṃ kathesi. Paññānissitamānaniggahatthañca dvikkhattuṃ pucchito pañhaṃ na kathesi. Ettha ca punappunaṃ chanduppādanaṃ tosanaṃ viya hotīti chandassa upaṭṭhānasadisatā vuttā, thāmabhāvato vīriyassa sūrattasadisatā, “chadvārādhipati rājā”ti (dha. pa. aṭṭha. 2.erakapattanāgarājavatthu) vacanato pubbaṅgamatā cittassa visiṭṭhajātisadisatā.

By making the mind foremost, the mind the leader, the mind the precursor, one should be seen as a producer of the supramundane Dhamma, like the Elder Sambhūta (Theragāthā Aṭṭhakathā 2, Sambhūtattheragāthāvaṇṇanā), who was as if he had attained a high position by virtue of birth. For indeed, that venerable one made the mind foremost, the mind the leader, the mind the precursor, and thereby produced the supramundane Dhamma. Like one who has attained a high position by relying on a sacred formula, by making investigation foremost, investigation the leader, investigation the precursor, one should be seen as a producer of the supramundane Dhamma, like the Elder Mogharājā (Sutta Nipāta 1122, etc.; Cūḷaniddesa, Mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddeso 85). For indeed, that venerable one made investigation foremost, investigation the leader, investigation the precursor, and thereby produced the supramundane Dhamma. To him, the Blessed One spoke the discourse on emptiness, saying, 'Look upon the world as empty' (Sutta Nipāta 1125; Cūḷaniddesa, Mogharājamāṇavapucchāniddeso 88). And for the sake of subduing the pride based on wisdom, though questioned twice, he did not explain the question. Herein, the repeated arising of desire is like giving satisfaction, thus it is said that desire is similar to attendance; from its state of strength, energy is similar to heroism; and because it is said, 'The king is the lord of the six doors' (Dhammapada Aṭṭhakathā 2, Erakapattanāgarājavatthu), the preeminence of the mind is similar to distinguished birth.

402-406. Attano saddhādhureti attano saddhākicce saddahanakiriyāya. Indaṭṭhaṃ kāretīti anuvattanavasena sampayuttadhammesu indaṭṭhaṃ kāreti, tasmā ādhipateyyaṭṭhena saddhā eva indriyanti saddhindriyaṃ. Tathā vīriyādīnaṃ sakasakakiccesūti āha – “vīriyindriyādīsupi eseva nayo”ti. Visodhentoti vipakkhavivajjanasapakkhanisevanasarikkhūpanissayasaṅgaṇhanalakkhaṇehi tīhi kāraṇehi visodhanavasena sodhento.

402-406. 'In one's own burden of faith' means in one's own function of faith, by the act of believing. 'Makes it stand as chief' means making it stand as chief among associated states through conformity; therefore faith itself is a faculty in the sense of dominance, thus the faculty of faith. Regarding 'Similarly, for energy and the others in their respective duties,' he says: 'This same method applies also to the faculties of energy and so on.' 'Purifying' means purifying by way of cleansing through three causes: the avoidance of opposing things, the cultivation of favorable things, and the grasping of similar supporting conditions.

Assaddhe puggale parivajjayatoti buddhādīsu pasādasinehābhāvena saddhārahite lūkhapuggale sabbaso vajjayato. Saddhe puggale sevatoti [M 1.0248] buddhādīsu saddhādhimutte vakkalittherasadise sevato. Pasādanīyeti pasādāvahe sampasādanīyasuttādike (dī. ni. 3.141 ādayo). Paccavekkhatoti pāḷito atthato ca pati pati avekkhantassa cintentassa. Visujjhatīti paṭipakkhamalavigamato paccayavasena sabhāvasaṃsuddhito visuddhaphalanibbattito ca saddhindriyaṃ visujjhati. Esa nayo sesesupi. Sammappadhāneti sammappadhānappaṭisaṃyutte (saṃ. ni. 5.651-662 ādayo) suttante. Esa nayo sesesupi. Jhānavimokkheti paṭhamajjhānādijjhānāni [V 1.0234] ceva paṭhamavimokkhādivimokkhe ca. Kāmañcettha jhānāniyeva vimokkhā, pavattiākāravasena pana visuṃ gahaṇaṃ.

Avoiding the faithless person: this means completely avoiding coarse persons who lack faith, being devoid of confidence and affection toward the Buddha and others. Associating with the faithful: this means associating with those resolved by faith in the Buddha and others, like the Elder Vakkali. The delightful: this refers to discourses that inspire confidence, such as the Sampasādanīya Sutta (Dīgha Nikāya 3.141, etc.). Reflecting: this means repeatedly examining and contemplating both the text and the meaning. It becomes purified: the faculty of faith is purified through the removal of opposing defilements, through natural purity by way of its conditions, and through the production of a purified result. This method applies to the others as well. Right effort: this refers to the discourses connected with right effort (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.651–662, etc.). This method applies to the others as well. Jhānas and liberations: this refers to the first jhāna and other jhānas, and the first liberation and other liberations. And here, the jhānas are themselves the liberations, but they are taken separately based on their mode of occurrence.

Gambhīrañāṇacariyanti gambhīrānaṃ ñāṇānaṃ pavattiṭṭhānaṃ. Tenāha – “saṇhasukhuma”ntiādi. Khandhantaranti sabhāvajātibhūmiādivasena khandhānaṃ nānattaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi. Akatābhinivesoti pubbe akatabhāvanābhiniveso. Saddhādhurādīsūti saddhādhure paññādhure ca. Avasāneti bhāvanāpariyosāne. Vivaṭṭetvāti saṅkhārārammaṇato vivaṭṭetvā nibbānaṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā. Arahattaṃ gaṇhātīti maggaparamparāya arahattaṃ gaṇhāti. Akampiyaṭṭhenāti paṭipakkhehi akampiyabhāvena. Etenevassa sampayuttadhammesu thirabhāvopi vibhāvito daṭṭhabbo. Na hi sampayuttadhammesu thirabhāvena vinā paṭipakkhehi akampiyatā sambhavati. Sampayuttadhammesu thirabhāveneva hi akusalānaṃ abyākatānañca nesaṃ balavabhāvūpapatti. Assaddhiyeti assaddhiyahetu. Nimittatthe hetaṃ bhummavacanaṃ. Esa nayo sesesupi.

'The course of profound knowledge' means the place of occurrence of profound knowledges. Hence it is said: 'gentle and subtle,' etc. 'Difference of aggregates' means the diversity of the aggregates in terms of nature, genus, ground, and so on. This method applies to the others as well. 'Adherence to the uncultivated' means adherence to the cultivation of what was previously uncultivated. 'In the duties of faith, etc.' means in the burden of faith and the burden of wisdom. 'At the end' means at the conclusion of the development. 'Having turned away' means having turned away from formations as an object and having made Nibbāna the object. 'Attains arahantship' means attaining arahantship through the succession of paths. 'By way of the unshakable state' means by the state of being unshaken by opposing factors. Through this, one should understand that the firmness in associated states is also made clear. For without firmness in associated states, being unshaken by opposing factors is impossible. Indeed, it is through firmness in associated states that the arising of their strength over unwholesome and indeterminate states comes about. 'Due to lack of faith' means due to the cause of faithlessness. This is a locative term used in the sense of cause. This method applies to the others as well.

418. Ādipadānanti satiādipadānaṃ. Saraṇaṭṭhenāti cirakatacirabhāsitānaṃ anussaraṇaṭṭhena. Upaṭṭhānalakkhaṇāti kāyādīsu asubhākārādisallakkhaṇamukhena tattha upatiṭṭhanasabhāvā. Upatiṭṭhanañca ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā ṭhānaṃ, avissajjanaṃ vā ārammaṇassa. Apilāpanalakkhaṇāti asammussanasabhāvā, udake alābu viya ārammaṇe plavitvā gantuṃ appadānaṃ, pāsāṇassa viya niccalassa ārammaṇassa ṭhapanaṃ sāraṇaṃ asammuṭṭhakaraṇaṃ apilāpanaṃ. Sāpateyyanti santakaṃ. Apilāpanaṃ asammuṭṭhaṃ karoti apilāpeti, sāyaṃ pātañca rājānaṃ issariyasampattiṃ sallakkhāpeti sāretīti attho. Kaṇhasukkasappaṭibhāge dhammeti kaṇhasukkasaṅkhāte sappaṭibhāge dhamme. Kaṇho hi dhammo sukkena, sukko [M 1.0249] ca kaṇhena sappaṭibhāgo. Vitthāra-saddo ādisaddattho. Tena “ime cattāro dhammā sammappadhānā, ime cattāro iddhipādā, imāni pañcindriyāni, imāni pañca balāni, ime satta bojjhaṅgā, ayaṃ ariyo aṭṭhaṅgiko maggo, ayaṃ samatho, ayaṃ vipassanā, ayaṃ vijjā, ayaṃ vimutti, ime lokuttaradhammāti evaṃ kho, mahārāja, apilāpanalakkhaṇā satī”ti (mi. pa. 2.1.13) imaṃ pāḷisesaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Therenāti nāgasenattherena. So hi dhammānaṃ kiccaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ katvā asseti “apilāpanalakkhaṇā sati, ākoṭanalakkhaṇo vitakko”tiādinā. Evañhi dhammā subodhā hontīti. Sammosapaccanīkaṃ kiccaṃ asammoso, na sammosābhāvamattanti āha – “asammosarasā vā”ti. Yassa dhammassa balena sampayuttadhammā ārammaṇābhimukhā bhavanti, sā sati. Tasmā sā tesaṃ ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpesi, sayaṃ vā ārammaṇābhimukhabhāvena paccupatiṭṭhatīti [V 1.0235] vuttaṃ – “gocarābhimukhībhāvapaccupaṭṭhānā”ti. Sammā pasattho bojjhaṅgoti sambojjhaṅgo. Bodhiyā vakkhamānāya dhammasāmaggiyā, bodhissa vā ariyasāvakassa aṅgoti bojjhaṅgo. Yā hītiādinā tameva saṅkhepato vuttamatthaṃ vivarati. “Yā hi ayaṃ dhammasāmaggī”ti etassa “bodhīti vuccatī”ti iminā sambandho. Dhammasāmaggiyāti dhammasamūhena, yāya dhammasāmaggiyāti sambandho. Patiṭṭhānāyūhanā oghataraṇasuttavaṇṇanāyaṃ (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.1) “kilesavasena patiṭṭhānaṃ, abhisaṅkhāravasena āyūhanā. Taṇhā diṭṭhivasena patiṭṭhānaṃ, avasesakilesābhisaṅkhārehi āyūhanā. Taṇhāvasena patiṭṭhānaṃ, diṭṭhivasena āyūhanā. Sassatadiṭṭhiyā patiṭṭhānaṃ, ucchedadiṭṭhiyā āyūhanā. Līnavasena patiṭṭhānaṃ, uddhaccavasena āyūhanā. Kāmasukhallikānuyogavasena patiṭṭhānaṃ, attakilamathānuyogavasena āyūhanā. Sabbākusalābhisaṅkhāravasena patiṭṭhānaṃ, sabbalokiyakusalābhisaṅkhāravasena āyūhanā”ti evaṃ vuttesu sattasu pakāresu idha avuttānaṃ vasena veditabbā. Paṭipakkhabhūtāyāti ettha līnappatiṭṭhānakāmasukhallikānuyogaucchedābhinivesānaṃ dhammavicayavīriyapītippadhānā dhammasāmaggī paṭipakkho, uddhaccāyūhanaattakilamathānuyogasassatābhinivesānaṃ passaddhisamādhiupekkhāpadhānā dhammasāmaggī paṭipakkho. Sati pana ubhayatthāpi icchitabbā. Tathā hi sā “sabbatthikā”ti vuttā.

418. “The initial terms” means the terms beginning with mindfulness. “In the sense of remembering” means in the sense of recollecting what has been long done and long spoken. “The characteristic of being present” is the nature of attending to the object by way of observing aspects such as foulness in the body. And “being present” means approaching and remaining with the object, or not abandoning the object. “The characteristic of not letting slip” is the nature of not forgetting. It is not allowing the mind to float away from the object, like a gourd on water; it is placing the object firmly, like a stone. Remembering, making it unforgotten, is “not letting slip.” “One's own property” means one's possession. “Not letting slip” makes it unforgotten; the meaning is that it makes the king reflect upon and remember his sovereign prosperity both evening and morning. “In the phenomena that are counterparts, dark and bright” refers to the phenomena designated as dark and bright, which are counterparts. For the dark phenomenon is the counterpart of the bright, and the bright of the dark. The word “elaboration” has the meaning of “etc.” By this, it includes the remainder of the Pāli text: “These four right strivings, these four bases of spiritual power, these five faculties, these five powers, these seven factors of enlightenment, this Noble Eightfold Path, this serenity, this insight, this knowledge, this liberation, these are the supramundane phenomena. Thus, great king, mindfulness has the characteristic of not letting slip.” “By the Elder” refers to the Elder Nāgasena. For he explains by stating the function and characteristic of phenomena, saying: “Mindfulness has the characteristic of not letting slip, applied thought has the characteristic of striking,” and so on. For in this way phenomena are easily understood. Its function, non-confusion, is the opponent of confusion, not merely the absence of confusion; thus he says: “or has non-confusion as its essence.” Mindfulness is that by the power of which associated phenomena face the object. Therefore, it presents them as facing the object, or it itself is present with the nature of facing the object; thus it is said: “its manifestation is the state of facing its domain.” “A rightly praised factor of enlightenment” is a “true factor of enlightenment” (sambojjhaṅgo). It is a “factor of enlightenment” (bojjhaṅgo) because it is a factor (aṅga) of the assemblage of phenomena, to be described, which is enlightenment (bodhi), or a factor of the enlightenment of a noble disciple. With “For that which…” and so on, he explains in brief the meaning just stated. “For this assemblage of phenomena” is connected with “is called enlightenment.” “By the assemblage of phenomena” means by the collection of phenomena; the connection is “by which assemblage of phenomena.” Regarding “getting established and striving,” in the commentary on the Oghataraṇa Sutta it is said: “Getting established is by way of defilements, striving is by way of volitional formations. Getting established is by way of craving and views, striving is by the remaining defilements and volitional formations. Getting established is by way of craving, striving is by way of views. Getting established is by eternalist view, striving is by annihilationist view. Getting established is by way of sluggishness, striving is by way of restlessness. Getting established is by way of indulgence in sensual pleasure, striving is by way of self-mortification. Getting established is by way of all unwholesome volitional formations, striving is by way of all mundane wholesome volitional formations.” Among these seven types mentioned, those not mentioned here should be understood accordingly. “Being a counterpart”: Here, the assemblage of dhammas in which investigation-of-dhammas, energy, and joy are prominent is the counterpart to being established in sluggishness, indulgence in sensual pleasures, and adherence to annihilationism. The assemblage of dhammas in which tranquility, concentration, and equanimity are prominent is the counterpart to striving with restlessness, self-mortification, and adherence to eternalism. Mindfulness, however, is to be desired in both cases, for it is said to be “needed everywhere.”

Kilesasantānaniddāya [M 1.0250] uṭṭhahatīti etena sikhāppattavipassanāya sahagatānampi satiādīnaṃ bojjhaṅgabhāvaṃ dasseti. Vuṭṭhānagāminivipassanā hi kilese nirodhentī eva pavattatīti. Cattāri vātiādinā pana maggaphalasahagatānaṃ bojjhaṅgabhāvaṃ dasseti. Sattahi bojjhaṅgehi bhāvitehi saccappaṭivedho hotīti kathamidaṃ jānitabbanti codanaṃ sandhāyāha – “yathāhā”tiādi. Jhānaṅgamaggaṅgādayo viyāti etena bodhibojjhaṅgasaddānaṃ samudāyāvayavavisayataṃ dasseti. Senaṅgarathaṅgādayo viyāti etena puggalapaññattiyā avijjamānapaññattibhāvaṃ dasseti.

“It rises up from the sleep that is the continuity of defilements”—by this, it shows that even mindfulness and other factors associated with insight that has attained its peak possess the nature of enlightenment factors. For insight leading to emergence occurs by suppressing the defilements. And with the phrase “four or…” and so on, it shows that those factors associated with the path and fruition possess the nature of enlightenment factors. “How is it to be known that the penetration of the truths occurs through the development of the seven enlightenment factors?”—addressing this question, it is said: “Just as…” and so on. “Like the factors of jhāna and path factors…”—by this, it shows that the terms “bodhi” and “bojjhaṅga” relate to the whole and its parts. “Like the constituents of an army, the parts of a chariot…” and so on—by this, it shows that, like the concept of a person, it is a designation for something that does not exist in itself.

Bodhāya saṃvattantīti bojjhaṅgāti kāraṇattho aṅgasaddoti katvā vuttaṃ. Bujjhantīti bodhiyo, bodhiyo eva aṅgāni bojjhaṅgānīti vuttaṃ – “bujjhantīti bojjhaṅgā”ti. Vipassanādīnaṃ kāraṇādīnaṃ bujjhitabbānañca saccānaṃ anurūpaṃ paccakkhabhāvena paṭimukhaṃ aviparītatāya sammā ca bujjhantīti evaṃ atthavisesadīpakehi upasaggehi “anubujjhantī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Bodhisaddo hi sabbavisesayuttabujjhanaṃ sāmaññena saṅgaṇhāti. Saṃ-saddo pasaṃsāyaṃ sundarabhāve ca dissatīti āha – “pasattho sundaro ca bojjhaṅgo sambojjhaṅgo”ti.

“They conduce to enlightenment, thus they are enlightenment factors”—this is stated by taking the word ‘aṅga’ in the sense of cause. “They awaken, thus they are enlightenments (bodhiyo); enlightenments themselves are the factors (aṅgāni), therefore they are enlightenment factors,” as it is said: “They awaken, hence they are enlightenment factors.” Because they awaken rightly and unerringly, face to face and directly, in conformity with the truths to be awakened to and their causes, such as insight, it is thus stated with prefixes indicating specific meanings, such as “they awaken accordingly” (anubujjhanti). For the word ‘bodhi’ generally includes awakening endowed with all its distinctions. The prefix ‘saṃ-’ is seen in the sense of praise and beauty, hence it is said: “The enlightenment factor is praised and beautiful, thus it is a ‘true enlightenment factor’ (sambojjhaṅgo).”

Dhamme [V 1.0236] vicinatīti dhammavicayo. Tattha dhammeti catusaccadhamme tabbinimuttassa sabhāvadhammassa abhāvato. Tato eva so pavicayalakkhaṇo. Obhāsanarasoti visayobhāsanaraso. Asammuyhanākārena paccupatiṭṭhatīti asammohapaccupaṭṭhāno.

“He investigates phenomena, thus it is investigation-of-phenomena” (dhammavicaya). Here, “phenomena” refers to the phenomena of the four truths, because there is no intrinsic phenomenon apart from them. For that very reason, it has the characteristic of investigation. Its function is to illuminate its object. It manifests as non-delusion.

Vīrassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vāti vīriyaṃ. Īrayitabbatoti pavattetabbato. Paggahalakkhaṇanti kosajjapakkhe patituṃ adatvā sampayuttadhammānaṃ paggahalakkhaṇaṃ. Tato eva sampayuttadhamme upatthambhanarasaṃ. Anosīdanaṃ asaṃsīdanaṃ.

The state of a hero, or his action, is energy (vīriya). Because it is to be exerted, it is to be set in motion. Its characteristic is the uplifting of associated states, not allowing them to fall to the side of laziness. For that very reason, its function is to support associated states. Its manifestation is non-sinking, non-collapse.

Pīṇayatīti tappeti. Pīṇanakiccena sampayuttadhammānaṃ viya taṃsamuṭṭhānapaṇītarūpehi kāyassābyapanaṃ. Pharaṇapītivasena hetaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ vuttaṃ, tathā rasoti. Udaggabhāvo odagyaṃ, taṃ paccupaṭṭhapetīti odagyapaccupaṭṭhānā. Ubbegapītivasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ.

“It gladdens,” thus it satisfies. With its function of gladdening, it suffuses the body with the excellent materiality produced from it, just as it does the associated states. This characteristic is stated by way of pervading joy, and likewise its function. The state of elation is upliftment; because it presents that, its manifestation is upliftment. And this is stated by way of transporting joy.

Kāyacittadarathappassambhanatoti kāyadarathassa cittadarathassa ca passambhanato vūpasamanato. Tenāha – “upasamalakkhaṇā”ti, kāyacittadarathānaṃ [M 1.0251] vūpasamanalakkhaṇāti attho. Kāyoti cettha vedanādayo tayo khandhā. Daratho sārambho, dukkhadomanassapaccayānaṃ uddhaccādikānaṃ kilesānaṃ, tathāpavattānaṃ vā catunnaṃ khandhānametaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Darathanimmaddanena pariḷāhaparipphandanavirahito sītibhāvo aparipphandanasītibhāvo.

Because of the calming of bodily and mental distress, that is, because of the calming and pacifying of bodily and mental distress. Hence it is said: “it has the characteristic of peace,” meaning it has the characteristic of pacifying bodily and mental distress. Here, “body” refers to the three aggregates beginning with feeling. “Distress” means agitation; it is a term for the defilements such as restlessness that are conditioned by pain and displeasure, or for the four aggregates occurring in such a state. Through the crushing of distress, there is a state of coolness free from feverish agitation and throbbing—the coolness of non-throbbing.

Sammā cittassa ṭhapanaṃ samādhānaṃ. Avikkhepo sampayuttānaṃ avikkhittatā. Yena sampayuttā avikkhittā honti, so dhammo avikkhepo. Avisāro attano eva avisaraṇabhāvo. Atha vā vikkhepappaṭipakkhatāya avikkhepalakkhaṇo. Nhānīyacuṇṇassa udakaṃ viya sampayuttadhammānaṃ sampiṇḍanakiccatāya avisārabhāvena lakkhitabbo avisāralakkhaṇo. Nivāte dīpacciṭṭhiti viya cetaso ṭhitibhāvena paccupatiṭṭhatīti cittaṭṭhitipaccupaṭṭhāno.

The right placing of the mind is concentration. Non-distraction is the undistractedness of associated states; that state by which associated states are undistracted is non-distraction. Non-scattering is the state of not scattering of itself; or alternatively, it is characterized by non-distraction as the opposite of distraction. It is to be known by the characteristic of non-scattering through its function of binding together associated states, like water with bath powder. It is manifested as the stability of mind, like the steadiness of a lamp's flame in a windless place.

Ajjhupekkhanatoti samappavattesu assesu sārathi viya sampayuttadhammānaṃ ajjhupekkhanato. Paṭisaṅkhānalakkhaṇāti majjhattabhāve ṭhatvā vīmaṃsanasaṅkhātappaṭisaṅkhānalakkhaṇā. Samavāhitalakkhaṇāti samaṃ avisamaṃ yathāsakakiccesu sampayuttadhammānaṃ pavattanalakkhaṇā. Udāsīnabhāvena pavattamānāpi sesasampayuttadhamme yathāsakakiccesu pavatteti, yathā rājā tuṇhī nisinnopi atthakaraṇe dhammaṭṭhe yathāsakaṃ kiccesu appamatto pavatteti. Alīnānuddhatappavattipaccayattā ūnādhikanivāraṇarasā. Pakkhapātupacchedanarasāti “idaṃ nihīnakiccaṃ [V 1.0237] hotu, idaṃ atirekatarakicca”nti evaṃ pakkhapātanavasena viya pavatti pakkhapāto, taṃ upacchindantī viya hotīti pakkhapātupacchedanarasā. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ sakasakakicce majjhattabhāvena paccupatiṭṭhatīti majjhattabhāvapaccupaṭṭhāno. Bojjhaṅgānaṃ uparūpari uppādanameva brūhanaṃ vaḍḍhanañcāti āha – “uppādetī”ti.

Equanimity means observing associated states, like a charioteer watching evenly moving horses. It is characterized by reflection, meaning it has the characteristic of examination called reflection while abiding in neutrality. It is characterized by balanced conveyance, meaning it has the characteristic of causing associated states to proceed evenly in their respective duties. Though proceeding with indifference, it causes the remaining associated states to function in their respective duties, just as a king, though sitting silently, causes judges to diligently perform their respective duties in matters of justice. Because it is a condition for functioning without sluggishness or agitation, its function is to prevent deficiency and excess. Its function is to cut off partiality; partiality is the functioning as if by taking a side, saying, 'Let this be a lesser duty, let this be a greater duty,' and it has this function because it acts as if to cut that off. It is manifested as neutrality regarding the respective duties of associated states. The repeated arising of the enlightenment factors is itself development and growth; hence it is said: 'arouses.'

Sati ca sampajaññañca satisampajaññaṃ, satipadhānaṃ vā sampajaññaṃ satisampajaññaṃ. Taṃ sabbattha satokāribhāvāvahattā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya hoti. Yathā paccanīkadhammappahānaṃ anurūpadhammasevanā ca anuppannānaṃ kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ uppādāya hoti, evaṃ satirahitapuggalavivajjanā, satokāripuggalasevanā, tattha ca yuttatā satisambojjhaṅgassa uppādāya [M 1.0252] hotīti imamatthaṃ dasseti, “satisampajañña”ntiādinā. Sattasu ṭhānesūti “abhikkante paṭikkante sampajānakārī hoti, ālokite vilokite sampajānakārī hoti, samiñjite pasārite sampajānakārī hoti, saṅghāṭipattacīvaradhāraṇe sampajānakārī hoti, asite pīte khāyite sāyite sampajānakārī hoti, uccārapassāvakamme sampajānakārī hoti, gate ṭhite nisinne sutte jāgarite bhāsite tuṇhībhāve sampajānakārī hotī”ti (dī. ni. 2.376; ma. ni. 1.109) evaṃ vuttesu abhikkantādīsu sattasu ṭhānesu. Tissadattatthero nāma yo bodhimaṇḍe suvaṇṇasalākaṃ gahetvā “aṭṭhārasasu bhāsāsu katarabhāsāya dhammaṃ kathemī”ti parisaṃ padhāresi. Abhayattheroti dattābhayattheramāha. Abhinivesanti vipassanābhinivesaṃ.

Mindfulness and clear comprehension means mindfulness and clear comprehension; or, clear comprehension with mindfulness as its basis. This, because it brings about the state of acting mindfully in all instances, leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. Just as abandoning opposing qualities and cultivating suitable qualities leads to the arising of unarisen wholesome qualities, so too avoiding individuals devoid of mindfulness, associating with mindful individuals, and applying oneself properly in that regard leads to the arising of the enlightenment factor of mindfulness. This meaning is shown by the phrase 'mindfulness and clear comprehension,' and so on. 'In the seven instances' refers to the seven instances stated thus: 'in going forward and returning, one acts with clear comprehension; in looking ahead and looking around, one acts with clear comprehension; in bending and stretching, one acts with clear comprehension; in wearing the outer robe and carrying the bowl and other robes, one acts with clear comprehension; in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting, one acts with clear comprehension; in defecating and urinating, one acts with clear comprehension; in walking, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent, one acts with clear comprehension.' The elder Tissadatta is the one who, at the Bodhi Tree, took a golden stylus and considered the assembly, thinking, 'In which of the eighteen languages shall I teach the Dhamma?' 'The elder Abhaya' refers to Dattābhaya Thera. 'Adherence' refers to adherence to insight.

Paripucchakatāti pariyogāhetvā pucchakabhāvo. Ācariye payirupāsitvā pañcapi nikāye saha aṭṭhakathāya pariyogāhetvā yaṃ yaṃ tattha gaṇṭhiṭṭhānabhūtaṃ, taṃ taṃ “idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ, imassa ko attho”ti khandhāyatanādiatthaṃ pucchantassa hi dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgo uppajjati. Tenāha – “khandhadhātu…pe… bahulatā”ti.

The state of questioning means the state of being a questioner after having thoroughly grasped the teachings. Having attended upon a teacher and thoroughly grasped the five Nikāyas together with their commentaries, whatever has become a knotty point therein, one questions about it thus: 'Venerable sir, how is this? What is the meaning of this?' For one who thus questions about the meaning of the aggregates, sense bases, and so on, the enlightenment factor of investigation of states arises. Therefore it is said: 'Aggregates, elements... frequently.'

Vatthuvisadakiriyāti ettha cittacetasikānaṃ pavattiṭṭhānabhāvato sarīraṃ tappaṭibaddhāni cīvarādīni ca vatthūnīti adhippetāni. Tāni yathā cittassa sukhāvahāni honti, tathā karaṇaṃ tesaṃ visadakiriyā. Tenāha – “ajjhattikabāhirāna”ntiādi. Ussannadosanti vātapittādivasena upacitadosaṃ. Sedamalamakkhitanti sedena ceva jallikāsaṅkhātena sarīramalena ca makkhitaṃ. Ca-saddena aññampi sarīrassa pīḷāvahaṃ accāsanādiṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Senāsanaṃ vāti vā-saddena malaggahitapattādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Paribhaṇḍakaraṇādīhīti ādi-saddena pattapacanādīnaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Avisadeti vatthumhi avisade sati, visayabhūte vā. Kathaṃ bhāvanamanuyuttassa [V 1.0238] tāni ajjhattikabāhiravatthūni visayo? Antarantarā pavattanakacittuppādavaseneva vuttaṃ. Te hi cittuppādā cittekaggatāya aparisuddhabhāvāya saṃvattanti. Cittacetasikesūti nissayādipaccayabhūtesu cittacetasikesu. Ñāṇampīti api-saddo sampiṇḍanattho. Tena “na kevalaṃ vatthuyeva, atha kho tasmiṃ aparisuddhe ñāṇampi aparisuddhaṃ [M 1.0253] hotī”ti nissayāparisuddhiyā taṃnissitāparisuddhi viya visayassa aparisuddhatāya visayino aparisuddhiṃ dasseti.

The cleansing of the basis: Here, the body, being the place of occurrence for mind and mental factors, and the robes and other requisites connected to it, are intended as the 'bases.' Making them conducive to the mind’s well-being is the cleansing of them. Hence it is said: 'internal and external,' and so on. 'Abundant ailments' means accumulated ailments due to wind, bile, and so on. 'Smeared with sweat and grime' means smeared with sweat and bodily grime. The word 'and' also includes other things that afflict the body, such as overeating. 'Or the lodging': by the word 'or,' the inclusion of bowls and so on that are covered in dirt should be understood. 'By preparing the requisites, etc.': by the word 'etc.,' the inclusion of cooking pots and so on should be understood. 'When it is not clean': when the basis is not clean, or when it has become an object of mind. How do these internal and external bases become objects for one devoted to meditation? This is said with reference to the arising of thoughts that occur from time to time. For those mental arisings conduce to the impurity of one-pointedness of mind. 'In mind and mental factors' means in the mind and mental factors that are the support, condition, and so on. 'Knowledge also': the word 'also' has the sense of inclusion. Thus it shows: 'Not only is the basis impure, but when it is impure, knowledge also becomes impure.' Just as the impurity of the support leads to the impurity of that which is supported by it, so the impurity of the object shows the impurity of the subject.

Samabhāvakaraṇanti kiccato anūnādhikabhāvakaraṇaṃ. Saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti, saddheyyavatthusmiṃ paccayavasena adhimokkhakiccassa paṭutarabhāvena paññāya avisadatāya vīriyādīnañca sithilatādinā saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ hoti. Tenāha – “itarāni mandānī”ti. Tatoti tasmā, saddhindriyassa balavabhāvato itaresañca mandattāti attho. Kosajjapakkhe patituṃ adatvā sampayuttadhammānaṃ paggaṇhanaṃ anubalappadānaṃ paggaho. Paggahova kiccaṃ paggahakiccaṃ. Kātuṃ na sakkotīti ānetvā sambandhitabbaṃ. Ārammaṇaṃ upagantvā ṭhānaṃ, anissajjanaṃ vā upaṭṭhānaṃ. Vikkhepappaṭipakkho, yena vā sampayuttā avikkhittā honti, so avikkhepo. Rūpagataṃ viya cakkhunā yena yāthāvato visayasabhāvaṃ passati, taṃ dassanakiccaṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti balavatā saddhindriyena adhibhūtattā. Sahajātadhammesu hi indaṭṭhaṃ kārentānaṃ sahapavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ ekadesatāvaseneva atthasiddhi, na aññathā. Tasmāti vuttamevatthaṃ kāraṇabhāvena paccāmasati. Tanti saddhindriyaṃ. Dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇenāti yassa saddheyyassa vatthuno uḷāratādiguṇe adhimuccanassa sātisayappavattiyā saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ jātaṃ, tassa paccayapaccayuppannatādivibhāgato yāthāvato vīmaṃsanena. Evañhi evaṃdhammatānayena yāthāvasarasato pariggayhamāne savipphāro adhimokkho na hoti “ayaṃ imesaṃ dhammānaṃ sabhāvo”ti parijānanavasena paññābyāpārassa sātisayattā. Dhuriyadhammesu hi yathā saddhāya balavabhāve paññāya mandabhāvo hoti, evaṃ paññāya balavabhāve saddhāya mandabhāvo hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “taṃ dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena hāpetabba”nti.

Equalizing means making something neither deficient nor excessive in its function. The faculty of faith becomes strong when, due to the condition of faith in an object worthy of faith, the function of resolution is prominent, because wisdom lacks clarity and energy and the like are slack. Hence it is said: 'The others are weak.' Therefore, this means that the faculty of faith is strong and the others are weak. Not giving way to the side of sloth, the upholding of associated states is exertion, the giving of support. Exertion itself is the function of exertion. 'Unable to do' should be brought in and connected. Approaching an object and establishing it, or non-abandonment, is attending. It is the opposite of distraction, or it is non-distraction, by which the associated states are undistracted. Just as with the eye one sees the true nature of an object such as form, so one cannot perform the function of seeing, because it is overpowered by the strong faculty of faith. For in co-arisen states, the accomplishment of the purpose occurs only through the one-sided dominance of states occurring together, not otherwise. Therefore, it refers back to what has been said as the reason. 'That' means the faculty of faith. By reviewing the nature of phenomena: that is, for one whose faculty of faith has become strong due to the exceedingly great arising of resolution regarding the superior qualities of an object worthy of faith, by thoroughly examining it as it truly is, in terms of the division into conditions, conditioned phenomena, and so on. For when things are grasped according to their true nature in this way, there is no intense resolution with full force, because the function of wisdom is exceedingly great in comprehending: 'This is the nature of these phenomena,' by way of fully knowing. Indeed, in the leading states, just as when faith is strong, wisdom is weak, so too when wisdom is strong, faith is weak. Therefore, it is said: 'It should be diminished by reviewing the nature of phenomena.'

Tathā amanasikārenāti yenākārena bhāvanamanuyuñjantassa saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ jātaṃ, tenākārena bhāvanāya ananuyuñjanatoti vuttaṃ hoti. Idha duvidhena saddhindriyassa balavabhāvo attano vā paccayavisesena kiccuttariyato vīriyādīnaṃ vā mandakiccatāya. Tattha paṭhamavikappe hāpanavidhi dassito, dutiyavikappe pana yathā manasikaroto vīriyādīnaṃ mandakiccatāya saddhindriyaṃ balavaṃ jātaṃ, tathā amanasikārena vīriyādīnaṃ [M 1.0254] paṭukiccabhāvāvahena manasikārena [V 1.0239] saddhindriyaṃ tehi samarasaṃ karontena hāpetabbaṃ. Iminā nayena sesindriyesupi hāpanavidhi veditabbo.

'Likewise, by not giving attention' means this: by not engaging in cultivation in that way in which the faculty of faith became strong when one was engaging in it. Here, the strength of the faculty of faith arises in two ways: either through its own particular conditions causing excellence in its function, or due to the weakened activity of energy and other faculties. In the first alternative, the method of diminishing has been shown. But in the second alternative, just as the faculty of faith becomes strong due to the weakened activity of energy and other faculties when one gives attention in a certain way, so too, by not giving attention—that is, through attention that brings about the keen activity of energy and other faculties—one should diminish it by making the faculty of faith harmonious with them. In this way, the method of diminishing should be understood for the remaining faculties as well.

Vakkalittheravatthūti so hi āyasmā saddhādhimuttatāya katādhikāro satthu rūpadassanappasuto eva hutvā viharanto satthārā “kiṃ te, vakkali, iminā pūtikāyena diṭṭhena, yo kho, vakkali, dhammaṃ passati, so maṃ passatī”tiādinā (saṃ. ni. 3.87) nayena ovaditvā kammaṭṭhāne niyojitopi taṃ ananuyuñjanto paṇāmito attānaṃ vinipātetuṃ papātaṭṭhānaṃ abhiruhi. Atha naṃ satthā yathānisinnova obhāsavissajjanena attānaṃ dassetvā –

The story of Venerable Vakkali—for he, being inclined by faith and having made a foundation, was eager to see the Teacher’s form and dwelt thus. The Teacher admonished him, saying, “What is it to you, Vakkali, to see this foul body? One who sees the Dhamma, Vakkali, sees me,” and so on (Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.87). Though he was assigned a meditation subject, not applying himself to it, he was dismissed and climbed to a precipice where he intended to hurl himself to destruction. Then the Teacher, just as he was seated, showed himself by emitting a ray of light, saying:

“Pāmojjabahulo bhikkhu, pasanno buddhasāsane;

Adhigacche padaṃ santaṃ, saṅkhārūpasamaṃ sukha”nti. (dha. pa. 381) –

“The monk, abounding in joy, confident in the Buddha’s teaching, would attain the peaceful state, the blissful subsiding of formations.”

Gāthaṃ vatvā “ehi, vakkalī”ti āha. So teneva amatena abhisitto haṭṭhatuṭṭho hutvā vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapesi, saddhāya pana balavabhāvena vipassanāvīthiṃ na otari. Taṃ ñatvā bhagavā tassa indriyasamattappaṭipādanāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ sodhetvā adāsi. So satthārā dinnanaye ṭhatvā vipassanaṃ ussukkāpetvā maggappaṭipāṭiyā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ – “vakkalittheravatthu cettha nidassana”nti. Etthāti saddhindriyassa adhimattabhāve sesindriyānaṃ sakiccākaraṇe. Itarakiccabhedanti upaṭṭhānādikiccavisesaṃ. Passaddhādīti ādi-saddena samādhiupekkhāsambojjhaṅgānaṃ saṅgaho. Hāpetabbanti yathā saddhindriyassa balavabhāvo dhammasabhāvapaccavekkhaṇena hāyati, evaṃ vīriyindriyassa adhimattatā passaddhiādibhāvanāya hāyati samādhipakkhiyattā tassā. Tathā hi samādhindriyassa adhimattataṃ kosajjapātato rakkhantī vīriyādibhāvanā viya vīriyindriyassa adhimattataṃ uddhaccapātato rakkhantī passaddhādibhāvanā ekaṃsato hāpeti. Tena vuttaṃ – “passaddhādibhāvanāya hāpetabba”nti.

Having recited the verse, he said, 'Come, Vakkali.' Then, being anointed with that very nectar, he became joyful and elated and began to establish insight. However, due to the overwhelming strength of his faith, he did not enter the avenue of insight. Knowing this, the Blessed One refined the meditation subject for him to bring his faculties to equilibrium and gave it to him. Standing firm in the method given by the Teacher, he earnestly applied himself to insight and attained arahantship through the order of the path. Therefore, it is said: 'Here, the story of Venerable Vakkali serves as an illustration.' 'Here' means in the case of the excessive faculty of faith when the other faculties do not perform their functions. 'The distinction of other functions' means the specific functions such as attending and so on. 'Tranquility, etc.'—by the word 'etc.,' the enlightenment factors of concentration and equanimity are included. 'Should be diminished'—just as the powerfulness of the faculty of faith diminishes through reflection on the nature of phenomena, so too the excessive strength of the faculty of energy diminishes through the development of tranquility, etc., because that belongs to the concentration group. For indeed, just as the development of energy, etc., protects the excessive strength of the faculty of concentration from the downfall of sloth, so too the development of tranquility, etc., protecting the excessive strength of the faculty of energy from the downfall of restlessness, certainly diminishes it. Therefore, it is said: 'It should be diminished through the development of tranquility, etc.'

Soṇattherassa vatthūti sukhumālasoṇattherassa vatthu. So hi āyasmā satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā sītavane viharanto “mama sarīraṃ sukhumālaṃ, na ca sakkā sukheneva sukhaṃ adhigantuṃ, kilametvāpi samaṇadhammo [M 1.0255] kātabbo”ti ṭhānacaṅkamameva adhiṭṭhāya padhānamanuyuñjanto pādatalesu phoṭesu uṭṭhitesupi vedanaṃ ajjhupekkhitvā daḷhavīriyaṃ karonto accāraddhavīriyatāya visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Satthā tattha gantvā vīṇūpamovādena ovaditvā [V 1.0240] vīriyasamatāyojanavidhiṃ dassento kammaṭṭhānaṃ visodhetvā gijjhakūṭaṃ gato. Theropi satthārā dinnanayena vīriyasamataṃ yojetvā bhāvento vipassanampi ussukkāpetvā arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ – “soṇattherassa vatthu dassetabba”nti. Sesesupīti satisamādhipaññindriyesupi.

The story of Elder Soṇa is about the delicate Elder Soṇa. Indeed, this venerable one, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, dwelt in the Cool Grove, thinking: 'My body is delicate, and it is not possible to attain happiness with ease. Even if I exhaust myself, the duty of a recluse must be done.' He resolved to practice only standing and walking meditation and applied himself to the striving; although blisters arose on the soles of his feet, he endured the pain with equanimity, exerting strong effort. Yet, due to excessive exertion, he could not achieve distinction. The Teacher, going there, advised him with the simile of the lute, showing the method of balancing energy and purifying his meditation subject, then went to Vulture Peak. The elder, following the method given by the Teacher, balanced his energy and, developing it, strove diligently in insight and was established in arahantship. Therefore, it is said: 'The story of Elder Soṇa should be told.' 'As for the rest' means also in the case of the faculties of mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.

Samatanti saddhāpaññānaṃ aññamaññaṃ anūnādhikabhāvaṃ, tathā samādhivīriyānaṃ. Yathā hi saddhāpaññānaṃ visuṃ dhuriyadhammabhūtānaṃ kiccato aññamaññānativattanaṃ visesato icchitabbaṃ, yato nesaṃ samadhuratāya appanā sampajjati, evaṃ samādhivīriyānaṃ kosajjuddhaccapakkhikānaṃ samarasatāya sati aññamaññūpatthambhanato sampayuttadhammānaṃ antadvayapātābhāvena sammadeva appanā ijjhati. Balavasaddhotiādi byatirekamukhena vuttassevatthassa samatthanaṃ. Tassattho – yo balavatiyā saddhāya samannāgato avisadañāṇo, so mudhappasanno hoti, na aveccappasanno. Tathā hi avatthusmiṃ pasīdati seyyathāpi titthiyasāvakā. Kerāṭikapakkhanti sāṭheyyapakkhaṃ bhajati. Saddhāhīnāya paññāya atidhāvanto “deyyavatthupariccāgena vinā cittuppādamattenapi dānamayaṃ puññaṃ hotī”tiādīni parikappeti hetuppaṭirūpakehi vañcito, evaṃbhūto sukkhatakkaviluttacitto paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ nādiyati, saññattiṃ na gacchati. Tenāha – “bhesajjasamuṭṭhito viya rogo atekiccho hotī”ti. Yathā cettha saddhāpaññānaṃ aññamaññaṃ samabhāvo atthāvaho, anatthāvaho visamabhāvo, evaṃ samādhivīriyānaṃ aññamaññaṃ avikkhepāvaho samabhāvo, itaro vikkhepāvaho cāti kosajjaṃ abhibhavati, tena appanaṃ na pāpuṇātīti adhippāyo. Uddhaccaṃ abhibhavatīti etthāpi eseva nayo. Taṃ ubhayanti saddhāpaññādvayaṃ samādhivīriyadvayañca. Samaṃ kattabbanti samarasaṃ kātabbaṃ.

Balance means that faith and wisdom are neither deficient nor excessive in relation to each other, and similarly with concentration and energy. For just as it is especially desirable that faith and wisdom, being distinct leading qualities, do not overstep each other in function, since from their balanced harmony absorption is accomplished; so too with concentration and energy, which are respectively allied with sloth and restlessness, their equilibrium, through mutual support, ensures that the associated states avoid falling into either extreme, thus rightly achieving absorption. The phrase 'strong faith,' etc., is a confirmation of the meaning already stated by way of contrast. The meaning is this: one endowed with strong faith but lacking clear knowledge becomes blindly devoted, not devoted with understanding. For they have confidence in what is not a proper basis, just like the disciples of heretics. They incline toward the deceitful faction. One who rushes ahead with wisdom devoid of faith speculates, 'Even without giving up material gifts, meritorious giving arises by a mere thought-moment,' and so on—thus deceived by plausible reasoning. Such a person, whose mind is ruined by dry speculation, does not heed the words of the wise and cannot be brought to understanding. Hence it is said, 'Like a disease arising from medicine, it becomes incurable.' Just as in this case, the balance of faith and wisdom brings benefit, while imbalance brings harm, so too with concentration and energy—their balance prevents distraction, whereas imbalance causes distraction. Sloth overpowers, preventing absorption—this is the meaning. Similarly, restlessness overpowers—the principle is the same. 'Both' refers to the pair of faith and wisdom, and the pair of concentration and energy. 'They should be made equal' means they should be harmonized.

Samādhikammikassāti samathakammaṭṭhānikassa. Evanti evaṃ sante, saddhāya thokaṃ balavabhāve satīti attho. Saddahantoti “pathavī pathavīti manasikaraṇamattena [M 1.0256] kathaṃ jhānuppattī”ti acintetvā “addhā sammāsambuddhena vuttavidhi ijjhissatī”ti saddahanto saddhaṃ janento. Okappentoti ārammaṇaṃ anuppavisitvā viya adhimuccanavasena avakappento pakkhandanto. Ekaggatā balavatī vaṭṭati samādhippadhānattā jhānassa. Ubhinnanti samādhipaññānaṃ. Samādhikammikassa samādhino adhimattatā viya paññāya adhimattatāpi icchitabbāti āha – “samatāyapī”ti, samabhāvenapīti attho. Appanāti lokiyaappanā. Tathā hi “hotiyevā”ti sāsaṅkaṃ vadati. Lokuttarappanā pana tesaṃ samabhāveneva icchitā. Yathāha – “samathavipassanaṃ yuganaddhaṃ bhāvetī”ti (a. ni. 4.170; paṭi. ma. 2.5).

'One devoted to concentration work' means one whose meditation subject is serenity. 'Thus' means, this being so, when faith is somewhat strong. 'One who believes' means one who, without thinking, 'How can absorption arise merely by attending to “earth, earth”?', generates faith and believes, 'Surely, the method taught by the Perfectly Enlightened One will succeed.' 'One who trusts' means one who places confidence and plunges into the object, as if entering it, by way of determination. One-pointedness should be strong, because concentration is predominant in jhāna. 'Of both' means of concentration and wisdom. For one devoted to concentration work, just as a preponderance of concentration is desired, so too is a preponderance of wisdom desired. Thus it is said, 'even in balance,' meaning 'even in a state of balance.' 'Absorption' here refers to mundane absorption. For indeed, one says 'it might be' with doubt. Supramundane absorption, however, is desired only with their balance, as it is said: 'One develops serenity and insight yoked together.'

Yadi [V 1.0241] visesato saddhāpaññānaṃ samādhivīriyānañca samatāva icchitā, kathaṃ satīti āha – “sati pana sabbattha balavatī vaṭṭatī”ti. Sabbatthāti līnuddhaccapakkhikesu pañcasu indriyesu. Uddhaccapakkhike gaṇhanto “saddhāvīriyapaññāna”nti āha. Aññathāpīti ca gahetabbā siyā. Tathā hi kosajjapakkhikena ca samādhināicceva vuttaṃ, na “passaddhisamādhiupekkhāhī”ti. Sāti sati. Sabbesu rājakammesu niyutto sabbakammiko. Tenāti tena sabbattha icchitabbatthena kāraṇena. Āha aṭṭhakathāyaṃ. Sabbattha niyuttā sabbatthikā sabbattha līne uddhate ca citte icchitabbattā, sabbena vā līnuddhaccapakkhiyena bojjhaṅgagaṇena atthetabbāti sabbatthā, sāva sabbatthikā. Cittanti kusalacittaṃ. Tassa hi satipaṭisaraṇaṃ parāyaṇaṃ appattassa pattiyā anadhigatassa adhigamāya. Tenāha – “ārakkhapaccupaṭṭhānā”tiādi.

If the balance of faith and wisdom, and of concentration and energy, is particularly desired, what of mindfulness? It is said: 'But mindfulness should be strong everywhere.' 'Everywhere' means in the five faculties, which are allied with sluggishness and restlessness. Taking those allied with restlessness, it says: 'faith, energy, and wisdom.' And it could be taken otherwise. For it is said only 'with concentration,' which is allied with sloth, not 'with tranquility, concentration, and equanimity.' 'That' is mindfulness. Like a servant engaged in all royal duties, an all-duties worker. 'Therefore' means for that reason, that it is to be desired everywhere. It is said in the commentary: 'Engaged everywhere, universally applicable, because it is to be desired everywhere, whether the mind is sluggish or restless; or, because it is needed by the entire group of awakening factors allied with sloth and restlessness, it is everywhere; that itself is universally applicable.' 'The mind' means the wholesome mind. For it, mindfulness is the refuge, the final resort—for the attainment of the unattained, for the realization of the unrealized. Therefore, it is said: 'Its manifestation is protection,' and so on.

Khandhādibhedesu anogāḷhapaññānanti pariyattibāhusaccavasenapi khandhāyatanādīsu appatiṭṭhitabuddhīnaṃ. Bahussutasevanā hi sutamayañāṇāvahā. Taruṇavipassanāsamaṅgīpi bhāvanāmayañāṇe ṭhitattā ekaṃsato paññavā eva nāma hotīti āha – “samapaññāsa…pe… puggalasevanā”ti. Ñeyyadhammassa gambhīrabhāvavasena tapparicchedakañāṇassa gambhīrabhāvaggahaṇanti āha – “gambhīresu khandhādīsu pavattāya gambhīrapaññāyā”ti. Tañhi ñeyyaṃ tādisāya paññāya caritabbato gambhīrañāṇacariyaṃ. Tassā vā paññāya tattha pabhedato pavatti gambhīrañāṇacariyā, tassā paccavekkhaṇāti āha – “gambhīrapaññāya pabhedapaccavekkhaṇā”ti.

'Those whose wisdom is not deeply rooted in the divisions of aggregates and so on' means those whose understanding is not established in the aggregates, sense bases, and so on, even by way of extensive learning. For associating with the very learned brings about knowledge based on learning. Even one endowed with newly arisen insight is indeed called wise in a definitive sense because they are established in knowledge born of meditation—thus it is said: 'Association with persons... of equal wisdom.' Due to the profundity of the knowable phenomena, it is the grasping of the profound nature of the knowledge that discerns them—thus it is said: 'by profound wisdom operating in the profound aggregates and so on.' For that knowable should be traversed by such wisdom, hence it is the conduct of profound knowledge. Alternatively, the proceeding of that wisdom there according to its divisions is the conduct of profound knowledge, and its reviewing—thus it is said: 'the reviewing of the divisions by means of profound wisdom.'

Pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇaṃ [M 1.0257] niraye nibbattasattassa yebhuyyena sabbapaṭhamaṃ karontīti devadūtasuttādīsu ādito vuttattā ca āha – “pañcavidhabandhanakammakāraṇato paṭṭhāyā”ti. Sakaṭavahanādikāleti ādi-saddena tadaññaṃ manussehi tiracchānehi ca vibādhitabbakālaṃ saṅgaṇhāti. Ekaṃ buddhantaranti idaṃ aparāparesu petesuyeva uppajjanakasattavasena vuttaṃ, ekaccānaṃ vā petānaṃ ekaccatiracchānānaṃ viya dīghāyukatā siyāti tathā vuttaṃ. Tathā hi kāḷo nāgarājā catunnaṃ buddhānaṃ sammukhībhāvaṃ labhitvā ṭhitopi metteyyassapi bhagavato sammukhībhāvaṃ labhissatīti vadanti, yatassa kappāyukatā vuttā.

The performing of the fivefold binding action is done first of all and for the most part to a being reborn in hell, as stated from the beginning in the Devadūta Sutta and others. Therefore, it is said: 'Starting from the performing of the fivefold binding action.' The phrase 'at the time of cart-pulling, etc.' includes, by the word 'etc.,' other times when they are to be troubled by humans or animals. 'One Buddha-interval' is said with reference to a being who arises as a ghost again and again, or it is said thus because some ghosts, like certain animals, may have long lifespans. For example, it is said that the Nāga King Kāḷa, having been in the presence of four Buddhas, will also be in the presence of the Blessed One Metteyya, since his lifespan is said to last an eon.

Evaṃ ānisaṃsadassāvinoti vīriyāyatto eva sabbo lokiyo lokuttaro ca visesādhigamoti evaṃ vīriye ānisaṃsadassanasīlassa. Gamanavīthinti sapubbabhāgaṃ nibbānagāminipaṭipadaṃ[V 1.0242], saha vipassanāya ariyamaggappaṭipāṭi, sattavisuddhiparamparā vā. Sā hi “bhikkhuno vaṭṭaniyyānāya gantabbā paṭipajjitabbā paṭipadā”ti katvā gamanavīthi nāma.

'Of one who sees the benefits thus' means: of one who is accustomed to seeing the benefits in energy in this way: 'All special attainments, both worldly and supramundane, depend solely on energy.' 'The path of progress' means the practice leading to Nibbāna together with its preliminary part; or the order of the noble path together with insight; or the succession of the seven purifications. For, because it is 'the path to be gone along and practiced by a bhikkhu for the escape from the round,' it is called the path of progress.

Kāyadaḷhībahuloti yathā tathā kāyassa daḷhīkammappasuto. Piṇḍapātanti raṭṭhapiṇḍaṃ. Paccayadāyakānaṃ attani kārassa attano sammāpaṭipattiyā mahapphalabhāvassa karaṇena piṇḍassa bhikkhāya paṭipūjanā piṇḍapātāpacāyanaṃ.

'Devoted to bodily fortitude' means one who is intent on the act of strengthening the body in any way whatsoever. 'Almsfood' means alms from the country. 'Respect for almsfood' is the honoring of the alms received by begging, which is done by making the service rendered to oneself by the donors of requisites become of great fruit through one's own right practice.

Nīharantoti pattatthavikato nīharanto. Taṃ saddaṃ sutvāti taṃ upāsikāya vacanaṃ paṇṇasālādvāre ṭhitova pañcābhiññatāya dibbasotena sutvā. Manussasampatti, dibbasampatti, nibbānasampattīti imā tisso sampattiyo. Dātuṃ sakkhissasīti tayi katena dānamayena veyyāvaccamayena ca puññakammena khettavisesabhāvūpagamanena aparāparaṃ devamanussānaṃ sampattiyo ante nibbānasampattiñca dātuṃ sakkhissasīti thero attānaṃ pucchati. Sitaṃ karontoti “akiccheneva mayā vaṭṭadukkhaṃ samatikkanta”nti paccavekkhaṇāvasāne sañjātapāmojjavasena sitaṃ karonto.

'He removes it' means he removes it from the bowl-stand. 'Hearing that sound,' he heard the laywoman’s words, standing at the door of the leaf-hut, with his divine ear, by the power of the five higher knowledges. Human attainment, divine attainment, and Nibbāna attainment—these are the three attainments. 'You will be able to give'—the elder asks himself whether, through the merit of giving and service done by you, and by becoming a special field of merit, you will successively be able to give the attainments of devas and humans, and ultimately the attainment of Nibbāna. 'Smiling,' he smiles with joy arising at the end of reflection, thinking, 'Without difficulty, I have crossed over the suffering of the round of existence.'

Nipparissayakāloti nirupaddavakālo, tadā bhikkhusaṅghassa sulabhā paccayā hontīti paccayahetukā cittapīḷā natthīti adhippāyo. Passantānaṃyevāti anādare sāmivacanaṃ. Khīradhenunti khīradāyikaṃ dhenuṃ[M 1.0258]. Kiñcideva katvāti kiñcideva bhatikammaṃ katvā. Ucchuyantakammanti ucchuyantasālāya kātabbaṃ kiccaṃ. Tameva magganti upāsakena paṭipannamaggaṃ. Upakaṭṭhāyāti āsannāya. Vippaṭipannanti jātidhammakuladhammādilaṅghanena asammāpaṭipannaṃ. Evanti yathā asammāpaṭipanno putto tāya eva asammāpaṭipattiyā kulasantānato bāhiro hutvā pitu santikā dāyajjassa na bhāgī, evaṃ kusītopi teneva kusītabhāvena na sammāpaṭipanno satthu santikā laddhabbaariyadhanadāyajjassa na bhāgī. Āraddhavīriyova labhati sammāpaṭipajjanato. Uppajjati vīriyasambojjhaṅgoti yojanā, evaṃ sabbattha.

'Time without danger' means a time free from calamities, the intention being that requisites are easily obtained for the community of monks, so there is no mental distress caused by the need for requisites. 'For those who see' is a genitive case indicating disregard. 'A milk cow' means a cow that gives milk. 'Having done some work' means having done some menial labor. 'The task of the sugarcane press' means the work to be done at the sugarcane press hall. 'That very path' means the path undertaken by the lay follower. 'Nearby' means close at hand. 'Gone astray' means one who has deviated wrongly by transgressing norms of birth, family, and so on, not practicing rightly. 'Thus,' just as a son who behaves wrongly, due to that very wrong behavior, becomes an outsider to the family lineage and does not share in the father’s inheritance, so too a lazy person, due to that very laziness, not practicing rightly, does not share in the inheritance of noble wealth to be gained from the Teacher. Only one with aroused energy gains it by practicing rightly. 'The enlightenment factor of energy arises'—this is the connection; the same applies throughout.

Mahāti sīlādiguṇehi mahanto vipulo anaññasādhāraṇo. Taṃ panassa guṇamahattaṃ dasasahassilokadhātukampanena loke pākaṭanti dassento “satthuno hī”tiādimāha.

'Great' means great and vast in virtues such as morality, unsurpassed, and unique to him. And to show how the greatness of his virtues became evident in the world through the shaking of the ten-thousandfold world-system, he said, 'of the Teacher,' and so on.

Yasmā [V 1.0243] satthusāsane pabbajitassa pabbajjūpagamanena sakyaputtiyabhāvo sañjāyati, tasmā buddhaputtabhāvaṃ dassento “asambhinnāyā”tiādimāha.

Because for one who has gone forth in the Teacher’s dispensation, the state of being a son of the Sakyan arises upon undertaking the going forth, therefore, showing the state of being a son of the Buddha, he says, 'unbroken,' and so on.

Alasānaṃ bhāvanāya nāmamattampi ajānantānaṃ kāyadaḷhībahulānaṃ yāvadatthaṃ bhuñjitvā seyyasukhādianuyuñjanakānaṃ tiracchānagatikānaṃ puggalānaṃ dūrato vajjanā kusītapuggalaparivajjanāti āha – “kucchiṃ pūretvā ṭhitaajagarasadise”tiādi. “Divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya āvaraṇīyehi dhammehi cittaṃ parisodhessāmā”tiādinā bhāvanārambhavasena āraddhavīriyānaṃ daḷhaparakkamānaṃ kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamanā āraddhavīriyapuggalasevanāti āha – “āraddhavīriye”tiādi. Visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.64-65) pana jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇā sabrahmacārimahattapaccavekkhaṇāti idaṃ dvayaṃ na gahitaṃ, thinamiddhavinodanatā sammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇatāti idaṃ dvayaṃ gahitaṃ. Tattha ānisaṃsadassāvitāya eva sammappadhānapaccavekkhaṇā gahitā hoti lokiyalokuttaravisesādhigamassa vīriyāyattatādassanabhāvato, thinamiddhavinodanaṃ pana tadadhimuttatāya eva gahitaṃ hoti. Vīriyuppādane yuttappayuttassa thinamiddhavinodanaṃ atthasiddhamevāti. Tattha [M 1.0259] thinamiddhavinodanakusītapuggalaparivajjanaāraddhavīriyapuggalasevanatadadhi- muttatāpaṭipakkhavidhamanapaccayūpasaṃhāravasena apāyabhayapaccavekkhaṇādayo samuttejanavasena vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa uppādakā daṭṭhabbā.

Avoiding persons who are lazy, who do not even know the name of development, who are much given to physical sluggishness, who eat their fill and indulge in the pleasure of lying down and so forth, who are bound for the animal realm—this is called avoiding lazy individuals, as stated: ‘Like a python that has filled its belly and remains motionless,’ and so on. Associating from time to to time with persons who have aroused energy and are steadfast in their effort, with the intention of beginning development, thinking, ‘I will purify my mind by walking and sitting throughout the day, removing obstructive states’—this is called associating with energetic individuals, as stated: ‘With those who are energetic,’ and so on. In the Visuddhimagga, however, these two—reflection on the greatness of birth and reflection on the greatness of fellow monastics—are not included, while these two—the removal of sloth and torpor and reflection on right effort—are included. There, reflection on right effort is included precisely to show its benefits, as the achievement of worldly and supramundane distinctions depends on energy. The removal of sloth and torpor, on the other hand, is included precisely because of one’s strong conviction in it. Indeed, the removal of sloth and torpor is necessarily accomplished by the proper application of effort in generating energy. Here, the removal of sloth and torpor, avoiding lazy individuals, associating with energetic individuals, strong conviction in these practices, the application of antidotes, the removal of adverse conditions, reflection on the fear of the lower realms, and so on—these should be seen as the causes for arousing the enlightenment factor of energy, by way of encouragement.

Buddhānussatiyā upacārasamādhiniṭṭhattā vuttaṃ – “yāva upacārā”ti. Sakalasarīraṃ pharamānoti pītisamuṭṭhānehi paṇītarūpehi sakalasarīraṃ pharamāno, dhammasaṅghaguṇe anussarantassapi yāva upacārā sakalasarīraṃ pharamāno pītisambojjhaṅgo uppajjatīti evaṃ sesaanussatīsu, pasādanīyasuttantapaccavekkhaṇāya ca yojetabbaṃ tassāpi vimuttāyatanabhāvena taggatikattā. Evarūpe kāleti “dubbhikkhabhayādīsū”ti vuttakāle. Samāpatti…pe… na samudācarantīti idaṃ upasamānussatiyā vasena vuttaṃ. Saṅkhārānañhi vasena sappadesavūpasamepi nippadesavūpasame viya tathā saññāya pavattito bhāvanāmanasikāro kilesavikkhambhanasamattho hutvā upacārasamādhiṃ āvahanto tathārūpapītisomanassasamannāgato pītisambojjhaṅgassa upādāya hotīti. Tattha “vikkhambhitā kilesā”ti pāṭho. Na samudācarantīti iti-saddo kāraṇattho. Yasmā na samudācaranti, tasmā taṃ nesaṃ asamudācāraṃ paccavekkhantassāti yojanā. Na hi kilese paccavekkhantassa bojjhaṅguppatti yuttā, pasādanīyesu ṭhānesu pasādasinehābhāvena lūkhahadayatāya lūkhatā. Sā tattha ādaragāravākaraṇena viññāyatīti āha – “asakkaccakiriyāya saṃsūcitalūkhabhāve”ti.

Because the recollection of the Buddha culminates in access concentration, it is said: ‘up to access’. ‘Pervading the entire body’ means pervading the entire body with refined forms arisen from joy. And for one recollecting the qualities of the Dhamma and the Sangha, the joy enlightenment factor arises, pervading the entire body up to access concentration. Thus it should be applied to the remaining recollections. And it should be connected with the contemplation of inspiring suttas, for they too are a basis for liberation, leading to that state. ‘During a time such as this’ refers to the time mentioned as ‘famine, fear, and so forth’. ‘Attainment…pe… do not occur’—this is said regarding the recollection of peace. For, indeed, by way of formations, even in a partial subsiding, the mental attention in development proceeds with the perception as if it were a complete subsiding without remainder, being capable of suppressing defilements and bringing access concentration. Being endowed with such joy and gladness, it becomes a condition for the joy enlightenment factor. Here, the reading is ‘defilements are suppressed.’ The word ‘iti’ in ‘na samudācaranti’ (they do not occur) has a causal meaning. The connection is: ‘Because they do not occur, therefore for one reflecting on their non-occurrence’. For the arising of the enlightenment factors is not appropriate for one reflecting on defilements. Due to the absence of delight and affection for inspiring things, there is a coarseness of heart, a harshness. That harshness is recognized by acting with disrespect and irreverence, thus it is said: ‘in the state of harshness indicated by careless action’.

Paṇītabhojanasevanatāti [V 1.0244] paṇītasappāyabhojanasevanatā. Utuiriyāpathasukhaggahaṇena sappāyautuiriyāpathaggahaṇaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tañhi tividhampi sappāyaṃ seviyamānaṃ kāyassa kalyatāpādanavasena cittassa kalyataṃ āvahantaṃ duvidhāyapi passaddhiyā kāraṇaṃ hoti. Ahetukasattesu labbhamānaṃ sukhadukkhanti ayameko anto, issarādivisamahetukanti pana ayaṃ dutiyo. Ete ubho ante anupagamma yathāsakaṃ kammunā hotīti ayaṃ majjhimā paṭipatti. Majjhatto payogo yassa so majjhattapayogo, tassa bhāvo majjhattapayogatā. Ayañhi sabhāvāsāraddhatāya taṃpassaddhakāyatāya kāraṇaṃ hoti, passaddhidvayaṃ [M 1.0260] āvahati. Eteneva sāraddhakāyapuggalaparivajjanapassaddhakāyapuggalasevanānaṃ tadāvahanatā saṃvaṇṇitāti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

The enjoyment of refined food means the enjoyment of suitable and agreeable food. By taking up comfortable postures and a suitable climate, the adoption of suitable postures and climate should be understood. For when this threefold suitability is practiced, it brings about the well-being of the body, and thereby brings well-being to the mind, becoming the cause of both kinds of tranquility. Pleasure and pain obtained among causeless beings—this is one extreme. But the unequal cause of a creator, etc.—this is the second. Not approaching these two extremes, one fares according to one's own kamma—this is the Middle Way. The state of balanced application is that in which one's application is balanced. For this, because of its natural non-agitation and the tranquility of the body in that state, becomes the cause, bringing about both kinds of tranquility. By this, it should be understood that the avoidance of persons with agitated bodies and the association with persons of tranquil bodies, which brings about that tranquility, has been described.

Vatthuvisadakiriyā indriyasamattappaṭipādanā ca paññāvahā vuttā, samādhānāvahāpi tā honti. Samādhānāvahabhāveneva paññāvahabhāvatoti vuttaṃ – “vatthuvisadakiriyā…pe… veditabbā”ti.

The clarification of the object and the accomplishment of balanced faculties are said to bring wisdom; they also bring concentration. It is said that it is precisely because they bring concentration that they bring wisdom—thus it is said: ‘The clarification of the object…pe… should be understood’.

Kāraṇakosallabhāvanākosallānaṃ nānantariyabhāvato rakkhanākosallassa ca taṃmūlakattā “nimittakusalatā nāma kasiṇanimittassa uggahakusalatā”icceva vuttaṃ. Kasiṇanimittassāti ca nidassanamattaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ. Asubhanimittādikassapi hi yassa kassaci jhānuppattinimittassa uggahakosallaṃ nimittakusalatā evāti. Atisithilavīriyatādīhīti ādi-saddena paññāpayogamandataṃ payogavekallañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tassa paggaṇhananti tassa līnassa cittassa dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādisamuṭṭhāpanena layāpattito samuddharaṇaṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

Because skill in the cause and skill in development are not immediate conditions, and because skill in protection is rooted in them, it is said: ‘Skill in the sign is skill in apprehending the kasiṇa sign.’ And ‘the kasiṇa sign’ should be seen as merely an illustration. For skill in apprehending any sign that leads to the arising of jhāna, such as the sign of the unattractive, etc., is also called skill in the sign. ‘Through excessive slackness of energy, etc.’—here, the word ‘etc.’ includes weakness in the application of wisdom and deficiency in striving. ‘Lifting it up’ means raising the mind that has fallen into sluggishness from that state by arousing the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor and so on. For this was said by the Blessed One—

“Yasmiñca kho, bhikkhave, samaye līnaṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo vīriyasambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo pītisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Līnaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi susamuṭṭhāpayaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletukāmo assa. So tattha sukkhāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni ca gomayāni pakkhipeyya, sukkhāni ca kaṭṭhāni pakkhipeyya, mukhavātañca dadeyya, na ca paṃsukena okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so puriso parittaṃ aggiṃ ujjāletunti? Evaṃ, bhante”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234).

“Monks, when the mind is sluggish, that is the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of investigation of phenomena, the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of energy, the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of rapture. Why is that? A sluggish mind, monks, is easily aroused by these qualities. Suppose, monks, a man wanted to kindle a small fire. He would put dry grass in it, dry cow dung, and dry sticks, blow on it with his mouth, and not sprinkle dust on it. Would that man be able to kindle a small fire?” “Yes, venerable sir.”

Ettha [V 1.0245] ca yathāsakaṃ āhāravasena dhammavicayasambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanā samuṭṭhāpanāti veditabbā, sā anantaraṃ vibhāvitā eva.

Here, it should be understood that the cultivation and arising of the investigation-of-states enlightenment factor and the others occurs according to their respective nutriment, as has just been explained.

Accāraddhavīriyatādīhīti ādi-saddena paññāpayogabalavataṃ pamoduppilāpanañca saṅgaṇhāti. Tassa niggaṇhananti tassa uddhatassa cittassa samādhisambojjhaṅgādisamuṭṭhāpanena uddhatāpattito nisedhanaṃ. Vuttampi cetaṃ bhagavatā –

‘Through excessive energy, etc.’—here, the word ‘etc.’ includes the strength of the application of wisdom and excessive elation. ‘Suppressing it’ means preventing that agitated mind from falling into agitation by arousing the concentration enlightenment factor and so on. This was also stated by the Blessed One:

“Yasmiñca [M 1.0261] kho, bhikkhave, samaye uddhataṃ cittaṃ hoti, kālo tasmiṃ samaye passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo samādhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya, kālo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanāya. Taṃ kissa hetu? Uddhataṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ, taṃ etehi dhammehi suvūpasamaṃ hoti. Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetukāmo assa, so tattha allāni ceva tiṇāni pakkhipeyya, allāni ca gomayāni nikkhipeyya, allāni ca kaṭṭhāni pakkhipeyya, mukhavātañca na dadeyya, paṃsukena ca okireyya, bhabbo nu kho so puriso mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ nibbāpetunti? Evaṃ, bhante”ti (saṃ. ni. 5.234).

“Monks, when the mind is agitated, that is the time to cultivate the enlightenment factor of tranquility, the enlightenment factor of concentration, and the enlightenment factor of equanimity. Why is that? An agitated mind, monks, is easily calmed by these qualities. Suppose, monks, a man wanted to extinguish a great mass of fire. He would throw wet grass on it, throw wet cow dung on it, throw wet wood on it, would not blow on it with his mouth, and would sprinkle it with dust. Would that man be able to extinguish the great mass of fire?” “Yes, venerable sir.”

Etthāpi yathāsakaṃ āhāravasena passaddhisambojjhaṅgādīnaṃ bhāvanā samuṭṭhāpanāti veditabbā. Tattha passaddhisambojjhaṅgassa bhāvanā vuttā eva, samādhisambojjhaṅgassa vuccamānā, itarassa anantaraṃ vakkhati.

Here too, it should be understood that the cultivation and arising of the enlightenment factors, beginning with tranquility, occurs according to their respective nutriment. In this context, the cultivation of the enlightenment factor of tranquility has already been stated; that of the enlightenment factor of concentration is being stated, and the other will be explained immediately after.

Paññāpayogamandatāyāti paññābyāpārassa appakabhāvena. Yathā hi dānaṃ alobhappadhānaṃ, sīlaṃ adosappadhānaṃ, evaṃ bhāvanā amohappadhānā. Tattha yadā paññā na balavatī hoti, tadā bhāvanā pubbenāparaṃ visesāvahā na hoti. Anabhisaṅgato viya āhāro purisassa, yogino cittassa abhiruciṃ na janeti, tena taṃ nirassādaṃ hoti. Tathā bhāvanāya sammadeva avīthipaṭipattiyā upasamasukhaṃ na vindati, tenapi cittaṃ nirassādaṃ hoti. Tena vuttaṃ – “paññāpayogamandatāyā…pe… nirassādaṃ hotī”ti. Tassa saṃveguppādanaṃ pasāduppādanañca tikicchananti taṃ dassento, “aṭṭha saṃvegavatthūnī”tiādimāha. Tattha jātijarābyādhimaraṇāni yathārahaṃ sugatiyaṃ duggatiyañca hontīti tadaññameva pañcavidhabandhanādikhuppipāsādiaññamaññaviheṭhanādihetukaṃ apāyadukkhaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ.
