Tayidaṃ sabbaṃ tesaṃ tesaṃ sattānaṃ paccuppannabhavanissitaṃ gahitanti atīte anāgate ca kāle vaṭṭamūlakadukkhāni visuṃ gahitāni[V 1.0246]. Ye pana sattā āhārūpajīvino, tattha ca uṭṭhānaphalūpajīvino, tesaṃ aññehi asādhāraṇajīvitadukkhaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ saṃvegavatthu gahitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Ayaṃ vuccati samaye sampahaṃsanatāti ayaṃ bhāvanācittassa sampahaṃsitabbasamaye vuttanayeneva saṃvegajananavasena [M 1.0262] ceva pasāduppādanavasena ca sammadeva pahaṃsanā, saṃvegajananapubbakapasāduppādanena tosanāti attho.

“Due to weakness in the application of wisdom” means due to the scarcity of the engagement of wisdom. Just as generosity is chiefly characterized by non-greed, and virtue by non-hatred, so too is cultivation chiefly characterized by non-delusion. When wisdom is not strong, cultivation does not bring successive progress. Like food that is not agreeable to a person, it fails to delight the meditator’s mind, making it joyless. Similarly, by not following the path of meditation properly, one does not find the bliss of tranquility, and thus the mind remains joyless. Therefore, it is said: “Due to the weakness in the application of wisdom... it becomes joyless.” Showing that the treatment for this is the arousing of urgency and the generation of serenity, he said, “the eight grounds for urgency,” and so on. Here, birth, aging, sickness, and death occur in both fortunate and unfortunate realms as is appropriate; other than these, the suffering of the lower realms—caused by the fivefold bondage, hunger, thirst, mutual harm, etc.—should be understood. All this is taken as being based on the present existence of those beings, while sufferings rooted in the cycle of rebirth in the past and future are taken separately. As for beings who live by seeking food and who live on the fruits of their labor, their unique suffering of livelihood is taken as the eighth ground for urgency. This is called “gladdening at the appropriate time.” This means the proper gladdening of the meditative mind at the time it should be gladdened, in the way that was stated, by means of arousing urgency and generating serenity. The meaning is satisfaction through generating serenity, which is preceded by the arousing of urgency.

Sammāpaṭipattiṃ āgammāti līnuddhaccavirahena samathavīthipaṭipattiyā ca sammā avisamaṃ sammadeva bhāvanāpaṭipattiṃ āgamma. Alīnantiādīsu kosajjapakkhiyānaṃ dhammānaṃ anadhimattatāya alīnaṃ, uddhaccapakkhikānaṃ anadhimattatāya anuddhataṃ, paññāpayogasampattiyā upasamasukhādhigamena ca anirassādaṃ, tato eva ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ. Alīnānuddhatāhi vā ārammaṇe samappavattaṃ, anirassādatāya samathavīthipaṭipannaṃ. Samappavattiyā vā alīnaṃ anuddhataṃ, samathavīthipaṭipattiyā anirassādanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Tattha alīnatāya paggahe, anuddhatatāya niggahe, anirassādatāya sampahaṃsane na byāpāraṃ āpajjati. Ayaṃ vuccati samaye ajjhupekkhanatāti ayaṃ ajjhupekkhitabbasamaye bhāvanācittassa paggahaniggahasampahaṃsanesu byāvaṭatāsaṅkhātaṃ paṭipakkhaṃ abhibhuyya ajjhupekkhanā vuccati. Paṭipakkhavikkhambhanato vipassanāya adhiṭṭhānabhāvūpagamanato ca upacārajjhānampi samādhānakiccanipphattiyā puggalassa samāhitabhāvasādhanamevāti tattha samadhurabhāvenāha – “upacāraṃ vā appanaṃ vā”ti. Esa uppajjatīti esa samādhisambojjhaṅgo anuppanno uppajjati.

“Having arrived at right practice” means having arrived at the right and undistorted practice of meditation by the path of tranquility, through the absence of sluggishness and agitation. “Not sluggish,” etc.: because the states on the side of laziness are not excessive, it is not sluggish; because the states on the side of restlessness are not excessive, it is not restless; and because of the accomplishment of the application of wisdom and the attainment of peaceful happiness, it is not joyless. Therefore, it proceeds evenly on the object, having entered the path of tranquility. Alternatively, because of being not sluggish and not restless, it proceeds evenly on its object; because of not being joyless, it is engaged in the path of tranquility. Or, it should be understood that due to even progression, it is not sluggish or restless; and due to the practice of the tranquility path, it is not joyless. In that state, because it is not sluggish, it does not engage in the activity of exertion; because it is not restless, it does not engage in the activity of restraint; and because it is not joyless, it does not engage in the activity of gladdening. This is called “equanimity at the proper time.” This is equanimity, so called because at the time when equanimity should be applied, it overcomes the opposing factor, which is the meditative mind’s engagement in exertion, restraint, and gladdening. Due to the suppression of opposing states and its becoming a basis for insight, even access concentration accomplishes the function of concentration, establishing the individual in a composed state. Therefore, due to its similar quality, it is said: “either access or absorption.” “This arises” means this concentration enlightenment factor, unarisen, arises.

Anurodhavirodhappahānavasena majjhattabhāvo upekkhāsambojjhaṅgassa kāraṇaṃ tasmiṃ sati sijjhanato, asati ca asijjhanato, so ca majjhattabhāvo visayavasena duvidhoti āha – “sattamajjhattatā saṅkhāramajjhattatā”ti. Tadubhayena ca virujjhanaṃ passaddhisambojjhaṅgabhāvanāya eva dūrīkatanti anurujjhanasseva pahānavidhiṃ dassetuṃ – “sattamajjhattatā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tenāha – “sattasaṅkhārakelāyanapuggalaparivajjanatā”ti. Upekkhāya hi visesato rāgo paṭipakkho. Tathā cāha – “upekkhā rāgabahulassa visuddhimaggo”ti (visuddhi. 1.269). Dvīhākārehīti kammassakatāpaccavekkhaṇaṃ, attasuññatāpaccavekkhaṇanti, imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi. Dvīhevāti avadhāraṇaṃ saṅkhyāsamānatādassanatthaṃ. Saṅkhyā eva hettha samānā, na saṅkhyeyyaṃ sabbathā samānanti. Assāmikabhāvo anattaniyatā. Sati hi attani tassa kiñcanabhāvena cīvaraṃ aññaṃ vā kiñci attaniyaṃ nāma siyā, so [M 1.0263] pana koci natthevāti adhippāyo. Anaddhaniyanti na addhānakkhamaṃ, na ciraṭṭhāyī ittaraṃ aniccanti attho. Tāvakālikanti tasseva vevacanaṃ.

The state of neutrality, by abandoning both attraction and aversion, is the cause for the equanimity enlightenment factor; for when that is present, it is accomplished, and when absent, it is not accomplished. That state of neutrality is twofold in terms of its object—thus it is said: "neutrality toward beings and neutrality toward formations." And conflict with both of these is removed precisely by the cultivation of the tranquility enlightenment factor. To show the method of abandoning attraction, it is said: "neutrality toward beings," etc. Therefore, it is stated: "by avoiding persons who are weary of beings and formations." For equanimity, lust is especially the opponent. As it is said: "Equanimity is the path of purification for one who is full of lust" (Visuddhimagga 1.269). 'In two ways' means by these two causes: by reflecting on the ownership of deeds and by reflecting on the emptiness of self. 'Only two'—this is an emphasis to show equality in number. Here, only the number is equal, but the objects counted are not entirely equal. The state of being ownerless is not belonging to a self. For if there were a self, by its being something, a robe or any other thing might be called 'belonging to a self'; but since there is no such thing at all, this is the meaning. 'Not enduring' means not capable of lasting, not long-standing, but transient and impermanent. 'Temporary' is a synonym for that.

Mamāyatīti [V 1.0247] mamattaṃ karoti, mamāti taṇhāya pariggayha tiṭṭhati. Dhanāyantāti dhanaṃ dabbaṃ karontā.

To 'make it mine' means to make it one's own; to stand grasping it with craving as 'mine'. 'Those who desire wealth' means those who make wealth their possessions.

419. Sammādassanalakkhaṇāti sammā aviparītaṃ aniccādivasena dassanasabhāvā. Sammāabhiniropanalakkhaṇoti sammadeva ārammaṇe cittassa abhiniropanasabhāvo. Caturaṅgasamannāgatā vācā janaṃ saṅgaṇhātīti tabbipakkhaviratisabhāvā sammāvācā bhedakaramicchāvācāpahānena jane sampayutte ca pariggaṇhanakiccavatī hotīti “pariggahalakkhaṇā”ti vuttā. Visaṃvādanādikiccatāya hi lūkhānaṃ apariggāhakānaṃ musāvādādīnaṃ paṭipakkhabhūtā siniddhabhāvena pariggahaṇasabhāvā sammājappanakiccā sammāvācā tappaccayasubhāsitasampaṭiggāhake jane sampayuttadhamme ca pariggaṇhantī pavattatīti pariggahalakkhaṇā. Yathā cīvarakammādippayogasaṅkhāto kammanto kātabbaṃ cīvararajanādikaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti nipphādeti, taṃtaṃkiriyānipphādako vā cetanāsaṅkhāto kammanto hatthacalanādikaṃ kiriyaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, evaṃ sāvajjakattabbakiriyāsamuṭṭhāpakamicchākammantappahānena sammākammanto niravajjassa kattabbassa niravajjākārena samuṭṭhāpanakiccavā hotīti āha – “sammāsamuṭṭhāpanalakkhaṇo”ti. Sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā ukkhipanaṃ samuṭṭhāpanaṃ kāyikakiriyāya bhārukkhipanaṃ viya. Sammāvodāpanalakkhaṇoti jīvamānassa puggalassa, sampayuttadhammānaṃ vā jīvitindriyavuttiyā, ājīvasseva vā sammadeva sodhanaṃ vodāpanaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ etassāti sammāvodāpanalakkhaṇo. Atha vā kāyavācānaṃ khandhasantānassa ca saṃkilesabhūtamicchāājīvappahānena sammāājīvo “vodāpanalakkhaṇo”ti vutto. Sammāvāyāmasatisamādhīsu vattabbaṃ heṭṭhā vuttameva.

419. The characteristic of right view is the nature of seeing correctly, without distortion, in terms of impermanence and so forth. The characteristic of right intention is the nature of correctly directing the mind toward its object. Because speech endowed with four factors gathers people, right speech, which has the nature of abstaining from its opposite, by abandoning divisive wrong speech, has the function of gathering people and associated states. Therefore, it is called 'having the characteristic of gathering.' For, being the opposite of false speech and so on—which are harsh and do not gather, due to their function of deception and the like—right speech, with its function of right speaking and its nature of gathering through gentleness, proceeds by gathering people who are receptive to the well-spoken words that depend on it, and associated wholesome states. Thus, it has the characteristic of gathering. Just as the activity called 'work,' such as making robes, brings about and accomplishes the task of dyeing robes and so on, or as the intention called 'action' brings about an action like the moving of a hand, so too right action, by abandoning wrong action that brings about blameworthy deeds, has the function of rightly bringing about a blameless deed in a blameless manner. Hence it is said: 'It has the characteristic of right production.' Alternatively, the uplifting of associated states is 'production,' like the lifting of a burden by a bodily action. The characteristic of right livelihood is the proper purification and cleansing of a living being, of the functioning of the life faculty of associated states, or of livelihood itself. Alternatively, right livelihood, by abandoning wrong livelihood that defiles the continuity of the aggregates of body and speech, is said to have 'the characteristic of cleansing.' As for right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration, what was stated before applies here as well.

Paññāya kusalānaṃ dhammānaṃ pubbaṅgamabhāvato sabbepi akusalā dhammā tassā paṭipakkhāvāti vuttaṃ – “aññehipi attano paccanīkakilesehi saddhi”nti. Atha vā attano paccanīkakilesā diṭṭhekaṭṭhā avijjādayo paññāya ujupaccanīkabhāvato. Passatīti passantī [M 1.0264] viya hoti vibandhābhāvato. Tenāha – “tappaṭicchādaka…pe… asammohato”ti. Sammāsaṅkappādīnaṃ micchāsaṅkappādayo ujuvipaccanīkāti āha – “sammāsaṅkappādayo…pe… pajahantī”ti. Tathevāti iminā attano paccanīkakilesehi saddhinti imamatthaṃ anukaḍḍhati. Visesatoti sammādiṭṭhiyā vuttakiccato visesena. Etthāti etesu sammāsaṅkappādīsu.

Because wisdom is the forerunner of wholesome states, all unwholesome states are its opponents—thus it is said: 'along with other defilements that are its own opponents.' Alternatively, its own opposing defilements, such as ignorance and so on, which share a basis with wrong view, are directly opposed by wisdom due to its being a direct opponent. 'It sees' means it is as if seeing, because there is no obstruction. Therefore, it is said: 'because it does not conceal... due to non-delusion.' Wrong thoughts and so on are the direct opponents of right thoughts and so on—thus it is said: 'right thoughts and so on... abandon.' 'Similarly'—by this, the meaning of 'along with its own opposing defilements' is drawn in. 'As a distinction'—as a distinction from the function stated for right view. 'Here'—in these, right thoughts and so on.

Esā sammādiṭṭhi nāmāti lokiyaṃ lokuttarañca ekajjhaṃ katvā vadati missakatābhāvato[V 1.0248]. Tenāha – “pubbabhāge”tiādi. Ekārammaṇā nibbānārammaṇattā. Kiccatoti pubbabhāge dukkhādīhi ñāṇehi kātabbakiccassa idha nipphattito, imasseva vā ñāṇassa dukkhādippakāsanakiccato. Cattāri nāmāni labhati dukkhapariññādicatukiccasādhanato. Tīṇi nāmāni labhati kāmasaṅkappādippahānakiccanipphattito. Sikkhāpadavibhaṅge (vibha. 703 ādayo) “viraticetanā taṃsampayuttā ca dhammā sikkhāpadānī”ti vuttāni, tattha padhānānaṃ viraticetanānaṃ vasena “viratiyopi honti cetanādayopī”ti āha. “Sammā vadati etāyā”tiādinā atthasambhavato sammāvācādayo tayo viratiyopi honti cetanādayopi. Musāvādādīhi viramaṇakāle viratiyo, subhāsitādivācābhāsanādikāle cetanādayo yojetabbā. Maggakkhaṇe pana viratiyova maggalakkhaṇappattito. Na hi cetanā niyyānasabhāvā. Atha vā ekassa ñāṇassa dukkhādiñāṇatā viya ekāya viratiyā musāvādādiviratibhāvo viya ca ekāya cetanāya sammāvācādikiccattayasādhanasabhāvā sammāvācādibhāvāsiddhito “maggakkhaṇe viratiyovā”ti vuttaṃ.

“This is called right view,” he says, speaking of the mundane and the supramundane combined, because they are of a mixed nature. Hence he says, “in the preliminary stage,” etc. It has a single object because its object is Nibbāna. As for its function: because the task to be done in the preliminary stage by the knowledges of suffering etc. is here accomplished, or because of this very knowledge's function of illuminating suffering etc. It acquires four names due to accomplishing the fourfold function of fully understanding suffering etc. It acquires three names due to accomplishing the function of abandoning sensual thought etc. In the Vibhaṅga on the Training Rules (Vibh. 703 ff.), it is said: “The volition of abstinence and the states associated with it are the training rules.” There, by virtue of the prominence of the volitions of abstinence, he says: “There are both abstinences and volitions, etc.” From the derivation of meaning “one speaks rightly by this,” etc., the three—right speech etc.—are both abstinences and volitions. At the time of abstaining from false speech etc., they are abstinences; at the time of uttering well-spoken words etc., volitions etc. should be applied. However, at the moment of the path, they are only abstinences, because they attain the characteristic of the path. For volition does not have the nature of leading out. Alternatively, just as a single knowledge has the nature of being the knowledge of suffering etc., and just as a single abstinence has the nature of being abstinence from false speech etc., so too, because the state of being right speech etc. is not established for a single volition having the nature of accomplishing the threefold function of right speech etc., it is said: “At the moment of the path, there are only abstinences.”

Cattāri nāmāni labhatīti catusammappadhānacatusatipaṭṭhānavasena labhati. Maggakkhaṇeti ānetvā sambandho. Pubbabhāgepi maggakkhaṇepi sammāsamādhi evāti yadipi samādhiupakārakānaṃ abhiniropanānumajjanasampiyāyanabrūhanasantasukhānaṃ vitakkādīnaṃ vasena catūhi jhānehi sammāsamādhi vibhatto, tathāpi vāyāmo viya anuppannākusalānuppādanādicatuvāyāmakiccaṃ, sati viya ca asubhāsukhāniccānattesu kāyādīsu subhādisaññāpahānalakkhaṇaṃ catusatikiccaṃ, eko samādhi catujjhānasamādhikiccaṃ na sādhetīti pubbabhāgepi paṭhamajjhānasamādhi, paṭhamajjhānasamādhi [M 1.0265] eva maggakkhaṇepi, tathā pubbabhāgepi catutthajjhānasamādhi, catutthajjhānasamādhi eva maggakkhaṇepīti attho.

‘It acquires four names’—it acquires them by means of the four right strivings and the four foundations of mindfulness. The connection is made by bringing in “at the moment of the path.” Right concentration is the same both in the preliminary stage and at the moment of the path. Although right concentration is divided into the four jhānas by way of thought and so on, which are factors assisting concentration—directing, stroking, gladdening, intensifying, pacifying, and happiness—nevertheless, just as effort accomplishes the fourfold task of striving, such as preventing the arising of unarisen unwholesome states, and just as mindfulness accomplishes the fourfold task of mindfulness, characterized by abandoning the perception of beauty and so on in the body and so on, which are foul, painful, impermanent, and not-self, so a single concentration does not accomplish the task of the concentration of the four jhānas. Thus, the concentration of the first jhāna in the preliminary stage is the very concentration of the first jhāna at the moment of the path. Likewise, the concentration of the fourth jhāna in the preliminary stage is the very concentration of the fourth jhāna at the moment of the path—this is the meaning.

“Kiṃ panāyaṃ maggadhammānaṃ desanānukkamo, kevalaṃ vācāya kamavattinibhāvato, udāhu kañci visesaṃ upādāyā”ti vicāraṇāyaṃ kañci visesaṃ upādāyāti dassento āha – “imesū”tiādi. Tattha bhāvanānubhāvā hitaphalāya sātisayaṃ tikkhavisadabhāvappattiyā acchariyabbhutasamatthatāyogena sabbaso paṭipakkhavidhamanena yāthāvato dhammasabhāvabodhanena ca sammādiṭṭhiyā bahukāratā veditabbā. Tenāha – “ayaṃ hī”tiādi.

In considering the question, “What, then, is the sequence of teaching these path factors? Is it merely a verbal arrangement, due to the order of words, or is it based on some special consideration?”, he says, showing that it is indeed based on some special consideration: “In these,” etc. Here, the great helpfulness of right view should be understood through the power of development, as supremely effective for a beneficial result, through the attainment of an exceedingly sharp and clear state, by virtue of its wondrous and amazing capacity, by utterly dispelling opposing factors, and by rightly awakening to the true nature of phenomena. Therefore, he says: “For this,” etc.

Tassāti [V 1.0249] sammādiṭṭhiyā. Bahukāroti dhammasampaṭivedhe bahūpakāro. Idāni tamatthaṃ upamāhi vibhāvetuṃ, “yathā hī”tiādi vuttaṃ.

‘Tassā’ means ‘of right view.’ ‘Bahukāro’ means greatly helpful in the penetration of the Dhamma. Now, to clarify that meaning with similes, ‘Just as,’ etc., is said.

Vacībhedassa kārako vitakko sāvajjānavajjavacībhedanivattanappavattanākārāya sammāvācāyapi upakārako evāti āha – “svāyaṃ…pe… sammāvācāyapi upakārako”ti. Sammāsaṅkappo hi saccavācāya virativācāyapi visesapaccayo micchāsaṅkappatadekaṭṭhakilesappahānato.

Thought is the cause of verbal breach. It is also helpful for right speech, which takes the form of refraining from blameworthy verbal breaches and engaging in blameless ones. Thus he says: “This very... indeed, it is helpful even for right speech.” For right intention is a specific condition for truthful speech and speech of abstinence, because of the abandoning of wrong intention and the defilements associated with it.

Saṃvidahitvātiādīsu sammā vidahanaṃ kammantappayojanañca ekantānavajjavacīkāyakammavasena icchitabbanti virativācāvasena saṃvidahanaṃ viratikammantasseva payojanañca nidassitanti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Evaṃ hissa sammāvācāya sammākammantassāpi bahukāratā jotitā siyā. Vacībhedaniyāmikā hi vacīduccaritavirati kāyikakiriyaniyāmikāya kāyaduccaritaviratiyā upakārikā. Tathā hi visaṃvādanādimicchāvācato avirato micchākammantatopi na viramateva. Yathāha – “ekaṃ dhammaṃ atītassa…pe… natthi pāpaṃ akāriya”nti. Tasmā avisaṃvādanādisammāvācāya ṭhito sammākammantampi pūretiyevāti vacīduccaritavirati kāyaduccaritaviratiyā upakārikā.

In ‘Saṃvidahitvāti’ etc., since proper arrangement and the purpose of action are desired by way of entirely blameless verbal and bodily action, it should be seen that arranging by way of speech of abstinence, and the purpose of the very action of abstinence, are thereby demonstrated. For in this way, the great helpfulness of right speech for right action would also be illuminated. For restraint from verbal misconduct, which governs verbal deviation, is helpful to restraint from bodily misconduct, which governs bodily action. For one who is unrestrained from false speech and so on does not abstain from wrong action either. As it is said: ‘For one who has transgressed the one thing... there is no evil that cannot be done.’ Therefore, one established in right speech, such as not speaking falsely, fulfills right action as well; thus, restraint from verbal misconduct is helpful to restraint from bodily misconduct.

Yasmā ājīvapārisuddhi nāma dussīlyappahānapubbikā, tasmā sammāvācākammantānantaraṃ sammāājīvo desitoti dassetuṃ – “catubbidhaṃ panā”tiādi [M 1.0266] vuttaṃ. Ettāvatāti parisuddhasīlājīvikāmattena. Idaṃ vīriyanti catusammappadhānavīriyaṃ.

Because purity of livelihood is preceded by the abandoning of evil conduct, therefore, to show that right livelihood is taught immediately after right speech and right action, ‘Fourfold indeed,’ etc., is said. ‘Ettāvatā’ means by means of pure virtue and livelihood. ‘Idaṃ vīriyaṃ’ means the energy of the four right efforts.

Vīriyārambhopi sammāsatipariggahito eva nibbānāvaho, na kevaloti dassetuṃ – “tato”tiādi vuttaṃ. Sūpaṭṭhitāti bahiddhāvikkhepaṃ pahāya suṭṭhu upaṭṭhitā kātabbā. Samādhissa upakāradhammā nāma yathāvuttavatthuvisadakiriyādayo. Tappaṭipakkhato anupakāradhammā veditabbā. Gatiyoti nipphattiyo. Samanvesitvāti sammā pariyesitvā.

To show that the exertion of effort, only when well-supported by right mindfulness, leads to Nibbāna, and not by itself alone, ‘Thence,’ etc., is said. ‘Sūpaṭṭhitā’ means it should be well established by abandoning external distraction. Supporting factors of concentration are such things as making the object clear, as was stated, and so on. Factors opposing these should be understood as unhelpful. ‘Gatiyo’ means accomplishments. ‘Samanvesitvā’ means having thoroughly investigated.

427. Yathā itthīsu kathā pavattā adhitthīti vuccati, evaṃ attānaṃ adhikicca pavattā ajjhattaṃ. “Evaṃ pavattamānā mayaṃ ‘attā’ti gahaṇaṃ gamissāmā”ti iminā viya adhippāyena attānaṃ adhikicca uddissa pavattā sattasantatipariyāpannā ajjhattaṃ. Tasmiṃ ajjhattarūpe, attano kesādivatthuke kasiṇarūpeti attho. Parikammavasena ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññīti parikammakaraṇavasena [V 1.0250] ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī, na appanāvasena. Na hi paṭibhāganimittārammaṇā appanā ajjhattavisayā sambhavati. Taṃ pana ajjhattaṃ parikammavasena laddhaṃ kasiṇanimittaṃ avisuddhameva hoti, na bahiddhā parikammavasena laddhaṃ viya visuddhaṃ. Tenāha – “taṃ panā”tiādi.

427. Just as a conversation about women is called ‘regarding women,’ so too, what arises concerning oneself is internal. As if with the intention, ‘In this way, we will grasp the notion of “self,”’ what arises concerning oneself, included in the continuity of a being, is internal. In that internal form, it means the kasiṇa form based on one's own hair etc. ‘Parikammavasena ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī’ means perceiving form internally through preparatory work, not through absorption. For absorption, which takes the counterpart sign as its object, is not possible with an internal object. However, that kasiṇa sign obtained internally through preparatory work is indeed impure, not pure like the one obtained externally through preparatory work. Therefore, he says: ‘But that...’ etc.

Yassevaṃ parikammaṃ ajjhattaṃ uppannanti yassa puggalassa evaṃ vuttappakārena ajjhattaṃ parikammaṃ jātaṃ. Nimittaṃ pana bahiddhāti paṭibhāganimittaṃ sasantatipariyāpannaṃ na hotīti bahiddhā. Parittānīti yathāladdhāni suppasarāvamattāni. Tenāha – “avaḍḍhitānī”ti. Parittavasenevāti vaṇṇavasena ābhoge vijjamānepi parittavaseneva idaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ vuttaṃ parittatā hettha abhibhavanassa kāraṇaṃ. Vaṇṇābhoge satipi asatipi abhibhavatīti abhibhu, parikammaṃ, ñāṇaṃ vā. Abhibhu āyatanaṃ etassāti abhibhāyatanaṃ, jhānaṃ. Abhibhavitabbaṃ vā ārammaṇasaṅkhātaṃ āyatanaṃ etassāti abhibhāyatanaṃ. Atha vā ārammaṇābhibhavanato abhibhu ca taṃ āyatanañca yogino sukhavisesānaṃ adhiṭṭhānabhāvato manāyatanadhammāyatanabhāvato cāti sasampayuttajjhānaṃ abhibhāyatanaṃ. Abhibhāyatanabhāvanā nāma tikkhapaññasseva sambhavati, na itarassāti āha – “ñāṇuttariko puggalo”ti. Abhibhavitvā samāpajjatīti ettha abhibhavanaṃ [M 1.0267] samāpajjanañca upacārajjhānādhigamanasamanantarameva appanājhānuppādananti āha – “saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ pāpetī”ti. Saha nimittuppādenāti ca appanāparivāsābhāvassa lakkhaṇavacanametaṃ. Yo khippābhiññoti vuccati, tatopi ñāṇuttarasseva abhibhāyatanabhāvanā. Etthāti etasmiṃ nimitte. Appanaṃ pāpetīti bhāvanāappanaṃ neti.

‘Yassevaṃ parikammaṃ ajjhattaṃ uppannaṃ’ means for that individual for whom preparation has arisen internally in the manner described. ‘Nimittaṃ pana bahiddhā’ means the counterpart sign is external because it is not included within one’s own continuity. ‘Parittāni’ means as obtained, merely the size of a small bowl. Therefore, he says: ‘unexpanded.’ ‘Parittavaseneva’ means this base of mastery is spoken of as being by means of a limited aspect, even though there may be adverting to color, for here, limitation is the cause of mastery. ‘Whether there is adverting to color or not, one masters it’—thus, ‘mastery’ (abhibhu), which is the preparatory work, or the knowledge. ‘Abhibhu āyatanaṃ etassa’ means ‘the base of mastery’ (abhibhāyatana), the jhāna. Or alternatively, ‘that which is to be mastered, the object, is its base’—hence, abhibhāyatana. Or else, due to the mastery of the object, it is called ‘mastery’ (abhibhu), and because it serves as the foundation for the meditator’s special happiness, and as the domain of the mind-base and mind-object base, the associated jhāna is the base of mastery. The development of the base of mastery is possible only for one of sharp wisdom, not for others—thus he says: ‘a person superior in knowledge.’ ‘Abhibhavitvā samāpajjati’ means here, mastery and attainment refer to producing absorption jhāna immediately after achieving access concentration. Therefore, he says: ‘here, one attains absorption simultaneously with the arising of the sign.’ ‘Saha nimittuppādena’—this phrase indicates the absence of a probationary period for absorption. The development of the base of mastery belongs only to one who is superior in knowledge, even more so than one called ‘swift in direct knowledge.’ ‘Ettha’ means in this sign. ‘Appanaṃ pāpeti’ means leads to the absorption of development.

Ettha ca keci “uppanne upacārajjhāne taṃ ārabbha ye heṭṭhimantena dve tayo javanavārā pavattanti, te upacārajjhānapakkhikā eva, tadanantaraṃ bhavaṅgaparivāsena upacārasevanāya ca vinā appanā hoti, saha nimittuppādeneva appanaṃ pāpetī”ti vadanti, taṃ tesaṃ matimattaṃ. Na hi pārivāsikaparikammena appanāvāro icchito, nāpi mahaggatappamāṇajjhānesu viya upacārajjhāne ekantato paccavekkhaṇā icchitabbā. Tasmā upacārajjhānādhigamato paraṃ katipayabhavaṅgacittāvasāne appanaṃ pāpuṇanto “saha nimittuppādenevettha appanaṃ pāpetī”ti vutto. Saha nimittuppādenāti ca adhippāyikamidaṃ vacanaṃ, na nītatthaṃ, tattha adhippāyo vuttanayeneva veditabbo. Na antosamāpattiyaṃ tadā tathārūpassa ābhogassa asambhavato. Samāpattito vuṭṭhitassa ābhogo pubbabhāgabhāvanāvasena jhānakkhaṇe pavattaṃ abhibhavanākāraṃ gahetvā pavattoti daṭṭhabbaṃ. Abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana “imināssa pubbābhogo kathito”ti vuttaṃ. Antosamāpattiyaṃ [V 1.0251] tadā tathā ābhogābhāve kasmā jhānasaññāyapīti vuttanti āha – “abhibhavasaññā hissa antosamāpattiyampi atthī”ti.

Here, some say: 'When access concentration has arisen, two or three impulsion-courses of lesser intensity occur based on it; these belong only to the side of access concentration. Immediately after, absorption occurs without a probationary period of the life-continuum and without the cultivation of access; one attains absorption simultaneously with the arising of the sign.' This is merely their opinion. For an absorption-occasion with a probationary preliminary action is not intended, nor is reviewing to be absolutely expected in access concentration as it is in the sublime and immeasurable jhānas. Therefore, one who attains absorption after the cessation of a few life-continuum mind-moments subsequent to the attainment of access concentration is said to 'attain absorption here simultaneously with the arising of the sign.' And this statement, 'simultaneously with the arising of the sign,' is one of implicit meaning, not of explicit meaning. The implicit meaning there should be understood in the way that has been stated. For at that time, within the attainment, such an adverting of the mind is impossible. The adverting of one who has arisen from the attainment should be understood as proceeding by grasping the mode of mastery that occurred at the moment of jhāna by way of the preliminary-part development. In the Abhidhamma commentary, however, it is said: 'By this his preliminary adverting is stated.' If there is no such adverting at that time within the attainment, why is it said 'even with the perception of jhāna'? He says: 'For the perception of mastery exists for him even within the attainment.'

Vaḍḍhitappamāṇānīti vipulappamāṇānīti attho, na ekaṅguladvaṅgulādivaḍḍhiṃ pāpitāni tathā vaḍḍhanassevettha asambhavato. Tenāha – “mahantānī”ti. Bhattavaḍḍhitakanti bhuñjanabhājane vaḍḍhetvā dinnaṃ bhattaṃ, ekāsane purisena bhuñjitabbabhattato upaḍḍhabhattanti attho.

`Vaḍḍhitappamāṇāni` means of extensive measure, not increased by one or two finger-breadths, for such an increase is impossible here. Hence it is said: `mahantāni`, 'great.' `Bhattavaḍḍhitakaṃ` is food given after having been served in the eating bowl; the meaning is half the food that should be eaten by a man at one sitting.

Rūpe saññā rūpasaññā, sā assa atthīti rūpasaññī, na rūpasaññī arūpasaññī. Saññāsīsena jhānaṃ vadati. Rūpasaññāya anuppādanamevettha alābhitā. Bahiddhāva uppannanti bahiddhāvatthusmiṃyeva uppannaṃ. Ettha ca –

Perception of form is form-perception. One who possesses it is a form-perceiver; one who is not a form-perceiver is a formless-perceiver. He speaks of jhāna with perception as its head. Here, the non-arising of form-perception is simply non-attainment. What arises externally arises only in an external object. And here—

“Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni. Ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni[M 1.0268]. Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni. Ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti (dī. ni. 3.338, 358; a. ni. 8.65; 10.29) –

“Perceiving form internally, one sees external forms, limited, beautiful and ugly. Perceiving form internally, one sees external forms, immeasurable, beautiful and ugly. Perceiving formlessness internally, one sees external forms, limited, beautiful and ugly. Perceiving formlessness internally, one sees external forms, immeasurable, beautiful and ugly.”

Evamidha cattāri abhibhāyatanāni āgatāni. Abhidhamme (dha. sa. 244-245) pana “ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññī bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni, appamāṇāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānī”ti evamāgatāni. Tattha ca kāraṇaṃ abhidhammaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vuttameva. Tathā hi vuttaṃ aṭṭhasāliniyaṃ (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 204) –

Thus here four bases of overcoming have come down. In the Abhidhamma (Dhs. 244–245), however, they have come down thus: “Perceiving formlessness internally, one sees external forms, limited, beautiful and ugly, and immeasurable, beautiful and ugly.” The reason for this has been stated in the Abhidhamma commentary. For so it is said in the Atthasālinī (DhsA. 204):

“Kasmā pana yathā suttante ‘ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī eko bahiddhā rūpāni passati parittānī’tiādi vuttaṃ, evaṃ avatvā idha catūsupi abhibhāyatanesu ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññitāva vuttāti. Ajjhattarūpānaṃ anabhibhavanīyato. Tattha vā hi idha vā bahiddhā rūpāneva abhibhavitabbāni, tasmā tāni niyamato vattabbānī”ti.

“But why, instead of stating as in the Suttanta, ‘One perceiving form internally sees external forms as limited,’ and so on, is it stated here that in all four bases of overcoming one perceives formlessness internally? Because internal forms are not to be overcome. For whether there or here, it is only external forms that are to be overcome; therefore, these must be stated as a rule.”

Tatrāpi idhapi vuttāni “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññīti idaṃ pana satthu desanāvilāsamattamevā”ti. Ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – idha vaṇṇābhogarahitāni sahitāni ca sabbāni parittāni suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇāni abhibhuyyāti. Pariyāyakathā hi suttantadesanāti. Abhidhamme [V 1.0252] pana nippariyāyadesanattā vaṇṇābhogarahitāni visuṃ vuttāni, tathā sahitāni. Atthi hi ubhayattha abhibhavanavisesoti. Tathā idha pariyāyadesanattā vimokkhānampi abhibhavanapariyāyo atthīti “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī”tiādinā paṭhamadutiyaabhibhāyatanesu paṭhamavimokkho, tatiyacatutthaabhibhāyatanesu dutiyavimokkho, vaṇṇābhibhāyatanesu tatiyavimokkho ca abhibhavanapattito saṅgahito. Abhidhamme pana nippariyāyadesanattā vimokkhābhibhāyatanāni asaṅkarato desetuṃ vimokkhe vajjetvā abhibhāyatanāni kathitāni. Sabbāni ca vimokkhakiccāni jhānāni vimokkhadesanāyaṃ vuttāni. Tadetaṃ “ajjhattaṃ rūpasaññī”ti āgatassa abhibhāyatanadvayassa abhidhamme abhibhāyatanesu avacanato “rūpī rūpāni passatī”tiādīnañca sabbavimokkhakiccasādhāraṇavacanabhāvato vavatthānaṃ katanti viññāyati.

What is stated both there and here, 'perceiving form internally' and 'perceiving formlessness internally,' is merely the Teacher's stylistic elegance in teaching. This is the intention here: here all limited, beautiful and ugly forms, both those devoid of advertence to color and those accompanied by it, are overcome. For the Suttanta teaching is a discourse with an indirect meaning. But in the Abhidhamma, because the teaching is direct, those devoid of advertence to color are stated separately, and likewise those accompanied by it. For in both cases there is a distinction in the overcoming. Similarly, here, because the teaching is indirect, the method of overcoming of the liberations is also included. Thus, by the words 'perceiving form internally,' etc., the first liberation is included in the first and second bases of overcoming, the second liberation in the third and fourth bases of overcoming, and the third liberation in the bases of overcoming of color, since they have attained overcoming. But in the Abhidhamma, because the teaching is direct, in order to teach the liberations and the bases of overcoming without mixing them up, the bases of overcoming are stated having omitted the liberations. And all the jhānas that have the function of liberation are stated in the teaching on the liberations. Thus it is understood that this distinction is made because the two bases of overcoming that have come down as 'perceiving form internally' are not stated in the Abhidhamma among the bases of overcoming, and because statements such as 'one with form sees forms' are common to the function of all the liberations.

Ajjhattarūpānaṃ [M 1.0269] anabhibhavanīyatoti idaṃ abhidhamme katthacipi “ajjhattarūpāni passatī”ti avatvā sabbattha yaṃ vuttaṃ – “bahiddhā rūpāni passatī”ti, tassa kāraṇavacanaṃ. Tena yaṃ aññahetukaṃ suttante “bahiddhā rūpāni passatī”ti vacanaṃ, taṃ tena hetunā vuttaṃ. Yaṃ pana desanāvilāsahetukaṃ ajjhattaṃ arūpasaññitāya eva abhidhamme vacanaṃ, na tassa aññaṃ kāraṇaṃ maggitabbanti dasseti. Ajjhattarūpānaṃ anabhibhavanīyatā ca tesaṃ bahiddhārūpānaṃ viya avibhūtattā. Desanāvilāso ca yathāvuttavavatthānavasena veditabbo veneyyajjhāsayavasena vijjamānapariyāyakathanabhāvato. Desanāvilāso hi nāma veneyyajjhāsayānurūpaṃ vijjamānassa ca pariyāyassa vibhāvanaṃ, na yassa kassaci, tasmā “idha pariyāyadesanattā”tiādinā vuttappakāraṃ vavatthānaṃ desanāvilāsanibandhananti daṭṭhabbaṃ.

'Because internal forms are not to be overcome': this is the statement of the reason why in the Abhidhamma it is nowhere said 'one sees internal forms,' but everywhere it is said 'one sees external forms.' By this it shows that the statement in the Suttanta 'one sees external forms,' which has another cause, is said for that reason, whereas for the statement in the Abhidhamma about perceiving formlessness internally, which is caused by stylistic elegance, another reason should not be sought. And the non-overcomability of internal forms is due to their not being manifest like external forms. The stylistic elegance should be understood by way of the distinction stated above, as it is a statement of an existing indirect meaning in accordance with the disposition of the trainee. For stylistic elegance is the clarification of an existing indirect meaning in conformity with the disposition of the trainee, not just any meaning. Therefore, the distinction made in the way stated beginning with 'because here the teaching is indirect' should be seen as founded on stylistic elegance.

Suvaṇṇadubbaṇṇānīti eteneva siddhattā na nīlādiabhibhāyatanāni vattabbānīti ce? Na nīlādīsu katādhikārānaṃ nīlādibhāvasseva abhibhavanakāraṇattā. Na hi tesaṃ parisuddhāparisuddhavaṇṇānaṃ parittatā appamāṇatā vā abhibhavanakāraṇaṃ, atha kho nīlādibhāvo evāti. Etesu ca parittādikasiṇarūpesu yaṃyaṃcaritassa imāni abhibhāyatanāni ijjhanti, taṃ dassetuṃ – “imesu panā”tiādi vuttaṃ.

'Beautiful and ugly': If it is said that since it is established by this alone, the bases of overcoming of blue, etc., need not be stated, we reply: No. Because for those who have made an aspiration regarding blue, etc., it is precisely the state of being blue, etc., that is the cause of overcoming. It is not the limitedness or immeasurability of those pure and impure colors that is the cause of overcoming, but rather precisely the state of being blue, etc. And to show for which temperament these bases of overcoming succeed with which of these limited, etc., kasiṇa-forms, it is said: 'But in these,' etc.

Sabbasaṅgāhikavasenāti nīlavaṇṇanīlanidassananīlanibhāsānaṃ sādhāraṇavasena. Vaṇṇavasenāti sabhāvavaṇṇavasena. Nidassanavasenāti passitabbatāvasena, cakkhuviññāṇavīthiyā gahetabbatāvasena[V 1.0253]. Obhāsavasenāti sappabhāsatāya avabhāsanavasena. Vaṇṇadhātuyā vāti añjanarajatavatthādivaṇṇadhātuyā. Lokiyāneva rūpāvacarajjhānabhāvato.

`Sabbasaṅgāhikavasena` means by way of being common to blue color, blue appearance, and blue radiance. `Vaṇṇavasena` means by way of its natural color. `Nidassanavasena` means by way of its visibility, by way of its being graspable by the process of eye-consciousness. `Obhāsavasena` means by way of its shining forth with lustre. `Vaṇṇadhātuyā vā` means by way of the color element of kohl, silver, cloth, and so on. They are only mundane because they are form-sphere jhānas.

435. Rūpīti ettha yenāyaṃ sasantatipariyāpannena rūpena samannāgato, taṃ yassa jhānassa hetubhāvena visiṭṭharūpaṃ hoti. Yena visiṭṭhena rūpīti vucceyya, tadeva sasantatipariyāpannarūpanimittaṃ jhānaṃ. Idha pana paramatthato rūpibhāvasādhakanti āha – “ajjhattaṃ kesādīsū”tiādi. Rūpajjhānaṃ rūpanti uttarapadalopena vuttaṃ – “rūpūpapattiyā”tiādīsu (dha. sa. 160-161, 185-190 ādayo, 244-245 ādayo; vibha. 625) viya.

435. 'One with form' (`rūpī`): Here, the form included in one's own continuity with which one is endowed is the distinguished form that is the cause of that jhāna. That very distinguished form by which one would be called 'one with form' is itself the jhāna that has as its sign a form included in one's own continuity. But here, he says what establishes the state of being 'one with form' in the ultimate sense: 'internally, in the hair of the head, etc.' The term `rūpa` is used for `rūpajjhāna` with the elision of the final word, as in such phrases as 'for rebirth in the form realm,' etc. (Dhammasaṅgaṇī 160–161, 185–190, etc.; Vibhaṅga 625).

Subhantveva [M 1.0270] adhimutto hotīti ayaṃ tatiyavimokkho. Idha suparisuddhanīlādivaṇṇakasiṇajjhānavasena vuttoti dassetvā idāni paṭisambhidāpāḷiyaṃ tassa brahmavihārajjhānavasena āgatabhāvaṃ dassetuṃ – “paṭisambhidāmagge panā”tiādi āraddhaṃ. Idha pana uparipāḷiyaṃyeva brahmavihārānaṃ āgatattā taṃ nayaṃ paṭikkhipitvā parisuddhanīlādivaṇṇakasiṇavaseneva subhavimokkho anuññāto.

'He is intent only on the beautiful'—this is the third liberation. Having shown that here it is stated by way of the jhāna on the perfectly pure blue, etc., color kasiṇa, now, to show that in the Paṭisambhidāmagga text it has come down by way of the jhāna on the divine abidings, the passage beginning 'But in the Paṭisambhidāmagga...' is started. Here, however, since the divine abidings have come down in the main text itself above, that method is rejected, and the beautiful liberation is approved only by way of the jhāna on the perfectly pure blue, etc., color kasiṇa.

443. Parikammapathaviyāpīti akatāya vā katāya vā daḷhamaṇḍalādisaṅkhātaparikammapathaviyāpi. Uggahanimittādīnaṃ pathavīkasiṇanti nāmaṃ nissite nissayavohāravasena vuttanti daṭṭhabbaṃ, yathā “mañcā ukkuṭṭhiṃ karontī”ti.

443. 'Even on the preliminary earth kasiṇa': this refers to the preliminary earth kasiṇa designated as a firm circle, etc., whether it is unmade or made. It should be understood that the name 'earth kasiṇa' is applied to the uptake-sign, etc., by way of dependent designation, referring to what is dependent on it, just as when it is said, 'The beds are shouting.'

Sīlānīti pātimokkhasaṃvarādīni cattāri sīlāni. Sodhetvāti anāpajjanena āpannavuṭṭhāpanena kilesehi appaṭipīḷanena ca visodhetvā. Tividhañhi sīlassa visodhanaṃ nāma – anāpajjanaṃ āpannavuṭṭhāpanaṃ kilesehi ca appaṭipīḷananti. Kammaṭṭhānabhāvanaṃ paribundheti uparodheti pavattituṃ na detīti palibodho rakārassa lakāraṃ katvā, paribandhoti attho. Upacchinditvāti samāpannena saṅgāhaṇena vā uparundhitvā, apalibodhaṃ katvāti attho. Kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvāti –

"Virtues" are the four kinds of virtue, such as the restraint of the Pātimokkha. "Having purified" means having done so by not incurring offenses, by rectifying incurred offenses, and by not being oppressed by the defilements. For the purification of virtue is threefold: not incurring offenses, rectifying incurred offenses, and not being oppressed by the defilements. A hindrance (palibodha) is so called because it hinders, obstructs, and prevents the development of the meditation subject from proceeding; the meaning is 'impediment' (paribandha), with the 'ra' changed to 'la'. "Having cut off" means restraining it through attainment or control, that is, having made it free from hindrances. "Having approached a good friend"—

“Piyo garu bhāvanīyo, vattā ca vacanakkhamo;

Gambhīrañca kathaṃ kattā, no caṭṭhāne niyojako”ti. (a. ni. 7.37) –

"Beloved, revered, and esteemed; a counselor and one patient with counsel; a speaker of profound discourse, and one who does not engage you in a wrong course."

Evamādiguṇasamannāgataṃ ekantahitesiṃ vuddhipakkhe ṭhitaṃ kalyāṇamittaṃ upasaṅkamitvā.

Having approached a good friend endowed with these and other such qualities, one who is entirely intent on one's welfare and established on the side of growth.

Ananurūpaṃ [V 1.0254] vihāranti aṭṭhārasannaṃ dosānaṃ aññatarena samannāgataṃ. Vuttañhetaṃ aṭṭhakathāsu –

"An unsuitable dwelling" is one endowed with any of the eighteen faults. For this has been said in the commentaries:

“Mahāvāsaṃ navāvāsaṃ, jarāvāsañca panthaniṃ;

Soṇḍiṃ paṇṇañca pupphañca, phalaṃ patthitameva ca.

"A large dwelling, a new dwelling, a dilapidated dwelling, and one on a roadside; a tavern, a place for leaves, flowers, and fruit, and a place of sought-after things.

“Nagaraṃ dārunā khettaṃ, visabhāgena paṭṭanaṃ;

Paccantasīmā sappāyaṃ, yattha mitto na labbhati.

"A town, a timber-yard, a field, a port with dissimilar people; a border region, a suitable place, and where a friend is not found.

“Aṭṭhārasetāni ṭhānāni, iti viññāya paṇḍito;

Ārakā parivajjeyya, maggaṃ sappaṭibhayaṃ yathā”ti. (visuddhi. 1.52);

"The wise, knowing these eighteen grounds, should avoid them from afar, as one avoids a perilous road."

Anurūpeti [M 1.0271] gocaragāmato nātidūranaccāsannatādīhi pañcahi aṅgehi samannāgate. Vuttañhetaṃ bhagavatā –

"Suitable" means endowed with five factors, such as not being too far from nor too near to the alms-village. For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ nātidūraṃ hoti naccāsannaṃ gamanāgamanasampannaṃ divā appākiṇṇaṃ rattiṃ appasaddaṃ appanigghosaṃ appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassaṃ. Tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane viharantassa appakasirena uppajjanti cīvarapiṇḍapātasenāsanagilānapaccayabhesajjaparikkhārā. Tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane therā bhikkhū viharanti bahussutā āgatāgamā dhammadharā vinayadharā mātikādharā. Te kālena kālaṃ upasaṅkamitvā paripucchati paripañhati ‘idaṃ, bhante, kathaṃ imassa ko attho’ti. Tassa te āyasmanto avivaṭañceva vivaranti, anuttānīkatañca uttāniṃ karonti, anekavihitesu ca kaṅkhāṭhāniyesu dhammesu kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodenti. Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, senāsanaṃ pañcaṅgasamannāgataṃ hotī”ti (a. ni. 10.11).

"And how, bhikkhus, is a dwelling endowed with five factors? Here, bhikkhus, a dwelling is neither too far nor too near, it is suitable for coming and going; by day it is not crowded and by night it is quiet and still, with little contact from gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things. While dwelling there, one obtains with little difficulty the requisites of robes, almsfood, lodging, and medicinal supplies for the sick. In that dwelling there reside elder bhikkhus who are learned, who have preserved the tradition, who are custodians of the Dhamma, custodians of the Vinaya, custodians of the mātikās. From time to time one approaches them and asks and inquires: 'Venerable sirs, how is this? What is the meaning of this?' Those venerable ones then reveal what has not been revealed, make plain what has not been made plain, and dispel doubt regarding various doubtful points in the Dhamma. It is in this way, bhikkhus, that a dwelling is endowed with five factors."

Ettha ca nātidūraṃ naccāsannaṃ gamanāgamanasampannanti ekaṃ aṅgaṃ, divā appākiṇṇaṃ rattiṃ appasaddaṃ appanigghosanti ekaṃ, appaḍaṃsamakasavātātapasarīsapasamphassanti ekaṃ, tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane viharantassa…pe… parikkhārāti ekaṃ, tasmiṃ kho pana senāsane therā…pe… kaṅkhaṃ paṭivinodentīti ekanti evaṃ pañcaṅgāni veditabbāni.

Here, "not too far nor too near, suitable for coming and going" is one factor. "By day uncrowded, by night quiet, with little noise and clamor" is the second. "With little contact from gadflies, mosquitoes, wind, sun, and creeping things" is the third. "For one dwelling in that lodging... the requisites are obtained" is the fourth. "In that lodging, elder monks... dispel doubt" is the fifth. Thus, these five factors should be understood.

Khuddakapalibodhaṃ [V 1.0255] upacchinditvāti dīghakesanakhalomānaṃ chedanena cīvarakammacīvararajanapattapacanamañcapīṭhādisodhanavasena khuddakapalibodhaṃ upacchinditvā.

"Having cut off minor impediments" means having cut off minor impediments by cutting long hair, nails, and body hair, and by way of attending to robe-work, robe-dyeing, bowl-curing, and the cleaning of beds, seats, and so forth.

453. Uddhumātakādīsūti ettha ādi-saddena vinīlakavipubbakavicchiddakavikkhāyitakahatavikkhittakalohitakapuḷavakaaṭṭhikānaṃ saṅgaho daṭṭhabbo. Tattha bhastā viya vāyunā uddhaṃ jīvitapariyādānā yathānukkamaṃ samuggatena sūnabhāvena dhumātattā uddhumātaṃ, uddhumātameva uddhumātakaṃ, paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ uddhumātanti uddhumātakaṃ, tathārūpassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vinīlaṃ vuccati viparibhinnanīlavaṇṇaṃ, vinīlameva vinīlakaṃ, paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vinīlanti vinīlakaṃ, maṃsussadaṭṭhānesu rattavaṇṇassa[M 1.0272], pubbasannicayaṭṭhānesu setavaṇṇassa, yebhuyyena ca nīlavaṇṇassa nilaṭṭhāne nīlasāṭakapārutasseva chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Paribhinnaṭṭhānesu vissandamānapubbaṃ vipubbaṃ, vipubbameva vipubbakaṃ, paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vipubbanti vipubbakaṃ, tathārūpassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Vicchiddaṃ vuccati dvidhā chindanena apadhāritaṃ, vicchiddameva vicchiddakaṃ, paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vicchiddanti vicchiddakaṃ, vemajjhe chinnassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Ito ca etto ca vividhākārena soṇasiṅgālādīhi khāyitaṃ vikkhāyitaṃ, vikkhāyitameva vikkhāyitakaṃ, paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vikkhāyitanti vikkhāyitakaṃ, tathārūpassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ.

453. In the phrase "Uddhumātakādīsu," the word "ādī" should be understood to include the discoloured, the festering, the fissured, the gnawed, the hacked and scattered, the bloody, the worm-infested, and the skeletal. Here, "the bloated" (uddhumātaka) is a designation for a corpse that is bloated like a bellows, progressively swollen and distended, having been puffed up by wind after the cessation of life. Or it is called "the bloated" because it is repulsive and disgusting. This term denotes such a corpse. "The discoloured" (vinīlaka) is a designation for a corpse that is discoloured blue, or it is called "the discoloured" because it is repulsive and disgusting. This term refers to a corpse where the flesh appears red in places of swelling, white where pus has accumulated, and predominantly blue in blue areas, resembling a body draped in a blue cloth. "The festering" (vipubbaka) is a designation for a corpse that is oozing pus from broken areas, or it is called "the festering" because it is repulsive and disgusting. This term denotes such a corpse. "The fissured" (vicchiddaka) is a designation for a corpse that is distinctly cut by being split in two, or it is called "the fissured" because it is repulsive and disgusting. This term refers to a corpse cut in the middle. "The gnawed" (vikkhāyitaka) is a designation for a corpse that has been gnawed in various ways, here and there, by dogs, jackals, and so on, or it is called "the gnawed" because it is repulsive and disgusting. This term denotes such a corpse.

Vividhā khittaṃ vikkhittaṃ, vikkhittameva vikkhittakaṃ, paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ vikkhittanti vikkhittakaṃ, aññena hatthaṃ, aññena pādaṃ, aññena sīsanti evaṃ tato tato vikkhittassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Hatañca taṃ purimanayeneva vikkhittakañcāti hatavikkhittakaṃ, kākapadākārena aṅgapaccaṅgesu satthena hanitvā vuttanayeneva vikkhittassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Lohitaṃ kirati vikkhipati ito cito ca paggharatīti lohitakaṃ, paggharitalohitamakkhitassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Puḷavā vuccanti kimayo, puḷave kiratīti puḷavakaṃ, kimiparipuṇṇassa chavasarīrassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Aṭṭhiyeva aṭṭhikaṃ, paṭikūlattā vā kucchitaṃ aṭṭhīti aṭṭhikaṃ, aṭṭhisaṅkhalikāyapi ekaṭṭhikassapi etaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Imesu dasasu asubhesu paṭhamajjhānameva uppajjati, na dutiyādīni. Tenāha – idha “paṭhamajjhānasahagatā saññā”ti. Tathā hi aparisaṇṭhitajalāya sīghasotāya nadiyā arittabaleneva nāvā tiṭṭhati, vinā arittena na sakkā ṭhapetuṃ. Evamevaṃ dubbalattā ārammaṇassa vitakkabaleneva cittaṃ ekaggaṃ hutvā tiṭṭhati, vinā vitakkena na sakkā ṭhapetuṃ[V 1.0256]. Tasmā paṭhamajjhānamevettha hoti, na dutiyādīni. Ārammaṇassa dubbalatā cettha paṭikūlabhāvena cittaṃ ṭhapetuṃ asamatthatā.

"The scattered" (vikkhittaka) is so called because it is scattered in various ways, or it is called "the scattered" because it is repulsive and disgusting; it is a designation for a corpse with a hand in one place, a foot in another, the head in another, thus scattered hither and thither. "The hacked and scattered" (hatavikkhittaka) is a corpse that is both hacked in the previously mentioned way and scattered; it is a designation for a corpse that has been hacked with a weapon in its limbs and minor limbs in the shape of a crow's foot and scattered in the way already stated. "The bloody" (lohitaka) is so called because it oozes and scatters blood, flowing hither and thither; it is a designation for a corpse smeared with oozing blood. Worms (kimayo) are called puḷavā. Since it scatters worms, it is called "the worm-infested" (puḷavaka); it is a designation for a corpse full of worms. "The skeletal" (aṭṭhika) refers to bones, or it is called "the skeletal" because it is repulsive and disgusting. This term applies both to a skeleton of connected bones and to a single bone. Among these ten foul objects, only the first jhāna arises, not the second or higher. Therefore, it is said: "Here, the perception associated with the first jhāna." Just as a boat cannot stay steady in a river with unsettled water and a swift current without the strength of a rudder, so too, due to the weakness of the object, the mind becomes one-pointed and stays steady only through the power of applied thought. Without applied thought, it cannot be steadied. Thus, here only the first jhāna arises, not the second or higher. The weakness of the object here is its inability to steady the mind due to its repulsive nature.

“Rukkho mato, lohaṃ mata”ntiādīsu yaṃ khandhappabandhaṃ upādāya rukkhādisamaññā, tasmiṃ anupacchinnepi allatādivigamanaṃ nissāya matavohāro sammutimaraṇaṃ. Saṅkhārānaṃ khaṇabhaṅgasaṅkhātaṃ khaṇikamaraṇaṃ. Samucchedamaraṇanti arahato santānassa sabbaso ucchedabhūtaṃ maraṇaṃ. Vipassanābhāvanāvasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Maraṇānussatibhāvanāyaṃ pana tividhampetaṃ nādhippetaṃ [M 1.0273] asaṃvegavatthuto anupaṭṭhahanato abāhullato ca. Maraṇānussatiyañhi ekena bhavena paricchinnassa jīvitindriyappabandhassa vicchedo maraṇanti adhippeto saṃvegavatthuto upaṭṭhahanato bāhullato ca. Idāni imameva maraṇaṃ sandhāya vikappantaraṃ dassento, “heṭṭhā vuttalakkhaṇā vā”tiādimāha.

In the phrases 'The tree is dead, the metal is dead,' etc., the designation 'tree' and so on is based on the continuity of the aggregates; in this case, even when that continuity is unbroken, the conventional expression 'dead' arises due to the disappearance of moisture and other qualities—this is conventional death. Momentary death is the dissolution of formations at each instant, known as momentary disintegration. Death of cessation is the death consisting of the complete cutting off of the continuity of an arahant—this is death by annihilation. This is stated in the context of insight meditation. However, in the development of mindfulness of death, these three types are not intended, as they do not provide a basis for urgency, are not directly applicable, and are not frequent. For mindfulness of death, what is intended is the cutting off of the continuity of the life faculty limited to a single existence—this is intended as a basis for urgency, as directly applicable, and as frequent. Now, to present an alternative distinction concerning this very death, it is said, 'Or as defined below,' etc.

Asitapītādibhedeti asitapītakhāyitasāyitappabhede, asitabbakhāditabbasāyitabbavibhāgeti attho kālabhedavacanicchāya abhāvato yathā “duddha”nti. Kabaḷaṃ karīyatīti kabaḷīkāro, āharīyatīti āhāro, kabaḷīkāro ca so āhāro cāti kabaḷīkārāhāro. Vatthuvasena cetaṃ vuttaṃ. Savatthuko eva hi āhāro idha kammaṭṭhānabhāvena adhippeto. Ojālakkhaṇo pana āhāro ojaṭṭhamakaṃ rūpaṃ āharatīti āhāroti vuccati. So idha nādhippeto paṭikūlākāraggahaṇassa asambhavato. Nava paṭikūlānīti gamanapariyesanaparibhogāsayanidānaaparipakkaparipakkaphalanissandappaṭikūlavasena nava paṭikūlāni. Samakkhanappaṭikūlaṃ pana paribhogādīsu labbhamānattā idha visuṃ na gahitaṃ, aññathā tena saddhiṃ “dasa paṭikūlānī”ti vattabbaṃ. Visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.303-304) pana samakkhanaṃ paribhogādīsu labbhamānampi nissandavasena visesato paṭikūlanti visuṃ gahetvā dasahākārehi paṭikūlatā vuttā.

Regarding the division into kinds such as what is eaten, drunk, chewed, and savored, the meaning is the distinction between what is to be eaten, chewed, and savored. The absence of terms indicating time divisions is like the word "milk." A morsel is made, thus 'morsel-making' (kabaḷīkāra); it is brought, thus 'food' (āhāra); and that which is both morsel-making and food is 'morsel-food' (kabaḷīkārāhāra). This is said with reference to the substance. Indeed, food with substance is intended here as a meditation subject. However, food characterized by nutritive essence is called "food" (āhāra) because it brings matter with nutritive essence as the eighth constituent (ojaṭṭhamakaṃ rūpaṃ). That is not intended here because the perception of the repulsive aspect is not possible in it. The nine repulsive aspects are: repulsiveness based on movement, seeking, consumption, abiding, origin, unripeness, ripeness, result, and exudation. However, the repulsiveness of anointing is not separately mentioned here because it is found in consumption, etc. Otherwise, it should be stated as "ten repulsive aspects." In the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 1.303–304), although anointing is found in consumption, etc., it is separately taken as especially repulsive due to exudation, and repulsiveness is explained in ten ways.

Uppajjanakasaññanti paṭikūlākāraggahaṇavasena uppajjanakasaññaṃ. Saññāsaddo cāyaṃ “rūpasaññā saddasaññā”tiādīsu (saṃ. ni. 3.57) sañjānanalakkhaṇe dhamme āgato, “aniccasaññā dukkhasaññā”tiādīsu vipassanāya āgato, “uddhumātakasaññāti vā sopākarūpasaññāti vā ime dhammā ekaṭṭhā, udāhu nānaṭṭhā”tiādīsu samathe āgato. Idha pana samathassa parikamme daṭṭhabbo. Āhārehi paṭikūlākāraggahaṇaṃ, tappabhāvitaṃ vā upacārajjhānaṃ idha “āhāre paṭikūlasaññā”ti adhippetaṃ.

By 'perception that arises' (uppajjanakasaññā) is meant the perception that arises by way of grasping the repulsive aspect. The word "perception" here, as in "perception of form, perception of sound," etc., (SN 3.57) occurs referring to the characteristic of recognition; as in "perception of impermanence, perception of suffering," etc., it occurs referring to insight; as in "Is the perception of a bloated corpse or the perception of a decomposing corpse, are these qualities the same, or are they different?" etc., it occurs referring to serenity. Here, however, it should be regarded as preliminary practice for serenity. The grasping of the repulsive aspect in food, or the access jhāna developed based on that, is what is intended here by "perception of repulsiveness regarding food" (āhāre paṭikūlasaññā).

Ukkaṇṭhitasaññanti [V 1.0257] nibbindanākārena uppajjanakasaññaṃ. Aniccasaññanti ettha aniccaṃ khandhapañcakaṃ uppādavayaññathattabhāvato, hutvā abhāvato vā, tasmiṃ anicce khandhapañcake aniccanti uppajjamānā aniccalakkhaṇapariggāhikā saññā aniccasaññā. Tenāha – “pañcannaṃ upādānakkhandhāna”ntiādi. Tattha udayo [M 1.0274] nibbattilakkhaṇaṃ, vayo vipariṇāmalakkhaṇaṃ, aññathattaṃ jarā. Udayabbayaññathattaggahaṇena aniccalakkhaṇaṃ dasseti. Uppādavayaññathattabhāvato hi khandhapañcakaṃ aniccanti vuccati. Yassa ca sabhāvena khandhapañcakaṃ aniccanti vuccati, taṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ. Tena hi taṃ aniccanti lakkhīyati, aniccalakkhaṇañca udayabbayānaṃ amanasikārā santatiyā paṭicchannattā na upaṭṭhāti, udayabbayaṃ pana pariggahetvā santatiyā vikopitāya aniccalakkhaṇaṃ yāthāvasarasato upaṭṭhāti. Na hi sammadeva udayabbayaṃ sallakkhentassa pubbāpariyena pavattamānānaṃ dhammānaṃ aññoññabhāvaṃ sallakkhaṇena santatiyā ugghāṭitāya dhammā sambandhabhāvena upaṭṭhahanti, atha kho ayosalākā viya asambandhabhāvenāti suṭṭhutaraṃ aniccalakkhaṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ hoti.

"The perception of discontent" (ukkaṇṭhitasaññā) refers to the perception that arises in the manner of weariness. "The perception of impermanence" (aniccasaññā) here refers to the five aggregates as impermanent due to their nature of arising, passing away, and alteration, or because they cease after existing. The perception that arises regarding these impermanent five aggregates, grasping the characteristic of impermanence, is called the perception of impermanence. Hence it is said: "of the five aggregates subject to clinging," etc. Therein, "arising" signifies the characteristic of production, "passing away" signifies the characteristic of dissolution, and "alteration" signifies aging. By grasping arising, passing away, and alteration, the characteristic of impermanence is shown. For the five aggregates are called impermanent due to their nature of arising, passing away, and alteration. That by which the five aggregates are called impermanent in their intrinsic nature is the characteristic of impermanence. Thus, that is discerned as impermanent, but the characteristic of impermanence does not appear due to its concealment by continuity when one does not attend to arising and passing away. However, when one grasps arising and passing away and disrupts the continuity, the characteristic of impermanence appears clearly as it truly is. For one who rightly discerns arising and passing away, phenomena that occur sequentially do not appear as interconnected when their mutual distinction is discerned and continuity is uprooted. Rather, they appear as disconnected, like pieces of iron. Thus, the characteristic of impermanence becomes thoroughly evident.

“Yadaniccaṃ, taṃ dukkha”nti (saṃ. ni. 3.15, 45, 46, 76, 77, 85; 2.4.1, 4) vacanato tadeva khandhapañcakaṃ abhiṇhappaṭipīḷanato dukkhaṃ, abhiṇhappaṭipīḷanākāro pana dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ. Tenevāha – “anicce khandhapañcake…pe… saññaṃ bhāvetī”ti. Tattha paṭipīḷanaṃ nāma yathāpariggahitaṃ udayavayavasena saṅkhārānaṃ nirantaraṃ paṭipīḷiyamānatā vibādhiyamānatā. Dukkhalakkhaṇañca abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanassa amanasikārā iriyāpathehi paṭicchannattā na upaṭṭhāti, abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanaṃ pana manasi karitvā iriyāpathe labbhamānadukkhappaṭicchādakabhāve ugghāṭite dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ yāthāvasarasato upaṭṭhāti. Tathā hi iriyāpathehi paṭicchannattā dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ na upaṭṭhāti, te ca iriyāpathā abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanāmanasikārena paṭicchādakā jātā. Ekasmiñhi iriyāpathe uppannassa dukkhassa vinodakaṃ iriyāpathantaraṃ tassa paṭicchādakaṃ viya hoti, evaṃ sesāpi. Iriyāpathānaṃ pana taṃtaṃdukkhapatitākārabhāve yāthāvato ñāte tesaṃ dukkhappaṭicchādakabhāvo ugghāṭito nāma hoti saṅkhārānaṃ nirantaraṃ dukkhābhitunnatāya pākaṭabhāvato. Tasmā abhiṇhasampaṭipīḷanaṃ manasi karitvā iriyāpathe labbhamānadukkhappaṭicchādakabhāve ugghāṭite dukkhalakkhaṇaṃ yāthāvasarasato upaṭṭhāti.

"What is impermanent, that is suffering," (Saṃ. Ni. 3.15, 45, 46, 76, 77, 85; 2.4.1, 4). According to this statement, that very same five aggregates are suffering due to constant oppression, and the characteristic of suffering is the manner of constant oppression. Hence it is said: "In the impermanent five aggregates...one develops the perception of suffering." Here, oppression means the continuous and uninterrupted crushing and affliction of formations due to their arising and passing away as they are apprehended. The characteristic of suffering does not appear because one does not attend to the constant oppression, and because it is concealed by postures. However, when one attends to the constant oppression and the way the suffering is concealed by postures is uncovered, the characteristic of suffering becomes clearly evident as it truly is. Indeed, because the characteristic of suffering is concealed by postures, it does not appear, and these postures arise as concealers because of inattention to the constant oppression. For instance, when suffering arises in one posture, another posture that serves to dispel it acts as a concealer—and so on for the others. When the postures are known as they truly are, in their individual instances of suffering, their role as concealers of suffering is removed, that is, the continuous affliction by suffering on formations becomes manifest. Therefore, when one attends to the constant oppression and the way the suffering is concealed by postures is uncovered, the characteristic of suffering becomes clearly evident as it truly is.

“Yaṃ dukkhaṃ, tadanattā”ti vacanato tadeva khandhapañcakaṃ avasavattanato anattā, avasavattanākāro pana anattalakkhaṇaṃ. Tenāha – “paṭipīḷanaṭṭhenā”tiādi[M 1.0275]. Anattalakkhaṇañca nānādhātuvinibbhogassa [V 1.0258] amanasikārā ghanena paṭicchannattā na upaṭṭhāti, nānādhātuyo pana vinibbhujjitvā “aññā pathavīdhātu, aññā āpodhātū”tiādinā, “añño phasso, aññā vedanā”tiādinā ca visuṃ visuṃ katvā ghanavinibbhoge kate samūhaghane kiccārammaṇaghane ca bhedite anattalakkhaṇaṃ yāthāvasarasato upaṭṭhāti. Yā hesā aññamaññūpatthambhesu samuditesu rūpārūpadhammesu ekattābhinivesavasena aparimadditasaṅkhārehi mamāyamānā samūhaghanatā, tathā tesaṃ tesaṃ dhammānaṃ kiccabhedassa satipi paṭiniyatabhāve ekato gayhamānā kiccaghanatā, tathā sārammaṇadhammānaṃ satipi ārammaṇakaraṇabhede ekato gayhamānā ārammaṇaghanatā. Sā catūsu dhātūsu ñāṇena vinibbhujitvā dissamānāsu hatthena parimaddiyamāno pheṇapiṇḍo viya vilīnaṃ āgacchati, yathāpaccayaṃ pavattamānā suññā ete dhammamattāti avasavattanākārasaṅkhātaṃ anattalakkhaṇaṃ pākaṭataraṃ hoti.

In accordance with the saying, 'Whatever is suffering, that is not-self,' that very fivefold aggregate is not-self because it is uncontrollable. The aspect of uncontrollability, however, is the characteristic of not-self. Therefore, it is said: 'In the sense of oppression,' and so on. The characteristic of not-self does not become evident, as it is concealed by compactness due to the failure to attend to the analysis of the various elements. But when the elements are analyzed—such as 'the earth element is one thing, the water element is another,' or 'contact is one thing, feeling is another,' and so on—and when the compactness of mass, of function, and of object are broken, then the characteristic of not-self becomes evident as it is. For this is the compactness of mass, where material and immaterial phenomena, arising in mutual dependence, are appropriated as 'mine' by those who have not thoroughly examined the formations due to their adherence to unity. Similarly, there is the compactness of function, where the distinct functions of various phenomena are grasped as one; and the compactness of object, where the distinct roles of phenomena as objects are grasped as one. When these are discerned and analyzed by wisdom in the four elements, they dissolve like a lump of foam being rubbed by the hand. As they proceed according to conditions, it is seen that these are mere empty phenomena. Thus, the characteristic of not-self, described as the aspect of uncontrollability, becomes more apparent.

Aparaaccharāsaṅghātavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The commentary on the Aparaaccharāsaṅghātavagga is completed.

19. Kāyagatāsativaggavaṇṇanā

19. The Exposition of the Section on Mindfulness of the Body

563. Cetasā [V 1.0259] phuṭoti cittena pharito. Cittena pharaṇañca samuddassa dvidhā sambhavatīti āha – “duvidhaṃ pharaṇa”ntiādi. Purimena atthenāti “sampayogavasena vijjaṃ bhajantī”ti vuttena atthena. Pacchimenāti “vijjābhāge vijjākoṭṭhāse vattantī”ti vuttena.

563. 'Cetasā phuṭo' means permeated by mind, pervaded by mind. Pervasion by mind, it is said, occurs in two ways with respect to the ocean, hence it is said: 'There are two kinds of pervasion,' etc. By the former meaning is meant what was stated as: 'Partaking of knowledge by way of association.' By the latter is meant what was stated as: 'Operating in the realm of knowledge, in the division of knowledge.'

564. Mahato saṃvegāya saṃvattatītiādīsu ayaṃ pana aparo nayo. Yāthāvato kāyasabhāvappavedanato mahato saṃvegāya saṃvattati. Atthāyāti diṭṭhadhammikādiatthāya. Yogakkhemāyāti catūhi yogehi khemabhāvāya. Satisampajaññāyāti sabbattha satiavippavāsāya sattaṭṭhāniyasampajaññāya ca. Ñāṇadassanappaṭilābhāyāti vipassanāñāṇādhigamāya. Vijjāvimuttiphalasacchikiriyāyāti tisso vijjā cittassa adhimutti nibbānaṃ cattāri sāmaññaphalānīti etesaṃ paccakkhakaraṇāya.

564. In the phrase 'leads to great urgency,' and so on, this is another method. From truly declaring the nature of the body, it leads to great urgency. 'For the sake of benefit' means for benefits in this present life and so forth. 'For the sake of security from bondage' means for a state of security from the four bonds. 'For mindfulness and clear comprehension' means for the non-abandonment of mindfulness everywhere and for clear comprehension in the seven instances. 'For the attainment of knowledge and vision' means for achieving insight knowledge. 'For the realization of the fruits of true knowledge and liberation' means for directly experiencing the three knowledges, the mind's resolve, Nibbāna, and the four fruits of recluseship.

584. Paññāpaṭilābhāyātiādīsu [M 1.0276] soḷasasu padesu paññāpaṭilābhāya paññāvuddhiyā paññāvepullāya paññābāhullāyāti imāni cattāri paññāvasena bhāvavacanāni, sesāni dvādasa puggalavasena bhāvavacanāni. Sappurisasaṃsevoti sappurisānaṃ bhajanaṃ. Saddhammassavananti tesaṃ sappurisānaṃ santike sīlādippaṭipattidīpakassa saddhammavacanassa savanaṃ. Yoniso manasikāroti sutānaṃ dhammānaṃ atthūpaparikkhāvasena upāyena manasikāro. Dhammānudhammappaṭipattīti lokuttaradhamme anugatassa sīlādippaṭipadādhammassa paṭipajjanaṃ.

584. In the sixteen instances such as 'for the attainment of wisdom,' etc., the four terms—'for the attainment of wisdom,' 'for the growth of wisdom,' 'for the increase of wisdom,' and 'for the abundance of wisdom'—are expressions concerning the development in respect of wisdom. The remaining twelve are expressions concerning the development in respect of individuals. 'Associating with good people' means associating with the virtuous. 'Listening to the true Dhamma' refers to hearing the teachings of the true Dhamma, which illuminates the practice of morality and so forth, in the presence of those good people. 'Proper attention' is the application of the mind by way of examining the meaning of the teachings heard with skillful attention. 'Practicing in accordance with the Dhamma' is practicing the qualities of morality and so forth that accord with the supramundane Dhamma.

Channaṃ abhiññāñāṇānanti iddhividhadibbasotacetopariyapubbenivāsadibbacakkhuāsavakkhayañāṇānaṃ. Tesattatīnaṃ ñāṇānanti paṭisambhidāpāḷiyaṃ (paṭi. ma. 1.1-2 mātikā) “sotāvadhāne paññā sutamaye ñāṇaṃ, sutvāna saṃvare paññā sīlamaye ñāṇa”ntiādinā ñāṇakathāya niddiṭṭhānaṃ sāvakasādhāraṇāsādhāraṇānaṃ ñāṇānaṃ. Imesañhi tesattatiñāṇānaṃ sutamayañāṇādīni sattasaṭṭhiñāṇāni sāvakassa sādhāraṇāni, “indriyaparopariyatte ñāṇaṃ, sattānaṃ āsayānusaye ñāṇaṃ, yamakapāṭihīre ñāṇaṃ, mahākaruṇāsamāpattiyā ñāṇaṃ, sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ, anāvaraṇañāṇa”nti (paṭi. ma. 1.68-73 mātikā) imāni cha asādhāraṇañāṇāni sāvakehi.

The six higher knowledges are the knowledges of psychic powers, the divine ear, penetration of minds, recollection of past lives, the divine eye, and the destruction of the taints. The seventy-three knowledges are those explained in the section on knowledge in the Paṭisambhidāmagga (Paṭi. Ma. 1.1-2, mātikā): 'The wisdom in attending is knowledge born of learning; the wisdom in restraint after hearing is knowledge born of virtue,' and so on, which include knowledges common to disciples and knowledges not common to disciples. For among these seventy-three knowledges, sixty-seven knowledges beginning with knowledge born of learning are common to disciples, while these six knowledges not common to disciples are: 'Knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of others; knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies of beings; knowledge of the twin miracle; knowledge of the attainment of great compassion; omniscient knowledge; and unobstructed knowledge' (Paṭi. Ma. 1.68-73, mātikā).

Sattasattatīnaṃ [V 1.0260] ñāṇānanti ettha –

'Of the seventy-seven knowledges' – here,

“Jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti ñāṇaṃ, asati jātiyā natthi jarāmaraṇanti ñāṇaṃ. Atītampi addhānaṃ jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti ñāṇaṃ, asati jātiyā natthi jarāmaraṇanti ñāṇaṃ. Anāgatampi addhānaṃ jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇanti ñāṇaṃ, asati jātiyā natthi jarāmaraṇanti ñāṇaṃ. Yampissa taṃ dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ, tampi khayadhammaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ nirodhadhammanti ñāṇaṃ. Bhavapaccayā jātīti ñāṇaṃ…pe… upādānapaccayā bhavoti ñāṇaṃ, taṇhāpaccayā upādānanti ñāṇaṃ, vedanāpaccayā taṇhāti ñāṇaṃ, phassapaccayā vedanāti ñāṇaṃ, saḷāyatanapaccayā phassoti ñāṇaṃ, nāmarūpapaccayā saḷāyatananti ñāṇaṃ, viññāṇapaccayā nāmarūpanti ñāṇaṃ, saṅkhārapaccayā viññāṇanti ñāṇaṃ, avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti ñāṇaṃ, asati [M 1.0277] avijjāya natthi saṅkhārāti ñāṇaṃ, atītampi addhānaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti ñāṇaṃ, asati avijjāya natthi saṅkhārāti ñāṇaṃ, anāgatampi addhānaṃ avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārāti ñāṇaṃ, asati avijjāya natthi saṅkhārāti ñāṇaṃ, yampissa taṃ dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ, tampi khayadhamaṃ vayadhammaṃ virāgadhammaṃ nirodhadhammanti ñāṇa”nti –

“With birth as condition, aging and death arise”—this is knowledge. “When there is no birth, there is no aging and death”—this is knowledge. “In the past, with birth as condition, aging and death arose”—this is knowledge. “When there was no birth, there was no aging and death”—this is knowledge. “In the future, with birth as condition, aging and death will arise”—this is knowledge. “When there is no birth, there will be no aging and death”—this is knowledge. And that knowledge of the fixed nature of the Dhamma is also knowledge of its nature of decay, vanishing, fading away, and cessation. “With becoming as condition, birth arises”—this is knowledge... “With clinging as condition, becoming arises”—this is knowledge. “With craving as condition, clinging arises”—this is knowledge. “With feeling as condition, craving arises”—this is knowledge. “With contact as condition, feeling arises”—this is knowledge. “With the six sense bases as condition, contact arises”—this is knowledge. “With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases arise”—this is knowledge. “With consciousness as condition, name-and-form arises”—this is knowledge. “With volitional formations as condition, consciousness arises”—this is knowledge. “With ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise”—this is knowledge. “When there is no ignorance, there are no volitional formations”—this is knowledge. “In the past, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arose”—this is knowledge. “When there was no ignorance, there were no volitional formations”—this is knowledge. “In the future, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations will arise”—this is knowledge. “When there is no ignorance, there will be no volitional formations”—this is knowledge. And that knowledge of the fixed nature of the Dhamma is also knowledge of its nature of decay, vanishing, fading away, and cessation.”

Bhagavatā nidānavagge (saṃ. ni. 2.34-35) jarāmaraṇādīsu ekādasasu paṭiccasamuppādaṅgesu paccekaṃ satta satta katvā vuttāni sattasattatiñāṇāni.

The Blessed One, in the Nidānavagga (Saṃ. Ni. 2.34-35), spoke of seventy-seven knowledges, explaining each of the eleven factors of dependent origination, such as aging and death, in seven ways.

Tattha dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇanti paccayākārañāṇaṃ. Paccayākāro hi dhammānaṃ pavattisaṅkhātāya ṭhitiyā kāraṇattā “dhammaṭṭhitī”ti vuccati, tattha ñāṇaṃ dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇaṃ, “jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇa”ntiādinā vuttasseva chabbidhassa ñāṇassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Khayadhammanti khayagamanasabhāvaṃ. Vayadhammanti vayagamanasabhāvaṃ. Virāgadhammanti virajjanasabhāvaṃ. Nirodhadhammanti nirujjhanasabhāvanti attho.

Here, the knowledge of the fixed nature of the Dhamma is the knowledge of the mode of conditions. The mode of conditions is called 'the fixed nature of the Dhamma' because it is the cause of the continuity of phenomena, which is termed 'stability.' Knowledge of that is the knowledge of the fixed nature of the Dhamma. This is another term for the sixfold knowledge stated as 'with birth as condition, aging and death,' etc. 'Subject to destruction' means having the nature of going to destruction. 'Subject to vanishing' means having the nature of going to vanishing. 'Subject to fading away' means having the nature of fading away. 'Subject to cessation' means having the nature of ceasing—this is the meaning.

Lābhotiādīsu lābhoyeva upasaggena visesetvā “paṭilābho”ti vutto. Puna tasseva atthavivaraṇavasena “patti sampattī”ti vuttaṃ. Phusanāti adhigamanavasena phusanā. Sacchikiriyāti paṭilābhasacchikiriyā. Upasampadāti nipphādanā.

In terms like 'lābho,' it is specifically 'lābho' that is distinguished by a prefix and called 'paṭilābho.' Furthermore, elaborating on the meaning of that same term, 'patti' and 'sampatti' are stated. 'Phusanā' means touching in the sense of attainment. 'Sacchikiriyā' means realization of acquisition. 'Upasampadā' means completion.

Sattannañca [V 1.0261] sekkhānanti tisso sikkhā sikkhantīti sekkhasaññitānaṃ sotāpattimaggaṭṭhādīnaṃ sattannaṃ. Puthujjanakalyāṇakassa cāti nibbānagāminiyā paṭipadāya yuttattā sundaraṭṭhena kalyāṇasaññitassa puthujjanassa. Vaḍḍhitaṃ vaḍḍhanaṃ ekāyāti vaḍḍhitavaḍḍhanā. Yathāvuttānaṃ aṭṭhannampi paññānaṃ vasena visesatova arahato paññāvasena paññāvuddhiyā. Tathā paññāvepullāya.

And of the seven learners: of the seven, from the one standing on the path of stream-entry upwards, who are designated as learners because they train in the three trainings. And of the ordinary virtuous person: of the ordinary person designated as virtuous in the sense of being excellent, since they are endowed with the practice leading to Nibbāna. 'Growth and increase in one way' means growth and increase. As stated, through the increase of wisdom, by way of the wisdom of the aforementioned eight persons, and especially by way of the wisdom of the Arahant. Likewise, through the abundance of wisdom.

Yassa kassacipi visesato anurūpadhammassa mahantaṃ nāma kiccasiddhiyā veditabbanti tadassa kiccasiddhiyā dassento “mahante atthe pariggaṇhātī”tiādimāha. Tattha atthādīnaṃ mahantabhāvo mahāvisayatāya veditabbo, mahāvisayatā ca tesaṃ paṭisambhidāmagge āgatanayena veditabbā. Sīlakkhandhassa pana hetumahantatāya, paccayamahantatāya, nissayamahantatāya[M 1.0278], pabhedamahantatāya, kiccamahantatāya, phalamahantatāya, ānisaṃsamahantatāya ca mahantabhāvo veditabbo. Tattha hetu alobhādayo. Paccayo hirottappasaddhāsativīriyādayo. Nissayo sāvakabodhipaccekabodhiniyatatā taṃsamaṅgino ca purisavisesā. Pabhedo cārittavārittādivibhāgo. Kiccaṃ tadaṅgādivasena paṭipakkhavidhamanaṃ. Phalaṃ saggasampadā nibbānasampadā ca. Ānisaṃso piyamanāpatādi. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana visuddhimagge (visuddhi. 1.9) ākaṅkheyyasuttādīsu (ma. ni. 1.64 ādayo) ca āgatanayena veditabbo. Iminā nayena samādhikkhandhādīnampi mahantatā yathārahaṃ niddhāretvā vattabbā. Ṭhānāṭṭhānādīnaṃ mahantabhāvo pana mahāvisayatāya veditabbo. Tattha ṭhānāṭṭhānānaṃ mahāvisayatā bahudhātukasuttādīsu āgatanayena veditabbā.

For anyone with a particularly suitable quality, a great thing should be known by the accomplishment of a task; showing this accomplishment of his task, he said, 'He encompasses great meanings,' and so on. Here, the greatness of meanings and so on should be understood by their vast scope, and their vast scope should be understood according to the method presented in the Paṭisambhidāmagga. As for the greatness of the aggregate of virtue, it should be understood through the greatness of its cause, condition, support, divisions, duty, fruit, and benefit. Here, the cause is non-greed and so on. The condition is shame, moral dread, faith, mindfulness, energy, and so on. The support is the state of being destined for a disciple's awakening or for a Paccekabuddha's awakening, and the exceptional individuals endowed with it. The divisions are the classifications of conduct and restraint, and so on. The duty is the destruction of opposing states by way of their respective factors, and so on. The fruit is the attainment of heaven and the attainment of Nibbāna. The benefit includes being dear and agreeable, and so on. This is the summary here. The detailed explanation should be understood according to the method found in the Visuddhimagga (Visuddhi. 1.9) and in the Ākaṅkheyyasutta and others (M. Ni. 1.64, etc.). In this way, the greatness of the aggregate of concentration and others should also be determined and explained appropriately.
