The greatness of what is possible and impossible, and so on, should be understood by their vast scope. Here, the vast scope of what is possible and impossible should be understood according to the method presented in the Bahudhātukasutta and others.

Vihārasamāpattīnaṃ mahāvisayatā samādhikkhandhe mahāvisayatāniddhāraṇanayena veditabbā, ariyasaccānaṃ sakalayānasaṅgāhakato saccavibhaṅge (vibha. 189 ādayo) taṃsaṃvaṇṇanāsu (vibha. aṭṭha. 189 ādayo) ca āgatanayena, satipaṭṭhānādīnaṃ satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅgādīsu (vibha. 355 ādayo) taṃsaṃvaṇṇanādīsu (vibha. aṭṭha. 355 ādayo) ca āgatanayena, sāmaññaphalānaṃ mahato hitassa mahato sukhassa mahato atthassa mahato yogakkhemassa nipphattibhāvato santapaṇītaatakkāvacarapaṇḍitavedanīyabhāvato, abhiññānaṃ mahāsambhārato mahāvisayato mahākiccato mahānubhāvato mahānipphattito, nibbānassa madanimmadanādimahatthasiddhito ca mahantabhāvo veditabbo. Pariggaṇhātīti sabhāvādito paricchijja gaṇhāti jānāti, paṭivijjhatīti attho.

The great scope of meditative attainments should be understood by the method of determining the great scope in the aggregate of concentration. The greatness of the Noble Truths is to be understood from their inclusion of all vehicles, in the way that has come down in the Saccavibhaṅga (Vibh. 189 ff.) and its commentaries (Vibh. Aṭṭha. 189 ff.). The greatness of the foundations of mindfulness and so on is to be understood in the way they are presented in the Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga (Vibh. 355 ff.) and its commentaries (Vibh. Aṭṭha. 355 ff.). The greatness of the fruits of recluseship is to be understood from their accomplishment of great benefit, great happiness, great welfare, and great security from bondage, and from their being peaceful, sublime, beyond the range of logic, and to be experienced by the wise. The greatness of the higher knowledges is to be understood from their great accumulation, great scope, great function, great power, and great accomplishment. The greatness of Nibbāna is to be understood from its achievement of great aims, such as the crushing of intoxication. 'Comprehends' means to grasp and know by defining according to intrinsic nature; the meaning is 'penetrates'.

Puthupaññāti [V 1.0262] etthāpi vuttanayānusārena attho veditabbo. Ayaṃ pana viseso – puthu nānākkhandhesu ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti “ayaṃ rūpakkhandho nāma…pe… ayaṃ viññāṇakkhandho nāmā”ti evaṃ pañcannaṃ khandhānaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati. Tesupi ekavidhena rūpakkhandho…pe… ekādasavidhena rūpakkhandho. Ekavidhena vedanākkhandho…pe… bahuvidhena vedanākkhandho. Ekavidhena saññākkhandho…pe… bahuvidhena saññākkhandho. Ekavidhena saṅkhārakkhandho…pe… bahuvidhena saṅkhārakkhandho. Ekavidhena viññāṇakkhandho…pe… bahuvidhena [M 1.0279] viññāṇakkhandhoti evaṃ ekekassa khandhassa ekavidhādivasena atītādivasenapi nānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati.

Regarding 'diverse wisdom,' here too the meaning should be understood in accordance with the method stated. This, however, is the distinction: knowledge operates with regard to the various aggregates, in the sense that 'this is called the aggregate of form... (and so forth) ...this is called the aggregate of consciousness.' Thus, knowledge operates in dependence on the diversification of the five aggregates. Among these, too: the aggregate of form is of one kind... (and so forth) ...the aggregate of form is of eleven kinds. The aggregate of feeling is of one kind... (and so forth) ...the aggregate of feeling is of many kinds. The aggregate of perception is of one kind... (and so forth) ...the aggregate of perception is of many kinds. The aggregate of formations is of one kind... (and so forth) ...the aggregate of formations is of many kinds. The aggregate of consciousness is of one kind... (and so forth) ...the aggregate of consciousness is of many kinds. Thus, knowledge operates in dependence on the diversification of each aggregate by way of being of one kind and so forth, and also by way of being past and so forth.

Puthu nānādhātūsūti “ayaṃ cakkhudhātu nāma…pe… ayaṃ manoviññāṇadhātu nāma. Tattha soḷasa dhātuyo kāmāvacarā, dve cātubhūmikā”ti evaṃ dhātūsu nānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati. Tayidaṃ upādinnadhātuvasena vuttaṃ. Paccekabuddhānañhi dvinnañca aggasāvakānaṃ upādinnadhātūsu eva nānākaraṇaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati, tañca kho ekadesatova, na nippadesato. Bahiddhā anupādinnadhātūnaṃ nānākaraṇaṃ tesaṃ avisayova, sabbaññubuddhānaṃyeva pana “imāya dhātuyā ussannattā imassa rukkhassa khandho seto hoti, imassa kāḷo, imassa maṭṭho, imassa kharo, imassa bahalataco, imassa sukkhataco. Imassa pattaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānādivasena evarūpaṃ. Imassa pupphaṃ nīlaṃ, pītaṃ, lohitaṃ, odātaṃ, sugandhaṃ, duggandhaṃ, missakagandhaṃ. Phalaṃ khuddakaṃ, mahantaṃ, dīghaṃ, vaṭṭaṃ, suvaṇṇaṃ, dubbaṇṇaṃ, maṭṭhaṃ, pharusaṃ, sugandhaṃ, duggandhaṃ, madhuraṃ, tittakaṃ, ambilaṃ, kaṭukaṃ, kasāvaṃ. Kaṇṭako tikhiṇo, atikhiṇo, ujuko, kuṭilo, tambo, nīlo, lohito, odāto”tiādinā dhātunānattaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati.

With regard to the various elements: in the sense that 'this is called the eye element... (and so forth) ...this is called the mind-consciousness element.' Among them, sixteen elements belong to the sense-sphere, and two to the four planes. Thus, knowledge operates in dependence on the diversification among the elements. This is stated with respect to the appropriated elements. For Paccekabuddhas and the two chief disciples, knowledge operates in dependence on the diversification among the appropriated elements only, and that too, only partially, not completely. The diversification of external, unappropriated elements is beyond their range. For the Omniscient Buddhas alone, however, knowledge operates in dependence on the diversity of elements, such as: 'Due to the predominance of this element, the trunk of this tree is white, of that one black, of another smooth, of another rough, of one thick-barked, of another thin-barked. The leaf of this one is of such a color and shape, and so forth. The flower of this one is blue, yellow, red, or white; fragrant, foul-smelling, or of mixed scent. The fruit is small, large, long, round, of good color, of bad color, smooth, rough, fragrant, foul-smelling, sweet, bitter, sour, pungent, or astringent. The thorn is sharp, very sharp, straight, crooked, copper-colored, blue, red, or white.' Thus, knowledge operates in dependence on the diversity of elements.

Puthu nānāāyatanesūti “idaṃ cakkhāyatanaṃ nāma…pe… idaṃ dhammāyatanaṃ nāma. Tattha dasāyatanā kāmāvacarā, dve cātubhūmakā”ti evaṃ āyatananānattaṃ paṭicca ñāṇaṃ pavattati.

With regard to the various bases: in the sense that 'this is called the eye base... (and so forth) ...this is called the mind-object base.' Among them, ten bases belong to the sense-sphere, and two to the four planes. Thus, knowledge operates in dependence on the diversity of the bases.

Puthu nānāpaṭiccasamuppādesūti ajjhattabahiddhābhedato santānabhedato ca nānappabhedesu paṭiccasamuppādaṅgesu. Avijjādiaṅgāni hi paccekaṃ paṭiccasamuppādasaññitāni. Tenāha – saṅkhārapiṭake “dvādasa paccayā dvādasa paṭiccasamuppādā”ti (saṃ. ni. ṭī. 1.1.110).

With regard to the various dependent originations: this means in the factors of dependent origination, which are of various kinds due to the distinction between internal and external, and due to the distinction of continuities. For the factors, ignorance and so on, are each designated as 'dependent origination.' Therefore it is said in the Saṅkhāra Piṭaka: 'Twelve conditions, twelve dependent originations' (Saṃ. Ni. Ṭī. 1.1.110).

Puthu nānāsuññatamanupalabbhesūti nānāsabhāvesu niccasārādivirahitesu suññasabhāvesu, tato eva itthipurisaattattaniyādivasena anupalabbhamānasabhāvesu. Ma-kāro hettha padasandhikaro.

With regard to the various unapprehended emptinesses: this means in things of diverse natures, which are of an empty nature, being devoid of permanence, essence, and so forth; and for that very reason, in things whose nature is not apprehended in terms of woman, man, self, what belongs to self, and so forth. Here, the letter 'm' is a euphonic connector.

Puthu [V 1.0263] nānāatthesūti atthapaṭisambhidāvisayesu paccayuppannādinānāatthesu. Dhammesūti dhammapaṭisambhidāvisayesu paccayādinānādhammesu. Niruttīsūti [M 1.0280] tesaṃyeva atthadhammānaṃ niddhāraṇavacanasaṅkhātesu nānāniruttīsu. Puthu nānāpaṭibhānesūti atthapaṭisambhidādivisayesu imāni ñāṇāni idamatthajotakānīti tathā tathā paṭibhānato upatiṭṭhanato paṭibhānānīti laddhanāmesu nānāñāṇesu.

With regard to the various meanings: in the various meanings, such as those arisen from conditions and so forth, which are the domain of the discrimination of meaning. With regard to phenomena: in the various phenomena, such as conditions and so forth, which are the domain of the discrimination of phenomena. With regard to expressions: in the various expressions which are designated as the defining terms for those very meanings and phenomena. With regard to the various insights: in the various knowledges that have received the name 'insights' because they appear and are present in such and such a way—as 'these knowledges illuminate this meaning'—within the domain of the discrimination of meaning and so forth.

Puthu nānāsīlakkhandhesūtiādīsu sīlassa puthuttaṃ nānattañca vuttameva, itaresaṃ pana vuttanayānusārena suviññeyyattā pākaṭameva. Yaṃ pana abhinnaṃ ekameva nibbānaṃ, tattha upacāravasena puthuttaṃ gahetabbanti āha – “puthu nānājanasādhāraṇe dhamme samatikkammā”ti. Tenassa madanimmadanādipariyāyena puthuttaṃ paridīpitaṃ hoti.

Regarding the various sections on virtue and so forth, the multiplicity and diversity of virtue have already been explained. As for the others, their intelligibility is evident following the method stated above. However, regarding Nibbāna, which is indivisible and singular, its multiplicity should be understood figuratively. Therefore it is said: "by transcending the various states common to beings." Thus its multiplicity is illustrated through terms like "subduing pride" and so forth.

Vipule attheti mahante atthe. Mahantapariyāyo hi vipulasaddo. Gambhīresūti sasādīhi viya mahāsamuddo anupacitañāṇasambhārehi alabbhaneyyappatiṭṭhesu khandhesu ñāṇaṃ pavattatīti visayassa gambhīratāya ñāṇassa gambhīratā vibhāvitā.

"Vast in meaning" means great in meaning. The word "vast" is indeed a synonym for great. "Profound" means that knowledge operates in the aggregates, which are difficult to access and establish for those without accumulated stores of knowledge, like the great ocean for hares and so forth. Thus, the profundity of knowledge is demonstrated by the profundity of its object.

Tikkhavisadabhāvādiguṇehi asādhāraṇattā paresaṃ paññāya na sāmantā, atha kho suvidūravidūreti asamantapaññā ākārassa rassattaṃ katvā. Keci “asamatthapaññā”ti paṭhanti, tesaṃ yathāvuttaguṇehi aññehi asādhāraṇattā natthi etissā kāyaci samatthanti asamatthā paññāti yojanā. Atthavavatthānatoti atthappabhedassa yāthāvato sanniṭṭhānato. Na añño koci sakkoti abhisambhavitunti ñāṇagatiyā sampāpuṇituṃ na añño kocipi sakkoti, tasmā ayaṃ suvidūravidūreti asamantapaññā. Idāni puggalantaravasena asamantapaññaṃ vibhāvetuṃ, “puthujjanakalyāṇakassā”tiādi āraddhaṃ.

Because it is unique due to qualities such as sharpness and clarity, it is not near the wisdom of others, but rather very, very far away. This is "incomparable wisdom" (`asamantapaññā`), with the vowel of the first syllable shortened. Some read `asamatthapaññā` (incapable wisdom). For them, the explanation is that because it is unique due to the qualities stated above, no other wisdom is capable of it, hence "incapable wisdom." By "discernment of meaning" is meant the precise ascertainment of the divisions of meaning as they actually are. By "no one else can attain" is meant that no one else is capable of reaching it by means of the range of knowledge. Therefore, this is "incomparable wisdom." Now, in order to demonstrate incomparable wisdom in terms of different individuals, the passage beginning "for the ordinary virtuous person" and so forth is commenced.

“Paññāpabhedakusalo abhinnañāṇo adhigatappaṭisambhido catuvesārajjappatto dasabaladhārī purisāsabho purisasīho purisanāgo purisājañño purisadhorayho anantañāṇo anantatejo anantayaso aḍḍho mahaddhano balavā netā vinetā anunetā paññāpetā vinijjhāpetā pekkhatā pasādetā. So hi bhagavā anuppannassa maggassa uppādetā, asañjātassa maggassa sañjanetā, anakkhātassa maggassa akkhātā, maggaññū maggavidū maggakovido. Maggānugāmī ca pana etarahi sāvakā viharanti pacchā samannāgatā.

"Skilled in the distinctions of wisdom, possessing unimpeded knowledge, having attained the analytical knowledges, having attained the four kinds of confidence, bearer of the ten powers, the bull among men, the lion among men, the great nāga among men, the thoroughbred among men, the beast of burden among men, of boundless knowledge, boundless splendor, boundless fame, rich, greatly wealthy, powerful, a guide, a trainer, an instructor, an expounder, a clarifier, one who observes, one who gladdens. Indeed, the Blessed One is the producer of the unarisen path, the generator of the unproduced path, the proclaimer of the undeclared path, the knower of the path, the expert in the path, the skilled in the path. And now his disciples dwell following the path, having attained it afterwards."

“So [V 1.0264][M 1.0281] hi bhagavā jānaṃ jānāti, passaṃ passati, cakkhubhūto ñāṇabhūto dhammabhūto brahmabhūto vattā pavattā atthassa ninnetā amatassa dātā dhammassāmī tathāgato, natthi tassa bhagavato aññātaṃ adiṭṭhaṃ aviditaṃ asacchikataṃ aphassitaṃ paññāya. Atītaṃ anāgataṃ paccuppannaṃ upādāya sabbe dhammā sabbākārena buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇamukhe āpāthaṃ āgacchanti, yaṃ kiñci neyyaṃ nāma atthi taṃ sabbaṃ jānitabbaṃ, attattho vā parattho vā ubhayattho vā diṭṭhadhammiko vā attho samparāyiko vā attho uttāno vā attho gambhīro vā attho gūḷho vā attho paṭicchanno vā attho neyyo vā attho nīto vā attho anavajjo vā attho nikkileso vā attho vodāno vā attho paramattho vā attho, sabbaṃ taṃ antobuddhañāṇe parivattati.

"The Blessed One, knowing, knows; seeing, sees. He is the eye, he is knowledge, he is the Dhamma, he is Brahma. He is the speaker, the proclaimer, the elucidator of meaning, the giver of the Deathless, the lord of the Dhamma, the Tathāgata. There is nothing unknown, unseen, ununderstood, unrealized, or untouched by the Blessed One’s wisdom. All phenomena, past, future, and present, in every way, come within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge. Whatever is knowable is all to be known—whether it concerns one’s own welfare, another’s, or both; whether it is a benefit in this life or a benefit in a future life; whether the meaning is plain or profound, hidden or covered, to be inferred or explicit, blameless or without defilement, pure or supreme—all of it revolves within the Buddha’s knowledge."

“Sabbaṃ kāyakammaṃ buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇānuparivatti, sabbaṃ vacīkammaṃ buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇānuparivatti, sabbaṃ manokammaṃ buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇānuparivatti. Atīte buddhassa bhagavato appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ, anāgate buddhassa bhagavato appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ, paccuppanne buddhassa bhagavato appaṭihataṃ ñāṇaṃ, yāvatakaṃ neyyaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Yāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tāvatakaṃ neyyaṃ. Neyyapariyantikaṃ ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇapariyantikaṃ neyyaṃ, neyyaṃ atikkamitvā ñāṇaṃ nappavattati, ñāṇaṃ atikkamitvā neyyapatho natthi, aññamaññapariyantaṭṭhāyino te dhammā, yathā dvinnaṃ samuggapaṭalānaṃ sammā phusitānaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ samuggapaṭalaṃ uparimaṃ nātivattati, uparimaṃ samuggapaṭalaṃ heṭṭhimaṃ nātivattati, aññamaññapariyantaṭṭhāyino, evamevaṃ buddhassa bhagavato neyyañca ñāṇañca aññamaññapariyantaṭṭhāyino. Yāvatakaṃ neyyaṃ, tāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ. Yāvatakaṃ ñāṇaṃ, tāvatakaṃ neyyaṃ, neyyapariyantikaṃ ñāṇaṃ, ñāṇapariyantikaṃ neyyaṃ, neyyaṃ atikkamitvā ñāṇaṃ nappavattati, ñāṇaṃ atikkamitvā neyyapatho natthi. Aññamaññapariyantaṭṭhāyino te dhammā. Sabbadhammesu buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇaṃ pavattati.

"All bodily actions of the Buddha, the Blessed One, accord with his knowledge; all verbal actions of the Buddha, the Blessed One, accord with his knowledge; all mental actions of the Buddha, the Blessed One, accord with his knowledge. In the past, the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, was unimpeded; in the future, the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is unimpeded; in the present, the knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, is unimpeded. As far as there is the knowable, so far extends his knowledge; as far as there is knowledge, so far extends the knowable. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, and there is no path of the knowable beyond knowledge. These states exist with mutual limits, just as with two well-fitted parts of a casket—the lower part does not exceed the upper, nor does the upper exceed the lower—they exist with mutual limits. In the same way, for the Buddha, the Blessed One, the knowable and knowledge exist with mutual limits. As far as there is the knowable, so far extends his knowledge; as far as there is knowledge, so far extends the knowable. Knowledge has the knowable as its limit; the knowable has knowledge as its limit. Knowledge does not proceed beyond the knowable, and there is no path of the knowable beyond knowledge. These states exist with mutual limits. The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, proceeds in all phenomena."

“Sabbe [M 1.0282] dhammā buddhassa bhagavato āvajjanappaṭibaddhā ākaṅkhappaṭibaddhā manasikārappaṭibaddhā cittuppādappaṭibaddhā, sabbasattesu buddhassa bhagavato ñāṇaṃ pavattati. Sabbesaṃ sattānaṃ buddho āsayaṃ jānāti, anusayaṃ jānāti, caritaṃ jānāti, adhimuttiṃ jānāti, apparajakkhe mahārajakkhe tikkhindriye mudindriye svākāre dvākāre suviññāpaye duviññāpaye bhabbā sabbe satte pajānāti, sadevako loko [V 1.0265] samārako sabrahmako sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī pajā sadevamanussā antobuddhañāṇe parivattati.

"All phenomena are bound to the advertence, aspiration, mental application, and arising of consciousness of the Buddha, the Blessed One. The knowledge of the Buddha, the Blessed One, proceeds in all beings. The Buddha knows the dispositions, the latent tendencies, the characters, and the inclinations of all beings. He understands all beings: those with little dust in their eyes and those with much, those with keen faculties and those with dull faculties, those with good dispositions and those with bad dispositions, those easy to instruct and those difficult to instruct, and those who are capable. The world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, the generation of ascetics and brahmins, devas and humans—all revolve within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge."

“Yathā ye keci macchakacchapā antamaso timitimiṅgalaṃ upādāya antomahāsamudde parivattanti, evameva sadevako loko samārako sabrahmako sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī pajā sadevamanussā antobuddhañāṇe parivattati. Yathā ye keci pakkhino antamaso garuḷaṃ venateyyaṃ upādāya ākāsassa padese parivattanti, evameva yepi te sāriputtasamā paññāya, tepi buddhañāṇassa padese parivattanti, buddhañāṇaṃ devamanussānaṃ paññaṃ pharitvā atighaṃsitvā tiṭṭhati. Yepi te khattiyapaṇḍitā brāhmaṇapaṇḍitā gahapatipaṇḍitā samaṇapaṇḍitā nipuṇā kataparappavādā vālavedhirūpā, vobhindantā maññe caranti paññāgatena diṭṭhigatāni, te te pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā abhisaṅkharitvā”ti (paṭi. ma. 3.5) –

"Just as all fish and turtles, even down to the timitimiṅgala, move about within the great ocean, so too the world with its devas, with Māra, with Brahmā, the generation of ascetics and brahmins, devas and humans, revolves within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge. Just as all birds, even down to the garuḷa, the son of Vinatā, move about in the regions of the sky, so too even those like Sāriputta in wisdom revolve within the range of the Buddha’s knowledge. The Buddha’s knowledge pervades and surpasses the wisdom of devas and humans. Those Khattiya scholars, brahmin scholars, householder scholars, and ascetic scholars—clever, versed in the doctrines of others, like hair-splitters, who wander about, one might think, shattering views with their wisdom—they, having repeatedly formulated questions..." (Paṭis I 5)

Ādinā niddiṭṭhapāḷiṃ peyyālamukhena saṃkhipitvā dassento “paññāpabhedakusalo pabhinnañāṇo…pe… te pañhaṃ abhisaṅkharitvā abhisaṅkharitvā”tiādimāha.

Showing the Pāli text indicated by `ādi` by abbreviating it with the `peyyāla` marker, he said: "Skilled in the divisions of wisdom, with differentiated knowledge...pe...they, having repeatedly formulated questions..." and so forth.

Tattha pabhinnañāṇoti atthādīsu pabhedagatañāṇo. “Pabhedañāṇo”tipi paṭhanti, soyeva attho. Te pañhanti te te attanā adhippetaṃ pañhaṃ. Niddiṭṭhakāraṇāti vissajjitakāraṇā. Upakkhittakāti bhagavato paññāveyyattiyena samīpe khittakā antevāsikā sampajjanti.

There, `pabhinnañāṇa` means one whose knowledge has reached differentiation regarding meanings and so forth. Some also read `pabhedañāṇa`; the meaning is the same. `Te pañhaṃ` means those various questions that they themselves intend. `Niddiṭṭhakāraṇā` means those for whom the reason has been explained. `Upakkhittakā` means the disciples who, through the Blessed One's wisdom and skill, are brought near and succeed.

Bhavati [M 1.0283] abhibhavatīti bhūri. Kiṃ? Rāgādiṃ. Upasagge satipi tadeva padaṃ tamatthaṃ vadatīti upasaggena vināpi so attho viññeyyo anekatthattā dhātūnanti vuttaṃ – “abhibhuyyatī”ti. Kārakabyattayena cetaṃ vuttaṃ, tasmā rāgaṃ abhibhuyyatīti sā sā maggapaññā attanā attanā vajjhaṃ rāgaṃ abhibhuyyati abhibhavati, madatīti attho. Abhibhavatīti sā sā phalapaññā taṃ taṃ rāgaṃ bhavi abhibhavi maddīti bhūripaññā. “Abhibhavitā”ti vā pāṭho, “abhibhavitvā”tipi paṭhanti. Abhibhavitvāti ca kiriyāya siddhabhāvadassanaṃ. Paññā ce siddhā, rāgābhibhavo ca siddho evāti. Sesesupi eseva nayo.

It is, it overcomes, thus it is bhūri. What? Lust and so on. Even when a prefix is present, that same word conveys that meaning; thus, the meaning is to be understood even without a prefix because of the multiple meanings of roots—as it is said: 'it is overcome.' This is said with a change of voice; therefore, 'lust is overcome' means that the respective path-wisdom, by its own power, overcomes and crushes the lust that is to be destroyed; that is the meaning. The respective fruition-wisdom was, overcame, and crushed that lust; thus, it is bhūripaññā. Alternatively, the reading is 'abhibhavitā'; some also read it as 'abhibhavitvā'. And 'having overcome' indicates the accomplished state of the action. If the wisdom is accomplished, the overcoming of lust is also indeed accomplished. This same method applies in the remaining cases.

Rāgādīsu pana rajjanalakkhaṇo rāgo. Dussanalakkhaṇo doso. Muyhanalakkhaṇo moho. Kujjhanalakkhaṇo [V 1.0266] kodho, upanandhanalakkhaṇo upanāho. Pubbakālaṃ kodho, aparakālaṃ upanāho. Paraguṇamakkhanalakkhaṇo makkho, yugaggāhalakkhaṇo palāso. Parasampattikhīyanalakkhaṇā issā, attano sampattiniggūhanalakkhaṇaṃ macchariyaṃ. Attanā katapāpappaṭicchādanalakkhaṇā māyā, attano avijjamānaguṇappakāsanalakkhaṇaṃ sāṭheyyaṃ. Cittassa uddhumātabhāvalakkhaṇo thambho, karaṇuttariyalakkhaṇo sārambho. Unnatilakkhaṇo māno, abbhunnatilakkhaṇo atimāno. Mattabhāvalakkhaṇo mado, pañcakāmaguṇesu cittavossaggalakkhaṇo pamādo. Bhavati abhibhavati arinti bhūri asarūpato parassa akārassa lopaṃ katvā. Tenāha – “ariṃ maddanipaññāti bhūripaññā”ti. Bhavati ettha thāvarajaṅgamanti bhūri vuccati pathavī yathā “bhūmī”ti bhūri viyāti bhūripaññā vitthatavipulaṭṭhena sabbaṃ sahatāya ca. Tenāha – “tāyā”tiādi. Tattha pathavisamāyāti vitthatavipulaṭṭheneva pathavisamāya. Vitthatāyāti pajānitabbe visaye vitthatāya, na ekadese vattamānāya. Vipulāyāti uḷārabhūtāya. Samannāgatoti puggalo. Iti-saddo kāraṇatthe, iminā kāraṇena puggalassa bhūripaññāya samannāgatattā tassa paññā bhūripaññā nāmāti attho. “Bhūripaññassa paññā bhūripaññapaññā”ti vattabbe ekassa paññāsaddassa lopaṃ katvā “bhūripaññā”ti vuttaṃ.

Now, regarding lust and so on: lust has the characteristic of attachment; hatred, the characteristic of aversion; delusion, the characteristic of confusion; anger, the characteristic of fury; resentment, the characteristic of lingering hostility. Anger is of the earlier time, resentment of the later time. Denigration has the characteristic of disparaging others' virtues; rivalry, the characteristic of contentious opposition. Envy has the characteristic of being vexed at others' success; stinginess, the characteristic of concealing one's own success. Deceit has the characteristic of concealing the evil one has done; fraud, the characteristic of proclaiming virtues one does not possess. Stubbornness has the characteristic of a puffed-up state of mind; presumption, the characteristic of rivalry in action. Conceit has the characteristic of self-exaltation; arrogance, the characteristic of extreme self-exaltation. Intoxication has the characteristic of infatuation; heedlessness, the characteristic of abandoning the mind to the five strands of sensual pleasure. It is, it overcomes the foe, thus it is bhūri, by eliding the letter 'a' of the latter word, which is not its proper form. Hence it is said: 'The wisdom that crushes the foe is bhūripaññā.' The earth is called bhūri because stable and moving things exist (bhavati) on it, just as it is called bhūmi. Wisdom is like the bhūri (earth), thus it is bhūripaññā, in the sense of being vast and extensive, and because it endures all. Hence it is said: 'by that [wisdom] like the earth,' and so on. Therein, 'like the earth' means like the earth in the sense of being vast and extensive. 'Vast' means vast in the domain of what is to be known, not existing in only one part. 'Extensive' means it is lofty. 'Endowed' refers to the person. The word iti is in the sense of a reason; the meaning is: for this reason, because a person is endowed with bhūripaññā, their wisdom is named bhūripaññā. Although it should be said, 'The wisdom of one with abundant wisdom is bhūripaññapaññā,' it is called bhūripaññā by eliding one instance of the word paññā.

Apicāti [M 1.0284] paññāpariyāyadassanatthaṃ vuttaṃ. Paññāyametanti paññāya etaṃ. Adhivacananti adhikaṃ vacanaṃ. Bhūrīti bhūte atthe khandhādike ramati saccasabhāvena, diṭṭhi viya na abhūteti bhūri. Medhāti asani viya siluccaye kilese medhati hiṃsatīti medhā, khippaṃ gahaṇadhāraṇaṭṭhena vā medhā. Pariṇāyikāti yassuppajjati, taṃ sattaṃ attahitappaṭipattiyaṃ sampayuttadhamme ca yāthāvalakkhaṇappaṭivedhe pariṇetīti pariṇāyikā. Imeheva aññānipi paññāpariyāyavacanāni honti.

The word 'Moreover' is stated to show the synonyms for wisdom. 'Paññāyametaṃ' means 'this is by wisdom.' 'Adhivacana' means a superior term. It is bhūri because it delights (ramati) in what is real (bhūte), in the aggregates and so on, with its true nature; unlike a view, it is not in what is unreal, hence it is bhūri. It is medhā because it harms (medhati) or destroys the defilements like lightning on a mountain peak; or it is medhā in the sense of swift grasping and retaining. It is pariṇāyikā because, for the being in whom it arises, it leads (pariṇeti) them to the practice for their own welfare and to the penetration of the characteristics as they really are of associated states, hence it is pariṇāyikā. These and other terms are also synonyms for wisdom.

Paññābāhullanti paññā bahulā assāti paññābahulo, tassa bhāvo paññābāhullaṃ. Tañca paññāya bāhullaṃ pavatti evāti tamatthaṃ paññāgarukassa puggalassa vasena dassento, “idhekacco paññāgaruko hotī”tiādimāha. Tattha idhekaccoti puthujjanakalyāṇako, ariyo vā. Paññā garu ekassāti paññāgaruko. Paññāya carito pavattito paññācarito, paññāya caritaṃ pavattaṃ assāti vā paññācarito. Anulomikakhantiādivibhāgā paññā āsayo etassāti paññāsayo. Paññāya adhimutto tanninnoti paññādhimutto. Samussitaṭṭhena paññā dhajo etassāti paññādhajo. Paññāketūti tasseva vevacanaṃ. Paññānimittaṃ ādhipateyyaṃ etassāti paññādhipateyyo. Paññāsaṅkhāto vicayo, dhammasabhāvavicinanaṃ vā bahulaṃ etassāti vicayabahulo[V 1.0267]. Nānappakārena dhammasabhāvavicinanaṃ bahulaṃ assāti pavicayabahulo. Okkhāyanaṃ yāthāvato dhammānaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ bahulaṃ etassāti okkhāyanabahulo. Paññāya tassa tassa dhammassa sammāpekkhanā sampekkhā, sampekkhāya ayanaṃ pavattanaṃ sampekkhāyanaṃ, sampekkhāyanaṃ dhammo pakati assāti sampekkhāyanadhammo. Sampekkhāyanaṃ vā yāthāvato dassanadhammo sabhāvo etassāti sampekkhāyanadhammo. Sabbaṃ dhammajātaṃ vibhūtaṃ vibhāvitaṃ katvā viharaṇasīloti vibhūtavihārī.

'Abundance of wisdom' (paññābāhullaṃ): one for whom wisdom is abundant is paññābahulo; the state of that is paññābāhullaṃ. And since this abundance of wisdom is simply its activity, showing this meaning with reference to a person who esteems wisdom, he said, 'Here, a certain person esteems wisdom,' and so on. Herein, 'a certain person' is a virtuous worldling or a noble one. 'One who esteems wisdom' (paññāgaruko) is one for whom wisdom is important. 'One whose conduct is wisdom' (paññācarito) is one whose conduct is impelled by wisdom, or one for whom the conduct of wisdom is active. 'One whose resort is wisdom' (paññāsayo) is one whose resort is wisdom, which is divided into conforming patience and so on. 'One resolved on wisdom' (paññādhimutto) is one who is inclined and bent towards wisdom. 'One whose banner is wisdom' (paññādhajo) is one for whom wisdom is a raised banner. 'Wisdom-pennant' (paññāketu) is a synonym for that. 'One for whom wisdom is sovereignty' (paññādhipateyyo) is one for whom wisdom is the sign and ruling principle. 'One abundant in investigation' (vicayabahulo) is one for whom investigation—called wisdom, or the examination of the nature of things—is abundant. 'One abundant in thorough investigation' (pavicayabahulo) is one for whom the examination of the nature of things in various ways is abundant. 'One abundant in analysis' (okkhāyanabahulo) is one for whom analysis—the presentation of things as they really are—is abundant. 'One whose nature is reflective examination' (sampekkhāyanadhammo): reflective examination (sampekkhā) is the proper consideration of this and that phenomenon by means of wisdom; the going or activity of that is sampekkhāyanaṃ; one whose nature or habit is that is sampekkhāyanadhammo. Or, one whose nature is the quality of seeing things as they really are. 'A dweller in clarity' (vibhūtavihārī) is one who is in the habit of dwelling having made all classes of phenomena clear and manifest.

Taccaritotiādīsu taṃ-saddena paññā paccāmaṭṭhā, tasmā tattha “paññācarito”tiādinā attho veditabbo. Sā paññā caritā garukā bahulā assāti taccarito taggaruko tabbahulo. Tassaṃ paññāyaṃ ninno poṇo pabbhāro adhimuttoti tanninno tappoṇo tappabbhāro tadadhimutto. Sā paññā adhipati tadadhipati, tadadhipatito āgato [M 1.0285] tadādhipateyyo. Paññāgarukotiādīni “kāmaṃ sevantaṃyeva jānāti, ayaṃ puggalo nekkhammagaruko”tiādīsu (paṭi. ma. 1.114) viya purimajātito pabhuti vuttāni. Taccaritotiādīni imissā jātiyā vuttāni. Idāni vuttamevatthaṃ nidassanavasenapi dassetuṃ – “yathā”tiādi vuttaṃ. Evamevantiādīni dassitabbanigamanaṃ.

In terms such as taccarita, wisdom is referred to by the word taṃ; therefore, the meaning there should be understood as paññācarita, and so on. That wisdom is practiced, esteemed, and abundant for one; thus, one is taccarita, taggaruka, tabbahula. One is inclined, bent, prone, and resolved toward that wisdom; thus, one is tanninno, tappoṇo, tappabbhāro, tadadhimutta. That wisdom is one's authority, thus tadadhipati; come from having that as authority is tadādhipateyya. Terms like paññāgaruka are stated with reference to the time from a previous birth onwards, similar to the passage, 'Even while indulging in sensual pleasures, one knows, "This person esteems renunciation"' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.114). Terms like taccarita are stated with reference to this present life. Now, to show the meaning already stated also by way of an example, 'just as,' and so on, is said. 'In the very same way,' and so on, is the conclusion that was to be shown.

Sīghapaññāti attano visaye sīghappavattikā paññā, yā samāraddhā attano paññākiccaṃ adandhāyantī avitthāyantī khippameva sampāpeti. Tenāha – “sīghaṃ sīghaṃ sīlāni paripūretī”tiādi. Tattha sīghaṃ sīghanti bahūnaṃ sīlādīnaṃ saṅgahatthaṃ dvikkhattuṃ vuttaṃ. Sīlānīti cārittavārittavasena paññattāni pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlāni, ṭhapetvā vā indriyasaṃvaraṃ tassa visuṃ gahitattā itarāni tividhasīlāni. Indriyasaṃvaranti cakkhādīnaṃ channaṃ indriyānaṃ rāgappaṭighappavesaṃ akatvā satikavāṭena nivāraṇaṃ thakanaṃ. Bhojane mattaññutanti paccavekkhitaparibhogavasena bhojane pamāṇaññubhāvaṃ. Jāgariyānuyoganti divasassa tīsu koṭṭhāsesu rattiyā paṭhamamajjhimakoṭṭhāsesu ca jāgarati na niddāyati, samaṇadhammameva karotīti jāgaro, jāgarassa bhāvo, kammaṃ vā jāgariyaṃ, jāgariyassa anuyogo jāgariyānuyogo, taṃ jāgariyānuyogaṃ. Sīlakkhandhanti sekkhaṃ vā asekkhaṃ vā sīlakkhandhaṃ. Evamitarepi khandhā veditabbā. Paññākkhandhanti maggapaññā ca sekkhāsekkhānaṃ lokiyapaññā ca. Vimuttikkhandhanti phalavimutti. Vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandhanti paccavekkhaṇañāṇaṃ. Sīghapaññāniddesasadisoyeva lahupaññāniddeso, tathā hāsapaññāniddeso. Javanapaññāniddeso pana kalāpasammasananayena pavatto. Tikkhapaññāniddeso vīriyassa ussukkāpanavasena, nibbedhikapaññāniddeso [V 1.0268] sabbaloke anabhiratasaññāvasena pavatto. Tattha turitakiriyā sīghatā. Adandhatā lahutā. Vegāyitattaṃ khippatā.

"Swift in wisdom" (sīghapaññā) means wisdom that operates quickly in its domain, which, once aroused, accomplishes its task without delay or hesitation. Hence it is said, "quickly, quickly fulfills the moral habits," and so on. Here, "quickly, quickly" is repeated twice to encompass many moral habits and other qualities. "Moral habits" (sīlāni) refers to the precepts of moral restraint (pātimokkhasaṃvara), enjoined by way of conduct and avoidance, excluding sense restraint, which is separately mentioned; thus the other three kinds of moral habits. "Sense restraint" (indriyasaṃvara) means guarding the six senses—eye, etc.—by not allowing lust or aversion to enter, warding them off and blocking them with the gate of mindfulness. "Moderation in eating" (bhojane mattaññutā) is knowing the proper measure in food through reflective consumption. "Devotion to wakefulness" (jāgariyānuyoga) means staying awake during the three divisions of the day and the first and middle divisions of the night, not indulging in sleep, but practicing the duties of an ascetic—thus, he is one who is awake; the state of one who is awake, or the action of wakefulness, is wakefulness; the devotion to wakefulness is jāgariyānuyoga; that devotion to wakefulness. "Aggregate of virtue" (sīlakkhandha) refers to the aggregate of virtue whether of a trainee or an adept. Similarly, the other aggregates should be understood. "Aggregate of wisdom" (paññākkhandha) includes the wisdom of the path and the mundane wisdom of trainees and adepts. "Aggregate of liberation" (vimuttikkhandha) refers to the fruition of liberation. "Aggregate of knowledge and vision of liberation" (vimuttiñāṇadassanakkhandha) is the reviewing knowledge. The exposition of "swift wisdom" is similar to that of "light wisdom," and likewise for "joyful wisdom." The exposition of "rapid wisdom," however, proceeds by way of contemplating the groups of phenomena. The exposition of "sharp wisdom" proceeds by way of stirring up energy, and the exposition of "penetrative wisdom" proceeds by way of the perception of non-delight in all the world. Here, swiftness is rapid action. Lightness is absence of sluggishness. Quickness is being speedy.

Hāsabahuloti pītibahulo. Sesapadāni tasseva vevacanāni. Atha vā hāsabahuloti mūlapadaṃ. Vedabahuloti tassā eva pītiyā sampayuttasomanassavedanāvasena niddesapadaṃ. Tuṭṭhibahuloti nātibalavapītiyā tuṭṭhākāravasena. Pāmojjabahuloti balavapītiyā pamuditabhāvavasena. Sīlāni paripūretīti haṭṭhappahaṭṭho udaggūdaggo [M 1.0286] sampiyāyamāno sīlāni sampādeti. Pītisomanassasahagatā hi paññā abhirativasena ārammaṇe phullitā vikasitā viya pavattati, na evaṃ upekkhāsahagatāti.

"Abundant in joy" (hāsabahulo) means abundant in rapture (pītibahulo). The remaining terms are synonyms for that. Alternatively, "abundant in joy" is the root term. "Abundant in feeling" (vedabahulo) is a descriptive term by way of the pleasant feeling of gladness associated with that very rapture. "Abundant in delight" (tuṭṭhibahulo) is by way of the aspect of satisfaction due to rapture that is not too strong. "Abundant in gladness" (pāmojjabahulo) is by way of the state of being gladdened due to strong rapture. "He fulfills the moral habits" (sīlāni paripūreti) means that, being delighted, exceedingly uplifted, and rejoicing, he accomplishes the moral habits. For wisdom accompanied by rapture and pleasant feeling operates as if blooming and unfolding in its object by way of delight, but not so wisdom accompanied by equanimity.

Aniccato khippaṃ javatīti “khandhapañcakaṃ anicca”nti vegāyitena pavattati, paṭipakkhadūrībhāvena pubbābhisaṅkhārassa sātisayattā indena vissaṭṭhavajiraṃ viya lakkhaṇaṃ avirajjhantī adandhāyantī aniccalakkhaṇaṃ vegasā paṭivijjhati, tasmā sā javanapaññā nāmāti attho. Sesapadesupi eseva nayo. Evaṃ lakkhaṇārammaṇikavipassanāvasena javanapaññaṃ dassetvā balavavipassanāvasena dassetuṃ – “rūpa”ntiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha khayaṭṭhenāti yattha yattha uppajjati, tattha tattheva bhijjanato khayasabhāvattā. Bhayaṭṭhenāti bhayānakabhāvato. Asārakaṭṭhenāti attasāravirahato niccasārādivirahato ca. Tulayitvāti tulābhūtāya vipassanāpaññāya tuletvā. Tīrayitvāti tāya eva tīraṇabhūtāya tīretvā. Vibhāvayitvāti yāthāvato pakāsetvā pākaṭaṃ katvā. Atha vā tulayitvāti kalāpasammasanavasena tulayitvā. Tīrayitvāti udayabbayānupassanāvasena tīretvā. Vibhāvayitvāti bhaṅgānupassanādivasena pākaṭaṃ katvā. Vibhūtaṃ katvāti saṅkhārupekkhānulomavasena phuṭaṃ katvā. Rūpanirodheti rūpakkhandhassa nirodhabhūte nibbāne. Khippaṃ javatīti ninnapoṇapabbhāravasena javati pavattati. Idāni sikhāppattavipassanāvasena javanapaññaṃ dassetuṃ, puna “rūpa”ntiādi vuttaṃ.

"It swiftly moves as impermanent" means that, as "the five aggregates are impermanent," it proceeds with impetus. Due to the absence of opposing forces and the exceeding strength of past formations, like a thunderbolt released by Indra, not missing the characteristic and not being sluggish, it penetrates the characteristic of impermanence with speed. Therefore, that is the meaning of it being called "rapid wisdom" (javanapaññā). The same applies to the remaining terms. Having shown rapid wisdom by way of insight focused on the characteristics, to further illustrate it by way of strong insight, "form," etc., is stated. Therein, "by the meaning of destruction" (khayaṭṭhena) means that wherever it arises, there it disintegrates, being of the nature of destruction. "By the meaning of danger" (bhayaṭṭhena) refers to its fearful nature. "By the meaning of essencelessness" (asārakaṭṭhena) means it lacks intrinsic essence and is devoid of permanent essence, etc. "Having weighed" (tulayitvā) means having weighed with insight wisdom as the weighing balance. "Having examined" (tīrayitvā) means having examined with that same wisdom as the means of examination. "Having clarified" (vibhāvayitvā) means having revealed it as it truly is, making it evident. Alternatively, "having weighed" means having weighed through the contemplation of the groups of phenomena. "Having examined" means having examined through the observation of arising and passing away. "Having clarified" means having made it evident through the contemplation of dissolution, etc. "Having made it manifest" (vibhūtaṃ katvā) means having made it clear in accordance with equanimity regarding formations. "The cessation of form" (rūpanirodha) refers to Nibbāna, which is the cessation of the form aggregate. "It swiftly moves" means it proceeds by way of inclining, leaning, and flowing downwards. Now, to illustrate rapid wisdom by way of insight that has reached its culmination, again "form," etc., is stated.

Ñāṇassa tikkhabhāvo nāma savisesaṃ paṭipakkhasamucchindanena veditabboti “khippaṃ kilese chindatīti tikkhapaññā”ti vatvā te pana kilese vibhāgena dassento, “uppannaṃ kāmavitakka”ntiādimāha. Samathavipassanāhi vikkhambhanatadaṅgavasena pahīnampi ariyamaggena asamūhatattā uppattidhammataṃ anatītatāya asamūhatuppannanti vuccati, taṃ idha “uppanna”nti adhippetaṃ. Nādhivāsetīti santānaṃ āropetvā na vāseti. Pajahatīti samucchedavasena pajahati. Vinodetīti khipati. Byantiṃ karotīti vigatantaṃ karoti. Anabhāvaṃ gametīti anu abhāvaṃ [V 1.0269] gameti, vipassanākkamena ariyamaggaṃ patvā samucchedavaseneva abhāvaṃ gamayatīti attho. Ettha ca kāmappaṭisaṃyutto vitakko kāmavitakko. “Ime sattā [M 1.0287] marantū”ti paresaṃ maraṇappaṭisaṃyutto vitakko byāpādavitakko. “Ime sattā vihiṃsiyantū”ti paresaṃ vihiṃsāpaṭisaṃyutto vitakko vihiṃsāvitakko. Pāpaketi lāmake. Akusale dhammeti akosallasambhūte dhamme. Tikkhapañño nāma khippābhiñño hoti, paṭipadā cassa na calatīti āha – “ekamhi āsane cattāro ariyamaggā”tiādi.

The sharpness of wisdom (ñāṇa) is to be understood by way of the special cutting off of the opponents, as it is said: "One with sharp wisdom (tikkhapaññā) quickly cuts off defilements." Then, to explain those defilements in detail, he begins with "arisen sensual thought," and so on. Even though defilements are abandoned through suppression (vikkhambhana) or temporary abandonment (tadaṅga) by tranquility (samatha) and insight (vipassanā), they are not eradicated by the noble path and thus remain capable of arising again, not transcending the nature of origination. Hence, being not eradicated but arisen, they are called "arisen," which is what is meant by "arisen" in this context. "Does not tolerate" (nādhivāseti) means one does not let them dwell after they have arisen in the mental continuum. "Abandons" (pajahati) means abandoning them through eradication (samuccheda). "Dispels" (vinodeti) means casting them away. "Brings to an end" (byantiṃ karoti) means makes them gone to an end. "Annihilates" (anabhāvaṃ gameti) means causes to go to non-existence successively; the meaning is that by the stages of insight, having attained the noble path, one causes them to go to non-existence by way of eradication. Here, a thought connected with sensuality is a sensual thought (kāmavitakka). A thought connected with the death of others, such as "May these beings die," is a thought of ill will (byāpādavitakka). A thought connected with harming others, such as "May these beings be harmed," is a thought of harm (vihiṃsāvitakka). "Evil" (pāpaka) refers to what is base. "Unskillful states" (akusale dhamme) are those born of unskillfulness. One with sharp wisdom is one who quickly comprehends, and his practice does not waver, as stated: "In one sitting, the four noble paths," etc.

“Sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā dukkhā vipariṇāmadhammā saṅkhatā paṭiccasamuppannā khayadhammā vayadhammā virāgadhammā nirodhadhammā”ti yāthāvato dassanena saccappaṭivedho ijjhati, na aññathāti kāraṇamukhena nibbedhikapaññaṃ dassetuṃ – “sabbasaṅkhāresu ubbegabahulo hotī”tiādi vuttaṃ. Tattha ubbegabahuloti “sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”tiādinā (dha. pa. 277) nayena sabbasaṅkhāresu abhiṇhappavattasaṃvego. Uttāsabahuloti ñāṇabhayavasena sabbasaṅkhāresu bahuso utrastamānaso. Tena ādīnavānupassanamāha. Ukkaṇṭhanabahuloti saṅkhārato uddhaṃ visaṅkhārābhimukhatāya ukkaṇṭhanabahulo. Iminā nibbidānupassanamāha. Aratibahulotiādinā tassā eva aparāparūpapattiṃ. Bahimukhoti sabbasaṅkhārato bahibhūtaṃ nibbānaṃ uddissa pavattañāṇamukho. Tathā pavattitavimokkhamukho. Nibbijjhanaṃ paṭivijjhanaṃ nibbedho, so etissā atthīti nibbedhikā, nibbijjhatīti vā nibbedhikā, sā eva paññā nibbedhikapaññā. Anibbiddhapubbanti anamatagge saṃsāre antaṃ pāpetvā anividdhapubbaṃ. Appadālitapubbanti tasseva atthavacanaṃ, antakaraṇeneva appadālitapubbanti attho. Lobhakkhandhanti lobharāsiṃ, lobhakoṭṭhāsaṃ vā.

"All conditioned things are impermanent, suffering, subject to change, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to decay, subject to vanishing, subject to fading away, subject to cessation." Seeing this truth as it really is leads to the penetration of the truth, not otherwise—this is the reason for showing the penetrative wisdom (nibbedhikapaññā). Hence, it is said: "One is often agitated regarding all conditioned phenomena," and so on. Here, "often agitated" (ubbegabahulo) means a frequent sense of urgency regarding all conditioned phenomena through the method of "All conditioned things are impermanent," etc. (Dhammapada 277). "Often terrified" (uttāsabahulo) means being frequently frightened in all conditioned phenomena due to the fear arising from knowledge. Through this, the contemplation of danger is indicated. "Often disenchanted" (ukkaṇṭhanabahulo) means being frequently longing for the unconditioned due to being directed upwards from conditioned phenomena towards the unconditioned. By this, the contemplation of aversion is indicated. "Often averse" (aratibahulo) and so on indicate the repeated occurrence of that same aversion. "Outward-turned" (bahimukho) means one whose knowledge is directed toward Nibbāna, which is outside of all conditioned phenomena; similarly, one whose liberation is so directed. Penetration (nibbedho) is piercing through, piercing into; it is called "penetrative" (nibbedhikā) because it has this, or it is penetrative because it penetrates; that very wisdom is penetrative wisdom. "Never before penetrated" (anibbiddhapubba) means never before pierced through, having reached the end in the beginningless cycle of existence. "Never before split open" (appadālitapubba) is another term for the same meaning; the meaning is that it was never before split open by making an end of defilements. "The mass of greed" (lobhakkhandha) refers to the heap of greed or the portion of greed.

Kāyagatāsativaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The explanation of the chapter on mindfulness directed to the body is completed.

20. Amatavaggavaṇṇanā

20. The Commentary on the Chapter on the Deathless

600-611. Natthi [V 1.0270] ettha mataṃ maraṇaṃ vināsoti amataṃ, nibbānanti āha – “maraṇavirahitaṃ nibbānaṃ paribhuñjantī”ti. Amatassa vā nibbānassa adhigamahetutāya [M 1.0288] amatasadisaatappakasukhapatitatāya ca kāyagatāsati “amata”nti vuttā. Paribhuñjantīti jhānasamāpajjanena vaḷañjanti. Viraddhanti anadhigamena virajjhitaṃ. Tenāha – “virādhitaṃ nādhigata”nti. Āraddhanti sādhitaṃ nipphāditaṃ. Tañca paripuṇṇaṃ nāma hotīti āha – “āraddhanti paripuṇṇa”nti. Pamādiṃsūti kālabyattayenedaṃ vuttanti āha – “pamajjantī”ti.

600-611. Because there is no death, dying, or destruction herein, it is the Deathless, that is, Nibbāna. It is said: 'they enjoy Nibbāna, which is free from death.' Or, because it is a cause for the attainment of the Deathless, Nibbāna, and because it partakes of a bliss free from torment, similar to the Deathless, mindfulness directed to the body is called 'the Deathless.' 'They enjoy' means they make use of it by attaining jhāna. 'Missed' means it is missed through non-attainment. Therefore it is said: 'missed means not attained.' 'Begun' means it is accomplished, brought to completion. And that is called complete. Thus it is said: 'begun means complete.' 'They were negligent'—this is said with reference to the passage of time. Thus it is said: 'they are negligent.'

Amatavaggavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

The Commentary on the Chapter on the Deathless is finished.

Iti manorathapūraṇiyā aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathāya

Thus in the Manorathapūraṇī, the Commentary on the Aṅguttara Nikāya,

Ekakanipātavaṇṇanāya anuttānatthadīpanā samattā.

the Elucidation of the Profound Meaning of the Commentary on the Book of Ones is complete.

Paṭhamo bhāgo niṭṭhito.

The first part is finished.
